_childDocuments_.review: I've seen some disagreements among the reviews so I'll just chime in with my own 2cMomodora: MF is a typical Metroidvania and it follows suit of the earlier entries in the Momodora series. It doesn't exactly improve on the formula but all the same carries a very satisfying air of confidence and just works very well in almost every aspect (gameplay, visuals, music).First, if you haven't played Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight, I'd definitely recommend playing that first. Overall, it's a tighter game (nuanced comparison following) and probably the best all-around entry in the Momodora series.MF mostly follows up on all the elements introduced in RutM and earlier series. Graphically, MF deviates through expanded visuals. MF is simply gorgeous, and the more cartoony pixel-art renditions have been replaced by lush effects, gorgeously rendered backgrounds, and some incredibly appealing animations for different characters and monsters. There are some amazing standout scenes that are just brimming with atmosphere.One of the drawbacks to the new visuals I did find while playing—the areas do seem a little more samey. Especially the first 3-4 sections of the game feel more similar in visual tone (black stones, green-blue background) to easily distinguish themselves. One of the strong suits of RutM was how each new environment really did feel like a different place you're visiting, but here that effect is diminished. That said, a few of the late-game settings are truly different from common ones found in a lot of Metroidvanias through a more morose or creepy setting.The musical score is just very well done—the songs didn't stand out enough that I'd listen to all of them individually, but as a whole, I definitely enjoyed the different themes (especially the village!) and never grew tired of them.Gameplay-wise, everything just feels very rounded and well-polished. The controls are a joy, and enemy and level design is very intuitive and paced excellently. One of the things I most appreciated was just playing a Metroidvania from creators who are so sure of the product they deliver, and have the experience and background to create a product that delivers consistently.The difficulty is, I found, not very high, save for some of the later areas. I don't consider myself the best at platformers, but on normal difficulty, I think I only died a handful of times. Most of the bosses were easy and quick to adapt to (the majority can be beaten on the first try). The second-to-last area in particular stood out as more challenging but never really required meticulous effort to beat. That said, there is a continuous level of challenge present that is fun and rewarding.The item mechanics borrow from other Metroidvania games mostly but are varied enough to keep your attention. There's a sigil system similar to Hollow Knight's badge system, and it's fun at any given moment to try out new combinations and see which work. There's also a companion system but to be honest, I never really found it having much effect on the gameplay. Mostly, it's just fun to pick a companion you think is funny/appeals to you.There's lots of secrets to navigate in the world map, but all are marked by a very obvious '?'. I sort of dislike this since I always like the feeling of exploring for secrets but it has no real bearing either way on the gaming experience.The bosses have been criticized for being too repetitive, and I can sort of agree. Most have a 3-sequence attack pattern or something akin to that which repeats. It gives the fights a little bit of a stale feel at times, but it's not really that noticeable.In comparison with other Momodora games, the story is less implicit, more spelled out. It's actually rather cute and expands on background lore that's fun as a backdrop without ever becoming overbearing. The character design, though, is very lovely (you'll find your fair share of big-breasted anime characters—if you're averse to that, fair warning). I particularly enjoyed the interplay between Momodora and some of the other female characters she encounters along the way. As a whole, if I can describe MF in two words, it is just: very satisfying. It doesn't have the distinctiveness of RutM down quite as much in equal amounts, yet the components are just very solidly implemented which makes for a very welcoming gameplay experience. Especially with what feels like many games being released that skimp on just delivering good gameplay, playing MF is so refreshing.Verdict: A satisfying end to a great series. Would recommend. Length (7.5 hours for 100% completion) is perfect for what it delivers too.

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first time playing a Momodora game so I can't compare it to past entries but it was pretty good for a first game. Took about 10 hours to finish the story and then another 2 hours to clean some things up for 111% completion of the first playthrough.The game looks, sounds and plays great. The combat is almost a 2D Souls-like where you have to make use of dodges, the enemies can be really punishing if you let yourself get hit and you have a (mostly) fixed number of heals that can (mostly) only be recovered at save points. It's a bit more forgiving than a true Souls-like, though.Some minor negative points:The metroidvania aspects are pretty minimal. You can do almost everything the first time going through an area so there are only a handful of times you have to backtrack for any reason, especially since the map will specifically tell you whether there's a collectible in the room or not. Also, the sigil system is pretty weak for most of the game. There are only a handful of good sigils and you spend like 80% of the game with only 1 or 2 slots so you very rarely change them up. Near the very end of the game you get most of the good sigils and the last 2 slots one after the other, at which point you can finally play with sigil combinations. If some of the crappier cards were buffed and you got the 3rd slot a bit sooner it would have made the system a lot more interesting.Overall, though, I had a lot of fun and I'll be checking out at least Reverie Under the Moonlight soon. I recommend this if you like metroidvanias/combat platformers and want something on the short & sweet side.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the Momodora series this is more of the same but improving on every aspect. The story is nice but the characters, including some recurring ones are the highlight narratively. There's also some platforming puzzles for optional stuff strewn in that are a very fun addition, just be aware that you get a temporary ability that also buffs your jump later on in the game so if you get stuck on one it might be worth coming back later.I have some minor issues with the story hinting at some things that ultimately don't happen – seeing as this is supposed to be the end of the series there obviously won't be a big setup for a sequel.I've still got to try the arrange mode which seems to be doing a bit more than just shuffling items around and there's a boss challenge mode that lets you try and fight the bosses and harder versions of them as fast as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played and liked all the previous titles I went into this game with high expectations and was not disappointed. Below are some spoiler free general thoughts after my first playthrough.- With a playthrough time of around 8h it fits well into the price range of similar titles- Difficulty wise it's sligthly on the easier side (with an even easier game mode for people new to the genre) but can be made harder with the help of items and on consecutive runs- The world is well designed and there is tons to explore and find (equipable charm/sigil system makes loot feel valuable)- Controls are tight and almost all deaths are the users fault (particle effects can be distracting but they can be turned down in the options)- Mechanics are well implemented. Don't expect anything new that is ground breaking to the genre though- Some side content and extra modes do exist (don't expect hollow knight level side content though)- Music is from the same composer as RUTM and you can expect to hear something to the same degree. It fits the environments well and was never discracting to the gameplay. OST will be added to my playlist of things to listen to while working <3- The pixel art and animation is amazing and shows lots of love to small character and environment details- Good mix of areas (indoor vs outdoor / moody vs comfy)- Players of previous titles can find a lots of familiar faces all around- No hit boss rewards no longer exist. Good for some dissapointing for others (take your pick)- Boss cutscenes cannot be skipped (they are not too long but become noticable when retrying)Overall it was a very pleasent experience and was well worth the money.Recommended

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, this is the "Momodora at home" to Reverie under the Moonlight.Firstly, it's full of half-baked or pointless features. To elaborate:- MP are only used for healing yourself and some optional sigil effects.- Sigils are imbalanced; at least half of them are useless or outclassed by other sigils.- Why the stamina bar? Because Dark Souls had it?- There are a lot of companions, but they only do one of three things (attack, restore mana, or give you useless currency).- Fishing is pointless. It only awards currency which becomes redundant halfway through the game.- At some points in the game, you plant seeds and have to wait 10 minutes to harvest them. WHY?- Towns are entirely useless since the NPCs have nothing of value to say.- (minor spoiler) The boss refights in the postgame are not only lazily designed, but also sporadic in difficulty owing to the lazy design. Better not have extra boss fights at all before you resort to red instant death blocks to make them "harder".Also, the map is cumbersome to traverse and full of bland environments. Regular enemies are annoying (especially when they're invisible until you draw near) and boss fights are way too easy for the most part.OVERALL: Get RutM instead or wait for a deep sale on this one. Feels like a huge step back compared to its predecessor.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not horrible and even not as bad as Minoria, but it's a huuuuge step back compared to RUtM.First of all, why is there a stamina meter? In the previous games I was able to sprint or dodge thing whenever I wanted. But here I'm wasting my time waiting for stamina to recover in order to perform some trivial actions! Like, why is this even here? Is this a blind copying of Dark Souls mechanics? Or perhaps it's just a trick to make the game a bit longer?But there's another reason why you cannot freely sprint or dodge-roll across the map. You see, there are a lot of enemies that pops up out of thin air right in front of your face. Yeah, just like in Minoria. It does not make the game harder or more surprising. It's just annoying. Should I even explain why invisible enemies is not a fun thing in action platformers?Also something is wrong with controls. The movement is kinda stiff - it feels like inertia is increased or something. Attack animation cannot be cancelled into the dodge roll. And sometimes attacks are delayed after dodging enemies. Maybe it's all just a bugs which will be fixed later, but for now controls are not as responsive as I expected.Of course there are a lot of minor issues. Like collectibles with 10 minutes timer straight out of mobile games. Or barely visible instakill traps in the Lunar Palace (or whatever it is called). Most of the sigils are fricking useless. Dodge roll is so short that sometimes the game forcibly pushes you out of the big enemies. Sometimes I couldn't even find Momo on the screen because of visual effects. Some enemies are literally copypated from RUtM, without even changing their size for new resolution...But still this game is not that bad. It is okayish little metroidvania if you haven't played RUtM before. But in this case I would recommend you to play Reverie Under the Moonlight instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Set five years after the events of , Moonlit Farewell tells the story of Momo Reinol, high priestess of the village of Koho, which is assaulted by demons after they steal a powerful artifact called the Black Bell. The matriarch sends Momo to retrieve the bell and investigate the source of the calamity, which is located in a dungeon underneath the village. It is not necessary to have played the previous games in the series because there are notes about Momodora’s past adventures, but it is highly recommended if you want to experience the whole journey (they are also very good games). The story is minimal and mainly narrated through recurrent interactions with different characters. Some old characters make their return to assist Momo with her task, and new characters are introduced (like Cereza). Oh, and if you love cats, this is the game for you.Being a classic metroidvania, the game delivers 2D platforming through large and interconnected maps mixed with combat and boss fights sections. Momo’s movements feel smooth and responsive, with beautiful animations for attacking, dodging and jumping. Such actions consume your stamina meter, so it is important to plan your combat strategy and quickly adapt to enemies’ diverse range of attacks. Momo’s main weapons are a maple leaf that acts as a blade and a bow, plus a magical bell that can be used to heal and, when upgraded, damage nearby enemies. It is also possible to heal and save your progress in specific checkpoint shrines by simply hitting the bell. The game also auto-saves after certain events (such as defeating bosses), but it’s still recommended to manually save every time you can. Progression features some special cards known as Sigils, which need to be found by exploring every corner of the world, or purchased from Cereza. These cards add different boosts to stats, increase weapons’ damage, unlock new effects and much more, allowing you to customize your playstyle in multiple ways. You can equip a max of 5 Sigils, but first you must unlock each slot by collecting Grimoires. You can also choose between different types of familiars, which will follow Momo and provide minor assistance (such as mana healing or scouting the map for Lunar Crystals). Thanks to these mechanics, exploration and combat always feel smooth and rewarding. There is a great variety of bosses too, each one with a unique design and patterns; some of them require perfectly timed attacks and dodges. Despite the use of Sigils and familiars, you will never feel overpowered, which is great for the game’s balance, but on the other hand it makes combat more difficult (particularly towards the end). Thankfully, difficulty can be switched to easy at any time, so the game is very accessible for those who are not used to metroidvanias. Graphically speaking, the game looks gorgeous with its unique 2D pixel art style, combined with cute character design and a wonderful soundtrack that enhances every encounter and each relevant moment of the story.Now onto the only negative I found: non-linear exploration. While still rewarding, it can also be confusing at times. There is a map but, except for some question mark symbols for important areas, there isn’t anything else to guide you and you will casually move around until you find the next boss area. This unfortunately proves to be even more frustrating when backtracking and looking for secrets and missed items. The game also seems to be quite short (especially when compared to metroidvanias like  or ) and probably could have included more side content or optional locations.  Nevertheless it is very addictive and the price seems fair for the content proposed.Momodora: Moonlit Farewell represents a satisfying conclusion for the series. It doesn’t innovate the genre and probably never had this ambition, but it’s a delightful experience from start to finish. If you enjoy metroidvanias you will love this one too; if you’ve played all the previous Momodora games, you will love this one even more.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, the game IS really well done, with incredible graphics, tight controls, and good performance overall (played the entire thing on the Steam Deck, never experienced bugs of any kind).But would I recommend it? Well, I really thinks it depends on who is asking.If you played lots of similar games and want to know if this game is also worth your time, I'd say yes, go for it.If you never played other metroidvanias, or only played a handful, I'd say there's better games to get into first, including the previous entry in this very series, Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight. It is very hard to talk about this game without comparing it to the previous one, and I think it falls short in many aspects where RUtM thrived. But at the same time, I understand that this kind of comparison is unfair and we should always threat each new game as their own standalone product.So, instead of giving the game a negative review, I'll leave it as positive, but listed below are the points that I wish were better, in my opinion of course. (Minor spoilers where I indicate things that happen late in the game, but I don't give enough detail, I think...)-The game is too slow, Momo walks too slow, and too many things slow you down even more, like mud floors, patterns that make you wait, and enemy attacks (even one of the first enemies you encounter is an unkillable thing that slows you down ). Plants that grow in real minutes to give you an upgrade are kinda boring too, because you either stand around waiting, or forget where they were afterwards. Also, near the end of the game there is an elevator section that could simply move twice as fast.-Level design is very linear, with lots of slow backtracking with few interesting things in the way back. There are none of those moments where you feel like you could have done an entire area of the game in a different order, and even when the map is all zig-zaguey, in reality you're just moving in a straight line that was bent and turned. Navigating the world feels more like a chore than a fun and rewarding exploration, even when you consider the "metroidvania" progression, which is very limited in this game.-Bosses are uninteresting, most of them I died once figuring the patterns, and then it's just a slog of repeating the same things over and over - they might as well just have half the health bar, so we can move on quicker. Even bosses in the end of the game, with multiple phases, were a mix of "what is going on I can't see anything" stages with "just mash the attack button until it's dead" stages.-The UI is subpar, with the pause menu somewhat hard to use. Selecting options on dialogues is also hard, because the option you select looks almost the same as the others, and when there's only 2, you don't know which is which. And that thing where the map and health bars move when you change which half of the screen you're on is terrible, because now I have to think where the relevant info is on the screen, instead of simply looking at it. I think some people might like that, but I wish I could turn it off to have the elements fixed, even if they end up on top of my character.-Because of the UI, I oftentimes cannot track my health, and I die because I didn't know I was low at health. I wish there was a health bar above my character, or some better indication that I'm almost dead. There IS a sound that plays when my health gets low, but I have the impression that sometimes you get one shots that don't even trigger that sound, and often times you get comboed with 2 or 3 attacks that connect so fast that, when you hear the low health sound, it is already too late to do anything. Also, the bleeding effect is very difficult to see and I always die without even knowing I was under that affliction - in fact, other status effects like Tired are also difficult to see, while effects like Cursed are very well represented.-There were some moments during the game that I got somewhat lost because I thought I had done everything I could until that point in time, and I think the game could do a better job showing you what's missing. Two examples, I spent like an hour trying to find where to go next, thinking I had visited every place, to finally see that one room had an open connection I didn't enter - the problem here is that that region of the map uses two similar colours on the border and the background of the rooms, so I could barely see that the line had a hole indicating a door. Another example was a situation where my path was blocked and I had to talk to an NPC that was right beside the door. I talked to it, nothing happened, I thought I had to do something else, and went on searching the whole map. An hour later I came back to the same NPC and talked to it again, but this time I talked a second time and the NPC unblocked the path. Why did the game let me walk away mid-dialogue the first time around? All these points might be very minor and a little nitpicky, but I think that's because this is a really well done game that could be even better, like it's predecessor. And I really hope the devs keep doing great games, even if in another style, genre or series.

_childDocuments_.review: Moonlit Farewell is a disappointing sequel that feels slower, emptier, and less imaginative than its predecessors. Gameplay-wise: Common enemies almost never pose a threat, bosses are forgettable, the number of linear monster corridors gave me flashbacks to Order of Ecclesia on the DS. Dashing is tied to a stamina bar so good luck running around the bloated, empty map. The sigil abilities range from 'nearly worthless' to 'very helpful' but they don't offer anything that actually influences how you play the game. The main currency is only useful for buying sigils and temporary powerups from altars, so the majority of the game you're hoarding money you don't need - there's no sense of satisfaction. The indie metroidvania market is beyond saturated in 2024 and it takes a lot to stand out; weren't this a Momodora game I wouldn't have bothered playing it. Stick to Team Ladybug. C+

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, this game is a mixed bag, about on par with the previous game. Most of the time you're traversing through colorful environments that offer plenty of eye-candy for pixel art aficionados. That doesn't last for very long, though, as later in the game you'll have to wander through dark and boring environments where you can only see what's immediately surrounding you.Combat boils down to striking, dodging, and shooting arrows from afar, with certain actions depleting from a stamina meter. Dodging just before an enemy attack lands replenishes your stamina but you can take damage anyway. You also have a magic meter, its only purpose being a healing mechanism. Along the way, you'll find sigils that change your character's attributes slightly, often with trade-offs such as greater attack power but lower defense. You also come across companions that follow you around and passively aid you by replenishing your magic meter or generating currency.Enemy encounters are where this game was meant to shine, but doesn't. Big or small, airborne or on the ground, they are dispatched mostly in the same way, by mashing attack and dodging occasionally, with very little variety in how you're supposed to engage with them. Early encounters, in particular, are pretty much brainless mashing. It gets boring pretty quickly and, since the only incentive in defeating enemies is getting the money they drop, and money becomes a trivial matter pretty early in the game, it won't take long until you start avoiding combat altogether and looking at enemies not as an obstacle or a bounty, but as a nuisance.Fights are often punctuated by lots of visual effects like hit sparks, explosions and smoke clouds, visual clutter which is not too bad for individual enemies but terribly affects readability when fighting mobs, particularly mobs of smaller enemies in dark rooms or in areas where they blend in with the background. Imminent attacks from enemies are obnoxiously indicated by flashing red circles instead of a proper visual tell like a wind up animation, further affecting readability in some situations. Some enemies attack by simply touching you, whereas you can sometimes touch enemies without taking damage, but there's no indication as to when it's safe to get too close to an enemy, you just have to know. One enemy in particular attacks by shooting a whirlwind that causes no damage but pushes you around a bit. You can hide behind the sprite of one of the bosses so you'll have a really hard time telling if you're behind it or not while trying to dodge its attacks.As a Metroidvania, this game encourages exploration by offering permanent attribute buffs, sigils and money. Your character's normal movement speed, however, is really slow, and a slightly faster speed comes at the cost of your stamina meter, a decision that contributes with nothing to the game itself and just punishes the player for the sake of it, something that's further aggravated by the uninspired level design that often consists in long empty corridors or vertical shafts. One of the rooms in particular is just one long, narrow pit that you're supposed to climb out of while avoiding spikes. Another room has a sign that says "Please come back later", an invisible wall and no in-game explanation as to why you can't go in; you're not missing an item or ability to access it, like most Metroidvanias would imply, you just can't go in because the game doesn't want you to. Later in the game, you're given the option to fast-travel between some (but not all) save points.The HUD moves around supposedly so it doesn't get in the way of the action. If you move to the upper half of the screen, the HUD moves to the lower half and vice-versa. In a game like this, however, where you can die in three or so hits depending on what you're fighting against, ideally you'll want the HUD to remain in place so you can see how you're doing at a glance during combat without losing track of the action, but here often you'll find yourself chasing the HUD around with your eyes, which gets particularly aggravating when the action is taking place in the vertical middle of the screen. A toggle to disable this behavior would've been much appreciated, or the HUD's opacity could just change accordingly instead.There's also a half-baked fishing "minigame" here. You push a button to cast the line, wait for the indicator to appear, and then push that same button to reel it in and that's it. With each catch, you get rewarded with money. There's no catalog for the fish you caught, and no interactive component for reeling the fish in (e.g., Sea of Stars, Stardew Valley). Why this was even added to the game is a mystery.I liked RutM and even that game had its flaws. Moonlit Farewell, however, is riddled with questionable design decisions and the sense that it was just made to check it off the list, with no real passion or interest behind it. Therefore, I sadly can't recommend it. If you're interested in Metroidvanias with good pixel art and gameplay, I recommend checking out Team Ladybug's catalog.

_childDocuments_.review: The latest Momodora series is out and i have a couple things to say about this game :The Artwork I will say that this is similar to the previous one, so if you enjoy the last one you will enjoy this one too.PlatformingEasy to traverse and map that easy to understand. Varies of areas are distinct and vibrant. Platform and enemy position in this game i fell like is not quite tight just like the last game but they are overall solid and i think design choice is appeal to more newcomers for metroidvania/platform game.Combat You have melee and range as two main of attack. Melee will be main way to deal damage to enemy while range will do moderate damage from distance. By design, you will mostly engage enemy and boss in point blank range which you will usually get hit by attack in which the game also introduce dodge. Dodge will allow you to roll pass an attack up on you without taking damage, and if you timing the moment where attack is hitting you while you at rolling dodge animation you will gain invincibility frame for a few second, allowing you to deal continuous damage.BossThey are very solid bosses but they are not aggressive and leave a lot opening opening for you to deal damage and anticipate the attack with fixed pattern which i found to be quite miss opportunity as this game bosses has quite potential for dedicated/experienced player who enjoy tense unpredictable anticipated combat to replay this game all over again.(Which you can also re-fought the bosses after completed the game) I do hope that there will be an update to make bosses fell more satisfy to engage.StoryI wish that the game could have more world building lore and dramatic compelling moment with momo and dora which there are rarely interact at each other in the story and the new casts that should have been more backstory and interaction, i think story will definitely be more memorable. Therefore i fell like story for this game is quite flat across the journey that left me unsatisfied but by its foundation it is still a solid story with missed opportunity to be compelling.Sigil Basically a slot for you to select passive ability to Momo.(stating at 2 and be unlocked up to 5 by exploration.) I found this to be solid system which allow to you customize your playstyle the way you comfortably the most, you can be melee aggressive, passive healing, or dedicated ranged built. Only downside is that some of the sigils are practically underbalanced and not worth using it. I hope this to be address so that they become more appealing choice.OverallVery solid game action platform game that i believe everyone will enjoy. Despite some downsides, i am glad that i enjoy my time playing this game but at the same time i wish that the game could potential ended up better. I wish luck for rdein and the rest for the next project.

_childDocuments_.review: TL/DR: Nearly perfect 8-10 hour experience. Not insane value, but otherwise an easy recommendation.I just finished this with 110% completion (the map makes this really easy), and I've loved it. _childDocuments_.review: As much as I respect the Momodora series for being simple and knowing it, this entry was too plain for me to really enjoy. I think  worked because every element there was just good enough to form a balanced whole, even though none of them were exceptional. Here, it’s clear that loads of effort went into sprites, animations and presentation, yet the core gameplay remained equally simplistic (if not more so), and the contrast actually undermines the experience.Momodora 2 and 3 worked too, but only since they were both 1-2 hours long. Moonlit Farewell lasts about 10 hours for no good reason, because the majority of this time is spent on a typical "hit, hit, i-frame dodge" combat. There’s no token platforming with spikes like before; only basic traversal.You get many boss fights, but all of them are utterly straightforward, and the best battles are where the aforementioned contrast gets downright jarring. Beautiful animations, lush special effects, cool cutscene intermissions, badass music… and barely anything to do. The final boss has three completely different stages yet attacks so rarely and simply that many harder 2D action games would barely count this as a tutorial fight.You could say there’s an attempt to get more mechanically complex using the Sigils system (basically your regular "many perks, limited slots" thing leading to different builds), except there’s really not enough balance for it to work. Some perks barely deserve a glance, while others are too good to not use all the time unless you’re doing a challenge run.The game also invites min-maxing through its occasional awkward attempts at increasing difficulty, trapping you in tiny areas with large enemies or giving their attacks brutal status effects like bleeding (there is, of course, an immunity perk that negates all that). There’s a post-game boss rush section with no recovery between fights, and it might feel like you’re finally in for some challenging test of attrition… except the mana regeneration perk negates such handicap entirely. So even when you die in this game, the answer is usually "use a more OP build" instead of "git gut".The story got an upgrade, but only in quantity of conversations and characters, not in their quality. RUtM was more of a typical moody dark fantasy; Moonlit Farewell is a typical JRPG-inspired romp about fighting a god with a double sprinkling of fan service. There’s a new girl Cereza acting as an NPC companion + shop, but she contributes absolutely nothing other than her cute cat ears. Momo and Dora are actually having chats here for the first time, except I couldn’t find any personalities in their lines beyond the most basic archetypes that were already established before.Lastly, it’s disappointing how the extra modes and achievements have almost zero variety this time. RUtM had a pacifist achievement that meant moving through the same areas differently, as well as higher difficulties that at least invited you to do the battles near-flawlessly, and Momodora 3 had pacifist and speedrun achievements too. Here, instead, there’s a YOLO mode (which forces you to rely on OP perks even more) and the "arrange" mode (which mirrors the map, removes one hit from the base combo, and changes pretty much nothing else), so getting 100% basically means repeating the same thing 3 times in a row. Naturally, by the end of it the already simplistic and overused combat starts to feel like nothing but a chore.Big props to the developer for making and finishing this game, despite the reported severe burnout, but there’s no denying that larger scope comes with its own set of challenges, and sometimes you just need a bigger team or even more time to make it work.

_childDocuments_.review: Did i like this game?  Can i truly and honestly recommend this game? I loved this game and its experience, overall. But there are parts of it that have actually left a rather bitter taste with me, and i want to let these grievances be known.I have played Momodora Reverie Under The Moonlight, this was my only other Momodora experience.Without a doubt, this game does not live up to that game. This game has lovely graphics, somewhat interesting environments, and killer music.Unlike many other negative reviews, i do think running around and exploring the map is fun... when you're allowed to actually explore, that is.I would say i really enjoyed the combat overall, as it does  good. But it isn't the best.Like many others, though, my gripes with the game are as follows:1. I dislike that enemy attacks are sometimes not indicated on really quick attacks, or attack take a full  after the indicator to actually come out. It's very awkward and unintuitive.2. While i love the combat, bosses feel either lacking in complexity and intrigue, or entirely too slow. Some bosses are damage sponges, others deal far too much damage 3. Post-game content is about as absent as i expected it to be, which is fine.. but what is there is lacluster. A boss refight area is good. But the "harder" versions of the bosses are just adding bland, boring, instant death squares to the arena or firing at you. If you fight these bosses correctly, you will actually find the nightmare version equal to or easier than the original.4. The final boss is just. Easy. Far too bland. A pretty spectacle, but.. i am feeling sad it was not a harder experience, and upset that there is not really going to be a good difficult experience with said boss.Overall.. i think its okay, as a game. I still love it. i will still play it probably to full achievement completion, if i have the patience for hardcore mode... But i just can't in good faith recommend it. Maybe if it was on sale, or if you really are wanting more of Reverie Under the Moonlight and feel like you can handle a bit more lackluster of an experience.If i were to recommend anything to the devs, i understand that Momodora games are getting tiring, but if you update this game.. please re-tune some boss health or damage values. Also, please tune up things about the refights. Make bosses attack  and hit slightly harder than normal. Or, find unique ways like forcing certain sigils on, changing the arenas.. etc. Those would be big changes, though, and i understand they likely wont happen.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Gorgeous sprite work and animations. Wonderful music. The plot is very straightforward but it has the same enchanting feeling as other Momodora games, which is to say that it feels like there's a real world behind the story.There are a few balance oddities with sigils, but my only real criticism is that several plot threads seem to abruptly end. This normally wouldn't be a problem since a sequel would flesh them out, except this was billed as the end of Momodora's overall story so the cases where this happened ended up feeling a bit unsatisfying.Honestly though, absolutely worth the price. Highly recommended for anybody who likes metroidvanias, especially if you like exploring and piecing together lore in games. I picked it up and didn't put it down until I beat the game. _childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: The game locked far too many common/basic movement options behind upgrades. Couple that with a really bad stamina system and you got yourself a slog of an early/mid game. Only way to make those parts of the game go by reasonably fast is to cap yourself to 1HP and let the stamina regen that kicks in at low HP to help you.Also, most of the "arena" situations take place in really boring or awkward parts of the map that massively restrict your movement options, which is REALLY not fun. These also mess with your expectations in the worst of ways because the enemies in them often have altered stats.I feel like this game misses the mark on so many small things that slowly add up to a cumbersome and frustrating experience. It was SO close in so many different aspects. Still, it has its fair share of enjoyable moments. I commend the dev team for sticking with it 'till the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful followup to Momodora:RotM and exactly what I've been hoping and dreaming about for almost a decade. This game is glistening and with quality and attention to detail. It follows the metroidvania methodology, similar to the previous game, and with some additional skills and companions and other enticing features (like fishing!), also taking some inspiration from Hollow Knight.The setting is less dark compared to RotM (whose world had more of a Bloodborne vibe), with this game feeling like medieval fantasy or Zelda. I still thought it was charming though, and enjoyed exploring all the various areas with their unique enemies, music, bosses, characters and themes. I look forward to diving back in to try the other difficulty modes, especially as I felt very overpowered on the normal setting.It's hard to poke holes in this game, it was definitely worth the wait. It's overall just a very high quality, wholesome game and a satisfying experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good short metroidvania. Expect 7-9 hours to complete it, 10+ for getting all the content. The focus is on lore and exploration. Fans of the series will enjoy all the lore. The graphics are the best in the series. The pixel art style is consistent with RutM but even better. The animation is so good!The movement feels very sluggish compared to the previous entries but I got used to it quickly. The combat is fine and the new sigil system is okay but not very deep.My only complaint is that the boss are *super* easy compared to the previous titles. Fighting enemies during exploration is more challenging than the bosses. I kept waiting for bosses to get harder.. they did not.  I guess they wanted this game to be more accessible to most players but it could really use an actual hard mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora Moonlit Farewell was in the end still a game that I enjoyed yet it lacked the simple charm of Momodora 1-3 and didn't reach the heights of RUTM and Minoria when it comes to map design, enemy design, gameplay, story and overall world design. To me there were no real strong points in this entry, aside from some of the sprites (I really enjoyed the ones in the swamp area) but also no real weak points either, an alright entry of the series but nothing great.  rdein peaked with Minoria and RUTM in my opinion. I had hoped Moonlit Farewell would continue to develop in the direction of those two titles, but it feels like rdein played it very safe and didn't want to experiment.Moonlit Farewell is still a good game but definitley not good enough for me to come back to every couple of years unlike RUTM and Minoria. I still recommend this game if you are a fan of the franchise but if you are new you should start with any other title.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Hate to give this one a negative review after how much I liked Reverie under the Moonlight but this is game is a mess. It feels like the game completely runs out of ideas a few hours in. There's so much contradictory design. Why is there a stamina bar? Why are so many sigils useless or overlapping? The companions do very little and are visually distracting, especially because some of them use the same sprites as enemies. Enemies drop tons of currency but there's almost nothing to spend it on. The level design is by-the-numbers and the areas are bland. The art and animation is still great, but these little inconsistencies and contradictions overpower what is otherwise a very simple game. It doesn't feel like there's a vision bringing the game together, just a bunch of elements cribbed from Castlevania and similar games without a feeling for why those mechanics work.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game, but... It's half as long and twice as easy as the previous title in the series. If you're new to metroidvanias are dislike difficulty, this would be the Momodora game for you, but otherwise, there's no reason to play this when you could play Reverie Under the Moonlight. At least it's pretty.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: When Starbound came out of early access, I tried it out and it felt a lot like Terraria but prettier, and with some new ideas. This compares favorably to that experience, being Starbound for Momodora: Reverie under the Moonlight (4). There's a lot of spectacle here, the backgrounds are off the chain gorgeous, and I really enjoyed exploring to the vibe set by all that and the music. That said, the gameplay itself felt kind of mindless a lot of the time. Combat was pretty easy overall, especially the boss fights. Environmental puzzles didn't get all that interesting, either. Still, if I could give it a 20/10 on presentation, I would, and that definitely counts for a lot for me. That, and the gameplay was never bad, nor boring, just that I was hoping for more of a challenge, or more of something new. This is definitely an evolution of Momodora 4 though it kind of feels like it takes more after Momodora 3 artistically.  I'd highly recommend it to anyone looking for a Metroidvania to dive into, but it's not quite the titan of the genre I felt Momodora 4 was at the time. Took me a bit less than 5 hours to get 110% completion.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: [+] artwork is exceptionally pretty[+] music is also very pretty and fits perfectly with the atmosphere[+] strong atmosphere to each area[+] large breasts[+] includes a post game boss rush mode, as well as a couple bonus difficulties[+] little bits of tech that the game lets you figure out on your own (e.g.  ) [~] there is an indicator on the map that shows you where all the secrets/items are, which makes it less tedious to find everything, but also less rewarding since all the locations are given to you as you play, I might prefer that you are given all the locations after you beat the game or maybe you can spend munnies for hints or something[-] the game overall is a bit short and a bit linear--one side or secret area would feel nice as well as having a few options for routes through the game, for $15 it's not bad but I would absolutely pay more if it was a bit bigger[-] no crouch in this game, which I really liked from the previous game since it added depth (had to crouch to hit shorter enemies with the bow, and you could dodge high attacks like lasers), and it was satisfying to do[-] there is no buffer window for jumping or rolling from a landing (as of writing this), which feels a little bit clunky at least until you get double jump, and I feel like it's pretty standard for most 2D games nowadays to have this buffer window[-] not enough things to spend munnies on, had a huge surplus the whole game
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's a fine game, less so for people that enjoy a good metroidvania or like difficulty. I think maybe HC mode, Arrange or some boss rushes can be interesting but otherwise most of the game was too easily passable by just bruteforcing. I played one other momodora title before, reverie of the moonlight or something and I thought it was less interesting than that but just okay to play through. There's no real intrigue, the story is kinda there but bland, the art and the music are great, movement and hit feedback are great. Some other opinions are detailed below, especially in regards to after completing the base game and other modes.Edit 1: The Boss Rush mode was disappointing, I completed all encounters in one or two sittings by just brute forcing. Arrange Mode seems to mostly the same but areas are mirrored plus there is supposed to be new stuff. I'm not sure I will continue with this game at the moment, just because the exploration aspect wasnt the strongest and the combat is quite weak. But sometime I'm definitely interested in HC mode because i think this will make the game challenging because bruteforcing isn't all that viable or consistent in some sections when one death means a complete game reset.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Map is small, not very interconnected and ability checks seem forced.Locations look nice but they are pretty random and boring. There isn't really any environmental storytelling in them, they are just here.I guess they might be explained in a story but i could not get myself to care.Some enemy attacks don't have attack indicators which makes them very fast,this would normally not be an issue, but when you attack you get stuck in a lengthy attack animation and so if you misstimed your attack, you get hit.Some enemy attacks show attack indicator just to hover and do nothing for 3s before hitting youI understand a little delay, but  i needed a damn mental alarm clock for this. Tank god for forgiving dodge frames.Some enemies just walk into you dealing damage instead of stopping in front of you to attack. Some enemies spawn from thin air and deal damage instantly.Some enemies spawn with indicators and attack immediately after, which as you can guess makes you feel quite bad as you just wanted to punish indicated spawn point.You can't do any movement tech in midair, which makes jumping over some enemies a death sentence.Hurt boxes are not clear at all, funny toxic clouds look like they are gone but they aren't, and look like they should still deal damage but don't.Bosses hurt you when you come in contact with them, except for those that don't and just push you away insteadGame looks nice but when you equip some sigils you can't see anything.Its not that big of an issue as combat is mostly memory game and you don't really need to react to attacks anyway.You either need to play safe to avoid undodgable attacks and random 3s timers or learn all and 1-2 per common enemy.I could see some fun in mastering combat system at the end of the game as you get a way to shorten your attack animations but the game is not worth the time.

_childDocuments_.review: very slight spoiler alertMaybe for some it's still a decent platformer but after playing Reverie under the Moonlight I had very high hopes for this game and been waiting eagerly for years.Sadly it did not live up to my expectations.Combat is ok early game but late game made no sense. Sigil system is a decent try at customization but has severe balancing issue and the immersion is nowhere near as good as reverie under the moonlight.Story telling is much, much worse than RUTMMusic wise is actually ok, I'm just VERY disappointed I didn't hear the Momodora theme song throughout my play through. There is also no fights in this game as memorable as the Fennel fight in RUTM.Artwork feels rushed, a lot of background and characters like the big snake clearly lacks detail.Overall 5/10, it's ok for a normal platformer but if you want another Reverie Under The Moonlight experience you will be disappointed.However, after actually finishing the game, it's not bad at all.Sure it's no where near Reverie under the moonlightBut it is still pretty good.Cheers
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who couldn't enjoy reverie under the moonlight to save my life because of flaws I pointed out about the game.I'm so glad to see those flaws fully removed in this game, leaving me with an exceptional experience akin to the first 3 games, which I loved so much.-There's an autosave feature now.-Enemies and bosses now deal fair amounts of damage as opposed to dealing next to no damage or straight up instakilling you like in reverie.-Boss attacks are now REACT-ABLE. Thank god, almighty. One of my biggest nitpicks with reverie was how it felt that it was neigh impossible for a boss to be beaten first try because their attacks were undodgable unless you knew what to do ahead of time. This is not an issue anymore and I'm glad to report that I have beaten many of this game's bosses first try.I guess my only gripe with the game can be that it can be too easy at time, but the game does have higher difficulty stuff post completion so that's easily written off.Honestly, 10/10. Glad to see one of my favorite indie platformer series end on such a satisfying note.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a sequel to the series that much is for sure. Story:Looks like it is drawing around to the time for another sacrifice. The game gives note to get you up to speed on past events, and given the layout of some areas. It also might have a connection to Minoria. Which really has me curious how this game will go. The highlight for Minoria were those documents that expanded more on the situation and the main. Here there isn't much, aside from the notes. That aside, the plot of this one are two warring deities, which leads into the problem. And the way it is going, I have some scenarios on how it might end at the current point. To add on a bit more, while it has connections to previous entries. It does appear it will be its own thing as well for a continuation. This is a sequel to Momodora III, which might be taking place before the events of Minoria, if I am tracking this correctly. Anyway, could be wrong on this. Either way, general run down. Is a goddess who gave life had her eye stolen by her brother. The two were put into a deep sleep because of their feud. When they awoken, the sister searched out her brother, intending to kill him. Part of it is protecting the world, and also hatred.The brother grew jealous of his sister, and wanted her light. Hence, it gets into the conflict of the game.Mechanics:There is more to it in this game, such as Sigils, companions, etc. It has the crafting, so that is not new. As well as the usual stuff.Gameplay:There is a difficulty option with adaptive gameplay, so it is an easier game compared to the rest. Which is not a bad thing, choose to play how you want. The one thing that can put a series in a bad light is when it does not account for player ability. You spend money on this, and saying not every game has to be finished is dumb, since money was spent. The difficulty options is a great addition to it. I didn't have issues with some of the previous games, but that is not the same for everyone.Maps:Usual fashion, if not feeling a bit larger than the rest. Get power ups, explore new places. There are many stat ups in the game, and these can likely be found in hidden area with a glow or a question mark on the map. Save:Autosave can be a bit weird, to manually save hit the bell with your weapon. Also, the bell can provide a temporary buff.Other stuff:There is fishing, and growing stuff for stats. Some side quests, etc.Overall:This is a great game, and I'd recommend checking it out. If you're new to the genre, you can get a feel for it quite well with this game. It also has two great clash scene, and final one that concludes the game. All in all, it was quite a fun experience. If you do everything, it should take about 8 or 9 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exactly what I expected after having played Reverie under the Moonlight.Really fun game, story is not groundbreaking but works and is compelling enough to want to find out what happens next at all moments, and in general I think the game is really well designed as a lightweight metroidvainia that you can finish in a couple of days.I've been waiting for this game since I first played Reverie under the Moonlight, and starting 2024 with this gives makes me optimist and gives me hope towards what this year can be regarding this kind of games.If you like metroidvanias, you'll like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this series and was extremely excited for this one to release, it was perfect! Gameplay felt really smooth, story was very fun and I loved the interactions with Cereza (npc character who travels with you). Some bosses felt easier than they could have been but hardcore mode is a good way to manage with that, plus the sigils allow for alot of different builds that are real satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: So far it feels great and looks like it's taking a much deeper approach to the narrative and character arcs (especially compared to the days of reading a short blurb in a .txt file). _childDocuments_.review: This was my first anticipated release of 2024 and it totally met and even exceeded my expectations. All I have left to do for 111% is the final boss rush, so I've seen a lot of the game, but I already plan to keep playing for full achievements and maybe even speedruns. This game is sick!

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little metroidvania that's not trying to re-invent anything, no crazy power-ups or unique methods of traversal, no difficult bosses, no real chance to get completely lost, not very difficult to find hidden items and invisible walls.$15 is about the right price for this and what you get. _childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: The 5th and possibly final entry in the Momodora series, Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a celebration of the franchise that brings everything you love from the previous games while adding its own flavor to it. The game feels easier than the previous entry (not counting Minoria), as there are initially only 2 difficulty options. Level design is pretty good, with some secrets and objectives causing me to spend minutes figuring out where to go or what to do. Music is also fantastic with some battle tracks sticking with me even after finishing the game (which took 8 hours). The biggest critiques I have are with the gameplay, mainly the introduction of the stamina meter. I think while the idea is to add a level of challenge and stop dodge roll spamming is good, the implementation of a stamina meter just slows the pace down and detracts a bit from the moment to moment gameplay of previous entries. Also some of the control mechanics baffle me, in the past Momodora game you had a dedicated ranged button, now it's holding up while hitting attack. This doesn't make sense to me especially since the R1 and L1 buttons have no use, it really just feels like an odd change that for no real reason.Overall if you're a fan of the series or a Metroidvania fan you will really enjoy this fun sendoff to a great indie series.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: We've just started the year and I already have a contender for Game of the year. I had been waiting for this game for so long and I'm happy to say that it did not disappoint, The controls from Momodora 4 have been polished even further and while at first I wasn't all that into the running button after a bit it felt satisfying to move around the map, combine that with the double and wall jump and its just incredible. The bosses are also still just as fun as before with the right amount of challenge, I'm also happy we finally get expanded more on the lore of this franchise which is something that's been built up little by little with each game.  Soundtrack and pixel graphics are outstanding as well. It's quite commendable how Rdein and his team leveled up their skills starting with a love letter to Cave Story to now this, I'm so happy to have played this and I look forward to whatever future projects they bring in the future. sincerely Thank you Rdein and team.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed it but not nearly as much as RUtM. Game feels pretty linear and the final boss was a major disappointment. I never felt a need to learn attack patterns for enemies as most of the time you can power through them easily enough or avoid them. Bosses aren't engaging and are very easy. _childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: There isn't much in this game that hasn't been done before in the metroidvania genre, all the traversal mechanics are your standard sprint, double jump and wall jump, a bit disappointing as the previous game had a fairly unique cat transformation. What this game does do well is combat and atmosphere, it's a very relaxing game to play, but simultaneously fairly challenging as enemies and bosses can take you by surprise if you're careless. Death isn't too frustrating as your only penalty for dying is re-spawning at the last bell you rang.Despite the game's simplicity, there is a healthy amount of character customisation in the form of equip-able sigils that you find constantly throughout the game, that give you passive bonuses, and it can be fun to experiment with different load-outs for different scenarios.The game's art and character designs are worth the price alone in my opinion, I frequently found myself in awe of some of the goofy, weird, and creepy enemy designs. Just be aware that you'll probably see everything the game has to offer in less than 10 hours if you're an experienced player, outside of replaying the game on a harder difficulty.

Movement feels more sluggish and unresponsive and the dodge telegraphs just don't exist for half the moves. Which in a game that wants you to no-hit bosses is a really stupid move. _childDocuments_.review: This is a very hard game to recommend. Not because it's bad or even mediocre, but because If you're a fan of Momodora you're pretty much guaranteed to be disappointed, at least in terms of gameplay. I'm honestly pretty conflicted. I had a lot of fun with the game and I intend to replay it, but as a send-off for the series, it just leaves a bad taste in my mouth. Most of the changes are arguably improvements, but it sort of comes off as fixing what wasn't broken.For some context, the other Momodora games available on Steam are essentially Mini-Metroidvanias. Reverie Under the Moonlight can easily be beaten in under an hour if you know what you're doing. Momodora 3 can be beaten on your lunch break. Mechanically they don't do anything revolutionary, But they're both dense with fun missables. To start on a positive note the game looks and sounds amazing, and the higher resolution is one area where I think the Moonlit Farewell succeeds as the culmination of the series. The previous games used a lower aspect ratio. 3 had very small sprites, and due to the limited detail, the combat was very simple. But Rutm's larger sprites have a more blatant tradeoff. They take up so much space that all of the rooms have to be very compact to accommodate them. Despite being larger than 3's the map feels claustrophobically thin at points. In a way, Farewell has the best of both worlds. Varied enemies with detailed sprites and animations, as well as wider and more varied layouts for platforming and exploration. My main issue is that the game feels a lot more streamlined. First off the combat and controls received some changes. Where before you only had health, now you also have stamina and mana to manage. They both function as you'd expect.The Healing bell (your only spell) really just replaces items, but stamina is a bit more complex. It decreases whenever you roll, or sprint, but by timing a perfect roll you can get some stamina back. You can also automatically perform a potent shot (essentially a charged shot) with full stamina. It's a lot of fun to time your dodges and strike back, and the upgrades gradually make this more rewarding. The problem is that this is pretty much all there is to the combat. You can't crouch anymore for some reason, and the air-dash is also strangely absent. You have to rely on I-frames to avoid damage more than the game relied on fanservice for marketing, but your best option in the air is a sigil that gives you a shield after using the healing bell.  Most of the enemies are designed around this, but some of the more hectic encounters in the final area made me miss the air-dash. To play devils advocate, an air-dash would likely break some of the trickier platforming, but I'd welcome any sort of air option at this point.This is more of a nitpick but I also preferred charging shots manually. Bow shots have been remapped to up + attack, as opposed to having a dedicated button. Potent shots fill a similar role, but they simplify the execution by a lot. It's also annoying to have to roll or sprint for a second to deplete your stamina every time you want to save a Potent shot. Anyways, this streamlining bleeds into the overall structure of the game. Because of the new gauges most of the collectibles are simple boosts to your HP, MP, and Stamina, most meaningful upgrades are necessary for progression. The only real exception to this are Sigils. These are essentially just Hollow Knights charm except with rigid slots instead of a notch system to balance them. I'm gonna go out on a limb and say that this is a straight downgrade, charms are overrated and I don't see why games keep copying this system. The result is a much greater emphasis on completing almost everything in a single playthrough rather than having interesting options for repeat playthroughs. Reverie has less main content, but most of the optional missables offer meaningful changes to the gameplay. If you beat the first boss of Reverie hitless, it will drop an equipable that adds poison damage to your arrows. More precisely it creates a small cloud wherever they hit, so if you're not careful you can accidentally poison yourself. Or you can combo this with the impurity flask (which gives you regen while poisoned) and poison yourself on purpose. These are the kinds of rewards that kept me playing and replaying the other games, and Farewell doesn't live up to this at all. You can't even do a proper pacifist run because the game is padded out with mandatory enemy rushes.Again, I'd like to stress that I did enjoy my first playthrough, and most of my issues are due to my expectations. I honestly can't recommend this as a sequel, but if you've never played the series before this is a pretty easy recommendation. Obviously, I think the others are better, but as a general Metroidvania, you could do much worse.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: I suppose the game is meant for those who have played the previous titles. As my first entry into the Momodora series, the story feels lackluster and the NPCs have little significance. Some enemies can be a little troublesome at times only because they deal a lot of damage, for example, the bandit archer/spear thrower in Heikan village dealing 750 damage when your HP is around 1250, and equipping the stamina sigil will make it worse. However, it becomes very easy once you get the shield sigil, even the nightmare bosses in post game (in normal difficulty) don't pose much challenge. Puzzles are almost non-existent, except just one or two in the sky castle. I did not anticipate the story and gameplay to be this short and felt disappointed. Clearing the game once + clear all reminiscent bosses + clear three nightmare bosses will get you all but three achievements. Clearing the arrange and hardcore modes will unlock all achievements but the game simply doesn't provide enough motivation for me to do that.On the up side, the graphics is good and there are some pretty nice BGMS. Overall movement and combat actions are smooth. Perfect dodge framing is pretty lenient, so it is pretty easy to get used to. There is also not much time-wasting backtracking because of the limited fetch quests in the game. If you are a fan of the series, I think the game would be recommended. But if you are not, wait for the game to have a bigger discount before giving it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: This was my favorite in the series. Did not seem as difficult, but I think I enjoyed it more because of that. I also didn't feel like I needed to have played the previous titles to enjoy this one. I did not see any noteworthy bugs in the game, was very clean. I highly recommend playing!Thanks to the team that brought us this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell does not tick the spot (personally.)Compare to Momodora: Reveries Under the Moonlight (2 previous title perhaps?), the tone was far less gloomy. I remember the first time I jump to Momodora: RUtM the story was vague and mysterious, there are hardly anyone in the game  mention anything about the story, yet it make the story to me seem very interesting in a special way. The atmosphere was sombre and grim, the lacks of friendly NPC to interact make the situation the more believable.But Momodora: Moonlit Farewell (the newest title) in my opinion have the opposite approach to the story. Now you have plenty of friendly faces to interact with, no mad people unlike the previous mentioned title. Also in this title, they try to explain so much about the story that I feel is just the way to ruin the mysteriousness it once has. Not to mention I personally felt the ways stories were told are somewhat considerable as plot hole. Minor spoiler? They mention life exist because part of the moon fell to the earth but "who" can possibly possess that kind of knowledge to tell the story? The combat in this game is okay, I wouldn't say that Momodora: RUtM has better combat, I would argue that this title does it better. I saw some controversy over the bow consuming SP on full stamina. I personally like this mechanic, it's a way to ditch quick damage in fast paced combat environment, well if you find it difficult to fight on low stamina the simple solution is not to use bow of course. There are also a trick for stamina management for sprinting. If you perform spinning attack: i.e. holding sprint and jump attack, you can carry the sprinting momentum and consume less stamina, it's somewhat just like RUtM cat morph jump attack. A final talk about the combat if you could count as one that is. The environmental hazard in this game was lack luster in term of challenges. There are reasons why Miyazaki love his poison swamp (every soul title have one, sorta.) Well, let say Moonlit Farewell doesn't have poison meter, also water doesn't slow you down. I can understand that it could be an annoying design rather than the feature if the water slow player down, but it could also be presented as a challenge for player.Lastly, the music. I don't have any particular memorable piece in this title unlike the RUtM the music was good because it compliment the gloomy atmosphere, and there is a piece I like way too much.Conclusion, if you're looking for Momodora: Reveries Under the Moonlit 2, this isn't the one. Despite giving a negative review, I could actually recommended you to play this game, it's still a solid choice.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played any past Momodora game, but I decided to give this one a chance and unfortunately I was pretty disappointed. The spritework and animations are pretty great, and the music is decent - it's purely the gameplay that lets it down. Despite being perfectly polished and functional, Moonlit Farewell manages to miss pretty much everything that usually makes Metroidvanias fun or interesting, and the end result is a game that's pretty flavourless.Let's start with the level design: this game resembles a Metroidvania, but it's fairly linear. Each area acts like a self-contained level and you progress through them in a mostly static order. Most branching paths are not that substantial. If you're hoping for a sprawling map of interconnected areas, you're not going to get that here. The real problem though is that most collectables are just sitting there in plain sight. I finished the game with 106% completion (out of a presumed maximum of 111% according to the achievements) so it seems like I grabbed almost everything just on my first pass through. I think I can safely say that exploration is not a big part of this game.If not exploration, maybe it's meant to be more of a straight action game with some slight nonlinearity? Unfortunately the combat isn't standout either. Most normal enemies take several hits to take down, but attacking them stunlocks them so it's just about getting in their face and whaling on them til they die. I think if they just went down in one hit it would be not much less difficult, but certainly less tedious. The combat doesn't evolve much either. You have a magic meter, so naturally I expected that you would progressively unlock cool attacks that cost magic, but it never happens. The closest thing is there are sigils that buff your arrows at the cost of magic, but each arrow costs a huge amount of MP and you can't choose to shoot a normal arrow without using MP unless you unequip the sigil, so it's super not worth using. The boss fights are where the game shines the most - the first fight with the black cat is excellent - however even the bosses are inconsistent. Some bosses barely move so you just mash attack until they telegraph to dodge. Again, I think it would be a lot better if bosses were more active but had less health, and it was more about finding spots to land one or two hits rather than mashing attack then dodging at the last second. Worse yet is that the difficulty balancing is all over the place. By the end of the game you can get so many overpowered effects that you basically become immortal. The final boss with like five forms is probably easier than the very first boss of the game.Beyond that the game is just full of strange, half-baked systems that don't mesh well. I already mentioned the puzzling magic system - there's barely any interactivity with it. To compare to a much better game, in Hollow Knight, your soul gauge can be used for both healing and attacking, healing takes a second and leaves you vulnerable, and you regain soul from successfully hitting enemies with melee attacks. These mechanics combine into a beautiful gameplay loop that let the player make choices with risk and reward. Meanwhile in Moonlit Farewell, MP is pretty much only used for healing, healing is safe and instant, and MP is only restored from checkpoints or very specific drops, so your MP is basically just glorified reserve health except you need to remember to press the button to use it. You start to wonder what the point was of even having it. The same could be said of the companion system which I'm still not really sure what they do, or the almost useless currency. I feel like a lot of effort went into these systems only for them to not feel worth it because they just weren't planned well.And then there's the sigil system. Similar to Hollow Knight's charms, you can equip sigils which grant special effects with a limited number of slots, however Hollow Knight had the sense to have different charms come with different equip costs, allowing for a great variance in charm effects while still maintaining balance. In Moonlit Farewell, sigils are wildly imbalanced in how useful they and yet they all cost exactly one slot, and the number of slots you get is frustratingly limited for most of the game. I only had two slots for what felt like ages while I kept picking up new sigils that weren't worth it compared to the overpowered ones I already had. One of said overpowered sigils nullifies all status effects with no downsides, and you get it shockingly early. I basically forgot the status effect system even existed because as soon as I got cursed once, I equipped the sigil to nullify status effects and left it on for the rest of the game. There's also a sigil that lets you regain health from enemy drops, which is a must-have because it lets you explore much longer without needing a checkpoint - that is, until it's made obselete by the sigil that automatically restores your MP at a pretty fast rate, giving you effectively infinite health unless you're face-tanking every other hit. Meanwhile other sigils have mediocre effects like increasing the speed of arrows, which could be nice to have if not for having to give up something massively more powerful in exchange, and it leads to so many sigils not being worth using unless you're purposely restricting yourself from the broken ones. It's unfortunate because a simple change of having different costs could have made it so much more interesting and strategic, but it's just another case of missed potential.Overall, Momodora: Moonlit Farewell may not be a terrible game, but I feel like it's so bland that it wouldn't be worth playing even if it was free. If you want a great Metroidvania, play Hollow Knight. If you're looking for a 2D sidescroller with cute girls, I highly recommend Shantae and the Pirate's Curse. Give this one a miss.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I play a Momodora game, and it will be the last I enjoyed the game in the begining, but the more I progressed the more frustrating and dissapointing the experience became.Uninspired boss fights, (especially the final boss, who I beat while being almost completely stoic and not bothering to dodge his attacks at all) The only time i moved was in phase 3 when he started walking around, i moved so i can be right next to him and attack, i again did not dodge his attacks.Overall frustrating things like, enemies respawning upon re-entering a room, attacks of both the player and enemy passing trough walls, enemies seeing you through walls or from very far away and just shooting the crap out of you from 3 different directions while u struggle to reach them.The Lunar Attunment, what's it even for but to pass trough mist? By the way the serpent explained it I thought it would be used agains the final boss, but it was not needed at all, I could make damage with my normal attacks and still beat him easily.The long coridors or elevators you had to pass trough felt, pointless, you'd expect that during the slow moments you will show something special with the art, make it worth to look at for longer, but the art stayed the same, nothing particularly stunning was show to give you some enviromental exposition, it just stayed the same as it is in the rest of the enviroment.The world itself felt very artificial, the characters were excisting purely for the player, they did not feel like individuals and none of them left a lasting impression on me. One of the things that made me feel this way was when first visiting the fairy village, you see all those fairys on the ground begging for help, but you are not given an option to help them, even though you have a healing ability. You just leave them on the ground. No one in the village itself mentions them. To enter one specific area you have to talk to a fish person, so that he can let you pass, he says how humans are cruel and kill his fellow fish people, you promise you're different, than you enter the area, and the fish people attack u with no option to speak with them, and u kill them. Why? What was the point of the fish person talking to u and saying how cruel humans are to his kind, only to just massicare everyone without beeing given the option to talk to anyone....The festival at the end of the game felt dry, all the villagers were at the exact same place they were as in the begining of the game, just lifeless and lacking of personality. I was expecting everyone at the village to gather, together including the Matriarch, but I didn't even bother going to her location since it's so far away from the village and I just did not care to.The plot itself was not particularly interesting, it felt pretty genering if I'm being honest, It did not make me care about the world, i liked some ideas like the priestesses, but that's about it. The rest of the world felt really underdeveloped.The only thing i liked about the game is the graphics, I love pixel art and that's one of the reasons I got attracted to the game.
