_childDocuments_.review: Sheesh, I know this review is not recommended but that was after a lot of deliberations, the game isn't bad in the sense that its beautiful, it runs well, and isn't like a waste of money but there is something critically missing. I love this series and absolutely fell in love with RUTM I was waiting on the edge of my seat for this to release only to find that like others have said its really half baked. The movement the combat and all the supporting mechanics fall completely short of the previous title, the writing is also much worse. The original didn't really have much dialogue which really worked for the cryptic heavy atmosphere they were laying down it had a really show don't tell style that made it shine. Back to the combat, in RUTM you would spend hours on one boss learning the mechanics dodging weaving shooting a bow here getting in swipes there, carefully planning out item usage and even being greatly rewarded for no hitting a boss with a special item. All of that has been erased in this title, every fight is the same, spank it until you manage to get hit by some attack at random and if you need to pop your healing throw it out for free. The whole experience is cheap and bad now especially when compared to the previous game there is nothing dynamic about the bosses and while there are more in this game they are kinda just thrown about haphazardly with no sense of pacing or reward at all for defeating them, they are not unique at all every single one follows that same flowchart of tank>spank>heal there is no skill involved or fun to be had really its a true shame. The level design is also significantly lacking, there's nothing exciting about the rooms they all just seem to hold one mundane enemy after the next all of which can just be beaten down in the same manner as bosses without any real thought or strategy. The overall flow of zones is also much more linear and doesn't feel like exploring like the previous did. Overall the game is much easier, and not even in a fun way just in a whats the point of playing it kind of way. Its a real shame to see this game in this state after all this time waiting, did the entire dev team quit or something? Like I have no idea how it could be such a drastic shift in quality when they had such solid gold in terms of game design previously. That being said, save your money, go play Reverie Under the Moonlight, it still remains to be fantastic and a completely amazing metroidvania that this sequel could only hope to come close to. If you do however want something super casual and cheap that you dont need to try too hard to beat and dont really care much for story I guess you will have fun with this game that runs decently well and doesnt take much out of you.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, this feels very much like a generic indie Metroidvania game and less like Reverie which, in a way, felt like the antidote to that kind of game: a concise, tight game with a good sense of challenge. By contrast, this game feels as if it was designed not with a mind towards making every room interesting, but with a mind towards making every room because it's additional content. The bosses so far have been fairly trivial, and they also highlight how thin the mechanics are – there's only so much you can do with a Dark Souls dodge-roll, a melee attack and arrows. There's also a hefty amount of backtracking. Switching tack for a moment, I do think the game is generally well-executed. The controls feel good. The player animations are good. A lot of effort has gone into this game. But it's let down by the gameplay design, and that's a shame, because wasted effort is PAINFUL.edit: the section where you have to run back through an already-explored level, but with barriers forcing you to take a more circuitous route, was awful. It's given no justification until the end of the section, so after seeing the barriers at first I assumed I was being deliberately prevented from going down there by some kind of arbitrary force (ie. lazy design), and instead went pretty much everywhere else before figuring out that there was one route that wasn't blocked. OH, and the bosses have way too much HP. Again, the mechanics are very simple, so this just amounts to tedium.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited 8 years for this game. _childDocuments_.review: Oof. This game feel just ain't it. Super slow and floaty compared to previous Momodora games or any fun platformer. The camera is also way zoomed out, perhaps due to the 16:9 aspect ratio, but that's no excuse. And the music was putting me to sleep. Usually, you wanna make sure the basic controls feel fun and tight in a metroidvania, and then add some wild movement abilities to unlock on top of that. In the trailer, you can see Momo sprint and double jump, but I think even if I got to that point in the game, the low gravity would still result in terrible game feel. For me, it's a massive red flag when I launch a platformer for the first time and immediately resent the movement. Who knows, maybe I wouldn't have fallen in love with video games as a kid if Mario 64 had featured slow floaty movement. This is important stuff.There was some sort of home town with far too many NPCs and their usual pointless chatter, which you know I can't stand in a platformer. You can plant stuff there and wait 10 real-life minutes for it to grow. I wish I was making this up. I didn't stick around to find out what happens after 10 minutes, but I'm willing to bet the next plant would have cost more money and have taken exponentially longer to grow. I guess wait timers are the pinnacle of game design. Just not a very positive first impression.Then, y'know, you start the actual game, and you notice they keep spamming the same "mini-thwomp" enemies, along with some big thwomps. It was some pretty uninspired enemy design. Like the enemies looked and felt generic. I remember in Reverie, the grenade throwers were cute female enemies. Well, here they were replaced with annoying little one-eyed buggers, even though mechanically, they were the same enemy. How to make your sequel feel like a direct downgrade. I mean, at least deliver on the main appeal the series is known for. Again, poor first impression.The first boss kinda made me feel empty inside. The sound design and music were very boring, there was no build-up, no stakes, no tension & release. The fight went like this: I took a hit from the big projectile attack cause I wasn't expecting it, then I tried jumping over it since y'know, it's a 2D platformer, but you can't jump high enough to avoid the attack. That's when I realized the only thing to do was dodge left and right and mash attack, which is a pretty boring thing to do in a 2D platformer. You're not taking advantage of your genre's strengths here. So anyway, I obeyed until the boss died. But instead of perishing, the boss decided to smash the floor and we both fell. After that, a cutscene teleported me back to town. I think the boss escaped, but narratively, I don't get what was the point of this. It wasn't some cool character that I'm gonna look forward to fighting again later or something. It was just some generic monster. What emotion were they trying to make me feel here? It's like the game just does random things for no reason.The next part hidden by the spoiler tag is a funny goof on my part. Feel free to read it for chuckles but it's not a valid complaint. It turns out, you have to attack the checkpoints in order to activate them. But you can also interact with them for a buff which costs money. Somehow, I thought this meant you had to pay to use the save point. The interact prompt is a little misleading, but that's mostly my own fault for misunderstanding it.I don't know. Maybe this is a lot of thought for like 30 minutes of gameplay, but it's true what they say: if the player isn't hooked within 30 minutes, you've failed somewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the last Momodora game ok (Reverie Under the Moonlight), but this latest entry is a snoozer. I played for more than 3 hours in a single sitting and there was no rising tension, no sense of danger or urgency in any moment. I suspect that this franchise is supposed to be more easy-going than other Metroidvanias, but there was nothing for me to invest in.The layout of the world is uninteresting. It's basically a downward plunge with no sprawl, no memorable spaces. There's barely a story being told. Every once in a while, a character will dump some text on the screen. After 2 hours, I stopped reading anything.The bosses can pose a challenge, but some of their attacks are so subtle that they can't be read at the speed they happen. The game compensates for this by adjusting the difficulty in response to your failures (even if you play on "Normal" mode, apparently); random hits from bosses don't damage you, and sometimes you start dealing ridiculous damage. Honestly, it was a relief for the Snake boss, as that was my third attempt and I considered it a war of attrition.Maybe a lot of people like the cutesy scenes with the characters. I thought they were too twee and do nothing to improve the story. In fact, the game feels like it has one foot in Cutesy-Ville and the other in a porno. The Fairy queen looks like a baby with stripper tits.I finally stopped playing when I took 4 (FOUR!) VERY SLOW elevators down from the fairy queen to a pond and was given an obligatory fishing rod and told to fish. I really don't like fishing minigames, but what really turned me off was anticipating the slow ascent back up and out of there. At that moment, I was D-O-N-E.~~~I feel that this Momodora entry is too sleepy for its own good. Its story is uninteresting and poorly told. I have heard that it is continuing a story from earlier entries, but even if I knew every part of that story, I would not be interested learning more about it the way it is presented in this game. I would rather be a participant in the story (as in Hollow Knight) than have lore regurgitated to me through dialog bubbles or walls of text. Show, don't tell, whenever possible. The enemies in the game are mostly just critter fodder and none of the areas feel "lived in". There were no memorable landmarks that I thought, "oh, I wonder what's there? I can't wait to come back later and find out!" Maybe--MAYBE!--there is an interesting secret that improves the story way later in the game, but I didn't think it was worth trudging aimlessly downward for 3 more hours to find out.

Spawning the same easy boring enemies you've been fighting the entire game with triple the normal health and poise does not make it more engaging nor less boring. All the npc interactions and dialogue just don't really go anywhere and feel like there's something missing.Other than that, the pixel art, music and animation are really good and I still enjoyed playing through it and would still recommend it but the game just felt like it was a major step down in a lot of ways compared to their last entry in the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice farewell to the Momodora series.  I liked it slightly less than Reverie overall.  I feel like the boss fights in Moonlit Farewell were a little too easy. I imagine most players will show up to the final battle as prepared as I was.  Definitely go on the highest difficulty mode that it offers you if you're the slightest bit familiar with the genre.All the assets like art and music are beautiful though, and the game is still really fun to play.  I just liked Reverie better.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fitting and satisfying end to the Momodora saga. _childDocuments_.review: After finishing Momodora III and Momodora - Reverie Under the Moonlight I finally finished Moonlit Farewell.Right off the bat you see that this is bigger than the previous Games but in the End it is still not that big.So of all the Momodora Games this is probably the most Metroidvania.The Map is also a bit better than in the previous Game, this time you have Question Marks when you are missing something, although  .First I thought they also wanted to go the "soulslike" Route because of a Stamina Bar, but I have to say, the Stamina Bar in this Game is almost of no concern.Also this Game has much more lore than the previous ones. Enemy Types are the familiar ones from the previous Games with just few variations.Bosses are quite nice, not the best you've ever seen, but still pretty good.Overall you could see that much more work and polish went into this Game than the previous ones. Everything was more detailed and felt really good to play.This time around I also had the feeling that exploration and progression were more fun and both felt more rewarding.Another QOL thing that I also liked was, that this time when you die, it isn't that frustrating because you keep everything you found up to that point. And it's nice to play this Game in "Widescreen".Music was excellent again and the Pixel Graphics and the Artstyle was pretty good.I read that this is supposedly the last Momodora Game, so if that's the case then this series had a good run and a good ending.I definitely liked it, a bitesized and again tight Metroidvania. Although I would get it on sale.Only thing for me to do is playing Minoria by the same dev(s).Thumbs up for this one...
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr, Momodora Moonlit Farewell is a cute timewaster metroidvania, but most of its features are overall underutilized. Get it on sale or wait for more content (Or buy Reverie Under the Moonlight).Momodora Moonlit Farewell is an ok game. Standalone I'd give it 6.5/10, as the cap off of the Momodora series, and the follow-up to Reverie Under the Moonlight, I'd probably give it a 5/10. Every part of this game is pretty underutilized and/or underdeveloped. The bosses for the most part follow a set pattern of attacks that gets pretty boring once you see it a few times. The fishing minigame is a single button press and offers nothing of substance. The characters as well feel pretty underutilized. There's a lot of things I'd want out of this game before I can recommend it as anything other than a cute lil' platformer to spend some time on. End game could be better. Seeing Lineth hang out in the town at the end of the game lead me to believe she'd be doing something post-game, perhaps even a "Play as Lineth" alt gamemode of some sort. But there's very little to do once you've completed the game. The alternate gamemodes are fine. Arrange gamemode reverses the game's map and adds more enemies. A fun way to replay the game if it's been a while since your first playthrough. "Insane" difficult (one-hit KO) from the last game was replaced with Hardcore, where your save-file gets deleted on death. I much prefer Insane difficulty, but with the way that items were redesigned, it wasn't really feasible for the most part. I think Reverie Under the Moonlight is a better game overall, but Moonlit Farewell has much more playtime and is more polished overall. The art is gorgeous (though I like the tone of the last game more), and the music is pretty nice. Ashen Hinterlands can leave the room though.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: A followup to Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight with cute art and vibes. But I personally prefer Reverie under the moonlight more. The trailer also shows items and mechanics that you don't get until later in the game, such as the triple arrows on the snake lady boss.This game had the same features, but the combat introduced different mechanics that I disliked, such as a stamina system that is tied to both your dodge and your bow attacks. The items found throughtout the world are also general upgrades to your stats instead of unique items, making backtracking less fulfilling to me. I also have a problem with the scale of the sprites, since its hard to keep track of your character when they are so small compared to the rest of the screen. This game will still give you a nice experience as a first metroidvania, despite being the last entry to the momodora series.Movement and combat still feels great compared to other indie metroidvanias, especially after you get the double jump.

_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: I have thoroughly enjoyed each of rdein's games, and although Minoria probably remains my favorite, Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a genuinely great game. It isn't particularly innovative, nor is it especially remarkable in design or execution. But that's okay! It plays exactly the way a Metroidvania game should play. It's neither too forgiving nor too cruel, all attacks and movement abilities are intuitive and fun, and, perhaps most importantly for a Metroidvania, every area is memorable and highly distinct in atmosphere. I'd also say the game is the perfect length.If you're only here because of the Metroidvania tag and have no prior experience with Momodora, you may not find much of interest aside from an enjoyable gameplay experience and beautiful pixel art.If you're here because you're a Momodora fan, however... you won't be disappointed! Finally, we see some quite substantial world-building on top of the simple story that started 14 years ago. All previous games are acknowledged here in satisfying ways, and I'm very glad I decided to quickly replay Momodora 1-3 before picking up this one.Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm stuck at home sick today, so I'm gonna go on ahead and replay Reverie Under the Moonlight now...

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely wish I could recommend this game, because I absolutely loved the artstyle and the mood it conveyed, but there's just too many things that are poorly designed for me to recommend the game.Stamina is incredibly infuriating in this game as it runs out way too fast when you try to run through the various rooms, as well as when you use it against your will because you decided to use the bow at full stamina. _childDocuments_.review: Momodora Moonlit Farewell is RDein's masterpiece. Having played Reverie Under the Moonlight, Minoria, and a bit of the first game, I can see the years of experience that went into designing the game. Minoria's combat was too overpowered, so Moonlit dials it back, giving the gameplay more weight and challenge so that the player can build up to that level of power. Reverie was a masterpiece, but getting 100 percent could be quite difficult without a guide, and the map was rather simplistic. Perhaps it's because the last two games were such big hits, but RDein and his team were about to craft a much more detailed map. This isn't to say that Reverie's map was bad, but you can tell how sectioned off pieces were. Minoria had the same problem, but that was likely due to them using 3D models over pixel art, and wanting to focus more on improving the combat from Reverie. The extra customization options were also a massive improvement from the previous games. Reverie didn't lack customization options, Moonlit simply expands upon it. There are also a lot more bosses than previous games. The bosses are always great, and thanks to improvements in gameplay and design, they're some of RDein's best. The final boss especially. WIthout spoiling, but the previous final bosses have felt lacking in their climactic feel. Moonlit gives one of RDein's best final bosses of what I've experienced. Hit boxes are also a lot better, as Minoria and Reverie had a few bosses where the hit boxes for enemies or for their attacks were inflated in places, leading to some cheap deaths or overly easy battles. These were minor issues, but it's great to have them fixed for this game. Some enemies are troublesome though, as there's a section that's just incredibly, almost cheapily difficult. it wasn't awful, but it had enemies with larger, faster attacks, mixed with smaller spaces. Reverie had some of these as well, so I'd put them at about the same. Then there is the art style. The dev room outright states that they changed artists a bit. RDein is still clearly involved, but you can tell something's different. Minoria and Reverie had more colors that popped against darker backdrops. Reverie had one of my favorite styles, with so many blacks and reds. Moonlit is much more colorful and varied. It's a beautiful game in every sense of the word, I wouldn't say it's better than Reverie, though I do prefer the blacks and reds of Reverie. The settings aren't as to my tastes either, as Reverie had more gothic architecture, while Moonlit takes place in nature. It's very lovely and rustic, which is refreshing and appearing for a metroidvania, since most don't go for such a simple, down to earth feel. I do prefer a bit of gothic architecture though. They both blow Minoria out of the water. Minoria was very lacking in color in places and the 3D models looked fine, but were lacking compared to the simple pixel art. Now with two more points, the metroidvania design itself. This is connected to the world, but RDein really knows how to make a smaller metroidvania work. There will be rooms and hallways that have nothing or just add some imagery. That, I feel, is a key component to making a metroidvania work. If everything is tightly designed, that works, but the bits of additions really help make the world alive. While it's not Hollow Knight levels, RDein is able to really make a world feel real with the more limited size. Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is one of the best gaming experiences I've had this year, if not in a while, and I hope I have more opportunities to play it again, as well as see what RDein does next.Also, a personal gripe. I really wish RDein would give his games some yuri. His female characters tend to really have chemistry and are often hot. The writing also just always feels like it's one step away from Yuri in places. At least, since Minoria. I just kind of want to see that lol

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a beautiful game. We see here the culmination of everything great about the prior entry, iterated upon and often surpassed in all new ways. The Sigil mechanic allows for an exciting degree of customization that RUTM did not have, however, you can absolutely capital B BREAK the combat with it. _childDocuments_.review: Moonlit Farewell is a serviceable enough metroidvania, but a disappointment when examined next to the previous iteration in the series: Reverie Under the Moonlight.  While I enjoyed my time with the game - the pixelart is gorgeous and the music/sound design fit the aesthetic very well - I'm glad my first playthrough only took about 7 hours, as any longer and I likely would have dropped it.The combat is a bit simplistic (attack, attack, dodge roll behind enemy, attack), but your attacks feel weighty and satisfying, and you can stunlock a monster by dealing enough damage in a certain amount of time. For the length of the game and the complexity of the encounters, it is more than sufficient, but it definitely lacks the "oomf" that combat in games like Hollow Knight or Metroid: Dread achieve. Thankfully, there is a system in place called "Sigils", or special effects that grant you some kind of boon. You are limited to a small number of sigils active at once, and the effects are significant and varied enough to allow you to tackle challenges how you prefer. For example, I stacked sigils that gave my melee attacks a chance to proc special effects, making my melee damage explode. There are also sigils to make your ranged attacks more powerful, to add extra effects to your healing item, and even one that prevents stamina depletion at the cost of lower defenses. These sigils added much needed variety to the combat, and kept it from ever feeling too stale.The map/level design feels rather lack-luster. In most areas, there's a single path to the objective with a few side branches that never go too far out of the way. There are a number of instances where you can open up a shortcut to create a more linear path through an area, but it feels less like a tool that the devs uses to connect the map together and more like something they felt obligated to use since they were creating a metroidvania. Traversing certain sections of the game can be very tedious, as you'll just be running along mostly flat ground with your very-limited stamina meter depleting every few seconds of sprinting. Luckily, backtracking is fairly minimal, so unless you're trying to 100% the game, you can avoid much of said tedium. That all being said, there are some clever and fun room designs that force you to engage with enemies in different ways, especially in the final area of the game.The art is gorgeous, though you probably don't need me to tell you that. The music doesn't stand out as particularly good or bad, but it fits the theme and vibe of the game very well. Bosses are particularly visually interesting.Speaking of bosses, they're mostly pushovers. The movesets for many bosses don't seem to be randomized at all, and a lot of their attacks will be telegraphed to the point where you would have to TRY to be hit by them.Finally, the writing and story is pretty 'eh'. Perhaps if you're a huge fan of the series, it's more engaging, but as someone who doesn't really remember the story of the prequel and never played the first 3 games, I found myself severely unimpressed. None of the characters are particularly charming, and the dialogue all feels stilted and awkward. There were a few hints of interesting world-building sprinkled here and there, but none of it ever amounted to anything.All in, I enjoyed my time with Moonlit Farewell, and don't regret purchasing. If you're in the mood for an easily digestible metroidvania, give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: B+I have some personal history with the Momodora franchise. After stumbling across Reverie Under the Moonlight while browsing steam, I picked it up without knowing much about it. I was hooked. The dense atmosphere, the heavy music, the gorgeous pixel art all had me enraptured. After beating the game several times, I went back and played the previous entries in the franchise. That one experience made me a fan, not just of the developers but of Metroidvanias generally. To say I was eager for this, the final entry in the series, would be an understatement.  Having played it now, simply put, it is another wonderful game. While it may succeed in the broad strokes, there are several small aspects which prevent it from reaching the apex of the series.  Let’s start positive though. The art continues to be a stand-out. The detailed and vibrant pixel art has an undeniable charm. Each area feels distinct with landscapes being dominated by a particular color and supported through the little touches which make it feel alive. It is unmistakable when you have entered a new area. Music further helps drive the mood and energy. The soundtrack is once again phenomenal and I have several songs I listen to from time-to-time (Harpy Attack! is a personal favorite).  Playing the game itself is smooth and frictionless. Exploring the world constantly yields rewards from simple upgrades to entirely new abilities. New to this entry are passive abilities called ‘sigils’ which typically provide fairly substantial improvements—too substantial. Over the course of the game, you can equip more sigils and gain access to more powerful abilities. By the end, combat becomes entirely trivialized. Bosses melt and you become almost unkillable.  While feeling strong can provide fun experiences, the sheer power of the sigils, especially in combination, forces the difficulty curve of the game sharply down. The bosses, while fun with some absolutely incredible music, can only slow down your path of destruction. Even the final boss poses little threat. A wonderful time, if you do not mind the game being a bit flimsy in the back half.

The one exception to this was  but it was still a relatively easy fight thanks to all your sigils.The game could've left a better impression if they had cut down some bosses but increased boss fight complexity to make up for your sigils. _childDocuments_.review: A solid Metrovania. Fun bosses, pretty environments, and interesting gear to find. I would say the DIFFICULTY is a 4/10. + Well designed bosses, with the exception of a couple. There are a couple bosses that never touch the ground, and attacking in the air in this game doesn't feel too good. + Gear (Sigils/Artifacts) are diverse and fun to use. I can't remember the exact amount, but there are a decent amount of them.+ Environments are nice looking and fun to explore.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------   - Having achievements for replaying the game 2 more times on 2 different difficulty modes isn't it chief, especially for a Metrovania. I rather would have had those achievements be for finishing the boss rush fully, which is unlocked at the end of the game, and using my existing gear. - Rolling can feel slightly not responsive, since you can't roll until your attack animations are fully finished.- Attacking in this game causes so much particles effects to feel the screen, that I would purposely tank hits sometimes because I couldn't be bothered to see through the red smoke that happens every time I attack something. _childDocuments_.review: If you're like me you probably will read some Negative Reviews as well to try to get a more balanced idea of the game. Most of them point that the game is a bit too easy, have difficult spikes, is too basic, doesn't add anything new etc. And... that's mostly true for everything *LOL*This is why I enjoyed this game so much and am giving it a POSITIVE review: it doesn't try to overdo it. If you want a nice Metroidvania where you'll feel right at home, with tight controls, cute visuals, nice exploration and not too long (it's a 8h-10h game, depending on your skill level or whether you want to explore everything or not) you'll find all that in here.While it's nice to see devs trying different stuff with their games, I'd say most of the Metroidvanias try too hard to add something new, or try to mix so many mechanics and styles from different genres that they end up creating more of a mess than an enjoyable game (enphasys on "enjoyable". Some aren't bad games per se, but are not very fun).The positives here:+ You have a certain freedom to explore the map right from the beggining;+ *EVERY*thing you find is significant. You find a fruit that raises your HP? Here, take some extra 50HP. You find a flower that raises your attack? Here, have an attack increase. You found a different skill? Here, you can equip and use it right away, you don't need to find a savepoint to equip it;+ The map progresses as you go. You don't need to find someone selling a map nor having to find a save spot for it to update;+ There aren't tons of dialogues, just enough to tell you what's goind on and then you keep playing. The story is basic and doesn't get in the way as well.The "could've been better":+- While there is a quick travel mechanic, it's not available from start. You'll get it around a 1/4, 1/3 of the game. Until then... yes, you'll have to backtrack on foot;+- Some things ARE underused and could've been better implemented, such as spell usage for example.Also the special skills unlocked by cards called Sigils you get A LOT of them, but you start the game with only two slots, somewhere in the middle of the game you get one extra slots and by the very end you find the two five slots (a total of Five, in the end). Could've been better spread out.So you have dozens of skills and only two/three slots to use them;+- Fishing is fun but useless;The negative:- There is a spike of difficulty in the last two bits of the map which will take you by surprise.Suddenly there will be enemies that can kill you with a couple of hits, ranged enemies throwing spells OFF SCREEN and so on.A bit unbalanced there, but nothing to the point of making you give up.- When you die you go back to the last save point. While there are enough saving points, when you start dying in the end of the game by those OP/cheaply placed enemies, it can become a bit annoying as well.In the end, if you just want a nicely done metroidvania where you pick up and start playing right away, that doesn't try to reinvent the wheel, you'll feel right at home here.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay, I'd say Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a harmless game at worst, decent at best.If you liked Momodora: Reverie under the moonlight then there's a good chance you'll be able to get some enjoyment out of this game, but if you didn't then this game probably won't change your mind. The graphics are definitely the strongest point of this game, infact it kind of carries it, it's really good, the sprites look great and the animations especially on Momo are very nice looking too. However the rest of the game isn't really anything to write home about, the story, characters, music and gameplay are all kinda meh.The characters all talk with a kind of stiffness that feels unnatural, it reads like a badly translated story lacking certain nuance but at the same time... it doesn't feel like it's translated? I don't know it's kinda weird, I'm not sure what language this game was original written in, but if it was English then oof (I played in English and switched to Japanese part way). I didn't hate or even dislike any of the characters per-say but none of them really stuck out to me. They're all just fine or passable. The story builds on the established lore of the Momodora series and there are even some call backs to older games events and that's pretty cool. But the overarching story doesn't really evolve past a "villain of the week" kind of formula, it's kinda straightforward until the very end. Again, it's not bad, but not great either, it's just fine. I didn't really take note of the music, it's mostly atmospheric, I probably couldn't give you an opinion on it even if my life depended on it, it's just kinda there.The gameplay isn't that different from Reverie under the moonlight. It's a metroidvania, you've got a map, you look for items sprinkled throughout the world to get stronger blah blah blah all that stuff. The most interesting things you'll find are sigils which are like perks that you can have a set number active at any given time by selecting them from the ones you have. I'd say this is the biggest addition from the last game and it's definitely the best, being able to mix and match sigils is kinda fun. However aside from sigils nothing else is really different, you'll probably end up using the same few sigils over the course of your adventure too.As for the combat, it's the same as last time, you whack things with your 1-2-3 melee combo, roll to dodge and sometimes shoot things with arrows. There isn't much or any variety in how you choose to take on enemies, you'll be doing that the whole game. There are some unique moves that activate out of a dash but they aren't really anything to write home about. Later in the game you get a  and I was so freaking hyped about it when I got it, but it mostly ended up being a means to travel kinda faster from place to place while using less stamina, I didn't really use it in combat other than to dodge some things with the . It's a tiny bit more interesting than last time but nothing game changing really, all in all it's the same gig as Reverie under the moonlight.To summarise, again, great looking game, "meh" everything else but overall it's still not bad, I'd say I can still recommend this game despite all that. If you want to give it a try I'd say wait for a sale before grabbing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is an exercise in fundamentals. The series has always achieved the right balance of detailed pixel art, interesting playstyle modifiers, and tricky-but-fair platforming challenges. Moonlit Farewell nails those pillars while expanding its scope, creating a beautifully hefty game where each room requires a careful approach and each upgrade is worth investigating. The downside is that some of the more interesting experiments from past games (multiple playable characters, a darker tone, and free form Metroidvania exploration) take a back seat or are absent entirely. That is most definitely a shame, but an absence of experimentation doesn't detract from the finely-tuned throwback gameplay this entry offers.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: I had never played a Momodora game prior to this game, but I am a big fan of the genre. I had always been offput from these games because I am not really a fan of magical girl types; however, the lore in this world sucked me in. It is understated and subtle but so alive. The music was probably my favorite part, but the artwork is ever so charming as well. The greatest compliment I can give a metroidvania is that it had engaging boss fights, captivating exploration, and doesn't overstate its welcome. Momodora: A Moonlit Farewell passes these with flying colors. 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Really darn good 8-hour-ish Metroidvania. The extra modes all seem like a chore, though.IMHO, the soundtrack is the best one in the entire series so far, it's freaking incredible!
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Sequel to the acclaimed ,  is the next installment in rdein's Momodora franchise. Following on lessons learned from making the Momodora spiritual successor, , rdein refines the core of the fantastic metroidvania style exploration and combat that the Momdora franchise is known for. With 36 "sigils" to change your gameplay, the inclusion of an "install drive" style mechanic, typical exploration upgrades, Moonlight Farewell is a fast paced and very customizable game. Completion time on one playthrough is approximately 6 hours, and is a perfect "rainy weekend" game, providing great music and good vibes the entire way through.As someone who began playing rdein's games with RUtM a few years ago;  shows me as a fan that he understand exactly what makes the Momodora franchise tick and what makes it stick with so many people. Thanks again for making another great game, and I look forward to whatever comes next, be it Momodora or not!

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora series visits us once again and it brings back it’s cozy blanket of on-brand aesthetics, good combat feel and compact-sized world that is fun to explore.Not much changed since the last installment - Reverie Under the Moonlight - but there is a good argument that it is A Good Thing™. This series oozes with an unique charm that fills you up with positive feelings, not unlike your favorite comfort food from your nearby bakery.While artstyle is being kept intact, there is a noticeable improvement in cleanliness of the pixel art. Game also got a widescreen makeover (making you more zoomed-out than in RuTM) and there is much less of a depressing theming this time around. Game world is much more colorful but still very stylish. Soundtrack also got a production values buff. Familiar nostalgia, gentleness and regality is being kept, while effort put into music pieces did noticeably increase, especially for boss encounters.Gameplay for the most part does keep up the pace with quality of the presentation, but not without some hiccups. Controls feel terribly sluggish at the very start of the game. I did get used to them over time and stopped noticing the issue after an hour or so, but first impression was very bad.Game world is slightly bigger than in RUtM, but it doesn’t feel terribly so, so complaints about game feeling short are not without basis.There is also a weird issue where it comes to difficulty balancing. Some bossfights feel too easy or too hard at random. I think the issue lies in the function of you gaining tons of power via upgrades, enemies hitting you like a truck (usually 2-3 hits to KO), but also you having tons of impromptu healing at your disposal. Some of the tells and enemy attacks do seem to be a little off with visual and sound feedback. Unfortunately, this can sometimes result in fights being attritional slap-matches.That being said, there are still many banger fights that delivered the goods both on audiovisual and gameplay fronts (shoutouts to a certain black cat!). And, all in all, Momodora V is still a pretty cute experience. It won’t blow your mind, but it will make you feel very warm inside and that’s really all I expected from new game from this series.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: An awesome game. I loved it. A calm game to just relax with. The story is touching and the game play is perfect for a "rainy in doors day"...or whenever. But still rewarding. The length is perfect for a weekend or so, a bit more if you want to see everything. All in all, I highly recommend Moonlit Farewell, especially if you enjoy the series. Ten thumbs up!

_childDocuments_.review: Really loved this one. The last one I played was RUTM, which was one of my favourite games of that year. This one improves on all the elements present there. There's a feeling of weight, momentum to the movement and attacks. It's a really great way to cap off a fantastic, but unfortunately underrated, series of games. I'm looking forward to whatever they work on next.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun metroidvania. It's pretty standard as far as traversal upgrades go (you can probably guess all of the traversal upgrades you'll get throughout the game), but it's got a good density of secrets that make exploration feel rewarding.There's a cool 'sigil' system where you can pick up cards to upgrade your character in interesting ways. Every sigil feels like a little 'rule breaking' upgrade. In general, one of the game's biggest strengths is that upgrading your character feels really impactful. Your attack power will increase like 8 fold throughout the game. The sigils and permanent upgrades you get from certain quests feel really meaningful and strong. Some examples: One sigil makes you shoot 3 arrows instead of 1. Another gives you infinite stamina but you take more damage. Another one spawns these cool magic swords when you attack, etcI love the pixel art and the music is great as well. The game has a ton of QoL, like showing you on the map where every secret is. Not sure if I think this is positive or not, since it makes finding secrets feel a little too easy. It's pretty simple to get 100%+ completion as a result without hunting everything down.My only "complaint" is that it's quite easy. With the exception of 1 boss, there aren't many bosses with threatening attack patterns. The bosses are all very fair, but they spend a lot of time standing around and their attacks are usually very easy to dodge.But that's okay, I don't think every game has to be dark souls-level difficult. The best way I can describe this game is that it's a very SMOOTH experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a fitting conclusion to the long running Momodora series, with beautiful music and pixel art, very nice to see throwbacks to where this all started as a reward for beating the game.Pros:- Addition of the bow is great and changes up how you play the game.- Beautiful pixel art.- Soundtrack for the game is amazing, calm and relaxing at points, intense at others.- Sigil system is great, allows you to change up how you character plays, can make you melee weapon more effective or use it to power up your arrows.- You can pet the cat(s).Cons:- Contact damage.- Enemy attacks were difficult to spot in some of the latter parts of the game.- Some of the combat/boss encounters can get very busy, making it very difficult to spot your character.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: A well polished and thoroughly enjoyable indie game. There are critiques to be made especially when comparing the game to its incredible predecessor Reverie Under the Moonlight, however this game presents more improvements than not on the most important mechanical aspects. The sigil system is very enjoyable and was excited to see what interesting bonuses the next one would provide. The animations and controls are nearly perfect with little room for improvement and I thoroughly enjoy the new map system, knowing that there was a secret around made me want to look for it, rather than in most games where they could be anywhere and I almost never bother looking. My biggest gripes are with the way the story made me feel like we were going to get more character interactions than we did, and with some of the boss fights. While most of the boss fights were enjoyable if easier than I was expecting some were overly simple or boring while only a few presented really outstanding and interesting challenges. The bosses get more interesting towards the end of the game, but also a bit more gimmicky. One late game mini-boss's only mechanic is to dodge the same 2 attacks while his health goes down overtime, an interesting idea, but it wasn't that interesting to play. Overall, I hope my criticisms don't dissuade anyone from playing the game. It didn't quite meet my sky-high expectations, but it's a great game that I'm sure I'm going to be playing through more than once.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. Some things aren't all there like the dialogue can be weak, the game can feel linear, and the early exploration and backtracking can be rather tedious. But, overall, it was ~9 hours well spent. I did feel that RutM was the right level of difficulty. In Moonlit Farewell, the difficulty is more up to the player. If you collect everything and kit well with sigils etc., you can evaporate anything. That can be fun, but I feel like metroidvania games are the type that should be challenging and reward appropriately.The aesthetic and the art all feel really good. The music is nice and sinks into the background well. The combat is good, although the dodge rolls can be a bit clunky and the timings can be really funky at times. The movement gets better later on, but the times where it felt limited don't drag on long.Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the game, and if you enjoy metroidvanias, you probably will too!
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: The Momodoras as a whole are great cozy, accessible metroidvanias with relatively short playtimes. Moonlit Farewell is probably the most polished and smooth-feeling of them, although you might be slightly lost if you're not familiar with the overall plot.And this might be the rare review where I've said everything I have to say in one paragraph. If you're looking for a high difficulty or a super long runtime, this probably isn't going to be your thing. Otherwise it's a good entry from a neat indie studio.I hope the vibes of it being the final game in the series aren't true. I'd love to see more of this world.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first Momodora game, and I absolutely enjoyed it! Was looking for something to scratch the Metroidvania itch and this definitely did just that! Lemme slap in some spoiler-free pro's and cons.PROS:-Gorgeous pixel art-Fluid combat system-Solid pacing-Fun boss fights-Composer did a great job with the music-Fun sound design-Enemies don't feel repetitive-Big booba lady yowza wowie dayum hello???CONS:-Dialogue felt super stiff most of the time-Not really much going on exploration-wise-Some of the area/level designs were super cool, just felt sort of under-utilized-Some super fun bosses, but a lot of em' were pretty forgettable-There's variety in the abilities (sigils), but a lot of them felt underwhelming-Companions could've used more variety, also sort of underwhelming-The entire end section of the game feels super rushedOverall the difficulty felt pretty middle of the road - had some challenging bits here and there, but nothing that'll make you wanna rip your butt hairs out one by one, especially for the seasoned Metroidvania players. _childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Another great Momodora game, maintaining a very comfortable size and great pixel animations alongside smooth, if not relatively simple combat gameplay. I appreciated the ease of exploration with the map marking unexplored rooms, and it made (at least for me) the pacing and secret-hunting never hit a slow spot. If I had any gripes, I'd have liked to have some some cool platforming challenges or harder areas that utilise all of the movement options in succession, although I understand that it's not necessarily that kind of the game in the first place.It's relatively short, but I don't see that as much of a negative, and the level of polish and quality of the design make me happy to recommend this to any metroidvania enjoyers, or fans of the series.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a metroidvania fan like me, who likes to be able to 100% (or 111% in the case of this game) a game without having to resort to endless grinding and searching, and who likes to get all achievements on a game without having to be a god gamer, this is the one for you.The story and characters are cute and wholesome as well, controls are solid and the graphics and music are lovely. I'm 12 hours in and on my second playthrough (of 3 required to get all achievements) and can recommend this game to likehearted peers.Getting 111% took me 8 hours, so if you simply pay attention and are reasonably adept at some platforming, that's about the threshold for completing the base game.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the previous Momodoras, you will like this one too as it is pretty much more of the same but with a step or two above in animations upgrade and combat.
