_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Fun addition to the Momo franchise and a solid metroidvania experience. Unfortunately I found that the sigils system didn't have as much depth as I'd hope, comparing with something like Castlevania: Circle of the Moon. I completed with 105% completion on my first run (out of 110? unclear, but I didn't get *everything*) in around 6 hours.Pro:- Lovely art and soundtrack- Movement feels more fluid than previous games- Clear progression and flow of "metroidvania" aspects; I never felt like I was stuck or lost.- You can eat lunch with your cat girlfriend; many other game designers overlook this crucial featureCon:- Not the longest core game, unless I just got the bad end.- Combat felt a little one-note.- Many of the sigils didn't seem to hold much value for me. - Why the time gated plants?- Would have liked more side events or secrets that weren't just fetch quests.7/10, worth the pickup if you're a fan of the series or genre, grab it on sale otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: The easiest comparison for this game is its predecessor, Reverie Under the Moonlight. And unfortunately, that game feels like a much stronger entry. This is still a good game, its just weird how the whole time I was playing it, I couldn't shake the feeling that this game was made first, but localized second. Moonlit Farewell has all the same features, they just seem less good or meaningful. There are upgrades you can collect that slowly bring everything up to the median of RUtM, but there's nothing that lets you go totally crazy off the rails if you're willing to push things anymore.Maybe that's actually the sign of a more "mature" design. The highs are lower, the lows are a little higher. Unfortunately, it comes across more as trying to get used to driving a minivan around after having a tricked out rat-rod as your daily driver.Maybe I was just doing it wrong. Maybe the problem was that I was trying to push the limits of the game in the same way, by going for the same low HP, high attack power play style. Maybe I should have swapped around a bit more, and seen if there was something crazy hidden away in archery in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: A worry successor to RutM! Very grateful for the hard work of the developers. It's lovely to track Momodora's progression across time. I greatly enjoyed Moonlit Farewell. The Sigil system is interesting and the characteristic tight and fast paced metriodvania gameplay with tight story telling makes for a lovely experience. All love to the creators!
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Moonlit Farewell is a perfect sendoff and culmination of rdein's prior work. Bombservice takes all these past projects and influences, then synthesizes them together to make something of its own. Moonlit Farewell has the most clear sense of identity and vision out of all the games, and I am all for it.I doubt rdein will see this review, but I want to say that I hope he and the team gets the rest they need. It'd be great to see them working on something new in some years from now, but moreso I hope they are healthy and are enjoying life. Enjoy sleeping for 20 hours as soon as the patch updates slow down, please.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: A while back I played through RUtM and Minoria, and while there are criticisms for those games and they're far from my favorite metroidvanias, for some reason they just stuck with me. The art, the music, and just overall vibes of both games I fell in love with, so needless to say I was pretty excited for Moonlit Farewell.Let me just say, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is gorgeous. That aside, I really enjoyed this as well. The combat, while far from challenging, is very satisfying and is definitely my favorite from the previous games I mentioned. I see some people saying that the game is too easy, but honestly in my opinion it's just as hard as any of the other games, but this time there's no incentive to no hit bosses (other than a single boss for an achievement) which for me made up for nearly all the difficulty of the other two games. While I can see why some people are upset about the removal of special items for no hitting bosses, it's definitely a good change let's be honest lol. Now if you want to challenge yourself to no hit bosses, it's completely up to you, rather than feeling kind of mandatory for the best gear in the game. Personally, I beat the final boss without any sigils. It's not hard or anything, but you can kinda chew through bosses with the right setup, and honestly I completely ♥♥♥♥ with it.Some aspects I wasn't too fond of though, not that they detracted too much from the overall experience. The interconnectivity of metroidvanias is basically absent here, although in my opinion, that makes this game a pretty decent choice for people looking to get into the genre. Additionally, the story was just okay. It's nothing special, not particularly captivating either, but again I came in hoping for some cool art, fun gameplay, and just general vibes so I don't really care that much lmao. Now the music in this game is kind of a toss up for me, there aren't any tracks I didn't like, and generally it was all really fun to listen to. That being said, I don't see myself listening to any of the tracks in my free time like I do with something like Pardoner's Dance from RUtM. To be fair though, "really good music but I probably won't go out of my way to listen to it" isn't really that much of a complaint. Lastly, I mentioned the vague idea of vibes earlier, and while this game sure has it, in my eyes it doesn't come close to Minoria, and maaaayyybe RUtM?Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed Moonlit Farewell, enough to get 111% on my first playthrough, and for me it more than delivered. While it is the fifth entry into the series, along with there being Minoria if you want something a little different, honestly I think this would make a very good introduction into the metroidvania genre; it's not too complicated, I'd be surprised if you got lost, and it's not particularly difficult all while looking beautiful and only being around 7-10 hours long. Also there's more huge, massive, absolutely enormous tits so just throw out any complaints I had before

_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: The quintessential metroidvania experience, subtly tinged with wholesome/chaste girl love vibes and Cave-Story-adjacent nostalgia!Light on backtracking filler thanks to a comparatively modest map, Momodora: Moonlit Farewell definitely feels like the most polished entry in the series... but it's also not doing anything surprising or revolutionary with the Momodora formula, either.When paired with the light, relatively angst-and-drama-free story, this makes for a very smooth journey that's as comfy as Cereza's cooking, but part of me hopes that the "Farewell" moniker and "Culmination of the series" marketing copy indicates that Rdein and friends are planning on bringing their talents to something totally fresh next time; I love the Momodora series, but it feels like they've been remaking and spiritually succeeding the same metroidvania for a very long time now!This probably explains the numerous missed opportunities for dramatic twists and revelatory character growth; it feels like M:MF wants to close on a very sated and satisfying note, with warmth and gratitude taking priority over melodrama and surprise.That said, this experience might just make you want to replay the entire series from the top!
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a well-paced Metroidvania style game. It's overall quite forgiving for casual players, and gamers that are more experienced with the genre may find their first run through to be quite enjoyable without getting caught up in needlessly frustrating moments. This makes it a low-stress introduction, but it it does a good job keeping things fresh through the combination of different Sigils to enhance your combat strategy, and companions can help level the playing field if you choose to use them, as well.I didn't need to experience the previous games to enjoy Momodora: Moonlit Farewell, and am glad the story was overall lightweight because the gameplay is really the most compelling aspect of the game. At the start of the game, you may notice that mechanics don't exist: sprinting, double jumping, and wall-jumping...but be assured they do exist in the game, but you have to unlock them, and that they are introduced gradually with intention. It might make the game feel a bit slower at the start, but it didn't deter me and I liked how they introduced them.I find a lot of parallel elements to the game Chasm, which I also enjoyed, without some of the "same-same" feeling since Momodora's maps are not procedurally generated. Momodora: Moonlit Farewell has a level layout that feels intentional and like a labor of love, and each environment introduces their own difficulties as well as a new set of enemies that require different strategies or combinations of Sigils to best them.I like that you had both options for archery and melee, but I do feel as though I spent much less time with the archery, but there are different Sigils that will make archery much more appealing, but with some limitations.If you're the type of person who wants an experience wrought with difficulty, you'll want to unlock the hardcore mode with permadeath and more challenging enemies. And for folks who play on standard difficulty or adaptive difficulty, there is still some post-game content if you are interested in upping the ante with more challenging battles.This is a game that I only found out about days before it released, and I tried it out on a whim because I really liked the art direction, and I'm really glad I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this game is good.The plot seems straight out of kirby milkway wishes. But instead of the moon fighting the sun, it just so happens to be two moons lol.About the save thing, I was also confused at first, but I was able to understand that in like, 10 seconds. What is wrong with people?? Argh.. one way to solve the issue would be to add the ability to ALSO save when you select UP at a save point. besides the healthy boost.the game is VERY easy. by the end, having 5 sigil slots is wayy to powerful. If you use healthy + the mp healing card + shield card you are almost invulnerable. I saw someone complain about the last boss making 1-hit-kill attacks but that did not happen to me whatsoever. The progression actually remind me of the last time I played zelda oot. You can actually collect 11 hearts IIRC before becoming an adult. That makes the game very very easy. You can also pick up way too many berries in this game to make it easy.The only thing I found weird is that almost every upgrade is marked on the map, but I'm still at 110%? Seems I'm missing something, but I don't know what it is. its not marked on the map.About the 10 minute thing, it doesn't disrupt the game at all. It just seems to be a very very random ass mechanic, but its not an issue as people are pointing.  Besides, there's only 3 in the whole game.I like the minimap. it helps a lot to avoid opening the map all the time. Although it could be more zoomed out perhaps.The level design is overall OK. Movement is OK also.Positives:- Good art- I like the map & mini-map VERY much, very informative- Good variety of enemiesNegatives:- It suffers from the same issue as previous momodora titles, the bow is too OP, and trivialize 60% of the game -- just stay at a safe distance and spam shot the bow- The bosses are so easy if you pick up the powerups, that they can be easily tanked, you dont even need to learn their patterns. I learn patterns for the first boss, and the good cat goddess boss only- I did not like how the lunar power work whatsoever. I always forgot to keep re-triggering it. It would be better if it was charged with dealing/receiving damage- There was some very tight platforming which was very uncalled for, since the jumps are very floatyall in all, this is the first momodora I (almost) 100%'ted. _childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Some unlock spoilers ahead, but nothing major.Very good and having played RutM, I have no understanding of anyone who genuinely prefers RutM's systems to this.After about the first hour adjusting to the new control schema it felt much smoother to work with.Likewise, I don't think that people who complained about floatiness ever really experimented with their kit.After getting Sprint unlocked, attacking during a sprint jump (The portion of the animation where you're spinning midair) will downslash, which carries momentum and keeps you from consuming stamina. This becomes a VERY convenient and enjoyable standard movement option for the entire rest of the game, as well as for getting cheeky hits on bosses in otherwise inconvenient timing windows.This is actually one of my very few things I'd request for the game-- (More story important unlock spoiler here) The [1/19/24 update: Like RutM, bow now has the option to use its own button.] Was the bow not being on its own button a little weird to get used to at first? Yes, but I don't think that it was at all strange past the first hour, and the gameplay benefitted massively from the changes to stamina/melee/ranged combat. Where RutM often devolved into standing away from the boss and spamming your bow, Moonlit Farewell encourages players to get a cheeky shot in before closing the distance and going full-send in melee range. With the addition of perfect dodge mechanics which give you a brief window of lingering iframes to DPS, and your bow being generally much weaker outside the first shot, it's very clear that Moonlit Farewell wants you to play more engaged with its combat.RutM players may also note the lack of an ability to crouch, which is admittedly a little unfortunate if just for the emotive potential. Even with later mechanics utilizing down inputs I didn't really see a clear reason *not* to add it, though there weren't exactly super strong reasons to keep it either.This game is as easy or as hard as you want to make it with your sigils, Late game, your build is likely to be incredibly cracked. RutM had a lot of "Gotcha ♥♥♥♥♥!" kinds of screens where there was a lot of death potential on blind playthrough to random things like spikes down a screen, but I didn't really get that vibe with any of the setups in Moonlit. When I died, I felt like I deserved the death. But again, you start scaling pretty dang quickly toward the mid-lategame, so most of those deaths were probably early-midgame or so. In terms of difficulty, both first run and postgame runs have two difficulty options, Light(with adaptive toggle), or Normal. Post first-run your new slots have an additional modifier you can choose between Normal, Arranged (Mirrored map, some other changes I'm not so sure of yet, some palettes are changed in the brief look I've taken into it, and I noticed that the base moveset doesn't have the leaf throw at the very beginning at least.), and Hardcore (Permadeath for the file, apparently some new enemy locations and things of that nature).At time of writing my main save is 110% completion of 111%. There is some post-game; (Nature of postgame content, no lore spoilers) I don't think you need to play RutM to enjoy this game. I recommend reading your Notes section whenever you get new stuff in there. The story, or at least the slice of the story we experience here, isn't super deep. I think the world they've built has a lot more potential to have that depth and be explored, but this game in particular is more about simple crisis resolution than diving into an expansive lore. It's enjoyable for what it is. Is the game a little on the shorter side? Sure. But honestly it doesn't overstay its welcome at all, and I enjoyed the whole thing quite a bit, and will probably be doing at least one other run through of it on the Arranged mode just for giggles. If you ask any of my friends you'd know immediately that I'm the first person to pick a game apart with little nitpicks and gripes and things to complain about but honestly, I genuinely didn't have any real complaints about this game. "I wish we got to talk more with X+Y characters", "I wish the game was longer", and similar thoughts sure, but that's not complaining about the game, that's wanting more of it. As it is and short though it is, the game feels complete as it is and doesn't *need* any DLC or anything similar to shore up its experience. That said, if it happened to get any for whatever reason I won't be hesitating to pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Very well designed Metroidvania style game with a fantastic story and art design. Very high quality environments with amazing detail and plenty of care to make every area feel different and lively. The map design is less complex than other recent games in the genre like Bloodstained or Metroid Dread but makes good use of this simplicity to focus on preventing backtracking getting stale. Attacks and abilities feel very satisfying and progression is very smooth for the most part with only a minor drag between the mid to late game. This is excusable as the best abilities all come in the last section of the game. Bosses are all fun to fight and the inclusion of a Boss Rush mode is great, allowing me to go back and fight my favorite ones without having to start a new game just for that fight. My only gripes with Moonlit Farewell would be that it doesn't feel good to play on larger screens like a TV. With how the HUD moves to prevent being in the way of the player it means I may have to look much further down or up than I'd like to in order to get an idea of my current HP and MP when I'm in a fight. I'd say this game is best played on a 24 inch screen or smaller. The game also runs and feels great on the Steam Deck with it's smaller handheld size screen.

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a really solid metroidvania, if only a little short. Too short is a good problem to have though, as it means I want more of it! It took twelve hours to beat the game and get every achievement that doesn't require a second play through on a different game mode. The characters are likable, the areas are fun to explore, the controls are smooth, and the story is simple, but effective.I'd say the games biggest strength though is the art and animation. It has a certain charm to it that I absolutely love, and it gives the characters and enemies so much personality that can sometimes be lacking in pixel art games. However, there are a few character designs that either feel too simplistic for the art style (the big one being a certain snake,) or overly suggestive (another snake, this time the snake lady in the promotional images,) though I suppose that sort of thing is up to personal preference.The biggest flaw in terms of game play would be that the game is a little too easy to brute force your way through with healing. There are several late game bosses that I never learned how to fight at all(even the hard mode versions), as I just healed through them while tanking all the damage. This isn't to say that the bosses are designed badly though. They are amazingly designed, with well telegraphed moves that are satisfying to dodge. It's just a little too easy to heal through all of their damage.I also think the systems surrounding collectibles and currency could have been expanded somewhat. It felt like there wasn't much variety in what you could find, the main collectibles being either stat boosts, companions, or equipable sigils. There's also nothing to spend your money on once you've emptied out the single shop in the game. One small addition could help both of these problems, though I don't know what. Perhaps something could be done with the fishing mechanic, as right now all that is is another source of money. One other minor complaint. There are certain collectibles that can only be collected after spending 10 currency and then waiting 10 minutes. I really don't get why you have to wait like this. It was a minor inconvenience that probably added about 20 minutes to my playtime.Over all, Momodora: Moonlit Farewell is a fantastic game that is absolutely worth the price, and I enjoyed every minute of it. I loved the previous game, Momodora 4, and this game did a wonderful job following up on how 4 changed the series while also adding new elements that make it unique. I'm looking forward to what the future holds for this series.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fun honestly.It's a very nice package and experience, especially from my experience as somebody who's played all previous games in the series and who's thus a bit invested in said series lol.Quite similar to Momodora 4 in many ways, but also expanded upon and tweaked in a few ways which I think  benefit the game overall.So ye, its good imo.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: If you like classic style metroidvanias this is as solid as it gets.Moonlit Farewell is a great sequel to the saga and a great game on its own, just a very fun action platformer. Exploration is fun and easy to follow if you have a good sense of direction, and never feels handholdy, with each scenario being distinct, having different enemies and introducing new exploration mechanics and/or status effects. Combat is simple but engaging: Time dodges, then unleash, then dodge, repeat. Some enemies can be stunned out of attacks or simply ignored if fast enough, and learning each pattern makes exploration much simpler and fast, feels very rewarding.The bosses, as always, stand out as being not only fun, but also beautifully animated. The ending, specially, is a veritable spectacle of setpieces and animations. It's extremely worth it to play it to max completion just to get to see everything, it's a very pretty game.I really can't say no more, it's just a fun and good game, at a good price, get it, play it, then play it again, then at least 3 times, and if you've the littlest love for its genre you'll assuredly fall for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: A good follow-up to Reverie Under the Moonlight, and overall a solid closer for the Momodora series. Music works well with the gameplay, sprite-art graphics are very well-rendered and pair nicely with newer lighting engines that have shadows baked into the sprites , and whilst it  reference earlier Momodora games, the claim that you don't need to play those entries is quite true. Though I'll fully admit, I forgot some of the details from the earlier games even after having played the games a few years ago, and had to look things up here or there as some comments had me go "wait,  is that person, and how does Momo know her?"The one major negative I suppose I can think of is that one of the post-game things has an  idea of what Nightmare difficulty is for combat. It's not  that it would increase difficulty, but I don't feel that it's for me, personally.Meanwhile, the Arrange mode seems like an interesting change-up to the game, at least on first blush. What-all changes beyond Mirror Mode remains to be seen, but I'll likely give it a proper run over the next couple of weeks to see if much is different. It doesn't seem to have a way to play as Dora, but as a follow-up to the more story-focused Reverie Under the Moonlight and Minoria, I can only imagine adding a  mode that allows for this in a way that remains congruent with the characters would increase development time by another few months. So I'll accept the cool moments Dora has whilst I'm busy slapping things with Momo.If you enjoyed Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight, it's a safe bet to say you'll like this one. Well worth the price of entry!

_childDocuments_.review: Moonlit Farewell is a good little Metroidvania, however I honestly expected more from the 5th installment.Most bosses are way undercooked, except for the one you fight twice. In my opinion, Momodora 4 was a better game overall.That's not to say that this wasn't an enjoyable experience, I had a lot of fun with it, I just hoped for more based on the previous 2 games.4/5 Bakman
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far the most solid and polished game in the series.The difficulty feels solid and balanced right from the start.I love the new upgrade system since it provides a steady feeling of progression. It's truly rewarding to check every nook.The power system is rewarding to play around with and try different things with subtle differences between even passives that seem to have overlap. The story and characters are endearing. One of the persistent complaints I had about the 4th game was the tendency for enemies to spawn or attack on top of you with little to no warning. This has been completely fixed. Not only are new enemies less likely to appear directly on top of you, they are always preceded by a bright red summoning circle, giving you plenty of time to move.The pixel art is beautifully vibrant and you can really see how the artist has improved from previous installments. Unlike the 4th game, which was mostly dark and creepy bordering on horror in the majority of areas, there are a wide variety of different environments and atmospheres.The level design is a step up, and just as backtracking was becoming slightly tedious, a fast travel system was introduced.My only nitpick I can think of (and it's very small) is that certain NPCs you can talk to in a certain western area remain there after the area has been cleared, when it makes little sense for them to still remain since the enemies all vanish.All and all, if this is the last game in the series it's a lovely one. If the developer ever decides to revisit the series again in the distant future after doing other things it would be just as welcome.
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. It's a solid sidescroller soulslike metroidvania. Think of games like Hollow Knight it that game had Souls combat. The exploration feels rewarding and the controls (on controller) are fresh and crisp. Every movement and attack feels like you're truly Momo. The combat is amazing and fairly challenging if you set your difficulty high. The game boasts some of the best 2D animations I've ever seen. The game truly is something that only comes once in a lifetime. That is, a product straight from the heart onto the screen. The game feels inspired at any corner. Not so much that you'll think, "Hey, that's from [insert your favorite Souls or Hollow Knight]!" but just enough to where you'll think to yourself, "This is familiar, but so different from anything I've seen before." The story is secondary to the gameplay but that's not to say that there's none! The game is sprinkled with lore all throughout and catching up on the story thus far is offered to the player basically immediately. The player could go through the entire game without even knowing any of the story though! I'm only an hour in but I can tell this will be a game I constantly return to. I wish this game was more popular because everything down to the music feels like a product of pure love and inspiration. But I suppose that's why we review things. This game is worth the pricetag and then some! If I knew what I was getting into, I wouldn't mind paying upwards of $60 for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've started to write longer form reviews as not only a way to test my skills and improve but also to give people a genuinely good rundown. That being said, it's hard to do that with Momodora, not because I can't, but more because this series represents a place of comfort for me. Finding Reverie and being introduced to this series was an awesome and inspiring find, seeing that for its majority it was a one man band has me hoping I could do the same someday. These games have all had their great spots, annoying spots, and everything inbetween, but they're all so comforting to play. I can just sit back and relax and enjoy great music and awesome art while exploring around for secrets. Moonlit Farewell is arguably the best in this regard, as its secret system keeps things from getting "needle-in-a-haystack" hard by giving you a marker, but still keeping it up to the player to find said secrets. This game was one I had been waiting to play for a long time, and it did everything I asked, the story felt like a great all around narrative that with its expanded amount of dialogue compared to games prior opens up the characters and allows for the rich history of relationships to naturally come back. Everything about it felt like a celebration and a "farewell" to what came before, while not making it have to feel like a bad thing. It makes me excited for whatever comes next, and to Rdein and all the others at Bombservice, Thank you for making such a wonderful game that oozed so much passion from start to finish, I hope you know you've inspired me and likely many more, and I hope that you feel equally as proud of what you've accomplished here. I could name "better", but none have captured the feeling this series exudes so effortlessly, and I'll always come back to Momodora: Moonlit Farewell and the rest when looking for my favorite metroidvania/platformers down the line.I'd say Momodora Moonlit Farewell is Totally worth completing. :)(Ended up writing a bunch anyways, whoops.)
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: +You get an achievement for petting too many kitty cats+Giant fairy mommy+The game is gorgeous+The music is AMAZING+Solid story+I really loved the contrasts in the different areas as I transitioned from one to the nextIt is pretty linear, but I don't think it's a bad thing.  I never got lost when playing, and even when I tried to explore side rooms - it was *usually* apparent where I needed to go, and I still had a really fun time with it.  My biggest complaint about the game is:(Prefacing this by saying I am basing this off of my initial play-through of the game.  The only 2 difficulty options were Easy and Normal.  I chose Normal.)-*SOME* boss fights in the game aren't super engaging.  There are multiple fights in the game where bosses have 1 to 3 moves, and then they do those moves over and over *in that order* every time.  I don't think I died in a boss fight until I was a little over halfway through the game.  This problem is *kinda* fixed whenever you beat the game and unlock the re-fights with Nightmare difficulty.  In Nightmare difficulty, you have limited space in boss arenas and have to play around a mechanic that can one shot you.  So instead of staying in one place doing the same attack over and over until the boss dies, you actually have to move around while also paying attention to the boss patterns.  Definitely more engaging there and I enjoyed that!-Common enemies weren't that threatening until the second half of the game, most of them can just be stun locked.  Later on enemies get better attacks and can be annoying, while also having increased health and damage compared to the beginning of the game.I really enjoyed this game, it was fun and wasn't too complex.  Would recommend to anyone who wants a simple metroidvania to play.

_childDocuments_.review: this is my review after beating the 1.0 game once and not playing much of the new modes you unlock then, though i'll definitely play them soon.the map is beautiful and fun to explore, there's a lot of enemy variety and cool bosses, everything nicely animated with gorgeous pixel art and well-readable attacks. i found the lore and story with all the characters to be interesting and could really immerse myself in the game. the music is also nice and fits the areas.the overall atmosphere of the game is kind of cute and optimistic, but serious and dark at the same time.one of the core mechanics, the sigils, are basically quite similar to the equippable items seen in previous installments, but i'd say it's more in-depth and quite fun to try out different builds/combinations (you can switch your sigils on the fly except in boss battles, so you can experiment freely)the only problem i had is that it could have been just a bit more challenging, especially in the first half. if there'd been a "hard" difficulty setting, i'd have picked it for sure. that's not to say the game is easy; the "normal" difficulty was basically what you'd expect for a difficult game on normal.after your fist playthrough, you unlock some game modes which i haven't had much time to play yet, but so far it seems like a good challenge and replayability.there are many callbacks to the previous games from the series, which i liked. however, i'm pretty sure you can follow the story without playing the previous games (although i'd recommend them nonetheless)All in all a very good and well-polished entry to the Momodora series.

_childDocuments_.review: Momodora Moonlit farewell definitely feels like the peak of the momodora games including minoria in many ways, the animations are varied smooth very readable and simply beautiful, the same goes for the Designs and general color usage. _childDocuments_.review: wow this was the metroidvania i needed last year to replace the void silksong left. in seemingly everyway this game is exceeding my expectations. i loved the last game. and this game is giving me exactly what i wanted. the same great momodora action with a much more fully realized world. secrets aplenty. the graphics look so good and set a standard for pixel art metroidvanias. I love the animations, the lighting effects, the creative use of colors and darkness. the characters are lively. we are truly in the golden age of metroidvanias, starting with afterimage and this game. games like rune fencer and castle in the darkness 2 have a lot to live up to with this latest momodora installment. introductory offer just the icing on the cake. oh and dont get me started on the music and the menus, all inlayed with those nostalgic waves of songs that immediately feel like home. cant wait to play the rest. the world is already opening up with many paths to explore and its just fun to get lost. it amazes me the price on a lot of these value packed indie metroidvanias. after image, souldiers, aterna noctis, and games like these really do offer that 30-45 dollar package for 5-20 bucks. and for that reason i am giving this game an early 10/10. an honor bestowed only upon resident evil 4 from me in recent memory. maybe silksong going MIA aint so bad

_childDocuments_.review: Always want more good Metroidvanias to play. This was a good time.If you have played other Momodora games and enjoyed them, this delivers on several fronts previous Momodora games have: A pleasant atmosphere with some dark undertones, fantastic pixel art, and some properly cute ♥♥♥♥. On top of this, the overall presentation of this game is something of a step up from previous games. There is a good variety of environmental details that really make each zone feel distinct and polished. Different zones of the map are designed in such a concise way that I never felt stuck in a place for longer than it was welcome. The pace of combat and movement was relatively slow and intentional giving a feeling of proper weight to most of the player's inputs. Along with this, the enemy and level design seem very carefully and intentionally balanced around the player's options. There is clear effort to showcase the charms of individual characters so their personalities shine through in what amounts to a short and fairly minimalist story. You can pet cats, and I guess that's nice too. I have no misgivings recommending this game to anyone who likes Metroidvanias or any of the other stuff I rambled about above.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing game!!!!! I could not recommend this enough to fans of the series or fans of action platformers in general!! _childDocuments_.review: I've played every Momodora and have been eagerly awaiting this one since it was announced, and luckily, it delivers!It clocks in at around 8 hours for 100% save completion, which is pretty on par for your average action-exploration type game. The game has a slower combat pacing than Reverie, more reminiscent of the older Dark Souls games, where stamina management is a big deal, and you need to consider your options carefully in combat. Although, real gamers will find a way around that. The sigil system is fun and engaging, with great synergy and loads of room for different playstyles. The progression items you get are more meaningful than any of the previous entries, which is always a plus.The art is obviously fantastic, with high framerates and lots of small detail. My biggest complaint is probably the story, which isn't bad, just a bit generic. It fails to have much punch or weight to it aside from a couple neat moments, and it's pretty predictable. Character writing is pretty bland, but it's not annoying. It's a bit disappointing coming from the melancholy, desolate atmosphere of the prior entries, but the game's fun so it's not really a problem.While some may complain about the slower combat or more linear progression, and that's valid, this is still a strong recommendation from me. Beautiful, fun, and a worthy entry in one of the oldest running indie game series.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is kind of a steal at the current price, especially if you already own Momodora IV. A beautiful and well-designed Metroidvania title that continues to uphold a subdued, Cave Story-style aesthetic, it's an entry on par with the previous game. The Metroidvania genre is pretty saturated nowadays, but the charm of this game makes it stand out even now. It was clearly a labor of love, and feels polished, with excellent graphics and animations, exactly as I expected.The game takes no small amount of inspiration from Soulslikes, with weighty movement, punchy hits, a "poise" mechanic, bonfir-- I mean, save bells, and dodge rolls. There are equippable cards with the same role as rings from said series.Still, the game isn't totally perfect. As with the other Momodora games, story is a distinct weakpoint and is pretty barebones. Even though this game makes the biggest attempt in the series to weave a full narrative of characters and interactions, I feel more like I am exploring to explore, while generally not paying much attention to the plot. A lack of character portraits, making it difficult to keep track of who's who, doesn't help matters.I feel like people will end up liking IV or this one more depending on how much they enjoy the setting. But it's nigh impossible to say I wouldn't recommend this game to someone who wants a Metroidvania with extremely impressive pixel art. It will probably be something that goes on my list of Metroidvanias to recommend in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Another fantastic entry to the series!The pixel art has gotten even better with this one. It looks downright gorgeous! The animations look great too!I will say, there were some story beats I found a bit strange, but overall I enjoyed it (it is possible I am just missing some context too).There are a bunch of extra customization options too to mix up gameplay and a ton of simple stat increases. Needless to say, exploration is heavily rewarded.If you want to play a solid Metroidvania, then this is a solid pick!

_childDocuments_.review: Now this is a lovely game! The pixel art looks great, I loved the feeling of steadily getting stronger as I explored the world, and I appreciated the way the map automatically indicates when there's something to find. It was nice to have those markers for later!There's one other thing I want to point out, because I do think it's a good change: there's nothing restricted behind beating bosses without taking damage, aside from an achievement. This might be a "me" thing, but in past games, I'd grind early fights for the rewards at the cost of enjoying the rest of the game, or I'd have to resign myself to the feeling of missing out on cool things. So with that in mind, it's honestly liberating that the reward for doing so here is a point of pride! Let yourself enjoy the game without holding yourself to imposing standards!Also there are plenty of cute girls
_childDocuments_.name: Momodora: Moonlit Farewell

_childDocuments_.review: Been loving this series since Reverie Under The Moonlight and now that Moonlit Farewell is here, it's hard to express just how much I appreciate this series.Even if you have not played a prior Momodora title, there is a lot in here that does it's own thing that it makes all that extra background reading unneeded (you also get a synopsis of each game in your notes).Story is a bit more important this time (such as hinting you in the right direction). It's a serious-toned story, well worth paying attention to, that is finely paced with charming characters that assist you along the way. (I'm not done the game as of writing, but I've loved each piece thus far.)The gameplay is similar enough to RutM that if you have played that game, this one might seem a bit easier. But Moonlit Farewell does a lot of extra in it's own way that it does not feel monotonous to go from one game to the next.Finding collectables and upgrades are no longer a chore and the game genuinely rewards you for exploring each of it's nook and crannies. The game marks where certain things might be if you've been there before, so you don't have to worry about leaving and then forgetting it was even there. It might be a bit hand-holdy, but for somebody who is a bit scatter-brained like myself, it definitely felt good to be able to know once I have been there.My only problem is that certain enemies will cast moves that block your movement in very small hallways for lengths of time even after they have died which makes going through certain areas irritatingly slow when there is no need to. As well as sprites being... distractedly flashy sometimes in more dimly lit places that make it hard to see certain enemies even in a well and open spot.I'm usually not a fan of Metroidvania's, but Momodora has a certain place in my heart for forever now and Moonlit Farewell hits that want really nicely. I would definitely recommend picking up Moonlit Farewell and giving it a fair shake. You might find that the journey is well worth the admission.

_childDocuments_.review: Another fantastic entry in the Momodora series and either from playing these games too much or im getting better at playing games in general but the game felt a lot easier than its predecessors.While I have yet to do absolutley everything (as far as I'm aware I have like 4 things left to pick up and a couple of map squares I cannot find at all) I have completed the story and some of the time trial bosses that unlock after completing it.The movement abilities unlock in a timely fashion and each one makes getting around feel much nicer.All of the collectables feed into your combat ability, you have 3 fruits for health, mana and stamina upgrades, a flower for overall damage, sigils which are equipable buffs/debuffs, crystal shard flowers which is your currency, companions which either drop mana, attack enemies or find crystal shards and finally fairies which once you save the NPC looking for them (it took me longer since I personally left the boss alone because I'm bad at video games) will give you a mix of relics (ability items), crystal shards and sigils.The sigil system allows for varied play with a range of different builds.The bosses are all visually appealing with a varied moveset making them a good challenge and attaining victory with no damage an even harder challenge.EDIT: At the end you unlock a  and honestly I haven't seen one of these in years, it made me smile so much, its a really cute little detail

_childDocuments_.review: Final thoughts on Momodora MFReally Solid 8/10I very very much wanted to give this a 10/10 after beating it on the intended difficulty, the game is unfortunately not perfect. I very much enjoyed the experience I got out of it. it just wasnt pants shiddingly good.And I think the biggest problem with why I feel that way very much stems from its difficulty, its difficulty is split into an easy mode and a normal mode. leaving no room for a harder mode to engage with on your first playthrough. The game has this issue, where you never really hit a wall, and the stat buffs perpetuate and make this issue worse. I was showing my friends the game, and I was around 80% done (found every secret up till that point and was as powerful as one could get at that time) I showed them the secret spider boss and to my and their suprise. i melted it in 12 seconds without takeing a single hit. Alot of the bosses later in the game started to feel this way, I'd have more trouble navigating through the game because of common enemies then I would fighting the bosses. This issue doesn't just arise because because I'm more powerful then the bosses, the bosses are all also a little linear, the only exceptions being the moon gods. Them two are the only bosses in the game that felt really fun and absurdly challenging. Why is the game easy? Once you take a look at what the game gives you. its not hard to tell why.Sigils are busted, Dont get me wrong. they are a cool mechanic for sure. but they require some extra checks and balances to make sure the game is still challenging. Which is a wierd thing to say because there are specific sigils that litterally attempt to make the game less challenging. Sure I get it, gaming needs to be accessible, but it also needs to have a hardcore option for players who want to get sat on by a giant mommy snake.I see a few complaints about how the movement is floaty in the game. Yeah it is, but its tight, responsive and the combat perfect parry mechanic is fun af. Rdein is the god of pixel graphics. you will never find a game this good looking, for this price. each area immerses you and makes you feel something, its a form of storytelling prominent in some of earliest games, and this one does it by far the best. (through out the whole game I litterally had thoughts in the back of my head that the starting village "Koho" would eventually burn and everyone would die at somepoint, because it just seemed TOO Peaceful and it was like a red herring in the back of my head for over 90% of my play time.) and I'm not gonna lie to you. Rdein would totally ♥♥♥♥ with people like that, I know how he writes and so do you.This game is a very complete new, and unique experience. It might not be a super challenging one, but if your looking for an entertaining metrodvania epic with some pretty graphics and a fun and highly exploitable combat system. this game stands up. I'm hoping in the future that a "hard mode" will be added for newer players, as I felt "Normal" was just not cutting it for me, and made the game in its entirety a little soft.But hell, I've been waiting 3 years for this game. maybe longer. it was worth the wait, the time and the money. I hope in the future, Rdein proceeds to innovate and create, maybe even remaster the first 3 momo games into one experience. I feel like that would be really cool.

_childDocuments_.review: Moonlit Farewell continues to push the best of what Momodora is known for - An enjoyable story with interesting characters, challenging fights, responsive controls, a well-crafted world, superb music which felt like a part of the world rather than a 'game soundtrack', and gorgeous artwork throughout.It's as good of an entry for those new to the series and veterans alike. Definitely worth the money. I'm motivated to get every achievement and replay the game at least once over, my first playthrough at 110% took 11 hours to complete, on Normal.The sigil system is aware that the game is singleplayer, and thus the buffs you get from them are each very impactful - perhaps too much, in the case of a select few that allow you to go face-first into anything and come out on top without much thought. You can still just choose not to use them, it's your experience to have and, much like Easy mode, it serves to make the game more enjoyable.I would recommend this game without a second thought. Hopefully the team continues to develop more games, Momodora or not.

_childDocuments_.review:
"Momodora: Moonlit Farewell" is the latest installment in the Momodora series. Join Momo, High Priestess of the village of Koho, as she embarks on a divine mission to save her people from imminent destruction at the hands of the demon hordes summoned by a malevolent bellringer.

Momodora: Moonlit Farewell presents the account of the greatest calamity to befall the village of Koho, five years after the events of Momodora III. Once the toll of an ominous bell is heard, the village is soon threatened by a demon invasion.

The village's matriarch sends Momo Reinol, their most capable priestess, to investigate the bell and find the bellringer responsible for summoning demons. It is their hope that by finding the culprit, they will also be able to secure the village's safety, and most importantly, the sacred Lun Tree's, a source of life and healing for Koho...

_childDocuments_.review: I was planning to wait until after I finished the game to write a review but I feel bad for the developer, so I will just write one after three hours.As a sequel, this is the type of game that improves on the original's base design without exploring new territory. Which is by no means a bad thing. If this is the type of gameplay style you want, it delivers while expanding on the novel idea of a grandfather telling his grandchildren a story. For those who don't know, sometimes the children will fight over the direction of the story (like if the enemies are snails or wolfs) and the player will decide which it should be. It was hardly used in the first game, so I'm glad it has appeared more often. Some optional puzzles can even be decided by the player, which is cool.I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone looking for an engaging story, because there isn't one. It's a basic save the sibling plot and most twists are so standard that they are hardly twists. However, given the premise and the focus on gameplay, it's more than acceptable and isn't bad by any means.If you ask me what the biggest problem with the game is, it would be lack of charm. Take the characters. Lily's animations are all functional but offer nothing fun to look at. No emotions, expressions, or personality. She has no  defining character traits to latch onto. I get that she's a blank slate for the player, but the world around her doesn't make up for this. In these types of games, the protagonist has a companion with a lot of personality and has to do all the talking, but Lily doesn't have one. The children sort of work like that because they will chime in every so often, but we never see them, so it's easy to forget they exist. Like when Lily gets a new item, have her do a little dance or high five herself, anything besides lifting the item with a blank expressionless face. I could give more examples but that would be nitpicky. In short, I wish the character models could be more expressive.Lastly, I want to touch on the music. It's a very relaxed soundtrack that has a few highs when against bosses, but needs a more clear melody to feel more impactful. It all fit the mood, but I struggle to remember what it sounded like. Credit where credit is due, this game is a fairy tale and the instruments make the music sound straight out of a fairy tale. I still recommend this game because it's fun and that is all that matters. This game deserves way more than 5 reviews at the time of writing. Hopefully it can reach 10 soon because steam will bury it otherwise.Update: After finishing the game and doing some side content, I still stand by what I said with two exceptions.While the music mostly never grabbed me, the final area of the map has the best song in the game. It's tense, dramatic, and ear-grabbing in a way the rest of the soundtrack wasn't. Again, the soundtrack as a whole isn't bad, but it would have been better if all the songs matched the quality of the labyrinth music.Second, in addition to a lack of charm, I think the story suffers by not having meaningful character interactions. New characters are often introduced but leave no impact because they are never given screen time to do anything. Take Lily's grandmother. She ends up having a role in reaching the final boss. Once she does her thing, she disappears and serves no other purpose. It would have been great to see her character have meaningful reactions to her grandson disappearing, but we don't get that. She doesn't even have a name, she is just a grandmother and that's it.Still, this is a functional and fun game. I enjoyed my time with it and if there is a third game, I'll buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you just want a simple Zelda romp, it's fine.  But if you're looking to really explore and complete, it's honestly too much padding.  Everything is just "too much."  And the game is just too small.Too many letters, too many apples to collect, push the statue way too far, wait too long for the too many rolling spike bars, wait too long for the balloon to pick you up if you play your instrument, too many hits to kill things, too much waiting for fish and too many fish required to brew the potions to see the dead people, too much randomness in fishing, too many potions needed to speed up your movement, falling platforms trails go on too long, too many treasures are just more gold, too many trades with too many ingredients.The items you get just aren't interesting enough with the padding.  The most interesting new tool teleports you and the dungeon's puzzle scheme makes good use of it, but otherwise you're just avoiding lasers and spiky rolly bars.It's like people said they want more Blossom Tales, but developers heard "we want more pointless wandering back and forth."

_childDocuments_.review: Blossom Tales 2 is a great adventure worthy to be played by anbody, who is a fan of Linkt to the Past, A Link Between Worlds, Ocean's Heart or other RPG-style adventure games that focus on exploration. It does a lot of things right, but still has some minor flaws. +Great art style that makes the most of what you can do with 16-Bit+Awesome soundtrack that is catchy and underlines what is happening in a great way+Interesting story and characters, that keep you tied to the game and make you want to explore every nook and cranny+Great humour!-the story doesn't develop as organically as in Sleeping King: It felt to me like the world wasn't a whole. In the Sleeping King areas and characters were diverse, but felt like individual parts of that world. In Minotaur Prince it felt like I roamed through different DLCs of a game. This is not necessarily bad, but I liked the vibe in Sleeping King way more.-all the little caves with just coins in them feel not rewarding after some time. And not being able to spend those in a way that matters just make them feel unnecessary.-there hasn't been as much development as I had hoped for. In Sleeping King you could upgrade so many of your items, but here this aspect falls way too short.Overall definitely I clearly recommend you to give this gem a whirl. And I hope the developers will continue their awesome work!8/10 for gamers in general9/10 for Zelda fans

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game until the end.  The first Blossom Tales was already a pretty decent Zelda-like, and this sequel has taken that game and improved it in every aspect.The story's pretty simple, but all the characters you meet along the way have a fun charm to them.  The music is very pleasing and the graphics are good; not great, but definitely not medicore.The way potions were presented in this game is also an improvement, instead of stuffing your inventory with a fat stack of healing potions and resurrecting flowers, the devs brought Zelda's "empty bottle" gimmick into the design, thus putting a hard limit on how many potions you can carry.  This has been coupled with a brewing mechanic, where instead of buying your potions from a shop, you gather and toss ingredients into a cauldron based on various recipes you can discover.What really put a smile on my face though was going out and learning the different sword techniques.  I absolutely adored the swordplay in Minish Cap (My favorite Zelda title by the way), and how you'd steadily learn more techniques as you progressed and explored.Overall I'd give this game an 8 out of 10.  While there's a lot to love about this game, it's not without any flaws...-----------------while some of the puzzles were fun to solve, otherwise felt rather tedious or just plain frustrating.  Though to be fair I don't consider myself to be very competent at puzzles, I'm more in it for the action.  So take this comment with a grain of salt.I'm also not a huge fan of how fishing works; it seems like you could fish just about anything from anywhere, with a few exceptions where certain species can only be fished from certain regions.  The problem is that the fish are required for certain brewing recipes as well as certain fetch quests, and the sheer randomness of what you could fish up may leave you sitting around for a good while.  Honestly, this could be solved by having more of a limit on which areas certain fish can appear in.And lastly...  There seems to be a lack of post-game content.  Like, once you beat the big bad, that's it; you've overcome the biggest challenge the game has to offer.  Actually, the only content you're offered post-game is the fact that the big bad is really gone, his lair can no longer be entered, and some NPCs will comment and how you're the hero and all; which IS a nice change of pace from what Zelda typically does, where you always reload your save from just before defeating Ganon or whoever, and never actually get to see the world after his defeat.All I'm really trying to say is, I wish there was another optional challenge or two post-game.  Like a boss rush, or another arena match like the one you find in the desert; you know, the thing the game only lets you run once and wont let you back in after you've beaten it.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game. I kept the game open during 2 nights, so the actual hours played is quite a bit lower.Much as I would like to recommend the game, I cannot do so because it has one fatal flaw compared to the Zelda game A Link To The Past. The entire combat system is extremely poor. In Zelda, hitboxes and movement speed are tuned such that you can properly evade enemy attacks. You have to evade them because enemies have decent AI and shielding. You often need to find and exploit their one weakness to defeat them. You cannot simply mash a button, especially for dungeon bosses, for which you need to discover and use the right strategy. It is a difficult and fun challenge.In Blossom Tales 2, hitboxes are not precise and movement speed is slow, so evading is often not possible. Many enemies have no defense that you need to circumvent, and their AI is dumb. Trying to evade during boss fights is essentially pointless. There is so much stuff flying around so fast that it is nearly impossible to avoid getting hit because of the low movement speed. But there is also no need for this. You only receive damage every few seconds, so you can effectively just go full berserker mode on all bosses. Just tank the damage, stay close to him, and keep mashing the Z button. When your health gets low, just drink a health potion. When you get knocked away, just run towards him and keep hacking away. This works like a charm even on the end boss, which you can defeat in probably less than a minute by standing next to him and just mashing Z.In Zelda, the boss fight is an exciting reward at the end of a dungeon. In Blossom Tales 2, it is a trivial and boring slug fest.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll start by saying if you liked the first Blossom Tales game, you’ll probably like this one. However, like its predecessor, if you’re looking for something new, this might not be what you’re looking for. That being said, if you’re looking for a short, sweet game that applies the classic Zelda formula of exploration, puzzles, collectibles, and dungeon crawling, this might be right up your alley.The game features a cute frame story, with a grandfather telling the story of the Minotaur Prince as a sort of parable to his two grandchildren. It’s full of references to classic games and movies ranging from Zelda (obviously) to The Princess Bride and Labyrinth, but it doesn’t lean on them too heavily. It’s just enough easter eggs to give people who grew up playing Zelda a sprinkling of nostalgia, while still being accessible for a younger audience that might not understand those references.The graphics and music are good, stylized and retro while fitting the tone and world of the game. The gameplay loop generally feels good, although on occasion the collecting and exploring felt a little tedious this time (I’m looking at you fishing mini-game). The special items and potion system added a lot of new little features, especially the teleporter, which proved to be one of the most unique items I’ve seen in this kind of game.As with its predecessor, Blossom Tales 2 is short, not particularly challenging, and follows the Zelda formula in a predictable way. If you’re looking for something new, this one might not be for you. If you are looking for something to scratch that classic game itch, or you’ve never played a Zelda game and are looking for a starting point, this game is a great fit.

_childDocuments_.review: Another game where the thumbs up or thumbs down rating system makes this rough. I feel like the first game was superior. In this sequel, the amount of times I have to pause to switch items is crazy. Some rooms need 3 or 4 items to progress, and if you have to fight that's another pause screen. I don't know, I feel like I didn't experience this nearly as much in the original game.The later level room layouts are infuriating when every room has respawning enemies. It's not a single hit to kill, nearly every enemy is two or three hits. Some enemies are far too tanky for their own good. The further I got into the game, the more I just stopped fighting and ran through. There's no penalty for dying - you just respawn in the same room with full hearts. There's no incentive to use potions - just save those for boss fights where you can face-tank everything.I loved the original, but can't help but feel let down by the sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Good, fun, easy Zelda-like. Probably aimed at kids.Storyline reminds me of the Labyrinth movie, and a little of the Princess Bride, as it is a bedtime tale told to kids who occasionally interrupt.Feels a bit short, the world map is a bit small, there are 3 main dungeons, plus a final dungeon.No need to manage ammunition: all the tools, be they bombs, bow & arrows, yo-yo's, whathaveyou, they're all based on an energy or stamina bar which auto-recovers pretty fast.Once you get your hands on some bombs, and are at least somewhat sharp-eyed, you'll never have to grind for cash again, as there are plenty of chests about, and most of them are filled with cash. Rather than grinding for cash, I felt like I was grinding fish, trying to get enough of the right ones for trades and potion ingredients.When you earn new special moves, the kids make recommendations on what they want to see learned, but regardless of what gets picked, you won't miss out on any. Instead, you just pick what order you get them in: there are 4 special moves, and both kids make 2 requests.

_childDocuments_.review: 17h when using a map to mark collectibles down while playing, otherwise more around 19h 2/10 1 No, there is a lot of info about this game, but at separate places, she the bottom of this review to check what I have used No No No No No No No No difficulty option NoBlossom Tales 2 is an awesome action-adventure very inspired by the old-school Zelda games. A grandpa is telling his 2 grandchildren a bedtime story where the girl is the main character in the story and the boy is kidnapped by the Minotaur King. What is unique in this setting is that a few times the kids will start bickering about something and you get the choice of which suggestions you want to follow. For example what kind of musical instrument the hero will use, or what kind of mount she has, but also at least one point which enemies the character is fighting, so you can choose the one you prefer.  And you got some unique choices, I took a pig as my mount over a horse... just because I could. The game is quite easy but has some tough enemies, altho you can make it easier if you would seek out the Heart pieces and maybe get the better sword before fighting the final boss. What helps a lot is that the game always saves when you enter a new screen, so you don't lose much progress at all when you die. I also found the first dungeon the most difficult one to understand, but I have very bad memories of the water dungeon in "Ocarina of Time" so I can say for sure that water dungeons aren't my favorite. This one isn't as challenging as the water temple but I just had a hard time wrapping my mind around it. The others were easier to figure out for me, but I can totally see that this is a personal thing. The achievements are totally what you expect. It is great that the game doesn't have any missable achievements, this way you can play through the story without worrying about them, but doing it this way may make you backtrack and search a lot harder for missing things at the end. I totally wish that I had used a map, not to find my way but just to mark off which item I found so that when cleaning up I knew what I had still to get. Gladly the developers provide those maps on the steam forum. I took the liberty to combine those different maps into one big one so you can just use one map if you want to mark things off. You can find it , just save it on your computer and open it in some sort of paint program to mark things off.For the rest, I have used all different kinds of videos and guides. The Youtuber  has some very handy videos for "Blossom Tales 2" and   shows 3 heart pieces and an energy piece at the beginning which are very easy to miss. So I would recommend tracking what you have found (not necessarily what to hunt for) on a map, but I can totally see why that would destroy a bit of the fun while playing through the game, so know that it still is possible to get all the achievements if you didn't do it or don't want to do that.

_childDocuments_.review: A short, simple, fun and light hearted 2D Zelda inspired game. I personally think this game is way better than the first game. The story told like a different bedtime story so you don't have to play the first game if you don't want to.You have your standard Zelda like items like sword, shield, bow, bomb, boomerang, etc. Besides the sword, the items uses an energy system that regenerates over time.In addition to heart/energy pieces, there are miscellaneous of materials to collect that can be used to make potions, sell for money, turn in to related quest, and scrolls that give you various new sword moves mostly tied to the charged spinning slash.The story is a frame narrative. This has some impact on the game such as deciding which enemies to fight in certain locations and what type of puzzle to solve. There are a few bigger decision such as having your musical instrument be either a guitar or an accordion and your mount being either a horse or a pig. Overall doesn't really change the gameplay too much.The game is rather short, probably beaten and 100% within 15 hours. The game also isn't too difficult and you have access to a large amount of bottles for healing if needed.Some of the changes from the first game:-there is actually a sword upgrade that increases the sword's base damage. In the first game, outside the sword beam, the sword was the weakest weapon in the game. Almost every other weapon out damages the sword. Good change in this game.-the shield has an upgrade, giving it a few more uses over its uses in the first game-they reduced the amount of push blocks and memory puzzles in this game, which imo was probably the hardest thing in the first game-subjective but I think this game looks better overallNitpicks:-you need to fish a lot for 100%-warping in this game takes way longer than it does in the first game because of the music mechanicYeah it is a good game. I would recommend this game way more than the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the simpler (and shorter) Zelda-likes. A few more tools and fun things compared to the first. Not really anything unique about what tools you get, just the versions of them (hookshot is a yoyo for example), though there is one that's a bit different than other Zelda games. All in all worth a playthrough, but nothing groundbreaking.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10 A very well-refined modern take on the OG Zelda games.I thought I was in for a mediocre LoZ clone or, at best, passion project. I was way off. Blossom Tales 2 sports great gameplay, visuals, skill/item loadout, music, even silly story choices. Lots of thoughtful finishing touches. Even the storytelling setting is a great hat tip to old favorites. It's not easy to stand tall and proud on the shoulders of giants. Blossom Tales 2 pulls it off.Notes:- Difficulty: kid-friendly- Length: beat it at close to 100% in 16 hrs (IMO a good length)- Only thing I don't understand is having to pause to switch items so frequently when there are plenty of unused buttons. I assume this was a design choice, given the amount of thought put into everything else, but I don't get it.

_childDocuments_.review: "Sorry...gotta trash your house or i can't afford that empty bottle..."More Blossom Tales time. Seriously, the best way to make money is to walk in and out of someones house and just become a destructive cyclone (which makes it even more fun to do in the shop when trying to save up to buy from after on their dime).But yes it is more Blossom Tales. The first one was a lot of fun, and this is...pretty good so far. It feels a little less smooth than the last in character movement, but it is hardly noticeable. Also this time you need to get ingredients for potions..but it isn't that bad. Really if you are lawn mowering the world as you go to each location, you shouldn't have to worry. I had enough ingredients to make 25 health potions by the time I got the recipe in the beginning of the game.So if you are still a fan of Zelda: A Link to the Past after playing the last Blossom Tales, then go for this one too. _childDocuments_.review: Blossom Tales 2, much like the first game, could best be described as a "zelda-like". This is not a negative - in a time where top-down Zelda has largely been neglected, it is nice to have indie games that fill the gap left behind.For anyone familiar with this format, the gameplay of Blossom Tales 2 is close to what one would expect. You traverse an overworld while collecting items and completing the occasional dungeon to advance the plot and open up more areas of the world. Exploration is encouraged with a variety of optional secrets, granting various benefits to the player upon discovery. Along the way you will have to solve puzzles and defeat enemies. Though Blossom Tales 2 does not feature any major innovations, it implements this formula well, creating what is in my opinion a fun, yet familiar (whether this is positive or negative is up to you) experience. However, I personally found the difficulty a bit lacking. If you explore a decent bit, you will uncover powerful new techniques, gain lots of health, and come across overpowered potions. As a baseline difficulty, I think this is excellent - it ensures the game is accessible to players of varying skill levels. However, players who want a more challenging experience may find themselves disappointed. The inclusion of a hard difficulty as an optional choice (for example perhaps increasing enemy damage/decreasing your damage, severely nerfing the healing and rejuvenation potions, etc.) would have remedied this issue without affecting players who do not want this challenge. Some smaller issues are that the game relies on coins as a minor reward a lot, but there aren't sufficient monetary sinks after the mid-game to keep this reward meaningful, and that you need to go into the item menu more often that I'd like to switch items - perhaps the game could have had an extra item button.The narrative of Blossom Tales 2 is a story told by Grandpa to his grandchildren over a campfire. This is integrated into the game in some fun ways - for example, at particular points the children will argue about what types of enemies or puzzles the player should encounter, what a particular thing should be, etc., with it being up to the player to decide between the two children's arguments. In addition to giving the player some minor agency over the game, it also provides a cute touch of whimsy to the narrative. The actual story being told is fairly weak and sparse, with too little focus given to the world or any of the characters beside the main two. This also results in the plot feeling quite impersonal. For example, the majority of NPCs in settlements share the same pool of dialogue which quickly repeats, and they just feel like they're there for the sake of it. Even the characters with plot relevancy, after doing their thing in one part of the story, generally just stay static for the rest of the game. However, in these kinds of games, gameplay (in my opinion) tends to be more important. This, combined with the unique framing of the plot, means that I think it is generally satisfactory for the plot to remain little more than a cute background. Players who expect or strongly want a deep or compelling story will likely find themselves disappointed.The graphics are not particularly exceptional, but they are fairly cute and generally done well, complimenting the rest of the game. Similarly, the soundtrack mostly varies from average to good, with a few excellent standout tracks.It is also worth mentioning that is is not necessary to play the first Blossom Tales to enjoy this one. Blossom Tales 2 contains a small amount of references to the first game, but the plots are otherwise completely independent, and as mentioned the actual plot is not a highlight of the game.Overall I would generally recommend Blossom Tales 2. With that said, if you didn't like the first game (or don't want to play another with a similar direction and setting), don't like this game genre, or really want a compelling story, you will probably be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Blossom Tales II: The Minotaur Prince

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to have to leave this review, but the warning needs to be here.  The game looks, feels, and sounds so nice with the music being especially good, but the dungeons and bosses are bland and some of the puzzles feel just pure evil, breaking previously established rules or randomly going off the rails into what I'd call romhack difficulty.  What really breaks the game for me though is that there's just no answers to be found anywhere if you get stuck.  There's no solutions in the guides sections, no gamefaqs, no one reading the forums.  If you get stuck, you're done.  That's what happened to me.  There's a puzzle I just can't figure out, I couldn't find any answers, couldn't get any help, and I'm sick of looking at it, so I'm bailing.  Too many other games to play.  Don't get me wrong, this is by no means a bad game, in fact I'm really more just sad I'll never see the rest of it because of this one stupid puzzle.  It's not the first time I've gotten stuck for way too long though, and I can only assume it'll inevitably happen again even if I did manage to progress.  Exact same thing prevented me from finishing the first game, and right near the end, too.  Guess I should have learned me lesson then.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the first game in this series quite a bit. It was similar to , but was more streamlined and less tedious. I didn't find  to be Game of the Year-quality or anything, but I liked it enough to have no hesitation when it came to picking up and playing the sequel.My initial roadblock came when attempting to get a bow from the Blacksmith, who needed things to be sorted first in Anchortown. I learned that pirates were disrupting shipments to Anchortown and I went and killed them, but no one in Anchortown seemed to care or acknowledge that I did so. I wandered back and forth, from screen to screen, over and over in an attempt to figure out what I was supposed to do or what I did wrong. I even posted on the Steam discussion boards in an attempt to get some direction.Shortly thereafter I made it into a Purple Turtle dungeon of some sort, only to learn that pirates had invaded it as well! So I guess this is what I was missing before? That there was a second battalion of pirates that were somehow inside of this giant turtle whose mouth was closed?
