_childDocuments_.review: There are very few times I feel compelled to write a bad review for a game. But I make this here with the hope that my favorite game and its devs wake up and get their ♥♥♥♥ together.I want preface this with saying that there is no other game like tekken for me. I like fighting games in general, but tekken scratches an itch that simply cannot be scratched by anything else.To the new players:Stay away from this game for a while. The most recent patches have all been undercooked spaghetti thrown at the wall. Nothing is sticking.To the devs:You need to introduce a test environment. That would directly lead avoiding massive review drops like this. You cannot treat the main branch as your experimental play ground. That's just basic software development 101. It needs to be opt in with you taking in as much data as possible. Or at least have a test environment for QA, because I guarantee that some of your most recent blunders would've been caught instantly with a good QA/dev pipeline. I know you guys aren't used to these sorts of modern methodologies cause you used to have your "test environment" be the arcade release. This will not cut it anymore, it isn't the 90s.Now for the actual analysis of this most recent patch. The idea that we should be matched based off of "tekken prowess". This change is obviously bad if you consider it for more than 5 seconds. We need to look at why this patch exists and what problems the devs were attempting to solve as a problem. The problem that the devs wanted to solve was that low ranked players are sometimes matched against a much higher ranked player who is using an alt character (therefore having a lower rank as rank isn't universal). This as a problem has been present since tekken 7 with high blue rank players having their alts put into red ranks. This is more understandable in tekken 7 for reasons I will get to later. This patch attempted to address this by basing match making on prowess AND rank together. This is a naive but somewhat understandable logic. There are a couple of key large problems with this approach:1. Tekken prowess was never a hard science for who is better than anyone else. It was at best a neat little thing that showed you if you were better at sidestepping than the average bear, but let's not pretend its elo. If you got carried by a prenerf top tier character then tried to play an alt, you would find that you get absolutely washed as you have to now engage with parts of the tekken engine that you never had to before. This can single handedly ruin your experience. For those that say you deserve this for playing dragunov or whatever, you should consider that this is a double failing of the devs (drag is too strong and matchmaking poorly thought out)2. This change doesn't even make sense in the context of new players. So picture this, you just got your friend into tekken for the first time. They ask themselves what every new player asks themselves "Who should I play?" We give them the correct answer which is "whoever you want". They decide to try out a bunch of different characters. They first boot up unranked (a not unreasonable thing for a new player to do). They realize that unranked puts them against much better players so they switch to ranked. They are still uncertain who their main will be (or even if they want to main anyone). They play many different characters in ranked. This player has just unknowingly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ themselves, they will now have an inflated tekken prowess despite being brand new to the game. They will get matched against much better players than them (as if it was unranked) and will get washed again. This new player is now frustrated at the game and is likely to quit.3. This change MASSIVELY inflates the matchmaking times. Now you must be at a similar rank + prowess to get a match. This disproportionately affects people who play multiple characters. You now must fight people who also play a similar amount of alt characters at a similar rank. Hope you enjoy playing against the same dude every 15 minutes, because that is now your exclusive ranked reality.4. On the other end of the spectrum, people who are experienced character specialists or just main one character exclusively now have matches against people that are likely far below their skill level (as prowess is a terrible measure of one's ability to win).Before this patch people would ♥♥♥♥ post about ranked not actually meaning anything. Which was dumb. Now though? Ranked actually means nothing. I haven't seen a bigger blunder than this since ds2 soul memory and that's impressive.There's a wise saying in game dev that goes as follows "Listen to the players that say something is bad, but don't listen to their solutions" This is no doubt true of this patch which was actually requested by a non zero amount of players. And as a player, take this next two suggestions with a grain of salt but I'm gonna offer them anyway.1. Have a public test environment for the love of god. Pushing everything to main is exceedingly outdated as a method of changing whole systems. Get one of your new devs to tell you about what they learned in school. ♥♥♥♥ has changed for better and you need to catch up2. Because you've made the change where people don't lose rank until gold, you've made it so that the range of skill levels are more varied per rank. This is why the median player rank is in red and why people have such a chaotic experience there. Despite this change you've kept the tekken 7 formula of having alts be SIGNIFICANTLY lower ranked than our mains. An exceedingly simple solution is to have alts be only 3 or 4 ranks down from mains and not an entire 7 ranks. As I write this I see so many of my friends list boot up tekken 7. A nearly 10 year+ old game. I recommend changing this sooner rather than later so you don't tail spin out of control. I am going to skip out on this game until this reverted. Absolutely insane

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I'm 2 full rank sets higher than when I made my first review and quadrupled my playtime (Garyu -> Fujin), I figured I'd update it with my current thoughts on the game.Tekken 8 is very aggressive and with the current state of the game, defense isn't really a valid strategy. Most characters have chunky unreactable attacks with ambiguous animations & very high damage combos.This by itself wouldn't really be a complete deal-breaker, however with 30+ characters, each having ~80 moves each (and only around 10% of the moveset being universal) ranked turns into a cluster♥♥♥♥ where both parties are scrambling to knowledge check eachother. In real world terms, this means that many of the things that boost your winrate (e.g indiscriminately power-crushing/low jabbing strings you're unfamiliar with, spamming command grabs, "combo hunting", etc) give you no extra progress towards being good, making the ranked mode almost meaningless.For a game to work in a format such as this without requiring an investment of 3000 hours to learn every matchup and every character's intricacies, characters would either have to share upwards of 90% of their moveset with a few "signature moves" setting them apart, or if they insist on keeping the degree of variety identical, there would need to be very few characters - maybe 4-6.In contrast to my first review, where I recommended Tekken 8 overall & added that picking it up with friends is the cherry on top, I now believe that picking the game up with friends to set up an "arms race" of sorts is the only way to enjoy the game - as the constant cycle of innovation & adaptation leads to a far less overwhelming, bottom-up approach of learning a few character matchups. This is important as playing a matchup both parties are familiar with is quite fun and is how Tekken is best enjoyed - it feels like a glorified version of rock-paper-scissors, with a heavy focus on mindgames and reading.If you have no friends, there's not much for you to do. Ranked is quite unfun, and even if it wasn't, grinding solo in a game where it takes almost a thousand hours to be considered "decent" and start playing the game as it was intended is frustrating, intimidating and just plain not worth it.tl;dr - only buy if you have a group of friends willing to start grinding simultaneously

_childDocuments_.review: New Gameplay Mechanics: As a fan of Tekken, you might find Tekken 8 to be a thrilling addition to the series with several enhancements and new features. The game introduces a new Heat system, which adds more excitement to battles without leading to mindless button mashing. This system allows for strategic use of Heat Smash attacks, which are visually impressive and inject more personality into each match.Character Roster and Design: The game features a robust roster of 32 characters, each with distinct visual and gameplay styles. This includes returning favorites and three new characters: Azucena, Victor, and Reina, each bringing unique fighting styles to the table. Veterans of the series will appreciate new moves and abilities for returning characters, providing a fresh learning curve.Game Modes: Beyond the main story modes, Tekken 8 offers various game modes. These include Character Episodes, a short-burst arcade mode with backstory elements; Arcade Quest, a survival-style challenge; and Super Ghost Battle, where you fight against an AI that learns from your moves. However, some modes like 'Tekken Ball', a beach volleyball mini-game, may not hold long-term appeal.Combat Experience: Fans of the series will find Tekken 8's combat to be smooth and satisfying. The game is designed to encourage aggressive play over defensive tactics, appealing to both new and veteran players. There are also plenty of new moves and combos to discover for each character.Customization: The game offers extensive customization options for characters, allowing players to personalize their favorite fighters with various clothing and accessories, purchasable with in-game currency.Visuals and Presentation: Tekken 8 impresses with its stunning visuals, although some have noted that the pre-rendered cutscenes don't quite match up to the real-time ones.Accessibility and Learning Curve: The game is considered accessible to new players while still offering depth and complexity for veterans to explore. Discovering new moves and strategies is part of the fun.Overall Reception: Tekken 8 is described as one of the most satisfying and fun 3D fighting games in recent years. It's particularly noted for its smooth combat mechanics and the introduction of new gameplay systems.While it holds onto the core elements that have defined the Tekken series, it also introduces enough new features to feel fresh and exciting for both veterans and new players.In conclusion, Tekken 8 seems to have struck a balance between innovating within the fighting game genre and maintaining the beloved core mechanics of the Tekken series. Its emphasis on offensive gameplay, combined with the new Heat system and diverse character roster, offers a fresh and engaging experience for fans of the series and newcomers alike. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I'm giving the game a "NO" on recommending it now simply because they have predatory FOMO battle pass additions that were never mentioned before. The whole bait-and-switch behind their monetization has left a really sour taste in the community and this practice should not be encouraged. Selling cosmetics was fine, but tying it to time limited events that require grinding to unlock content is not okay. Thumbs way down now.Original review follows below:Great version of the Tekken franchise. Has a large list of characters, feels really smooth, new systems that help players comeback / do cool combos, has options to make the game easier for people, practice modes, and lots of other things. The story is pretty meh overall and very "anime"-like, which took me out of it a bit. Plus, in the story you're playing as Jin like 90% of the time instead of jumping around and learning about other characters and what they are doing. I think MK9 did it much better in terms of a playable fighting game story. Should have really focused on multiple characters and had more things than just the same few fights over and over (and the wonky fighting masses of 3D enemies).Either way, this is a great continuation of the Tekken franchise. Just wish it had more practice tools, macro setup, a few more characters (saving them for DLC, I guess), and more game modes (Tekken Ball is fun but give us more). Still think Tekken Tag Tournament is better because of the 2v2 dynamic, but this is very solid. Oh, and I wish they brought back Paul Phoenix's "Rapid Fire to Stone Breaker" move... I miss it so much!8/10

_childDocuments_.review: As an off again on again Tekken fan I was only semi excited for 8's release, but as more and more features were presented I realized just what a beast this game actually is. Every aspect of this game was designed by people who love the franchise, and it absolutely shows. Fighting games can certainly feel like "more of the same" when the next iteration drops, but every part of T8 has changed (at least slightly) and after some time with the beta and now full game, I can confidently say it has changed for the better.The loading is insanely fast, the graphics and flare are top quality, even the story this time around was a blast. However, the one defining set of features that make Tekken 8 the BEST fighting game out there are its practice tools. My god, to say they went above and beyond is  doing it justice. The practice mode bot is super customizable, there's wiff punishing training, followup training, combo trainings for each character, ghost fighting, and oh my god it just keeps going! These features are doing massive work, helping newer (or even older and just not as good players like myself) learn how to play Tekken to its fullest potential.The one specific training tool that needs a callout is Replays. You can watch your recent matches sure, but you can also PAUSE AND HAVE IT TELL YOU WHAT YOU COULD HAVE DONE BETTER. And as if that wasn't the coolest thing yet, you can then TAKE CONTROL of EITHER CHARACTER and play out the next 10 seconds! I cannot stress enough just how cool and USEFUL this is when learning. So yes, absolutely recommend, even if you're not a Tekken fan. Even if you hate online there's a full campaign, full arcade campaign, 32 character battles, arcade mode, ghost fight mode, etc etc. I don't know what the future holds for Tekken 8, but I am excited and confident that it will be bright.  EDIT:88 Hours (Post Tekken Shop Launch)Current state, I am Vanquiser on my main and working on getting the entire roster to Warrior. Still having a great time. Every now and then I get smacked by someone not rank adjusted yet, but much less so than on release. However that's not the topic I'm amending this review for. That topic is the Tekken Shop. I have 2 things to say, and then I'm out.1st) It's predatory. Yes because you get leftover coins, but ALSO because it was never mentioned in the leadup to the release of the game. It was purposefully left out content that evaded major reviewers and has made its way back in when it could be downplayed between major updates. I want the game to be successful, I want them to offer microtransactions if they believe its best for the game, but I do not want them to be dishonest about their practices. If I could change my review to meh, I would.  2nd) Not only is the shop abysmally small, the costumes are all full-body. This feels like such a wasted opportunity. We're headed back into T7 where we will seemingly receive no other smaller customization options, but ONLY full body changes. Thankfully there's already a lot of options, but they are missing a golden opportunity to expand on already implemented features. EDIT: 161 hours (post battlepass + eddy launch)Man, rough time. Still loving the game, got garyu with eddy and almost there with steve. The battlepass is just awful, its nice that it pays for itself and its quite cheap, but damn did they not care about it in the slightest. Hopefully this was just a test run for more interesting content in season 2. EVO is a few days away and we're getting the next character reveal alongside a huge balance patch. Hope to see some good changes. EDIT:  232 hours (release of battlepass 2 + lidia)Battlepass 2 is better, but more importantly the game state overall has become much more balanced. The design team has made some incredible choices. This is the best state that tekken has ever been in, hands down. I can't wait to see what the future holds. Chipotle free content is pretty funny.

_childDocuments_.review: Refreshing coming from Guilty Gear: STRIVE, yet very challenging, often in a way that makes me frustrated.Despite that, it's hard not to like TEKKEN 8, as the visual style is incredibly beautiful, and the gameplay is awesome. It's super hard, that much is true, but the typical air combo nonsense is not present here, unlike in 100 hit combo anime fighters. There are a few cons though. For one, the ranking system. I went into this game excited that there was a proper unranked mode, and that delivered. Casual-esque gameplay that I could enjoy without the stress of ranked modes. Ranked mode, however, Is probably just as bad as Guilty Gear: STRIVE. The ranking is not a cumulative score as a player, but by each CHARACTER. You may be Ranger with Jin, but if you try ranked with Asuka, you'll be playing as the Fighter rank. This makes the ranking system both accurate and innacurate. Sure, a really good Jin player wouldn't be even half as good at playing even another Mishima, but confidence and proper basics can make learning substantially easier. The aforementioned Jin will hop in training with Reina for an hour or so and get ready to stomp people at lower ranks. This essentially makes smurfing an actual system in the game. SO much more frustrating than the innacurate floor system of Guilty Gear: STRIVE. All in all, the game is still just so cool. I suck at the game, but the gameplay has so much impact and the characters are so badass that it's hard to not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: They managed to kill every good mechanic and skill gap from the previous game, while shoving in corporate greed at its finest . Literally putting MTX 1 month after release followed by a Battlepass in order to avoid review bombing is enough to show how pitiful they are. Not mentioning the amount of laziness in porting items from Tekken 7 from Unreal 4 to Unreal 5 and locking it behind the previously mentioned battle pass or a pay wall (you can buy a wonderful textureless sphere from the default UE shapes catalogue for only a couple of euros). Giving early access to DLC characters to whoever bought at least the deluxe edition is an unfair advantage and you can't even use the replay feature in order to learn how to play against said DLC characters unless you own them.The entire roster is unbalanced like hell, forcing 50/50's with no risk while punishing you for a good defense is the biggest red flag that points out what kind of product the saga has become and the audience which aims towards.They favor mashing and pressing the escape button (also known as Heat system, I'll come back to this later) instead of motivating players in getting better even in the most fundamental skills you need to learn in Tekken: movement, positioning and sidestepping.Movement and positioning are completely gone, utterly disintegrated and substituted with homing projectiles ready tohit you when you least expect them. Sadly, sidestepping has met the same fate, one of the most useful mechanics to punish and deal a good amount of damage if successful, turned into a nightmare (quoting Murray's own words "Why would you want to sidewalk if you can block and launch... If you know it is coming, like all other moves...).Now the main dish, the Heat system. Pressing a button to escape a combo and restore a fairly good amount of game changing health proves how this system wasn't even designed in the slightest towards competitive game enviroments.Instead of working on the already refined rage art/drive system and working on its flaws, they radically changed everything and took the easy route. Certain heat engagers and heat bursts are so broken that they make certain matches tedious and monotonous often causing players to run away after a single match (this is also a huge issue in the competitive field).Ranked matches are in the worst state they have ever been, they should've kept the Tekken 7 system instead of turning everything into a gambling session, hoping you don't lose 1k points randomly if you lose once. They still don't punish pluggers properly and most importantly they don't give points whenever you are a victim of plugging, sure they banned a couple of them but they instantly came back with alt accounts, bravo Namco.They're pursuing legal actions against mod creators in general and they give little to 0 communication at all to the community when they expose the real problems of the whole game.The game is fun? Indeed. Do I recomend it? Not in its current state unless they do some soul-searching and finally start addressing the issues the community has been highlighting for months.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely fun and fast games, great moments with chunky heat engagers and slow mos. Backdash is nerfed but sidestep is buffed so its a fair trade. Story mode is good only as a throwback to previous Tekken games, otherwise very cliche and mediocre, but I can still appreciate the effort they put in this time around.Arcade Quest is essentially a tutorial and a great way for new players to get acquainted with how the game works and tries to transition them into becoming an intermediate and beyond level player. Every character has had massive overhauls in terms of appearance and gameplay so you feel tempted to play every character to some degree. Ghost battle is super underrated as it lets you figure out your own weaknesses and also gives you a chance to lab certain matchups and see what people generally like to do with a character. Jukebox mode is back and lets you change the music for all stages/menus using music from any Tekken game from Tekken 1 to Tekken 8 (including tag 1 & 2 and revolution). Its been just about 2 weeks since the game released and there has already been a minor balance patch with notes from the team addressing some overtuned characters and bugs, which means that the dev team certainly cares about maintaining the balance of this game. Online is the best its ever been in terms of connection quality and input response, though your experience will vary if the opponent is on WiFi or has a toaster for a computer. There is a block list at least so you can ensure you don't rematch with an opponent who doesn't have a good setup.Training mode is very robust and is now accessible while searching for a match. New options are available including the ability to see what you can do in response to an opponent's attack (this setting is called "Punish"). Frame data is detailed and free unlike Tekken 7. Quick select now allows you to view a map of all the characters, and stage selection is also a part of quick select now. Loading times are incredibly fast both offline and online (provided you're playing on console or PC with the game on an SSD).Replay mode is the greatest new feature to this game as it allows you to rewatch games and reflect on your gameplay. If there was a string you could have ducked, the game will tell you. If there was a move that could be block punished, the game will tell you (and what to punish with as well so knowledge of frame data is not necessary, but helpful). And if something could not be ducked or block punished, you can take control of the replay and figure out what your options are in terms of sidestepping, reversals, counter hits, etc. You can also take control of your opponent and figure out what they could have done against you. If you messed up a combo in game you can go back and fix it. If you could have won a round by optimizing your combo or spending heat, you can go back and verify that. If there was a weird okizeme situation that you don't understand, you can go and see what the grounded options and counterplay are. There really is no excuse to not improve as a player with this feature included.In conclusion, if you want a fun game to pickup as a beginner but also want something that has a long and fulfilling path to improvement as a player, get this game.Overall: 10/10Fighting game of the decade.

_childDocuments_.review: While many of the negative reviews will talk about the micro transactions they added, imo the biggest problems this game has are on the gameplay side.They buffed offense whith things like HEAT and chip damage while nerfing defensive tools like backdashing, making the game way too offense oriented.Heat / Heat Dash have made it so that every character has OP 50/50s that are so strong that every round feels like your either just guessing or forcing your opponent to guess because that is the most optimal way to play. Overall HEAT is just too strong.The Prowess based matchmaking punishes you for playing more than one character by only matching you against other people with the same prowess and similar rank. While this may seem like a good thing its actually really bad if you get high in the rankings with one character because there are less people with the same prowess at the ranks your secondary characters are at, so you get longer que times and your more likely to run into the same people.They still haven't fixed the rage quitting issue. While you can report people it still feels bittersweet because you don't get the points. This issue feels especially bad because they had almost 10 years of this being an issue in T7 and they still didn't fix it for this game, It honestly just feels like the devs don't give AF about ranked at this point.Overall the game feels very unbalanced and i don't trust the developers will make the changes needed to fix it, It feels like they want to cater to the casual audience while alienating the hardcore player base. i can look past the scummy micro transactions if the gameplay is good enough but this game fails to deliver even on that side, so i can't in good faith recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The most amount of fun I’ve had online in the longest time. It’s a true joy to discover how rich and layered a fighting game can be, especially after being frustrated with the current state of Mortal Kombat. _childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is really, really good. This is my first fighting game since the days of KoF '97, when all I did as a kid was button mashing. I've always heard that fighting games are like rock-paper-scissors, and while that's not entirely wrong, it's better described as a series of fast decision-making based on both reactions and predictions, with many available options. In particular, with Tekken 8 being a 3D fighting game, it offers even more choices and strategies than traditional 2D fighting games. On top of that, it amazes me how smooth and realistic the fighting animations have evolved to be over the years.Now, for the bad part—the micro-transactions are really, really sucky. They weren’t mentioned at all prior to launch and were added shortly after to lure people in and avoid bad publicity on release. I was disappointed to see so few customization options in the base game, which is a big part for a fighting game. It all made sense when an in-game shop asking for real money was added. When the shop was only selling costumes, it was disgusting but at least understandable. However, when a new stage arrived, it wasn’t free and wasn’t even included in the deluxe or ultimate editions? What a joke.Thumbs up for the game itself. Absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for the micro-transactions.

_childDocuments_.review: I spent $100 dollars on the pre-order for this game. In the ensuing 8 months, Bandai Namco has prioritized how they can ask me for even more money over any gameplay enhancements.Changes the community has been crying out for are not happening, but more battle passes are. A stage with a character is something we're being charged for, when that never happened in the last installment of the series.The netcode is once again some bizarre in-house amalgam of delay and rollback because Japanese developers are too arrogant and xenophobic to use technology that already works, and would rather implement something that doesn't so they can say they made it.Matchmaking in ranked regularly pits you against opponents far better than you, and punishes you for losing to them as though you were playing someone of similar skill all the same. The massive ranked points swings seem designed to incite an emotional response and rewards behavior the game allows you to report people for.High level ranked is rife with players with poor connection quality, people who leave after one round, bored Twitch streamers fishing for clips or some combination of all of the above.Rather than feeling accomplished and motivated to keep playing after hitting Tekken King in April, I have had very little fun playing the game since.Bandai Namco needs to get their act together before Capcom, ArcSys, or even an indie FG eats their lunch.

_childDocuments_.review: So the, polaris error has been resolved for 900 and 1k series nvidia gfx card users, and as the game no longer crashes every few minutes I have updated this review. A number of players still have these issues though, so try the demo before you buy - this is still the most buggy game I have played.Anyway gameplay wise:* The game has had a number of updates now so its not quite as much of a 50/50 mash fest as it was on release, and side stepping is now worthwhile. * They wanted a more aggressive/less passive game which is fine (in T7 you could play defensively, and back into a corner waiting for the right time to strike), but they could have achieved this by speeding up gameplay by 20% or so (compared to tekken 7) without the heat mechanic (as it is currently).* The heat mechanic is ok, but it really is a missed opportunity - It's pretty much used to do extra damage and force 50/50 situations. If they used it in a more strategic way to enhance moves or as a combo breaker or similar then the game would be a lot better for it. * In a bid to encourage new players they have also dumbed down the game, the problem with this, is that kind of gameplay really isn't rewarding, negatively impacts depth and skill, and will hurt longevity of the game. While i get that you need to draw in new players, there are better ways to introduce complexity than giving characters one button combos for instance or adding speshal style controls.* Character selection also doesn't give players a sense of how complex/easy a character is and what their strengths/weaknesses are, there is just a bit of fluff about fighting style, weight and height. Not that is matters much since a lot of characters now have moves to counter their weaknesses, all of which leads to a number of characters feeling a bit more samey compared to previous entries and losing a bit of their identity.Don't get me wrong, visuals aside it's still the best readily available tekken but it could have been a lot better if they made some tweaks and adjusted their approach.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, an outstanding return to form for the series and one of the best entries in decades. Tekken 8 is held firmly by more of the deep, technical, and ultimately satisfying gameplay the series is known for, made even more exciting to both play and spectate with the new Heat System. All three newcomers are well designed and evoke nostalgia whilst bringing something to Tekken never seen before. The training and replay systems are extremely robust, promoting intuitive learning without tedium. The graphics are stunning, boasting high quality character models with a noticeable improvement in the stages themselves.However, the game is marred by its mediocre single player. The story mode is a fun 4 hour romp, and leans heavily into shonen anime tropes, which can make it polarizing for players not already invested in the story. The character episodes are simply 5 AI fights to watch a 45 second ending, and can be tedious just to find out your favorite character gets a silly cutaway gag as an ending. Arcade Quest is a short tutorial mode that does its job decently, but fails to deliver how exciting high level gameplay can be or give a player a better reason to sit down and learn the fundamentals rather than to just go online and mash buttons. I will say that something is better than nothing over Tekken 7's absolute lack of a tutorial mode.The online netcode is markedly better than Tekken 7, but the netcode still isn't up to snuff with near perfect implementations of its competitors, namely Guilty Gear Strive and Street Fighter 6. An unfortunate side effect of the high fidelity graphics is that if your opponent's PC struggles with performance, you also feel it as well to keep the game in sync. Many players online do not optimize their graphics settings leading to unplayable matches, exacerbated by poor wifi connections. The online play experience is passable, but I will applaud the vast improvement over Tekken 7. It's fine and playable but not perfect.Despite this, Tekken 8 still has some of the most exciting gameplay in the gaming market today. It hits all the important points of a fighting game as hard as it can, while making decent attempts at welcoming and retaining new players with more single player options and improved netcode. All of this adds up to be a outstanding game I will be playing for many years to come.

_childDocuments_.review: The so-called "aggressive gameplay" direction has been implemented in a shockingly poor manner. Numerous aspects of the game are flawed:1. The heat mechanics make the gameplay feel like a 50/50 gamble.2. The defense is nerfed like crazy. Almost every move feel like its safe. the lows are not that punishable now. i think the developers want us to press the button throughout the round.3. The excessive use of particle effects has become a concern for my eyes.4. The sound effects are disproportionately loud; a normal punch sounds like an atomic bomb. Special moves, heat-bound moves, and power crushes all contribute to a relentless barrage of noise. A few explosive sounds per round are acceptable, but constant blasting over 60 seconds is unbearable.5. Some characters, like Victor, are overdesigned with an abundance of spammable moves.6. The fighting game community (FGC) is already small, and games like Tekken 8 are unlikely to retain new players. They might try it initially, but once the novelty wears off, they are likely to leave.The only positives out of this game i can take are - Buff to side step, cool graphics and developer support. Devs are making a lot of effort to correct the game but there are some inherent issues in this game which cannot be fixed.Steam will show that i have 1 hour in the game but i have played this game on my brother's PC for good 70 80 hours before i finally decided to own it but later refunded timely.

_childDocuments_.review: The current state of this game is comically bad. The online is nearly unplayable - constant disconnects, crashes, bad netcode, pluggers running wild because the game doesn't really have a system in place to punish them and the devs prefer to meme about it on social media than actually take action to improve their product.If you don't run into any of these issues the gameplay is also very rough. The new heat system is unfun and unfair to use or defend against. There are lots of moves with little to no counterplay. The over emphasis on aggression has turned the game into a series of guesses and scrapping. Its genuinely difficult to cover all the dumb gameplay changes from T7. Theres a chance they tune some parts of the game but the entire thing is built on a system mechanic that is fundamentally anti-fun.The DLC practices are insultingly scummy. Of the many blunders in this area the one that sticks out to me as the best example of incompetence in this game is how they've handled the first DLC character, Eddy. This is a character synonymous with trickery. He has a moveset with a million unorthodox moves that is balanced by the fact that you can take him into practice mode and dissect everything one by one. In T8, you once again have to buy this character. But it doesnt stop there - anyone playing this character starts at the lowest rank possible. So new tekken players are forced to fight hundreds of eddy players that should be playing vs much higher ranks and the only way for them to learn to counter this character full of tricks is to buy him on top of the $70 price tag for a game that isn't even complete.You will occasionally get to enjoy a little bit of good ol tekken here and there. Its still fun to KBD around and out maneuver your opponent. Its still fun to experiment with the giant movelists and come up with some wild stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a near Masterpiece. Unfortunately I've run into performances issues, including Several "Initialize error" messages and long load times. That could be my fault however as my CPU processor is old. Other than that this game has so much to over. The amazing fighting mechanics that Tekken has always been known for are present and over thirty characters in the base roster. This game has something to offer for every fighting game player. The Cinematic story mode titled The Dark Awakens is quite possibly the most ambitious, epic, and memorable fighting game story mode every produced. Its shorter than what you may be used to if you play MK and Injustice but it packs quite a punch. Jin Kazama goes through a tremendous character arc, one that brought genuine goosebumps and heartfelt moments. The final fight is beautifully choreographed and concludes the story with a bang. The ending leaves you wants more as expect and there are still loose ends to be tied up and explained but its good that we have a solid story arc to prop us into the next generation of Tekken after the somewhat lackluster Tekken 7 story mode.       Besides that there is a lot to do. The Arcade Quest is a fun little mini game reminiscent of old school Arcade play as well as a clever nod to Tekken world Tour competitive gaming. The new Replay and Tips feature adds so many tools to help player improve their skills and the New Super Ghost Battle ensures that you can play against anyone you want even when they are not available Online. You can even fight yourself. Its a brilliant feature and one I hope they will continue to build on in the future. The Presentation of this game is sublime. Namco really stepped it up with the visuals and this is apparent in the epic redesigns many of the characters have. I look forward to playing this for many years to come and to see the Tekken fandom and community grow after this new release. This is phenomenal and the best game to come out of this three decade old franchise since Tekken 5. What a time to be alive!

_childDocuments_.review: TEKKEN 8? A Fiery New Chapter in the Iconic Franchise! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)"TEKKEN 8 dazzles with its groundbreaking graphics and dynamic new 'Heat' battle system, delivering thrilling fights and a deep story, though it faces initial online playability issues."TEKKEN 8 storms onto the scene, reviving the legendary fighting game series with breathtaking new-generation visuals and an immersive battle atmosphere. The game introduces a roster of 32 fighters, each meticulously designed with elaborate detail, showcasing the power of new hardware capabilities. The environments are vivid and dynamic, with destructible stages adding an exhilarating layer to every match. This installment's standout feature is the Heat battle system, an aggressive and thrilling addition that maintains the unique play feel of the TEKKEN series. It enhances the intensity of fights, making each bout more exciting and visually stunning. Rage Arts return, adding a dramatic flair to battles and appealing to both players and spectators alike.TEKKEN 8 isn't just about fierce battles; it also introduces the Arcade Quest mode, allowing players to create their avatars and embark on a personalized TEKKEN journey. This mode is a refreshing change of pace, providing a more individualized experience in the TEKKEN universe. The game’s storyline continues the tragic saga of the Mishima and Kazama bloodlines, picking up six months after the previous installment. This continuation of the longest-running video game storyline adds depth and context to the battles, making them more than just random matchups. For longtime fans of the series, this narrative progression offers a satisfying dose of nostalgia mixed with new twists.However, TEKKEN 8 hasn't been without its share of criticism. User reviews reflect a mix of admiration and frustration. The game's online playability, a critical aspect for modern fighting games, has faced scrutiny. Players have reported issues with server stability and online matches, which are crucial elements for a game that relies heavily on its multiplayer experience. Additionally, the trend of offering early access to content for more expensive versions of the game has been a point of contention. This business model raises concerns about fairness and accessibility for all players. While these issues don't detract from the game's core appeal, they are significant enough to warrant attention from the developers.In conclusion, TEKKEN 8 is a bold step forward for the franchise, offering stunning visuals, an engaging story, and innovative gameplay mechanics. While it captivates with its high-octane battles and character customization, the game's online issues and business model practices have left some players feeling short-changed. Despite these drawbacks, TEKKEN 8 remains a compelling addition to the fighting game genre, promising hours of exhilarating entertainment for both new and veteran players.Interested in discovering great Steam games? _childDocuments_.review: i'm a tekken fan and this game is a great sequel to tekken 7, that's the short of it.Edit : i'm changing the review to bad for the reason that they decided to add micro transactions post launch.this in itself is not a huge issue but they employ dark pattern monetization meaning the prices of the things you can buy cannot be bought directly but rather the currency you need to buy is in packages of just too little, or just too much incentivising you to go for the next package up or simply buy more to even get rid of the rest of your coins burning a hole in your pocket, THIS is my REAL issue with the way they handle post launch monetization.further criticism is that the costumes are ports from older games, nostalgic yes, but add those in for free later at some point and actually put effort and money into making new and unique costumes, work for it.the fighter pass/ battle pass is again a practice i don't agree with as i'm forced to pay for a bunch of stuff i don't want to get to the stuff i do want.the objectives are unimaginative, basically just play games and win, herein lies the crux of a mission based system, if you want to add anything imaginative it becomes a chore for some, you don't wanna do some of the missions that are layed out before you, it doesn't fit a fighting game because there's very few things everyone wants to do or will do as they play the game. a battlepass doesn't belong in a fighting game.and here again the rewards are lackluster, some eyecolors, re-textures and a literal default 3D modeling software ball.all i can say is that the post launch support is not representative of the success and sales it made at launch.my fix : remove the premium currency, display actual prices in actual currenciesput the battlepass items on sale in the regular store, focus on the game and making it as fun as possible so that people want to play because they want to play and not because they need to complete their daily and weekly tasks like fomo sheep.it's incredibly short sighted and greedy, i don't know bandai namco's financial situation(with blue protocol notoriously being a massive money sink) but i do know i feel pissed on as someone who planned to be here for the next 10 years. : i think it's really good, the heatmode is fun, the passives it gives are fun and create risk/reward, ofcourse tekken just feels so good to play, and doing combo's is fun.the only complaint i have is being unable to decide if a move activates heat or not, i would have liked maybe HOLD to activate heat on hit, it often removes those moves on the movelist when it comes approaching the enemy if you don't want to use heat yet. : the actual story mode is about 6-7 hours long and FAR better then tekken 7's story, arcade story mode can vary from 4-10 depending on if you beat every single guy at the arcades or if you just rail straight through to the end.there is also Super ghost battles that uses the surprisingly good AI learning mode they have so you can fight your friends or random people from all across the world forever and increase your rank.then there is also the character stories and i'm so happy to see a return to form with these slightly short but very entertaining and fun little snippets of what the characters are up to, we'll see if they can keep it up with the upcoming DLC characters too.i sat at round 27 hours after beating all the singleplayer content. : the meat of the game, this is what is gonna keep you playing for hundreds of hours.the online is not as good as street fighter 6 but far better then tekken 7's netcode, i can play with my friend on the other side of the earth and i get 1 frame of rollback.if you'e having a terrible connection it's not because the game's netcode is bad, but it's because your wifi is dropping more packets then Amazon does in a day : this is where i live, i often just get fighting games to figure out the characters and do cool combo's. this practice mode is extremely good, the features that have been added are monumental timesavers for setting up situations and, for instance saving your position and state and being able to reset to it in a flash.Watching back replays lets the game analyze it and give you tips on how to punish moves and then lets you actually practice it instantly which is a HUGE feature for people wanting to get serious with the game. : another fun part of any 3D fighting game is character customization, it's an improvement, quality of over quantity this time around, fabric sticks closer to the skin in most regards, the fidelity is obviously higher,  and you can color basically everything, compared to previous entries there are few items to choose from (i don't consider a T-shirt with a different picture on it a unique item)there are misc items that you can put all over your body and you can get creative, but you can't put any item anywhere you want which i guess it to prevent people from making characters with D*cks : there are some strange quality of life features that have still not been added.you can't host a tekken ball game online in player match, you have to go to the arcade lobby and then to the beach area.no tournament mode, my friends and i like to run a tournament now and then, the tournament mode in T7 was incredible for that, but now we just have to keep our own bracket.this is definitely a very personal take but tekken ball is not very interesting, it does nothing particularly well compared to games with balls that are also fighting games like lethal league. : 70 euros is pretty steep if you're not planning to play with friends or online but you must put value to your own time, it's quality over quantity and overtime i have no doubt they'll add a lot more content.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never seen a game start out so amazing and fall this hard. When the game came out, it was awesome. Character creation was cool, they added a better assisted mode so people could just pick up and play the game, the story was neat, the gameplay was very solid. It wasn't perfect, but it was a very good start and they had plenty of time to fix the issues. Then, they added a store. This store only takes Tekken coins, which have to be bought. You have to buy a preset amount of coins with the lowest being 500 for 5 bucks. A skin costs 400, which means you'll be spending 5 bucks on a 4 buck costume with 1 buck left over. This is a scummy way to encourage people to buy more coins to get their full money's worth. This update didn't fix a lot of the issues the game had at launch. Then they added a battle pass. There's a free battle pass, but that's more of an ad for the paid battle pass. Once again, they didn't fix the issues the game had at launch. Now pluggers are put into the plugger pool, but it still feels like they're putting more effort into adding these money making features than features that will actually improve the game. I'm really disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I didn't play single player outside of training mode, I don't care about micro transactions and character customisationThe combat feels unrewarding and less interactive due to too many plus frames, armored moves and forced 50/50s. A lot of strings jail now, so no more sidestepping between blocks. Too many interactions feel unpolished, like characters flipping out of strings if you're slightly off-axis - same with stage hazards - or moves that have weird tracking properties. Heat feels braindead and I would like to see it leading to more interesting player decisions in the future. Overall I think T8 skews too much towards aggression (the dumb kind) and I wish Bamco found more of a middle ground between T7 and the current version of T8. Good thing is, everything is fixable with patches but it'll probably take quite a while until the game is somewhat polished. Netcode is decent enough and an improvement over 7, though not nearly as great as SF6's netcode.

_childDocuments_.review: I know that words are boring and reading sucks, but I feel like expressing some thoughts at the moment.Tekken 8, in my opinion, is the best fighting game compared to the two other titans: SF6 and MK1. I say this as a 20 YEAR mortal kombat enthusiast- I've been playing since MK:Deception. The problem is, it's eating ♥♥♥♥ commercially. Tekken is the weakest of the three at the moment- SF6 offers more bang for your buck, and WB is just as greedy as Bamco if not more- but they've delivered more content; earlier.With all this pretext, making an arena not included in the year pass is the equivalent of shooting yourself below the knee with a 4gauge shotgun in terms of just how much of a bad faith move it is. Whoever approved this decision is a demon. Not putting your stage in your season pass (that is supposed to have all the content in that season) is such a weird hill to die on.Since release, we got three characters, a bunch of clothes you have to pay extra for, and two maps. The second map, you also need to pay extra for. Make a good game, act on good faith, the money will come. Happy customers make you money. The extreme fetishist fixation on short term gain with more money in the CEO/Investor pockets and pennies for devs works, but your product WILL be more shallow compared to the competition. I am not very knowledgeable about SF6, but I do know that MK1 will end up with around ~35 characters, that is not including your kameo pairings making up for way more versatility in gameplay. They will end up with a good number of maps. They even have been gifting free costumes and palettes for multiple weeks before their expansion release.Serious changes in philosophy needed for the execs at Bandai Namco. You don't just need to "not do less"; you need to start doing more. The FGC is flourishing right now. So much hype, so many events, so much traffic. Tekken needs to aim above mediocre. Yes, you're a company- yes, you aim to make money. But "Money, NOOWW!!" is not the only thing there is, and I'm tired of monkeys pretending this is the only possible strategy for commercial purposes.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first fighting game I have ever purchased and the only one I have played other than super smash bros (which I haven't played in quite a few years).  I normally don't particularly care too much about in game cosmetics or battle passes to purchase them, so most of the talk of battle-passes and cosmetic purchases don't affect me at all (though I know I am probably in the minority). The way this game feels to play is awesome. Whenever I win, it's because I feel like I legitimately outplayed my opponent, while if I lose 99% of the time it's due to a lack of knowledge or skill against a certain character. The roster is, from my understanding, not very large for a fighting game, but it feels like every time I play the game I discover something new about playing it, whether that be the character I play or the character I play against. I guess my only slight complaint would be that it feels like in order to go up ranks you have to win significantly more than you lose, otherwise you will be stuck. Overall, if you don't care about the cosmetics/battle pass shenanigans the developers pulled I would highly recommend the game, it's very fun and rewarding.

_childDocuments_.review: Recent steam reviews criticizing Bandai Namco for banning a Chinese player from a tournament after the player came to a tournament and made it to top 8 in the bracket have been removed, so I'm adding mine.T8 has poor netcode, skins that were ported over from past games and look awful that are sold at a premium price, stages that aren't included in the DLC pass despite the fact that they impact balance and your online matchmaking pool, and generally less enjoyable gameplay than Tekken 7.The Heat system  encourages a hyper-aggressive style of play, leaning into risky 50/50 mix and chip damage.  Heat activation plus frames into 50/50 into heat extender into 50/50 into heat extender into 50/50 into plus frames and one more 50/50.  If the opponent is still alive, they can heat activate and are at rage art %.  Prepare to be snowballed into the corner and die.Low parry follow up damage has been nerfed into the ground.  The online lobby mode is garbage and way too difficult to actually play people in.3D fighting games need more competition.

Balance is another topic but I suppose Tekken isn't a game well known for a balanced roster.- 70 dollar base game with 100+ euro editions. _childDocuments_.review: Really love this game. It will remain to be seen how heat played out but right now during the honey moon phase the game is really fun. The game continues to do what Tekken does best: offer a fighting game package in which there is enough depth that you can pour 1000's of hours into the game and still have things to explore, but is also accessible enough that new players can hop in, find a character that seems cool and mash away. Heat is definitely a powerful mechanic, but I was surprised to find that there is quite a bit of strategy and decision making surrounding how to use it effectively. The meta does fall into how well you can use heat so it is absolutely the defining factor in matches but how to use heat has some depth to it. I think that in subsequent patches, the strength of some heat moves will be tuned down, as T7 slowly lowered the power of certain characters over time. But I think we're in a period now where the game feels explosive and fun, which honestly is great for the first season of a game. Refinement can be the flavor of the game over a long lifespan, but the first few months-year I'm okay with being a slugfest personally.To me the biggest drawbacks are QOL and optimization. Currently there is no benchmark to play online, so if another player's PC cannot properly run the game, the game will stutter. They really need to add a benchmark / recommended for online setting type of system to 1) reduce stuttering 2) not alienate the players on lower power PC's but instead guide them to the correct settings to reduce stuttering. There are many upscaling options but how they work are a blackbox. The other issue is the complete lack of infinite matches and poorly optimized user experience. FT2 in ranked is fine, but having player matches and lounge matches also be FT2 makes no sense. In a game as difficult as Tekken, it can be really difficult to learn match ups if new players are only encountering 1 character on a 32 roster every once in a while and then for only a 2, maybe 3 games at best. Also searching for lobbies needs to be implemented. I am part of a discord community and when we are trying to play with players in other platforms and are unable to invite via stream, it becomes a game of refreshing the available lobbies over and over until our lobby comes up. Overall, I love Tekken and I think this is a great game for newcomers and veterans a lot. If you go into this game with the right mindset, it's just the best.

_childDocuments_.review: Decades of being a gamer but I've never been a Tekken player. Played a decent amount of Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter, but the few times I tried Tekken it felt sluggish with characters not as appealing as the other ones I liked. Then tried Tekken 8 demo during a time I was playing Street Fighter 6 and thought to myself: "this gameplay sucks, they can't even jump".But watching that story so far video with Brian Cox and learning about the plot of the whole thing made me curious about the story mode. And Azucena's gameplay trailer made me realize the gameplay can be faster than two muscly guys punching each other like in the demo. So that's how I got into it.Played the story mode first and... well... it was underwhelming to say the least. Especially compared to Netherrealm Studios' story modes. Most of the time you play as Jin and even when you aren't, you keep fighting against Kazuya. It was super boring, at least for me as a newcomer even after watching all the "previously on Tekken" videos.But that is the only negative I've felt against the game. Once I realized how technically rich and unique the game is and how every single character is the same in some ways but different at the same time, I've been trying to get better at it like I've never done before. The Arcade Quest mode is a wonderful entry point for the newcomers and taught me a lot. I now feel like this is the ultimate fighting game with the best gameplay mechanics. Even bought a fight stick as I wanted to be more precise. Because ranked play is an addiction.

_childDocuments_.review: The devs intentionally hid their desire to monetize just about every system in the game and, after a few weeks of being out, are now revealing a premium currency shop, which will effectively render in-game currency totally useless, while charging players for even more than the prior Tekken did. The devs knew people wouldn't like it, and they waited so they could sneak it past ratings boards, so they could get the goodwill of the players, before revealing their intentions. All characters will (of course) continue to be monetized, all character cosmetics will be monetized (including costumes and various pieces of clothing), all player avatar cosmetics will be monetized, and no word on how egregious premium currency bundles will be., so even if prices end up theoretically being low, there still may be a high buy-in cost, having to buy more currency than you need.All of this, in a $70 game :) since, you know, increasing the price by $10 for just the basic version wasn't enough.The devs knew people would be upset, and they wanted the glowing reviews and good PR, as well as not having this practice put on their game by ratings boards. They knowingly kept this from players, and lied by omission to ensure that more people would get into this, and to keep review scores high, as well as ensuring that physical releases of the game would have no mention of their in-game spending by ratings boards.Harada's a conman lol.Still no rollback netcode btw. It would be cool if their antics at least went toward making a better game, but instead, it's just gonna end up in someone's pockets.As far as gameplay goes, this game is a lot of fun, and, from a gameplay feel, is without a doubt the best Tekken that's been made in a very long time. The story feels like it needed way more time and budget, its boss fights are its lowest points, and I wouldn't recommend approaching it from anything even resembling a critical perspective xD Customization is pretty good, a big step up from Tekken 7, but it's all going to be monetized, going forward, so enjoy having everything that comes next locked behind a paywall lol.Gameplay is fun, game's monetization is bad, the devs just want to fleece you and take advantage of your passion. I wouldn't recommend unless you want to enable the unethical, exploitative, practices a corpo pretending to be part of the FGC.--updating to say: I told you so.---

But the big question is...is it BETTER? In most ways yes. However for right now the game is completely BANANAS in terms of balancing. Characters like Devil Jin have an instant, full screen, plus on block, leading to okie heat smashes. If that sounds bloated to you....it's cause it is. However stuff like this will matter little to your average Joe who just wants to play some Tekken. While the game may be crazy for competitive players, anyone who's casual is going to be hard pressed to find a better Tekken game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tekken 8 is my first Tekken game ever. I'm not huge into fighting games, however I probably have about 125-150 hours across the Mortal Kombat and Soul Calibur  franchises.Getting right into it, I am in love with Tekken 8. Clocking about 30 hours so far, the game has a way of teaching you the mechanics like non other through the various modes then game provides, right down to specific character mechanics. The practice tool is extremely versatile and helps you practice specific moves as much as you wish, where as the Arcade Quest Mode teaches you the generic mechanics of the game while facing seemingly more and more difficult challengers as you progress and learn to use the taught mechanics. Definitely recommend Arcade Quest to be your first stop as a new Tekken player.The AI Ghost Battles are a fantastic addition to fighting games in general and I hope to see it in more games going forward as it is another great tool for practice.Online play has been challenging as veteran players make there way up the ranks from the bottom.I can see and feel myself improving at a steady pace with lots of practice, which keeps me coming back for more. Those wanting a more social aspect to their fighting games will love the Tekken Fight Lounge, a virtual space in which your player avatar from the Arcade Quest Mode can walk around and interact with other players.Customization of characters is very good in Tekken 8 and allows players to feel as though there characters are truly their own. It can leave me wanting more in some areas when it come to customizing, but I don't think that what makes a fighting game great, so I can't let that hold it back.Tekken 8 is a 9/10 fighting game that is worth every penny to those willing to put in the time to learn the game at a controlled pace. I truly do not have many if any, negative things to say about the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Wanted to write a new review after clocking over 100 hours. I'm deeply in love with the game, but it has some big issues so I want to list both the good and the bad!The good:-It's Tekken. Deep and complex mechanics, with a large roster and huge movelists. A detriment to those who want a game to pick up easy wins with (cheese stops working once people start passing knowledge checks), but for those who have an improvement mindset this game is an absolute DRUG as there is a near-infinite amount of meaningful player skill progression.-General gameplay and visual polish is pretty high quality, be in its animations, visual effects, graphics, etc. Really great newcomers too.-Training mode and replay functions are INSANELY well featured. Punishment training, ability to take control of your character during replays, comprehensive attack and frame data, and combo trials are just a few notable features. This game REALLY gives you the tools to actually learn the game, and this is easily the best training mode in all of Tekken, as well as one of the best in all of fighting games.-It has a tutorial! Arcade quest is actually pretty decent for teaching new players Tekken 8's mechanics, even if it is a bit ugly and should actually just be...labeled as the tutorial.-Lots of content between story mode, character stories, Tekken ball, ranked, quick play, and Tekken lounge. Lobby system seems to be decently robust too.-Rollback netcode exists and the online is very playable with wired to wired on systems that can run the game at a consistent 60FPS. Much better than Tekken 7's netcode imo, but this will often fall apart with wifi and low-end PCs, which I will touch on in the bad sectionThe mixed bag:-Heat system. IMO it is really interesting since it adds new mechanics to each character on activation, but there are many who dislike it due to its ability to tack on 50/50s. I'm not as quick to write it off because there is 1000% counterplay to heat mechanics (a lot of people just... lack the knowledge and skill), but I do get that a lot of people dislike 50/50 mechanics in their fighting games. People will have different preferences/tolerances to this, so into the mixed section it goes.-Tekken shop. The price for skins at $4 is very reasonable IMHO. What is less reasonable is Bandai Namco implementing the shop a month after release and forcing you to pay $5 for credits to buy $4 skins. Scummy for SURE, but I think $5 is also... fine? It is stupid, but whatever it is still fairly cheap. Doesn't affect me that much cause you don't need cosmetics to play the game (and I don't plan on buying many if at all), but a lot of people do care so this is here for awareness sake.-The community. If you can find friendly players who are improvement driven and have small egos, you'll have a great time. There are a number of wholesome content creators and communities for this game out there. Local scenes are great too if you have access to them. On the other hand, the general online community for Tekken 8 has kind of become a negative echo chamber, and the issues with the online listed in the next section below combined with a lot of people's fragile egos REALLY exacerbate this. Reddit and Steam forums for T8 have kind of become miserable to be around and I recommend not spending too much time in those places for mental health purposes.The bad:-Online can be a hitch-filled crap-shoot when wifi gets thrown into the mix since the netcode is not great at handling packet loss. On top of that, if you are matched against a PC that can't run the game at 60FPS, the game slows down for everyone. There really needs to be an online benchmark that requires 60FPS to go online. If you're on older lower-end hardware, I implore you to lower settings so the game runs at 60. It will be better for everyone, yourself included-Performance issues and crashes are still a thing. It's less buggy than day 1 but I still hear people getting issues from time to time so more definitely can be done by the devs at this front.-Ragequitting is a big issue. Disconnecting on a game before the match ends does not count as a loss, so many players will plug before the game is over. This creates an inconsistent and toxic online ranked experience, and it hurts other people's promotions and winstreaks for even being in the same match. Bandai Namco is starting to ban people for serial disconnects, but this doesn't really solve the problem as serial pluggers can just buy the game again. The obvious simple solution would be to make it so that disconnecting = a loss for the one who disconnected, and serial ragequitters should be put into a matchmaking queue with other serial ragequitters until they've played enough sets to reset their disconnection rate. This is well-documented to work in other online fighting games and I don't get why Tekken isn't doing the same.My Recommendation:I do recommend Tekken 8, though it unfortunately has some pretty glaring issues in its online and ranked systems in its current state, and the Tekken devs keep skirting around the issue of ragequitting, which mind you has been a long running problem since the series has had online functionality. Still well worth picking up imo, especially if you have friends, a group, or a local scene to play with. But dear god, all the devs have to do is just make it so disconnect = loss. If my power, internet, or game goes out during a set, that's my L to hold. The same should go for intentional disconnects. That is simply just the fairest way.Additional thoughts:This game is HARD AS HELL. No matter what, at some point there are going to be other players that will DESTROY you, and there is no getting around it. If you are someone looking for constant wins to boost your pride, this game will eventually give you the hardest reality check, and if you can't get past that you won't last very long. But if you are are able to swallow your pride, take the time to gain the knowledge and learn from your mistakes, and relish in small incremental victories of improving your skills bit by bit rather than the color of your rank, you will have a long and rewarding journey with this franchise as a whole.

_childDocuments_.review: "Tekken 8: A Visual Feast, But Missing the Classic Tekken Force Mode"Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)Tekken 8 delivers a stunning visual spectacle that surpasses its predecessors, showcasing the capabilities of modern gaming technology. The character models are incredibly detailed, animations are smooth, and the environments are a treat for the eyes. The vibrant colors and attention to detail make each battle feel like a cinematic experience, truly elevating the overall aesthetic of the game.The character roster boasts a diverse range of fighters, each with their unique fighting styles and flashy moves. The fluidity of combat animations adds a layer of realism, making every punch, kick, and special move visually captivating. The game's visuals contribute significantly to the immersive nature of the battles, creating a visually engaging experience for both casual players and competitive fighters.However, the absence of the beloved Tekken Force mode is a notable disappointment. Fans of the series have come to expect this classic beat 'em up mode as a staple in Tekken titles. The lack of Tekken Force in Tekken 8 feels like a missed opportunity to provide players with an additional layer of gameplay variety. This mode added a unique blend of action and storytelling, and its exclusion leaves a void in the overall content package.

_childDocuments_.review: For as interesting as it is, Tekken 8 is a hot mess. Nothing glaring stands out from a distance; an addition to a long time fighting game. It kinda achieves that, kinda not. This game is hyper monetized to it's own undoing. 70 dollar game has 40 dollar better "edition", which gives you 4 of the likely many more DLC characters, and a handful of little skin items. This does not include the paid Battlepass with mostly recycled skins and content, or the entire slew of paid skin options for every single character. Micro-transaction heaven.I can't tell if this game is a really poor port to PC, or it's just straight up broken. Immediately after download it crashed on launch first itself, then my whole computer saying "Not enough VRAM". I have 24GB. The Recommended amount is 8GB. After some googling, it seems to be an issue people have at seemingly random, have been having since release, and is not hardware dependent at all. (Happening on both Intel and AMD CPUs,  nor caring if it was a Nvidia or  AMD GPU) Some of the ways people were citing to fix this include but are not limited to: Changing the .exe file to a windows 7 compatibility setting, running the program as Admin every time you launch it, using the steam launcher settings to run DirectX11/12, and launching the game in windowed mode. From the looks of it the developers have not fixed, nor acknowledged this issue, nor provided any support or information for those having this issue After some combination of these, the game appeared to function "normal", if normal means punching your CPU's usage through the roof in the character selection screen. The optimization of several portions of this game are atrocious. So poorly optimized and drinking of hardware problems, that it brought a motherboard bios inconsistency into the light being had with high end Intel CPUs drawing insane amounts of power and degrading the silicon to the point of nonfunctional. Granted this is due in part to Intel's motherboard manufacturers not being held on a leash, and pushing the power limits to ungodly heights in the sake of allowing the customer that little ounce more power, but at the same time, I have *never* seen any game hit my CPU that hard. Cinebench and 3Dmark do that, but they're supposed to. A character selection screen should not be doing this. Paying 70+ USD for a game that requires you change seemingly random settings on the files of the game itself just to be functional is not acceptable in my eyes. Much less with the anticipation that you then go and spend more money on all number of little things.If you can look past these pains, the 70+ dollar game is alright. Visually it's pretty pleasing, a large step over it's predecessors. The music and art of the maps is brimming with life and detail. I have yet to try the story mode, but doubt it'll change my opinion on the game as a whole. Game play is interesting, yet weird. There's no defined balance in anything, and the game has possibly become over-bloated compared to what the initial intent of the series was. Characters have so many moves that each individual player can use a totally unique combination of them and present a totally different fighting experience compared to any other combination. Enough so that the individual characteristics of any given character starts to become blurred, while the focus is forced to shift to learning the handful of openers that your opponent uses, and just counter those. Or if it's someone using a selection you're not used to, good luck. That's not inherently a bad thing, but even compared to Tekken 7, Tekken 8 feels like it's purpose has dulled of sorts. Every character has more over match abilities, damage can be dealt through blocks, making rounds even quicker then they already are. A nondescript healing system was added to seemingly counteract that damage among other things, and try and make matches slightly longer/less predetermined. It doesn't feel very effectual. The balancing of these powerful moves feels quite distant, even after supposedly several patches trying to change this precedent a bit. Maybe I'm thinking too hard into it and I'm really just bad at the game. TL:DR Too pricey for extreme lackluster. Wait for sale if you must. Not recommended, but somewhat fun if you do purchase.
