_childDocuments_.review: A lot has changed since the game's release. Upon release, it had bare-bones customisation for characters. With a later emphasis on "unlocking more" by purchasing cosmetics with real money, to then release a Battle Pass system, in a fully priced triple-A game. To the consistent nerfing of Leroy, to "balance changes" that ruin creativity, this game is worse than Tekken 7 in its current form as of this review. Need I remind you that Tekken 8 sold millions per gaming platform. It didn't need this.This isn't an "Early Access" game. It has its issues, which may or may not be ironed out, however it is the price of a full triple-A game, which you have to remember before making any financial purchasing decisions, The story picks off after Tekken 7. During, we only saw Jin once, at its end. Now, we play as him for the majority of T8. The story is about 4 hours long, has its spectacular moments, but isn't groundbreaking either. It ends on a cliffhanger and doesn't feel fulfilling. The cutscenes, animation, voice lines, good. see you playing as other characters. Which is a great way to encourage the player to use more than one character! Each character story has its own ending. Some are funny, some are awkward.The roster is good, having many returning characters from Tekken 7. Each and every character has changed, in either good, or bad ways. It has been argued that  and that is true for what's on offer. The counter play to strong opponents now, bounds down to a "50/50 casino guessing game". It gets boring fast, regardless of how skilled you are as a player. What I'm saying is, yes, characters like Victor or Dragonuv can be labbed, (practice mode) but when you're up against 50/50 mixup pressure, all you can do is make reads and guess what your opponent is going to do. At times, It feels less like a fighting game and more like a guessing game. However, this isn't always the case.The first DLC character to come to Tekken 8 is Eddy, whom previously came with the main game of Tekken 7. He wasn't the most popular character. In Tekken 8, it appears he has a few simplified "easy" combos. Namely, pressing 3,3,3,3,3,3,3,3 gives him a 61dmg combo.Some characters from the previous game, are now simply too strong. Dragonuv, for example. He went from a safe, poking, counter-hit seeking character, into a pressure-into-CH guessing game tool. Feng Wei is another example. He has every tool in the game. Evasiveness, parries, great throw game, pressure into safe 50/50 mixups, and insanely strong low attacks.The Heat System is a unique take on Tekken, where it temporarily gives the player a very strong buff to where they can produce a strong 50/50 mix-up, leaving your opponent to guess how you're going to attack. It can lead your character dealing half health damage to your opponent if used correctly.Heat Burst activation gives your character the armor property, meaning you can push through opponents attacks, resulting in yours connecting. On connection, it deals a quarter if not more of the opponent's health bar. It's a "haha, I win!" button. The only difference between Heat Burst and Rage Art, is that on block, the Heat Burst is safe, AND gives you a 50/50.Rage Art is a carry-over from Tekken 7. A move that becomes available when your character is around 15% health. It turns your health bar red, and you get access to two options. You deal more damage, and you have a one-time use attack, which is punishable on block. Rage Arts changed in Tekken 8, where the punishment frames are now 15, meaning most 16 frame (and above) launchers don't connect. It is a dumb change, because the attack itself deals nearly half your health bar. It can be used in combos as an "ender", but due to damage mitigation after each hit, it doesn't do AS much damage, thankfully.Overall, it takes me out of the experience of having pre-ordered the most expensive version of Tekken 8. It is the reason I made this negative review.One month after the game's initial release, Namco released an update where players could purchase cosmetic items for $4 each. Some of these were  re-used assets from previous Tekken games. (pictured: Tekken 6 Kazuya costume, a game from 2007.) Two months after release, Namco unveiled the "Tekken Pass", another take on the popular "Battle-Pass" which Freemium games use to make money.The practice itself preys on "FOMO", the "fear of missing out". Overall , as it requires them to contribute their time, and money. It also means, that for the participating player to level up the pass, they will play the game even when they don't want to.  as your payment does not guarantee you the items included in the pass, as you are given an arbitrary time limit to complete the pass.---Another way Battle Pass systems encourage the damaging of mental health. A player will see other players with cosmetics, that they want. They then become addicted to the system, playing the game 24/7, draining their social and mental batteries. This will not affect everyone,  It is important to avoid games with time-exclusive Battle Pass systems if you have these issues.---In the past, I myself have suffered at the hands of another game and succumbed to "brain rot". I couldn't not play this other game, because I wanted to level up the BP each month. I couldn't think for myself, or do anything else. It was difficult to recover from. I could only think about this one game, and its fancy, shiny cosmetics. It took my time, money, and mental stability away from me. This was years ago, I'm fine now. This will unfortunately encourage players to purchase it, so they can "reap the rewards" of the paid tier up to that point.  Not to mention, the items included in the pass (which costs $10) are FROM PREVIOUS TEKKEN GAMES. Character profiles, cosmetics,  The Tekken Pass could very well change the player community as a whole. The gameplay itself between players was already very aggressive, due to the inclusion of the Heat system. And now with the Battle Pass, it will encourage players (whom are addicted to FOMO) to play even more aggressively, possibly increasing the frustration of the base players if not leading to other emotions.Tekken is in no-way under financial ruin. With millions of copies sold per gaming platform, it didn't need this. Now, during gameplay of my paid game, I will have to put up with  advertised to me, IN A PAID GAME. No thank you!Every character in the game has been nerfed, due to Devil Jin's ability to floor break stages, which had an issue with damage scaling. Wall and Floor Breaks no longer work during combos. Whether or not this is patched, we've yet to see. It was likely an unintentional change, but it could've been handled better.This recent change destroys creativity during combos, as floor breaks, etc, were key to pulling off flashy moves.A common meme, but true; Thank you for reading my review! (ran out of txt space.)

_childDocuments_.review: Tekken 8, while undeniably more accessible than its predecessors, has stripped away much of the tactical depth that defined the series. The game feels like it's been simplified to cater to a larger player base, but at the cost of what made Tekken unique. What we're left with is a game that's largely about 50/50 situations, with little room for the nuanced, defensive play that even 2D fighting games manage to preserve.One of the biggest disappointments for me is how defense is not only unrewarded but outright punished, particularly with the introduction of chip damage. In other fighting games, there are defensive tools to counterbalance aggressive play, but in Tekken 8, it feels like the game is designed to reward the player who can memorize the best combos and apply pressure non-stop. The Ranked matches exacerbate this issue, becoming a toxic experience where opponents either quit after one match, have unbearable lag, or exhibit other frustrating behaviors.After over 100 hours of trying to give this game a chance, I've lost the drive to continue. I might revisit it if Kunimitsu is reintroduced, but for now, Tekken 8 is getting uninstalled. I'm finding more satisfaction in games like Guilty Gear Strive or Granblue Fantasy Versus Rising, where my efforts in practicing hit confirms are actually rewarded, unlike in Tekken 8, where any attempt at analysis seems to get me punished anyway.The final straw for me is the Battle Pass system, which feels even more intrusive and unpleasant in Tekken 8 than in Rising. It's a feature I genuinely dislike and it only adds to my overall disappointment with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: So I just got to God of Destruction with King and felt the need to leave a review. So I understand that people feel that this game is a casino game and that it isn't tekken. I believe that there is still a lot of older tekken in there, but it doesn't give crazy reward to turtling like 7 did. Yes aggression is key and I don't hate it. I was also a player who prefered clean telken and defense in 7. So obviously heat being a big addition, many people do not know how to use it correctly and many people do not know the weaknesses and how to counterplay other characters stuff including their heat. I don't know how to deal with high level hworangs stance pressure does that make the character broken? No. Same thing applies to heat with exceptions of course like dvj heat smash being damn near homing  Kings heat smash is also very strong in terms of damage, however the unbreakble grab is reactavle to duck to and a lot of people don't practice that so of course its gonna feel broken. Also I notice a lot of players that try to move and get punished and conplain that the character is broken or certain moves are too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Remember, with some exceptions in the game, there is counterplay, and just because sidestep block or duck isn't the answer for everything doesn't make the game a casino. It means you have to think and time your buttons, while incorporating sidestep, watching out for grabs so you can break on reaction, finding opportunities to use your characters full potential, observe and understand the offense and defense of your opponent to make educated guesses on their move choice and timings. Yes it is hard and if you find yourself getting washed, don't think the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, cause you only have the right to say that once you learn why it is and if you are even good enough at tekken 8 to make an opinion. If you are fujin and you feel as if azucena is too busted, yet so many people of different characters have fought the same character and play style and manage to win then is it the characters or is it your gameplay that is the problem.  The game does have consistent ways to play, are some characters too strong sure, but there were characters that were too strong tekken 7 like akuma that can do death combos. The game is easier to pick up than 7 and people think it is easier because alot of new players are facing each other and getting to blue ranks. Once you make it tekken king atleast where you start to learn the deeper intricacies of the game, of course there is gonna be players at every rank where you think how did this guy get here. But in general, alot of matchups can be learned up here and I find it fun slowly seeing counterplay to things that I thought there were no answers to. In conclusion, my opinion is that the game is fun and good. _childDocuments_.review: Yes, I highly recommend buying Tekken 8. This game will please both the newcomer and the veteran fighting game player. In terms of content, this game has much to offer since the basic game has 32 characters, which is quite the feat for a fighting game. And do you want to know the neat part ? On average, every character has at least a 100 different moves in their movelist. Yep, you read that right, so needless to say that there's a lot of complexity in this game, the gameplay is rich as it's always been the case for the Tekken serie, and this game introduces a new mechanic called "Heat" that encourages offensive plays. Now, as a complete beginner, that might scare you off, but fear not, as this game also clear tutorials and different modes to learn how to play. Everything is well explained, and there's even a new tool in replay mode where you can actually watch your games and replay some actions to understand how to counter some moves. In terms of solo content, this game does the job in fighting game standards, there's a complete story mode with nice cinematics and an arcade mode for each character. Unfortunately, it's not a perfect game because a few things here and there are still "questionnable" to say the least : - While the customization is way better than what you can find in other fighting games, it's kind of annoying that they didn't put some features present in older games, and the base content regarding custom items is rather small. - It's a been a month since release and there are some problems regarding ranked ( cheaters and "pluggers"; people who ragequit games ) and nothing has been done yet. - They introduced microtransactions a few weeks after release, whereas it doesn't annoy me that much since it's only for cosmetics, some people mightt not like it and it was kind of a shady move to wait reviews before bringing them. All in all, excellent game, they clearly didn't miss the mark with Tekken 8 and released a very solid entry, this will be one of the best fighting game for years to come. However, it's a shame that there are still some problems online ( that were also in Tekken 7 ) and that they haven't solved them yet, but with some qol changes that might come in the next months, Tekken 8 might become even better.

_childDocuments_.review: One line review: Tekken8 is amazing.Slightly expanded review: Probably the biggest leap in quality since Tekken2->3, 8 refines the mechanics from T7, adds modern controls a la SF6, hugely improves the graphics and sound, adds cross play and PvP rematches and makes the game much more accessible to boot. It also adds a real money shop, which, well, is not popular, but is also entirely ignorable.The sound in particular is great - a blocked quick jab might sound a bit mid, but most hits sound like a damn gunshot and add a heck of a lot to the atmosphere.The cast of characters is also diverse and fascinating, from giant hugely hard hitting war robots to a hyperfast peruvean coffee-saleswoman who likes nothing more than doging your attacks to hit you from the back, literal devils and demons, a chavvy kind of boxer, a hotheaded taekwando expert, happy shopper bruce lee, a giant championship wrestler who think he's a cat, two kinds of bear, knock-off magic Blade, a gun-toting cyro-frozen irish assassin, a french spymaster who thinks karambit knives are somehow acceptable in a fist fight, a space alien octopus robin hood ninja thing, an egyptian lady who has the literal god of war stuck in her hand somehow and a good two dozen more. More will come with DLC, ofc, but there are plenty to choose from and lots to experiment with.The really great thing about tekken is that it has an almost abyssal level of depth, with so many mechanics, both new and old. Now this might seem like it would make the game hard to learn, especially if you're new to the series, but it's also really intuitive. You have four buttons, left and right kicks, and left and right punches. That's it! If you want to do a quick right left combo, you press right punch, then left punch. Easy.If you have good timing, are patient and understand distancing even a little bit, you really don't even need a tutorial, it's that welcoming.Now, all the above is really only about the PvP mode(s). SP has always been a bit thin in tekken games, but fwiw, I think it's probably at it's best here; there's the campaign which to its credit has tried to mix things up a bit, character episodes which also focus on the non-mainstream characters a bit more, arcade and arcade quest mode and also ghost battles. I guess it's alright? Tekken ball makes a return from 3, which is great, but you can't play it online for no good reason I can think of (e: you can, im just a big dummy, see comments), but the SP definitely takes a back-seat to the PvP modes.There's also a bunch of nice touches, like how you can play as Tekken3 Jin, how the characters have rivalries and neat fight intros with their nemeses, replays which have advice when you watch them, kazuya's tits are FINALLY splashed all over the main menu*, there is the customary Tekken silliness, weirdness and ott anime moves and also Heihachi Mishima, possibly literally the most terrible person in the world, and easily the worst parent ever has died**. And then reincarnated as his own illegitimate daughter who is, if anything, even more horrifying to fight against. And she also has the devil gene that is basically the reason for everyone fighting in the first place, because of course she does.*: Now you can choose which character you see**: He's alive now, ofcIf you want an example of how silly it can get, here's Panda winning the tournament and then failing to deal with a chair: I like it. I think it's great and i'm going to play some more right now. But I'm still terrible at it.

_childDocuments_.review: TEKKEN 8 continues the tragic saga of the Mishima bloodline and its world-shaking father-and-son grudge matches. This latest saga begins with Jin Kazama facing off against Kazuya Mishima in a city-shattering face-to-face showdown. After defeating his father, Heihachi Mishima, Kazuya continues his conquest for global domination, using the forces of G Corporation to wage war on the world. Jin is forced to face his fate head on as he is reunited with his long lost mother, and seeks to stop his father Kazuya's reign of terror. Absent for over 25 years, Jun Kazama re-joins TEKKEN 8 as a playable character. [Bandai Namco]

name: Pine Hearts
detailed_description: Welcome to Pine Hearts Caravan Park! As Tyke, hop into your hiking boots and explore the paths and rivers of this cosy little world. Rummage around the park and find handy tools that will help you on your journey as you fill out your trusty hillwalking journal. Rediscover memories of Tyke's time in the park many summers ago and unearth the heartfelt story of his childhood. 👩‍🌾 Make new friends 🛠️ Unlock tools and abilities 🏕️ Rediscover memories 🐶 Pet cute dogs Every inch of the park has little surprises waiting for you to discover! A Touching Tale Pine Hearts is a warm, thoughtful game about love, life, memories, and family. It tells a story of the loss of a family member with tenderness and care, but please be aware of this subject matter before playing the game ❤️ Wholesome Classics Pine Hearts takes the item-based progression of Zelda, combines it with Souls-like level design and wraps it all up in a wholesome aesthetic with a focus on puzzles, not combat 🌳 No Barriers To Play We’ve worked hard to make Pine Hearts as accessible as possible. Some of the key Accessibility features include: Simplified Controls Colour Blocking Mode Black and White Mode High Contrast Mode Visual FX Toggles Font Scaling Full Controller/KB+M Remapping

_childDocuments_.review: is a short and cozy exploration game with a small emotional story to guide you along the way.From an isometric perspective, you control a cute and colorful nugget character as he wanders the tranquil world of Pine Hearts Caravan Park, meets various NPCs and helps them with their tasks. The map is rather vast and the game is heavily focused on exploring it, as there are no quest markers (neither to distinguish the NPCs that can give you a quest from the rest of the NPCs, nor for the items you are required to fetch), nor a detailed map of all paths possible. Available is only a top-level map of the game world that displays the regions, but not the connections between them or any other details such as paths or points of interest.However, the game is split into distinctive regions, and accessing them requires obtaining a specific ability, which is unlocked by gathering enough “droplets”. These can be obtained not only by completing quests but also by interacting with various objects in the game world or simply collecting them from your path, as you explore the maze-like environment. Without a map, navigating the world is not exactly trivial (especially for those without a clear sense of direction like me), as you have to project the zones visited in your mind and obviously remember their location, together with which NPC gives you which quest. Unfortunately, only the quests belonging to the main storyline are shown and not the side quests (which are encountered in much higher numbers than the former).While I could think of several QoL features that I would like to see in the game, I’m deeply appreciative of how much effort was put into accessibility options. There are several color palettes to choose from, and the interactable objects (including the NPCs) are brightly colored to distinguish them from the muted colors of the environment. To be honest, this was extremely helpful to me during the end game (even if I don’t have any disabilities) for gathering those last difficult-to-find droplets required for the hardest achievement of the game: gathering all 1500 of them. While roughly 1300 are obtained through quests and from wandering around, the last ~200 come from object interactions or other areas reachable only after unlocking all abilities. The map is also designed so that even the early zones contain areas accessible only with fully unlocked abilities, thus a full traversal through the entire map will be required for this achievement. I would have really liked to see from which of these zones I can still collect droplets, as opposed to wandering around aimlessly until I find something to interact with, but unfortunately, this information is not available to the player. The rest of the achievements are naturally unlocked as you play and complete quests. None of them are missable, as you can always return to the previous zones to obtain them and they’re color-coded based on the region they belong to, which is quite helpful.’ story is not the one that drives the gameplay forward, as it consists only of five miniature memories of the character and his father. However, they’re quite emotional and are bound to touch your heart, even if they’re short-lived. These memories, together with all the cute interactions that you can do with the objects in the environment and the colorful, positive visuals give the game a heartfelt, wholesome vibe.  is certainly a chill and enjoyable ride that will take you between five and seven hours to complete, depending on how much you like to dawdle, yet pretty expensive for the content that it offers.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure why  hasn't had more publicity. I was surprised to see that it only has 41 reviews so I wanted to write a nice review about it because I really enjoyed the game, and you will too if you like exploration and quests. Straight away from the train journey into Pine Hearts you will get cosy and heart-warming vibes just from the upbeat music and colourful graphics. Of course, everyone is super friendly in Pine Hearts and it is the sort of place where you would probably like to live, with camaraderie abundant to see, and loads of colourful characters to meet who are more than happy to lay all their chores on you. The game is very much quest based, performing tasks for people who have mislaid something, or want something delivered, or want you to collect items to fix something. You know how it goes. The characters are very interesting and you will spot connections between them which gives a nice community feel to the game. Often, you walk into situations where people are socialising or performing goofy stuff which will make you smile. Just interacting with everyone is fun because they will either give you a quest or have a humorous answer. It's definitely a feel-good game. Even though some characters do briefly show you where items are, with the camera shooting off to their location and back, you have to pay attention as there is no second chance, although occasionally characters will remind you of your task if you ask again. There’s also an active quest reminder in your journal but it just tells you what the quest is and gives no other information. Completing quests earns you equipment which is needed to progress and also gives you droplets which is sort of the currency in the game. You will need to collect enough droplets to unlock memories which in turn give you extra skills. There are four skills to collect and learn which open up areas which would have been previously inaccessible. The skills are climbing, jumping, moving blocks, and pushing trees to bridge gaps. All these skills are easy to perform but you will have to action a simple sequence of button pushes and thumb stick movement to do these. Personally, I would have just preferred pressing one button to action these skills as it felt a little frustrating going through the motions of pressing ‘A’ then ‘up’ on the thumb stick or similar. There was no challenge in doing the sequence so why bother? Game play is arranged so that early on quests are manageable with the equipment you already own but you will notice that lots of areas are inaccessible because they are blocked by rocks or chasms or need to be reached through climbing. These areas get unlocked by completing quests and earning enough droplets to unlock a memory which gives you a skill. Pine Hearts is reasonably big and although there is a very crude map there are no quest locators or any other help to aid you in finding characters or items you need. This means you will be doing a lot of backtracking, hitting brick walls, and getting lost. Your main tool will be your memory and remembering shortcuts and how areas fit together. There can be a lot of time saved through shortcuts, like a fallen tree saving you going around the long way, but there will always be a path to adjacent areas. Getting lost is a source of frustration but I guess if everything was laid out for you it would be too easy. There is a small story which plays out as you unlock memories and is quite poignant and sad. There are five memory clips, but because they are spaced out throughout the game they can be easily forgotten, but for such a brief story it leaves quite a powerful impression and ties together quests and stories you may have heard throughout the game and brings everything together. _childDocuments_.review: 7 hours 3/10 1 I wrote . No No Maybe the 1500 collectibles, finding the last ones you're missing can be a challenge No No No No No, you can use the accessibility features freely and still unlock everything NoSometimes you instantly fall in love with a game in the first 30 minutes. Pine Hearts did this for me! When the game starts and your first quest is to pet the dog, it is a great start! And after that, it only got better and better. However, I also want to mention that Pine Hearts has very emotional moments. It is based on the creative developer losing his dad in a very short time and while the game is wholesome it also touches on the sad feelings of losing your dad. The implementation of those feelings is done in such a beautiful way. I can imagine how challenging the development must have been with a project so close to his heart, but the love and beautiful memories he has shines through the game and I hope it also helped focus on those beautiful memories. So why did I fall in love so quickly? It starts with how cute this game looks and there went so much attention to detail. What I love about that is how they highlight all those little details by making it reward you with collectibles.  Do you see a crab with a crow? Pet it to get a collectible! Do you see a sea otter? wave at it to get a collectible. There are canons broken? Fix them to get a collectible. What is also implemented in a great way is the interactions you do with a controller for each interaction you want to do. There is a headlight and it can run out of battery, then you have to take it off your head and recharge it by rotating your left thumbstick. If you want to dig you pick up your shovel and first press the left thumbstick down and then press it up.  If you don't like this or can't do this, the accessibility settings have the option to turn this off and have simple controls. Speaking about the accessibility settings, there are so many great settings in this menu. For example, there is the option to standard run, or standard walk, or switch between them with a button press. There also is an option to highlight all the interactive things so it is easier to differentiate between things that are for show and things that are important to the game. It is so nice when a developer wants to include everybody and find ways to implement accessibility features to make the game playable for a wider audience.Another thing that I love about Pine Hearts is how it uses the Steam achievements to challenge you to do more and find more things to do than the main quest line. Almost every easter egg and little activity is tied to an achievement and this way a lot of people will get to see everything in the game. It is also done well how the achievements are color-coded and by seeing which color you're missing you can know in which area to look for it. And it gets major bonus points for not having missable achievements, so you really can just walk around and find everything for yourself without worrying about missing out on something. The only downside the game had for me is that there is an achievement to find all 1500 collectibles, without knowing in which area of the game you're missing some. I was lucky with this achievement. I had looked at most places, so I only missed 3 at the end of the game, and I could deduct which area I had not looked hard enough and quickly get them that way, but it can be such a struggle and annoyance to find those last ones without a clue where to look. luckily the accessibility feature to highlight interactive things is very helpful when walking around looking for those last few collectibles. I highly recommend Pine Hearts and give it a 4,5 out of 5 stars.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: A quick first look:So far this game is absolutely cute and relaxing. Just explore at your leisure, solve little quests for people, and discover more tools and skills little by little while unfolding the story.I'll post a more proper review later, but I know it's early reviews that can help out small developers and publishers a lot.Now if you excuse me, I have to jump back in - I have people to help in game and a ton of exploring left to do.Edit: little over 5 hours later and fully played out. I still think this game is cute, relaxing and absolutely wholesome. The only thing that changed is that my eye sockets are very very wet right now due to the story. It was brought beautifully and with kindness. Very well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Another "wholesome adventure", similar in style to A short hike and Lil Gator Game, where you solve various problems for the people around you while you work towards your main goal (in this case it's actually the same as in A short Hike, to climb a mountain). It's a pleasant couple of hours (my playtime got a bit inflated due to having to restart), but i really enjoyed it.  But there where quite a few glitches that need to be resolved, nothing outright gamebreaking, and i'm sure they will be fixed in time, the game hasn't been out that long and the devs are active in the forums awnsering bug reports. 1) Some places where there is a hotspot where you interact with a tool are invisible. The key prompt is there, but the graphics for what you interact with isn't (for me it was a message in a bottle) it is marked on your map so you will be able to find it but it's stil anoying. 2) One minor quest in one area glitched out several times in a row, because i accidentally skiped a step and went directly to the solution, you have to restart the game and do the quest correctly and it will work. 3) The most significant one is that it's possible to sequence break the game. This only matters if you want to 100% the game, you are not locked out of finishing it. But if you start the quest in another area before finishing the one in your quest log you will not get a reward when you actually finish the quest, making it so that you will be short of the 1500 drops that you need for the completionist achievement. I'm not suire if this happens in more than one area, but it does in the Castle at least. That said, the glitches aside, this was a cute little adventure and I very much enjoyed my time with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Pine Hearts is a cute and quaint little adventure game that reminded me of my childhood favourites such as Scooby doo Night of 100 frights for the PS2. which is ironic due to the nature of Pine Hearts narrative surrounding early-life memory's. I found the gameplay simple yet engaging, collecting different tools to unlock new areas for exploration and NPC's to discover provided more of a thrill than I was anticipating. Searching every nook and cranny for the necessary 1500 tears achievement was a little annoying, but nothing i'd deduct points for as I 100% Pine Hearts in about 7 hours of gameplay. (provided sitting in main menu doesn't register as steam playtime as I was AFK to do house chores.)The Main story of our protagonist Tyke is told through a series of Charming Animatics that convey to us the reason for tykes venture to the park and the emotional significance of his journey of which I won't spoil but will say that I thoroughly enjoyed and said story hit me in the feels. The Music Supplements the gameplay perfectly as each area of the Pine Hearts park has a unique song that play's on a loop during your questing. I worried that listening to such music for hours on end might irritate me but fortunately the music doesn't outstay its welcome, And of course, there is music that tugs on the heart strings during the games more serious moment's. If the developers of Pine Hearts ever attempted this type of game in the future I'd like to see more puzzles, riddles and perhaps some PG combat to spice up gameplay as though there were instances of gameplay diversity throughout pine hearts such as the lawnmower and sowing section the core gameplay loop of walking around to pick up items can get a bit repetitive. Overall Pine Hearts was a lovely experience that I recommend to anyone who desired a palate cleanser from real life woes and would grade this game an 85/100.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: A welcomed change of pace, this game delivers a lovely and at times tear jerking story, with an adorable aesthetic. Each area invokes a range of emotion, with cute/funny interactions, to heart felt memory sequences. There is a lot of to take from this short yet charming experience, and I look forward to what comes next from this team.A true delight!
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Cute and short game with some suprisingly dark moments. Gameplay is incredibly simple, i would very much say this is a kids game. You do like button prompts to lift stuff or use tools to progress through the map and then you do fetch quests for npcs until you have unlocked all the memories and done the major quests where you can scale the mountain, Not really complaining it's nice to have something simple once in awhile. Nice accesibility options, but i don't understand why the map system isn't more fleshed out or there isn't like a hint system if you want to get the 1500 drops. I got 1499 and gave up after looking for the last one for an hour, with the color change mode on ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ Play it if you like simple short games and if that isn't your vibe skip this.

_childDocuments_.review: The concept artist for this game must have one hell of a glorious moustache! _childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: I played a demo of this game last year at EGX and met the some of the lovely team. I couldn't wait for the game to come out and it didn't disappoint. I love the sweet story line and the amazing artwork - plus you get to pet dogs - what more could you need? I love the different areas and the variety of tasks and challenges and the beautiful ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Its a cute and decent game.While some have compared the game to a short hike, i feel that such a comparison will leave you disapointed. This game is only superficially similar. Exploration is highly on rails, unlike a short hike. There are also issues like the 'local map' is not navigatable, and there isnt good quest tracking on misc quests (or said tracking is bugged).So, was it fun? Sure. Was i disapointed after hearing it compared to a short hike and then playing it? Extreamly.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: I played a demo of this game at EGX last year and have had it on my wishlist ever since - Tyke's waddle was the hook. So far I've been really surprised at how much more content there is than I expected, I've unlocked 4 areas of the map and the variety in scenery has been really nice, plus plenty of mini missions, lots of characters to talk to, and background animations that are funny if you take the time to stop and watch what the animals/characters/objects do when you're not directly interacting with them.The game is immediately charming and the main character (Tyke) so endearing that even though I've only unlocked 2 memories so far (about 50 droplets off the third) my heart broke seeing baby Tyke cry. Again, his waddle is also solid.I can see myself working through this game in 1 hour chunks over the next few weeks the same way I have so far. It's chill and casual and sometimes it's nice just to waddle around and enjoy the bright scenery.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve written probably ten review drafts of this title and none of them seem to do it justice. So back to basics. Buy it. This is a beautiful game that manages to incorporate the complexity of losing someone into a wholesome, heartfelt narrative adventure game. Do tasks for the adorable people of Pine Hearts, grow emotionally and skill up. I am trying to avoid all spoilers with my wording here, because you must experience this beautiful story yourself. Technically speaking Pine Hearts feels crafted with love. The graphic design is cute and lighthearted, the music is just perfection, the story is a delight. It also has some clever accessibility options. A mix of mini games, light puzzles and NPC quests (the bulk of the game), Pine Hearts will take you on a relaxing, fun and at times, tear jerking adventure. Purchase it, it’s a rare gem of a game. Oh and I love how it leans into its Scottishness. I lived in Dundee for many years and this made me smile ear to ear. Bravo devs.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Pine Hearts has to be one of the most delightful cozy games that I've played in a while. In Pine Hearts, you play as Tyke. Your goal is to climb the mountain, but in order to even start your journey, you have to prove yourself. This game was wonderful from the sound track to the characters to the quests. I enjoyed everything about it. On top of that, the story was extremely touching as someone who has experienced loss before. Highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: the game is super cute and do a lot of things right.the only thing i found annoyed me was the "power checks". (a power check is when the game puts something in your way that require you to have a specific power to get past)every 30 seconds they made you climb up a wall, break a rock or cut down a tree. (not for shortcuts)thise would be okay if it was just for shortcuts or get to a new area,but to get to a new area i had to first break a rock then climb 2 walls then cut a tree down then break another rock and then push a tree over. (and this is not the first time it seems to get worse the more powers you get)so while i do give it a positive i recomend if you buy it play with simple controlls.TLDR: good game, too many checks, play with simple controlls

_childDocuments_.review: Cozy little metroidvania, if I use that genre loosely. There's no combat or platforming, but there is exploration, quest-doing, and physical barriers which will only let you through when you unlock the right tool for it. I enjoyed my time exploring it. No-pressure environment, too. Took me five hours to complete.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Played through in two wonderfully charming sessions and had to write a review to explain just how wonderful this indie really is.So much heart went into making this, you can just tell. The art direction is stunning, the writing is strong, the story is beautiful and the puzzles are fun and engaging.Genuine pleasure to experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Highly Recommend!!!Where to start when writing a review for Pine Hearts....In short: amazing looking game, smooth game play and great sounding soundtrack that hits you right in the feels.Longer version:What drew me to the game was the cute art style and the promise of a cosy experience (and ofc dogs to pet helps a lot too).This however did not prepare me for the gorgeously written story and the way it was brought. It was an emotional roller coaster based on one of the devs his story but it resonated deeply with me.Game play is fairly simple, lots of running back and forth collecting things and giving them to people. Pretty decent size map to do this on (don't be like me and not realise you have a zone map till almost the end of the game) with lots of extra's to find.Everything from the art style to the soundtrack, the story and the gameplay just made sense and made for a great experience so do yourself a favour and pick up this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend! This game is not to be rushed!! There are little things to do, characters that you will need to meet and do quests for and make sure to collect the memory water drops. The land/map layout is like a maze and it's a puzzle game with a story. The story felt vague but I understood the point of it. I wish there was a better zoom out camera method than just sitting on the bench. Controls were simple and easy to navigate. If you want a cozy game to chill out to, then this would be it!
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: I discovered Pine Hearts at WASD this year and played the demo. The full game does not disappoint. Cute art style, puzzle mechanics and an emotional underlying story. I was happy to be able to go back into Pine Hearts to continue exploring after finishing the main game so you can hoover up all the areas you may not have explored. Beautiful soundtrack and nice touches throughout. AND YOU CAN PET THE DOG!
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this game. Its very cozy and cute. I loved both of the art styles and how easy it is to play. I played on KB&M but you can use controller (I believe that's suggested). The music was very tone setting and beautiful. I did not find any bugs, played so smoothly. The story was cute and heartfelt and I may have shed a few tears. Also loved that a dyslexia setting was there to adjust text to your needs. Not something seen often and it is greatly appreciated. Cannot recommend this enough. Holding out hope that there is more coming.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Pine Hearts is a wonderful game teeming with personality. There are so many cute wee interactions with each character you meet, and the art style is particularly cozy.One thing I'll say about this game is that it's clear that it's been made with a lot of heart. The accessibility options are really fleshed out which shows it was a consideration from the very beginning of development. Also like the many nods to Scotland peppered throughout the dialogue as well, it's nice to see Scots words in a game!
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Pine Hearts A Cute and Emotional Adventure that is very charming and was a genuine joy to play. There are a total of seven areas of the map to discover and as you do you unlock memories of you past time in the Pine Hearts Park moving the main story forward. There are a ton of side quests in each area so I recommend you take the time to speak with everyone you meet and give them a hand.I very much enjoyed the art style of this game and found it really lended well to the relaxing cosy outdoor vibes. The soundtrack is very calming as well and changes for each area you can explore. Each area is also well designed and enjoyable to move through and don’t feel the same. Each area is very distinct and individualised making exploring that much more enjoyable. I really enjoyed this game and found it to be a nice refreshing experience,I really appreciated to emotional beats of the story and even shed some tears as the credits rolled.
_childDocuments_.name: Pine Hearts

_childDocuments_.review: Pine Hearts is a wholesome adventure that gives you delight without unnecessary complexity.It also does a fantastic job at being accessible to everyone, it's rare to find a game that embodies a safe space and this truly does. I finished the story today and it left me with such a warm and satisfied feeling. _childDocuments_.review:
Pine Hearts is an itsy-bitsy, open-world puzzle game! Explore the sleepy scenery of Pine Hearts Caravan Park as you uncover items, unlock new paths, and discover all the little secrets stuffed throughout the Park.

Pine Hearts takes the item-based progression of Zelda, combines it with Souls-like level design and wraps it all up in a Wholesome aesthetic with a focus on puzzles, not combat.

Pine Hearts is a gentle story about fond memories and growing up. A light touch narrative sets the scene for an affective experience that will tug at your heartstrings.

name: Promenade
detailed_description: In Promenade you have to collect golden cogs to fix the great elevator and unlock new worlds. To do so, you can engage with a bunch of diverse activities, like puzzles, races, cute NPCs, and many secrets scattered everywhere by using a dynamic moveset. Whether you like puzzles that require lateral thinking, technical platforming, or just wandering around, there's always something interesting awaiting for you around the corner. Use object's properties to your advantage : double jump by throwing an object down, glide when holding a chicken, run at insane speed with the rocket and a lot more to experiment ! And since you only need to collect some of the cogs to progress, you can follow your instinct and only engage with what interests you the most. Will it be platforming challenges ? Interacting with colorful characters ? Or facing the bosses that dwell in dungeons ? Wether you're a completionist, a cozy gamer, a speedrunner or a collectathon lover, you'll find your way to finish the game the way you like !

_childDocuments_.review: Promenade is a hidden gem amongst its platformer genre and its cute graphics should not be confused with it being a kids-only game.  Featuring extremely variable, challenging gameplay and smart puzzles with new mechanics introduced constantly, it always managed to keep me on the edge of my seat.There is not much of a story in the game. You fall into a watery cave and are saved by a cute octopus-like creature. This creature then joins you on your mission to repair the Great Elevator. Each time you repair a level, more cogs are scattered across the map for you to find.As I said in the introduction, Promenade is most definitely not just for kids, the gameplay is fairly challenging. Don’t let the cute aesthetic fool you! The core mechanic is that you can double jump once you’re holding something. This can be enemies or any random object that you can pick up. This will then propel the object down, thereby elevating you upwards. A double jump (when done in mid air). This simple, but unique premise evolves over time and there are constant new changes being introduced that help keep gameplay fresh and exciting. These jumps sometimes also need to be chained to reach high places, so grab something, jump, swing off a hook and then quickly grab another floating enemy in the air to propel yourself even higher. Falling does not result in any damage (as long as you land on the ground) but you will need to start climbing from the beginning again.While the protagonist does have a health bar, it refills at constant checkpoints and the game is fairly forgiving when you do die, or fall off the edge. Typically respawning you on the last solid ground you were at before.The main goal is to collect each of the parts of the cogs to be able to power up the elevator and get to the next phase. The cog parts can be found all over the place, with some easier to obtain than others. Some may be behind a large puzzle section and a boss fight, whereas others you may just be able to climb up a few obstacles to nab. Not all cog parts need to be done to progress the game, there are many extras here for completionists or achievement hunters to enjoy.I never knew what was around the corner in Promenade. Boost yourself through the level while riding a rocket, swing from chimpanzees hands, corral the chickens back in the coop, complete gravity puzzles or travel through space. The game is absolutely jam packed with creativity and many of the puzzles were exceptionally well designed and I could not help but admire the developers  ideas.This is the only part of the game that made me a tad frustrated but it is not necessarily a fault of the game. There are no indicators telling you where the remaining cog parts are, or where you have already been. There is a journal page that will tick off completed levels, but the universe is exceptionally large that I found it difficult to remember where things were, or how to get there again. I spent far too long aimlessly wandering around trying to find areas I hadn’t been to yet, or trying to find that one area by the beginning of the game that I need to return to. This is definitely a personal preference, or perhaps an accessibility feature, but it would be nice to be able to be shown some directions, or even a map when completely lost.The world of Promenade is undeniably wholesome, boasting its light, pastel aesthetic and cute creatures. There are no weapons, and you cannot kill any of the enemies. You can pick them up and throw them, but they will respawn shortly after and are the main way to traverse.There is no voice acting but the cheery upbeat soundtrack reminded me of older style platformers like Kirby. Each time you locate a cog, a little flute tune will play, representing a sort of congratulations, you did it! Did I mention the game was wholesome? 5 – 10 hours for a playthrough, but there is much content to discover to keep you going for double that. Yes, definitely. Yes, the game is brimming with things to do, especially for completionists.Promenade is a top-quality platformer that is bursting with creativity. From its smart puzzles, engaging and everchanging gameplay to its whimsical world, there is just so much to love here.  Its looks can be deceiving, and it is definitely more challenging than its cute graphics let on. I highly recommend this for all platformer fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Promenade

_childDocuments_.review: Do not be fooled by the cartoonish (and beautiful) design, this game is above all a true platforming masterpiece, rich with smart ideas, surprises, and the kind of puzzles that will make you think hard and then put a smile on your face when you solve them. It is refreshing, fast, beautiful, and engaging !

_childDocuments_.review: The most wholesome puzzle platformer I've ever played. Calling it a platformer is totally dismissive of what the game is. Sure, there is a lot of platforming, tight precision trials that will take you to your wits' ends, and boss fights, but there is so much more! It has puzzling, platforming, exploring, adventure, all in a very beautiful, child-friendly presentation.So, you play as Nemo, a young boy who fell down a long tunnel into a fantastic realm. You are rescued by, and befriend a little poulp (baby octopus). The goal is to fix the big elevator to get back up into the real world. In order to do that, you must find cog pieces scattered throughout the world, awarded after accomplishing something.  And the tasks you can do are so diverse! You'll have to cook some food, learn to juggle, do a little dance, help two snails have a romantic lunch together, overcome your fear of darkness, play Breakout and Pong and other retro games, water the plants, gather the chickens, do a sneaky bank heist, race a penguin, catch ghosts, paint pretty pictures, look for hidden treasure, brave a thunderstorm... There are literally  more than a hundred things to do. Some of them are obvious and easy, some require good precision platforming, some require deep exploration, some require a lot of lateral thinking. There's nothing like that feeling you get after finally figuring out the secret recipe, or the hidden house, or the peculiar list, or if you're more into platforming than puzzling, beating a timed trial.The elevator goes through many floors, each with its own theme: a sandy beach, space, a flowery garden, a temple full of monkeys, a mountain, an office building, snow, a haunted house, a thunderstorm. And each level teaches you something new about what you can do, with a trial course focused on a specific mechanic, from simple moving and jumping, using paper airplanes or rockets to fly, using objects to double/triple jump... To me, these don't feel like obstacles to overcome, but more like lessons being taught. They aren't in the way, blocking all progress, but after you complete the trials, you can better navigate the rest of the game.Other than the game contents, the presentation is superb. The graphics are very nice, cartoony but beautiful, the different worlds are well designed, the controls and mechanics are well done, beautiful sounds and music, plus a lot of extra features that make it a good modern game. Moderate, not too hard but not too easy. To reach the first end, you only need to collect a little over half of the cogs, so you don't really have to do all the hard things, except that you must finish at least five boss levels to get to the end. Timed trials are optional, but reaching the second end requires collecting almost all cogs and beating a few really really tough trials. At least 10 hours. I've really enjoyed it for more than 30 hours already, and I didn't yet try to speedrun it. Superb! Excellent! Excellent presentation, good UX, plenty of settings, multiple save slots, good Steam integration with cloud save, excellent achievements (including a few for speedrunning), Steam Deck support. A few bugs encountered that are being patched. Yes. Looking for secrets. I'm not really a fan of precision platforming, so that would be  most negative aspect, but that's not a bad thing about the game itself.,  and their new remakes, which this game reminded me of with its jump and roll mechanics, and the hunt for secrets., beautiful platforming with a lot of focus on puzzles., beautiful platforming/metroidvania with a lot more fighting, but also clever exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: While researching to add the appropriate links to my youtube video I came across their website where it says; "4 enthusiasts who want to create a unique video game experience". But I digress.I have some real-life stuff to do first before I can jump back in, at some point I'll update this review to have a full proper written review but for now I already wanted to show my love and support with a big thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing puzzle platformer that is a joy to play due to constant influx of new things.The story start when a kid falls into a cavern filled with water. Before he drowns, a little octopus appears out of nowhere and rescues him. They quickly became buddies. Everything is seen rather than told, therefore the majority of the enjoyment stems from the wonderful cartoon-like animations.The overall goal of the game is to take the large elevator to the top. However, the kid's evil side is attempting to thwart you by destroying cogs. This occurs with each new floor you reach. So your task is to build a new cog by completing short puzzles and challenges that reward you with cog parts. One cog requires three little parts.Because the game takes place in a dream-like realm, you are able to go to many locations. It looks great in motion since there are just enough details on the screen to not detract from the gameplay. It never gets dull because you are continuously seeing new places and encountering new inhabitants of this world. Although the octopus will rescue you if you fall in the water, or you’ll reappear immediately if you drop into a hole, you can still fail. If the kid loses all five hearts, you will respawn at the beginning of the stage. But don't worry; there are hammocks everywhere that will heal you.This is a platformer with puzzle components, so expect a lot of jumping. Although the child's only abilities are to jump once and roll, his octopus companion can assist him with the most essential actions. This involves flinging your friend at opponents or items. Once you have the enemy in your hands, you can hurl it at something or use it to double jump. Of course, you aren't limited to a double jump because you can jump whenever you have something in your hands. Enemies respawn after two to three seconds, so you won’t waste time waiting for them. Another octopus’ strength you will gain later is the ability to grip onto hooks. The game focuses on challenges and riddles. The imagination and fun factor are high because you never know what you're going to have to do next. You might have to protect a snail from cannon fire so he can reach a bowl of spaghetti, carry a jigsaw puzzle to finish the picture, bring chickens to a pen, jump inside a painting and match colours, battle a boss, and so on. Obviously, the majority of challenges involve platforming, and there are some that repeat, like the penguin that wants to race.All possible challenges by location are listed in your notebook; but you need to find the page first. Some problems require some extra work, while others must be solved twice. One of them is trials, which require you to complete a normal and time challenge that will put even the most die-hard platforming enthusiast to the test.One small annoyance I noticed is that puzzles reset when you switch locations. So if you do two steps out of three, you’ll have to do everything all over again unless you finish it. Another one is that since you’re always going higher, you’re bound to fall down. In this case, you need to climb up or ride the elevator. In the end, this is a one of those titles why I like indie games. It's simple to play, visually appealing, and will keep you entertained for a long time. I think it might be a hidden gem that many will overlook and discover much later. One warning: if you go into the game blind, the game has a bunch of achievements that are easy to miss. This might bother achievement hunters that like to take time exploring.
_childDocuments_.name: Promenade

_childDocuments_.review: is great for a cloudy sunday afternoon in your couch if you are looking for a chill / cute experience , on the other hand, it can also give you a nice challenge if you are of the completionist / competitive / speedrunner type.It's made by awesome, passionate and devoted people who managed to create a complete mix of what makes a game entertaining and satisfying to play.Give it a go, try the demo, get the game, and enjoy <3
_childDocuments_.name: Promenade

_childDocuments_.review: I play a lot of platformers. I love the genre, but it can have a lot of duds. Either games with repetitive mechanics or cheap deaths, or ones where the controls don't feel quite right or tight enough for the dexterity they demand.And then you have Promenade, a game that came seemingly out of nowhere and is the single best platformer I've played in years.The fact that this has only 86 reviews on steam right now is very troubling to me, because I hope it doesn't mean that it sold poorly. This game is a masterpiece.So what sets it apart? First of all, it's not structured like a traditional 2D platformer, but as something much more open. Think less metroidvania (a genre I'm not a fan of personally) and more Super Mario Odyssey but in 2D. A collectathon full of mini open worlds where collecting enough gears will allow you to progress to the next mini open world.Each level is absolutely stuffed full of charming secrets, fun mini games and platforming challenges that range from simple and quick to totally sweaty palm fodder. It's never excruciatingly difficult but maintains a good balance and is no pushover.I won't go on too long, but just be aware that Promenade is one of those rare platformers that has *almost* no flaws. It is incredibly charming and wholesome, oozes creativity and passion at every turn, controls well and feels amazing to play.There are two tiny problems:1. A few frustrating moments of cheap deaths (could probably count them on one hand)2. A "Unity stutter" problem that is fixed by locking your frame rate to a multiple of 50 (cap it to 60 fps on steam deck and you're golden).Play Promenade. Buy it on sale, buy it full price, just buy it. The best $20 I spent all year, and at 10 hours for basic completion plus a few side things, has plenty of content.
_childDocuments_.name: Promenade

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked good ol' collectathons and you kinda miss them, Promenade is for you. Holy Cap Studio not only fully understood the biggest games of this genre, but they also somehow find multiple new ways to let you enjoy it. Add the very pleasant and progressive moveset and it will be a pleasure to move the main character and his octupus throught the entire game.The artistic direction is wonderful but don't get it wrong : even while looking shimmering, the 100%-run will sometimes challenges you more than the cute animation might suggest.A tiny game full of creativity.
_childDocuments_.name: Promenade
