_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game in early access. It still seems somewhat unpolished due to bugs here and there (mostly with spawning npcs/structures inside one another in the environment) and occasional crashing (only once in my current 40hrs of gameplay). It is evident that the game is still in early access as there is no 'endgame' questline, but the gun play is in depth with the ability to add attachments and change bullet type, but still seems somewhat lackluster with customization options. It would be nice to be able to equip the weapons with more and there being more than just the single type of standard weapon mods but in different colors. A part of me wants to ask for a greater emphasis on the survival aspect of the game, namely the food/water/etc with more deathly options with water is not drunk or food is not eaten as the negative effects, although somewhat detrimental, are not horribly difficult to work around. However, the ability to turn off 'death from starvation/dehydration' would be excellent if the survival aspects were to be reworked.The gameplay besides the survival aspects and the modding of weapons involves either resource management or enemies. Let's start with the latter, enemies. The combat  is very tense throughout the game, although as of this version (0.40.23) the bandit faction are extremely easy in the late-game as they only have early- and mid-game counterparts and can be easily decimated. The ???/Watcher faction was an excellent addition to the game as it is interesting to see a new difficult type of enemy that is specifically in this iteration's final map. The monsters are terrifying as they will shred your health nearly as fast as the in game bosses do. Although they are squishy, they are fast, terrifying, and hit like a truck. Hoards of them genuinely send shivers down my spine. The Green Army and CC have an interesting feud, neither of which I would like to side with, but I am looking forward to a more in-depth questline, possibly returning us to previous maps with greater difficulty enemies. Overall, I just want more gameplay since I thoroughly enjoyed the game. Now onto the former, the resource management. Now  I do not mean the management as you open your inventory, but as in back at the base in the bunker(home location). I do wish that there was more substance to building yourself a home base and also I wish there was all around more to do with the modules that you build for the base. I feel as though I spent majority of my time in storage while in base then immediately leaving as there were no apparent benefits to using nearly any of the modules that you built. Final topic I will discuss is skills. Great addition allowing for more customization and allows me to really find my niche. Stealth sniper all the way baby!TL;DR, Great game, mildly lacking gun customization, great combat and gunplay, fair questline.(got bored and started procrastinating on hw)

_childDocuments_.review: While i really enjoy this game, i can't help but feel like its perspective is putting it at a massive disadvantage. The core gameplay is solid. Drop in one of several large areas, loot materials and quest items, get out alive, rinse repeat until you're a walking armory with more crackers than a limp bizkit concert. Its the first very solid extraction shooter out right now aside from Tarkov with its single player mod. The problem is hot infuriating the top-down perspective can be at times, and how many deaths are from simply walking into a boar or a mutant because you didn't 360 enough to see everything around you. Audio cues could fix this issue with proximity sounds around enemies, or even just more of a delay between "i see you" and "i attack you". I like the game, i really do, but i would LOVE the game if it was first person. A sequel with that perspective and same core gameplay would be amazing, maybe even Risk of Rain 2 levels of hype. Its great for the price and the dev is open to experimenting and adapting to feedback, so i can see this game being wildly different at 1.0 launch.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game but still needs a lot of work. With a lot of the gunplay changes, I don't think they really have an idea of how to make combat work with this top down format. The bullet glancing system is straight up bad. And because you NEED an SMG/shotgun (probably SMG) to kill the melee enemies that repeatedly run through you and you NEED a sniper (or something with a scope and high damage) for when there's an enemy sniper 2-shotting you from off screen, that's your loadout end game. Sniper and smg. That's all you can bring with unless you want to run into no-win scenarios. It's very limiting. The irony is that the devs made these gunplay changes with the intent of increasing weapon diversity but they ended up decreasing it instead.Also still lots of just bugs with mission objectives spawning inside walls and whatnot. Like a lot. But hey, it's early access. Overall a pretty fun game but I feel like the changes made over the past year (other than just adding content) have been misguided and sometimes even made the game worse. Kinda getting worried about where the game is gonna end up but holding out hope that they can get it back on track. Worst case, it's still worth $20 for the ~100 hours of fun I've had with it so far. Ignore the people with 50 hours of playtime saying it wasn't worth $20 lolUPDATE: Per their update on June 4th, looks like they were working on multiplayer a lot for the past few months and have tabled it cause the engine doesn't easily support it. They'll be focusing more on core gameplay and content again which is great to hear. Still think the gunplay could use some work (an M4 does not have this much recoil guys, it's 5.56) and I hope they add an option to remove the bullet glancing/efficient range mechanics entirely for those that don't like them. _childDocuments_.review: I love this game, but it's a little rough around the edges. I read another review saying it was made in gamemaker, so that explains some of them. It takes a while to load certain actions, to consolidate things from your stash when crafting items, things like that. So, naturally, because of this kind of optimization, the game can't have a very huge inventory/crafting system. Still, it feels like a lot for a game of this nature.It's difficult, but in a good way. Never played tarkov, but played a lot of stalker and I can see the obvious influence. My main problem is so much of the game is hard to experience if you don't spend a super long time in the maps. There are storms, sort of like the emissions from Stalker: Pripyat--where you must take cover or die. There are other storms that rain green clouds of toxic gas, which, I assume, increase radiation? But I always wear a science suit so I've never been affected by them. There are airdrops, which get fiercely defended and are risky, but the rewards are great.  The problem with these events is they only occur once every ten minutes or so. But. Your excursions into the zone, though tense, usually are over before they occur. I can fill my inventory with high quality loot and get out well before anything happens, unless on a mission into a facility. Also: you never really need to prepare with food or water. The survival system is there. And food and water are critical to your carry weight capacity. But you can refill these gauges at base for almost nothing, and they usually are never a problem within the timespan it takes to get good loot from the zone. So you bring ammo and medkits. Radiation is an annoying problem--but easily solved with the right armor gear. this leaves me feeling locked into science gear--but if annoying radiation management isn't a problem, different gear loadouts open up. the base modules are similar--certain ones just feel crucial, others feel like an afterthought. Money can solve all of my ammo problems, because ammo is cheap, so why craft ammunition? Buy it. Weird, considering it has more upgrades than anything else. Repairing armor on the other hand cost a LOT of money, and requires tedius inventory management with higher tier armors, so you kind of have to get the forge and the workshop. The scavenger mod is great until you find a certain merchant that sells junk, and after that, totally optional.the airdrops don't make much sense from in-game lore. There should be no way in or out of the zone--but the UN has planes constantly dropping supplies--so I guess air travel is not off limits? You'd figure people would find a way to escape, in this case. Anyway, I'm not going to critique the story in a game like this. The main draw is the gameplay loop. Get into the zone, get loot, sell it.I do wish faction relationships mattered more, and that there were more mutants/aliens. But in the end, despite all it's quirks, it's very atmospheric and fun.

_childDocuments_.review: still needs a lot of work and polish.a lot of people are singing its praises, but to be honest, I don't really get it.the balance is really janky, with enemies spawning in the lowest level area that will take multiple magazines to kill, right next to enemies which you can drop with a few bullets. and in the meantime you will pretty much always be a paper soldier, and if the enemy happens to have a powerful gun, you go down in one hit. this struggle is exasperated by how busy the wooded areas are visually, an issue the AI will never have because they dont see from a top down/ 3/4ths view, they just check for line of sight. their reaction time is also pretty quick, so it can be a challenge to compete in the more hectic situations. next, none of the items have descriptions. they just say "item description." as far as I can tell, this is just laziness. _childDocuments_.review: Edit: The developers have acknowledged what happened with the current update. Their plans going forward seem solid; the announcement is worth keeping in mind when deciding whether or not to buy "ZERO Sievert" in early access.As a preface, the game is in early access. I understand that it is not a complete product. However, the latest update completely breaks basic functionality.Half of the mechanics in the game do not work consistently; an entire section of the crafting station crashes to the desktop, you can become hard-locked due to main story quests being incompletable, and weapon attachments disappear without a trace.This update launched after the developers established a publicly accessible beta branch for testing game updates. It really makes you wonder if the developers even ran the game before pushing out the update, as all of the issues are immediately apparent and game-breaking.The mood around this update is strange. In the past, the developers had such great communication and even announced delays related to the update cycle. As a fellow developer, I understand being excited to share new content and features. However, the current release of the game is half-baked. With this release, the game took five steps forward and twenty steps back.As a request to the developers: please announce a delay if the update is not ready. Many great companies have released terrible products recently because they were forced to stick to a release date. I really enjoy this game, as evidenced by my playtime, and I don't want to see people (rightfully) toss it aside because it is a buggy mess.Building consumer trust back up is really hard. New players do not have the same understanding and background knowledge to see what the game is like when it works well. New consumers only experience what is present at the time.As much as I love the game, I cannot currently recommend Zero Sievert. I hope that this patch was a mistake rather than the start of a pattern. Even after all these game-breaking bugs are patched, I would be hesitant to recommend buying the game.As a consumer, wait until the developers show whether untested, bug-riddled updates become the norm.

_childDocuments_.review: As an Escape from Tarkov and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. player, I came to this game with high hopes of playing something similar, even if it is at a much smaller scale. Sadly, I was rather disappointed by how promising it was, yet how many concepts were badly implemented.- There are factions in the game with which you need to build up reputation in order to access better gear and supplies. You gain reputation with these factions by doing repeatable quests that refresh every (in game) day. These quests are not inspired, they are generic and brings memories of MMO type of daily quests. These quests get stale really fast and they can vary a lot in difficulty which may slow down your faction reputation progress down to a slog if the RNG gods hate you.TLDR: Reputation quests are boring and RNG dependent.- The gunplay is.. not great. Weapons have a maximum and a minimum range. I presume this is in order to balance out the weapons types, but it doesn't really do that. Bullets have different armour piercing values which determines if your bullets actually go through the enemy armour or not. The highest AP on SMG bullets allows penetration of tier 3 ( out of 6 ) armour which is never going to be enough especially in the end game, which results in you still using the same weapon types in the end game but they just feel bad. I forgot to mention that these penalties do not apply to the enemy, which creates an unfair playing field.- Enemies most of the time have high armour piercing bullets which just shred you no matter what, This wouldn't be so bad if the AI had more than 2 states: Braindead and Perfect Aimbot. End game felt extremely cheesy due to this, as the best and safest way ( by far ) to engage soldiers was to sit as far as possible and shoot them with the sniper, otherwise you will be swarmed and peppered with bullets incredibly fast.- I've also encountered several bugs, but I am not going to list them all. The most frustrating was when terrain generation was acting up and blocked up certain entrances making it impossible to enter buildings required for quests or such.Overall, this game had an incredible amount of potential, yet the implementation has lead to a rather frustrating experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Early Access review, November 24th 2022.Holy crap this game is fantastic! When out on a hunt, Zero Sievert constantly has me on the edge of my seat. The gunplay is as good as it gets in a 2D game, and the sound effects are great. The game also has very clever details that make the experience even more immersive. For example, if after an intense gunfight your enemy's corpses are spread out in tall grass, they can be very hard to spot. But at some point I realised the birds would come eat from the corpses, telling me where to collect my loot! It might seem like a minor detail, but to me little things like this can really make a game. If the early access stamp worries you: the game seems very stable and in my first 12 hours of gameplay I have encountered no bugs (apart from some typos and grammatical errors). I very highly recommend this game!Disclaimer: like so many pixel art indie games, Zero Sievert is tough as nails. Don't expect to just walk around guns blazing, clearing levels. You need to think about when, if at all, to engage, and with what type of ammo. You will die a LOT. Don't buy the game if this is not your jam.Edit: November 26th, 2022: In the 10 or so hours after writing this review, I actually encountered quite a few bugs. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: The game is not bad, but I can't recommend it either as certain mechanics annoy me too much.The game tries to be a mix of stalker and Escape From Tarkov in 2d and does so reasonably well and the story was good imo. I had fun and the game certainly improved constantly during early access, though the final release felt more like a cut corner than a final leap. The gameplay loop and looting is fine and certain difficulty aspects will certainly appeal to an audience. However some mechanics are more on the edge of bad than on difficult:- most important: Having red–green color blindness i must say that i found it next to impossible to distinguish most of the faction-npcs you meet on your raids. Which really does suck when you don't want to damage your reputation needlessly but also don't know whether they will just shoot you up when you come closer. At least the scientists and bandits (and some late game faction) were easy to tell. Maybe there could have been some reputation-/faction-/indicator pop up after aiming at somebody for a couple seconds - enemies engaged in melee combat sometimes "move along", preventing you to be able to hit them back. Feels ill-designed and annoying but getting meleed with a gun usually does not end well either so there is at least a point.- the fog of war has no near radius so you can just walk past enemies. Again, learn to watch your corners but i would argue for being able to perceive somebody breathing right into my neck- there is one main quest which requires you to find 2 keys that are random drops from cabinets. Wasted a lot of time on the last one and eventually cheated it in (either rare or i was just unlucky). Imho there should be a way to progress with the story without getting stuck on random chance- the enemies view-range is equal in the horizontal and vertical axis while yours is not. So fighting left-to-right is both safer and easier while i often got hit and killed despite looking as far as i could into the upwards direction without being able to see the enemy. And yes, i got sniped despite looking as far as i could with the best scope in game (did see the muzzle flash so there is that i guess)- There is no mechanic of making sure that you don't end up in the middle of a group of enemies when entering buildings or using the spawns on the last map, leading to rather unfair deaths- In some cases random map-objects had been blocking the entrances to key map parts needed for missions, requiring to come back with another raidTo be clear: I don't mind dying in "hardcore" games as long as there is something that can be learned from it. And sadly this does not always seem to be the case, and that is not just me being bad (which to be honest I kind of am).In the end i found myself trying to get the game over with instead of looking forward to it.

I don't need an item card that takes up a third of my screen, offering bare information. Additional information would be nice regarding certain statistics. For example, what is "Fragility"? What does the class armour number mean? Do higher numbers mean heavier weight class? There's so much space on item cards, it could have benefited from adding a little more to it.There's no comparison UI, often you will be moving the cursor back and forth between items. Moving items across, the norm is holding Shift and left-clicking. Here, it's Ctrl and left-clicking. Again, odd design choices. If it's worked in other games, there's no need to reinvent the wheel.That's what I've been able to pick up on in my short span of game time. As of writing this it is a short list, but the thing is I work in the interface and experience design industry and it irked me. People will enjoy this game, and I can recommend the gameplay to others. But it's a hard no for me and to others who appreciates more clarity and polish.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely promising isometric take on the, uh....STALKER genre? It's been two days now and I've already sunk 22 hours into it. Much dying and cursing and running right back out into the field to get vengeance on the next random NPC that spawns in my vicinity. Art direction is simple, yet solid. Lots of nice little details in the gear and animations when consuming items, firing weapons, or just running around. Plenty of customization in the firearms (with a nice spread of frames & parts to pick from - and all the ammo types). Environments are interesting with plenty of space to explore. The maps are just big enough and randomly generated every time you revisit them (similar to early Diablo games). They just take the environmental assets and NPCs then shake them up in a cup before spilling them out onto the map. The only constants are certain camps/structures but even those move around a bit when you re-load a map. Enemies are dangerous but fair. They hit as hard as you and die just as fast with the right application of ammunition. Plenty of visual variety in the two maps I've explored so far (Fores & Makeshift Camp). Audio is also very nice. Guns are loud, footsteps are noticeable, and I've been made to jump multiple times when I'm creeping through the forest at night and hear sudden gunfire or the growl of a nearby mutant.Only real gripe so far is that some locations will be decorated with shelves, tables, and drawers that *look* like they should be lootable/interactable but are in fact static and untouchable. That shelf clearly full of books? Nah, can't touch it. Would like to see some expansion on the lootable objects. Perhaps even just include some minor collision + physics with items placed on the ground like empty boxes and bottles. Overall I'm loving the game so far. Scratches the isometric loot n shoot STALKER longing I've been wanting.

_childDocuments_.review: [UPDATE: 01][YEAR: MARCH 2023][TIME: 21 HOURS][OVERVIEW]Overall, Zero Sievert is a Top-Down, Pixel Extraction-shooter game. This one is a hidden gem. Unlike other games simmilar to the extraction genre such as Tarkov or Marauders, ZS is a single player game as well so when you die on your run, it loads your last save right before you depart to your map of choosing. This changes the way you play the game overall as well as the day and night cycle. This review will be a simple overview of the games mechanics, my opinions as well as some tips and tricks![VENDORS]Currently there are 3 vendors in the game. The bartender and Medic are going to be your main vendors when starting out. The 3rd vendor is unlocked later in the game as you level up your character. The Bartender and Medic carry the majority of the quests in this game (so far). Some of the quests are similar to other games in the Extraction shooter genre such as fetch quests, kill people or animals, activate this, do that, etc. You dont level up vendors like you would in Tarkov, instead, better gear will unlock in their shops as you level your character. [MAPS]There is quite a variety of maps in this game and there are more to come as well. There is a bit of random generation in the world as there will always be the Central points on the map but smaller points vary each run. Orientation of where things are on the map changes with every run as well. The main roads stay the same so it really minimizes the overall RNG to the procedural generation. There are 2 maps that are easy, the rest of the maps are very difficult requiring high level gear. Stick with forest for a while and move up levels as you get better gear.[STASH & BASE]Your stash can hold quite a bit of loot as long as you can upgrade it. You can either build an upgrade kit using materials found through the game, or there are some quests that give them to you as a reward. When you upgrade your stash you upgrade a whole tab of space. there are 14 tabs of space in the game currently. Just like upgrading your stash, building your base requires you to build kits. Each kit is different and offers different benefits to the player. Ex;, Kitchen allows you to cook better foods, ammo station allows you to craft ammo, or bedroom giving heath regeneration and an ex boost for a moderate time. There are limited spaces so choose wisely.[GAMEPLAY]The overall gameplay is quite fun but could use some balancing when it comes to weapons and armors. When it comes to the weapons there are a good variety of weapons in the game....but not until mid game. Combat is fun once you get used to it and if anything quite addictive. The best advice on meta gameplay would be to play far and use either a sniper or a semi auto rifle. They are accurate and put out good damage. Its also easier to maintain ammo. There are a huge variety of weapon mods in the game and they will say in the description what weapons are compatible with what mods. The combat can use some work but for where its at, its a really good start.  [CONCLUSION]Overall this game has some major potential and I would highly advise supporting the devs and getting the game to help the dev(s) make this game into a banger.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say? I'm Hooked.I've heard this game described as a 2-D mashup of S.T.A.L.K.E.R, and Escape from Tarkov, which is pretty accurate.The style and flavor of S.T.A.L.K.E.R is there, you've got your post-apocalyptic zone, your anomalies and mutants, soldiers, scientists, 'hunters' and bandits. The general game-play loop will remind you of EFT: you bring whatever gear, ammo, and supplies you think you'll need into a mission on one of several maps in an attempt to loot and complete missions before extracting back to home-base. Mind you, you do not lose everything you brought in should you die. However, losing whatever you've gathered, or whatever quest progress you've made so far on that mission is plenty punishing enough.In this way, the game builds a lot of tension and forces you into some tough decisions: "Do I try to complete this quest before I leave, risking the precious loot I just picked up?"The S.T.A.L.K.E.R series is absolutely dear to my heart, but the 'survival game' shoe doesn't really fit on the vanilla games, where food and water become irrelevant after about two minutes. Food and water feel precious in this game as they should, and the survival elements stitch pretty seamlessly into the combat and overall game loop.The mechanics are likewise well-done and polished. Using good gear, ammo, positioning, tactics, and awareness will most often reward you with a successful run. The devs implemented a cover and line-of-sight system, and impressively dynamic enemy AI that make engagements even with enemies below your 'tier' engaging and non-trivial. There were only a handful of times that I've died on a mission and thrown up my hands as if "aw come on, you kidding me?" Most often I've had to admit to myself that I'd bungled my decision-making, execution, or both. Likewise, I've only encountered one crash and a couple of bugs, but those occurred during, or immediately after loading into a mission, and were rectified by re-launching the game, with no impact on my play-through.I'm not even remotely close to getting through the content available thus far and am having a blast. Great job devs, I'm excited to see where this game goes.

_childDocuments_.review: Hidden GemThis is the best 2D Tarkov style PVE extraction shooter in fact I would say its way more fun than the greedy russian game itself. Why have you never heard of this game because its one guy with zero marketing making it and boy is it impressive considering. Many people have quit Tarkov and The Cycle and for those people you will love this game in fact its a great game for many.Game has a great foundation, the systems feel right, walking around gunning as you eat drink heal etc feels overall good without being too oppressive. The gameplay loop of getting home with your goodies feels good and makes you care about your runs. There are plenty of maps and content to explore here getting 100% will probably take you a long time if you care to. The enemy AI is very good overall the bosses especially react in a way that instills real fear into you as it suddenly feels like a human is trying to hunt you down. The graphics and sound are great I love the art style the scale of being a small cube helps to make you feel like an underdog against the odds of the apocalypse background. There's plenty of enemies and creatures to and lots of guns to fight them with all with punchy sound effects.All this said the game is NOT FINISHED maybe 60% of the way there 3 maps are missing and there is a significant amount of polish and clean up that is needed. Sadly game issues are x10 their weight when it comes to permadeath extraction shooters as you may invest significant time and skill into a run/mission only for some BS to ruin it. We accept this as players when making mistakes but alot of stuff in the game is silly/broken and I will list them hoping for changes;-Aliens they are straight busted 2 shot you in 1 second when turning a corner feels super cheap-Weather is just annoyin I get the realism attempt but walking around at 1mph feels trash get rid of all weather speed debuffs it doesnt improve the gameplay experince AT ALL!-Ghool nests once you learn the trick to them are super boring to play against get rid of them thanks-The base upgrade system needs a TOTAL REWORK it is awful I would actually get rid of it entirely and just let the player use them if they gather mats then scale the mats to quality of reward. WHY CANT I HAVE EVERY BASE WORKBENCH ! silly-Missions pacing is awful and needs totally streamlining made more clear with more ways to find where you are supposed to go many missions you will be on youtube trying to figure out why your mission has not triggered etc.-Upgrade system and weapons acquired pacing is awful I feel like once I got my 2nd gun I didnt get any improvement for a long time. Many weapons feel pointless other than for style hence I stuck to my rifle  90% of the time and mines and nades are super clunky to use.-Get rid of player upgrade books and just have it go up as you play the game and do those related actions thanks. -Costs of items/upgrades etc are insanely expensive one example is the lighting in the base, 24 bulbs took me 40 hours to get are you insane. Also I had no idea what it was I thought it was going to give me ability to make torches or something lol-Faction system is not finished I want more choices on who I can align with would be nice if all 4 could be chosen from and weapons were NOT related to that. I think the game would be more fun it every map had the 4 factions present maybe I could be a mad scientist or a bandit etc. Make the bartender sell any weapon once you sell it to him.-Day/Night cycle feels annoyin feels like you have to be perfectly awake at 8am everyday not fun-Food/Drink system is annoyin -Game needs more NPCs to interact with-Change the home base architecture its annoying to run around and looks bad.-WAY too much geo on many maps from cars to trees why am I always bumping into things it even blocks mission access sometimes as its procedural. Less density please.-Far too much radiation to the point all armor other than science hazmat feels pointless #amongus-Confusing weapon mods I never had a clue what mods are for what please add a system to know easily.-Item reveal time is far too slow and pointless get rid of it we not in a pvp game here-Add co op at some point the game would be great with others-The swamp map is awful change it-Change the mall to be not dark its cool to look and therefore graphics are wasted-There is no counter to acid rain and lightning storms total BS-More tracking tools please-Add Drones-More weapons not just guns-Add sound meter like BOTW-Crystals and inject buffs feel pointless and annoying to use and make-Finish the menu map system Overall there maybe many problems/bugs/QOL here but they are EASY to fix and I can easily invision this game being a 10 if they polish it up and finish the games vital features and hopefully give us some good endings to aim for hopefully one for each faction. Extraction shooters are a huge investment in time and skill but this is probably the easiest one to get into so I strongly recommend people try this game to get a feel for why this genre is great and will dominate the next few years in the gaming space.psWord of warning to the developers please do not make the mistake that valhiem made not hiring enough devs to make the game great, this game will fade into the past if it is not reinvested into with its profits. Also to the players this game is best on the biggest screen you have so if you are steamdeck user make sure you have a dock.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: A solid game I have found enjoyable. There are a few flaws, but it's in early access.The premise of the game is to head out into a low-rez isometric environment filled with creatures and people that want to kill you, then return alive with loot to improve your equipment or quarters or to complete quests.Graphics: 3/10While this is a pixelated retro-styled game, there is a fair amount of detail to the those scenery sprites, especially the grasses. The characters are not great by retro-style pixel standards, so there is room for improvement without losing the feel of the game.Gameplay Loop: 7/10It can take a bit long to achieve anything notable, especially at the start. 'Breaking even' alone can be a bit tricky in middling difficulties simply because food and water is so expensive and the rewards for quest completion are considerably less. Despite this, each semi-randomly generated 'hunt' can feel brutal, a quick stop in the inventory screen can have you killed by a boar hiding behind a rock in no time, forcing you to start the hunt over. Making it to the extraction zone can feel like a relief. Audio: 4/10There's no music to speak of and the sound effects can be a bit bland. For example, using a Geiger counter crackle as a mouse-over sound. Music is only on the menu screen and is not good. Despite this, the sound does what it's supposed to.Story: 0/10There is no story save for the one you craft yourself.Verdict: 7/10While no single one of the above values is exceptional, the finished product is greater than the sum of its parts, and I look forward to seeing what is to come.Criticisms:The main one is that the game gets easier as you progress, rather than being more challenging.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Game good, you buy game.I do not normally leave reviews for games unless it leaves a lasting impression on me. Zero Sievert is one of these kind of games for me. I have always wished that Escape From Tarkov had a solo mode of some kind that did not include any PvP, but also saved progress. Zero Sievert, by far, has given me the closest experience to this to date. Zero Sievert, while clearly taking influence from Escape From Tarkov, gives a good mix of familiarity from that game and combines it with a completely new and different style of shooter (that I have ever played). After about 40 hours, (my steam time is bugged due to a docking issue with the Steam Deck) I think that Zero Sievert does a great job of balancing the level of difficulty. The game can be punishing, especially when starting a fresh character and learning the mechanics of the game. However, that was part of the fun for me. I can only remember a couple of deaths where I felt like I could not have done anything differently in order to survive. Sometimes an enemy would get inside of my character model and would not allow me to shoot them. And outside of that, the game seemed to be mostly bug free as well, for me at least. The only thing that I would like to see in the future is a bigger penalty for dying (I am ignorant to any future plans) and more stash space for hoarders like myself. Other than that I am excited to see where Zero Sievert goes in the future and will probably jump back in for every major update.

_childDocuments_.review: You're very limited on what you can do early game to survive and not waste resources. It's just not fun when ammo is scarce, meds are expensive and weapons you pick up are in the worst condition possible. You're forced to keep dying until you get that one run in the beginning that doesn't ruin your ammo supply or cash to get out of the newbie ditch. Even then you hardly make any cash to make up for the ammo/med/food/drinks you've spent. The weight limit also hinders how much you can bring back. The game saves as soon as you extract so if you left with no ammo left in your pockets, that's what your next run will be like. The bartender does sell ammo but he sells barely enough ammo to kill 2 enemies if you use a single type of ammo.I cannot recommend this game because the "fun" part of the game is locked behind an extreme resource management. If I was given a new loadout after dying, such as scavs in Tarkov or the beginner set of gear in Dark and Darker, I would have much more fun.

I originally gave this an upvote, even with the issues I mentioned below. but this ♥♥♥♥ has to go. I know I can hit a button and it unjams - which is a quicktime event. the worst invention ever and it is made for consoles and has no place on PC. especially when a gun can jam several times in a row. what turned out to be a major issue is the minimum distance you get to hit things if you use any good gun. I want to be able to craft stuff and get all the rooms. artificial limiting this does not make the game harder. it makes it more inconvenient and give you less to aspire towards."I want to build all the rooms" personal game goal gets reduced to "oh well... so I can't do that in this game. too bad. let's play something that does not force a negative with a positive"a lot of new devs do this now... after I figured out I can't in any way get around that limit or outgrow it, I thought of quitting the game.a lot of people are also pissed about the new downside of running with a long gun, i.e. that you can't hit anything at close range. others are upset about acid rain ruining their runs with no warning.I'm not even far enough into the game where this is an issue, but it reeks of the same design mindset: making things annoying, obnoxious and limiting is somehow a design goal and an inherent good.I think the dev needs to stop making things cancer and making them fun. and stop listening to the super serious, fiddly, limiting and obnoxious, go design something like Go or Chess.and if you want systems that are hyper real, you get all the garbage that fills reality these days, i.e. people rather play games than deal with that nonsense. if your game feels like real life, just as irrationally limited and nannied by arcane and abstruse rules, voila, people are gonna start hating the _childDocuments_.review: Don't expect a carbon copy of Tarkov or Stalker with this one. I really hope we get multiplayer in the future. If you're someone who enjoys a more methodical and slow pace, I highly recommend this game.Edit:I see lots of complaints about load times, though mine has never taken longer than 20 seconds to load into a game. Turning down dynamic grass in the settings should help a lot. After putting more time in, I can confidently say the gameplay loop is EXCELLENT. The use of the fog of war adds a gripping third dimension to an otherwise 2D game. You will get caught off guard often if you aren't careful. The game stays quite difficult into the endgame, with some enemies killing you almost instantly even when wearing top tier armor. It is extremely satisfying running around in top tier gear, instakilling foes that once gave you trouble. All in all a fantastic game and I can't wait to see where the devs take it next!

_childDocuments_.review: ZERO Sievert gets lots of comparisons to Escape from Tarkov, and I imagine the comparison would also hold for the similar game mode in The Division.  I've played neither, as competitive multiplayer games can be a pretty toxic experience and I really just don't like the premise of griefing as gameplay, I don't want to be the dude who ruined someone's lucky find.  So having a single player PvE version of that basic premise was interesting.I can certainly see the appeal.  As other reviews will mention, the mechanics of aiming, accuracy, damage falloff, and visibility all come together to force you to play cautiously and tactically, ambushing bandits from one spot before disappearing into the treeline to pop out at them from a flank, trying to think of where they might outflank you or if some random animal or monster might decide to come after you and force you to shoot it and give away your position.The loot is pretty straightforward to understand - you scoop up loot (in an enjoyably gradual way, as items reveal one by one to simulate your character having to look through containers to find everything, leaving you vulnerable and increasing the excitement), and then you have to get to an extraction point to keep that loot.  It's an enjoyable tension.However, the game despite apparently being in 1.0 is very unpolished in terms of presentation.  Items have inconsistent capitalizztions.  NPC's instnatly display their dialogue the moent you click it in a menu, givng an impression that you're simply reading through a log rather than actually holding a conversation - there's a reason most games break up NPC text into bite size chunks and have the words gradually appear, it gives the impression that they're actually talking to you.  They don't change what they say either in subsequent conversations, which just further gives the impression you're just reading a sign with an arbitrary name on it rather than a character.  Your character is very liable to get stuck in geometry, only for the UI to announce to you that you need to hold CTRL + WASD to nudge yourself free as I suppose the dev had no luck in fixing the clipping bugs.Menu elements like your inventory frequently have unspeakably awful UX from waht presumably came out of the dev simply not knowing how to make something work more elegantly - so for starters, dragging and dropping one item on top of another item in your grid-based inventory doesn't swap their locations, requiring annoying menu juggling when trying to squish things together in a stash.  There's no conveniences like a "stack all" or "deposit all" button to make offloading your loot quicker while at base while maintaining a set loadout, though mercifully crafting uses items in storage as well... though it just makes the annoyance of trying to sell items to a vendor more apparent.  This compounds issues with other jank in menus - weapon repair kits, for example, don't simply let you right click and then specify what weapon to repair, you can't drag and drop it on a weapon to repair it, you can't even double click it and then click on the weapon to repair.  No, what you have to do is first  of the weapon you actually want to repair.  I sure hope you have room in your inventory to hold your massive 4x2 weapon for a minute if you don't want to drop it on the gorund and start blinding feeling around for it in the tall grass to retrieve if you have to move for any reasonThese aren't deliberate design decisions, but just very obviously the attempts of a developer to work around their own limitaitons as best they can.  And I can't help but respect it, because they clearly do understand the gist of what people like about this genre and brought it to a single player audience, little touches and tweaks to very carefully manage player behavior to make sure eveyrthing ffeels tense.  I guess that's just the essence of eurojank, you're playing a game that struggles at some very seemingly basic things while giving you a completely unique experience, requiring you to trust the judgement of a man that doesn't undesrtand you can't just render clickable text in the exact same way as uninteractive text and expect players to know that that's supposed to be a menu tab.  I just tried to move my farm over so it'd be a little easier to grab the items it generates between runs, only to realize it just straights up deletes it outright with no refunds of hte many resources it took to build.People refer to this game as being Tarkov with QoL improvements, but seeing as my own expectations were never set so low my comparison point is most other games or just computer programs in general.  I do appreciate the QoL features that seem very obviously to have been nods to community feedback, like hitting a hotkey to teleport between locations in the bunker, but I can't do things like hold a key to split a stack and see one half of the split stack being dragged by my cursor so taht I can visually see that it's working and that I did the key combination right.  I am very spoiled by games putting a lot of thought into these sorts of ergonomics and ZERO Sievert is a lot like hanging out with a dear friend on their couch that has a spring poking through the fabric and poking you in the ass.  The reason you're here is still good, you're going to have fun and enjoy yourself, but you're going to be enjoying yourself in spite of constant discomfort.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not for everyone, and let's preface that with, I did finish the game, but I kinda enjoyed it? But also pretty much didn't. Doesn't make sense? I'll explain. What this game does great, is litter your early game with incredibly tense combat AND extremely satisfying victories. Combat itself is not difficult to pick up or master, and every early run will feel like a champion crawling back from a bloodstained pit clutching spoils torn from the viscera of whatever it is you've recently slain. It's great, it's satisfying, it doesn't last forever.What this game does poorly, is pretty much everything else. The AI on enemies will often flip flop wildly between, "Will run into their own thrown grenade" to "This mediocre bandit with an ill gotten sniper rifle has locked onto you in the dead of night without having night vision goggles, and will immediately two tap you once you scuttle out from that rock you hid behind." It's really not fun to have a suppressed weapon in the dead of night, shoot one guy, and suddenly the sniper that is beyond your field of vision has immediately locked onto you and is killing you from an area you quite literally cannot see. Speaking of, weapon balance is pretty poor, and most of your fighting will be done at the very edges of your screen. You 100% have to pick up a sniper rifle, because 95% of the fighting will happen at the edge of your screen. Subbing in an AR or an SMG just allows you to either waste stragglers when they charge you, or kill hordes of mutants when they get too close. All the guns feel same-samey, and you'll probably end up just picking the guns that have the highest armor penetration ammo. If you do pick up the game, the ZZ Vel will carry you throughout the entire game and can be acquired early. Loot balance AND faction reputation are pretty poor. There's an entire faction that quite literally cannot set up because they've been beset by mutants, so you single handedly go in and wipe all the mutants out, letting them proliferate across the maps. Oh but sorry, they won't let you buy the nicer weapons or high armor penetration ammo unless you officially join their faction, which will piss off another faction increasing the amount of danger per raid. But then, there will be random scavengers just out and about toting around full magazines said ammo, or just loose leaf ammo hanging around in boxes. Why? It's highly unlikely random scavs killed what was supposed to be an elite corporation of soldiers and scientists, but then again, they were dying to run of the mill irradiated cannibals. Regardless, joining a faction should offer benefits on price, free stockpiles of supplies, or free equipment every so often, it should not simply prevent players from getting to the equipment end-game.Difficulty is entirely artificial once you get into the meat and potatoes. At first, it'll seem difficult because you don't have nicer equipment, or full durability armor. Once you do, you'll realize the game is really only difficult cause everyone can die in 3 shots or 3 melee hits, but the game will spam 7-30 enemies at you all at once. Nothing says frustrating like having to repeat the same quest 6 or 7 times in a row because they want you to clear out an area filled with ranged units that can 3 tap you, while they hangout with the best protecting armor in the game, AND there's 30 of them in that area. Or earlier in the game, clear out this lab that has 4 mutant nests in it that spawn 10 mutants each, on top of the mutants that already live in the lab. It's just annoying. Doesn't help that melee attacks slow you, preventing your escape, AND all melee units will just sit on top of you hitting you over and over until you die. It also really doesn't help that said units are extremely fast, and all enemies offer basically 0 audio cues until they're right on top of you. Lastly, smaller mediocre gripes. Saving money is incredibly easy, and there's not really much to spend it on. At best you'll need repair kits, but those only cost like 4k each, and when you come home with 40-80k, you're not really making a dent. There's no point to offering an armor repair service if the guy can't repair any higher tier armor. Faction reputation AND skill levels need to be leveled up way faster than currently implemented. Higher tier armors could be more durable. The ending and overall story was really not satisfying or interesting at all. Some quest items being randomly generated instead of consistently lootable is complete nonsense. 50% faster loot speed perk should be the norm. Perks all in all seem tacked on rather than something useful. Why can't I shuffle stashes or at the very least rename them? How come when you're done with a questline it just cuts off rather than having any form of notice that says, "Hey this is the end of this questline."? What's the deal with weapon vendors selling you a weapon but not carrying all the attachments for it too? How come there's no mechanic to maintain your weapons? Why isn't penetration explained in "this bullet can pierce up to this armor class" instead of what we currently have, which is a random arbitrary value? All in all, it can be fun? But honestly it's still really, really jank for a "fully released" game, and there's a ton of areas that can be improved and expanded upon. For 20 dollars, it's an alright, "play it until it gets frustrating" game. I wouldn't recommend it to anyone that isn't super into Tarkov esque combat combined with Stalker vibes. 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:I'm a teacher on Half-Term for a week. I wanted to catch up on my marking but spent 31 Hours playing this instead. No regrets. Longer Review:I bought Zero Sievert based on a Reddit post about alternatives to Tarkov, now that COD's DMZ is pretty much dead. I'm a really busy guy, I've got kids, I work a full week and I run a business on top of that. I like my few moments of gaming to be immersive but with the option to drop in/out for quick sessions. Zero Sievert totally scratches that itch. The gameplay loop is great, it's easy enough to get into and has just the right level of challenge to keep me interested without being overly difficult. At the moment, the game is in a very playable but definitely early-access state. Bugs are rare, there are a few typos in dialogue and some of the quests can be a bit glitchy. At about 30 hours in, I've maxed out all the stats, fully built my base, defeated all the bosses, collected most of the weapons/armour and finished the main Questline, so I'm probably going to swing back later down the line when we hit 1.0 for a fuller experience. Tips:The Scavenger Base Module is brilliant, it'll give you a constant supply of items to sell or craft with and will help build the other modules. A Stealth/Sniper build is really viable and works great at night once you have NVGs Your biggest expense early on will be Armor repairs, armor with lower 'Fragility', like the police armor will save you lots of money in the long run, as will crafting armor repair kits. The Radiation and Nourishment Injectors allow you to travel very light and basically remove the need to carry anti-rad or food/drink items (which are generally plentiful anyway). Do Ivor's Quest in the forest - it's worth it. You also do not have to kill him when asked.When you're strong enough - farm Lazar and his guards a few times and sell their weapons, you'll have enough money from there on to finance your expeditions. When you've max levelled a base stat (like stamina), you can choose a specilization by clicking on it in the journal.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It's a good idea, and an "okay" game. Just overpriced for what you get, and I can't even recommend it to people with craptops since Stalker Anomaly exists, and Anomaly does everything this does better, *for free*.Zero Sievert attempts to make a S.T.A.L.K.E.R.-Tarkov hybrid rougelike set in a 2D space. This would be okay if you had room for tactics, but its a *2D* game. Meaning you're cutting a lot of the mechanics that make gunfights work in a 3D space, and by extension the life or death decisions that would normally decide your fate in the titles this game was inspired by are mostly thrown out the window. Couple that with the fact you can spend 20-30 minutes on the map trying to out-loot the attrition of spent ammo, meds, and food, just to die to a factor completely outside your control and you have a recipe for a frustrating game with a lackluster payoff.A few examples: -Elevation. No vertical space to work with means there are no advantageous positions to work with or take up before an engagement, its whatever open space you can catch the most enemies in before you open fire. No choke points or stairwells you can hold a good view on while you eat/drink/med. Its whoever turns the corner first and if you can out-prefire them or not. Thanks to instant reaction times on AI, this is more often, not.-Headshots and body damage multipliers. If you hit an enemy in Zero Sievert they take damage to their overall health, no modifiers for where they get hit to affect the damage they take, meaning enemies can eat a lot more damage even if you have the drop on them or have time to line up a shot. The guy you're shooting have good armor? You need to shoot him 5 more times before he dies and don't worry about his buddies who now have their guns up ready to dome you the second you try to get closer, all of whom will eat just as many shots.Grenades: Can't throw grenades because there is no "throwing" in a 2D playspace. Enemies dug into a position? Guy hiding around a corner you can't get an angle on? 2 dudes hanging out in a room with a good crossfire on the entrance? Sorry, no other option than rush them or wait until they come into your line of sight and hope the dice roll in your favor.You get the point. The style of gameplay its trying to achieve falls flat because of what the game is at its foundation. Dying to things you cannot counter is called artifical difficulty and Zero Sievert has a lot of it. No matter how careful you are, not matter how much you plan an engagement, no matter how outgunned you have your enemies, it comes down to a dice-roll. Thats the exact opposite of what you want in a game like this.As for the game loop: Its shallow, just loot and return. Crafting is RNG (materials), most buildings have a single lootable chest in them as a placeholder, you can't ID enemies in the beginning so you end up just shooting on sight because you can't tell whos friendly and who isn't, quests are just find X item or kill X enemies. Faction relations are non-existent and are "work in progress". Anomalies are obscure and checking with bolts is inconsistent (another thing you *really* don't want in a game like this). If you want the Tarkov experience, just go play Tarkov. If you want a better 2D shooter, play Synthetik. If you have a bad PC and want something with deep gunplay and much more fleshed out mechanics in a 3D space complete with a weather system, natural disasters, dynamic faction relations and with better variations on the quests with a full dynamic start for roleplaying and completely player-customized difficulty for even the biggest masochists or the easiest run-and-gun settings for the COD fanboy sick of Activision (Oh, AND ITS FREE!), go play Stalker Anomaly or Stalker Gamma. As a rougelike this is frustrating and doesn't provide a whole lot of payoff when you figure it out. This game isn't worth ~$20 USD. I'm not kidding when I say that everything this game does, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. does better.

_childDocuments_.review: In a game where individual runs can be anywhere from ten minutes to an hour, crashes can really try one's patience. For those whose may experience graphical bugs/shader deb prompts preceding a crash, do check and make sure that the game is not using your cpu's integrated gpu function (if you have it).Apparently this app is considered a low power app, thus any automatic graphics settings will defer it to the "energy efficient" option. This can be changed in your Nvidia control panel or AMD equivalent.Outside of that hiccup, the game is very enjoyable for what it is. _childDocuments_.review: Having been keeping an eye out for a game that is reminiscent of such great games focusing on the post-apocalypse setting after a nuclear disaster, such as Battlestate Games' Escape from Tarkov coming to mind alongside the likes of GSC Game World's own S.T.A.L.K.E.R that bears a close resemblance to this indie title, ZERO Sievert takes places not in America but instead set somewhere in Eastern Europe as you are tasked with familiarizing yourself with once-friendly and peaceful lands now ravaged by all the dangerous elements that a nuclear apocalypse comes with it as well as the savage mutated monstrosities and ruthless bandits that roam the lands freely, slowly building up your reputation and ferocity as a 'Hunter' as you explore the various areas in this game which, as of the writing of this review, currently stands at 5 with a sixth soon to be on it's way!Before getting straight into the gameplay, no doubt it will intrigue some as to what comparisons this game has between Stalker/Tarkov here and, seeing how I am more familiar with Bethesda's works as far as these types of games go, I don't exactly have the gameplay knowledge to commentate on the big differences other than that ZERO Sievert, as an indie game, puts it's focus on a less technical and graphically-impressive world but rather sets it's eyes on a more 2D plane of exploration with decent 16-bit graphics to support a more retro-styled type of gameplay by building it's horror through it's atmosphere and monsters that you can't quite fully make out, which only deepens when you are dealing with them when it turns dark or when the weather becomes dangerous and actively harms your character by being exposed to it!With that being said though, how does one exactly 'progress' in ZERO Sievert anyhow? Seeing as the goals presented in these types of games vary from one game to the next but usually carry a theme of 'survival' and coming up against the odds, overwhelming as they may be at first, and coming out on top by the end of or near the end of the game whilst attempting to resolve the nuclear post-apocalypse conflicts and, perhaps, come to some form of understanding of what triggered such a catastrophic event and how to move forward from there.To start off, the very first mission entails a simple 'survival of the elements', whereby you are brought to somewhere in the middle of the map by a train seen at the entrance to your main base of operations (more on this later) to the chosen area of your choice, seeing as it is simple enough to getting there but, in order to leave, one must make their way towards one of two green flares that is visualized as a small green circle on the map to fully leave and return to base, taking with them whatever goods they were able to acquire on the field with them.No doubt though that is only a mere fraction of what this game entails though, seeing how surviving the first map is only one of two objectives as ZERO Sievert is a game that tends to not go easy on it's players, even during it's tutorial, as it also assigns you to kill at least 5 wolves to prove that you are prepared to face danger and come out alive as a Hunter, seeing how combat works purely on a gun basis, meaning that when your firearm runs out of ammo and you have nothing else to fall back on, you had best hope you don't run into any other danger or let it catch up to you, less you risk dying to either human or animal eager to rob you or eat you alive, possibly both depending on what you're dealing with!Also not even getting into the fact that, just because you may be adept at combat does not necessarily mean you are free from danger either as both the environment affected by the nuclear incident itself as well as your very own body present problems that one needs to be constantly aware of in order to survive for another day, with how the former can quickly change from harmless sunny weather into severe fog that hinders one's sight, radioactive rain that will increase your radiation depending on the severity of the weather and even bizarre 'emissions' that, if waiting out in the open for too long, will emit deadly plasma waves that quickly harm and kill both you and enemies alike!As for the latter, it is safe to say that this is a tradition as old as time itself as far as the survival genre goes, seeing how one must tend to their character's primal needs to sustain life itself, that being food to eat, liquids to drink and energy to rest alongside the aforementioned radiation which is kept preferably to a near bottom-low. These can be found lain across the dangerous areas through various human enemies holding them as well as many containers that can possess them, albeit most of them will be 'rotten', meaning eating or drinking them will pose a risk to you getting sick by receiving small boost to radiation that, with enough dosage of it, will ensure you throw up and become more hungry/thirsty as well as injuring you through nose-bleeds and the likes that require bandages to properly treat, something that becomes increasingly harder to avoid as later areas will be near enough like hotspots for various radioactive sources, of which the only key way to identify them (outside of static when too close to it) is by avoiding any vehicles and specific large objects as these seem to be the primary source of radiation from personal experience.Once you return to the main base of operations, aptly named the 'Zero Sievert Bunker' which essentially acts as your official Hideout for the entirety of the game, this is where you are assigned most of your quests during the game as well as being where several vendors offer both goods and services to ensure that you have a good use for Roubles, this game's currency, although bearing in mind that there exists multiple groups within the bunker, each with their own reputation that can only be increased by completing quests for them, as having too low a reputation means you will not be able to access their services or goods and, even for those you start off with, some of the more 'premium' goods will not be for sale until you prove yourself to them.Alongside a neat feature that allows one to customize their own little 'base' in the bottom-left corner of the bunker through various 'modules' that require a wide variety of resources to build, it's safe to say that there is plenty for one to do in ZERO Sievert as they slowly become more accustomed to the intense and scary atmosphere that this game brings with it, no doubt about that!However, to bring up some issues I had with playing this indie here, ZERO Sievert is a fairly challenging game, of which I personally enjoyed a great deal, and whilst it offers various difficulties to balance this out somewhat, it does little to resolve the problem of gathering resources for a certain type of activity, that being crafting your own items, seeing as the modules are one-and-done deals whereby you are granted the benefits permanently and can enjoy them whenever you like, whilst ammo, medicine, food and equipment repairs among others are quite resource-intensive for what little you get out of them, since some are fairly reasonable whilst others you get far too little from that it's better just to buy a brand new firearm or armour instead!Other nitpicks include certain enemy behaviours, mainly bandits equipped with powerful shotguns or rifles, are hard to counter at a higher difficulty as often they can one-hit you before you even have time to react as well as no melee alternatives, weak as they may be, means you are essentially helpless if you ever run out of ammo on the field, which is only made worse with a limited inventory coupled by a weight limit before it slows you down greatly.In conclusion, I'd safely say that ZERO Sievert is a pretty solid entry as far as indies go, given it's focus on the Eastern Europe landscape, and I look forward to seeing how it progresses as it leaves Early Access in the months to come!

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for almost an hour, but this was with 4 attempts.To explain. This game has a lot going for it, the idea is very good, and I can't help the feeling, but keep opening it up again and again, but when I do open it up, and play for 10minutes, I get very frustrated and close it.The frustration comes from the absolutely awful user experience across the board.Like I mentioned, in my 45 minute gameplay, I have experienced several "features" in the game, that are very hard to wrap my head around why something like this would be implemented.To mention specific things.* When you loot an enemy, each item has a load time. That means, when you open the loot menu, each item slowly loads in. Since they are loading at constant times, i assume that is intentional. Before it has fully loaded, you cannot loot or even see the item. I can think why this is implemented, probably to make it more realistic how in the real world you don't see absolutely everything instantly and to make the player evaluate situations and loot more carefully, but in the end this comes off as just the worst looting implementation I have seen in my 20+ years of gaming. If you are looting an enemy, you probably are safe enough, and punishing me by making me wait 5-10 seconds every time I want to loot something, is just making me want to skip the looting process altogether.* Radiation. It is absolutely everywhere. every step, every breath, every thought I have about moving in any direction, there is radiation. I feel like this is very unfair to me as a player to have to go trough this "punishment" right off the beginning of the game, to probably just unlock some anti rad gear later on. If that is the case, this is even worse than just punishing the player for no reason other than playing your game. In the very first minutes of gameplay, try to at least allow me to enjoy the scenery, figure out the mechanics, try to get a feel for the shooting, etc.. But instead of that, there is this nerve wrecking radiation noise every second of the game outside main base.* UI item tooltip. This one is beyond me. There is no way to instantly see the tooltip by holding down a button or something (to my knowledge). The only way to see what this item is, is to mouse over it, and wait for half a second. When you are new to the game, and instantly get hit by 100 different items, this, combined with the insane loot loading mechanism, completely puts me off even trying to loot something. It is just a chore, nothing else. For a game that is tagged as a "looter shooter" to have a player be disgusted even by the thought of opening a chest... it's very odd.These are just the major user experience choices made by the developer that baffle me, there are several more minor ones.User experience for this game feels like it was developed by a very young child, with no idea of how the game will play and just pushed in every player limiting idea they could and the devs were just - "yup, this looks solid".So my rating for the game, if it had the user experience completely reworked from scratch - 8/10My rating as the game is now 4/10. I still recommend it because, maybe these things really just bug me, and other people are absolutely fine with them.

_childDocuments_.review: Having sunk an additional 20 hours into the demo on top of what I currently have, I think it's pretty fair to say I  enjoy this game. I am particularly fond of the butt clenching early game and the moderate learning curve that comes with it. On regular difficulty you will die quite often but not enough to halt your gradual accumulation of good gear. Learning how to navigate the somewhat random maps and where to best find particular materials is helpful. Exploring new maps for the first time is (rightfully) terrifying.The gameplay is very tactical, methodical even. You'll spend a lot of time peering into the distance in order to secure your safety and prepare for the fast, lethal firefights. Range is your friend, but close quarters is often necessary to reach new objectives or better loot.This is the sort of game where a sufficiently skilled and knowledgeable player could rush end game gear. So, while there is a slow and useful skill grind, you aren't locked out of using anything you find. The story exists. I haven't really followed it because I just like fighting for gear. The game is also updated fairly regularly, the devs listen to feedback, and there is a very pleasant discord community. I don't know what else you could want from a small indy game, so if whatever you've already seen interests you, get this game.

Granted i haven't played the new map quite yet so it could be great/big but that's still not what was hinted at in previous versions. _childDocuments_.review: I am forced to come back here and switch my review to Negative, after thoroughly enjoying the game, prior to the most recent big update.Another case of devs messing up the good thing they had going post success.The jist of it is, the devs changed the weapon system in an incredibly stupid way, making weapons ineffective.Imagine a circle around your character.Now imagine you are using a Pistol. The pistol does full damage in the first 1/3 of the circle, which drops off gradually in 2/3 of the circle, and does 0 damage in 3/3 of the circle.Makes sense right?Now imagine using an Assault Rifle.The AR goes from 0 damage to full damage in the first 1/3 of the circle....Yes, really. You get cornered by any mob and you are holding an AR, you die if you fight at close range, because it does 0 dmg, or a fraction of its regular damage at close range.Snipers are even worse - 0 damage at close range, which gradually increases at medium range.This has been in the game for months, and I have been patiently waiting for the devs to listen to the constant negative feedback on the new system, and with their latest blog they "acknowledge, and understand our frustrations, and bla bla bla" and do not mention any upcoming changes to this stupid system.I'm done waiting.I had a blast with this game and would have recommended it prior to this nonsensical update.I don't recommend it to anyone, simply because the devs don't know what they are doing, and will likely make it worse with further stupid decisions.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a single-player top-down extraction shooter. Heavily inspired by Escape from Tarkov and Stalker. You go into one of the several maps, explore, kill, loot, and head to the extraction point to exit the map. In between expeditions, you mod weapons, pick up tasks from npcs, build up your hideout, and manage your stash.Unlike Tarkov, you don't lose anything when you die - you go back to where you were prior to loading the mission with everything intact (unless you play hardcore mode). To offset the fact that there are no human players or loss of progress, this game includes mutants, anomalies, radiation, and emissions inspired by the Stalker games. If you want to play a casual Escape From Tarkov with much less frustration, pick this game up.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is solo top down Tarky Stalky bois. If that sounds exciting to you, it's very much worth a try.If it seems odd to say Tarkov can translate to a top down pixel art game, the devs have really done a good job at this. Everything is scaled just a little differently and tweaked to fit the style of the game. It's not as "hardcore" but the balance is there and it can definitely just take your guys life at a moments notice. It's fun, intense, gunfights feel weighty and can very in length. It's really up there with most of the other better looter shooter extraction hate yourself but then do another raid anyways games. It also takes roughly 30 seconds to go from desktop to being in raid, which is really really nice compared to many of these kinds of games where load times, crashes, messing with broken saves, etc. can eat a lot of time. I had two crashes happen before raid so they cost me maybe 45 seconds put together and I didn't lose anything. Can't wait to see where they take this next.A few suggestions:- The HUD sometime get's in the way of a gunfight where the enemy is in the top left of the screen.- The quests don't always tell you which map to go to, might be intentional.- It crashed twice on me in 6 hours. Not bad for day one EA. Both times it was shortly after clicking to load into Forest map.- It might be a good idea to have it so when you hold RMB to zoom around, the zoom is farther up and down then left and    right to compensate for the screen dimensions. It feels a little weird being able to see much further east and west then    north and south.- A few item suggestions(maybe some are already there but I haven't seen them yet): Grenades, headsets, melee weapon.- Would be cool to be able to change fire modes on rifles and such.

_childDocuments_.review: (Hardcore Hunter) ~700 hoursThis game's potential has so much head room, but we have a long, very long way to go. Currently with v.40 out it has divided the player base from what I've seen on reddit, and it is a tad concerning to me. For clarity I am pro v.40This game has helped me learn to focus and organize better, and has really helped my problem solving skills overall. With this new update, the game-play has slowed down immensely to what I have been accustomed to for months (and a year maybe?) and it's forcing me to slow down even more. I love it. However, the drastic change in pace is something I can see that has ultimately compromised the community and I'm going to try and fix that right here.The obvious changes now and what new players won't ever experience from the older versions is the grazing feature (enemy flashes red) where if the weapon you're currently using isn't being utilized at it's optimal distance, the hit will not register. For those of you just joining, you need to understand that everything that you once saw on the screen was a valid target, no matter the distance. The devs are obviously working extremely hard to provide more depth within the game and this new change has amplified that exponentially. This has caused me more anxiety, frustration, hair pulling, and desk smashing (consider grabbing yourself an XL mat to absorb some of the impact). This game is challenging me more and I welcome it. That being said, how we interpret the distance may not immediately make sense to use from a bird's-eye perspective at a glance. The gaps in which the weapons effective range respond to will take you HOURS to get comfortable with, and it will KICK - YOUR - ASS. I have a comfortable solution for this: an option for locking your cursor within the minimum and maximum diameters that your weapon's optimal range requires. This will EXTREMELY help those out that are on their Steam Decks with limited cursor movement.I would love to personally tell the staff that their hard work is not going unnoticed, and the vast majority of us appreciate the hard work that's going into this game. You guys rock!

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally buy early access games, I review them even less, but I needed to leave this review. Is this game worth it in its current state of early access at its current price point? Yes.I already have over 20 hours into it and am just as excited to play it as I was 15 hours ago. The game certainly isn't finished and some of the criticisms that have been levied in these review are warranted, they just don't come close to outweighing the positives to me. First off difficulty: I have no issues with the difficulty. If you are impatient you will be punished. Take things slowly and at distance and choose your engagements. Survivability: Your armor has a condition percentage. Once that condition goes to zero it isn't functioning as armor. That's why you're suddenly dying more often. The DR will repair your amour for a fee, I would recommend doing that every time you come in from a raid, it appears to be cheaper that way. - Hydration is an issue early on. Prioritize drinks over all loot. Buy all the water you can from the Barman, this resets every day at 7:30. Ammo: The type of ammo you use is hugely important. Don't try and go against heavily armored foes with the low penetrating ammo, you will use an entire magazine before you kill them. The same is true for you though, if you have high tier armor you will sponge rounds from low caliber wielding bandits. Things I would like to see: More content: Quests, maps, guns, attachments. I would like to see some more attachments that aren't just clear upgrades, give us some that require tradeoffs that can lead down different playstyles. - Throwables would be great, maybe remove a med slot or two for grenade types.All-in-all I think the current spot the game is in is excellent given how close we are to early access release and I'm excited for future content updates, but I never recommend buying a game on what the future might bring and the game is worth it in its current form.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - I strongly advise you to wait until release v1.0 before you buy this game. The game you're getting now may not be the game you want when released v1.0 eventually. Also, there's potential that this game will be in Early Access for a long time.Let me elaborate further.Based on the updates this game has been receiving, there's potential that the game mechanics will be constantly redesigned or maybe revamped. I'm not talking about changes like UI or QOL or minor stuff. It's about the core mechanics. Imagine a developer making an Action RPG, only for it to evolve to Active Battle System RPG. Or a Hold 'Em Poker turning into Draw Poker. Sure, it's still poker, or RPG with action in it., but now it's not what you wanted in the first place.The updates right now gives me an impression that the developer does not have a concrete idea or solid design specification / direction to the game. The development seems to be about throwing ideas at the wall and see what sticks. Or just throw it without seeing the results. This is not a good sign.Biggest example now is the recent update making changes to the core shooting mechanics. It is now the biggest source of contention of this game at this time. Expect lots of other things to change as it looks like the game design turns into a whack-a-mole session. i.e. Change something, and then try to change another thing in response to the previous change. Development hell.I bought this game to demo the first 2 hours. I liked it and had the impression that the development direction is already solid. I would have refunded it immediately if I knew otherwise. I stopped playing.Analogous to this, if you remember the Early Access period of this game called 'Starbound' ; Almost 10 years ago. The flip flop design where the mechanics (e.g. how the items stats work) kept changing to the point a number of people I know of got burned out and never touched the game again.Or AI Wars, where the core damage / RPS mechanics kept getting revamped, until I got tired from trying to relearn everything again.
