_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty decent. I would have liked to see more of the underworld in order to get a feel for the setting. But I think it sets out to tell the story it wants to. Fair warning the game is pretty light on gameplay and most of the battles are pretty easy, I think I died once out of apathy but outside of that it was straightforward.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: **Graphics are flawless. Feels like a high-quality earthbound crossed with a little bit of Gunple/Gunman's Proof. Adore the spritework and the backgrounds and the animations-- it was what first made me click on an ad for the game, and did not disappoint.**Characters are likable, but the sudden development is VERY sudden imo. Pacing really threw me off, but once I made a conscious choice to shrug and continue anyway it was... fine. I guess.**Music is... meh? I'd have liked to see some development go into this, as it feels like not a lot did? It's very forgettable and feels like an afterthought, when it can be used to do amazing things.**THIS IS NOT A FULL RPG.**This is not a bad thing, just not what you may think upon seeing that term used when advertised, exactly. You do not have stats that do anything (aside from getting meg's 'health/happiness' slightly increased after every battle. your attack+defense also go up but to no noticeable change). You don't have an actual inventory. The combat is far more akin to a puzzle, and there is a set number of battles in the entire game.**The story was quite cute, albeit extremely short and the ending wasn't the full experience I wanted or expected going into it, but by that time there was also enough flags to warn me that it wasn't going to go that way.I beat the entire thing in 4.7 hours, and that was with a couple of pause-menu-snack-breaks. Not an RPG, but a cute visual novel with some puzzles and walking around thrown in. I think if it was stated to be such from the start more people would know if they should go into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't cry but beautifully made story and everything, combat can get a little annoying sometimes but overall great. I also recommend playing their bear restaurant game that one put me through more emotional stuff than this game but it is both cute stories with dark/deep stuff but this one is more lighthearted in my opinion
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: I never do reviews I rarely do but I had to for this one:I just wanted to say, that I adored this game more than I thought i would. The characters are all very loveable and easy to get attached to!If you crave monster and human games kind of like the undertale series then this game is for sure it. I highly recommend it, and you'll cry a lot too, this game will pull your heartstrings.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: This is a story focused RPG, It sets out to tell a story not reinvent the wheel. The battle system was simple with QTE's that made them interesting and fun. It had an Undertale feel to it but it is no way a clone or copy. The Story tugs at your heart strings with great character dynamics. Those looking for a traditional copy & paste RPG or RPG maker game trying to compete with AAA titles or trying to bank on your nostalgia, this not it. The Story is the strongest part of the game the reason you should buy and play it. I do wish there was more story but it accomplished its goal in the time allotted. I recommend it especially if you love RPGs but are tired of the cheesy stories, false promises and just want to to enjoy a light-hearted story without needing to grind.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: A short, but sweet adventure with a Pokemon-esque battle system. Gameplay has some unique gimmicks throughout, but the story is the meat and potatoes here. Very charming characters, pleasant art style, gentle music, and unique world carry the experience till the end. Give this game your time and you won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: I came across this game on just a whim, browsing steam recommendations and here this was. I generally get how stories go, I've seen enough to know the tropes and can often see how it ends. This had suprising twists I did not see coming, but in looking back I can see the connections. I never took my headphones off, the ost is small but they are all fantastic and worthy of listening on their own. I found myself getting attached to the characters, feeling joy and sorrow through their journey. I can count the number of games I have cried at with one hand, and I am happy to say this has joined that short list. The strongest reason I recommend this, is at the end of it all, with having done everything there is to do and seeing this tale to the end, is the fact that I deeply want more, and I hope to see more from this team.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: Meg's Monster is beautiful journey filled with emotion, humor and great music. It is quite short, but the game doesn't overstay it's welcome. The turn-based combat gets challenging, which makes you think about your next move. I definitely recommend you play Meg's Monster, it's a game worth checking out!
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: Don't drop this game!! The first half of the game is a bit underwhelming and straightforward, but I promise that if you stick with the game after the first ending, you will be rewarded with a phenomenal experience with unexpected plot twists and loads of emotion and unique gameplay mechanics, up there with To The Moon, Undertale, and the like.The entire game is presented in a retro, GBA-inspired style that's right up my alley. The aesthetics are top-grade stuff, with stunning pixel art rivaling that of Mother 3. The music is also great: I'd expect no less from Reo Uratani, who also worked on music for Monster Hunter 3, Hyrule Warriors, and so on.Going into more detail about the game's plot, and my retrospective experience below.[HEAVY SPOILERS BEYOND THIS POINT!! BEWARE!!]The first half of the game felt rushed: The story lacked the polish that I saw in the second half (more on that later) and I felt like the story was going through the motions of similar stories that I'd seen in the past, without much intrigue, and with minimal gameplay mechanics. On a surface level, the story feels particularly inspired by Undertale's lore, where it almost feels like a rewritten fanfiction somehow (Underworld of monsters separated from humans w/a war between them; A flower bed resulting in the merging of monster+human; A dump where humans throw their waste and monsters find value in their contents; a large council member with a large foreboding silhouette wearing a cloak, protecting their citizens by preventing them from reaching the surface; and so on...)The similarities to Undertale are not necessarily a bad thing, however: I think there is always room for alternative takes on existing stories! Unfortunately though, I was struggling to find many positives beyond the aesthetics to continue playing the game beyond the first half: I felt that the gameplay was not very interesting (all the battles felt the same), and the plot developments were lacking intrigue. As for the plot developments that got my attention, I felt that they were revealed a bit too early by the other NPC characters, whenever the protagonist left the room. It was difficult to feel much for the argument between Meg and Roy when a council member came to visit and Meg fell, or when Gustav got shot by the humans, because by that point I was not invested enough in the characters.The second half of the game was truly a marvel though, and I'm very glad that I decided to stick with the game after the first ending, when the grown-up main heroine breaks down crying after discovering the truth about Roy. The game then travels back in time to the point where a council member cuts the rope leading back to the surface. Afterward, the protagonist needs to get a ladder to progress up to the nearby skull statue, and it's at this point where the game starts picking up in both story and gameplay. From this point on, the game introduces more unique gameplay elements, some which give characters more personality (card shuffling) and others which tie directly into the story (particularly, Sebastian testing Roy by pulling out a megaphone that has very similar mechanics to those seen later in the game). I also really enjoyed the battles against Nancy, Victor, and Meg, where the dialogue and game mechanics would help create tension between them and Roy.The second half of the game also focuses more deeply on the characters' backstories: Knowing the secret mission that Golan was sent out to do, we get to witness his struggle as the opportunity to betray Roy crosses his mind. We get to see his struggle after growing attached to Roy, and it's done so in a (very well-executed!) way that directly makes sense with the involved puzzle's level design. We also get to learn a lot more about Sebastian and his previous life, which also helps explain why he was so well-versed with humans and their technology, like fixing Joey the robot.My only concern about the second half of the game is that it leaves a bit of a sour note, that humanity will continue throwing waste down the cliff, and Roy detests eating the waste, on top of it being a dangerous idea to do so... I cannot recall if the waste was created solely by the now-defunct Lab? But worth mentioning here because it was still on my mind by the time I reached the final "THE END" screen...The game just came out very recently at the time of writing this review, and I genuinely hope that the game will perform well: I am writing this review out of love and support for the game, and I pray that those decide to pick up this game will stick with it to the very end, because I *guarantee* that Meg's Monster will deliver more than what it promises on the surface, as a unique, rich, and memorable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely wonderfully written story. The writing does a great job of getting you attached to the characters, and the setting is beautifully designed. Although on the short side, it's wrapped up and delivered in a well thought out package. Even the simple mechanics are pretty innovative, enjoyable for the ride, and blended really well with the narrative. Overall, would definitely recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: This game hit me right in the feels. I honestly cried. It's a heart-warming story between Meg and Roy and their adventures together. Despite being from different "worlds", their friendship rises above challenges they continuously encounter; aside from friendship, the game also showcases camaraderie and altruism. The music is very expressive and helps in creating an atmosphere for certain scenes. I love the piano version of Wishing Star so much that I can't wait to get sheet music; however, personally, it felt used as a BGM a bit too much; I still love it nonetheless!Would I recommend Meg's Monster? Yes, absolutely. It is worth it. I hope this game will get more attention. If you're an empath looking forward to playing this game, get some tissues ready. You have been warned.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally review games, and to be honest-- I'm not good at it. Nonetheless, I honestly felt I had to give this game a review just to express my experiences with it. Finding out about it just today, 2 days after its release due to Nintendo having dropped a trailer for the switch port, I found the artstyle intriguing and reminiscent of games like Mother 3-- The Mother/Earthbound Series has had major influence on modern RPGs, and I can see a fair bit in this game myself. It's a short and sweet game, with great humorous moments and it made me cry multiple times throughout it. Honestly, a certain segment in the second half was one of the funniest parts of the game just because of it derailing the story for a bit in a humorous way. Having released on console and PC, I feel like the game will very well reach a good audience, and I sincerely hope it does. It's one of those games that, if it has the chance and exposure, could very well end up a classic. Just might want to put a notice that the game isn't responsible for any onion-cutting ninjas in your vicinity.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: A short, but well-written, wholesome experience. I interpret the story as one of compassion and camaraderie. About the joy we can bring each other and how much better life becomes when we share it. It's a story about friendship, which I believe can never be overstated, but not one that is overdone or devoid of risk. The adventure has real stakes, for both the world and the characters, and I plowed through it in a single afternoon because I needed to know their fates. Meg's Monster plays more like a visual novel than a by-the-numbers JRPG. Most of the game is dialogue between characters and for the above reasons I was fine with that. It's a gem and I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: Yep, I'm the one who's left crying.A super wholesome and sad story with some unexpected twists and beautiful soundtrack. My only gripe is that there are some plot points near the finale that could have been explored further, but overall, a great game. Battles and puzzles can give a challenge but don't detract from, and in fact complement, the narrative that drives the game.If you have a few hours and enjoy immersing yourself in story-driven games, this is definitely something worth experiencing.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review: While extremely short, this 15 dollar investment was completely worth my time. In this gripping 5 hour long journey, you play as a grumpy monster named Roy who must escort a young Meg back to the surface world, where she wants to return to her mother. The gameplay is simple, but immersive when needed, and the writing is cute, yet it's encased in this rugged strong language to remind the player the kind of environment the world sets itself up to be.Extremely touching story with amazing music composed by the now independent sound designer Reo Uratani, who previously worked with the Monster Hunter series. His soulful approach to the soundtrack along with the beautiful motif throughout the game that was then vocalized by Laura Shigihara.This is a game you do NOT want to miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Meg's Monster

_childDocuments_.review:
Welcome to the Underworld - a land of monsters and mutants who eat humans for breakfast.

One such monster - a hulking ogre by the name of Roy - has no interest in eating humans. But one day, he and his best friend Golan stumble upon a lost little girl named Meg, and discover something truly terrifying: the moment she starts wailing in fear, a blood-red hue washes over the sky, and the earth itself begins to tremble and quake.

That's right: this small girl's tears hold the power to bring forth the apocalypse - and the only way to stop it is for them to help find her mother so she can make it safely back home.

Meg's Monster is a short, story-driven JRPG with a big twist. Players control Roy, who begins the game with 99,999 HP and is virtually untouchable - but the real concern is keeping Meg safe, because if she starts crying, it's game over for everyone. 

Players will have to master the unique mechanics and mini-games baked into each battle, all while protecting Meg and using her favorite toys to keep her pacified.

name: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss
detailed_description: Thalassa is a single player, first person psychological drama set in 1905. You play as Cam, a deep sea diver in a crew of adventurers and pioneers aboard Thalassa. As you prepare to raise a long-forgotten Spanish galleon from the ocean, what should be a great day for history takes a turn for the worst. Upon needing to take some time to heal from the event, you discover Thalassa has met a mysterious and unfortunate end. Your former crew mates are gone, and you'll need to descend into the depths to board the ship once more. Alone in the ocean, with your diving support Bailey guiding you from the surface, it's up to you to piece together the clues left behind in the wreckage and discover what really happened in the final moments onboard the ship. Immerse yourself in an atmospheric story of self-discovery and sorrow onboard Thalassa. Discover a story that delves into the complexities of human emotions and interactions, and learn about the intricate relationships between your crew members. You'll uncover the personal struggles of each member of Thalassa's crew and how grief can be experienced in different ways. Loss takes its toll in many shapes and forms, while life marches on. As the only diver left in the crew, it's up to you to return to Thalassa, now in its final resting place on the seabed. Navigate your way through the strange, but beautiful surroundings and discover the clues that will help you unravel the events leading up to the disaster. Experience the calm and isolation of deep-sea exploration as you navigate through debris of the shipwreck. In order to continue exploring the ship, you'll have to find the right tools to help unblock the obstructions in your path.

short_description: Uncover the mystery of Thalassa, a first-person psychological drama set under the sea. Ill-fate has fallen on your former crew and friends and it’s up to you to find answers onboard the wreckage. Experience the melancholic underwater journey of human stories facing life and loss.

_childDocuments_.review: This game took me into the depths of a sunken ship for just over 8 hours, exploring every square inch of the ship seeking answers as to why the crew of the ship met their demise.  After the 8 hours and solving 100% of the mysteries, I was sad the game was ending. I still wanted more, the game was that good. Highly recommend to play this game in the dark with headphones to get fully submersed in the experience.+ The atmosphere and underwater ambience is done to perfection.  I literally felt as I was in a diving suit underwater searching for answers of the late crew members.  Its just you and the ship, no jump scares, very mature well written game.+ There is a massive intricate web of events that led up to the demise of the ship, hats off to the developers for pulling the back stories of all the characters together. By the ending of the game I felt as if I knew all the characters personally.+ The sound effects were top tier, the screeching of the metal doors, the noises of the water and bubbles+ The voice acting was really well done, many different accents, some very emotionally performed dialog+ The layout and design of the ship was done to perfection, the developers carried your journey room to room, and then near the end of the game, up and around and over, it seems like every square inch of the ship was managed and specifically thought out for a purpose- The 10 minute prologue is a bit slow and a bit over the top on the emotional side, too sappy. This might turn off several people which is super unfortunate, because the main game after is superb- Some of the mysteries that needed to be solved on the mystery bulletin board were solved by guessing and seeing what fits, I couldn't make out some of the logic. This didn't happen often though, I would say 95% I would understand get first try.- I like to turn Subtitles off in games to get the full immersive experience and this game did not allow me to do this- There was a minor stutter in this game as I was walking around, the game isn't optimised 100%, however this wasn't as noticeable as in normal games because of the environment the game is in, being underwater with a diving suit, dirty glass and waves everywhere masked the problemThe small nitpicking negatives as a whole did not hinder the grand journey to the depths and the massive intricate web of character stories you uncover.  Wonderful and soothing experience.9 / 10
_childDocuments_.name: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this Indie game. After I saw the first couple of trailers, it really reminded me of the Bioshock 1 and 2's ocean atmosphere. Especially as you walking through the empty water filled halls and passage ways, kind of made you feel like Subject Delta from Bioshock 2.  A ship that was once your home is now an empty shell, the signs of life was once there. But now all that reminds is you, the ocean, silence and your thoughts.Overall though the game made you feel like Deep sea diver Sherlock Holmes or Hercule Poirot. You wanted to find out why the Thalassa sank,  well be ready. It is a spiderweb of mysteries entangling the entire crew of the ship. Everyone has a secret, but is the blame on one person or everyone. The theme of coming to terms of ones own guilt over a situation that they could not control and the depression that came afterward. It hits home, you can't save everyone. As much as we try or think about what we could of done, there nothing more we can do in the moment of terrible tragedy. Situations happen that are out of our control.Been a while since I sat down and played a single player game. And I was impressed. I have heard of people having technical issues. On my computer, it ran great. No shuddering, glitches, or crashes. It is bound to happen.I give it a 10/10 and this is rare for me. Most games I find something wrong, but this is the first one in years that I got this interested and wanted to find out the end of the Thalassa.
_childDocuments_.name: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss is a satisfactory combination of walking sim and detective game, despite a few notable problems. With a clunky start and some believability concerns, it takes a while before the game settles into an agreeable state. While most of the mysteries are easy to clear, there are prominent issues with some clues and deductions. Traipsing back and forth through the shipwreck is more irksome than interesting, despite a few good holographic memories to witness. And with the game’s stutters and audio problems, the modest underwater atmosphere is compromised. Conceptually, Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss is fine, but too often it feels like you're drowning while playing.***Neutral rating***
_childDocuments_.name: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: There is so much left to explore, and the oceans are one of the most mysterious place left on Earth. This is the mission of the SS Thalassa. The crew is full of hope. The atmosphere aboard is festive. They are about to complete the recovery of a lifetime, raising the St-Catherine, a long lost Spanish galleon. Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss is a first person psychological drama by the Sarepta studio. It is published by Team17 who are known for their extensive catalogue of indie games.The game takes place at sea, mostly underwater. Miss Isabel is a modern woman - a woman before her time. She has dreams and the money to make them happen. She owns the Thalassa and has big plan for it. Little does she know that tragedy is about to strike her and her crew on their voyage. You play as a deep-sea diver named Cam, one of a team of adventurers aboard the SS Thalassa. The game starts with the team preparing for a very important dive. Today is a special day. The Thalassa’s crew is getting ready to raise the St-Catherine. Bailey is helping you into your suit. He is the one responsible for the equipment aboard the Thalassa. The big moment as arrived, and you will finally get a first look at the Spanish galleon. It’s time for you to begin your descent. Chaos erupts! Something terrible has happened. You and Bailey are the only ones left alive.Now several months have passed since you lost your friends. You’ve barely had time to grieve, but you want answers. With the SS Thalassa and her crew at the bottom of the ocean, you and Bailey take to the sea, ready to dive to the Thalassa’s hulk. There are many mysteries to solve.The game is presented from a first person point of view. There are a couple instances where you are on the boat, but most of the game is played underwater. There is a lot of emphasis on the story. I found the slow build-up interesting - almost everything you encounter on your exploration will give you an additional piece of the narrative. There are wax rolls scattered around the ship that let you listen in on some interviews taken on the Thalassa, giving you even more context into the mysterious story.The main mechanic of the game consists of mysteries that you must solve. There is a screen that looks a bit like a family tree with all the mysteries, and by clicking on each one you will get more information. Clues can come from anywhere. These mysteries help to add depth to the story and also resolve some unanswered questions. Each mystery is a different question that needs to be deciphered. Only when you find the right clues can a mystery be solved by clicking the “conclude” button. At the conclusion of each of these, you will get another piece of the Thalassa’s tale. I had fun unravelling the mysteries, and it kept me engaged in the game and its story.The art is gorgeous, and the subdued colours and somewhat hazy graphics did a great job of making me feel like I was truly underwater. Bailey is there through the game helping you and giving you hints. I had a great time playing Thalassa, but there is one aspect that I found exasperating - when you fire up the game, get ready to wait. There are a lot of different screens to open throughout the game, and as the mysteries are the principal mechanic in this game, you will be opening this screen again and again. You can’t get around the extremely long waiting time since you will need to open your inventory and the mysteries several times during one playthrough. If you are not the patient type, this canbecome a real impediment.You can see the developers have paid great attention to details. The map of the ship is very lifelike. The Thalassa has several levels with many rooms, and the detailed map makes it easier to get around. It also highlights where you should look and the main areas of interest at each moment. My favourite part of the game is the way the creators have chosen to tell the story. Every aspect of the game is used to shape the narrative. You get bits of the story by listening to the characters on the wax rolls, and also from the objects you discover and the surroundings. The mysteries are also a big part of creating the tale.Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss is a stunning game with an emotional narrative. I especially loved the mystery mechanic where you get to be part of the investigation. I enjoyed uncovering the crew’s story bit by bit. If you don’t mind waiting for the different screens to load, and enjoy solving mysteries, Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss is sure to keep you entertained until the end.Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss is a touching psychological drama with an emotional narrative and some engaging mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game setting that recalls one of the most interesting stories of navigation, the titanic.the emotion that this game gives you is immense and as you advance you will discover a lot of secrets and interesting things.If you like games based on a story and little on the gameplay you will definitely like it. perhaps a little too slow and clumsy the movement of the character especially when taking objects.

_childDocuments_.review: Not the longest game (I finished in 11 hours with breaks included), but it has a well-done story, beautiful graphics, and gameplay that definitely captures the feeling of exploring a recently wrecked ship. I 100% recommend this game for people that really want to get into a story and can accept that there aren't always happy endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game with a few minor flaws. I played a lot of the time offline whilst travelling so I think actual playtime was around 15 hours.First the good; I think it has a compelling story, and made me want to learn as much as I could about the various mysteries on board. The setting was outstanding, I feel this is a really under-utilised setting in games over all, and would love to see more of this setting.The ship was big enough to explore and not get bored, there was some back tracking to open previously closed areas, but for some reason this was not a chore, it just made me want to unlock the different areas all the more.Having said I love the setting, I do feel the ship could have been lying on its side/at an angle - not many shipwrecks are sitting perfectly upright at the bottom of the sea. It would have been more interesting to have the boat on it's side for example, but I do appreciate that would have made it all the more difficult to navigate, and this brings me to my second criticism. I understand you are underwater and it takes a while to get around, however some of the animations were painfully - but I guess realistically - slow, it just made certain parts drag.The game doesn't seem to be that well optimised either, with my ROG Ally struggling to keep up, and a decent laptop faired no better either. FPS was all over the place from high 50's to 30 mainly (at medium), but this was very glitchy. There were some areas where this dropped to between 5-10fps at times. Annoying but not game breaking. Lastly (no spoilers) like a lot of games there is a point of no return, however I was in limbo with a few mysteries still to complete, and unsure whether by going beyond the point of no return I would be able to complete them - as it turned out I could, but I think the game could have done a better job of relaying this information. I stopped playing it at this point whilst trying to find out from the web, but the answers were ambiguous, so I just backed up my game saves and bit the bullet.Overall I really enjoyed the game, even given the comments above, and I would look forward to to the next adventure in this universe!Thanks for a great game devs - much appreciated!
_childDocuments_.name: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game/story & with a great exploration of grief & how people cope with certain tragic situations differently. Graphically beautiful & voice acting was top notch as well.Only negatives are for deck owners, which is what I played this on & why my game time is so long. It is not optimized well currently. A lot of crashes & random pop in even on medium or low settings especially when I first started playing that I almost gave up & had to switch to proton experimental as well to get it to even run. When I decided to boost the decks Watts to 15, that lowered the crashes & gave a better performance where I was able to complete the game & almost get every achievement. It’s such a great game & I was so invested in the story that I managed to just accept the deck issues which definitely played a role in taking so long for me to complete the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: A short but excellent narrative game, that delivers an emotional experience.  I highly recommend it if you enjoy character driven story and exploration. While the gameplay is centered around exploring the Thalassa, what keeps you engaged is the shifting perspectives you have on the crew and their actions.  Themes include grief, loss and responsibility.
_childDocuments_.name: Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss

_childDocuments_.review: You explore a shipwreck looking for clues as to what happened. Once you've gathered enough clues for a particular scenario, a message will appear on-screen and you use the in-game interface to put the clues together. It's very well done and I recommend it if you like relaxing adventure games. Took me about 12 hours to complete the first time. The only negatives are occasional stutter and low voice volume that seems unaffected by the settings.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a nice relaxing game with a unique mystery solving aspect. The environment is beautiful and highly detailed. The story is compelling and well written. Game play itself is fine, It's not very challenging and I think most children would have an easy time with it, although the story may not be entirely suitable for children, having themes of death and romance.The only negative things I have to say about it is that it seemed to be very demanding on my PC for some reason. While the environment is stunning, it's not very interactive. You just kind of move around and pick up objects, sometimes you can zoom in to take a closer look but that's about it. Without headphones the audio isn't very good, I could barely hear the dialogue at some points with the volume all the way up. Sometimes it seemed like they forgot to add sound effects at certain points which took away from the immersion. Also, there are these "wax rolls" throughout the game that you have to find, but they're all labeled the same thing: "Hans Interview" even if that character isn't in the recording... idk it's just something random that got to me after a while. The game has a cool way of guiding you throughout story by highlighting on your map which areas you still have to search, but there are times when this doesn't happen so you can feel stuck and end up just wandering around aimlessly searching for something. Overall I would give it a 6/10 when compared to similar games of this genre. Definitely worth a try especially if you like ships and such.

_childDocuments_.review: It's got some issues. Second issue would be that some clues only spawn at certain points in the story, so you can completely vacuum a room and then later find yourself back there, swearing you checked that cabinet and there were most definitely nothing there last time. Third is the wax cylinders, it's a little immersion breaking how they are spread out all over the ship, it makes no sense within the story. But it's makes the story and information flow better, much like the second issue, so it's a minor nitpick really.That's the negatives out of the way. Thalassa is a really competent story teller and investigation game, you're not exactly on the edge of your seat, but certainly craving for more answers all the way through. The plot just keeps thickening and I personally found it really satisfying and thought provoking at the end when you have all the answers. I would highly recommend the game, if you have the patience for it, it's a slow burn and no mistake.Bit of practical information at the end. Game ran like ass on ultra settings (not a hardware issue) FPS were fine when standing still or walking straight, but turning caused FPS drops and stuttering, lowering the graphics to High solved the issue entirely and I could frankly not see a difference in graphical fidelity. Sound, especially voice, is pretty low even at max volume, not an issue on its own, but if you have anything else playing at the same time, you might miss some voice work, there's subtitles for everything though.The game took me 7 hours to complete the first time and I were very thorough. _childDocuments_.review: I picked up the demo for this game during the Steam ‘NextFest’ and it was the only demo I grabbed this year which became a full purchase.I have been waiting for launch since the demo and the full game has not disappointed. I finished my playthrough in around 8 hours, but have missed some mysteries and apparently haven’t visited everywhere on the ship so I will be running this again.The environments are beautifully crafted and I loved exploring the wreck of the Thalassa. It is worth being aware this is a walking simulator that follows a story. I commented on this after the demo, but there were at least two instances in the game where I spotted items I should have been able to pick up but was blocked from doing so until I had advanced the story to the point my character ‘knew’ they had to pick them up. I suspect this is needed to stop the player jumping ahead, but it does occasionally create a moment where you feel like you are watching a movie character miss something obvious and are willing them to see it to little avail!Some of the puzzles (or Mysteries) didn’t, and still don’t make sense to me so I did find myself combining semi random items to solve them. The game doesn’t punish you for this though and the vast majority did make sense providing you take the time to read the documents and listen to the audio logs.For me this game was well worth purchasing at full price (in the UK at least, I know Steam does odd things with costs in some other countries). I experienced some issues with sound levels in the game. The voices in the prologue were almost impossible to hear, so having cranked my sound system up to the maximum the moment your character dons their diving suit the volume ramped up to the point it made the living room floor vibrate! I do have a 5.1 surround sound system, in the end I changed the sound setting to Stereo but I still found myself keeping my hands close to the volume controls. This isn’t the first game I’ve had this sort of issue with but it does feel like there is an issue with some of the volume levels at least.If you like narrative experiences that keep you wanting to know what happens next I think you’ll like this. If you aren’t sure but you’re here anyway try the demo, I think the developers have perfectly ‘sliced’ the game so that the demo is representative without giving away too much.I think that might be the longest review I’ve ever written (so far!)

_childDocuments_.review: Most of this review will be about the collectively-major problems i had with the game, so I want to emphasize: for most of the time, Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss is awesome. Mystery/detective games often struggle to actually give the player the experience of solving the mysteries, but Thalassa's mystery mechanics work very well -- guiding you toward which types of evidence to examine and what types of connections to look for, but you still need to mentally make those connections to be able to mark a mystery as complete. When the game is mechanically working, it's working very well.But there were a lot of pain points which significantly brought down the experience for me. To enjoy this game to its fullest, you really need to be able to weather an onslaught of in-your-face flaws. For me, those flaws started to dominate the experience toward the end of the game, and my experience suffered death by a thousand paper cuts.This is a very slow-paced game, so it's essential for the moment-to-moment interactions to be smooth, but they often aren't. You click interact, then the camera slowly moves one axis at a time to the magic spot to start the animation, which often is nonsensically far from the interaction trigger, and then most of the time, the start of the animation moves the camera back to near where you originally had it! This kind of micro-mechanical friction is pretty pervasive.The "proper" mechanics aren't perfect either. The map helpfully tells you whether there's something you missed in a room, but there are some rooms where, several times, the map will show that it's cleared, but later, it will show as having things to find. There is exactly one time in the whole game where this arguably makes sense, since you get a tool that lets you access more clues, but even then, I would've much preferred the treatment that the doors received, where when you get in interaction range, it says what you need to interact and leaves a marker on the map. Most of the time, it seems to just be the game withholding the interaction trigger until it feels like it. One room had a very interesting book on the shelf that was clearly signposted as a clue, but the game didn't let me interact with it until the third visit. This kind of thing turned clue gathering into an absolute chore near the end of the game, where I was running to one end of the ship, getting a newly-spawned clue, completing a mystery, and running to the other end of the ship to gather a clue that seemingly spawned in response to that one mystery. It's an especially bizarre decision since, for the most part, the game is comfortable letting you gather clues that you don't necessarily understand the context of yet -- as it should!The mystery/deduction mechanic, which to me is the highlight of the game, also stumbles sometimes. You'll understand the actual story the mystery node regards, but you're struggling to figure out which aspects of the story the node is wanting you to present to it. The clue and connection hints often describe multiple aspects of a situation, but only one will be marked correct. This problem ramped way up during the ending of the game. Narratively, the clues you find spell out the last mysteries in extreme clarity, but the ending events involve many people most of whom do many things, and trying to guess which one or two people and which one of each of their actions a given mystery node wants was absolutely infuriating. It was pretty awful not just because it happened at the ending, making it very hard to enjoy what was clearly supposed to be a set-piece moment, but also because the mystery screen becomes *patronizing* when you are incorrect during this part. Instead of getting even vaguely helpful "incorrect" messages, it gives messages like "oh, come on" and "it's so obvious". The story is obvious but the expectations of these mystery nodes are NOT. This next part might feel like a spoiler but it's mostly just the premise of the whole game, and I promise you won't miss out on anything by reading it: the absolute worst one was the last one, with the title "What Sank the Thalassa" and description "The Thalassa sank after [minor spoiler]. What had happened?". By the time you unlock the node, you are certain to have a clue tile for the exact event which sank the Thalassa, and a previous mystery will have hard confirmed that it sank the Thalassa. But the mystery node wants a connected pair of clues, and I could not for the life of me find anything on par with that event to pair with it. It was especially confusing since the failure message was "not significant enough". There's nothing more significant than that one clue! And there's nothing nearly as significant as it! I had to use a guide, and it turns out that "What Sank the Thalassa" DOESN'T WANT THE EVENT THAT SANK THE THALASSA. It wants two clues which were on the road to disaster, but for which the sinking was absolutely not an inevitable result. At that point I was so out of it that I could not engage at all with the interactive cut-scenes that followed. I just walked and tried unsuccessfully to follow the dialogue until the credits rolled.I originally played in a single sitting, so I didn't notice this issue until trying to double-check things for the review, but you cannot manually save! There is no "save" button in the pause menu. Since there's no explicit save button, I thought it might save when you click "Main Menu" or "Quit Game", but it does not! I collect a clue, I complete a mystery, I click "Main Menu" hoping it'll save so that I can review things with a 100% save file, but when I reload, clue is uncollected, mystery is uncompleted, and I need to rewatch the mystery's (long) completion cut-scene again to double-check things.Bonus problem: once you open "What Sank the Thalassa?", you're not allowed to look at other mysteries or to leave the tab menu, and as a consequence you cannot access the pause menu. I'm sure the developers thought this was a deeply meaningful decision but to me it was deeply outrageous.I know it's odd to have a "recommended" review that spends so much of its time on problems, but that's just the nature of problems sometimes -- they tend to stick with you and overshadow the parts that worked. I definitely enjoyed much of this game, but sadly, the bad parts dominate my memory of the experience.My advice if you run into the problems I described with the mystery mechanic: the mystery nodes are almost always in strict chronological order. If you're giving it connections about an event and it's not accepting anything, try giving it connections for an event that precedes what you thought the mystery node is talking about.

_childDocuments_.review: Thalassa is an evocative exploration/mystery/walking sim that takes place primarily on a sunken ship. The environments are beautiful, lush and detailed, and I enjoyed the weirdly slow, whooshing movements of my character moving through water while walking in a diving suit. I've played and enjoyed number of games that have this premise: you must find out what happened to the missing crew on an empty vessel by searching for clues (think Tacoma, Pollen, The Invincible). I really like this genre, and I like slow paced games that allow you to gradually discover new places and rifle through drawers and cabinets looking for secrets while a story builds around you. Thalassa has a fun system in which discovered "clues" are added to a sort of inventory and can be combined to solve "mysteries" on an inquiry map. I found that element of the gameplay satisfying and useful for keeping track of the numerous bits and pieces of storyline that you discover as you explore.I felt that the storyline and characters were very compelling -- and some of the scenes are quite emotionally intense. I appreciated the way that each character, who we get to know through clues and flashbacks, can be seen as the potential suspect in the mystery that unfolds, but each is also sympathetic with an interesting story arc. Although the playable character does not speak, we get a strong sense of their state of mind over the course of the game.I did have some issues with the game stuttering and the image splitting apart at times, and had to adjust the image quality, but I was able to play without much issue after making adjustments. There were pretty long pauses when I initially would open the map or the mystery board, and I thought the game had crashed. After the initial long pause, the maps open more quickly. If, like me, you are someone who requires an inverted Y axis, you'll be glad to know that's an option. The mechanics of the game were simple and intuitive, though some of the "mysteries" (the piecing together of the clues) took me a few tries. There is a fair amount of wandering back and forth through the large ship, and some "clues" do not appear or become acquirable until certain things have happened in the storyline -- so you do need to revisit areas that are potentially quite far from each other (while moving very slowly underwater) to double check that new items haven't appeared. I enjoyed the pacing, however, and thought that the order in which new parts of the ship became available through storytelling was clever. The game took me about 11 hours to play.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly brilliant game. Out the outside, it's a fairly straight-forward 'walking sim', trying to figure out what happened to the ship Thalassa as you explore the wreck. It leans into the Sherlock Holmes style of mystery solving. However, the narrative of Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss deals expertly with loss, grief, and the complex lives and decisions with which people have to contend. It weaves a fascinating narrative through that exploration, that was [for me at least] deeply moving, especially if you have dealt with grief. It's definitely not a game for everyone. It's a slower-paced game. The movement of the character, the animations, are all careful and deliberate. From a immersion perspective, it's logical; The game is set around 1900, where diving suits were big and cumbersome. That may not be for everyone though. However, the pace of the game works well with the narrative it's telling. It's a narrative that invites you to take time to think and carefully consider the various plot points as you uncover them.  If you've played and enjoyed games such as Firewatch, this type of gameplay will be immediately familiar. If you enjoy the face-paced games, try the demo first. The mystery solving side of the game may not be for everyone either. The mysteries can occasionally be 'brute forced' to a conclusion, taking away the satisfaction of figuring it out, or can be so obvious that it's barely a mystery. Some may find it 'easy'. But on the whole for me, it's enough to keep you guessing, while creating that 'just one more' feeling as the next thread of the story of the Thalassa is unveiled. Never did I feel the puzzles were rushed, or the narrative stalled because a puzzle was too complicated.Along with the narrative, Thalassa: Edge of the Abyss also shines with it's characters. Each one is brilliantly brought to life, as is the ship (almost a character in its own right). The writing never feels off, and the acting is fantastic. You really feel a connection to each of them, whether it's positive or negative. The game doesn't over-do the character interactions either. They are kept relevant.I cannot recommend this enough. It's a thought-provoking game; one that you experience as much as play. And certainly one that deserves more attention. It's become a personal favourite of mine

_childDocuments_.review: A decent puzzle game where you play a diver trying to uncover the events that led to the sinking of your ship. The plot is interesting (although having to  right in the prologue was pretty grim), the dialogue and voice acting is adequate, and the game mechanics work well. The character models are nothing to write home about, but in this kind of game I'm willing to overlook that.What I'm not willing to overlook, though, is that quite frequently objects are not accessible before certain puzzles have been solved, which leads to a lot of otherwise unnecessary backtracking. That's just bad design. Period. If you don't want the player to have access to certain objects prior to certain events: put them in places that aren't accessible before these events transpire.Despite this rather annoying design flaw, I did enjoy the game overall and recommend playing it if you're interested in a linear, story-driven experience. But I cannot give it the 4-star rating it would've gotten otherwise.Rating: ★★★☆☆

name: Winds & Leaves
detailed_description: From the developers of the award-winning game Prison Boss VR, Winds & Leaves is now coming to PC VR with enhanced visuals and room-scale support. Stranded in a barren landscape, you are the only one alive able to master the ancient art of growing vegetation. Your world is fragile, and you must find a way to end the recurring cataclysms that threaten it. Grow a verdant forest from nothing and create different tree species to adapt to the various biomes and weather. Transform the barren land into lush valleys, one tree at a time. Explore an intriguing ever-changing world on your stilts, a locomotion system designed for walking across the landscapes and climbing up in trees. Stumble on ancient structures and awaken them to discover their secrets. Enjoy a procedural living soundtrack that reacts to the world around you from award-winning composers Vibe Avenue and see the landscape transform into a forest one tree at a time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful, quiet, highly immersive adventure.As another user mentioned it is reminiscent of Journey in some ways - in great ways. But unique too. Any fan of journey will be glad to pick this up if they take the time needed to get used to it.And indeed you must get used to it. I was looking forward to this when it released then saw the initial negative reviews, and being on a very tight budget I was dissuaded on spending the money to buy Winds & Leaves. Fast forward a couple months, to my delight I won a free key from VRGrid.I recommend this even at full price. If this game sounds up your alley it probably is. It's a really wonderful game. (Edit: I've since completed the game. I loved it!).Detailed review follows.___________________________First, the elephant in the room. The negative reviews - all based on initial impressions and relating to controls/motion sickness - are understandable. About that:The opening 'tutorial' is built-in to the game world in a way I *theoretically* appreciate. But it's not accessible enough for a game that already has a challenging on-boarding process. If the devs have the funds to rework the tutorial, I would highly recommend checking out the tutorial for the game Déraciné on PSVR. This game has one of the best tutorials of any VR game I've played, and it also does it in a way that's 'in-world'. Devs: pick up Déraciné, learn from this tutorial. A better tutorial has the potential to drastically improve the on-boarding process for the player.The controls of Winds & Leaves are actually quite thoughtful and well done, but it takes time to realize this and acclimatize to your unusual equipment. On-boarding issues:- You have some choice of how to position your tools, but the choice is provided to you before you really understand what you're doing. After my first 1.5 hours I discovered that if I go to the 'calibrate' menu option, I can easily reposition the tools to my liking. It would be better if the game initially places your tools for you, then tells you to go to the calibration menu to change it.- Climbing feels like a mess until you understand how to consistently initiate climbing. For the first hour I kept trying to climb and it felt like half the time it didn't work. This is because I was holding both grips and trying to 'lift up'. Instead I would just move on my stilts. The trick is to initiate with one controller, grip and lift. This initiates climbing. The climbing is unusual but works really well once you get used to it. You can easily maneuver around a tree and it's quite pleasant.- It's only about 45 minutes in or so that you learn you can adjust the height of your stilts to change your movement speed. Too late!! Not only is this knowledge helpful for movement, it's also helpful for grabbing items. Once you get comfy with this you can easily lower yourself to the ground to pick up dropped fruit, or raise yourself high to grab fruit off lower branches. Overall it helps one grab precisely, which can otherwise be a little frustrating.- A tutorial segment that better encourages you to try the different movement settings may be helpful. I'm feeling happy with the roomscale 360 setup, but there's extensive options that allow you to pick from several different rotation methods. The existence of these options are not obvious at first glance, and I suspect that some users don't realize that all these rotation choices exist. Also to the devs: I suggest an additional smooth turning speed of 'very fast'.- I pretty much never ever experience motion sickness in VR, but I experienced a little in my first 30 minutes with this game. After that it went away. (I don't use any comfort options). Again a better tutorial might help the player tolerate this adjustment period and successfully acclimatize without quitting!- On Reverb G2 grip and trigger were flipped, adding confusion. I have created a public binding to fix this for any G2 users, but of course ideally this would be fixed by the devs (to be fair to the devs, I have spoken to many developers who have a miserable time trying to get G2 controls to work properly. So I blame HP and Valve for this issue!)The above on-boarding challenges are magnified because the game already takes a kind of Dark Souls approach to putting you in the world. Not in the sense of mechanical challenge - what I mean is that you learn about the world and how things work by experiencing the world, intuiting things, and trying things out. (For example, learning how your time speed tool works, learning about soil and how to understand the various hint images, etc). That's all great, I like this approach, but because of the messy on-boarding process it's inhibitive in that first hour.IN SHORT, for anyone who's just bought this, prepare yourself mentally for that first hour of getting used to everything and feeling clumsy and frustrated with controls and possibly even a little motion sick. You will get through it, and it's worth it.___________________________SO.What about the actual GAME???? Is this a decent game, a good game, a great game...?? Is it worth dealing with the messy first hour?In my opinion this is absolutely a great game, and totally worth dealing with the messy first hour.Immediately when I booted the game I was greeted with beautiful sounds and a gorgeous visual experienceEverything is designed fantastically to create one of the most immersive games I've played in VR. (And I've played a lot of heavily atmospheric games). The sound, the visuals, the art design, the spatial design, progression - everything works really really really well. This is a very pleasing, immersive, quiet but engaging adventure.Because of all that, the game world feels like a real world. I don't mean the art style is 'realism', it's not and doesn't need to be. I mean that it feels like you're in a world that lives and breathes and has a real presence to it.It's also really wonderful that you can climb some special tall trees and look up all across the world. Again it just feels like a real place, and being able to do that really enhances that feeling.As of writing this I am 2 hours in and eager to keep going (I gather it's a 7-8 hour adventure from a quick google, which sounds like a great length).___________________________Quick note on performance:My system has a laptop 3080 GPU, which is probably a touch worse than a standard 3070 GPU, a bit better than a 2070 GPU.I get full 90fps with the following settings:1) in-game quality set to Medium2) vr performance 'mod', . Foveated rendering didn't work for me. I used FSR, with renderScale of 0.64, sharpness of 1.0, radius of 1.0, applyMipBias false3) Steam SuperSampling set to 140%Looks great and plays great. If you don't want to worry about step 2 than just play with the in-game quality and SteamVR SuperSampling to see what works best for you. The game looks great on all 4 quality settings, and there is a noticeable performance improvement on the 'low' setting if you need to use that.___________________________This is a very high quality game, beautiful and unique, marred only by its frustrating on-boarding process. In my opinion the control system is thoughtful and well done... if only you take the time to get really comfy with it (about 45-90 minutes depending on the player).I hope that this review breathes some life into this game's sales. There's a large amount of people - people who enjoy games like Journey as the obvious example - that will really love this game and find it to be a breath of fresh air.I would love to see this game reduced to $20 to make it more enticing for people to buy, just because I know it's one of those 'hard sells'. But I do think it is worth the $30 asking price. It is impeccably designed and gorgeous besides that challenging on-boarding process mentioned in every review.

_childDocuments_.review: You can view my review & gameplay here: I really did enjoy this game. The visuals & sounds are excellent. It kind of reminds me of playing Journey. Unfortunately, the clunky controls & VR interactions really bring this experience down. It really does take you out of the flow state of regenerating the flora back to life. This game is so beautiful. The art style is really well done. The ambient sounds, sound mix, & musical soundtrack are all excellent. When it works, it's also very relaxing & enjoyable to play. However, a lot of the time I was struggling with the controls or trying to look past the clunky VR interactions. The climbing in this game is one of the worst I have ever experienced in VR. It's very easy to grab the wrong tool or object in this game.Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting variable frame rates from 90 to 45 fps on high graphical settings on my HP Reverb G2 (high native resolution, but it looks so stunning the trade off was worth it to me). You have arm swing locomotion and smooth & snap turning options, as well as several comfort options you can turn on or off. You can also lower the graphical settings (but why would you want to do that???!!!!). The placement of your tools was a bit cumbersome as well & you can try to move them, but I could never find a good spot.I did experience 2 crashes during my almost 2 hours of gameplay. The only other issues were clipping through just about everything and not always being able to control how fast you move (even slight movement on arm swing would move you too far when you're trying to get close to some objects). Other than that, like I said, the game overall lacks polish & needs better VR interactions either from using your tools or grabbing objects. Lastly, on WMR, the instructions were usually wrong on what to press for interactions.Still, it's a lovely game. Beautiful visuals & sounds just like Journey. Unfortunately, the gameplay, due to the poor VR interactions bring the experience down (unlike Journey where the gameplay goes with the flow of the game).
_childDocuments_.name: Winds & Leaves

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique VR experience that NAILS immersion and atmosphere but definitely will not be for everyone. The game is clearly designed to be as minimalist as possible and not spoonfeed any info to the player, but tries to make them learn through experimentation and environmental context. This can be frustrating gameplay-wise, but the tradeoff is that I found the game to be incredibly immersive and would feel during my play sessions that I was in a different world instead of a video game, which IMO is the greatest compliment you can give a VR game. The core gameplay loop itself of planting trees across the wasteland is honestly pretty tedious, but the game is carried hard by the sense of immersion, atmosphere and exploration. This is one of the very few VR games with a beautiful, well-designed open world to explore and a metroidvania-esque way to progress in the world. Overall, I really loved the game and wish there were more VR games out there like this. The closest comparison I can think of is Paper Beast.
_childDocuments_.name: Winds & Leaves

_childDocuments_.review: Like many others, anxiety and depression have been a struggle for most of my life. My sibling saw this game on my wishlist and, unbeknownst to me, bought it for me during the autumn sale. My gratitude is immense. At first sight, the visuals alone blew me away and gave me hope for stress ease, and after the initial struggle and confusion with some unclear instructions and direction, the gameplay became immediately healing. You control your own world, you are free to plant, explore, generate life... the world moves without you, but you are the root of the creation. Winds & Leaves allows you to escape your world for a little while and get lost exploring as well as creating a new one -- you heal the world, and the world acts as your lifeline in return. I would highly recommend this to anyone stressed, overworked, or in need of a break or some serenity  in their lives.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished and loved it. The controls were tricky to get used to at first and switching the play space mode really helped. Once I got the hang of those it became a beautiful, zen puzzle game. It had an unusual but deeply satisfying combination of the primitive—trudging through a desert at risk of death, cultivating an orchard, climbing through trees and encountering ancient art painted on rocks—to the godlike—freely controlling time, flying through the air, inhabiting foliage like a forest spirit and reestablishing what I can only describe as ley lines.

_childDocuments_.review: VR games are always a gamble for me as I do have to deal with VR sickness, but the way this one has handled it is so immersive, my 20-minute limit became nearly 2 hours the first time I played it.  The game itself is slower paced than many, but that just gives you more time to enjoy the simple things, such as watching your trees grow in high speed.  The only thing I could wish for is a bit of backstory, but perhaps that comes later in than I am.  Even not knowing who I am or why I'm reforesting the world, I'll definitely be coming back again and again to plant more trees and see new things.
_childDocuments_.name: Winds & Leaves

_childDocuments_.review: Winds and Leaves is a beautiful and atmospheric game, where you can spend you time wandering around, replanting trees to bring a barren world back to life. But no, this is not simply another "walking simulator 2.0"; you will need to learn to cross your seeds together to breed the right varieties of tree to survive in different terrains and hazards, from whirlwinds to acid rain.Although there were a few hiccups at the beginning figuring out how to interact with things, and the controls occasionally glitched, overall the problems were not bad enough to take away my enjoyment of the game. I recommend this - even if this style of game isn't generally your thing, it's worth checking out if you can get it on sale.(Hardware: HTC Vive. Didn't run into any hardware-related issues, as far as I could tell. And the game would no doubt be even prettier on a newer headset with higher display res.)
_childDocuments_.name: Winds & Leaves

_childDocuments_.review: Learn to read the signs of the various climates, awaken old landmarks, and grow your own forests in this PlayStation VR flora builder. Stranded in a barren landscape, you are the only being capable of mastering the ancient art of growing vegetation. Journey across the Steppe to discover landmarks left behind from a previous time. Uncover their secrets in order to unlock new equipment and gather ancient dormant seed varieties. Find the perfect conditions to plant them in and you'll witness magnificent trees grow to maturity and transform the landscape.

name: TopSpin 2K25
detailed_description: TopSpin 2K25 Grand Slam® Edition Compete on the world’s biggest stages with the TopSpin 2K25 Grand Slam® Edition! Get the Grand Slam® Champions Pack, plus the Under the Lights Pack, New Wave Pack, Rookie Rise Pack, and the All Access Pass. The Grand Slam® Edition includes: Grand Slam® Champions Pack, featuring a cosmetic Championship Racket and a Champion Serve. Under the Lights Pack featuring Serena Williams and Roger Federer Alternate Outfits, Wilson Nightfall Bundle, and Night-Time Majors. New Wave Pack containing Carlos Alcaraz, Iga Swiatek, and Frances Tiafoe Alternate Outfits, New Wave Glasses, New Wave Top, New Wave Bottoms, New Wave Shoes, and New Wave Wrist Bands. Rookie Rise Pack containing one MyPLAYER Boost to Level 10 and 1,700 VC. All Access Pass, including six Centre Court Season Passes, plus French Open, Wimbledon, US Open, and Australian Open T-Shirts. TopSpin 2K25 Deluxe Edition Rally on with TopSpin 2K25 Deluxe Edition! The Deluxe Edition includes: Under the Lights Pack featuring Serena Williams and Roger Federer Alternate Outfits, Wilson Nightfall Bundle, and Night-Time Majors. New Wave Pack containing Carlos Alcaraz, Iga Swiatek, and Frances Tiafoe Alternate Outfits, New Wave Glasses, New Wave Top, New Wave Bottoms, New Wave Shoes, and New Wave Wrist Bands. Rookie Rise Pack containing one MyPLAYER Boost to Level 10 and 1,700 VC. About the Game AUTHENTIC GAMEPLAY Advanced gameplay mechanics, realistic physics, and immersive visuals are at the heart of TopSpin 2K25. Several playable pros in TopSpin 2K25 have a custom forehand, backhand, and serve animation that’s been fine-tuned to replicate their real-life form. On clay, sliding across will kick up dust and leave scuff marks along the ground you’ve covered while on grass the court wear becomes more noticeable as you progress through a tournament. Deliver pinpoint precision on the court with the all-new Timing Meter, and hit the perfect serve with the new Serve Mechanic. LOCAL MULTIPLAYER Gather your friends and family to compete in intense, head-to-head matches on the same screen. Offline Exhibition supports up to two players in singles and up to four players in doubles, offering endless fun and rivalry. EXPERIMENT WITH PLAYSTYLES Do you gravitate toward a strong defensive strategy or will you lean more on dominating serves? TopSpin 2K25 features four different playstyles, each with their own upsides and unique Skills. Choose from All-Round, Offensive Baseline, Defensive Baseline, and Serve & Volley playstyles. Lean in to the playstyle of your favorite Pro or experiment and create hybrid MyPLAYERs based on these core playstyles. WIN THE CAREER GRAND SLAM® Travel the world as an up-and-coming pro, go toe-to-toe with the biggest names in tennis, and take Centre Court at Wimbledon, Roland-Garros, the US Open, and the Australian Open as you strive to become a Grand Slam® Champion online in MyCAREER. DOMINATE THE COURT ONLINE Test your MyPLAYER's mettle and showcase your tennis prowess on the World Tour or step into the 2K Tour as a playable pro challenging players around the world with cross-play support. Alternatively, have a friendly and invite your 2K friends and platform friends to online private singles matches in Online Exhibition! PERSONALIZE YOUR MyPLAYER Create a MyPLAYER tailored to your play style and define your look on the court! With a wide range of customization options, you can fine-tune your attributes and earn new Coaches, Fittings, and gear from adidas, HEAD, Lacoste, New Balance, Nike, Wilson, and more.

_childDocuments_.review: REALLY good gameplay, and I'm happy they've made it accessible on modern systems so I don't need to keep emulating Top Spin 4. These are the only positives you can say about it and the modernization is why I've purchased it, but I will not be supporting another followup if it's like this.The roster is pathetic, hosting SEVEN active ranked male players out of the top 100. The career mode is a drawn-out grindfest where you need to keep entering low level tournaments as a top 20 player, while doing increasingly annoying and arbitrarily difficult training minigames to progress. Including a pointless stamina system that adds nothing but downtime. There is a shocking lack of content, almost nothing at all added twelve years later. This game should have been half its price.The bs of premium currency, battle passes and always-online nonsense poisons every single aspect of this game. Doing ANYTHING in the single player MyCareer mode costs a premium currency. Necessary stuff like coaches, gear upgrades and homes can only be purchased with this currency. Unlocking new animations for your player is only available as extra purchases. Every menu in this game is exploding with challenges and progression and additional purchases and it just gives you the feeling that 2K's priority was on making a money printer, not a complete and functioning video game.Worst of all, we are now on day TWO of this game's life and the servers have been down all afternoon, rendering MyCareer mode (the SINGLE PLAYER CAREER) unplayable, it is grayed out in the main menu. You can't do other challenges to at least earn some currency, because nothing you do offline gives you any rewards. You can't play in any of the unlockable arenas (about 75% of them) or play AI on the two hardest difficulties for some reason. All because it's all online-only. Totally inexcusable.
_childDocuments_.name: TopSpin 2K25

_childDocuments_.review: I am glad top spin is finally back on PC but this is just a cash grab. This game is basically top spin 4 with fancier graphics, UI, and some minigames which cost 60 USD but have the same amount of micro-transactions to a free-to-play mobile game. Many better looking outfits, even animation need to be bought with real money, so you are struck with few outfits and default animations for every player for a long time when playing in career mode. Career mode is also so much grind, not to mention the "pay to level up faster" and requiring lots of in-game credits to re-spec your character. I would be okay if this is half the price but the state like this is just greedy.
_childDocuments_.name: TopSpin 2K25

_childDocuments_.review: ✅ Filled with microtransactions?✅ 3rd party account required for no reason?✅ Denuvo?✅ Aggressive anti-cheat that causes crashes for any number of programs?✅ Online-only single-player?✅ Constant server issues that therefore prevent you from even playing said single-player?✅ Online access terminated after 2½ years, likely therefore also preventing single-player access?Refunded? You bet.It's a joke to the point where it almost feels like they mixed up the 'things nobody wants in a videogame' list and used it as a checklist instead. In the end though, it's a tale as old as time: a good game ruined by a truly awful publisher.Never buying anything from 2K again. Consider yourselves blacklisted.

Whatever you do Avoid 2k games as they've now added micro transactions into single player PVE as well, want your char to progress so you don't have to play 100 seasons getting 40exp a match? The rest/energy system is.. yeah it’s ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up. You'll basically rest every other month or you get injured! _childDocuments_.review: The fact that I paid full price for this and have put 100+ hours into it is one of the great shames of my existence up to this point. I could honestly forgive the threadbare presentation and typically intrusive microtransactions if it wasn't full of insane balance issues and game-breaking bugs that make ranked matches almost unplayable. The basic physics of the game are solid and it maintains a lot of the feel of Top Spin 4 - when you're matched with a player of equal skill it forces a lot of careful and creative play that is pretty fun. The main issue here is that power is massively OP - if you dump all your XP into power you can just blast winners from any position in the court with no unforced errors. You can put zero points into serve and still slam down perfect 240kmh aces as long as you have 95+ in power. Ranked modes are full of French teenagers with identical build who just spam unplayable wide serves and flat power shots from the baseline with zero risk - there is almost no way to counterpunch or draw unforced errors, the only way to win is to quit as soon as your're matched with one of them. Insane to include all court players like Federer or defensive players like Medvedev in the meagre list of pro players considering their playstyles are simply not not viable in this system.Even if you do manage to stay toe to toe with power spammers there is a gamebreaking bug that forces faults even on perfectly timed serves. I have lost multiple matches from an even or winning position because the serves bugged out and I hit 4 double faults in a row. The devs are aware of this and have not patched it.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay wise it's currently the best tennis game. On the court it just feels right on how the game plays with not much room for improvement other than that with xbox controller the left analogue stick seems overly sensitive during serves which makes placing serves somewhat difficult.Graphics are okay but feel like they are a generation behind. A sports game shouldn't look this "bad" in 2024. Especially the player models don't look good at all, none of them do. Thankfully the game makes up with it's great gameplay on the court.Career mode is a bit slim with only 80 ranked players in the field and only monthly events. It would have been nicer to have a ranking list of 500 or 1000 players that you could slowly climb through weekly events. Tournaments are also quite short with lower tournaments only having 8 participants and bigger tournaments like grand slams 32 participants. Every month in career mode you can do 1 training, 1 special event and 1 tournament. Over time you gain XP and can rank up the skills of your player.Online has a world tour mode where you use your "myplayer" against others which has it's own leaderboard etc. It also has a ranked mode where players playing against each other with pro's instead of "myplayers". Overall multiplayer seems fun and competitive.The game has seasons that each seem to last around 2 months and have unlockable rewards similar to battle passes in other games, with around 40 unlocks being free and around 100 being unlockable if you have a season pass. You earn VC for doing literally anything which can be used to buy cosmetics in the shop or unlock tiers in the season pass or buy xp boosts etc. It does not feel pay to win though and VC can't be used directly to upgrade the skills of your myplayer, unlike NBA 2K where VC can be used to improve your myplayer.Overall currently the best tennis game around when it comes to overall presentation, gameplay, game modes etc. I'd say it's worth a buy if you like tennis games and don't mind the price tag. Otherwise wait for a discount as it's quite expensive for what you get. I'd give the game a 7.5/10.
