name: Song in the Smoke
detailed_description: Using the power of virtual reality, Song in the Smoke puts your survival directly in your own hands. Enter this dangerous world outside of time, where you must craft weapons, make clothes, build fires, and brew healing elixirs to steel yourself against its vicious predators. Whether you're either the hunter or the hunted, you can block, parry, and strike back with your club, or attack from a distance with your bow. True survivors will also need their wits to avoid some of the most lethal creatures that call this land their home. The world of Song in the Smoke holds equal parts salvation and danger. Use your senses to stalk prey: track their smell, follow their footprints, and plan your strike. When you’re ready, intuitive and responsive VR controls let you execute the perfect shot—a shot that could mean the difference between survival and death. The game uses a number of deeply-intertwined procedural systems, making every play-through unpredictable and unique. Animals seek water and shelter, while predators hunt for prey; as day transitions into night, the environment shifts and the creatures who inhabit it change their behaviors. A mystical narrative runs throughout the player’s journey as well, putting the experience into greater, transcendental context. Song in the Smoke is a beautiful and harrowing survival experience. How long will you last? Hunting : String bows to hunt your own prey, tracking their footprints and scents on the wind. Then hide among the ferns and bushes to line up the perfect shot, aiming naturally with your controllers before letting your handcrafted arrow fly. The player often takes the role of the hunted as well, requiring deft avoidance—or harrowing combat—to stay alive. Foraging : Find food, water, and the raw materials needed to build shelter and fire, as well as craft weapons and other items is essential for survival. Exploring : The wide open world of Song in the Smoke begs exploration, and moving through it requires curiosity and wit to unravel nature’s many mysteries. The song leads players forward, guiding them through this strange world and revealing a little more about the secret at its heart with each new discovery. Maximizing Resources : If you make the kill, make sure nothing is wasted. Stock up on meat, bones, and skins that you can use to keep yourself warm as you move through the world of Song in the Smoke, travelling from lush forests, through ancient valleys, to frozen glaciers. A deep crafting design allows players to build weapons, tools, shelter and fire from the raw materials nature provides. Total playthrough time: 12-20 hours REVIEWS Upload VR: “I am, if you couldn’t tell, quite in love with SitS ... An intoxicating trip, an experience directly connected to the beating heart of nature and acutely aware of the structure and interaction needed to make its survival gameplay work in VR.” Road to VR: 2021 PlayStation VR Game of the Year: 'In few words, Song in the Smoke is breathtaking, and definitely worth the tens of hours it will coax out of you.' USA Today: 'Top 5 VR Games of 2021.' Screenrant: “Song in the Smoke is an unrivaled VR survival game with horror elements, and it gives players complete freedom to explore, hunt in, and conquer the treacherous wilderness.' Shughead Gaming: “Maybe my biggest surprise of 2021. In the running for VR game of the year.” Gaming Nexus: “Excels with fantastic controls and VR mechanics, accomplishing some things that veteran VR developers still struggle with. Games like Song in the Smoke signal what VR games could be, which has restored a bit of my hope for the future of the format.” The VR Grid: “Song in the Smoke is an awesome blend of survival and fantasy” VR Focus: “Song in the Smoke looked like it was something special and it is, one of the best VR games of 2021.” Press Play Media: “A memorable experience the scope of which we’ve rarely seen on a headset like the Quest.” PSVR Without Parole: “GOTY. Best Survival Game in VR yet. Intuitive, Immersive, Incredible One of PlayStation VR's very best games.' PSVR Underground: “Game of the Year. A master class in survival.”

short_description: Using the power of virtual reality, Song in the Smoke puts your survival directly in your own hands. Enter this dangerous world outside of time, where you must craft weapons, make clothes, build fires, and brew healing elixirs to steel yourself against its vicious predators.

_childDocuments_.review: Saw this game had no review so decided to just try it out. Wow, great little survival game! You have to craft your own stuff, so creating arrows, knives, spears etc. You can hunt animals, eat berries, upgrade your clothing, gear and more. Only played an hour but it seems like a fun game! It can also definitely be a bit scary, so keep that in mindI had most settings on high, with AA turned off, and the game looks great and ran pretty much smoothly (the tutorial had some very minor stutters when explaining things). During the actual gameplay, there was pretty much no stuttering at all. Ran on an index @80hz, 100%SS, RTX 2080ti, i9 9900k.edit: Okay this game is genuinely scary at times, but so good!
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: This is, without a doubt, the most fun VR survival game I have played. When I saw the trailer, I thought it was a simple survival game that looked awesome but the more I play the more intricacies I discover. I keep finding new things that change how I interact with the world.Do yourself a favor and grab this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Song in the smoke is an unpolished gem. There are some glitches and fallbacks - I can't deny that. That said, however, this game is a one-of-a-kind. You will not find a survival crafting game of this caliber in VR. They exist, sure; but all are unfinished with game-breaking glitches.My first playthrough was on easy difficulty. It took about 15 hours to complete. Future playthroughs on higher difficulties may introduce more mechanics that I have not yet seen, either way, I'm aching to get back in and try a harder difficulty; perhaps even unlock those pesky hidden achievements.Song in the Smoke offers something no VR game has truly given me to date -- a survival crafting experience with a story to squeeze your heart and titillating game play that chaulk up to a phenomal VR experience. There are bugs. The occasional wood flying across the screen due to some strange collision mechanics, or items on the ground disappearing after you've slept off a night. None of these bugs are game breaking though and the game play and story make up for the cons of this game 10 fold. It's worth the price tag.It's not hard to see why UploadVR nominated SitS for PCVR game of the year.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Takes a few hours to get the hang of some of the finer game dynamics (best to do a quick check on youtube), but once you have the hang it is fantastic!It is suited to people who like exploring levels and taking the time to level up their gear - you could rush just to the objectives but i imagine it would quickly become very hard to kill anything you meet if you did!I find it lots of fun hunting around for good items and exploring the world anyway - so may as well take your time and get your money's worth from the game is my view!Great game.Tips it would be good to know from the start i have found:As you are searching around always look out for items with 3 teeth (stars) - they make significantly better weapons and armour so always try to have everything 2 or 3 teeth gradeFires - you need to build big fires to last the night while you sleep (or things will get you after the first couple of levels) - the trick to building fires is watching the circle that goes around the side of the fire pit - start your fire with bark and 3-4 small sticks - you will notice the circle goes around and goes past a point labelled M - this means the fire is big enough to take medium sticks, once you throw a few of those on it gets to a level to take large logs and a few of those should max out the ring and get you a good night's sleep! Also the extra long sticks can be grabbed at each end and snapped into a small and medium stick.You can also collect arrows you shoot that miss their target so definitely easier to go looking for them than making new ones all the timeLast one - you can leave liquids in your mortar and pestle so if you make a health potion and dont need to drink the whole thing then sip it and just keep the rest in the vessel for laterHave fun!

_childDocuments_.review: While it isn't without its flaws, Song in the Smoke is criminally under reported and underappreciated. At the time of writing, there are only 23 other Steam reviews. Oomph. The development team deserves better. This game is a well produced, functioning full length product with plenty of features. For these reasons along, it is a positive rating and well worth trying. Everything that follows may sounds negative, but Song in the Smoke is still an enjoyable VR experience of which there are far too few. Fighting the animals is a ton of fun. Being chased by the dinosaur sized animals is a ton of fun. Taking in the large forests in the twilight light, firefiles scattering through the air, is a ton of fun. If you liked the art of S&S, you should be at home here. It runs fantastic on a 4790k and 2080 Super. It has some of the largest environments that I've encountered in a VR game. Boneworks had giant street and building interiors, but they were mostly empty rectangular spaces. Subnautica has large waterways but, when I tried it, they were plagued with assets popping in once close enough to the player. Here, there are giant forest areas with many nooks and crannies to explore. The colors are vibrant and lush. Ok, it isn't super detailed, but I assume, like S&S, the developers were balancing style with VR performance. Both S&S and Song in the Smoke are masterclasses in the ethos of doing more with less. It felt like a mix of Turok and open world Zelda. There are lite, lite story elements. Personally a weak point. Dropped immediately into a caveman doing his thing. Your mission is collecting hidden orbs per zone and then fighting progressively harder animals. After you collect orbs, you're treated to a brief cinematic. There are also hidden power ups. The biggest flaw is its clunkiness, which is likely the result of being ported from the PSVR. Inventory management is more smooth and intuitive in PCVR first games like HL:A or Walking Dead: S&S. For example, there are two quick slots for inventory, but they're seemingly bound to specifically the left or right hand versus shoulder location. While you'll access them by reaching over your shoulder, if you reach your right hand over your left shoulder, you'll pull out the right hand item. It can be confusing until you realize what is happening. There are other nagging object and inventory interactions. New instructions are floating tool tips that can be easily missed, such as if you are in active pursuit of an animal. Between tracking down the orbs, you'll have to survive. Frankly, I liked S&S's or the Forest's survival balance better. There is no stamina meter. Instead, you'll progressively become hungrier and sleepier. The survival elements were on the tip of being overbearing. For example, you basically need to eat a couple pieces of meat or fruit each day. However, most of the animals only drop one piece of meat per kill, and the act of harvesting the single meat usually takes half the day cycle (it fast forwards). Unlike S&S or the Forest, where I could stockpile plenty of food materials during the day and then prepare meals to last several days, I basically just kept my head above water each day. It ended up being faster to skip harvesting meat and grab berries or mushrooms on the fly. Physically crafting each item, like knives, arrows and campfires, is really neat. Still, like the one to one meat experience noted above, crafting is one to one also. While quick, you will be hand crafting each and every arrow you use (unless you take time to find the hidden caches). After building your 10th campfire (which has to be rebuilt at least once or twice in the night), the experience starts to drift from game to chore. Plus, items tend to wear out really fast. The starting bow broke on the second or third hunting trip. Each item has an independent quality level, but you would be forgiven for overlooking that detail while scavenging. There is simply a lot of upkeep.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: The initial impressions of the game are very favorable. The crafting is satisfying and discovering new crafting recipes while exploring is great. You search for the required three items while trying to gear up and getting pumped to face your strongest foe yet.Then the game keeps repeating the same thing. Location after location  you're doing the same thing. Create camp, hunt local wildlife and gather local resources to upgrade yourself to next tier. Move to next area and repeat. Creating a storage sack is often very important but each storage is it's own thing. You're always starting with stuff on your back when moving between areas and all your previous work becomes moot. Having a Resident Evil style universal storage sack would be incredibly welcome and cut back on the repetitive tedium of the game.The last areas are very disappointing. Boss of the second to last area is nothing but a walking target, offering no resistance.  Last area is very arduous and frustrating.You need to feed yourself, keep warm and for some reason keep away the dark. Hunger is great and easy to handle. Staying warm doesn't seem to come into play until closer to the end of the game which feels like a missed opportunity. Cold snaps could have been a great thing.Keeping away the dark... it's not about the darkness. A magical floating goat that people usually call Wendigo will haunt you at night. It causes massive damage, clips through walls and can't be fought off without light. Game wants you to explore at night for upgrades but the Wendigo actively encourages you to hug your bonfire at night.I would recommend not building a bonfire at all but to simply have a torch in your inventory at all times. When the menace wakes you up at night, simply smack your torch against the wall to light it and it will go away. You have to do this twice a night to keep him away but you will save a lot of time fetching firewood each day.Repetitive and stretched out nature of the gameplay combined with the awful Wendigo mechanic is the reason why I'm giving this negative review.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying this game so far, gives off a Monster Hunter/Valheim vibe. The best VR survival I've played to date. All the systems/mechanics have some depth and feel meaningful, the creatures so far are varied and unique. The crafting feels very "VR" and less clicking buttons to make things appear, without being tedious. I find myself truly immersed, trying to plan out tomorrow's hunt/forage while I stack the night's campfire. I've only made it to the second area but can definitely recommend at this time.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't like in the beginning the way bow and club activation works (pressing left or right triggers, instead of grabbing the bow from behind the shoulder etc) and teleporting instead of jumping. But I got used to it the longer I played, so it wasn't a problem. Overall I really enjoyed the whole playthrough (I played the hardest difficulty). Some mechanics are not explained in written form, so you have to be aware of visual hints, which I liked, though I didn't pay enough attention sometimes and learned about stuff from videos. The overall feeling of loneliness and adverse world was fantastic. Gameplay loop of traveling into new territory and finding optimal camp sites and exploring the land for hunting places and materials was very satisfying. Especially the feeling of visually remembering and getting to know the place and creating your own paths etc, stuff that I am longing for in todays gaming industry where you are guided by gps from point to point and dont really see the world. The progression felt meaningful, because it wasn't just the stats of equipment. I was forced to try different approaches to my daily survival and learn, which led to becoming better at hunting, traversing the land, foraging etc. Fun game!
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a bit less than 17 hours on a single play through.  I started on hard and I was dying too quick while still learning controls and mechanics of the game play.  Restarting on regular difficulty it was a breeze difficulty wise.  There is only the main story to play and it is an excellent experience, but hardly any replay value.  It wasn't spectacular enough to play through on the hardest difficultly, though I probably should have switched to hard after the the first stage/learning how to play.Quite an underrated game by review count.  There were also a few unpleasant bugs.  I have a KatWalk and had to re-calibrate often.  I am not sure if the treadmill was at fault and couldn't pinpoint what exactly caused it.  It often had something to do with holding something in each hand.  There was also a bug that caused my bow to disappear twice.  It was in hand and I was putting a new bowstring on it... and gone.  Poof.  Not in inventory quick spot. Not on the ground.  Nothing.  Just had to reload a save to get it back.The troubles were worth it and I recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Song in the Smoke is an excellent game, and well priced for $30.It may soon list here that I've refunded the game. That is because I'm counting pennies and decided I can't justify spending the money right now. My situation is anomalous (compared to most PCVR users). You should buy it for $30. I very literally only drink tap water and never ever buy prepared meals, so I'm allowed to say that!!! I thoroughly enjoyed my first 1.5 hours with the game, even despite some controller binding issues with the G2 (this is a solved issue - it's expected these will be fixed in a patch soon, but also I've made a public binding for other G2 users that fixes the problem, so just select my public binding if the patch hasn't come yet).The game looks beautiful on the G2. It runs well. The crafting was engaging, the world was immersive, and felt like a world I wanted to spend more time with and learn more about.I only got a small abstract introduction to the story. So I can't comment much about what I feel about the story.The devs have been adding patches regularly since the game released on PSVR a couple months ago.Song in the Smoke seems like a polished, immersive, lengthy & replayable (from everything I've heard), interesting adventure survival story game made for VR. It got some stellar reviews on PSVR and it seems to me this is for good reason.I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I'm playing a different game than everyone else.  I really want to like it but the core game play is absolutely awful.  It is way too hard to aim the bow which I guess makes it more realistic.  That'd be fine if the resources to make arrows was easier to come by.  The hunting is awful.  Even after watching one of the developers tutorial videos I still have no idea what I'm doing wrong.  I just wasted the last 4 hours alone trying to finish the terrible hunting tutorial. (my steam playtime is off because it launches better from the oculus app).  The one time I did manage to finish it I was not able to save before dying.  That was after hunting the phantom deer for 2 hours.  My second attempt ended up in me hitting the phantom deer with countless arrows but ultimately dying form starvation because there is not enough food to forage and the hunting is awful.Part of the fun of these games is figuring out some of the mechanics on you own but tutorials are necessary for core game play mechanics.  I don't know if my game is glitching or what but "hints" pop up at the weirdest times and are confusing because they have nothing to do with what I'm doing or was information I could have used hours ago. They also only seem to pop up when I'm crouching ie in the middle of something.The controls are usually fine and actually fun for the crafting but they are terrible in combat.  It took me a very long time to figure out that you can equip items to RT and LT but that just causes me to whip out a club when I'm trying to nock an arrow.I rage quit earlier and then watched some of their tutorial videos.  Definitely watch those since the game does such an awful job at explain the actual game (seriously, how in the F are you supposed to know that there is a campfire "gauge" around it?).  I thought I'd enjoy it more but ended up rage quitting again.  Even knowing how to play more didn't make the game any more enjoyable because the hunting experience is so bad.  I hope they patch the game because I really liked it up until the hunting part. I can't see myself wasting any more time with it in its current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: This is THE BEST representation of the early VR Survival genera! Crafting is intuitive, making good use of motion controls to keep immersion high. Status effects such as cold, tired, hungry or bleeding, are shown subtly as a few floating HUD icons like ice-crystals, sleepy-eyes, or blood-drops. The fear can get pretty real as there are many dangers and encounters to avoid or conquer. The upgrades feel useful and rewarding by covering areas like larger-packs and higher armor/weapon stats. Keeping all your "meters happy" includes managing hunger, fatigue, temperature, and light-sources. Item management includes having enough firewood or light, with deadly consequences if neglected. Campfire system is unique that it requires a "pyramid" mix of timber using sticks, medium-Sticks, and logs.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Fun exploration, survival and combat. The crafting is well-done.Gorgeous environments with a nice art style.Not really an open world, but rather a series of medium sized to large levels.Runs great on minimum system requirements.My only gripe would be the inventory management, but hey, it's a survival game after all!"The ultimate caveman simulator" pretty much sums it up accurately.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: All around great VR survival game: cool setting and atmosphere, good looking stylized visuals, smooth difficulty curve and addictive gameplay loop. The only weak parts are awkward melee and teleportation climbing, but even that is tolerable.In my opinion, it is one of the best games that came out in the last 2 years.You play as a lone hunter in beautiful prehistoric environments that get more a more hostile as you progress. Stylized visuals look almost as good as Saints and Sinners, and later levels have those breathtaking vantage points where you can see almost whole map from high above. Forest sounds and realistic lighting with pitch black nights create thick atmosphere of wild nature and sometimes primal horror.All interactions are designed for VR with intuitive item crafting and building. Gameplay loop is addictive, you constantly have something to do as you hunt and gather to get better equipment or explore the land to progress in the story. Song in the Smoke never leaves survival phase for base building like many similar titles do. You are a hunter, not an industrial builder: food will always be scarce and nights - dangerous if you do not prepare enough wood for bonfire before dusk.Archery is deliberately slow: bowstring draw speed is limited, stopping you from becoming an arrow minigun like you usually do in VR archery titles:) And there is huge difference in damage between hitting a heart and anything else, further encouraging accurate shots. Melee is weightless and not very enjoyable, but it's usually only used to finish wounded animal with 1-2 hits to the head or block enemy charge.The campaign is quite long for VR and will take about 10-20 hours to finish depending on chosen difficulty and your playstyle.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what an underrated gem. You are a cave-person / native trying to survive and level up your equipment as you face increasingly dangerous animals in the prehistoric wild. It's exciting (& creepy at night), challenging (with a good difficulty ramp), uses VR mechanics (vs. simply being a survival port), great sounds (crank it up), and has a unique art style. I hope more serious players give it a chance as it is completely worth the journey. I'm probably 1/3 the way in at 9hrs. The survival aspects of the game have not been too consuming/distracting thus far. For me, hunting and exploring during the day are the most fun, and crafting / surviving are the means to that end. The game has no words (great) and the few dreams/hallucinations serve as hints. I am thoroughly enjoying the well-designed maps and heart-pumping moments.Areas for improvement: the grabbing/placement is imperfect and in key moments can feel like I am bumbling around for a key item. Example: In the day I use the bow and club, but at night, I find myself clamoring into the inventory to pull out a torch. I discovered couple rendering errors with objects hovering high in the air. Hearing gripes about auto-save and would generally agree that if you get back safe to a fire, the game should not require you to manually go save (immersion breaking).A gripe with my fellow Steam community - this game is well reviewed and popular on PSVR and Oculus (500+ positive reviews), yet has very few reviews (and I assume purchases) on Steam. Why? From reviews/chatter it feels like the bar is much higher here (and I can partly see why - better equipment, other platforms are lower res, often much younger...), but seriously this game deserves much more love...spread the good word!
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: Song in the Smoke is a full fledged, open world survival game that guides you further and furhter through various open maps.I find it strange and funny that this game is so low radar here on steam. You really wanna feel like grown up Mowgli without his pack to protect him? You really wanna feel like a caveman, 10000 bc surrounded by predators that rival you?You really wanna feel like a prey animal that, through bow and club, rises above the food chain?Then this game will give you exactly all of the above.There are not many games that can draq you outside of your comfort zone while being in your own room at the same time.The mechanics get intuitive quick, the graphics are good on the valve index and i enjoy sometimes not enjoying this ride, especially when night is drawing near starting at the thrid map onwards.A really good survival game, in VR, the best there currently is IMO.Its August 2022 now and there is, in my humble opinion, still no other VR-Prehistoric-Survival Game to rival this raw gem deeply hidden underneath the layer of sameish VR-Titels. Its kinda sad that this does not shine more.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review: What a cool game! I don't play alot of survival games, but this one was alot of fun. I really liked the mechanics and the story. Really got a Breath of the Wild vibe from the graphics which isn't a bad thing. I wish you could use your hands for climbing and/or grabbing items instead of trigger press, but that hardly takes away from the fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

_childDocuments_.review:
Song in the Smoke immerses players in a mysterious prehistoric world full of strange beasts where they must craft, forage, hunt, and fight to survive. Featuring art by famed illustrator Katsuya Terada (The Legend of Zelda, Blood: The Last Vampire, The Monkey King), Song in the Smoke has atmosphere and adventure in spades, with fantastical creatures and stylized scenery that pack an eerie, otherworldly punch.

Awoken by a three-headed crow at the edge of the woods, players will travel through eight stages including forests, valleys, and frozen terrain. You'll battle the elements and strange beasts alike, crafting tools, weapons, medicine, and more to stay alive. In true VR fashion, you'll identify threats by sound as well as sight. Intuitive controls mean you can line up the perfect shot with your bow, but you may not be the only one stalking its prey, so keep your wits about you.
_childDocuments_.name: Song in the Smoke

detailed_description: DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO Deluxe Edition The Deluxe Edition includes: • DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO • Season Pass - 3 Packs including Dragon Ball SUPER: SUPER HERO and Dragon Ball DAIMA content that contains more than 20 playable characters • Season Pass Bonus - Summon Shenron and 3 Days Early Access to the 3 DLC Packs DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO Ultimate Edition The Ultimate Edition includes: • DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO • Season Pass - 3 Packs including Dragon Ball SUPER: SUPER HERO and Dragon Ball DAIMA content • Season Pass Bonus - Summon Shenron and 3 Days Early Access to 3 DLC Packs • Ultimate Upgrade Pack • Ultimate Edition Bonus - Summon Super Shenron About the Game DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO takes the legendary gameplay of the Budokai Tenkaichi series and raises it to whole new levels. Become a super warrior and experience the earth-shaking, limit-breaking power of Dragon Ball battles! Unleash the strength of over 180 fighters from Dragon Ball Z, Dragon Ball Super, Dragon Ball GT, and selected Dragon Ball movies, all in the base game! Each character comes with their own signature abilities, transformations, and techniques. Make the destructive power of the strongest fighters ever to appear in Dragon Ball yours! Engage in heart-pounding, high-speed 3D battles that stay true to the anime and video game series, with breathtaking visuals and authentic combat moves like beam clashes, rush attacks, movements too quick for the eyes to see, and planet-razing ultimate attacks. Challenge other players online to test your skills, or sit down with friends offline to hone your skills exclusively in the Hyperbolic Time Chamber! Fight your way to become a champion across various tournament modes and victory conditions. Conquer the action-packed battles from the beloved original story, or discover and unlock new encounters for your favorite Z-Fighters and more. Relive your favorite moments from the series through cutscenes you can experience from the perspectives of eight characters! Recreate your favorite battles from throughout the Dragon Ball story, or set up your dream story battle with your favorite characters! Share your creations with other fans and experience the battles brought to life by imaginations around the world. *In addition to this edition, Deluxe Edition and Ultimate Edition are also available. Please be careful not to purchase the same content twice.

_childDocuments_.review: The story mode is a complete joke. It's just still frame images, sometimes without narration, sometimes with. The game play itself is really good and has a lot of depth. I suppose if all you care about is online pvp, then this game is for you. However, the EULA required to play this game is next level bs. I understand needing to agree to their terms to access their servers for online pvp and whatnot, but why am I forced to agree to this hot garbage if I don't plan on playing online at all? Would it not be better to allow to just play in offline mode? I suppose the general public have become so relaxed with giving up their rights and personal information that I can't really blame Bandai Namco for taking advantage of free money. That said, I spent $70 on this and would have kept it were it not for the garbage EULA you forced me to agree to. So instead, I'll just pick it up on the ol Pirate Bay in a few days when it's cracked. If you're going to stoop to anti-consumer practices, then I'll stoop to thievery.

_childDocuments_.review: Dragon Ball: Sparking! Zero is an exhilarating love letter to the franchise, blending explosive visuals with a colossal roster and chaotic, high-octane action that is both fun and strategically nuanced. While the campaign lacks depth and the limited map pool may disappoint, Sparking Zero’s true strength lies in its raw 3D arena-fighter appeal and its execution of it, firmly establishing it as a worthy successor to Budokai Tenkaichi 3. Sparking Zero condenses the DBZ storyline and beyond, focusing primarily on key moments from the perspectives of seven prominent characters. Each narrative unfolds through iconic battles and light character dialogues, intertwined with in-game stills and static interactions outside battle. Unfortunately, this is why the campaign falls short: it relies too much on superficial, static screenshots and brief exchanges to propel the story, failing to capture the depth and intensity each moment deserves. This leads to erratic pacing, iconic scenes come and go with little buildup or emotional payoff, making the story feel more like a checklist of fights throughout a slide-show presentation than an immersive journey with cinematic cutscenes befitting of DB.While additional What-If scenarios add unique twists and explore sick alternative outcomes, they still face the same issues as the campaign. Ultimately, the campaign does deliver thrilling battles and fresh takes on classic showdowns that fans of the series would love, but its shallow storytelling dilutes pivotal moments, leaving the experience feeling flat, especially for newcomers to the franchise. Dragon Ball: Sparking Zero delivers precisely what fans crave: a spectacular, high-speed, chaotic, but fun experience that builds upon the beloved formula of Budokai Tenkaichi 3. The combat may seem simplistic, but it is deceptively layered, with diverse and intricate mechanics. You can scrape by with button mashing in solo play, but fall into that trap, and you will be easy prey online. The combat revolves around high-octane action throughout the free-form stages, where every clash feels like a scene from the anime. Characters zip through the air, dash, and teleport across the massive stages. The combat flows seamlessly from incredibly satisfying melee combat to explosive ki blasts, letting you pivot between close-quarters brawls and long-range assaults instantly. But it's not just about offense; you have plenty of defensive options such as guards, vanishes, counters, bounce-back mechanics, and more to keep you engaged, demanding constant adaptation with a high-skill ceiling. The character roster has a staggering size of 182, from anime and movies to various transformations and eras, each with unique moves and abilities. As for stages, there are 12 different stages, each packed with destructible elements and vibrant, detailed visuals. The diverse roster keeps every match fresh and exciting and allows for experimentation with characters, strategies, and matchups. However, I can't help but wish for a few more maps.First off, the absence of crossplay is a disappointing oversight that could hinder the long-term viability of multiplayer on PC, compounded by the fact that there are no penalties for rage quitters. Multiplayer offers normal and ranked matches and four modes: singles, teams, DP battles, and tournaments with local play also available.DP battles are particularly notable and enjoyable due to its unique system that allocates 15 DP points to build your team. Stronger, canonically powerful characters cost more DP, while weaker ones require less. Due to the cap of DP, it fosters varied playstyles, challenging you to balance your squad without relying solely on powerhouses, effectively reflecting the series' established power levels without being overly unbalanced.With custom battles, you can create fully customized fights with options to change intros, voice lines, conditions, mid-cutscenes, and more, then share them with the world, which is a sick feature and helps alleviate skipped encounters. Sure, there are some limitations, and the UI can be a bit clunky, but having the ability to build showdowns beyond just pitting two characters against each other is incredibly fun and unique.As for character customization, in the shop, you can buy ability items that, when equipped, boost stats, and these carry over into multiplayer. Beyond that, you can grab costumes, music tracks, voice lines, and more. Outside of the shop, Shenron allows you to wish for additional stuff once you have all the dragon balls. The level of customization here is impressive, giving you tons of things to unlock.The visuals are nothing short of explosive, capturing the dynamic, high-energy feel of the anime. The character models and environments are polished and faithful to the source material. Each era of characters is beautifully represented and rendered with meticulous attention to detail, particularly in their animations, transformations, and ultimate moves. Each clash fills the screen with vibrant colors and dramatic effects, while crisp sound effects and a powerful OST heighten the impact of every ki blast and melee attack.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't recommend in the current state. The game desperately needs a significant update to improve stability, QOL, and input windows. It feels very inconsistent. Pros1) the game looks great. There's a lot of glitches as the maps load in, but the action itself is smooth and the animations are very satisfying. The art style was executed perfectlyCons1) there are two control schemes: classic and standard. There are significant advantages to using the Standard control scheme such as being able to trigger blocks and counters more effectively. If you're a classic player, you're going to find yourself at a disadvantage to players using standard controls. Very odd decision for a game that leans into being a casual fighter. The learning curve to switch from one to another is really tough as well. Not sure why they couldn't add an option to map your own controls. 2) Many controls are unresponsive both in single player and multiplayer. In single player, I don't think there's a problem with the game receiving inputs; rather that the input windows are too narrow. For comparison, the input windows for certain key counter commands is dramatically tighter than even From Soft games.Online is a different story. Lots of input lag, lots of failed connections, and no penalization for players dropping randomly. The poor connection quality creates input lag so you have to relearn all the timing for commands. It's very frustrating to finally tighten your counters only to get trashed online because the windows are different due to input lag. It's just not satisfying. You never feel like you're gaining mastery of the control set. Instead, it feels random and all about luck. The windows need to be adjusted immediately in a patch to make them more forgiving. 3) The story mode is not well executed. There are limited narratives, only a hand-full of what-if scenarios that are difficult to unlock because the criteria that must be met are not clear. Additionally, you have to play on the highest difficulty to unlock them. Why? For a casual game, I feel gate keeping the what if stories behind some arbitrary difficulty floor is not user friendly.  The difficulty also spikes randomly from battle to battle. For Goku the infamous Ape Vegeta battle might be the most difficult and must be cheesed to get beyond, but the Jiren fights are easy. Some narratives - like Gohan's - feel very rushed. You get one or two matches as child Gohan and are then thrust into the adult episodes. In sum it's only 5 or 6 fights. It's not like there's an absence of characters to setup canon fights for Teen Gohan: Garlic Jr, maybe Goku fights in the Time Chamber, etc. Very disappointing. Other characters suffer from this downside too. There are no fights from the movies, yet almost all of the movie characters are included in the base game. Why?4) There is almost no customization for characters. Only one character has an outfit that affects their move set. All other outfits are cosmetic, and most of them are recycled. Some variations are so subtle it's actually hard to tell what the difference is between the stock and unlocked outfit. There are only four accessories in the game, and they are only accessible by certain characters. 5) The game has a lot of characters but many of them feel the same because the move sets are essentially the same. There are multiple reskinned versions of the spirit bomb across several characters which makes them feel interchangeable.

_childDocuments_.review: All of this is just my humble opinion.Ok honestly, if you're getting the game for offline play (Episode Battle, Custom Battle, vs CPU, Split Screen), it's an amazing game and I'd say very much worth it if you're a Dragon Ball fan. If you're looking for online play however, I personally would not recommend it. Despite the game having such a huge roster of characters to choose from, you'll pretty much only see the same 5 or so characters in ranked online matches. Meanwhile, the unranked matchmaking system is absolutely horrible, and if it used the same matchmaking system that ranked used (select a preferred stage/bgm, select your character, queues you up to find an opponent) the online play would probably be miles better than it currently is, but as it stands right now if you try to go for unranked play, rather than queueing up, it puts you into a custom lobby as you wait for other people to join your lobby to play with. Sure you can just find someone else's room, but another problem is that usually there's more than just 2 slots in a room, so you're gonna be waiting for your turn to fight.Overall, taking the online play out of the equation, it's an amazing game, an absolute love letter to any Dragon Ball fan out there. But, if your main reason for getting it is the online play, unless they change some things, namely the unranked matchmaking system, I would not recommend this game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: The core fundamental foundation of the game is very solid, but a plethora of individually small issues ends up resulting in a death by a thousand cuts for me with regards to playing this game.In its current state I honestly don't recommend this game. Its foundation is there and it has a lot of potential to be absolutely excellent, but as it stands it has a few notable issues that detract from the overall experience to the point of complete frustration. The biggest issues to me personally, at least at the time of writing are super counters, vanish wars, and the overall lack of quality of life in the menus. There are other smaller issues I have with the game as well, which I'll bring up over time. First and foremost, the main menu screen for the game is gorgeous and filled with so much charm and detail it's hard not to love it, at first glance. But when you actually play the game, scrolling through the options on the menu mwill result in noticeable lag which makes the actual experience of going through the menus more tedious. Ontop of that, there are various points in the selection of modes where, when you back out, you will be taken directly back to the main menu as opposed to 1 step back in the overall process, the biggest example being shop and customization.For some reason, despite using a controller, my mouse is still "active". This has, on numerous occasions, caused my menuing inputs to be incorrect because my mouse just happened to be hovering over a certain selection, which results in a misinput I was never intending.Character selection also sucks. It's bland and boring, especially compared to previous games in the series.Custom battle was legitimately the one feature I was looking forward to most. As a kid I would constantly just do random battles and make up storylines in my head, and now that it's an actual feature in the game directly?! That's awesome. However, the experience of making battles is sullied by the overall lack of QOL within the menu itself. I understand why the game won't let you just write your own dialogue, but digging through the over 5k options available is tedious at best, frustrating at worst. All we need is a search function to find phrases and words that we want to use.Now onto the actual combat side of the game. It has a very strong baseline foundation that makes playing the game feel very fun and pretty rewarding but there are a number of things I personally take issue with that detract from it being the best experience it could be. For reference, I'm playing on standard controls.I'll start with the lack of customization in the controls settings. Despite playing on standard, I have swapped around my inputs via in game menus a little. However, the amount of freedom you have with changing and remapping your controls is very limiting, to the point of confusion. I personally never would, but if someone wanted to bind their basic attack button to say R1, why can't they?Despite not being in my initial paragraph, my absolute biggest issue is with the current state of inputs. They just don't work. There will be various times where I will say vanish a beam attack right next to my opponent, and then even when I'm no longer pressing the guard button, I'll grab. But since I'm not *quite* close enough to grab, it whiffs and I take a punish, despite said grab not being my intention in any way. Also, the moments when I'm doing a combo and I want to finish with a super attack, but instead of doing said super, my character either vanish follow ups or spams ki blasts or something. The last big thing in this regard is either transforming or swapping characters, for some reason when I bring up the menu half of the time I either can't transform or swap characters out despite the menu being open. Or the menu will open but kinda close shortly after, without doing what I want anyways?I don't know what the fixes to these problems could potentially be but as it stands it makes the actual combat of the game, the explicitly best part, into a grueling grog that is just very tedious to work around with. I've never had these issues with the previous tenkaichi games, so I'm not sure why they're an issue now.Now onto super counters and vanish wars: I'll preface this by saying I like that, as mechanics, they exist. I like that they're in the game. Just not in the current state they're in. Super counters are a very strong "get off me" tool that is useable in so many situations it's crazy, however the fact it costs no resources and isn't even that strict of an input is crazy. It's a fundamental defensive tool that is definitely necessary but they either need to make the input more difficult like in BT3 or add some sort of resource cost to it.Vanish wars on the other hand are just really boring. At a high enough level of play, EVERYONE is consistent enough with the vanish inputs that it boils down to just "more ki wins". And when both players are like 4+ bars of ki, it takes so long to finish said vanish war. There have been a ton of suggestions online as to how to fix it, be it either just costing more with each subsequent vanish, clashing after 4 or so vanishes or making them faster, thus harder inputs, with each subsequent vanish. I don't know which would be the ideal fix, but personally I think something needs to be done because as it stands vanish wars just completely ruin the flow and pacing of the fights in such a negative and boring way.There are of course other common complaints people have about Sparking Zero's combat, such as instant spark, unblockable ults, afterimage strike, senzu bean (which did get nerfed), giant characters, etc etc etc. But honestly, while they are frustrating, there is counter play to basically everything here. Frustrating to deal with, for sure, but you can work around them. But, saying that, I understand if some people dont want to work around them. I don't expect ranked to be the most balanced game mode in the world, on the contrary I expect it to be full of shenanigans and cheese. But I do think there is a distinct lack of non ranked quick play for online matchmaking. It can be fun, and even very rewarding, to beat up the meta characters in the game with someone like Babidi, but it can get really grueling after a while. Having a casual option where more people are more likely to explore more of the cast would go a long way to making the online experience more enjoyable, especially long term.Playing offline is an option of course, and it can be fun, but after reaching a certain point in skill level (which I will admit isn't even that high of a skill level), the CPUs even on the hardest difficult aren't really that challenging, at least not challenging enough to justify just spamming cpu matches over and over with no other goal in mind.Offline also has its own fair share of issues. I already mentioned my issues with custom battles. Story mode is fine, and while I can take it or leave it at the presentation, some of the choices made are just baffling. Some characters story modes are just super short when they really shouldn't be, and while some of the what ifs present are good, I feel they also dropped the ball on them to some extent.Honestly we need more offline game modes. Let us expand the roster size of tournaments to 16 or 32 people, give us 100 man battle where the fights get harder and harder with each subsequent fight. Give us more developer made custom battles. Just something *more*, because the offline options are leaving me wanting.Ultimately, this is an amazing game with a lot to offer and acts as a good love letter to fans, myself included. I do genuinely like this game, but all of the things mentioned made the game a very frustrating experience to enjoy. So many small things that add up to a death by a thousand cuts situation. Each of these problems individually aren't that bad, but when stacked ontop of one another it becomes a very frustrating experience.

Am i supposed to fight a regular AI to kill time, or am i supposed to throw hands with a hell-bent Mike Tyson? Its a genuine question because even i cannot tell at this point, sometimes i think i fight the lamest AI you can think of, sometimes i think i have accidentally provoked a really hungry polar bear that is ready to do unspeakable things to my poor ass. Which one is it chief? Make up your minds, will ya? Next up, Multiplayer.... Man all this time i thought DRAGON BALL LEGENDS had the worst PVP in the entire Globe, SOMEHOW, Sparking Zero proved me wrong by showing me the most unholy amalgamation of all the inconveniences you can come across in a Multiplayer, so lets list all of them in case you were that blind: Hackers!, yes, Hackers. a handful of them using scripts consequence free. Input Lag! Because the Netcode was probably made around the same time they invented the World Wide Web, no point in fixing it, if it works dont touch type ♥♥♥♥!Rage-Quitters! Probably 80% of the entire PlayerBase, The funniest part? Consequence Free! YAYYYY! What, you thought you were about to win with pure skill against someone that uses cancer teams as if their life depends on it? LMAO NO! ALT F4 IN THIS ♥♥♥♥♥! You wanted a Reward fair and square since he rage quitted? Too Bad! _childDocuments_.review: To start off, I have to give credit to the game for how well it was developed and designed. It is too pretty, and maintains a similar design to that of Dragon Ball, with quick movement, environments that glow with beauty, making one feel like they're in the heat of the moment. Well-Known CharactersThe Character Models are well made and recognized as wellShowing The Unique features from Each FighterWhich Adds on to the Overall Experience as the Unique CharacterBut, as well made as it is, I think the game just hits a wall at a certain point. Though the mechanics are fun to begin with, they can end up feeling a little repetitive, and its story may not prove to be as deep and satisfying as some experienced veterans of the series may hope for. The combat system is fun, but it also quickly falls into predictable patterns where you can understand who is going to achieve victory. This can sap the excitement from combat once the novelty wears thin.In summary I think the game has a lot of potential, but it also has a lot of just straight bad. Longer, expanded storylines or more diverse gameplay mechanics could add replay value to keep players engaged. Secondly, introducing a wider range of different missions or side quests could help replace the monotony and enhance the experience.Overall, Dragon Ball Sparking Zero is a visually creative, technically sound title but one that its core concept lacked of depth and breadth. It is a fun time if you care about the series and I hope we get something a little less predictable next update or series of updates.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR at the bottom.This game was fun for the first week, but I had to uninstall because people online prefer to cheese instead of just have fun. The game is deliberately unbalanced, which on paper, sounds fun - Until you understand that the playerbase can and will optimize the fun out of online play in favor of quick cheap wins with low skill ceiling fighters - And they have already done so at the time of this review. It goes to show how much gaming has changed since the last Budokai Tenkaichi, and how everyone has grown to prioritize virtual points over fun.You'd think that with a roster this enormous, there would be a huge diversity in the different fighters you'll be tackling. But if you buy this game with the intent to play online, you will go up against the same 12 characters, and your skilled plays will be punished with unskilled cheese (unblockable attacks, hyper armor, auto-dodge, stalling until the timer runs out and the person with the most health across their entire team wins by default).Oh, and I've never gotten a beam clash in Ranked. It's not meta to hit a beam attack with your own, apparently. It's fun to do with friends, it's extremely hype, but it's not optimal for quick and easy wins.  Okay, so some clarification since a lot of the comments on Reddit referring to this review gave me some ideas of what to talk about--1. The AI is a mixed bag. You'll either find it too easy or too hard, I can't comment on it because everyone's mileage does vary and so will yours.2. The online multiplayer is a direct influence on this review because I am reviewing the game based on my enjoyment of it, and everyone is obviously going to explore their PvP options at some point while playing this. I'm not gonna gloss over technical details like netcode or matchmaking, you can find other reviews for that from people with actual wrinkles in their brain.3. "Just play offline", no, I don't want to fight the CPU, I don't find that fun. That's like going to a movie theater by yourself, it's highkey miserable, don't do that.4. I am not harping on the "difficulty" of the game, and I am not having a "skill issue" - I am making commentary on whether or not I enjoyed it, and I simply did not enjoy Recoome popping Instant Sparking, dashing behind me, and triggering his unblockable AoE. Of course I could cheese it by popping Afterimage Strike or something, but frankly, I don't always run characters with auto-dodge skills, so 9 times out of 10 I have to eat poo.5. The dorks saying "online is easy", cool, I never asked though but I'm glad you're enjoying it, still kinda hate playing online.6. "You only play Ranked", no, I mentioned it exactly Once (1) in passing. Apparently some people think that because I wrote 'Ranked' exactly once, it's all I play, you're missing the point entirely, please focus on the bigger picture.

_childDocuments_.review: It's imperfect, it's hugely unbalanced, the AI is broken (and sometimes flat-out cheats in What-if episodes), Episode battles has a very repetitive nature and the camera can be nauseating.The combat has a surprising amount of depth and variety, there's an incredible amount of customization, the animations and effects are superb and custom battles and tournaments offer fantastic variety, be it online or offline.It might miss a few things that BT3 had (more maps, loading screen minigames...) but all these things, including its negatives is exactly the reason why people are praising this game. It doesn't need to be perfect, it doesn't need to be meta, it just needs to be Dragon Ball. It's a gift to Dragon Ball and BT fans. If you never touched a DB game before or don't bother with DB at all, it's very hard to recommend Sparking! ZERO, it's going to be a 6/10 at max. If you are a DB fan or enjoyed any of the BT installments, Sparking ZERO! is an easy 9/10 or more. A love letter to fans and to the great Akira Toriyama.

_childDocuments_.review: Noticeable FPS drops, shader compilation stutter (pair that with egregious texture pop-in even on an NVME), a 60FPS lock (paired with slowdown below that), and no ultrawide support on a game that the publisher (Bandai Namco) is charging $100+ for. If you buy it on a key-site (like Humble or GreenManGaming) then it's around $90 but you forfeit your right to a refund.The only positive thing I can say about the PC version is that it has some graphics options (DBZK was barebones in comparison), PlayStation button prompts, and actually lets you play the single-player mode on Proton/Steam Deck.The game is seemingly using Unreal Engine's Fixed Framerate settings which is bad news because if you raise the framerate with INI tweaks, it will slow the actual game speed down if you can't hit that target, and even with the default settings if you can't hit 60FPS it will slow down. Just use delta time normally like every other Unreal Engine game does.Alt-tabbing is completely busted as it won't hide the window when you focus another one.The HDR display mode looks incredibly washed out and dull (Probably poorly configured defaults in Unreal Engine striking yet again). At least on Linux (through Gamescope) it is, on Windows, it looks fine. Some people report it looks washed out for them on Windows, so your mileage may vary.This also isn't using the Unreal Engine 5 version that has built in PSO caching (This uses 5.1.1 if the exif metadata is anything to go by). Turning down the graphics options does squat to help improve performance or to fix the physical slowdowns.The online multiplayer doesn't work on Proton and the Steam Deck due to the anti-cheat shenanigans.Played a few matches, the game itself is fun, but they learned nothing from the DBZ Kakarot PC port. And despite their constant patches on that game to add more live service crap, they didn't fix anything that was wrong with that port, so I'm not holding out any breath that this game isn't going to be similar. I'll revise this review once Bandai Namco patches the game.There's a bunch of characters in Tenkaichi 3 that aren't in Sparking Zero.EDIT: Just got the game installed on my Steam Deck. Strangely enough the game doesn't have black bars with anything narrower than 16:9. I noticed this when I saw that there was a strange issue with Master Roshi's ultimate kamehameha and how the top and bottom were expanded.But from my time playing on the Steam Deck, no, it's not a stable 60FPS, even with low settings, and the game's speed does slow down using default settings (no INI tweaks).If the game didn't have the slowdown issue, you probably could cap it at 40 or 50 and have it stable.EDIT 2 (Mods to fix the issues):So it looks like this mod works for unlocking the framerate in Dragon Ball: Sparking Zero for me.You will need this which you then put into SparkingZero/Content/Paks/~mods:You will also need this mod to basically force the game to load signatureless .PAK files:As for ultrawide support, you can use this mod:

_childDocuments_.review: The game DRAGON BALL: Sparking! Zero is a game that can trigger nostalgia for you if you have previously played the previous Budokai games. There are times where the graphics can be a bit overwhelming, though it all depends on your setup.Downsides:Lack of moves- Now hear me out, while the moves (specials) are definitely nice looking, at the end of the day, there are only 2 moves you can use that is offensive and the others are mostly buffs/debuffs.**Character Slots**- SO THIS IS WHAT BRINGS IT DOWN FOR ME. I don't know why they do this now, but ever since Xenoverse (Correct me if I'm wrong), I don't understand why character's TRANSFORMATIONS (In example: Goku, SSJ Goku, SSJ2 Goku etc..) have to take up 1 character slot. DO NOT BE FOOLED INTO THINKING THAT THE GAME HAS A LOT OF CHARACTERS. The game only has more character slots that are taken by their transformations. That's it.Characters locked- Now, I understand that in some games they had this as well, but, why even lock characters to this day? If I want to play as a character, I don't want to GRIND LEVELS just to be able to BUY them. Not unlock, but BUY with the in-game currency. It makes it more of a drag.Now, as the time of me writing this, I only have 22 hours of playtime, so my review can be slightly less intriguing than from someone that invested 100+ hours into the game. However, I only speak from the viewpoint of someone who works, and does not have enough time to play the game all day.Verdict: It's a good game for nostalgic reasons, however, it can burn itself out really quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: With a heavy heart I have to say that I can't recommend this in its current state. You'll see a lot of issues repeated throughout the negative reviews, but the biggest are the following:1. PerformanceGame slows to a crawl if you are capable of a refresh rate higher than 60. Unreal unlocker currently isn't working, and engine.ini fixes will last until you open the options again or touch anything about the display. I'm playing on a 3070ti and I had to resize down to 1920x1080 with everything on low with engine.ini fixes just to get past the roadblocks in the story due to the performance. Even then this is a slog due to problems with the AI. Ironically, some of the slowdown helped since I just sat waiting for 20% speed telegraphs of attacks to punish but this felt like a cheap win on the harder fights. The AI is definitely inconsistent, broken, and over-tuned, to that end.2. OnlineOnline is broken and not working. A lot of work and love seems to have gone into encouraging longevity of the game through multiplayer but I'd be surprised if it lasts very long. I was never able to actually start a match. Maybe an hour of trying various things to actually get to one. I was face-to-face as Broly vs Kefla, all primed to actually fight...then "communication error". Stopped there.3. AnimationsMy biggest gripe. There's a noticeable discrepancy between characters animations and certain attacks, and the "weight" that the original BT's had is just not present here. I think this is a quirk of choosing Unreal along with Super's animation style being the audience preference, but this is a sequel to a game 17 years old. Most of us are above 30, and grew up with Z animations. There's no reason to NOT make the punches and kicks in a DB game feel satisfying, meaty, and heavy. Burter's Mach Attack might be the most underwhelming thing I've ever seen him do in virtually any dragon ball game ever. Seriously go compare the two on youtube. Normally I'd be able to overlook this type of thing but they had a perfect template for some of these characters from 3 previous games from the same publisher who owns rights to those assets and animations. If you're going to copy/paste them over for fan-service, then don't half-ass it. Design philosophy is all over the place. Spamming Hellzone Grenade was fun in BT2/3 strictly BECAUSE there was no cutscene associated with it. You can get incredibly far away distance wise, to the point that you can barely make out the explosions from your attacks! Awesome! Except if you sprint to the other side of Hyperbolic Time Chamber and use your ult, it'll render a cutscene and teleport you to a "normal" distance to the enemy. Actually, lots of ultimates and attacks that were previously "spectacle" are now just a rush attack with an associated cutscene, or come out so fast they just feel like win buttons. It wouldn't be so bad if the facial animations and voices were fleshed out for a lot of these attacks but they aren't. This sucks. I remember spending all day testing beam clashes with my friends to see what worked against what attacks. Now you'll just get a generic rush clash for a lot of specials. I get that it was done with the multiplayer "fairness" in mind but this is really egregious here. Nobody who's anybody cares about balance or ranking in a game like this. We want to try and win with our favorites. Plus, the whole draw of xenoverse 2 was making a custom character with your favorite attacks. Every character here has set specials and ultimates, so it makes no sense why you can't customize one character with whatever attacks are associated with them. There's a couple of outfits that change ultimate attacks, but one of them is 9.99 (more on that later). It would have made for far deeper and more engaging longevity with making each fighter do what you love watching them do most. It feels like just enough respect and fan-service from the previous games is here for them to ♥♥♥♥ it up and change it to make it one step worse than it needed to be. 4. Nickle and DimingThis is a Bamco game, so predation is expected. However, two categories for early access followed by not including music packs (which don't seem to include falconer scores) in those ultimate editions means that if you are making this purchase with any nostalgic motivation, be prepared for a 200$ purchase up front just to deal with the above issues 2 days early (because no preload is available). This coupled with the misleading marketing (30 of the "131 characters" are just goku and vegeta transformations) leads me to believe that future DLC is going to be piecemeal releases designed to milk you of your money and prey on your nostalgia. I get that its a business with a product to "upsell" but this thing sells itself. You really only stand to lose the respect of your audience by doing things this way.All-in-all, this feels like a monkey's paw'd wish of getting a Tenkaichi 4. Might be worth picking up the ACTUAL 'ultimate' edition in a year or two when they roll it all together like fighterz, but for now, go play your backlog, or wait for BT5.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, we're nealy 4 hours in, and not gonna lie. I've got some thoughts on this game so far.Menus are annoying as sin, between the UI sometimes requiring you to HOLD a button to make a decision and sometimes not requiring that, and the fact that the main menu forces you to sit through these animations, which while cool the first couple times, is just kinda tedious after that.The shop is more frustrating than it has any right to be, as Bulma can't shut the hell up with her 5 repeating voice lines on cycle every 5 seconds, it feels like.Gameplay is fine, mostly pretty snappy, though I do think it feels.... a little different from the past games. If you ever want to play with earlier arc characters, you're probably best served communicating that with the person you intend to play with, since power creep is VERY real, and you're not at all likely to be serving up much work with Early Z Goku against some of the later arc characters. But that's what we expect from Sparking, so it's not a bad thing, just something for people who might not know to be aware of.I do think some of the story flow is a little stunted by the constant switching in its presentation, flipping between fully animated cutscenes and slideshows. But we've all seen DBZ, it's not like we need to see this story in full AGAIN for the 9001st time.Story mode alt win conditions.... feel really unnecessarily difficult, and with no idea HOW it's even supposed to reward the effort, it just feels like a complete waste. I mean, in a fight where the alt win condition is "beat X" or "beat Y", but the characters seem to refuse to switch, it's not exactly lending you an opportunity to even achieve it, is it?Don't misunderstand the criticisms, I think this is a really fun game so far, but it has some pretty interesting flaws and pain points that can really stack up to some serious frustration.All that said, if you're a fan of DBZ/Super, and you loved playing BT1-3 or hell, even XV, you might well really like this game, and you might have already bought it. Just be aware of some of what you might be in for. If you're trying to use this game as an entry point? I wouldn't recommend it, unless you're perfectly fine diving into the deep end. Overall, I think I can safely recommend this game to anyone who's probably eyeballing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Return to the Budokai Tenkaichi series! Sparking Zero is a blast! 182 characters on launch with each character feeling fleshed out and different to one another. Even the giant characters are fun to play. This game has a variety of single player content: Episode Battle: Which is essentially story mode with a twist. Certain missions have alternate objectives which give you an alternate side path to go down which unlocks a new "what if" story. There are many different perspectives of the Dragon Ball iconic story to play from, it's not just Goku! There is Piccolo, Gohan, Vegeta and many more! World Tournament Mode:This is a staple in the classic BT games back in the day with having the option to disable flying and enable ring out. Its even more fun online with a whole tounrament flled with friends.Custom Battles:You get to create your own Dragon Ball episodes! Having an episode title screen that pops up at the beginning, being able to pick what characters say to each other. Being able to choose how the cutscenes plays out. Also, being able to change the actual battle with buffs or certain events that trigger in the midst of fighting. There's endless possibilities. (I do wish there was a search feature when choosing dialogue for your scene as there are over 5000 pieces of pre-made dialogue and it takes a long time to find the most fitting dialogue for your dream scene.) Another thing to add about Custom Battles is you can upload your completed battle to the network so that other people can play them and try and beat them. You can also download others too and you can search by difficulty or how popular a Custom Battle is and so on.Of course there is online mode that has Player and Ranked mode but what is brilliant about ranked team battles is there is a "DP" or  Destruction Point feature. Stronger characters have more DP, i.e. SS4 Gogeta, Beerus, Whis etc who have 10 DP. And the max DP for ranked is 15.  So, it's up to you if you want to have 5 man team of mid tier characters or 1 OP character with a mid tier tagging along. Its very interesting to see other peoples teams (Although every man and their dog runs fusion characters as they have more health and hit like a freight train being thrown at you by The Incredible Hulk)I cannot recommend this game enough if you are a Dragon Ball fan.Things i want in the future:Characters i would love to see as DLC in my opinion are:Fit Buu (DB Super)Chi-Chi (World Tournament and DB Super as optional skins)Bulma (Could be in some form of mech or have some form of weapon like her early DB days)Tambourine (OG DB)All the Shadow Dragons (DBGT)Towa (DB Xenoverse) and her many forms from DB HeroesEven Bonyu (DB Kakarot) as i really enjoy her design and how she fought. The list could go on and on...I hope they continue to support this game for years to come and continue to expand the roster, i want every niche, random, filler , unimportant character playable too. EVERYONE!Raid battles:Raid battles would be fun too. Similar to Xenoverse 2 where you have multiple people working together to take out one super powered enemy. Or, even like FighterZ raids too.More Episode Battles:I would like more from other perspectives as well as having the OG Dragon Ball as a story arc as well as GT.If you made it this far down my review then thank you so much for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: 17 years we've waited. The game -through the eyes of an avid fan- is amazing. Through the eyes of someone who's first BT experience is this? It leaves some distaste in your mouth. The combo system is rather easy to grasp, if a bit oversimplified. The AI is either tearing you apart with combos I don't even know how to do, nor have I found them in the tutorila/training missions, or you're steamrolling them. No in-between. There are bugs when certain moves (vanishing step) just won't work. That specific bug persisted until I restarted the game, and caused me a lot of grief with the Ape Vegeta fight.The graphics are beautiful, though certain cutscenes where only the character's mouth moves is disappointing (for me specifically, could be a one-off thing).The controls (since it's like 4 buttons) can be tricky, if you're in a pickle, and start mashing. I know I've used far more supers than I'd have wanted when things got dicey.Balance is weird, since in one of the side-missions I steamrolled 1st form Freeza as Nappa. (and I still lost somehow?)Speaking of side missions: Some require you to beat certain enemies in certain ways. And they tell you, which technique you need to defeat them with. Which is only a problem, because: it's a text message, that's barely readable. It could change while you're charging the attack, and you'll hit them, and lose.All in all: It's a good game, with a few bugs that need to be fixed, and perhaps some balancing too. (How does Krilling survive a Godly Final Kamehameha from Vegetto Blue? :) )

_childDocuments_.review: Peak. It captures that same perfect energy BT3 did. It's what we all wanted the BT4 mod to be. I have very few negatives, but i'll list them before I glaze the game.- Character transformations are listed alongside the characters as opposed "click on character from 'x' time period, list transformations of character" style it had in BT3, this makes the roster VERY hard to navigate. VERY.- Instead of including all of the music with something like the ultimate edition, which, mind you, was over 100$, they're packaging it as two different music packs priced at 15$ each. Again, it's just music, but still. I want to be able to play head-cha-la while i'm in sparking WITHOUT dropping 15$.- The story mode is a touch lacking in certain areas, I found myself left wanting when certain pivotal moments just didn't have cutscenes. It was still fun, and I adored the "sparking episodes" so very much.- Maps. I just wish there were more. The maps that we DO have are very nice and very pretty, not to mention the map destruction is amazing, I just wish there were more maps.- A few OG dragonball fans will be a little disappointed when they see the roster, aswell as GT fans. I'm sure they'll package them later on as a DLC, but not being able to play as fan favorites like Mercenary Tao or Super 17 definitely sucks.- Wishes. I |WISH| there was more to wish for. As of writing this, you can only wish for 2 characters, and they can both be acquired by just leveling up.That aside, time for the pros.+ literally everything else.+ The game is just beautiful, so very beautiful. It's definitely the best looking anime game to date in my opinion.+ The combat is just as fluid as you'd expect from a successor to the series, and it didn't leave me wishing for more.+ The CUSTOM BATTLE CREATOR.... this game includes the most expansive mario maker-esque custom battle creator and I absolutely adore it. Also, yes, there are atleast 20 levels of Cabba vs SSJ4 Gogeta, and yes, I also made one.+ THE SPARKING EPISODES. I have only experienced Goku's sparking episodes as of writing this, and I won't spoil it for anyone reading this that hasn't seen them. They're incredible. I found myself, literally, screaming at around 11PM at night because of them.+ Online tournaments. Need I say more? You can do world tournaments ONLINE, with RANDOMS... it's peak.+ Ranked/Casual, I mean, it's got online matchmaking. Which, admittedly, in this day and age isn't that big of a deal, but having online matchmaking in a tenkaichi game is something I literally dreamed of. It's so nice to actually have it.+ Voice acting. In stark contrast to the lack of cutscenes leaving me wanting, some of the voice acting in this game left me with the exact opposite feeling. At first, I was kind of expecting the delivery of some lines to not live up to my expectations as the lack of cutscenes had dimmed my expectations, but when I heard that first "YOU FOOL!" I knew I was in for a treat. Overall, I was EXTREMELY satisfied with the voice acting in this game, some of the iconic one liners are just delivered so perfectly. Though, no UI Goku roar does make me sad.+ Story mode DOES have positives outside of the sparking episodes, you can also go down different character's story routes. It's a nice touch, in my opinion, though it's still dimmed by the lack of cutscenes.Overall? The best anime game to come out in YEARS. Easily one of, if not, my favorite release of this year, and a must buy for dragonball fans everywhere.9.5/10

Roughly 95% of the ranked player list is a bunch of meta abusing, cheesy (& i use this term lightly) "Players".. They all pick the same 4 to 5 characters, & spam/abuse the same skills/supers/ultimates exclusively. Ranked is currently overrun by a bunch of people who decided to buy a fighting game, but literally will do ANYTHING except fight in the game. Then when they are going to lose to someone who knows how to actually play the game, they rage quit... I still love this game, & have been lucky to meet a small handful of some really wholesome players who are not only actually crazy good at the game, but also were willing to just have fun, & goof around a bit. I have hope that a lot of the smaller issues will be improved over time, & the community can hopefully stop destroying itself.

However, while thrilling in multiplayer, the single-player experience can feel somewhat repetitive due to straightforward strategies often being enough to win against the AI. Tutorials are also noted to be less intuitive, potentially challenging for newcomers to navigate effectively through the extensive options and controls.Overall, Dragon Ball: Sparking Zero is packed with content and offers something for both nostalgic fans and newcomers, though its menu design and tutorial system may be challenging for some players to navigate smoothly
