_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to start this review off by saying that the price of this collection for what's being offered here is too high. Wait for the price to go down in a future sale or just naturally over time if owning this collection isn't the most important thing to you.Additionally, as of the time of this review being written, the game uses Denuvo, and I have noticed some small stutters while playing. It's not impacting performance to the point that it will get you killed during gameplay, or screw up a jump or anything, but it does seem to be on occasion making the visuals on screen slightly less smooth than they really should be.With that out of the way, here are my thoughts on this collection:Personally, I'm overall really happy with what we got here. There are some potential sound balancing issues with some sound effects, such as the crumbling terrain sound in Green Hill Zone sounding a bit on the loud side, but otherwise the games themselves play very well. I do however feel rather dissatisfied by the lack of a toggle option to enable widescreen in classic mode and disable it in anniversary mode.Take note that the versions of the games here are not ports of the Genesis/Mega Drive originals, but rather are ports of the mobile remakes running on the Retro Engine, with exception to Sonic 3&K which was made new for this collection and is also on the Retro Engine. Each of the games has been updated to the most up to date version of the engine.The coins system in anniversary mode is very balanced. Everything that used to give you a 1-up will instead give you a coin, and instead of continues you will get 3 coins. You can retry special stages at the cost of 1 coin per attempt.Update: In retrospect I actually feel like coins are far too easy to obtain between the various game modes, being farmable so easily that you don't even really need to be trying to get them to have more than you could ever need. Just retrying for speedrun times in time attack or redoing missions a lot in mission mode will net you plenty of these things in ridiculously short timespans.The new mission mode is really fun, and is the fastest and easiest way to farm coins. From what I've seen so far, it seems like S ranking a mission will net you 5-10 coins and completing a mission for the first time will net you a bonus, I think 2 coins. Missions are composed of little trials in which you must complete time based objectives. In some cases, that means completing an objective such as collecting X number of rings within, for example, 1 minute. In other cases, you have infinite time to complete the mission but the faster you do it, the higher your rank. Even for missions that limit your time, completing them faster will still reward you with a higher rank.The Museum is very rich in content, and features a number of cool things such as concept art, complete game manuals, OST's, animations, etc. For the unlockable items you spend coins on in the Premium section, it seems as though individual items are very cheap, costing you a mere 5 coins per item. Unlocking everything might be a little on the time consuming side since you need to grind up coins, but it's otherwise very trivial. Outside of the Premium section items are unlocked through game progression rather than by spending coins.Sonic CD in this collection slightly differs from the previous Mobile/Steam release. In addition to running on a more updated version of the engine, it features a title screen that functions more closely to the original release. Tails is unlocked from the start, and Sonic can now use the Drop Dash by default (or at least, he can in anniversary. I haven't tested for it in classic yet). I can confirm that the intro cutscene does in fact include the vocals as well. Unfortunately, Sonic and Amy's voices in-game have been removed for some reason.As for Sonic 3&K, I haven't at the time of this review tested around super extensively, but it does seem to be exactly what you would expect. You might be aware of the legal issues/controversy around the Micheal Jackson/Brad Buxer involvement with the original Genesis/Mega Drive release of the game. A number of music tracks they were involved with were apparently not meant to make it into the final product, but somehow did anyway. This eventually led to a legal issue that stopped SEGA from re-releasing Sonic 3&K for years, and it seems as though they were still unable to obtain the rights to those music tracks. As such, they have been replaced in this collection. The replacements are remastered versions of the Prototype tracks, alternate versions of which were also used in the old PC release of the game. Personally, I think these new versions sound fine but a lot of people seem to not like them. Overall though, this is something to keep in mind. Multiple individuals have made note of how they are making it a priority to mod the Jackson/Buxer tracks back into the game.I'd also like to briefly touch up on the recent delisting of previous versions of these games on Steam. In particular, Sonic 3&K. A fan project by the name of Sonic 3 Angel Island Revisited, or Sonic 3 AIR for short, was able to fully remaster the 3&K experience with a huge number of toggle options and native modding support. In my opinion, it's still the better way to experience the game. To install the game legally, a steam copy of S3&K was required, and was fairly cheap to obtain. However, this is no longer possible, and so even if they manage to continue the project through requiring ownership of Origins or something, the cost of legally installing it will have gone up significantly, which feels like kicking the fanbase while it's down to me. Make of it what you will, however.Overall, I consider this to be worth owning, but as I warned at the start of this review, not for the release price. I will leave it up to you to decide whether you consider it worth it however, and spend your own money however you please.

_childDocuments_.review: Post-Plus Release Edit:As someone who bought the extra DLC at original launch, I went ahead and ate the cost of the Plus update too just for convenient access to the Game Gear games.Honestly? I can't say I'm entirely happy with the expansion content here. The Game Gear games are a lot of fun, but I was really hoping we'd get at least a modicum of some kind of bonus included as part of their presentation here -- infinite lives akin to the Origins versions of the core games at the very least -- but no go: these are just straight ports, right down to performance issues akin to the slowdown and audio issues the original hardware was known for.Don't get me wrong, I feel that having them included is nothing but a positive for the collection... but, well, they call the Game Gear version of Sonic 1 a port of the Genesis game. That should really tell you all you need to know about the effort put into their inclusion here.Having said that, let's be real: if you're getting the DLC as an extra, it's probably for the same reason I did: Playable. Retro. Amy. No problems there for me: she's got her hammer, and that's all that matters.Otherwise, my original review for the game stands. A little disappointed? Yeah: save states and being the first really complete collection of the Game Gear games on PC is great, but it really is a bare-minimum inclusion, checking a content box and nothing more. No new unlockable GG-related art, no new unlockable GG related songs, no Origins mode extras for the games... so yeah.Absolutely worth having the collection for the games. Just... don't go in expecting the GG stuff to be anything more than what they already were.Original Review:I mean, I'll be honest... it's good.Now, take this with a grain of salt, because computers are as varied as the people who use them, but personally, I haven't had a single significant issue while playing the games.That said, I'm a casual when it comes to Sonic. I enjoy the games, but I've never ground out perfect finishes in any of them, or gotten all the emeralds, or anything like that. At least, not until this release right here.For someone coming at the Sonic games from the angle of "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ isn't fun," on a gameplay front this package does a great job of mitigating a lot of the things that tend to be Not Fun (for me) about Sonic. Unlimited lives/no continues helps to soften the blow of some of the frustrating and outright mean level design and enemy placements, and the ability to re-try special stages means you're not punished unnecessarily for not being an expert at a mini-game that, if you miss it, you have to more or less start the entire game over to get a chance at again at worst, or can't practice harder ones until you DO master it at best.Classic Sonic games are short and fun in our memories because we block out the literal dozens of frustrated hours we spent as kiddos memorizing enemy placements, special stage layouts, and hazard routes.This package's presentation of them allows them to be that fun in real life.On the other hand, if you want the classic lives and continues back, or want to be punished for the game eating a jump input during a Blue Spheres minigame, then the classic versions of the games are here. I can't say much more about them, though, because I haven't touched them: I bought the package for the Origins versions specifically.And I haven't been disappointed.Are the games buggy? Yes. They're Sonic games; anyone who tries to claim they weren't buggy *before* this port is completely ignoring every time the Genesis version of 2 will subpixel you into the void or 1 will press you through a wall with a piston.Is the music different in 3? Yes. The new tracks arguably aren't as catchy as the originals, and the whole mix is a little weird, but it's nothing that makes the game unplayable, and if it means 3nK is now free of the noose hanging around its neck from music rights for years, then all the better.Is the package too expensive? Honestly, debatable. Leading up to release my thoughts were an unequivocal "yes," but having played the actual releases, seen the work that's gone into things, experienced the animations and everything else... it's harder to make that judgement. As individual titles, if SEGA has asked me for 8 bucks or so for each of these versions, I would have thought it was 100 percent worth it. Combine that with the bonus materials you have access to, the linked mode where you can play all the games as one continuous experience, and everything else?The value depends on how much you think MUCH more friendly versions of the Sonic games are worth. For me, yes, they're worth it.Is the DLC worth it? Not really. For 5 bucks on top of the normal price for the "deluxe" bundle it's at least less egregious than the 8 if you bought the two packs individually, but overall unless you're the type who loves delving into the sound tests and listening to Sonic music when you're not playing Sonic, or a hardcore fan who needs the hard missions and, let's face it, isn't reading this review because you already bought the whole package? They're skippable. The animations on the menus are fun, but aren't really a value add in any major way.So, Sonic Origins. It's fun. It's functional. Sure, it could be better, but as-is it's (in my opinion) the definitive versions of all 4 games featured in the package, and 100 percent the way I'll choose to play all of these games from this point on.Lots of people are angry at this release for what it isn't, but for what it is, it's solid.

name: Laika: Aged Through Blood
detailed_description: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a western-inspired motorvania set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland. It is the story about a tribe oppressed by occupant forces, and the personal story of a mother coyote warrior who descends on an endless path of vengeance to take back what her people lost. Drive, jump and fight your way through the huge hand-drawn world on your trustworthy motorbike. Race through the wasteland and perform dangerous jumps, shoot enemies in slowmo and reload your gun by performing a backflip! Use skill-based power-ups and persist challenging battles against big bosses ! Vehicular combat on a fast and agile motorbike. A beautiful, hand-painted and post-apocalyptic world. A deep story about a mother-daughter relationship, vengeance and loss. A varied world, epic boss battles and loads of missions. The very first MOTORVANIA!

_childDocuments_.review: If the story or style even mildly interests you, it will deliver beyond all expectations.Laika is a game that reignited what story telling means to me. Laika's story is a masterclass in misery. Between the terrible lows the story brings your emotions, stunning visuals, and the astonishing soundtrack, Laika is easily one of my favorite games of all time.Even if the gameplay isn't your style, it would be a disaster to not experience the story because of it. The story being told is worth it, even all the side content is worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Tight controls, and you feel like a god when you string together a good combo of shots, kills, reloads, blocks and deflects. Super killer soundtrack too, and a great story. Some of the level design can be a bit tedious, and there were a few minor camera bugs where you had to reload / suicide to be able to fix, but nothing egregious. I think this game was worth the full price of admission, and I wish the devs the best in their future games.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid gameplay that is simultaneously rewarding and infuriating with it's motorcross style movement, the game always feels good to play. As good as the gameplay is it was the soundtrack, and surprisingly the story that kept me playing. _childDocuments_.review: As stated in the opening load screen for Laika Aged Through Blood I feel it important to put at the top: "Warning this game contains depictions of extreme acts of violence towards children and suicide, and mention of sexual assault, which some players may find distressing."Laika Aged Through Blood is an emotionally devastating story about a Coyote named Laika, one in a long bloodline of women cursed to live. die. repeat, putting this mother of one on the front line of protecting her tribe from the Birds: a group of Zealous Militants who drove the world to nuclear ruin. The game is not shy about graphic violence, from the explosion of gibs when you shoot an enemy to the scenes of physical violence toward children in the pre warning (the disclaimer scenes are thankfully sparingly used and not a common theme you'll witness throughout the game).Beyond the violence is a beautifully desolate world with a phenomenal art style all brought together by an amazing soundtrack of folk music by Spanish singer Beícoli, be sure to check out her work.  The game is a hybrid of a twin stick Metroidvania and motorcycle control and trick games like Trials Fusion which the devs call a "motorvania" in the most satisfying way. Thematically your bike is a huge part of you and will have to master your balance, between angling the undercarriage of your bike to block bullets and using backflips to reload and frontflips to recharge your bullet parries in combat. Whilst retaining the Metroidvania game plan of learning maps, upgrading, backtracking and reasonably challenging bosses.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood has been one of my favorite games this year, with it's well drawn art style to pull you into it's many interesting locales, fast-paced action that makes you feel like a god once you get a grasp of the controls, and all the characters you meet- and lose along the way, make for a meaningful and sad story that I won't be forgetting for a long time.Not to mention how well it does as a Metroidvainia, with each little choice you take to explore having an impact in some way, be it an upgrade that changes how you roam the Wastelands or a little thought in the back of your head, I at least always felt like it was worth my while. There's much more I could say about this game, but I think it's worth discovering for yourself. Highly recommend in all regards.The only downside to this game is that the soundtrack isn't available for me to purchase by itself yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: great game only held back by it's lack of ability to communicate things to the player.the art style is incredible and in a more static game would have been an absolute highlight, but in a game this frenetic and twitchy, the extreme visual noise can make things way more difficult. I can't count the number of times i died because i simply lost track of where the hell my character was at on screen.i spent a lot of my play-through feeling extremely frustrated trying to find quest objectives because the journal only tells you what area to look in, rather than just giving you a simple objective marker or even some better instructions for finding things. I get that you want the player to be looking for things on their own and engaging with the world by searching for things, but the instructions given were far too vague and i often felt like i was just wasting my time looking for things and frustrated out of my mind because the instructions just give you nothing to go off. game-play and story are both pretty decent, i was definitely engaged, it was just the directionless in-between moments that brought it down for me.it also kinda goes downhill in the back half as you realise that they've kinda squandered a lot of the potential the game had. you only really get 2 movement upgrades, a shotgun that gives you a jump with recoil, and a boost you only unlock before the final level. i think calling it a metroid-vania is a massive stretch. the story works in a lot of ways, but also suffers from a similar kind of missed potential. the start of the story is pretty strong, but it should have included the move from "Where All Was Lost" to the new "Where We Live". as it is the background storytelling details are interesting, but ultimately underwhelming because everything is kind of exactly as it seems. there's not hidden story to uncover as you explore, just, "oh hey, there's a big boom here and the area is called "where doom fell", guess this is a nuclear apocalypse." that could have been an interesting story to hear, either through dialogue or flashbacks, but instead it's just taken at face value and no one really comments on it. how did life change for these people? were they always in the desert like this? the birds seem to live in cities so clearly this apocalyptic landscape is relatively contained right? i dunno, the whole thing feels weird and i have no idea where the stakes are meant to be. why are the birds developing giant ass war machines to take on our tiny little village of like 20 people? also, the whole "floating sky city" aspect is introduced in the last hour of the game and feels both super underutilised and incredibly under-explained. Honestly the whole game feels like the devs had way more ♥♥♥♥ planned out, but they ran out of time or funding or whatever and decided to just scrap most of the meat and potatoes of the game-play and story, which is understandable, but definitely leads to the game having this really disappointing  feeling of untapped potential.overall, i'd still recommend the game, but go in with lowered expectations, like a 6-7/10. what you see is what you're getting, there isn't anything else under the surface that'll come out strong in the later half to radically switch up the gameplay or take the story from mildly interesting to mind-blowing
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: So happy I found this in an Iron Pineapple video! Beautiful game, that has a wonderful story and characters, unique gameplay that you can master and an awesome soundtrack that I'll listen to even though I've just beaten this game. There's frustrating moments in here, but if you like souls-games and a bit harder games this is a great one. The weapons are fine, but I finished it basically only playing 3 and not feeling the need to experiment with them as it worked really well. A few parts were there in the end where the polish from the start was missing where I glitched through or into things 2-3 times, but restarting the game fixed all of that. I wish there were a bit more abilities that you get to move around in the levels, but you only get 2 really. The wheelie to go up a track is also sometimes a bit frustrating until you get the hang of it and I had some problems in the beginning seeing if Laika was turned correctly.All of that said: it will be difficult to beat this game for my game of the year, because it's so darn beautiful and the levels are really enjoyable. I would love to have a sequel, It was a great fun to play and really really enjoyable. I really recommend it to anyone that's fine with trials controls and has a soft spot for Souls-likes! You can beat it in ~20 hours, I took a bit longer, grinding and so on because it was just so enjoyable! I'm happy that I live in a time where such games get made!
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeous game with unique mechanics and a heart-tearing story.For what could sound like a silly idea - metroidvania on a motorbike - it pulls it off with aplomb, featuring tight controls and evolving mechanics that keep things fresh throughout the play-through. The setting is engaging, the characters and dialog are well written, and they nailed the graphical style. True to the store page and splash screen warnings about the content, the mature themes in the story do not pull punches, but  they are handled with appropriate care and seriousness so it does not feel out of place.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a great game, helps that the soundtrack has been living rent free in my head since I started playing it. There's definitely an adjustment period of getting used to driving the bike while also focusing on shooting and having to decide in bullet time if you have time to block that bullet with your bike while backflipping to reload or if you should burn a bullet parry. I honestly almost never used the fast travel system because travelling the world was just so fun to do and that soundtrack absolutely kills it, almost every track just feels like it belongs regardless of what's happening on screen and that's something that's super hard to nail. I never thought I'd say I loved unloading a full mag of revolver ammo into enemy birds while backflip reloading in bullet time to accoustic guitar and indie vocals but here I am in 2024 getting way too into the world and setting of another indie game that not a single person I know has even heard of before. It's not perfect by any means, I'll straight up say I don't like the level design of the water level and the boss of that zone was just painful but that's by far the lowest point of the game for me and it's about halfway through, also not a fan of the mine level's design of fighting the same boss 4 times but both of those are outliers compared to the levels and fights around them so I'll forgive it.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game enough to someone looking for a good story experience. The dark themes presented in this game are handled flawlessly, the wonderful personalities of each character makes for a welcoming world to learn about, and the beautiful yet often menacing locales tell a grim story of the world through fantastic visual design.There are warnings that the game contains disturbing topics, but any scenes of much darker subjects are either are completely optional or there is very little of it in the main story. Most importantly, they are given the proper degree of detachment from normal gameplay to allow their emotional impact to be given the attention it deserves and present proper character development to Laika.The movement and combat can be rather disorienting at first, but as I kept playing I found a beautiful rhythm which made me feel like an absolute badass. The guns feel great but sadly most of them are better used as special tools or are less effective than what you already are given, making the default revolver my most used weapon for the majority of my playtime. The enemies may sometimes be in some annoying places, and I find some behavior of unique enemy types may sometimes be rather inconsistent, which has been the cause of many deaths. I want to also add that the movement is not well designed for a certain location with one area specific mechanic which I will not spoil, but thankfully it is only used once and then forgotten.

If there's a sequel, I hope they can be polished. Still an excellent game.)

_childDocuments_.review: As stated in the description, its a motorvania.You ride a motorcycle throughout a metroidvania map system, shooting bad guys, and doing sick flips.But it is VERY fleshed out. Admittedly, the aiming with controller could be better, but Laika has very solid systems that works well with enemy/boss layouts, the map in general, and just making you feel like an absolute badass.For combat, you really can just go the whole game with the default pistol. The upgrades you get don't increase damage, but this game focuses more on skillfully maneuvering with the motorcycle rather than out damaging your opponents. However it is still fun to use other weapons, and the only "required" weapon you get during the story.Then the story, WHOO BOY IS IT GOOD. It really is a "you have to experience it for yourself" kind of story, but the stories as well as some of the side quests are so heart wrenching. It really does accurately portray the cruelty of the aftermath of war, and the pain it brings.I do recommend this game, but I will warn anyone looking to buy that there are difficult sections in the game, but much of your deaths will be based on your ability to maneuver your bike properly. Have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: The dark and gruesome post-apocalyptic story is excellent, the soundtrack is deeply emotive, and the combat and movement are tons of fun. But, that mainly comes to play with side quests which really only matter for achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: Be sure to give the demo a go to see if the gameplay clicks with you before buying.As others have already said, the game is like Trials+Guns+Mad Max esque story. I don't necessarily think the game is bad, I mean I bought it cause it looked fun and there are moments where I was having fun shooting birds and doing flips. It just kind of surprised me with a lot of other things I wasn't expecting and personally found too annoying to continue and finish.First, the world is like a big metroid style map and has quests. Kinda threw me off a bit cause I thought the game would lend itself well to a level based format. I really wasn't expecting to have to do so much back and forth between place to place and it gets tiring very quickly. In other metroidvanias this isn't a huge deal, but in Laika you're doing this on a Trials bike and starts to get annoying very quickly when you bump your head and die when all you're trying to do is drive back to a place you just were.The game offers fast travel but is very quickly undercut by the fact that it's use is tied to a resource. You have to collect wax and craft candles to be able to fast travel and I have no clue why. While playing I saved up some money and wanted to fast travel home to purchase an upgrade only to learn I had 0 candles. I had 30 pieces of wax but because I didn't realize the only place you can make more candles is at home base I was outta luck. I was annoyed and mainly just wondering why a basic game mechanic has to be tied to a resource to begin with. The wax isn't exactly rare, so it just feels like adding an unnecessary step to basic game mechanic. Then there's money and resources. The game uses a similar mechanic to that of Hollow Knight where when you die you lose a portion of your saved up money. If you can get back to the spot where you died you can pick it up again and there will be no loss. Otherwise if you die too much you'll just lose it for good. A mechanic that I think works fine for other games, but that's because there's a margin for error. If I died in Hollow Knight I can try and get back to that spot and have health as a buffer to help me get there through enemies and obstacles. As long as I don't make too many mistakes I can get back. Laika doesn't have health. Bullets, explosions, head hits the ground, those all result in instant death. There's no buffer, you make one mistake and that's it, so if you die in an awkward spot around enemies or difficult terrain you kinda just have to accept you're gonna lose your money.Again, I don't really think the game is bad, it just has some really odd design choices here and there. And at least for me, the annoyances of those choices simply reached a point where I felt the frustration outweighed the fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Backpedaled on this one pretty bad...The initial impression for Laika is extremely positive, but once the game starts rolling the frustrations start kicking in.First of all Laika is a very good looking game that radiates the passion that went into creating it. The OST is a longshot from my preference, but it's unique in its own way. The artstyle is unique and elaborate. The gameplay is simple (similar to those 2d flash bike games) and makes good use of the few rules it introduces. It's quite neat. The writing is, if very generous, mediocre. It's your average Deviantart-short story in game form; unnuanced "lol quirky xd" characters set in a universe that is thematically over-exploited.Unfortunately the frustration that started to kick in somewhere halfway in the game became a little too much for me. Laika is a pretty good experience, but it doesn't do a good job at being a good game. It communicates itself strikingly poorly and when met with new maps I constantly ran into (literally) geometry I couldn't see or couldn't make out from the background. There are too many overlapping elements, the camera likes to do its own thing making the player character hard to follow (their color scheme is nigh identical to the background). Color palettes are used inconsistently (one such example is the blue hue used for enemies is identical to the checkpoint. I can't begin to count the times I shot the checkpoint thinking it was an enemy when first appearing). Crafting materials that completely go against the grain and pace of the remainder of the design. Enemy corpses that block shots for no apparent reasons. Overlapping elements you have to shoot DURING boss-fights.It's a little too much of the bad for me. The pricepoint is more than fair, but Laika severely suffers not having had enough time to reflect upon itself. It's been a long time since I've seen a game with this blatantly many issues so prominently displayed.

_childDocuments_.review: What a damn beautiful game, must play. The story and world-building is incredible, leaves me asking questions and wanting to learn and play more of this game. The artwork and style is immaculate, pure vibes. Music delivers so well in reinforcing the atmosphere of the game, I would listen to it outside of the game just because of how good it is. Gameplay is also really good. Mechanics are simple in theory, but intensive enough at times to give you abit of a challenge, hits the perfect point to engage your mind. Boss fights are short, but great in its execution. (OPINION: this is a better Hollow Knight, the navigation and map design is much better for someone like me that likes to explore everything in a map without getting frustrated about ambiguous objectives. I guess I'm trying to say its not as hardcore as HK)

_childDocuments_.review: This game won't feel good, it won't feel satisfying like Hotline Miami would, it won't even be difficult like a "Souls-like" but it will be Unless you want to spend hours playing on a bike oddly similar to the controls of Happy Wheels then you're better off watching someone else play it I think.It's a shame, I tried a lot to like this game, others did too. But it's just a good idea for a videogame that has poor execution. I'm sure someone will come along and do it better and release something that feels genuinely satisfying to play.You're not going to be going fast, driving through a level, and shooting birds on the way. The trailer/gameplay footage would have you believe that's how the gameplay will be but it's much more slow paced and frustrating than that. You'll spend most of your time either teetering back and forth between spike-y hills or lost in the unmemorable maps.There are things the tutorial neglects to tell you, like double tapping W to speed boost and that a short press of spacebar will just parry an attack but a long press of spacebar will turn the bike around. You'll have to choose very carefully between the two in a lot of situations and you won't always get your choice, often resulting in you dying and/or tragically losing all momentum and joy.The game is a lot more fun when you have the dash ability but that's given to you near the end.

_childDocuments_.review: *A one-of-a-kind take on the genre, it mixes 2D action metroidvania with dirtbike stunts and fast-paced gunplay. Beautiful hand-drawn art style with great music and a compelling story. I highly recommend this, my only complaint was that I wanted more. Also, demo progress was immediately carried over to the full version without any issues.** Do be aware of very mature themes in story, presentation, and gameplay. It does not shy way from the brutality of survival in a post-apocalyptic world, despite a colorful cartoon style.Without spoilers, you play an anthropomorphic wolf riding a dirt bike and firing various firearms through a Mad Max style wasteland. You'll take on quests, trade items, and acquire weapons and equipment that will further your exploration. I'll try to give some explanation of the unique controls, but honestly it's best to jsut give the demo a go.I played with a gamepad, so I can't speak for other controls. They are very different from what I first expected, but it didn't take long to get the hang of it.Movement consists of controlling your bike through various 2D environments using hills and ramps to gain speed and launch yourself from platform to platform. The left stick is used to control the radial orientation of your bike, not the direction of movement (for example: hold right while in the air and moving to the right does a front flip, while doing it on the ground while facing right and stationary will balance you on your front tire). The right stick controls your aiming , while the triggers control your acceleration and firing your weapon. It might sound like a mess of a control scheme, but it really comes together in a fun way. You are fragile. If you take a direct shot from an enemy or land your bike upside-down, you're dead. There is however a very generous checkpoint system, but you mainly will use your speed and the bike itself to avoid or block enemy fire. Gunplay feels fast and rewarding, as you are always able to fire in any direction around you. The only gimmick here is that reloading is done by doing flips on your bike. Trust me, when you get in down, it feels incredible.It's wild, it's gory, it's sweet, it's heartbreaking. I can't recommend this enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I can hardly express in words how much I love this game! I never write reviews, but for this game I simply must write one. When I first launched the demo and saw how beautiful the art style was and heard the stunning music I knew I came across something special.It's not just the excellent audiovisual direction that's brilliant about this game, it's the deeply emotional story, the short but sweet animated sequences and of course the gameplay, which is somehow even better than all the other parts of the game!Riding the bike, doing backflips in slow motion while killing enemies all around me by deflecting bullets and shooting them in the face is just pure fun! And it somehow got better and better the further I progressed in the game! The level design, especially in the big tree, felt like an enormous amount of time and thought was put into every centimeter of the game, all the locations are visually distinctive and traversing them is a joy. I even enjoyed that more enemies appeared on the map as I got better equipment and got more skilled in using my abilities, it made sense storywise and created a nicely challenging difficulty curve that, at least for me, fitted perfectly in the sweet spot of not being too easy and boring, but also not being frustratingly difficult.I could praise all the aspects of this game for hours, but I will just say that for me this might be a perfect game. Thank you so much for making this masterpiece, it shows that so much heart and effort was put into it!

_childDocuments_.review: All in all, I really enjoyed Laika: Aged Through Blood. It's a tough, yet heartfelt experience and that goes for everything including the story, the gameplay, the visuals and the music. *Gameplay: Difficult, but rewarding. Hard to get used to and just when you thought it would finally become a breeze, the game will surprise you with another hurdle. Such is life. I think the difficulty adds a lot to the narrative; the grim situation you're in calls for riding that bike with a furrowed brow after all. But still, it's very rewarding. It simply asks for equal or more energy put into it. I personally like that, a lot. If you go into the game, expect it to challenge you. It also subverts some tropes regarding quest systems, which were very entertaining.*Story and writing in general: The story and lore had me on the edge of my seat all throughout. I desperately wanted to know more about the world and what will happen next every second I played. Every character is very believably written and multifaceted. Laika in particular is cool, but her coolness comes from her suffering, which again, is very realistically conveyed. This game adores and understands women in particular. Feminine pains and joys are a theme from beginning to end. I personally was really scared at the final mission when I put together in advance what will happen. I was relieved that things went a lot better than I expected. The game balances sadness and joy very well, and I was really happy to see that. After all, the story was about native people fighting back against colonization in a world where they already lost so much. Those crumbs of joy among the horrifying chaos are much appreciated. *Art direction and music: The music being diagetic on multiple levels blew my mind, it was so cleverly executed. All tapes are atmospheric and suit every location they play in really well. They're melancholic, yet not a slog in the slightest. They're comforting, especially when you've been listening to them for a while. The visuals strike a similar balance with the rest of the game. Everything is ruined and disordely and yet, every asset is lovingly rendered and the soft colors bring it all together so well. It never gets boring to look at. The animations are gorgeously done also. At first I felt that they were a little abrupt, but I found that kind of added to Laika's character? She has nothing to fear, killing a giant mutant is just another Wednesday for her. She wants no fan faire, just getting home, spend time with her daughter and getting some decent sleep.*The one thing I didn't like: The game doesn't communicate things clearly to the player both in text and visually. Textually because in quest descriptions, the locations tend to be either too vague or flat out inaccurate and I needed to look up walkthroughs at least 7 times, but I think it's closer to 10. Visually, I had a really hard time distinguishing the interactable objects and the ground  from the background. The game is absolutely gorgeous and works its lore into gameplay seamlessly but I feel like it was a little too seamless way too many times to ignore. There's so much detail and the important objects just get lost in them. This goes for puzzles and navigation too, unfortunately. I also feel like the buttom prompts either don't always show up, or just gets lost in the details also, because I found that with most places/objects of interest, I already passed by them.Another, problem that's just personal gripes: I wish the game was longer. It would have allowed for more practice, more lore, more story, but as is, I still think it works and creates a wonderful whole.For the reasons I brought up in the second to final paragraph I can only give it a 9/10, but I still wholeheartedly recommend it. Lovely, wonderful, fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: There aren't enough words to express how much I love Laika. This game is the only game that's made me cry so far in my almost a decade of active gaming. It's a soulslike in its depressiveness, but there is genuine hope for the future built within that core of pain.Of course there are pain points. One of the bosses in what I feel is "Act 2" is not communicated how to fight it and ruined an important emotional beat for me. Laika's behavior in "Act 3" is questionable and frustrating, yet also understandable if you squint. A lot of quests are backtracking and fetch quests, but I don't really care.I love this game. I will never not love this game. It has soul, passion, and genuine humanity pumped into every little detail. I'm unsure if I can bring myself to play it again simply because of how good it is.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll start this review by saying that Laika: Aged Through Blood is the best game I’ve played in quite a while. This is the first time I’ve felt compelled to pour my heart and soul into a review, and Laika deserves it 100%.This game first caught my eye while I was browsing Spotify, believe it or not. After a few hours of listening to the soundtrack, I knew I had to give it a shot. Music and sound design is a big deal to me, and is one of the main things I look for when selecting games, and Beícoli has created a true masterpiece. From the heartwarming thoughts of wonder in “Playing in the Sun” to the melancholy lyrics of “The Last Tear” to the pangs of regret in “No Return”, this soundtrack will tear your heart to pieces like no other. It complements the narrative of the game so well, matching perfectly with the somber storyline.Speaking of which, I’ll go so far as to say that this game has the best story out of everything I’ve played so far. You’re dropped right into a brutal and equally powerful scene of destruction and loss, and the game doesn’t stop there. This game will make you cry, and its continual onslaught lends particularly well to the perpetual feeling of hopelessness the village's inhabitants express in every interaction. You are the only member of your village that they can spare to fight the bird’s military power, and you owe it to them to make every battle count.The gameplay has also amazed me. Combat and movement are entirely based around your motorcycle. Put it in between you and enemies to block bullets, reload your weapons with a tactical backflip, and parry your bullets right back at the birds with your wheels. Once you’ve gotten the basics down, every encounter is a stylish mix of finesse and vengeance. On top of that, the terrain allows quite a bit of creativity when it comes to pulling off whatever vindictive plan you have in store.Overall, Laika: Aged Through Blood is a true gem of a game, and I’m so glad I had the opportunity to try it. I urge you to treat yourself to what it has in store. I can't recommend it enough.Laika is as heartfelt as it is gut-wrenching, and that’s precisely what makes it so beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this when it was released last October. I keep coming back to it when I think about what I love about the medium and how it creates these memorable experiences unlike any other kind of media and I wish more people were still talking about this one so I’m writing a review now. Laika manages to marry the short repeatable loops of games like My Friend Pedro or Celeste, where attempt after attempt and failure after failure bring you closer to a satisfying mastery of a 5-10 second feat, with the more contemplative exploration of a metroidvania. Both feel great and act as great counterbalances to each other as you make your way through Laika’s tale. Occasionally, and in boss battles in particular, the camera can get too far from the character and it becomes difficult to tell which way you’re facing. This can cause you to land on your head despite thinking you were about to nail a flawless landing after pulling off a double front flip and laying waste to the bosses weak points. Despite these occasional frustrations I found flipping around in slow motion over and over until I had mastered the moment largely satisfying. Both the exhilarating fights and the relaxing platforming exploration are wonderfully accompanied by the games almost entirely diegetic soundtrack written and performed by real wold artist Beícoli/in fiction artist Beicoli who’s poignant lyrics and haunting vocals beautifully if sometimes heavy handedly reinforce the games themes of parental anxiety about the things we pass (or try not to pass) down to our children and what that means for any one person caught in the middle of generational pulls. I continue to put the soundtrack on regularly as I’m working or driving. Laika’s dying world is beautifully rendered in hand drawn 2D art. Anthropomorphic animals ,friend and foe, populate the wasteland and lend the story just enough abstraction to really land the metaphor without veering into rote melodrama. The game largely strikes a somber tone which is enforced by contrast with its cartoon aesthetic and remains a world I wanted to keep inhabiting. All of these elements come together to tell a very moving and ultimately hopeful story that I have not been able to let go for the past year and change. I whole heartedly recommend you play this one and I eagerly await whatever these devs decide to do next.

_childDocuments_.review: Another excellent game that REALLY is sprinting through its third act. Dug the art-style, fantastic animation, haunting (if samey) score, and even its novel gameplay loop. First third I was hooked, even despite the learning curve when it came to the motorcycle. By that middle portion, its indie roots were starting to show, with its side quests offering too little in the way of narrative or gameplay treats for the lengths you go through. Most boil down to fetch quests and the little quips you get as a reward are cute, but so SO lacking when put against the main story beats. Its padding, sad to say.Certain boss fights were also a chore, especially the chicken boss (get that machine gun!!). They were, as a whole, the worst part of the gameplay loop, with basic traversal through the sprawling map being much MUCH more enjoyable.As I said before, ending was sudden and honestly, kinda weak. Not bad mind you, it just felt a bit lacking for the emotional punch it was trying to land. I get that traditional animation is just stupid expensive, but I felt the ending should've gotten a little more than, what, 30 seconds?In the end, great game. Would love to go through this world again if Brainwash decides to put out a sequel. Whatever quibbles I might've had, Laika is a damn good game and I suggest you give it shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I really really want to like this game. But it is seriously testing my patience.Laika's opening is really strong. If the entire game was as cool as the opening, I would strongly recommend it. I played for as long as the demo would allow me to, and immediately bought this game. I have always been a fan of metroidvania style games, sinking hundreds of hours into hollow knight alone. Therefore, with how sick and memorable the opening was in this game, and how good the core gameplay loop felt, I decided it was an easy purchase. However, if you are like me and considering purchasing this game after playing the demo, or have been sold it by word of mouth then I urge you to take this review as a caveat.The overall variety is lacking. And not just a little lacking. INCREDIBLY lacking. I have completed the first two major story objectives, and am well on my way to completing the third (more on that later), and I kid you not, there are only four basic enemy types that I have encountered in the overworld, or anywhere else for that matter. No, not four general types of enemy, LITERALLY only four unique enemies. To add insult to injury, all, and I mean ALL of these enemies stand in place, and fire at you. To compare this to a metroidvania with a much more varied sandbox, Hollow Knight has more variety in enemies in the FIRST AREA. You have a mix of enemies that charge you, slash you, and fire projectiles from afar. It's not a ton of variety, and hollow knight will retread enemy concepts in later areas, but in roughly the first seven zones of this game, I have not seen a single enemy other than the aforementioned four.  (I know there are boss fights, but those have their own issues).The lack of variety extends to the zones. While they are all visually distinct, and all offer worthwhile side paths, they really just feel like reskins of each other. Each section of the wastes could have had its own unique challenges to overcome, and unique obstacles to face, but instead you will be doing in each zone roughly what you were doing in the first: Driving up ramps and loops, and shooting bad guys. This could have been helped if it wasn't THE SAME FOUR BAD GUYS copy and pasted throughout the entire overworld. There could have been so much more done with these areas, but sadly, there wasn't. For an example of a game that does this better, Hollow Knight has unique obstacles and enemies in each area, in addition to having visually distinct areas. (There is one exception to this in Laika, which I will talk about later).These problems come to a head when we consider what genre of game this is. This is a metroidvania, where backtracking is often necessary to progress. To Laika's credit, there are lots of reasons to go back to previously traversed areas. There are tons of crafting resources to find throughout each level, each of which unlocks pretty useful and cool upgrades. There are also story items which help you complete quests for various NPC's. I have no problem with the quest system. However, with samey environments (gameplay-wise) and enemies that are LITERALLY all the same, going back to areas that you have already explored with new unlocks to collect their resources becomes a chore, which is sad, because returning to previous areas with new powers is usually a strength of this little genre. Once again, going back to hollow knight, returning to previous areas was awesome, because of their uniqueness, and because there was a sense of getting more powerful. This neatly leads into my next point.Laika Doesn't really have progression. I mean it technically does, but there isn't a very tangible sense of getting stronger. I challenged the Big Tree, what I can assume is meant to be a mid game or end game area, with essentially no upgrades. Basically none. I put a single upgrade into my revolver, and didn't even get another weapon slot. I'm not pretending to be some kind of pro at this game, in fact I'm kinda garbage at it to be completely honest. But I never once felt like there was a challenge I couldn't face with my early game character, or even one where the scales were stacked against me. Once again, going back to Hollow Knight, I remember getting my ass whooped by the Watcher Knights, because I had neglected to get any sword upgrades for this mid game boss. What makes this particularly sad is that after a point in Laika, I just stopped caring about getting upgrades in any way, shape or form, because beyond the usual metroidvania "You need item X to do Y", there was really no need at all to get them. This kneecaps the satisfaction of finding upgrade materials. Why should I care about getting the machine gun or the sniper rifle, when starting revolver can easily clear the entire game. All the doodads you pick up are kinda just meaningless bloat.Despite all this negativity, there are aspects of this game that are incredible. If you can look past all of the issues that I just mentioned, this might be the game for you. The visuals are drop dead gorgeous, in an art style that blends better than any game I have hitherto played beauty and bleakness. The wastelands feel like a living, breathing, yet harsh world. This alone might be enough for people to draw them in. People might like the soundtrack, but I'm personally not too much of a fan. I'm more of a heavy metal aficionado, and therefore blasted 80's hair metal the whole time I was playing, which I felt matched the setting nicely. Music taste is pretty subjective though, so you don't need to listen to my dumbass opinion. The story, while hamfisted at times (to the point where it feels like it's trying to hit you over the head with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sledgehammer sometimes) is effective. I like the main character, (not a silent one, but not an annoying one either) and I really felt like I was fighting to make the lives of all the little furry villagers better. I really wanted to help them, to make their cartoon world a better place, but I just couldn't bring myself to slog through more nigh identical gameplay. Anyway, to wrap this up, I have nothing against this game, its developers, its community, or anyone else who might enjoy it. It's just really not my cup of tea in any way, shape, or form. If you want a good metroidvania, there are much better examples in the genre (SOTN, Hollow Knight, Tunic, etc.) I really really want to like this game, but it just feels like it's wasting my time. TL;DR This game suffers from a lack of variety in terms of level design, variety in normal enemies, and an overall lack of progression. While it has excellent visuals and visual storytelling, those for me are not enough to rescue a game from bad gameplay, which I feel like this game has overall. If you have not done so already, go play Hollow Knight instead, as it is a fantastic game (with its own issues, of course).

In this game, you use a bike to get around, the bike has alot of utility being able to block and deflect bullets. _childDocuments_.review: Let me start this review off by saying how gorgeous of a game this is. I was immediately roped in by the art style and smooth animation, clearly the devs put in a lot of passion and work into this game. Although admittedly the game may not be for everyone as its unorthodox method of reloading and traversal is certainly something to get used to. I highly encourage you, reader, to download the demo and give it a try! If you like it, you're in for a treat! WHERE WE EXPLAINLAIKA is, as the devs put it, a 'MOTORVANIA!' Haha, It's basically a Metroidvana with a motorcycle, you can expect the same beats as any other metroidvania with this game. Progressing through areas and unlocking new abilities to unlock other areas of the map as the story goes along. The map is littered with resource nodes you can shoot to gather materials to upgrade or craft new weapons which also act as said upgrades for methods of traversal. One thing i really like about this game, like any good Metroidvania, is that you get a LOT of utility out of your weapon since they act both as your methods of killing and in the case of the Shotgun, your doublejump! Even as you unlock new weapons and abilities, your older weapons don't loose any utility, most enemies except for bosses are one shot, so no matter what weapon you use, all will be effective! This game requires a good level of strategic thinking, as you can only reload your weapons by doing a backflip off a ramp or a ledge, meaning if you rush into an engagement without thinking or picking important targets, you'll be out of ammo, or you'll misplace your shots by taking out less threatening enemies! Your bike is your shield, and using it to block fire is always effective, you can even drift and deflect the enemy round back to them! LAIKA has a soulslike mechanic, where once you die, your drop your currency and you'll need to fight back through hoards of enemies to retrieve your lost Viceria, you can craft various food items to give bonuses to the amount of Viceria you collect, or the amount of resources you get, or get a double parry charge, etc etc. A BIIIIIG note should be made on the music and the soundtrack, written and sung by an ingame character named "Beicoli," It really is a wonder to listen to. WHERE WE STORYTELLLaika's story takes place in a post apocalyptic setting, in the lands simply known as "The Wasteland." It's a tale as old as time, a jaded survivor of the wastes who simply wants to keep her friends and family safe and has become an excellent killer by doing exactly that. Laika possesses the curse passed down her mother which makes her immortal, each time she is slain, she rises again from Shrines spread across the Wastes. With her skills gained over the years and this power at her disposal, its up to Laika to defend her village from the onslaught of the Imperialist Birds. Laika's story, while on the more minimal side, is presented excellently and while I would have enjoyed a more worldbuilding, games like these don't require it to tell the story they want to tell. Quirky side characters fill the wastes as this games takes a more comical approach to the seriousness of a Post-Apocalypse setting, you can do sidequests for the villagers in your village and help mend old scars. Laika's story is solid, with a great beginning, middle, and end. I hope that we get another game in this universe, 'PUPPY: SECOND BLOOD?' haha.WHERE WE CAST JUDGEMENTOverall, Laika is a solid experience with satisfying gameplay and a complete story with adorable, funny, and heartstring pulling moments. Mitzfing gives this a 8/10 with a FUN Seal of approval!

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the most conflicted I've felt about a 2023 release. Like what a lot of people have already said, the mechanics are tough to wrap your head around with the mixture of Trials/Excitebike traversal and 2D twin-stick shooter combat with one-hit kills. It's incredibly thrilling and satisfying to pull off some of the motorbike bullet-time acrobatics, but this game also gave me two of the most frustrating combat sequences I've had all year. There are unnecessarily difficult mechanics that make some sections just tedious and aggravating. Still, I admire the boldness in the direction that really clicks when you get into a weird stop-and-start flow state a la Hotline Miami. Closest thing that plays like it is Rollerdrome, which I ultimately prefer on a mechanical level, especially with its decision to not punish the player for not landing on your feet. While there's a practical reason for the growing homogeneity of video game control schemes, I can't help but respect a game that bucks that trend and comes up with its own set of controls to create unique moment-to-moment gameplay.It's up there with Alan Wake 2, Hi-Fi Rush, and Season: A Letter to the Future for delivering the best aesthetic experiences in 2023 video games. Just a fantastic cartoony visual style reflected in the memorable character designs, striking background art, and the bombed-out brown and bloody red color palette. The soundtrack is appropriately somber yet has this driving undercurrent of pent-up emotion brought to life by the beautiful breathy reverb-heavy feminine vocals, soft and sometimes relentless percussions, clean plucky melodic guitars, and melancholic keys. It's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mood biking through the desert wasteland of your war-torn home country devastated by avian colonizers with evocative place names like "Where the Doom Fell", "Where the Waves Die", and "Where Iron Caresses the Sky". The narrative goes to some real dark places that aren't in any way softened by the cartoon animal characters. It's a game about dealing with the burdens of motherhood and the different ways of surviving and resisting under the brutal cruelty of imperialist forces. The cast goes about dealing with these challenges in very human ways, some of which are selfless and self-serving, all of which are written to be understandable if not relatable. The dialogue in particular is cutting in its raw honesty. It's not without moments of levity, but by and large it tells stories of suffering with a sense of poignancy. All in all, it really is a special kind of game that I have a hard time recommending to just anyone. It's uncompromising in its vision, both in its mechanics and in its narrative. You need to have a ton of patience for its difficulty, and you need to have a strong stomach for its storytelling turns.

_childDocuments_.review: I love hard games. I've played and beat Celeste, Cuphead, sekiro (platinum), I've SL1'd dark souls 3, blasphemous 1/2, lies of P Ng+, etc. I don't mind playing and replaying sequences over and over again to get it right. But after dying 50 times to the lighthouse boss I find myself not frustrated, but genuinely exhausted and uninterested to make another go. It's a shame because the story is great and there are some fantastic moments in the game. Read the positive reviews if you want to understand why people love it. Death should be an opportunity to learn from your mistakes, but that's not what's occurring here. It simply feels... random. Maybe I get through a 3/4 loop without getting hit by a perfectly aimed projectile, maybe not. Maybe the bubble hits me in a way where I'm properly oriented relative to the ground, maybe not. Maybe I have enough momentum to get up the ramp, maybe not. There's so much variance in each run. And apparently that's not even the most difficult/annoying boss. Perhaps it's better with a keyboard and mouse but I'm playing on the deck. Regardless, I'd appreciate either an (optional) checkpoint system, a way to reload my weapons without needing to do a specific kind of flip, or some kind of life bar/life count system. I want to love this game and experience the story without watching someone else play it on YouTube, but as it stands I'm going to put it down as being "not for me". ♥️

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I have never ever played a game which had a 10/10 soundtrack design, where every piece of music is a masterpiece, yet every other aspect of the game is 6/10 at best (in my opinion at least). My review will mostly build around this summary.-- THE GAMEPLAY --Riding your bike, balancing, trying to shoot accurately, trying to insert some flips into your movement to reload the gun, all this can be overwhelming at first, but you can get the hang of it pretty quickly, and it stays challenging, yet rewarding through the whole game. If this wouldn't be the case, the game would probably be too frustrating, and unplayable. So they did a good job on this part, yet I will still say that the game is only enjoyable around up to the 40% completion mark. The reasons are the following:-- THE NARRATIVE --Again, it starts off amazing. The characters, the story, the vibe; it is rough, unforgiving, realistic and sentimental. They (devs/art director) really give a good glimpse of the feelings and thoughts of this depressed, enervated woman, who's not even trying to do the right thing anymore, just doing something stuff that is expected from her because of her role. With motives so empty and hopeless, it was a great feeling to try to find something pleasant in the game, and I mean in the good sense. I wanted to seek comfort for Laika and he Puppy, which made me kept playing.But here, the 40% barrier shows up again. After that, the characters feel like NPCs in every game ever, giving out the basic "grab that from this area or inspect this in that area" type of quests, which were probably added to revisit areas, giving out more content, which is not a problem, but the backstories for the quests were really uninspired after a while.The thing that I missed the most was the option to choose an outcome, to control the flow of the story in any way. It was so predictable that  Why can't we do it if we choose to? Why does it have to be forced to just swear it to Puppy, but having other quests instead. Even if it's just two cards popping up with two choices, if they would have made the "war with the birds" quests feel like they really affect the safety of Where We live, choosing between that and your family would have been really hard and would have involved the player much better into the story and the hardships of Laika. Towards the end of the game, in some encounters you can either let enemies live or kill them, and I thought they are finally trying to add these options that the player can choose between, but as far as I now, these choices have zero impact on the game whatsoever. I don't know if this wanted to show how it doesn't amtter how you treat people, or how much Lika doesn't care at this point, but I rather felt like a missed opportunity, than an artistic choice.Towards the end of the game, all these just become worse. The characters, the motives, they start to get unpolished, the dialogues are lazy-written and do not carry as much weight, as before, even Laika's character starts to feel off.But the worst experience from the whole game, as already touched by the final boss topic, is the very ending of the game. Of course,  But what comes after you defeat the final boss? -- THE MUSIC --I don't know if these are valid categories for a game review, but I wanted to talk about this topic as well. I have said everything I have found problematic with the game so far. But I wouldn't care this much, nor would I have finished the game at all, if it wasn't for the music it provided. As said by the large cat creature in the game, Beícoli is a genius. And it was a really nice touch to add the music selection and collection as an in-game mechanic, since you will be hearing the songs a lot throughout the game. And to be honest, I had much more fun listening to the songs, trying to understand the lyrics, and trying to put together the backstory based on them, than playing the game itself. I have never analyzed songs to understand the lore in any videogame so far, and the fact that it came naturally, just by how powerful these songs are, made it really enjoyable. Since Laika is not a woman of words, her feelings can mostly be unserstood from these songs, and I really can't express how well these feelings come through. I have probably racked up half of the spotify listens on these tracks at this point.Overall, I wholeheartedly recommend Laika: Aged through Blood. Even with it's flaws, it has a soul you can connect to, and if this is the experience you are looking for, then I am sure this game will have something for you.I'll be looking forward to new projects by this studio, and more importantly, from Beícoli.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a revelation for me in terms of a new gaming experience. "Laika: Aged Through Blood" is an atmospheric metroidvania that stands out from others in its genre due to its unique combination of styles and mechanics, as well as its unusual aesthetic. Visually, the game impresses with its hand-drawn graphics, and its brutal violence and frequent scenes of brutality underscore the tense atmosphere of the game world.The main events take place in a post-apocalyptic world where birds have declared their racial superiority over other species and launched a brutal war of extermination. As a result of constant warfare and the depletion of resources, the land has turned into a desert. The other inhabitants of the wasteland hide, gather in small settlements and try to survive. The story follows Laika, a coyote warrior, as she tries to save her settlement from the invaders.The majority of the game is spent riding a motorcycle. You can balance the bike, perform various tricks and block enemy bullets. The combat system is implemented in an interesting and unconventional way: a backflip reloads the weapon, while a front flip gives the ability to ricochet bullets back at enemies. Holding down the fire button activates a slow-motion mode, allowing you to better aim and plan your next moves in battle. The one-shot system, where you and your enemies (except bosses) die with a single hit, keeps the tension high and forces you to be more careful. This set of abilities, along with the proper use of the world's terrain, allows for the effective destruction of enemies, even if it may seem a bit challenging at first. As you progress through the game, however, not only does your character improve, but so does your understanding of the game's mechanics.The game's painterly visual style is very pleasing. Characters, locations and effects are well done and stand out for their originality. The beautiful animated cutscenes are also worth mentioning, although there aren't many of them. The music in the game is wonderful - melancholic and effectively conveys the atmosphere of western post-apocalypse and hopelessness. I particularly enjoyed the mechanic of searching for new music tapes scattered around the world and listening to them on the player while riding a motorbikeNow for the aspects of the game that players may not like. The general description of the quests is well written, but the description of the specific task is often vague, which can make it difficult to complete the quest. For example, a quest may tell you to go to a certain place and find an item, but not give the exact location. This requires careful exploration of the location, which is fine if it is unexplored, but usually these are locations that have been fully explored several times and the item was not there before, or was non-interactive and seen as a decoration. There are also sometimes problems with the detection of interactive items, which can make finding quest items even more difficult. I had a situation where I couldn't find a quest item for a long time, even though I was driving right by it, because it looked like a normal decoration. In addition, quest items can be sold by merchants and are visually indistinguishable from other consumables, making them difficult to find, especially early in the game. The rewards for additional quests are usually small and insignificant.Bosses are not a strong aspect of the game. In fact, their attacks can be quite monotonous. Some bosses follow a pattern: dodge their attacks until the boss exposes his vulnerable spot for a hit. I expected a lot more from the last boss. In general, the bosses in the game are not bad, but they lack variety and complexity.As a result, I liked this game, with its beautiful hand-drawn visuals, great music, interesting story and lore, good and unusual gameplay, and was able to get into it and enjoy it. However, due to some of its features, it may not be suitable for everyone, but those who can accept it will get their share of emotion and enjoyment. I recommend trying the demo version first, which will give you a better understanding of the game. Also, if you buy the game, all your progress from the demo will be transferred to the main game.
