_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly good game that overall pulls off an amazing spectacle worthy of a playthrough.++PROS+++ Art, cutscenes are amazing.+++ Soundtrack is an absolute banger, SPECIFICALLY Playing in the Sun which is my song of the year.+ Gameplay is difficult but gets slightly easier over time and manages to be lovely throughout. People will likely complain about the difficulty but it's honestly not that bad at all once you get used to it [And as long as you DON'T use a controller with mouse and keyboard being an infinitely easier and more accurate control method with the autoaim for controller being liable to get you killed]+ Technically tons of content, although the sidequests are pretty bare.+ Kinda loved the anti-war message the game had going. Similarly I loved the Western style of everything.+ Animal people are an interesting decision and I found myself more interested with this then say, human characters. Like the Birds being literal BIRDS led to some real monstrosities you fight, while the friendly NPCs range from adorable to very memoral. [Also I'm biased sue me, but genuienly so many games fail to make human characters diverse enough to warrant remembering, it's going to be pretty hard to forget the western coyotes anytime soon, design wise, as they have no one else to blend into.]--CONS--- Gets a little edgy and very gory. While I'm cool with this and it's literally on the tin [It's not "Aged through Smiles"] but it's not the thing for everyone.- Map is ABSOLUTELY not accurate, or at least wasn't for me at a certain point which makes exploration a massive pain.- Screen transitions can get you killed by enemies you can't react too, or at least it did to me in a handful of areas. Not the biggest complaint but sometimes the camera will pan to let you see a "Cool" thing but then not pan fast enough once you rocket past it.- End game cinematic feels very unfinished and I really wanted a little bit more to feel more closure for the characters I grew to love by the end of it.- Hook upgrade wasn't used for general gameplay and is only used in two areas with it's second outing be FAR less interesting. ??MIXED??? Laika's hitbox can feel so bad at times.? There's a "Boost" for Laika from hitting accelerate twice in a quick succession which I had no idea about until near the end of the game. I don't know if I missed a tutorial or what but it's both entirely pointless and essential in certain bits making certain paths easier than prior.? Vendor - Craft - Upgrade system. Cooking for instance lets you make many different meals with passive gains that last 15 minutes, but overall it's going to be pretty rare to use as you don't always have access to it and you also don't really need it if you're bothering to do side stuff. Crafting upgrades involves bonus viscera sacks, the currency of the game is kept in there and they function as lives, however I didn't know you could upgrade them for a while as they are upgraded at a vendor to the left of your home and is not on screen unless you go all the way over there. The rest of the upgrades just feel like an excuse to heavily limit the weapons you get so you have to grind to level up the fun part of the game. Vendors are also pretty annoying as not all of them are near fast travel points but you have to routinely go back and forth to them to finish sidequests. ? Areas towards the backend of the game feel a little rushed. It wasn't that noticeable to the casual player I think but I noticed.? Combo meter isn't displayed and there is no option for it, at least not that I remember. Missed opportunity given how there's food dishes based on making it last longer.VERDICT: Laika, Aged through Blood is one of my favorites in this genre and for 20 bucks you're getting an INSANELY good deal, however don't expect it to be 100% perfect, you will likely find it to be 1000% enjoyable, especially when you get your combo going and you start pulling off sick moto-tricks by the end of the game. Really fun, memorable and filled with a mix of funny moments but also plenty of gory ones.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: For only 12$ and 15 hours of gameplay you will receive:•	full, completed game with nearly no bugs•	very fun and interesting dynamic exploring/shooting bloody game•	large, open, filled world, that is interesting to explore•	most memorable emotional rollercoaster of your life•	probably PTSDIf be serious, the game is perfect in every possible way. Under this cute and well-drawn game hides so much pain, suffering and difficult thoughts that surely not leave you indifferent. Adult topics that were raised is pretty unexpected and unusual, but they amaze with its simplicity and surprises with its depth. This is the first game where you really want to help NPCs and do their side quests because you really want to solve their problems and make their lives a little bit better, not because they give you XP or loot. The most valuable reward from them would be a few lines of dialogue, which would certainly be useful for a better understanding of them and Laika herself. Nearly all of the friendly characters in this game are memorable and leave some warm thoughts about them even if you don’t see them too often or even once...In addition, it is the first game in which children do not annoy, on the contrary they add contrast and more gloominess on the background of adult characters to this dark and unwelcome post-apocalyptic world. Main character`s daughter – Puppy, is an absolute gem of this game. After less than hour of playthrough, you officially become her co-parent along with Laika. You will became emotionally addicted to this innocent little fluffy cuteness and do anything to feel her happy and protected, despite everything.   The game has so many sudden heartbreaking and emotionally tense moments, that nearly the half of the game you will be emotionally devoured and play with teary eyes, trembling hands or just thoughtfully sad. These moments give you enough food for thought about, even after you fully completed the game.Along with emotionally hard and absorbing plot you would listen the angelic Beicoli music that will skyrocket your emotional instability and make all main story moments memorable and unforgettable (also after the end of the game you won't be able to listen some songs without start sobbing after a few notes). This music would lead you through the whole story and supports you in darkest and finest parts of Laika`s journey.The main therapy and emotional respite will be the fast reaction-oriented bloody gameplay with not necessary resource collecting (you can complete the whole game with basic nonupgraded gun) while listening to the Beicoli`s tapes that you collect through the wastelands.The game will have constantly emotional dominance over you. And rest assured you will love every second of this.Laika: Aged Through Blood is like a good psychologist whose shoulder you can cry on, think about your life and move forward. Despite the very depressing message of the game that will haunt you all the time, this game makes you think about very simple but important things that we rarely think about in everyday life. For example, how long have you been in contact with your elderly parents?Gameplay is fun and unique, the story will leave a deep scar on your heart for a while, the music is breathtaking. What else do you need from a game? You definitely won’t find another game like this. This is absolute perfection!
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence though most of this but I've just had enough and gave up. After the initial excitement wares off everything becomes so tedious, back tracking + collecting resources feels so unnecessarily time consuming. I usually play games consistently until I beat them but I've gotten so annoyed and fed up that I've taken multiple week breaks from the game, only for me to give up in the last area and just watch the end. It really seems like they focused on story too much as the game play feels lacking. Too many depressing things happen for you to care once your able to predict every story beat like "oh that guys gonna be dead when i get back", "that guys gonna be dead when i get there", or "go to place for good thing but find BaAaD thing happen". No map markers for quests, resources, or anything for that matter.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderfully unique game, oozing with style and emotional impact. The learning curve for the movement mechanics is a bit steep, and some sections of the game can feel rough around the edges. But I think "rough around the edges" is to be expected for any art trying to do something novel or unconventional. If you can spare it a bit of patience, the payoff is well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: A very moving game with an interesting, if a tad underdeveloped gameplay loop.The art is fantastic, I listen to the music regularly even months later, and the story is deeply tragic (But fantastic!)I think you could split the gameplay into three major areas:- Combat- Exploring- QuestsThe combat I think is quite unique, and I found it pretty enjoyable, however I will note that as you go through the game, you unlock new weapons that do different things, unfortunately most of the time the revolver you start with is almost always the best option, with most other weapons being confined to either beating a specific boss easier or augmenting your movementExploring was nice! There's plenty of world to roam about, and with your growing collection of mixtapes to keep you company, I found myself wanting to drive more often than fast travel (Which while not free, is awfully cheap)Quests are..Where my love wanes a lot. They feel like their only purpose is to provide character progression, and while I'm not strictly against that, the result can bring the game down at times:- You'll find yourself backtracking to areas often. You might explore an entire region on your own! Juuust to get a quest to go find an item you previously couldn't pick up- You're often misdirected, or given extremely vague information. At times I was told to go to a certain region for an item, only to give up, go to the wiki, and find it was in the neighbouring region- Sidequests are never not fetch quests, this led to disappointment. Here's a moment in particular that stuck with me: That all said.. Particularly with the questing. I want to say that this shouldn't turn you away from the game, it has its faults, perhaps those faults were due to limited time, budget, or something else. But the things it does do right, it excels in, and it's not often I can say a game makes me cry just from hearing certain tracks. If you want an experience to remember, this game is it!
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, bittersweet story about motherhood, loss, sacrifice, and vengeance among many other deep and messy topics it isn't afraid to get into. Throughout your travels you'll come across a number of funny and interesting characters who you’ll love, hate, adore, and make you reflect. The music for this game is so well done and incredibly moving, it really ties the whole game together. I was initially drawn to this game by the art/visuals and they did a fantastic job with them. The characters all look unique and amazing and some of the bosses and levels were very cool visually. I could recommend the game on just these aspects alone. The actual gameplay can be challenging and frustrating in regards to the controls and mechanics, but once you master them it can lead to some pretty satisfying moments. You will die a lot in this game whether it’s due to losing orientation of your bike and slamming poor Laika’s head on the ground, being unable to see a projectile amidst the flying bodies and gore, or simply mistiming a dodge (dying 1000 times is literally one of the achievements). It would've been nice to get more abilities to spruce up the gameplay considering you only really get one and that's towards the end of the game. 9/10 made me cry
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: At my first couple hours playing I wasn't gonna recommend because of how frustrating the bike controls are but the game won me over by the end. The soundtrack is very nice both on the vocal and non vocal sides, with a mad max esque setting having a more softer soundtrack over something like heavy metal was a nice change of pace. The back tracking can be annoying at times until the dash ability is unlocked late game which alleviates a lot of the pain the bike controls cause, just wish was added more earlier on or something. Some mechanics should have been cut, the wheelie for the tightrope section sucks hard because you never build enough speed for it and the hook is only really useful for one main quest and the statue side quest. The story is very touching on how Laika cares for her child throughout the game and still pushes on despite the odds and past traumas. Really hoping the devs make a sequel and make some improvements to gameplay specifically. Buy on full price if you played happy wheels a lot or light (10-15%) discount for newcomer.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a mixed bag of an experience, although it's one I would ultimately recommend due to its unique motorbike gameplay.The gameplay: the motorbike is the game's most standout feature, and I would say it delivers in all the ways that matter. Getting used to the controls and reload mechanics has a bit of a learning curve, but once mastered the game is very fluid and fun to control. Both you and the enemies die in a single hit, so the game stays challenging throughout, but riding through an area flawlessly while gunning down all the bad guys as soon as they appear onscreen while doing a backflip on the bike never stops making you feel like a badass.The story: Laika tries to tell a somber and mature story, but frequently stumbles  in ways that makes the script come out as amateurish and even a little cringeworthy at times. When it works it can tug at your heartstrings, but when it doesn't it will leave you scratching your head and wondering just what the writers were thinking. For the most part, the main plot tries to impose a sad and oppressing atmosphere; however, most of the side characters you meet around town and throughout your travels are zany looney toons characters that have exactly one character trait or verbal tick, such as considering everything to be "hilarious!" or being a Karen that complains about absolutely everything, which results in a tonal dissonance that pulls the player out of the experience.The dungeons: All the main dungeons in Laika are very well-designed, featuring plenty of navigational puzzles built around a central mechanic exclusive to that level. They're definitely a highlight of the game.The sidequests: sidequests are almost universally worthless in this game. 9 times out of 10 they consist of fetch quests that will have you travel to levels you've already completed to pick up items you could see on your first visit through the area but were not allowed to interact with originally. Even worse, since every secondary character is a cartoon parody of themselves, almost none of them have any narrative or emotional payoff and they will almost always get brushed aside as a joke that made you waste your time. And to make things even worse, most of the time the rewards consist of useless cooking resources or upgrade materials. I would recommend ignoring most sidequests and sticking to the main story for this game.The music: The OST in this game is fantastic and very atmospheric. One of the central collectibles in Laika are music cassettes which you can then listen to in the overworld while riding your bike. Pretty much all of them are very moody and very atmospheric songs and I was always excited to come across a new piece.The verdict: Laika is a very interesting and unique game you should play if you're a fan of metroidvanias or want to play a game with a unique central mechanic of riding bikes. The main quest is solid, but the side quests are almost universally worthless. The writing tries to be serious and emotional but suffers from a lot of tonal dissonance and come across as amateurish a lot of the time. I would recommend wishlisting Laika and picking it up on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: No one asked for Bike Souls, but Laika delivered a masterpiece anyway.Story: Darker than my morning coffee. Stands well on its own.Gameplay: simple yet satisfying with backflip-to-reload. Gratuitous flips translate to more style, more bullets, more combos, more loot... and more deaths. If the game is too hard, liberal use of bullet time and cooking will boost your survivability.Art: Very well polished 2D animations and backgrounds. Anything interactable will have stronger borders and saturation than the foreground, which makes the game easy to parse.Music: Grab those cassettes scattered through the map. Well worth the extra bit of exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: it was a great game, very fun it brought back those  motorcycle flash games feel with a fun twist.the story is pretty engaging even though laika was wayy too much of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the whole game,its not bad enough to be a deal breaker tho, its more as an bitter person kinda way. the boss fights get wayy too easy at the end as well too specially the last two.. the crab and the final boss... maybe i was using an exploit in the final boss but idk, just holding the dash to enter bullet time unload all the weapons on the boss then getting away with the invincible dash basically one shotted it.felt like a lot of upgrades where crammed in the end of the game as well, and the game for the final parts does overstay its welcome. great experinece overall tho, gonna keep an eye on these developers.

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I even start... This game is simply outstanding. An emotional rollercoaster that's as brutal and unapologetic as it is beautiful and heartwarming. Even by metroidvania standards the gameplay is rather unique due to controlling the bike rather than direct character movements which bears similarity to old Sonic games, but with gunplay. And gunplay is so damn satisfying here: picking enemies with different ranged weaponry in slow mo while doing 360 in the air never gets old.Music is a masterpiece that not only supplements what's happenning on the screen extremely well, but often also foreshadows future developments with song lyrics, and there's A LOT of vocal tracks. Hell, I don't usually like this kind of music genre, but it's so well done here that I can't get it out of my head.The story of badass biker furry mom is a must play and I can only hope we'll see more of this desolated, post-apocalyptic world
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically, imagine Excite Bike crossed with Metroid. That's what you'll be getting into, and it is beyond great. Seriously, just check the demo.Story wise, I can't possibly say enough about how good the story is so far. There's an incredibly dark, heavy opening that very much sets up just how utterly awful the future has become, and how hard some animals are trying to survive and help each other in the darkness. At the same time there are moments of geniune sweetness, caring, and heart that will absolutely make you smile, snicker, or even tear up a bit as these characters try their best to be there for each other.All between doing sick flips and firing guns on a magical dirtbike. Laika's something special, don't pass it up.Update: Dear god what an ending. Did not expect the story to hit that hard.

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a really neat concept of a game. A motorbike metroidvania game with guns and a backflip reload mechanic set in a western style anthropomorphic world is an awesome idea!  And while I do think the game struggled to build on top of that base design, overall I had a really good time with the game.The Story: Laika: Aged Through Blood's story is very bleak and dark with light moments of levity. Laika's struggles to deal with her responsibilities and the implications of them are very interesting in concept, but aren't touched on as much as I'd like and the scenes with her family while very emotional, are also a bit sparse in the overall runtime of the game. However, overall, the vibe of the game's story really hit me and I got pretty emotional in a few moments in the game.Graphics: You will almost certainly die a lot to enemies you didn't see or to not realizing you're upside down when you hit the ground as this game can get visually cluttered pretty easily, but I don't think this was often enough to be too much of an issue during my playtime. Beyond that this game is gorgeous. I love the 2d art style of this game. All the characters look so unique and interesting. I just wanted to know everything about how they ended looking the way they did and the same goes for the world around them.Sound: Also a mostly, big plus for me. Loved the music. It matches wonderfully with the lonely, dreary feeling of being on the road. Your mileage may vary on this strongly though as all the tapes are vocal tracks and even for me, towards the end of the game I turned them off occasionally.Gameplay: This game can feel fantastic at points. During boss fights or when the level design just has you keep moving constantly you can get into a groove that clicks real well between riding your back, doing back flips, and deflecting/shooting bullets. Unfortunately, there's only a few boss fights in the game and sometimes it can be a bit confusing where you need to go so you have to bring up the map which ends up breaking up that really nice feeling of just riding through the levels. Also, the game is a bit long for what gameplay is there. It really only has 2 unlockable movement abilities and the second one is gained at practically the end of the game and makes the first mostly pointless. So while Laika does have a lot of metroidvania elements I think going in expected a traditional metroidvania will leave you disappointed. The shooting is hella fun though and I loved spinning my bike to reload my guns. I really wish more games had interesting reload mechanics.Summary: While it struggles a bit to keep things interesting for its full runtime and has some frustrating design elements(traveling merchant, a missing fast travel point) overall I think the cohesive vibe of Laika: Aged Through Blood really pushed me into greatly enjoying my time with the game. So I give it a big old recommend, with the advice that ya try out the demo first to make sure it'll work as well for you.

_childDocuments_.review: right now, maybe i stink at the game. but it has caused me so much grief and frustration, that it makes it really hard to continue playing for a story i otherwise currently enjoy and think i will in the future. but the stinkin Radio Tower quest is so rough. not to mention that sometimes, you *know* you landed that shot, but the game says you didnt. you die. you do it again, this time really enjoying that bullet time to land that shot perfectly. you still miss. same thing with the flips; you know you flipped, but the game says you didnt. no ammo for you. which, by the way, is *very particularly frustrating* in the last encounter of this stinkin Radio Tower quest.im probably gonna keep playing it, but sheesh, man. it's rough. at least i like the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Do yourself a favor and please play it.This is one of the best experiences i've ever had ever.One of the biggest selling points for me was the story, it is incredible how you connect and feel compassionate with the characters in this game, even if the amount of dialogue with the "secondary" cast isn't super extensive. I especially liked how the game doesn't pull any punches. The story is absolutely brutal, acts of exterme violence are commonplace in this world, and, suprisingly, it is very tastefullly done, never feeling like violence is pushed on the player just for it's shock factor. By the end I felt completely inversted in the main characters story and how it would end. No game ever managed to make me shed a tear except this one, that's why it will always have a place in my heart.This game has some amazing ideas in terms of playability. Almost every single gameplay mechanic has been thought out and is well implemtented, especially the core combat loop, making incredibly fun to fly around keeping in mind your ammunition, parry, and figuring out the perfect time to do a flip to get all your abilities recharged. Also the variety of weapons you aquire througout the game made sure to keep the gameplay interesting.Beícoli, the creator of the sondtrack did an amazing work, making the discovery of casettes one of the biggest motivators for exploring. The soundtrack is superbly crafted to contrast the post-apocalyptic setting.The art style is incredybly well made, making the depressing world feel completely unique and beautiful, as well as keeping all the plethora of characters unique.I'd like to thank the developers for making such an amazing game.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to start off with saying that the Music and Art of this game is really good. It also has a pretty interesting story and some ideas that work really great. Unfortunately the game play is what killed this game for me. The entire premise of riding a bike is fine and we have seen it work great in Flash Games (Newgrounds baby), sadly for some reason the bike riding is atrocious. From the clunky environment and sometimes unresponsive controls. Playing with the Game Pad eases the riding a bit but makes the shooting near impossible since you need to shoot the enemies as quickly as possible or else you are screwed.Sometimes when my character stops to talk to an NPC(mostly the rude map Maker) the game spazzes out and my character rides into his death. After she respawns you get stuck and you gotta restart the game. The Game starts random radio sessions with your kid which just distracts you from the obstacles and enemies. The game really doesn't make clear which parts of the environment are background or not. This can lead to a great deal of restarting the level (or boss fights) because sometimes the environment blocks the rockets and sometimes its just a background and doesnt do ♥♥♥♥. The wep designers really need to know how a crossbow works lol (made the wrong choice for a second wep (pro tip crosbows dont work as spread shotguns lmao).There really are some great moments that await you if you can somehow get used to the atrocious controls, annoying Map Design and fetch quests.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: The game clocks at 18-ish hours of playtime, including the demo from which progress carries over (!). Mechanically, good, although I eventually turned on some assist to help with Laika's head bumping on the ceiling. I have enough headache keeping her bike straight up, so that's all. Very brutal one-shot-one-kill gameplay, meaning you're likely to repeat the same sequence over and over until you get it perfectly - there's a rush of satisfaction from executing a good encounter between checkpoints.In terms of story, the journey was exceptionally bleak and saddening, but the very end could have used a little more punch. Despite that, I highly recommend it for the emotional aspect.Traversing the map is satisfying, although tad repetitive by the end - even with the mechanic of teleporting between "bigger" checkpoints, I found their layout to be inconsistent (sometimes a checkpoint is just unused for the rest of the game, others are way too far out from everything important, etc.) but that's a minor complaint.Please give this game a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Before this review I'm going to say this: I understand.This was one of the most beautiful and heartbreaking games I've played.The music is lovely, the animations scenes are gorgeous, I seriously love the character designs, the story is compelling and makes me want to walltext about it, the gameplay is... not for everyone.Does anyone remember the motorbike flash games? Like that but with a ton of s*** going on. It was not easy to get used to it, the controls felt weird and by the time I taught of changing something my muscle memory was already glued in place. That doesn't mean I didn't enjoy the gameplay, far from it, but I can see how I can be annoying. I think its meant to be played in a semi-relaxed state, weird because of all of the shooting in between, but when you get used to the mechanics and enviroments, you can just enjoy the ride, hear the music, the sounds, the guts flying to your pockets...It's a shame that the gameplay will be so divisive, the game was made with tons of love and dedication. It shows everywhere that the devs really loved their project and I love it too.Try out the demo, if you can push through getting used to it I swear it's a game worthwhile
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: It's like a combination of Excitebike, Mad Max, and Castlevania. And it is beautiful, emotional and very fun. Can be challenging, and you'll die a lot, but it's not at all discouraging. There are many checkpoints, and respawn time is very minimal. I'm not normally very good at coping with games that require you to die frequently, but I don't have any problem with this one.The art is fantastic. The story is mature and emotional and very enjoyable. The music is fitting, reminds me a bit of some of the Low Roar stuff from Death Stranding. Not to mention the fact that you play a tough, battle-hardended, but clearly loving and maternal 'yote mama on a motorbike with guns. For furries, that might be enough reason to get it right there. But for everyone else, the game is actually simply incredible anyway, so you should also get it. =)
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game with a fantastic soundtrack.Be warned: The game can be very difficult.It's the first motor-vania. Balance is of utmost importance ala Trials, but so is making sure every shot is pitch perfect.Laika isn't perfect, there's definitely some rough edges and at times it feels more motor than vania, but it is firing on all cylinders at all times. The gameplay offers a unique spin on traditional platformers and metroidvanias that never feels like it overstays its welcome. In fact the longer you play the game, you get better at controlling the bike, and then pulling off the moves you need for the mechanics (backflips to reload guns, frontflips to reload parries, wheelies, blocking with the bottom of the bike) starts to feel natural.Beyond the gameplay Laika offers a feast for the eyes and ears. The artists did a wonderful job in bringing this post-apocalyptic anthropomorphic world to life. Every character in the game is dripping with visual flair and are well written as well.And the soundtrack. Oh. My. God. Beicoli is absolutely wonderful on every track. She IS the music of the game. I'm no music buff so I can't exactly describe what it is that makes the soundtrack so beautiful, but every single track feels fitting. The OST doesn't waste a single second and as you ride across the wastes, collecting tapes and fulfilling Laika's journey, it is impossible not to jam, cry, and feel pumped with the tracks that Beicoli has produced. I regularly listened to the OST to and from work for a month after finishing the game. I would put Beicoli's OST for Laika among my favorite video games OSTs: (Insert any of Supergiants OSTs), Doom 2016 & Eternal.Laika is a wonderful game and despite some frustrations and a few wonky design choices, it is a game I will remember fondly.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I received this game as a gift, and given that the themes and art style clicked with me, it seemed easy to give it a go right away and see what was there. I have never in my life, however, bounced harder off a core control scheme/gameplay loop than this one: the sheer act of moving from left to right is tedious and disempowering. Instead of feeling like I am an interesting or cool character in a world that is accordingly hostile, I feel like I'm a balloon tied to a bag of rocks that can't even turn said bag of rocks properly to block what looks and moves like a paper dart being thrown at me in slow motion. The idea of reloading by doing flips is cool, but *mandating* those flips just to be able to even functionally use your gun is beyond infuriating. You get so few bullets in said gun that you will do nothing but reload every few seconds, and this is not fun or interesting to do. The act of dying in a single hit in every single instance, even if your bike is slightly askew when landing, makes me feel like the least powerful and least fun to play character in the world.I have legit never hated a control scheme this much. You can't even just farm materials when you find them: you have to go find a section of slanted ground so you can do your stupid bike air reload flip to go back to shoot the rocks to pick up the stuff they drop. Supposedly this game has a 'souls like' currency system but I never noticed it because the core gameplay was so infuriating I couldn't be bothered to care whether or not I had any kind of 'currency'. You can't even reload your gun when stationary and out of combat, and that one of the stupidest and most unrealistic things I've ever heard in my life. This review is piss-poor but I really cannot convey how mad this game made me, because the setting and premise and storytelling all seem amazing, and right up my alley, but holy cow it has absolutely zero respect for the player's agency or time. What a colossal miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, but also has the worst boss fights I've ever seen in a good game. The main problem is the mechanics go against how it wants you to play. _childDocuments_.review: So .. Laika aged trough blood , I will be short and on point with this one.Pros:* The visuals are Amazing.* The soundtrack is amazing.* The mechanics of the game are interesting.Cons:* The music is buggy and sometimes just not plays so you stuck with some elevator songs.* The mechanics of the game become repetitive really quick and it loses its magic.* The map of the game is riddled with pointless Riddles , which are : " go to this place in map , and look for trash bin , in there , take the item " , zero direction the item or the place of the item has nothing outstanding in it , so it blends nicely with the surroundings.* Many places in the map gives you the illusion that you can go there while its a wall , that you cant go up or even interact with...* The bosses are multi-phase boss , that not only depends on your ability to handle their BS, but also to interact with the surroundings in middle fight , which causes many times going in a wrong corner and dying because simply that and going back to phase one of the boss fight.That's it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this game, but I couldn't personally get past its flaws. I don't think it's worth playing.Pros:* Real edgelord dialogue, game is very visceral and I don't think the writers felt like they had to hold anything back* Excellent animation, lots of shocking hyperviolence in cutscenes* The motorcycle gimmick is really creative (unfortunately becomes a con later)* Overall art and presentation is solid. Themes and atmosphere is consistent through the entire game.Cons* The movement with the motorcyle is sluggish. It takes seconds to complete a jump, you have limited control in the air, and there's jumps everywhere. Traversing the map was not fun after the first few hours, made worse by...* Too few travel points. Want to get that one item at the corner of the map? It'll take you 7-10 minutes to get there. This, and sluggish movement really don't work well in a metroidvania. Hollow knight also had few fast travel points, but you had so many things to whack and platforming in between areas to mitigate the pain.* Many of the bosses are autoscrollers and those are just not fun. You miss a jump, you start over. The lighthouse boss took me an embarrassingly long time to beat because I kept zoning out, it was so boring.* The music is not bad, but not really in my taste. Early in you have few songs and it was jarring hearing the first 2-3 tracks repeated in early exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel heartbroken about this game. There's something good in here, there's something genuinely as beautiful as harrowing that the game feels like it's getting across, with a particular take on anti-imperialism and actual empathy for its victims that I wanted to see more of - but I can't stand its design decisions. I don't know why they decided the game shouldn't be a linear experience but instead a metroidvania, I can't parse out why it has a million different progression systems - it has multiple different kinds of guns, it has sidequests, it has meals that give temporary buffs, it has resource collection that messes with the pacing. It has a playlist system, where the songs that were once placed perfectly in setpieces, swelling with the emotion of the scene - instead wear themselves out in open stages otherwise devoid of ambience, repeating over and over in a playlist in which they all blend in together with the other collectible tracks. The level of work this game puts into trying to make the player like it less is honestly astounding - there's something beautiful and unique here, but between its mechanical design being as inconfident as it is despite how confident the art design is as well as the simply baffling decisions (as another example - the first two bosses literally wait for you to enter a trigger zone before doing their single attack pattern, letting you take them slowly, easily, and tediously) - it starts to become intensely frustrating. Not because of any difficulty, but because of the way it simply refuses to let the player immerse themselves within the experience. I wish I had the patience to play it to the end, and I wish there was a version of this game that didn't require such patience.

_childDocuments_.review: **Spoilers Below. Fairly non-specific but read at your own risk.**An incredible game with a fair collection of flaws (namely, the bosses and pacing) that nonetheless earns a recommendation from me. It's a game that's trying a lot of new things and for the most part succeeds! The bike mechanics are novel and are built so that you're doing a maximum amount of flips all the time. It really shines in the open world exploration parts of the game -- racing along the road, shooting down enemies in between flips, calculating how many rounds are in your pistol, dying and finding the perfect "solution" to the fight -- this is where the gameplay was the most satisfying. In some ways, Laika reminds me of Katana Zero (die in one hit, respawn as a curse, high speed resource calculation, explosive gore) and that's a great thing! Exploration is a little tampered by the fact that it's hard to tell where you can return to once you gain new movement abilities. It feels like you're wandering aimlessly to find what you missed. Most metroidvanias include an upgrade to the map that shows locations the player hasn't been yet. This would've been a great quality of life improvement.Where the gameplay falters most, however, is in the boss design. The strengths listed above work best when death is cheap and you can respawn easily from a point seconds ago. The bosses, by design, are long and require near perfect execution because you die in one hit. So, if a boss takes a couple of minutes to beat, any mistake in that time means a restart from the very beginning. This is frustrating when compared to the high speed nature of the rest of the game! It's especially egregious with the crab boss. It would be a fun challenge with intermittent checkpoints. However, it's turned into a slog as you restart from phase one every time you die and have to redo all the easy parts (and the long animations) to get to what's killing you. Either adding checkpoints or taking a page from Katana Zero's boss fight (super short, but super difficult) might have improved the game.Laika's weapon system is also flawed. The only two weapons worth upgrading are the ones you acquire first (pistol and shotgun) and the rest aren't worth the money. While resources for crafting were fairly easy to come by, upgrade costs vastly outpaced the rate at which I collected currency. You simply finish the game's content way before you gather enough money to acquire and upgrade all your weapons. As such, the weapons system felt a little underbaked. This is a minor complaint, but just something I wanted to point out.In story, Laika is really good. The protagonist is a grizzled, middle-aged mother whose womanhood never needs to be commented on. Often in video games, women's primary characteristic is "Girl", and Laika is a fresh breath of air from that. Never did I feel Laika's ruthlessness or anger or age be tempered by some chivalrous idea of femininity... This game, for sure, didn't pull its punches. Themes of loss, of motherhood, of meaningless violence, of imperialist ambition seep throughout Laika's world. Laika and her mother's relationship sticks out to me as a highlight. They're dysfunctional and mean to each other in a way that feels real to this setting. Their actions individually hold truth, yet clash. So delicious! I'm so glad there isn't a morality system, letting the players make what they will of the story. I'm also grateful that Laika's violence against the imperialist birds is never questioned with "Aren't you becoming the oppressor if you enact violence against the oppressor?". This question has become a tired trope. Laika acknowledges this by letting players choose to have mercy on pacifist or child soldiers, but does not further comment on it. Indeed, you don't have to have mercy. Instead, the environment clearly shows the absolute systemic power of the birds and their history of exploitation and colonialism. It shows the facetiousness of the question without needing to speak.The story does stumble at the end, however. The final boss is strangely really really easy. I died A LOT to the crab boss, but only died twice to the final boss. In the sequence afterwards, Laika gains invulnerability, which I also feel cheapens the one-hit kill mechanic. If Laika didn't gain invincibility, I feel the short boss fight + this sequence would've made the ending much more satisfying gameplay-wise. It would've taken a few more tries, and the ending would have felt earned instead of inevitable. The final cinematic's pacing also felt very rushed. It suddenly jumps in time and ends abruptly. I get the impression that they ran out of time or funding to make the ending truly great, which is a shame.Overall, a wonderful, novel game that I hope more people enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a fantastic little indie game that I almost missed. I was browsing the Steam store one day, bored out of my mind when suddenly I came upon this little masterpiece! Brainwash Gang, a company I had not heard of up until this point have done very well with this one.Not only have they stuck to the Metroidvania formula and made a great game to boot, but they have also gone and invented a whole new hybrid of the genre; Motorvania. This certainly made me smirk at the very least. A game where you are for the most part bound to your motorbike. It combines Bullet Hell elements along with those of the Metroidvania genre to create a truly wonderful game play experience, whether you're achievement hunting, searching for secrets, or gunning it for the end of the game, you will have a great time.The plot of the game hooks you in immediately and along with the music really puts you in the shoes, or in this case on the motorbike of the protagonist. It tugs on my heartstrings every time I hear the music even now.

_childDocuments_.review: LAIKA's strongest selling point is definitely the motorcycle. I've played a lot of sidescrollers at this point, and it's highly engaging to have your method of traversal completely shifted in the way LAIKA shifts it. It reminds me, at times, of the way My Friend Pedro twists what "defensive gameplay" looks like; even at an intermediate skill level, good gameplay means becoming one with highly committal and violent STYLISHNESS. But to achieve that, you can't press buttons like you'd normally press them. You gotta press buttons like LAIKA wants you to press them. And that's rewarding to learn.    The levels themselves are quite distinct, and steadily extrapolate on the motorcycle-based movement. Traversing the world quickly, and farming for money + materials, involves an exercise in finding frequent opportunities to safely BACKFLIP (backflipping reloads your gun.) But the developers are aware of the value of those opportunities, and challenge you with tight jump timings, strange terrain, and intimidating enemy placements. Just blindly attempting backflips will get Laika killed, so you need to immerse yourself in the world and determine where to be confident and where to be cautious.    The tone of LAIKA is very somber. A post-apocalyptic story where characters in their different ways embody the pain of what has transpired (more or less, imperialism/colonialism doing their thing to the bitter end). This time, there is only sparing levity to be found through comedy or cuteness; instead, relief from the stressful world of the game is generally provided by beauty. The beauty of finding music that nourishes, of finding places where nature still flourishes (as much as it can in a sundered wasteland), and of connecting with people despite everything. Also the beauty of doing backflips on a dirtbike. LAIKA is unapologetically raw and it may scare some people off, but Brainwash Gang's vision is executed excellently.    Now, where LAIKA suffers most is a presence of bugs + jank, and a lack of overall accessibility.· I've encountered only one bug on the level of a softlock (essentially forced to quit to menu and reload the save), but there are a lot of cases of audio or visual elements continuing when they shouldn't, or dialogue cutting short before you can read it.· Overall presence of QoL (quality of life) features is pretty good, mostly marred by inconsistencies in where keyboard or mouse are useful in navigating menus.· If you have eyesight issues while gaming, LAIKA (at time of review) is probably highly strenuous. This is due to a combination of janky graphical effects (artistically amazing as the game may generally be), a dynamic camera that can make visual elements (like Laika herself) very small and unsteady, and occasional issues with overall color contrast.The devs are actively patching the game to fix issues like these, and I'm loving the game despite them, but they're worth mentioning.    I haven't finished the game yet, and I think it's important for Metroidvanias and open world games in particular to STICK THE LANDING. For the package to feel holistic... and it's doubly important for stories to stick the landing. But, LAIKA has the potential to do so in a big way. I'll check back in here when I finish my ride...    EDIT: I finished LAIKA, and it stuck the landing. It's a good game, thank you Brainwash Gang. <3

_childDocuments_.review: I love everything about this game, the artstyle is incredibly fitting, the combat and the movement are satisfying and, despite it being a difficult game, you will never feel it's difficulty is insurmountable. The story of the game is dark and depressing, yet incredibly satisfying, as any post-apocalyptic game story should be. The main character and side characters are in line with what you would expect from the world like that, yet all of them have their own unique charm to them. Majority of the characters are female and the game certainly has a feminist perspective to it, however it's in absolutely no way forced, pretentious or whatever you'd expect from the recent AAA games. Instead, this feminist perspective focuses on parent-child relations, motherhood and enduring in the world that was lost long ago. At the same time the story represents the only problem I have with the game, it leaves a little chance of there ever being a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad but it's lacking in many aspects. The gameplay doesn't really evolve much and a lack of meaningful upgrades makes it a bit bland by the end. However the music, art and overall story is good. More dialog would be nice, I had a few instances of the same conversation happening multiple times. _childDocuments_.review: Story, music, and gameplay are phenomenal, and only gets better as you get more upgrades and gear. This was so good in so many ways, but there are some shortcomings I experienced that frustrated me, which were just enough of an annoyance for me to feel the need to write review.There is a ton of side quests in this game that require you to go back into old areas and not tell you exactly where the thing you need is, like for example there was a sidequest that asked you to find root in a cave in an area where there seemingly are none, and there's even a sidequest where a guy looses his drumsticks and literally has no idea where they are, like you're supposed to scour the entire map looking for these things? On top of that, quest items don't spawn until you activate the quest, so you can't just stumble upon them early and have them in your inventory. The experience of thinking you know where the thing is, driving to where you think the thing is, then having to do the drive all the way back when you realise the thing is not there is a real pain, and useless filler in a game that doesn't need that kind of tedium to artificially increase the average playtime.To make matters worse, at the time of playing there are no guides on the internet for this game. I would say a solid 12 hours of my 18.6 hours on this game is just me backtracking and looking for things. The only saving grace is riding the motorcycle is fun, and when you do find a new area you haven't been to before it's a great feeling.Honestly, despite my frustration I could have easily overlooked this if it weren't for the ending and some missed story beats. Some of the following are nitpicky, some are a big issue imho;- The game starts off so strong but is never able to maintain that vibe, - If you get killed while talking to someone on the walkie-talkie, you just never get to hear that conversation ever again.- Minor gameplay thing, flipping your bike while you're spinning in mid-air stops your spin for some reason- Despite the birds spawning closer to the village as the story goes on, and everyone talking about how they are going to find the village eventually, they never find it. Missed foreshadowing IMHO- There is only one major event that unfolds after falling asleep in your house , and after that nothing interesting ever happens in the village.- There is a clip in the general/cinematic trailer of Laika in a sick solider outfit walking through a city with vendors, and people lying down on the street. This is an area you are immediately teleported to for some exposition, and then immediately teleported out of afterwards. Unfortunate that you can't go back there as it is probably the most interesting area in the game.- - Would absolutely have loved to see more animated cutscenes, the only problem is there are very few tense moments in the game where an animated cutscene could be applied.- Every single area in the game before a boss consists of "Oh, you want to do the cool thing? well, you have to do 3-4 tedious things before you can get to the cool thing!" It should all be cool thing.- Final boss is a bit easier than the boss before it, and isn't even half as cool as the 2nd boss - They never give you an opportunity to learn about the final boss through cutscenes, you never see him ordering an attack or doing anything evil, the moment you meet him is the moment you beat him. In that sense he just feels like a slightly harder enemy that invokes no emotional reaction, unlike finding - Ending was a 20 second cut scene with an immediate cut to the credits and no follow up. ENDING SPOILER: Imagine playing your favourite story-driven game and at the "point-of-no-return" you are immediately brought to the final boss, who is never talked about/you've never met before, kill him fairly easily, then you get a 20 second cutscene and the credits roll. I tried ignoring every shortcoming hoping that the ending would make it all worth it and come back together but it falls short as well. Which is such a shame, cause the story and gameplay had me captivated from the very beginning don't see this getting fixed in the future, would be happy to replay the game and change my review if it does.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Give me Mad Max, but give it a Native American influence with a killer soundtrack and breathtaking hand-drawn landscapes. I haven't had this much fun with a Metroidvania since Hollow Knight. Controls take some getting used to, but when it works, you feel like the coolest thing on the planet.--edit--I've played a bit more, and I'm still going to recommend this, but not as highly. The first 3 hours were polished and fantastic, but almost immediately after that, I ran into some really dissonant game design. Areas shrink and the game morphs into a precision platformer with Happy Wheels physics. Levels feel good only in one direction, which would be fine if there were shortcuts at the end to get you back to the start. Toeing the gas to gently bump your way backwards through a Sonic the Hedgehog level is exactly as much fun as it sounds, but never fear, the enemies all respawn behind you. I'm still playing, and still enjoying, but much less enthused than before.

I hate that there aren't "mixed" reviews but only GOOD or BAD and initially I was conflicted on what to say about this game but overall it was enjoyable enough to earn a YES from me.THE GOOD:- Game felt really good, hard enough with it's innovative gameplay.- I had a blast driving around, Sidequests were also good with bits of lore scattered around them.- Bosses weren't that hard and the last two were even pretty boring.- Music was top tier, probably the best part of the game followed by the Art Style.- Story wise it was really something... made me feel a roallercoaster of emotions, but to be fair i feel like the ending was rushed too much, I'm talking also about the Cutscenes.THE BAD:- Some sections were incredibly frustrating and boring.- you get the "cool Powers" too late in the game to even be able to enjoy them properly.- slow upgrading system, even with buffs your don't earn that much currency.- The Ending... this was the biggest letdown unfortunately, could've been way better without changing anything but adding that "something" that was needed in my opinionif you like Metroidvanias and want to try something different, this game is for you and it's worth it even at full price.

_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Expert writing, incredible art and worldbuilding, and unique mechanics. A story that is gripping and enthralling from start to finish, and when it was over, I found myself already starving for more. The movement mechanics with the bike are a bit tough to wrap your head around at the start, and a large portion of the arsenal feels a bit too niche to widely be useful, but those are really the only two criticisms I can find for a game that has clearly had so much passion poured into it.This game made me cry four times. 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: At first I didn't think the game would be for me. You die with one simple mistake and the game doesn't really mince that. However once I got past the beginning tutorial, the game started to really click with me. Getting a feel for how the bike handles, learning its momentum, blocking bullets with your bike and eventually getting your gun does a bit of time. If you can get past this, it all blends together amazingly while feeling really natural to play.That being said, while I love the darker and grim feeling of the story, it starts to feel kinda sparse after the first few hours. The game is rather on the short side, but I would've loved more interaction or moments in the story for things to grow. Instead it drip feeds you small interactions here and there to progress the story. Though once you reach about roughly the 3/4 mark, the game quickly races to a conclusion, the pacing rushing to resolve what should've felt like a major quest or and then pushing you toward the finale. Despite this what is there is rather nice, its dark and really makes you feel for Laika who remains stoic most of the time but deep down you can tell she's hurt but trying to stay strong for others. If you're a metroidvania fan who is looking for another game to get lost in, you're going to get very disappointed. Despite the marketing, the game doesn't really have much to encourage backtracking. Once you get the shotgun, very little is held back from the player. And what little left is just behind a quest you can do right after getting the shotgun. And the very very very little rest is a lategame upgrade thats locked almost right before the final area. There's not much of the 'Aha!' feeling you get from a usual metroidvania from discovering a way to get back a roadblock that stopped you earlier. There's also not that much reward besides weapon crafting materials which I will get into later. There's not much there to entertain a metroidvania fan. Sidequests give you little else besides a few cute interactions with npcs and a pittance of materials. Even close to the end-game, sidequests are never worth doing besides for seeing character interactions, giving you at most like 3 of a rare resource that you'd need 15 or 30 of for an upgrade, or 6 of a material you might already have well of a 100 in. This sounds harsh but sidequests are never difficult, usually just the standard fetch quest with the very rare combat trial. The interactions while small still give neat insight into a character or have a neat moment between them and Laika.Weapons...are a mixed bag.You will be using the revolver for 99% of the game. Besides for bosses, everything dies in a hit. The revolver is quick, accurate and easy. It will be a staple even into the end game.The shotgun is a vital part of your movement, and in fact some areas are locked off without it. The blast of it will give you a burst of momentum in the opposite direction, boosting you through the air to make tricky jumps or even correct yourself if you mess up a jump. Once unlocked it will always find a place in your arsenal for mobility mostly, and combat secondary.The rest are gimmicky.The machine gun is okay, the sniper rifle is awful and inaccurate, the crossbow requires you to reload it bolt by bolt, and the rocket launcher is impractical and slow with a high chance of killing you.On top of this all, the revolver and shotgun are cheap and easy to upgrade. The rest will require you to grind to do so and will still pale in usefulness.This all sounds rather terrible, right?Not really.The story is sparse but the game is so short that it doesn't feel as if it drags on with what you get from the story and short interactions with quests keeps it refreshing enough.Despite exploration being weak, the handling of the bike, the way you flow with its momentum, and the deadly rhythm of combat makes Laika feel like none other. The story while dark, doesn't dwell in over indulgent edginess. My biggest complaint being mostly "I want more" is kinda rooted in how short the game is, being roughly 10 hours if you focus on the story. Which honestly not that bad all things considered.  If you can stomach some gore and a bit of a rocky start, Laika is a great game

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game. The soundtrack, the story, visuals, little details — absolutely amazing. _childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is probably one of my favorite games of all time (also it's better with a controller) It's like Moto X3M as a metroidvania with guns. Both the story and the gameplay are amazing. The traversal is all done on a motorcycle that feels great to control. Just like any other metroidvania, you'll get tools throughout the game that help you get around. One of my favorite tools is the shotgun, which you can use to jump and redirect yourself in midair. Reloading is done through backflipping, and you have a parry which is recharged by doing frontflips. Also, you buy things using your enemies' viscera, which brings up a lot of questions about how viable that is realistically as a currency. Like where and how do you keep your money if it's made of guts that decompose and rot? The story follows Laika, a dog person living in the wasteland who has a daughter and a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mom. I think it's a wasteland because fascist birds dropped a big bomb and harvested all the resources. Also I think they might have evolved from humans or something? Anyways, Laika is cursed with the ability to respawn after dying and is thus the protector of her village from the fascist birds as the war begins to ramp up towards its conclusion. It's a pretty sad story that really got me to care about it. Music is also pretty good. Didn't think I'd like it at first, but it kind of grew on me. While riding around, you can find cassette tapes and manually play the songs you've unlocked, which is a really cool implementation on the music. The fictional character that made the music is named Beicoli, who appears in the game and shares a name with the real life artist, who actually made the music for this game in real life.All in all, Brainwash Gang kind of hit the nail on the head with this game, and then kept hammering. Highly recommend. Took about 20 hours to complete (review might say less 'cause it probably didn't count the offline steam deck hours.)
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely dark and unique Metroidvania romp. The bike handling + shooting is a welcome breath of fresh air. The moody soundtrack and gorgeous vistas really set the vibe. There is a bit more back tracking then I typically prefer, however the location's made each journey back a joy.Come for the tight 1 shot 1 kill action, stay for the moving story and characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing art and animations. Wonderful music. Well-crafted atmosphere and very interesting characters and world.Gameplay is frustrating, repetitive, and sluggish. I remember thinking I would not be able to keep up with how fast the gameplay trailers looked, but instead the bike feels like a bicycle being pedalled by an old lady. The backtracking is atrocious, and the movement is so clumsy in general that exploring the map never, ever feels good.Really sad, cause I really wanted to love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I give up. I've spent an hour driving through the first section of the game waiting for it to get good and it never has. It's just been more of that indie game trend of "difficulty via bad game design = good" that seems all too pervasive. The gameplay is supposed to consist of you riding around in a motorcycle and shooting the bad guys with a gun that has bullet time and reloads by backflipping. Sounds great on paper, but in practice balancing not being shot with actually shooting feels super awkward and I usually ended up overfixating on one or the other. Combine this with the fact that your  for some inexplicable reason only has TWO rounds in it, and it means in practice the game is encouraging you to stay back and farm for more bullets. Oh yeah, also why in Christ's name is PARRYING tied to a consumable? Does that not get rid of the entire skill factor in parrying? Awful design decision.The enemies aren't very good either. They stand in one area and fire a bullet that basically immediately flies towards you, with 100% precision, every time. Since your bike blocks bullets, you're intended to use that to block them as you take aim. So how does this work when there's multiple enemies at different heights? Simple; it doesn't. You once again are forced to take it slow. Take out enemies from a distance, because you can't realistically be expected to take them out normally due to the game's poorly thought-out mechanics.While the artstyle was fantastic, I also found the story lacking. I enjoyed the post-apocalyptic scenery, but I found a lot of the actual story beats were too much. At a certain point it just started feeling like a torture porn that was being needlessly edgy just for the sake of it. Also, and maybe this would have been addressed later in the game (God knows I'm not playing the game any longer to find out), but I can't help that the birds feel like extremely plain villains. I'm not asking for you to make us feel sympathy for the Nazis of course, but for God's sake we don't get even the slightest hint of even a single bird not being a bad person in the entire first section of the game. Keep in mind by the way that in-universe birds ARE just a race of people, not some hivemind species of hate and anguish that you'd think they are with how they seem to act. Again, maybe this is addressed later, but it almost feels like they flanderized the main villains, and that is not a good impression to make.And the artstyle almost makes it worse. I LOVE the artstyle, and I LOVE the animation within. But unfortunately, I have to live with the knowledge that this beautiful artstyle was wasted on a game without good game mechanics. I would LOVE to have seen this in a game with well thought-out gameplay and combat, but instead all of that hard work and effort is relegated to this and nothing else. It's a shame.All and all, for $20 I would recommend this if the game wasn't just SO unfun. This is not a cheap game, and I went in expecting much, much more out of it than I got. Sadly, I'll be refunding this game because it's not every day I get $20 of spending money, and I know I could spend it in much better ways than this game. Maybe next time.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. This game was such a nice surprise. Who knew I wanted an action game with light metroidvania elements and Trials controls!? The control scheme is a lot to learn at first, but once it starts clicking it's so satisfying. The art is incredible and the gameplay stays super fun throughout as you face new challenges. The one thing I would say is that if you're going to play this game, there are a few mechanics they don't make super clear. The first is that you use candles to fast travel but they only work at the BIG checkpoints, not the small ones. You have to hold down the interact button to access a menu where you can fast travel or change your loadout. The other thing that I didn't realize for a long time was that in the journal menu the main quest line is the one marked by a skull. I spent way too long chasing down sidequests for not much reward. By the time I finished this I was pretty ready to be done, but still enjoying it. So I'd say focus on the main quests for the most part. This is a fantastic gem that everyone should play. Get it!
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika's a 6 or 7/10. A good idea executed in a way that sucks a lot of the fun out of said idea.The story is engaging, depressing, and bloody as hell. I enjoyed that a lot, as well as some of the gorgeous locations, amazing animation especially after boss fights, and awesome soundtrack. If this game didn't look and sound as great as it does, I'd have refunded it.Exploring the world is tedious as hell. More interesting gameplay with weapon variety is locked behind that world exploration and a ton of side-questing. Combat difficulty comes down to boring, precise execution rather than exciting improvisation, as enemies will likely kill you and then you'll just pre-fire at where you know they will be. What could be exciting upgrades like the ability to deflect more shots is made inconvenient to use via the cooking system. The only fun upgrade you get comes very near the end of the game.Looks great on the Steam Deck though.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika's greatest strength is honestly in the sound design. The music, the sound effects, and its silence. How it all ties into the heart wrenching story is frankly inspirational. Everytime I hear the soundtrack, I can't help but tear up as I remember another detail about this game's story. Another memory of how it still, after making you think there was nothing left to fight for but one cute puppy, gives you such intense hope for the future.This game is masterful. I can't recommend it enough. It's a challenge, but not such a challenge that you can't push through it with some amount of dedication. If you have any interest in the game, do at least try the demo. It's fantastic.My only hope is that they put out the lyrics for all the game's music because I can't find that anywhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a unique blend of Trials and Metroidvania, a Motorvania. In a world which games with furry main characters are targeted for lovestruck tweens, this one is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dark twist that's grim, distressing, and utterly captivating. You'll find yourself bathed in the blood of enemies as you tear through them with bullets, collecting guts and gore as your currency. This is not a game for the faint-hearted.As someone not particularly keen on Metroidvanias due to a poor sense of direction and a disdain for retracing steps and mundane sidequests, Laika made me love all of that. The seamless integration of sidemissions next to your main objectives, coupled with the thrill of performing tricks on your bike, along with the challenge of equally annoying bosses, makes it a standout for beginners in the Metroidvania genre.Prepare to die—a lot—in mostly in the stupidest ways possible, like falling off your damn bike in a standstill or forgetting to land on your wheels. Thankfully, the developers are generous with their checkpoints, sparing you from tedious retracing. I always have a satisfying sense of accomplishment when I finally land that perfect triple barrel roll onto a wheelie, wiping out a horde of enemies that's more than the amount of bullets my gun can carry.Beicoli's soundtrack complements the barren wasteland setting beautifully. Despite the grim atmosphere, the story is deep and intriguing. Characters leave you wanting more, and the game strikes a perfect balance, keeping the lore mysterious but captivating. You won't get bored; you should definitely give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to beat the game before writing a review...But frankly I am devastated after the credits rolled.Ok...So I can't stress enough how good this game is. I think it's a game that everyone should play atleast once. The story is dark but so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good. If you want a good story this is a game for you. Music is amazing. It's still on loop on my spotify it's that good. It's calm, sad sometimes tense and somehow it fits so well with genocide you're committing. I can't explain it, it just works and I adore it.Gameplay is really satisfying. Yes it's hard but that's the point. You'll die a lot, but you'll learn with every death. It's the whole point of the game. Every combat is a puzzle that you need to figure out. Very satisfyingEdit: After 57h and after 30 hours of trying to beat the game without dying... Gameplay just got better. It's tough yes, but it is so satisfying to go through the whole thing memorizing and progression through this game with an outside challenge. Honestly I want a special challenge gamem mode. Pretty please.And the artstyle dear good. This game is a work of art for it's graphics. Backgrounds are just amazing, character designs are really good, and gore is somehow fitting where game just wants you to paint everything with that crimson blood.And every single thing I mentioned works together, creating one of the best experiences of 2023. It's cheap, buy it and enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: A prime example of the maturation of the indie scene and the creativity it can offer when devs roam away from traditional genre and subject combinations. Laika is short, sweet, and to the point, though perhaps too short overall for what's commonly expected of most games today. It's metroidvania aspects are also somewhat weak, with only three real abilities gating progression, the first two being mostly abandoned once you've used them to deal with the immediate utility-gate. It's also quite linear, and lacks optional exploration and gameplay. However, this is made up for by a very tight, very gripping story packed with emotion and mystery. You find yourself drawn into the tragedies, big and small, afflicting Laika and the people she lives with and meets. And the familiar world Laika inhabits is poked through with oddities. The skeletons of mountain sized creatures clash with modern feeling ruins and odd technology. The implications of a deeply troubled world rife with racial violence that ultimately culminated in a nuclear armageddon so long ago that nobody uses the names of the places they live anymore, just the purposes. And through it all is a distinct supernatural presence. And to accompany all of this is an absolutely first class soundtrack, tailor made to tug at your heartstrings. However, the cutscenes and the music get cut off several times throughout the game, damaging their impact somewhat.To conclude, Laika possesses creative, if simple gameplay, but a fascinating setting, an emotional story, and fantastic music make it worth your time. Like me, you'll probably be looking forward to a possible sequel one day.

_childDocuments_.review: I may not have the most time in this game so far, but I absolutely this is game is beautiful. It is heart wrenching as it is a blast to play and explore. My only frustration is during the boss fights visual clarity is sacrificed for spectacle. I can forgive it as respawning is quick and you are dropped at the start of the boss battle.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I am addicted to games with horribly bleak stories! I love being punched in the gut as a reward for experiencing the world and its many vibrant aspects! I love not realizing this until I've completed the game! I love Laika: Aged Through Blood because it less-so ages you in blood and more-so deepfries you in it. The gameplay and sound design are stellar, as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I don't see the praise for this overrated turkey. Aiming is randomly inconsistent.  Sometimes I can hit a small object across the map.  Other times I miss a shot with something an inch away with no clear feedback as to what is different between the two cases.  It is hard to tell which direction the bike is travelling especially during boss battles with the screen zoomed out.   I press the button to change direction and about 1/4 of the time it doesn't seem to work. All this leads to a frustrating mess. Story is interesting although a bit over the top.  I like the graphics style and world.  Music is great.  The inconsistencies of the controls and presentation just eventually lead me frustrated and angry.  Thumbs down for me.  Fail.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what this game did to me but its story made me incredibly emotionally invested for as long as I played and had it. The soundtrack really helps this game and despite its flaws being the bosses and the ending without an epilogue I would do it all over again if it was wiped from my mind.
