_childDocuments_.review: The Metal Slug games used to be one of my favorite genres that set the stage for my expectations of side scrolling shoot-em-ups.  I fear that Laika may have now have overshadowed my love of the classic genre by far and exceeding any expectations I had for this game.The story is gritty and doesnt hold back. The game play is solid and the progression is very well paced.  It doesnt let you explore the Overworld without first unlocking the next area through story progression but this limitation is understandable due to needing to keep the narrative moderately linear while giving the player limited choice.Though I'm only 4 hours into the game, I expect that it will keep surprising me with more heart wrenching plot twists and turns.  Great job Brainwash Gang! Hope to see more content in the Laika universe in the future!!

_childDocuments_.review: I wholeheartedly recommend Laika: Aged Through Blood. It is a metroidvania set in the post-apocalypse. It took me about 17 hours to finish and another 4 to 100%. You play as the titular character Laika trying to raise your daughter and not die while fighting against The Birds. Everything is done on a motorcycle. Combat, traversal, ability usage, all is tied to Laika's interaction with her motorcycle. I'm not usually a fan of metroidvanias, I always worry I'm going to miss an area, but I very much liked the gameplay.The game is very visceral, lots of blood and gore, which is interesting given its almost cutesy artstyle. Games like Darktide or Doom that involve a lot of viscera are more photorealistic, whereas Laika: Aged Through Blood is not. This doesn't detract from what it's trying to do. Backflipping in bullet time onto a group of unsuspecting birds, screen shading redder and redder with each subsequent kill feels more brutal than tearing the heart out of a Cacodemon or decapitating 7 Poxwalkers in a single swing. I do recommend the game based on its artstyle, and is HEAVILY boosted by the fact that you play as an anthro coyote.The story is fine, but what really shined was emotional impact. The game features several mature topics, death and torture of children, suicide, suicidal ideation, loss of innocence, alcoholism, etc. This is one of the very few games I have written reviews for and for good reason. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if it didn’t make me cry.In conclusion, Laika: Aged Through Blood deserves my wholehearted recommendation based on gameplay, visuals, and emotional experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The biking and gunplay feel really good together. Juggling bodies and blocking/reflecting shots by hurtling through the air makes Laika (and by extension you) feel like a serious badass. The cooking and upgrading doesn't feel out of place, as gathering what you need comes with the same loop as dealing with your foes. The monster designs are amazing and lead you to really wonder about the lore of the game's world, but that leads me to what I think is the game's weakest part: the story.The game's music, environment, and circumstances get you to the edge of intrigue and emotion but don't have that final push to leave an impact on your mind. We get bits of background information on the enemy Laika is dealing with, but it leaves more to be desired and can be missed very easily. At many critical story points, things go by so fast that you don't really attach to the events and characters in front of you. The game's story is very comparable to LISA: The Painful, if LISA was watered down a ton. Worst of all, things happen quicker and quicker the later into the story you get. While there is still plenty of side content, it's unfortunate the parts everyone will experience feel like a second thought.Ultimately, really interesting and fun game that I think could've done more with what it had. Very much worth buying and playing despite the story's pacing. Also feels like a perfect game to have a level editor system where you can share your creations with people.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Man, that ending sequence is something special. I would put this up there as one of the best stories in any metroidvania I've played. The wastelands are bleak, the birds who have invaded them cruel, but each night when you return to your home, slip into the bar for some blackjack, stand in front of the band and listen to their music, hand out news and items from the outside to the residents, and finally enter your house and go to sleep beside your daughter, there is a reassuring sense of peace. At least you have this one thing. At least you have her. This propels you to keep fighting, even when some of the game's less polished aspects rear their heads. The most consistent source of annoyance for me was difficulty telling where my character was facing midair. To reload a gun you have to do a backflip, but in the heat of combat, when you are blasting birds below, above, and alongside you, it quickly becomes disorienting. You also get progressively more covered in blood during gunfights, which makes it even more difficult to tell what way you are facing. By the end, muscle memory mostly covered for me, but there were still times when I would land on my head instead of my wheels.The other main annoyance I had while playing, which was really more of a disappointment, was enemy placement. There are some standout sections where it feels like enemies were placed deliberately to create a challenge when clearing them. Most of the time, however, they are just tossed into the room, and you can clear them with ease. There are also countless times where a single enemy appears in front of you, and it's trivial to kill them before they even get a chance to shoot. I didn't mind this because it did keep me on my toes during platforming-heavy sections, but it does feel a little pointless when you can kill half the enemies in the game before they even get a chance to shoot you.Some final positives: The auditory feedback when shooting and reloading is incredibly satisfying. Even though it didn't require much skill, continuously backflipping while spamming out shots to clear entire rooms never got dull. The air dash is also an incredibly fun ability, though it's unfortunate you don't get it until so late into the game. To be fair, it is pretty busted, so having it too early would completely change the combat. Lastly, the music is awesome. There's almost always something playing in the background, and the various tracks have a strong sense of cohesion while still remaining distinct from one another.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough game to review. I did enjoy it, but I had to use a mod to make it consistently enjoyable. Without the mod, it was difficult to the point of being frustrating and frustrating to the point of not being fun. You shouldn't have to mod a game to make it enjoyable. I don't suck at the game, it's just really hard and I don't have the time or patience to get good enough that I'm not dying over and over. Also, early in the game you are such a huge disadvantage that it feels unfair. This game desperately needs a difficulty setting and some tweaks of the mechanics. First the good. It is an interesting and original game. It is very polished and beautiful. The music isn't for me, but it's not bad and adds to the atmosphere of the game which is dark, but good. The controls feel tight and responsive. There are some great cutscenes. The story and dialog are pretty good and substantial for a video game, especially an indie game. There's a few rough translations, but nothing too bad. The combat is fun and engaging. When it works, it makes you feel a bad ass, flipping around blasting everyone. There's a lot to like.Now for the bad. Aside from the difficulty, there are a lot of really weird design decisions that contributed a lot of frustration for me:-The pacing is off. You won't fully unlock everything until just before the end of the game. And the later weapon upgrades are really expensive are require extensive backtracking, so you may not unlock all of them.-At least one of the abilities you unlock is completely useless other than to unlock part of the map. Actually two similar abilities, but they are used in slightly different ways in different parts of the map. This bugs me as not only is it a wasted opportunity, it makes me feel like the effort I put into unlocking the abilities was wasted.-In many cases, the upgrades aren't worth the hassle. Most of the weapons are designed in such a way that they're more trouble than they're worth. In particular, one weapon uses all its ammo regardless of how many bullets you fire. Another weapon is powerful, but it is really a pain to reload. In a game where reloading can be difficult or in some cases impossible, that's a big problem. I found myself just using the default pistol the vast majority of the time.-Level design is creative and interesting and maddening at the same time. Let me tell you, if you're a fan a backtracking, you're going to love this game. I can tolerate some backtracking, but this game really pushed me to my limits. Many of the levels are mazes, which I'm not a fan of. Not puzzles, but literal mazes where if you take the wrong turn you have to navigate the entire level all over again.-Unlocking music as a reward sounds like a good idea, but it means that in the first part of the game you're listening to the same three or four songs over and over and it gets old real fast. -The game has fast travel, but it's spaced out in a really weird way that severely limits its usefulness. In this game, it can be extra annoying because enemies respawn every time a new map loads (or you die), so if your path requires getting through a difficult cluster of enemies, fast travel often doesn't help. In any case, I'm glad there's something there, but it really doesn't save you much time. And with the amount of backtracking involved, it gets...you guessed it...irritating.Otherwise, the game's main mechanics are interesting and they can be fun, but they also contribute to the difficulty and frustration of the game. Reloading requires you to do a flip, but there's not always a ramp available and this puts you at risk of landing on your head, which kills you instantly. This bugged me probably the most. More on that later. The game isn't as cruel in its death mechanic as other games. You can usually find a respawn point not too far away and you lose about half your resources, but it's usually not too painful to get them back. That is, unless you lost them in an area with a million enemies. All in all I found it tolerable, though death punishment mechanics do grate on my nerves. So, the mechanic where you die if you flip your bike, I found really exasperating. I used to ride a motorcycle IRL and dropped it plenty of times and I'm not dead. In this game, if your head touches the ground, you're dead. What's more, your bike randomly backfires, giving you a little speed boost, but also causing your balance to go haywire. You'll die a lot just going straight. You get used to it kind of, but it's just another thing to add to the list. There is a setting that I think was added in the latest patch which gives you a little bit of a break on that front, but I didn't notice it until I was halfway through the game.If you're like me, you won't enjoy this game unless you mod the difficulty. If you're not lot me and have a lot of free time and patience to master a game's mechanics (and cat like reflexes), and/or enjoy dying 50 times in a row, you will probably enjoy this game without a mod. In any case, I still recommend you give it a shot. If it's too frustrating, try a mod. If it's still too frustrating, either refund it or be okay with a loss of at max $20.I'm only giving this a thumbs down because:a) The Steam hive mind overwhelmingly likes this game, so it doesn't need my endorsement andb) The average player who isn't a Dark Souls enthusiast type will most likely not enjoy this game without modding the difficulty.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I want to enjoy this game because it seems like it would have a fun story and the gameplay should be fun.However, the developers did not do a proper job of managing the difficulty level. There's no 'Balance' button to keep you from killing yourself in a required backflip or frontflip if you don't manage your movement. Time only slows down during aiming and that's timed with no way to cancel a shot so you can't use it to properly deal with hails of bullets. You only block bullets with your bike which, while it makes sense, will often leave you either getting shot trying to reload or getting crushed with the bike trying to block a bullet.There are areas where five or more birds can get shots at you with ease, they don't need time to aim and are most likely going to hit you. There's no Melee attack so if you fail to kill a bird and get close, you will die.Most of my deaths, and I got 100 in an hour and a half, were from hitting a platform while trying to do a flip or getting shot in one direction while blocking a shot from another.I want to see the creators of the game play and finish the game without using excessive time grinding out to get upgrades. Until then, I'm done.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely in my top 3 for 2023. Absolute gem. Difficult (frustratingly sometimes), but (mostly) fair. I think there are some late game pacing issues around some of the unlocks, but don't want to get into spoiler territory. Have already recommended to a few friends. Enjoy your time in the wastelands!
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I think the best recommendation I can give on this game is that it's the first one I've bothered to get all the achievements for in over ten years - because I was so engrossed by the gameplay, artwork and writing that I was already 90% of the way there by the time I hit credits. There are pain points here or there. You'll get fed up when you're trying to traverse the map and, half paying attention, wheelie so hard you slam your head into the ground. You learn pretty fast that the reward for most sidequests is a handful of crafting materials you could have gotten faster farming yourself. There is a *lot* of trekking back and forth to your fast travel points.But it's worth it. You really feel like you are mastering your bike, and within an hour or two you'll be doing frontflips with an inch of clearance off the ground while shooting across the screen. You'll find yourself picking up every sidequest so you can squeeze a few more sentences of lore out of NPCs and your journal. This game has collectible cassette tapes for background music and you will treasure each and every one of them as your faithful companions on those long drives through the lonely desert. This is not just a game with a fun motorcycle gimmick, this is a world that wants to pull you in, wants you to experience this beautiful nightmare of a setting. If you like metroidvanias, motorcycles, or world-building you can sink your teeth into, trust that this is best-in-class for all of the above and give Laika: Aged Through Blood a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Whoever thought mixing exitebike with a metroidvania was not right. Conceptually this is flawed, and even if it was not execution is horrible. Most of the time i had to fight the physics simply to get from A to B and that is without enemies. Fighting is terrible thanks to the reload mechanic, again spin to reload is a conceptually flawed thing Even then, Ghost and Goblins is hard, not because it was a well crafted difficult experience, like dark souls but because its creators lacked the ability and the know how to actually design for difficulty, it all came from poor aerial controls and weak weapons. this is similar, but on purpose.Despite being on a diet of souls like for the past decade or so this games show me that we have yet to grasp how to design for difficulty in mind and the overwhelming positive reviews also show me that we as a consumer still cannot tell the difference between difficulty stemming from poor mechanics and that coming from well crafted design choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: One of the rare games that I would call "Insanely good." It has a unique gameplay premise which doesn't get stale and introduces new mechanics, the boss fights are distinct from normal encounters, there's plenty of puzzles, collectibles, and sidequests, and the music and story mesh BEAUTIFULLY with the theme and each other. Every aspect of this game you can tell was handcrafted and polished. The only real criticisms you can make are 2 minor ones: Slight clarity issues, and slightly annoying fast travel system. However every other aspect of the game is near a 10/10 and it makes me wonder why this game isn't talked about more. Worth full price, solid 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game about 15 minutes ago, and I am currently in a completely incoherent state fueled by adrenaline and sadness. It has fun and satisfying gameplay, a captivating story, beautiful art, music and animation as well as art/music direction, great characters, bosses that are challenging (but not to the point where it isn't fun), and genuinely interesting and creative worldbuilding, which is all tied off with an absolutely top-notch soundtrack.Oh, and whatever the ♥♥♥♥ the writers for this game were on, I want some. NOW. They absolutely cooked with this ♥♥♥♥. Experiencing this game is basically like that scene in Ratatouille with Anton Ego eating the food and having a flashback to his childhood. The setting is a mix of post-apocalyptic with a bit of fantasy, and not only do the writers make great use of various writing techniques, they actually managed to turn the game mechanics into plot points. And ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, that ending.Its enough to leave the manliest of men broken down on the floor crying. Even just looking at the icon on my monitor makes that whole ending sequence along with the music replay again in my head. It was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beautiful.This game is a true work of art. If anyone comes to me saying "games aren't art" I'm going to show them this and their head will explode.If you still have doubts about it, play the demo. It is absolutely worth your time.TL;DR: This game left me crying like a little ♥♥♥♥♥ for the first time in years, and I will never emotionally recover. 10/10.Also, the banner art for this game goes hard as ♥♥♥♥. Just felt like I had to say that.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. The art style is fantastic. The animated cutscenes sprinkled throughout are such a treat. Absolutely beautiful soundtrack.  NPCs are fun and entertaining. The writing is wonderful, funny, and heartbreaking. There's a good variety in weapons, though keeping the pistol and shotgun in rotation feels almost necessary. Boss fights were always unique and interesting in concept (though not always in execution).Now, the things that I did not like. -The dash comes FAR too late in the game. For this to be a metroidvania that requires you to constantly backtrack, it takes FOREVER to go from area to area, especially when you aren't 100% sure where you need to be looking for whatever quest item is necessary. -The game desperately needs a better fast travel system. The fast travel points are oddly inconveniently placed. There are large parts of the map that are without them (especially central of the map) and you seem to have to go to those areas frequently. Not to mention the fast travel points ALSO cost a unique currency for much of the game. A currency that you have to gather in the world, and then make at the fast travel point, to use the fast travel point (stupid, STUPID).-The turn around function is not perfect. I don't know if it needed to be a shorter duration held but MANY of my deaths were because of thinking I had turned around only to ride in the same direction to my death.-The hook function is dicey at best and extremely difficult to use at its worst and made that whole boat area of the map feel like a pain to get through. It got so frustrating that I considered quitting the game. I'm glad I didn't, but that level of annoyance does not make for FUN. Having the dash there would have made it significantly easier to get through, but that was still 2/3 of the game away.-Upgrades cost FAR too much. Max upgrade costing 3000 of the currency when you typically get 5 (FIVE) for killing enemies is insane. Especially considering there's like 6 weapons and multiple bag upgrades. I didn't have it in me to grind it out just for achievement sake.-Nearly all the side quests were ridiculous fetch quests forcing you to go from corner to corner (again, the terrible fast travel does not help this) only to receive basic upgrade material you can easily get from respawnable chests. Make the side quests feel like they're worth doing. I don't care how interesting the NPCs are (and they are all quite varied) if I'm getting useless rewards in return for the quests.-I initially started this game on a controller, because that's how I expect to play a platformer, but I VERY quickly switched to mouse and keyboard. Godspeed to anyone that persevered with a controller, because having to move, aim, reload with the flips, use the hook, etc all on a controller feels absolutely awful (lol at console players).I really wish there had been another boss or area like the mines. That was one of the only times that the fact that you're on a motorbike felt fluid and fast. I understand that really isn't the crux of the game, but I still feel like it should have had a greater impact, rather than the start stop start stop precision gameplay.I know this is a review mostly focused on negatives, but the entire 30-35 hours I spent on this game (a bit of afk) I loved. But there is truly a laundry list of caveats. The game itself was never too difficult, but as I said above, I nearly quit from frustration over a poorly implemented core mechanic. Buy it full price, buy it on sale, just play this game. It really is beautiful. Just mind the bird ♥♥♥♥ that you will step in while playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: This game controls like ♥♥♥♥. OR rather, the one hit kills make this game control like ♥♥♥♥. Like I'm sure it controls pretty much how Trials controls but that makes the one-hit nature extremely untenable to me. I even enabled the "grace period" option and it was no different at all? Like I didn't notice any sort of grace period in anything related to crashes/deaths. I got up to where you get a pistol and have to escape I guess, but dying and being sent back to the check point after any sort of minor mistake made this completely unenjoyable for me. Shame, I think if it didn't start like or let you wipe out and have to get back on the bike or something I would enjoy it, but as it is now, it's completely unplayable.Nice art style though.

_childDocuments_.review: Just a really good, incredibly solid game. Do yourself a favor and pick this up. There is someone in this games story team that truly understands the tenants of telling a satisfying story. From the gameplay to the sidequests, everything about this game informs the arch of the story, incredibly strong.I will say the backtracking can get a bit tedious, but the quests that require it are so satisfying storywise, it didn't really bother me.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: This is the coolest metroidvania I have ever seen. Visuals are gorgeous, music is amazing. The story is painfully brutal and nihilistic, in a  great way. Its all very fitting with the feel of the world, being that life sucks ass a lot of the time. The gameplay is badass as hell, you backflip to reload and you can parry bullets back at the shooters, and there is a lot to explore that feel worthwhile.Some flaws with the game is that some parts of the main story feels like they go over too quickly, and should have been expanded on. It can also feel a little bit pointless to do sidequests since they don't really give you anything, but I found them enjoyable still if you just try to act as the character you are playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Not-quite-a-masterpiece. This game has interesting mechanics and feels fun to play. The music is memorable and a good fit, along with the atmosphere that comes together to tell a story worth experiencing for yourself. It isn't quite on the level of Hollow Knight or Ori, but with a different vibe and a different story, it's definitely worth the play if you enjoyed either of those games. I walked away from this game having thoroughly enjoyed it, but also feeling like if the developers had more to work with, they could have done even better. So I'm hoping they keep building up with stuff like this, more animation, more in-game "stuff" to do/collect, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot put into words how much i recommend everyone to play this game! It has been one of the best gaming expiriences recently for me, a fantastic piece of art that is criminally underrated! Especially at the asking price of 15 bucks there is no reason for you not to play it! Now for me personally it was a bit rough, i got some trouble dealing with emotions and this game will hit you in the feels every damn chance it gets so if you have trouble getting sad easily this is gonna be a hard journey. _childDocuments_.review: This game caught me totally off guard with how good it is.  At least for a certain kind of person,  a degenerate like me that takes getting killed personally and will take pleasure in the twenty plus tries it takes to make a perfect run through a section.  The controls are complicated and uncompromising,  it doesn't pull any punches with it's brutal storytelling,  and it asks a lot of you.  It feels like a game that was made with a vision and they stuck to it without worrying about simplifying things for broader appeal.  Once you click with it though,  your hands start doing what they need to without thinking about it and you're in for a treat.  A real masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I have ever played, which took me on a emotional journey, which I was not ready to take. The Story is really dark and depressing but is also quite beautiful at the same time and even got me crying once I got to the end. The gameplay was a bit hard at the beginning but once I mastered the bike movement and gunplay it was really fun to just cruise around the wastelands and shoot birds.There are plenty of missions and side quests, which offer rewards and some lore, which helped me to immerse myself into this game's world even more.And the music is just so beautiful, it really fits the game. It's both sad and beautiful at the same time and it just vibes so much.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game with a few flaws.This game has a super neat concept and amazing presentation, with a story that kept me interested for the whole runtime. However, the game does have some flaws. I experienced several bugs; dialogue repeating, bullets disappearing, etc. Although none of them were too game-breaking or difficult to deal with.My biggest issues with the game are some of the boss fights and level design.The first couple bosses were really good and fun to fight, but I found the rest of the bosses (except for the final boss) to be not as great. I found there is a lot of downtime where you are just slowly riding the motorcycle through the arena, waiting for the next phase of the boss so you can continue the fight. These sections aren't too big of a deal, but if you die on the final phase of the boss, you really realize how long they take to get through, they aren't difficult, just monotonous.As for the level design, I think the game excels in open areas with lots of ramps, or areas with lots of loops and jumps. However, I found the closed in areas where you are fighting lots of enemies in cramped spaces to be way less fun to play. You don't get the fun excitement of doing cool tricks and actions with the bike in a stage designed for it, it feels more like you're playing an area designed for a regular metroidvania, but you have to also worry about the bike.I still loved this game, it was super fun and unique, if a bit flawed. Definitely try the demo, I think it's more than enough to determine if you like the game, and the save data carries over to the main game, so there is really no reason to not start with the demo.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: TRY THE DEMO FIRST BEFORE PLAYING!!!Wonderful music, beautiful graphics, fun combat (if you can learn it) and a heavy story line; all things that make a great game and all things that Laika has. The first thing I'll say is that this game is not for the faint of heart. It gives you a brief warning about its contents upon startup, which I greatly appreciated. The motorcycle combat take a lot of getting used to, and that can throw a lot of people off, but once you understand how it works and start practicing, it gets much easier and actually begins to flow with the other aspects of gameplay very nicely. Again, this takes a lot of practice, but the better you get, the smoother it flows. It feels really rewarding when you manage to pull of a x6 kill streak without touching the ground. The art is stunning, and the music is as well. It is implemented in a very unique way, in the form of cassette tapes you can find around the world. Most are easy to come across. The story pulls no punches, which I appreciate.I have three main critiques.1) The bike upgrades are not very well implemented into the overall gameplay. One of them in particular you will only use in extremely specific circumstances and then never think of again.2) One specific story event felt disconnected from player choice and from the world itself, as your character apparently has the ability to travel to this place (that is only relevant for this event) but you yourself can't find it on the map and can never go back. Most of the event is like watching a cutscene, and I feel as though it could have been something better seeing as how it was a very important plot point.3) One major plot point surrounds you destroying something, and despite the characters acting like it is destroyed after you finish the quest, it's actually not????Overall, I absolutely loved this game despite the issues I have with it. Play the demo and see if you like it, too! It's a pretty good representation of what the rest of the game will be like.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very short and punchy and worth it to those who are a fans of metroidvania and looking for a good fleshed out experience. _childDocuments_.review: "Laika: Aged through Blood" is pretty darn unique, and it's hard to slot it neatly into any comparison. But, if I had to draw a parallel, it's like "Katana Zero" in an open-world setting with some quirky motorcycle combat.The connection to "Katana Zero" comes from the whole 'dying over and over, grinding through encounters' vibe. You'll face plenty of deaths, taking another shot at a challenge until you finally reach the next checkpoint. Now, let's talk about the combat; it's got its quirks. Reloading means doing a backflip, and a frontflip refreshes your parry, all while dodging and trying not to fall onto your face, as that is an instakill. It can get pretty annoying when you're dodging bullets, parrying like a champ, and then eat dirt because you couldn't nail a flip.However, when everything clicks, and you're parrying perfectly, sniping enemies, and blocking their shots, it's a satisfying rush.What really stands out in "Laika" are the cutscenes and the music. They're top-notch and add a ton of value. The combat is decent but can be a bit unwieldy.Now, here's the curveball – there are these moments where you have to do some platforming on a motorbike. To be honest, it feels out of place and doesn't jive well with the rest of the game.All things considered, Laika is an enjoyable ride. It's not a game-changer, but it's a load of fun, quirks and all.Upon completing Laika, my initial impressions have undergone some adjustments ( after all they were limited to the first 4 hours of gameplay). While I still recommend Laika, my overall experience is not without its criticisms.Laika undeniably excels in its storytelling, artistic presentation, and music. However, other aspects of the game are ranging from decent to problematic.Combat:The combat closely resembles Katana Zero, requiring the player to repeat stage sections until they are successful by chance. This repetitive nature can be frustrating, especially when a missed shot results in death and having to restart an annoying section. Notably, the probably best upgrade in the game only gets unlocked near the game's conclusion with the introduction of an ability that enhances both combat and traversal.Bosses:Boss fights, excluding the initial two, tend to be tedious and somewhat irritating. For instance, one boss battle involves a vertical sidescrolling format with combat sections interspersed. The challenge arises from dodging projectiles and waiting for the boss's vulnerable point to appear. Some boss fights become particularly frustrating due to issues with motorbike controls, adding an unwelcome layer of difficulty.Quests:Side quests are mixed in design, ranging from decent to poorly thought out. While some quests offer engaging challenges in specific areas, others involve mundane tasks like buying quest items from wandering merchants. The "Wastelanders" quests, in particular, lack inspiration, requiring players to reunite scattered musicians with nearly identical quest structures.Each on of these Wastelanders quest, 6 overall, have the EXACT SAME structure.-Encounter Wastelander-Receive their Quest-Buy their Item from a Wandering merchant-Return to the Wastelander-Give them the item and finish the questExploration:The game features numerous areas but offers few fast travel locations, resulting in extensive travel to reach quest locations and resources. This repetitive travel becomes tedious and may deter players from fully enjoying the exploration aspect, even more so, considering you will be forced to do it for quests. The excessive backtracking, especially for resource gathering, at some point made me groan when I had to enter an area for the fifth time and go there the long route because it lacks fast travel locations.Side Content:The limited side content consists of Blackjack and cooking. While Blackjack proves mundane, cooking lacks meaningful impact due to the scarcity of cooking spots. You will never have a boss encounter or a section in which you say that "X"-Buff would help here, simply because the cooking spots are so rare. A different approach to cooking would have made way more sense. Have it like in Bloodstained, whereas cooking a dish for the first time provides the player with a small permanent buff.Laika is still mostly a fun ride, primarily attributed to its outstanding soundtrack, captivating art, and compelling narrative. The game's strengths are for the most part in the initial and concluding hours, with a challenging and engaging experience despite occasional frustrations. It would have made way more sense for the developers to cut down the needed resources and tedious quests. Even if it makes the game shorter, it will leave the player with mostly good afterthoughts.The positive aspects, particularly the story, music, and challenge, make Laika a worthwhile experience nonetheless, although I recommend to wait for a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a near-Hades-caliber game. Do not miss it. It's incredibly powerful. This game has changed how I view games.The character design, the worldbuilding, the atmosphere, all phenomenal.  Furthermore, the pacing of exposition and the way the narrative is handled is just spectacular. As a gamedev and writer myself, it's so refreshing to experience a world without hamfisted, unnatural spoonfeedings of lore. Instead, we're offered glimpses of a world that does not exist to serve or inform the player. It makes exploring the world addictive and makes the emotional, often gut-wrenching revelations about the characters and world feel organic and genuine. At the start, I was also very vocal about bad writing choices they'd made to some friends. And the control scheme is unusual and was initially very frustrating. But honestly, I feel almost ashamed of my initial jaded assumptions, because it has become clear now that every single thing I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about in my first hour of playtime was done intentionally and for great effect. Just keep playing this game.I'm going to mourn when I finish this game and can't experience more of these characters' lives any longer.

_childDocuments_.review: Geniunely one of the best of the genre. The art is so beautiful that I avoid fast-travelling just to enjoy it, as well as the music, which comes in the form of cassettes that you can pick and choose whenever you want, cheers to the artists!! _childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: A game that tackles some extremely serious subjects with an incredible amount of grace and respect, a metroidvania about motherhood, a woman's coming of age, and a hell of an apocalyptic story on top of it all with a beautiful aesthetic combined with an absolutely top notch soundtrack. In a year of amazing games, Laika stands out even among them as one of the best I've ever played. A must-play.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Steam Deck specific review. This game is a headache. Not overall though, its music is legit incredible along with its atmosphere. Story telling isn't bad either. The actual gameplay design, or ideas, are quite good. It's just the execution and controls that need work. It all feels very clunky or unnatural even 6 hours in. You can "get used" to the controls but getting used to something doesn't excuse the fact that something is heavily flawed.This game expects you to land your bike after performing multiple actions in mid-air. Normally this would be fine, and maybe it is fine on a bigger screen, but it's genuinely annoying on Steam Deck's small screen. The game zooms out during combat, making it hard to see what position your bike is in. Often I feel like I'm failing an encounter not because of a mistake I made, but because the game fails at giving me the right information. I wish I could mess with settings and not zoom out so much. It's controller sensitivity is also wonky, making precise aiming feel not-so-great. However this might also be a Steam Deck specific issue.The one-hit-kill mechanic is probably a love or hate thing. I personally enjoy it. While you can die very easily and with one mistake, enemies also die in one shot. This makes for compelling gameplay and makes you feel like a badass when you finally execute your attacks or parries perfectly. Reminds me of a Ghostrunner. I'll probably complete this game because of the positive things I've mentioned, but I'll continue to roll my eyes at all the design flaws.7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: This Game needs to be played by more people. It genuinely and I mean it has one of the best stories in the Metroidvania genre, So Many complex characters and lore to dig into plus the soundtrack. The Soundtrack goes hard and I enjoy it dearly.My only cons are the Boss fights, The third act and the special metals being easy to buy instead of find,Besides that, the game was a easy 100% I just had to endure emotional damage to get it.I'd give it a 9.5/10 its closer to a 10 than a 9.Every Wastelander needs therapy Badly

_childDocuments_.review: Plays great. The music is to die for. Release the ost, I'll buy it day 1!Whatever, you already knew it. I'm here to tell you about the writing. How is it so good! Just from a few lines of dialogue! Every now and then the protagonist talks to the dead, someone she used to know, and it's such a treat every time. Bonus points for all game mechanics making sense within the lore.I'm gonna find out who wrote this and check out all their other games.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Mad Max: Furry RoadThat joke out of the way: Laika is one of the most fascinating titles I've played in recent years, a game that makes up in soul what it lacks in perfection.Everywhere you look, you can see the love and passion that went into its making. Gameplay, visuals, story and music echo each other, and the brutality of the action finds itself woven into a narrative about desperate survival, itself framed inside the hand-drawn beauty of a desolate wasteland, all carried by the soft melody of an absolutely haunting soundtrack.And what a soundtrack it is. The composer and singer's name is Beícoli, and I think she's earned her place among indie game giants like Darren Korb (Hades) or Andrew Prahlow (Outer Wilds). I hope we'll get to hear more of her work in the future.All in all, Laika isn't without flaws: the final confrontation is a bit underwhelming, and I think overall the game would have benefited from a more linear and focused storyline, rather than a quest-based design that lets players choose their own path also but hampers the sense of general progression. Thankfully, it only takes a few lines of well-written dialogue to make you instantly invested into Laika's world, characters, and story.Laika is not a perfect game, but it's a game I'll remember.

_childDocuments_.review: Been a long time since I loved a game as much as this one, I love everything about this game from the rich story and the music that perfectly fits the game, I would have paid more for it. This game is a shiny example of what the gaming community is missing, the passion poured into this game is amazing. I fully believe this game deserves game of the year. It is hard and I love it challenges you, but most of the time you are you own enemy in playing it. So I say thank you to all who worked on this game cause I was losing faith in the game company and seeing this has giving me hope, hope company will start to care again about their games and not money, hope that we wont continue the many years of disappointing and just okay game games.(update) I see that a lot of the neg reviews for this game is that it is too hard, guess those people never grew up in the years of NES and SNES with games like sliver surfer and Battle toads.

_childDocuments_.review: -Presentation is EVERYTHING-A motorcycle physics metroidvania is a decent gameplay base for a short game. Using guns to slow down time or to thrust our bike forward is great, and there's potential to revisit this concept on a sequel if they do one (long range weapons to hit specific spots, breaking shields with machine-gun fire rate?)The gameplay's fine. The presentation? Is EXCELLENT. Great 2D Animation, powerful narrative, and attention to story beats that aren't gameplay-heavy, but do wonders fot the story. Collecting the soundtrack piece by piece was a smart move, i paid attention to every new track i bought or unlocked.I couldn't help but do every side-quest, every tiny detail i could absorb. Do you want a full game that you can complete in like a week? Get LAIKA.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I hate metroidvanias. I would've nominated this for GOTY if I played it earlier. Incredible gameplay, even better story. I'm not very emotional, and this game nearly brought me to tears IN THE INTRO.Roughest part of the game is getting past the skill floor, so here's a few tips from my first playthrough.1: USE MOUSE AND KEYBOARD2: Don't upgrade weapon slots. Just use one gun you're comfortable with and the gun you build for a quest. My biggest mistake was getting another weapon slot, which killed all of my weapon swap muscle memory. 3: Your cursor shows what direction your head is pointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions;Laika is very fun. It's got all the best (and worst) aspects of the metroidvania genre when it comes to progression and map design, the movement and the combat are fluid and responsive. Easy to learn, hard to master, all that jazz. I  the art direction, even if the environments can be a little difficult to read at times, and a special commendation goes to the soundtrack, it fits the tone of the game perfectly. Playing In The Sun has burrowed its way into my brain, and I'm sure the rest of the cassette tape collection will follow suit.One flaw that I find rather critical and worth pointing out is that the game doesn't feel that well-optimised. Now, I haven't got the best rig out there, but I have been able to hit 60+ fps just fine for most of the game, even during hectic combat, but depending on the location and the scenario, the game can dip all the way to 20-30 fps seemingly at random (no stutters, at least). Some screens ran fine except for very specific parts even when nothing was happening in them, it all feels... uneven.I'm hoping future patches will include more framerate improvements, but even at the moment it's not unplayable.

_childDocuments_.review: This game captured the feel of a metroidvania perfectly. The music combined with the style and look of the world makes this world have the exact feeling that the developers were going for when designing the game. After beating this game and taking a couple months of hindsight I have seen some issues.The character development of the game is extremely lacklustre where you will often meet a character and in the next 15 mins they die, I am not even kidding it became an expected thing I kept noticing after the second area, whether this was intentional or not, it makes it feel like the people you meet are just bullets in a firing range, they are shot and introduced but after that you dont worry about them. Even worse is that your character will mention something once then have a short talk and then they are never mentioned again no sign of remembrance or care for the lose off life she just continues like nothing had changed. My other gripe with the game is that it felt way to structured and the mechanics of each areas was often never repeated anywhere else. I am going to use an example of a game like little big  planet three even with all its problems it gave one big show down at the end that allowed you to show off everything you had learned in previous areas of the game. Laika fails to do that having in my own opinion one of the most lacking final boss areas and fights of the entire game. youve met characters with better motives then this final boss throughout that game.one last final thing, this is not a game about being cool and riding a motorcycle its about going through puberty and having a period. thats it the whole game stems from something that girls go through every month. thats literally it, yes you fight in a war to save a village and yes you fight the big bad but if you didnt have a perioid you would be dead

_childDocuments_.review: I hesitate to refer to Laika: Aged Through Blood as a metroidvania, at least, not in the traditional sense; the game offers you very clear quests marked through a journal, and only contains, if I remember correctly, three items which change the way you progress throughout the world.This does not mean, however, that Laika is a bad game; my first blind playthrough lasted a little under 13 hours, which consisted of doing all the side quests I ran into (Though I do not think I did all of them) and exploring liberally; which, while not a supremely long amount of time, was thoroughly enjoyable all the way throughout.Laika isn't going to change your life, its not a genre defining game; neither the story nor the game play do anything all that extraordinary; what Laika is, however, is a polished game with an enjoyable story and world, that doesn't waste your time, which, at least to me, makes it worth every penny I spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a bittersweet tale from start to finish. It is a bleak, brutal and desolate world and you can see and feel it in everything you come across. From your own small tribe clinging desperately to life, to the bone-dry wastes, to the bullet-blasted ruins of yesteryears' wars, to even the chief antagonists' lot in life.Laika offers a heart-wrenching story with its gameplay that is heavily weighed towards precision in movement and in combat. You have no health, but neither do your enemies: everything except bosses die in one hit, so make every single shot count. You have a small arsenal of weapons, up to six if you find every single blueprint, though the game only really requires the revolver you begin the game with, and the shotgun you must unlock to progress. Notice, however, that your weapons generally have 1-4 shots loaded, depending on their upgrade level.Every weapon has four levels, with two-through-four giving small but important bonuses, such as increasing the magazine capacity of your weapon by 1, or giving you a more generous reload angle for faster and easier reloading. Though you will have to look around for materials to upgrade these items with, do not sleep on them. Naturally, you can carry between two and four weapons at a time, depending on how many times you upgrade your weapon bandolier.When it comes to the movement, if you have played any 2D game where you ride a motorbike, the movement should feel very familiar. You have acceleration, and you tilt your bike backwards and forwards to wheelie, or if in midair, flip the bike around. Flipping is extremely important for this game: backflipping is the only way for you to reload your active weapon, and front flipping refills your parry. Parry is your only active defense against a bullet careening towards Laika, though the timing can be very tight and sometimes frustratingly difficult to get right.The art and the music are some of the best Laika has to offer. You will be accompanied by a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack throughout the entire game as you ride through a wasteland that feels hand painted. In the bone-dry wastes, there is very little color: mostly the bleached white of dry bones, ashen grey of dead trees and the deep red of the blood you spill. Weapons sound punchy, the bike roars pleasantly and the wind howls to accompany the wistful soundtrack that accompanies you. There are a number of songs, though at first you only have a few cassette tapes and the same songs loop over and over. Later, as you explore and find cassette tapes, the repertoire of songs naturally expands. Also, back at your village, should you find musicians to play, you will hear them play at nights.Laika is an excellent showing, though it is not entirely without flaws. The most frustrating part is how finicky the bike occasionally feels to control. If you do not make a perfect landing and your attention wanders for a split second, you may find yourself unexpectedly dying because Laika's back briefly touches the ground, or because a pixel touched a surface that is considered ground.At times there are sudden difficulty spikes that force you to retry a sequence over and over again until you eventually master it and clear the stage. Thankfully Laika is very generous with checkpoints scattered everywhere so you never lose much progress, but at times it is aggravating to die in the same spot a dozen times or so. When I finished the game, I had 328 deaths total.The pacing of the game feels a little wonky. Though I ended up spending 20 hours playing the game, I did just about everything there was to do in the game, save for getting every single weapon upgrade. There are only three or four main story quests and they are over sooner than you might expect. That leaves the side content to fill the rest of the runtime, and while that is not a bad thing necessarily, it left the main story feeling a little short and bare-bones. Likewise for the animated cutscenes that are sparingly sprinkled here and there during the game; they are short and sweet and carry the emotion of the scene excellently, but they feel a little rushed, as though they were sped up or otherwise in a hurry.Finally, the weapons that you unlock feel largely superfluous. The crossbow is a shotgun that takes far too long to reload without investing tons of resources into it. The machine gun blasts its entire magazine in one go, so long as you hold down the trigger; if you stop, you might fire a single round at the cost of 5 or more, yet it does not excel better than the starting revolver. The sniper is effectively a second revolver that seemingly offers a slightly stronger bullet time effect, but not sure if anything else beyond that. And lastly, the rocket launcher arrives far too late in the game to be of much use, though you can use it to blow up the shielded machinegunners risk-free. It is a shame that most of the weapons are not very good at their jobs, so you can easily get through the game with just the revolver and the shotgun.Finally, what happened to all the men? There are only a small handful of men anywhere and most of them are either crazy or crippled. My only explanation is that most of them have died in the fighting of the past, but that leaves the game feeling strangely packed with almost exclusively women who never really even reference them. While this doesn't really impact the game much, it was something I couldn't stop noticing. Especially in a world as harsh as Laika's, you would expect to see fathers, brothers and husbands trying their damnedest to help their tribe and their family survive.Laika is a beautiful game that is close to perfection in many aspects. The story holds no punches and many of the stories end in the only way they could end in a world as harsh and brutal as Laika's. It is a story well worth experiencing, even if the gameplay can feel like a real struggle at times. It holds a similar place in my recommendations as Dust: An Elysian Tail, which is exceptionally high praise.

_childDocuments_.review: Close to one of the top 10 games I've ever played.  The game is super unique, has an insane utilization of simple controls, makes you actually care about crafting and food, has a very bold plot that feels personal, lots of colorful characters and quests, great visuals, nice little cinematics, and it has a wonderful soundtrack that feels almost contrary to the gameplay but actually transforms a high octane adventure into a contemplative, vibe.  You can absolutely annihilate enemies in this game especially after you've prepared and eaten.  But the game always requires focus and mastery no matter what you're fighting so when you do indulge in those moments it feels like you're a total god.It can be a little rough around the edges, I think they should have made reloads 340 degrees instead of 360 just cuz how some elevations work and there's a couple of camera issues I noticed a few times.  The bosses are not very well done.  There is a little more polish that could have been done in the backtracking, where it can feel like the game is wasting your time, especially if you didn't die so the enemies that you would have backtracked to aren't there.  It felt very friendly with checkpoints, fully aware of how difficult the game can be.  If the bosses were fantastic, this would be a top 3 game of all time for me even with the other issues just because the whole package ends up being so good.

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged through Blood has constructed a world that is utterly believable with characters that are written with a passion without compare. _childDocuments_.review: A great concept hampered by patchwork execution.This is more of a mixed recommendation, but I'm going with a thumbs up because the core gameplay is original enough to be worth a look. Combining Trials-style 2D biking with guns, bullet time, parries, air dashes, and backflips to reload your weapons is awesome. Moving Laika around has all the weight and momentum you'd expect of driving a clunky motorcycle around a Mad Max wasteland of the future, but in mastering it, you can chain together a series of actions that make you feel invincible. You're not just fighting the enemies, but the angle of your motorcycle, the speed of your jumps, the rounds left in your weapon, and the number of parries you have left to use. It's a lot to manage at first, which makes success all the more satisfying when you finally get the hang of it.This combined with a stylish aesthetic, some lovely animated vignettes, and a beautifully moody soundtrack are Laika's greatest strengths. It was an ambitious idea to meld this type of gameplay with a metroidvania-style world, something I can honestly say I've never seen done before, and unfortunately... it kind of doesn't work. That's not to the say the concept is inherently flawed, but I was pestered with constant annoyances that made me feel like this was the devs' first crack at an idea that could be done much better with a few revisions.Laika feels like adopts a ton of ideas from other metroidvanias without much concern for how well they fit its gameplay style. The biggest issue I ran into was the exploration. Despite having an open world, this is the kind of game that directs you everywhere with quests, the prerequisites for which don't spawn until you accept a blue checkmark from an NPC. You aren't rewarded for taking the initiative and getting yourself lost in the world, you're directed from point A to point B in a fashion that makes me wonder why this wasn't just a linear action game. There are upgrade and cooking materials to collect if you go a little off the beaten path, but the game's weapon upgrades are more limited by your universal currency than the items you find through exploration, and I never found it necessary to engage with the cooking system at all. While moving along linear paths and fighting enemies feels great, navigating complex environments and backtracking to pick up items that roll away from you often feels like a cumbersome chore.You only get one real movement upgrade all game, and it comes right at the end. This was the only point at which exploration actually felt rewarding to me, as the movement ability is pretty darn fun and completely changes the way you interact with the world. I can only imagine how cool it would've been to get more upgrades that let you fine-tune your mobility and pull off more crazy stuff in combat while simultaneously letting you access new areas. Every time I revisited areas prior to this, I felt like I was punished for trying to explore by hitting dead ends. The game's quests, similarly, feel like fluff that usually involves nothing more than reaching a spot on a map you've already explored before returning to the questgiver.There are some tedious bosses that are poorly designed around the game's movement, but also some fun ones that take advantage of it. Area maps need to be purchased from a vendor, but he almost always shows up right at the beginning of zones, rendering the process largely pointless. You get a bunch of different weapons to play with, but the default pistol is better than all of them in 90% of situations. Enemies are distinct, but the visual noise during combat is sometimes problematic. I could sit here listing minor annoyances that bugged me all day, but I don't want to be overcritical of a game I still enjoyed enough to complete. None of these issues are gamebreaking at the end of the day, they just feel like a big ball of fumbles that stifle Laika's core strengths.Finally, there's the story, which I feel is a fairly mixed bag as well. The pacing is sometimes jarring and intrusive, with too much time spent on too little substance followed by glossing over major developments that demand room to breathe. The main characters are sympathetic, and Laika's relationships with her mother and daughter are engaging ones, but the supporting cast are spread a bit thin, and the game's unsettlingly grimdark tone doesn't feel like it gets explored in any real depth beyond the basic emotional yank of getting upset about bad things happening to people.There's a lot of ambition and passion here, but the execution is rough. It's a whole lot of ideas pulled from similar games without the necessary tweaks to make them fit the unique gameplay style. I feel like with some relatively simple changes, I could've loved Laika, but it wound up being a bit of a 6/10 for me. I hope the devs try something like this again with more focus on polishing up the smaller details in the future, because it has a lot of potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: This was one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had. Initially a simple bike game, the depht of the story, characters and world blew my mind. Everything has a meaning, a porpouse and a cool background. Everything is alive and interesting. The story is captivating, tragic, dramatic, fun to be part of, with an ending that got me tears. And with "a simple bike game", I don't mean it's bad! The gameplay is just amazing to play, and keeps getting better at each new upgrade, each new weapon discovered, each new bike upgrade. And the Level Design is just as fun, I was always interested in doing some more side quests so I could explore the map with my new powers. Plus, the collectables, man... the songs are just one of the best soundtracks I've heard on a game. 10/10, this is a masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: Laika: Aged Through Blood

_childDocuments_.review: I will say that it is fantastic that we have a 2D Metroidvania that plays uniquely for once in our lives, thanks to the motorcycle and the level design accompanying it. I just don't think that the overall level design and progression suits the backtracking that a Metroidvania calls for; I often dreaded having to go to a location because it meant doing the same jumps, killing the same enemies (or worse!), and doing everything the same while the game-changing power-ups are few and far between to change up the core traversal.I hope this inspires more motorcycle Metroidvanias in the future and tweak the overall design.

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a game that lives and dies on it's ability to provide an insane amount of checkpoints to the player in order to lessen frustration, and it falls into a category of games that I would call an 'always on' sort of game.An 'always on' game, to me, is a game that requires concentration or is difficult for long periods of without any real break or pause. Games like Rusted Moss and CrossCode for example fall into this category of game for me. You will die a significant amount of times for the smallest thing, and some of these can feel extremely bad as well. The game provides a TON of checkpoints, though, and as another user pointed out it can feel a bit like Katana Zero where you will restart a section over and over repeatedly until you get your clean run. I don't consider these sorts of things a negative, but a cautionary note for players looking for a more traditional, perhaps relaxed, exploratory Metroidvania experience. With that out of the way. Laika's art, music, animation, and overall design are superb. It is easy to recommend to people as long as they understand what they're getting into. It's a unique experience that's kept me pretty engaged with it's overall visual style and story. Strongly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Laika: Aged Through Blood is a game that is hard to call any one thing, but might be best summarized by the name of the first mission: Rage & Sorrow. It's a game in which sorrow and rage pervade even the happiest moments.It's a game about womanhood, and wanting better for the generations that come after us even while we recognize how truly bleak the future seems.It's a game about somehow finding hope in hopelessness.It's one of the most emotionally taxing games I've ever played, and from a pure gameplay perspective I don't think I have ever encountered a game that so perfectly balances challenge and a call for finesse. The game asks you not just to play, but to dance.There is literally nothing else like this game. I have never come across a game so unflinching in what subjects it is willing to approach to achieve its vision.This is one of the best games I have ever played, and one of the most difficult to recommend. It's a hard experience. I strongly recommend paying attention to the content warnings.But if you are up for it, you'll find one of the most engaging pieces of media I have encountered.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo first, it made me cry. Naturally I had to buy it!Laika: Aged Through Blood is a spectacular game, perhaps not for a general audience. If you enjoy challenging, visually stunning games with heart wrenching stories then It may be for you! I am not talented in platformers, metroidvanias, or even the flash game Happy Wheels, but the story alone followed me even away from the PC. I was obsessed. I wanted to know what would happen to this motorcycle driving coyote mom and her loved ones! Laika is more than just a typical "Badass motorcycle riding woman" trope. Her character has depth and while you'll be carrying out excessive violence on her behalf, she's reluctantly carrying out her role as her tribe's defender. She's just as pained and uncertain of her future, and just wants to live a life of peace as much as any other poor critter out in the wastes.The soundtrack is perfect. You wouldn't think that Soft Folk Pop would be the tracks you'd want playing while doing flips and firing a revolver, but its irrevocably the best fit for this game. The artists even exists in-game, with characters opinions differing on them. Heck, even the respawn mechanic is a canon aspect in-game too. A few notes:The game is Dark: If you are sensitive to certain dark aspects of humanity, just be aware that this game wont shy away from showing you them. That said, you'll find brief moments of beauty and hope within the darkest moments, from amusing moments of childhood innocence and mother/daughter bonding, to bittersweet elegies. Be prepared to die. A lot.  Esepecially early on, encounters are more like puzzles for you to figure out than flowy, on-the-fly vehicular combat. It's a bit frustrating, but by the time you master the controls and mechanics, things will be more smooth. Upgrades are sparse: Some side quests will be essential for story progression, namely Maya, Shaza, and the Hectist's. Do note, some weapons and abilities may be used in clever ways. Also, the game doesn't tell you, but tapping the gas repeatedly can occasionally give your character a speed boost. I wish it was more consistent however.. Some cons:This game really should have a gentler difficulty mode, I'd love to see this story told to even more folks but I'm afraid most will be deterred or unable to see its entirety!Boss fights can be lackluster. A caterpillar Made of Sadness and the Hundered Hungry Beaks were the better two!  I loved how flowy they both were. The others are more stationary and are bullet hells and test your focus a little too much, it can be frustrating.Overall, if you were interested enough to read this entirely, I'd recommend giving it a shot, or at least the demo if it's still up!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is nice and freshens up the normal sidescroller metroidvania type of game experience with the biker twist, which alone makes it worth the buck for me.BUT you should know beforehand that the game is not really long and has a few design issues which are not really thought through.This review is also more about the bad things then the good cause bad things mark themselves more in your brain then good.  I needed around 20 hours to complete the story and have no open sidequests left, and also collected almost all the things which you do not need to farm a lot for. I guess you could complete it if you only focus on the story in around 10 to 12 hours or even shorter. (could spoil the general story experience a bit) The story is a depressing adventure which is interesting, but after a few hours, you notice that the game really wants to make you feel depressed and sad about the lives the characters live, which will affect you for a few characters, but for most of them not. This is just my experience, but it made the story a bit annoying and predictable for me because I don't really expect anything good happening to the characters I meet , which in conclusion makes you not really invest much emotion in the people you meet. Now to the MC of the story . The story of those characters is really nice . SO AMAZING! The art and music are so nice and really made the experience a lot better. The music was amazing and really matched the style and setting of the game and also made the exploring of the world more enjoyable. The art was also amazing; it wasn't top-notch but almost there. But the combination of the music and art made the atmosphere and feeling of the game insane. It really gave you the feeling of a lone rider who does what must be done, and that's all I wanted from it. I didn't have any crazy bugs or such; the only thing I had was that the game would drop fps to 50 or lower when I was in a menu and streamed the game with Discord at the same time, which was weird but easy to evade. The performance was also stable at 144fps constantly. SO MANY BAD DECISIONS! The game has a few bosses which were just awful to kill, and I know bosses need to be challenging, but these boss fights were one of two things: an easy first try or a frustrating 100 deaths try. This is because you have boss fights which are parkour and frontal boss fights in which you fight the boss with one ramp or so head-on. One of the parkour bosses was nice because it resembled the normal flow of the game, but the other bosses, oh god, help me, they made me hate parkour , because you needed to play everything perfectly or you need to repeat a 10-minute boss fight which could have been easily evaded just through a simple checkpoint. But the frontal bosses are a complete disaster; you literally one-shot EVERY SINGLE ONE if you have certain weapons. You literally need to handicap yourself and don't use other weapons except the starting weapon to make those boss fights last more than a few seconds. But well, that doesn't make the bosses a disaster; it makes them bad, but not more. The real problem lies in the part where they are really annoying to play against if you don't use the overpowered weapons, so you have either the choice to stomp the boss into the floor or every single boss makes you hate the game because of dumb projectiles and tiny platforms. The other thing is that the art is in some situations in your way of seeing yourself. What I mean is that if you, for example, do a , the screen gets almost completely blacked out as an effect, which makes it harder to see coming enemies, resulting in your death and therefore made me not do any of those anymore, which is bad design. The other part where art is in your way is that you really easily lose the overview of your character's direction or where your head is because the colors of your character fade into each other if you are faster or do 360s, which could also be avoided with a bit of outlining. . I really, really want to like it just because of the innovative ideas for a metroidvania, the insane music, art, and world, but the game doesn't really make it easy with the balancing, bosses, annoying mechanics, story, and character relations. I would recommend it, but only if you want to experience a depressing world as a lone biker which grabs you with its art and music with a few twists in the story and if you are ready to overlook a few flaws the game has which make you hate it at some points in its short time.(English is not my first language, so grammar is bad)

_childDocuments_.review: is an excellent “motorvania” with some great bullet-time action, emergent bad-ass moments, and substantive adult themes, all while packaged in a poignant post-apocalyptic world with a memorable soundtrack and anthropomorphic characters. It does a great job of balancing between fun action, explorative gameplay, and world building. And did I mention all of the 2D gore? This is a very satisfying game to play and experience (once you acclimate to the control scheme) and should be on your list of games-to-play. First and foremost, Laika is a metroidvania on a motorcycle, and it’s a genius combination. The thrill of exploring a 2D map while handling motorcycle physics makes movement itself a fun mechanic to build from. But it further commits to the vehicular traversal by incorporating back/front flips into the gameplay. Backflips reload your weapon, and front flips replenish your deflect ability. Why does this work thematically? No idea, and I don’t care, because it’s a ton a fun! On top of that, aiming your gun activates a bullet-time mode, allowing you to line up your shot accurately while you’re driving around. Combine this with all the flipping and reloading, and you get a constant sense of bad-assery! It never gets old flipping through the air to reload mid-gunplay, aligning your motorcycle to deflect the bullets, and then coming around and finishing off the enemy in a blaze of bloody galore! It’s such a strong basic gameplay loop that will keep you coming back for more.This is also a game where you’ll die all the time, but it’s not that big of a deal. Whether you get hit with a bullet, or miss your landing and smash into the ground, you’ll just respawn at the last checkpoint, which are all over the place. Furthermore, the death/revive function is incorporated into the story as a special ability, so you don’t feel like the story is ignoring your player deaths like most games do. It helps to keep your suspension-of-disbelief.Objective wise, you’re trying to fight back against a colonizing force. Luckily, your home tribe is hidden from the enemy and gives you a safe place to rest, collect small quests, and upgrade your gear. Having a home base to retreat to was a nice expansion of gameplay I wasn’t expecting in this title. There are no upgrade trees or anything, but you have some weapons to unlock and upgrade with materials you scavenge from the world map. There’s even a little blackjack side game you can play, though it’s mostly a gimmick.It also takes a novel thematic approach to currency: the  of your dead enemies. After every kill, instead of collecting coins, bloody viscera will fly to you in their bloody trails, often leaving you totally drenched in red blood. In case you had any doubts about the title “Aged Through Blood”…there’s plenty of it here.Overall, this is a very fun and satisfying game to play. The controls are going to take a minute to get comfortable with. I played on PC, and the default control scheme to move is:- W = Accelerate (facing left or right)- S = Brake- A = Flip Counterclockwise- D = Flip Clockwise- Space = Drift (deflect)- Dash = Left ShiftThis can be a little tricky to get used to. Intuitively, I wanted to default to holding A or D to move left/right, and then use W and S to flip clockwise or counterclockwise. But then there wouldn’t be an easy key to brake with. Space and Left Shift are already used for other actions. Anyway, it took a little bit to get used to. But once I did it made perfect sense and the game flowed really smoothly. (Since I’m weird and wanted to avoid using the spacebar, I set Drift to Left Shift and Dash to Left CTRL, and it worked fine for me.)If you’re turned off by the controls at first, don’t let it soar you to the game. Just stick with it and it’ll click. The atmosphere is an immersive one that pulls you in from the very first cutscene. You are a mother Coyote trying to protect her daughter and what’s left of her tribe (different types of animals) while dealing in bloody vengeance against the occupying army of Birds. I really like the idea of mixing a violent and heavy post-apocalyptic world populated with anthropomorphic characters. Mixing these two juxtaposing vibes gives the game a unique character while also making the heavy subject matter more digestible. It adds a nice artistic flare, instead of simply looking like some generic “realistic” rendering.The artstyle is really pleasing to watch on the screen. The colors can play on the emotions of the story really well, and allows for highly saturated effects to come out without feeling out of place. The animation of characters has a low frame-rate style, which works surprisingly well considering the action that can take place. There are also some really cool animated cutscenes that have some fantastic animation and presentation. Unfortunately, these are few and far between. I would have loved to see more of these.The music is also another hidden gem in this game. There’s a “game soundtrack” but also a soundtrack for the cassettes you play diegetically in-game. The acoustic songs from the cassette player throw in another fun twist to the "post-apocolypse + anthropomorphic" formula. I bought the cassette soundtrack as soon as I beat the game.The presentation in Laika is very strong, and creates a cohesive immersive experience. It’s probably about 25 hours or so to beat with 100%. However, I can’t be sure because my computer crashed and corrupted my file right before the final boss (you can only use one save slot for your playthrough). Thankfully, a kind soul on the Discord gave me their save file that I could continue from, so I didn’t have to replay the whole game. My advice, manually backup your game while you play this…  is a fantastic game that you should definitely invest in. It’s strong gameplay loop, slick visuals, heavy adult themes, and great art and soundtrack make it a solid experience you can sink your teeth into...once you're used to the controls. It’s just a really fun game. If they ever make a sequel, I will pick it up immediately. Easy Recommend.
