name: Redout 2
detailed_description: The fastest racing game in the universe. Redout 2 is a tribute to classic arcade racing games and the sequel to the critically acclaimed Redout, where racing through the dystopian wastelands of a semi-abandoned Earth is one of the galaxy’s most popular sports. Reach impossible speeds in exhilarating futuristic races across an extensive single-player campaign and competitive multiplayer. Deep control systems, robust hovership customization and a killer soundtrack make Redout 2 the premier anti-gravity racer. KEY FEATURES Speed and Control - In the tradition of Anti-Gravity racing classics like Wipeout and F-Zero, experience blazing fast speeds and an intuitive driving system that makes Redout 2 a blast to pick up and play, but also rewarding for those prepared to master the super-high skill ceiling. Bend, loop and swoop through the most insane twists and jumps in racing game history. Extensive Career Mode - Fly through hundreds of events across 36 unique racetracks - all of which are reversible! From Arena Races and Time Attacks to Last Man Standing and intense Boss Races, dart past the competition and dominate the finish line. Competitive Multiplayer - Race against others in intense 12-player online multiplayer action. Dive into fresh challenges with regularly-added custom content, alongside seasons that include unique aesthetic rewards. Comprehensive Customization - Choose from 12 distinct chassis and fully customize your own hovership with an incredible selection of propulsors, stabilizers, rudders, intercoolers, flaps, magnets, wings, spoilers, rocket engines, paints and more! Create and share your best high-speed highlights with Photo Mode. Jaw-Dropping Soundtrack - Featuring superstar electronic artists, including the legendary Giorgio Moroder and acclaimed talents like Zardonic and Dance with the Dead. Our music-master algorithms seamlessly and dynamically mix tracks based on real-time race data.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: New players, stay away until you see some patch notes about the difficulty curve. It's awful, and I'm saying that as a long time Redout enjoyer and advocate.     Redout 2 seems to be a game by game developers who have not spoken to anyone outside of their hardcore playerbase for the past decade. The difficulty curve is insane, and the campaign mode has an aggressive problem with the very idea of player agency.      The tutorials are blisteringly hard, and I'm saying that as a guy who has over 80 hours in the previous game. They slow time and assume control from you, that can occasionally put you into walls or off the track, as the only way to progress past them is to hold down the designated input. They are unhelpful at best, and mandatory.  I had to teach myself boost-stacking to complete the tutorial level you have to beat to unlock the tutorial about boost stacking. I got 3rd place in a tutorial that just shows you *text* explaining car stats. It is massively overtuned for the hardcore crowd.     As an additional screw-you, the game only half-explains some vital mechanics and locks them behind additional tutorials in the tutorial race league that you can only access after you have won some races in the B tier league. It's comical how bad this signposting is.     The campaign forces you to drive the ESA car. You do not get to choose your starting chassis. You are forced into this un-upgraded jalopy and asked to play the game against opponents that are genuinely just better than you, and race like they've been turning laps since before you were born. The idea that a player would have preferences about what kind of car they would like is not even considered. Progression is glacial and involves unlocking specific parts that arbitrarily raise different stats. It's impossible early game to determine if you have lost because you made driving mistakes, or because your numbers are not turgid enough to out-race the raid boss. This is a terrible sensation to foist upon players who may be losing due only to developer malice and no actual fault of their own.     Some of the earliest campaign events available to you as a player are one-lap time trials. Blind. You do not have any idea what you're getting into in a precision racing game that literally sells itself on near incomprehensible fastness. Hope you enjoy the restart button because you'll use it a lot chasing a gold that is physically impossible to achieve with the terrible car you are forced to drive at start.     My favorite bit though, after all of this crass mistrust of the player to make any meaningful decisions or observations, is that in the multiplayer mode the ONLY cars available to you are the un-upgraded junker you start with or fully kitted out max level versions of every other car. The idea that new players might form a small grid to teach themselves in a reasonable spread of their preferred low tier vehicles is apparently completely lost on 34 Big Things, and it is an absolute shame.     The new player experience for this game is a trainwreck. I'm sure the 10 people who show up to the weekly wallgrind are going to have a great time, but they are not about to find themselves many new friends with the launch of Redout 2.     All that said: For those of you who have not been scared away, the actual mechanical driving in this game is a thing of beauty. Cars handle with an amount of control and willingness to cooperate with long, boostful drifts that I could only have dreamed of playing Redout1. There are now boosters that live in the apexes of some corners and will still accelerate you accordingly even if you are fully sidewrong to their orientation. The boost pool is fully intertwined with your vehicle's health, and were it not for the fact that a single explosion means an entire race restart, is really fun to balance. The combination pressures of your auto-repair's time delay, your coolant temperatures begging you to go faster, and the flickering booster ahead of you forces you into a beautiful headspace balancing risk and reward.     Until you go slightly too far, explode, and the setback of exploding is so punishing it forces you to restart the map.       I don't have high hopes for 34big things having a functional response to feedback however. They have failed to provide proper lobbies, or for that matter proper lobby controls after that being a glaring issue for the entirety of Redout1. I fear that they may be too stubborn in their design convictions to realize that their tiny cabal of dedicated fans will be the only people interested in their future ranked league and season passes if this new player experience is not addressed.     The most pessimistic part of me is very looking forward to seeing how they cultivate a competitive scene without allowing for a casual one to exist. The cart is firmly before the horse there, and by we've seen how that plays out time and time again.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: I've updated this to reflect my growing thoughts on the netcode of this game if you intend to play at a high level in Multiplayer.This game is DIFFICULT to get good at. If you had played Redout 1 and expect this to play exactly like it, you'll be very surprised. It took me over 50 hours after completing an already 30+ hour campaign to get where I am now to be considered "good". This game rewards track knowledge and snappy decisions/control that takes a lot of getting used to. If you step into the world of Multiplayer, this problem gets worse; as you're competing with a VERY strong suite of players who have a lot of experience with this game and will thrash you.If you're willing to push through that skill barrier and want to race really fast in what I believe to be the most satisfying and rewarding racing game ever made, then keep reading. Otherwise, I might advise holding off if you're looking for a really fast multiplayer racer.The game has 10 primary environments you'll properly race in with 3 tracks each; that's 30 tracks which can go both Forwards and Reverse (except for VERTEX) for a total of 57 tracks. If you buy the summer/winter DLCs, that's an extra 3 reversible tracks each to bring the final total to 36 tracks (69 for reversible). Each track is gorgeous (and GPU intensive, mind you, this game is going to hit your PC HARD if you don't meet minimum specs) while incorporating crazy inversions, jumps, and track hazards that make it so no two tracks feel the same. I've enjoyed learning each one of these tracks (except Maidens of Karyai :P) and I'm still learning techniques and new racing lines even now. Each track is unique in what they try to show off, and each seems to have a "signature" section I'll call it that separates it from others, even if some tracks will share connecting sections back to the finish. Learning these tracks is half the fun of this game, and the makers have done an incredible job making tracks feel AMAZING.There are 12 unique ship teams that you unlock by playing through the campaign. While each ship has a unique starting stat spread that changes how they feel on the track and what they can be good at, you typically won't be at a major disadvantage in a multiplayer setting based on ships (usually, Lunare still sucks and Buran/Koen are still busted). However, there are some exceptions. Ship have had their hitboxes standardized that makes it so no ship is limited (at least I can tell) by their shape, and it's purely determined by the stat spread and your skill. There's unfortunately some ships which aren't strong, but your skill can offset this in multiplayer and to an extent in time trials. Play what you like, the game doesn't require you to be hyper-meta :)Instead of each ship being a static stat spread, you build off of a chassis using special parts you unlock during the campaign. While the community at large as already "optimized" the system, it provides some interesting control in making your ship feel how you want it to (floaty, stiff, ballistic missile, tank, glass cannon, literally undriveable, etc). However, some of the part choices are horribly balanced compared to others (i.e., the PSLN propulsor is no-question the best one in the game). Additionally, unlocking these parts takes a LOT of time in the campaign that I know some people disliked. You can import a 100%d save file, but then you don't get the learning experience offered by the campaign. I heavily recommend playing the campaign before trying to take on Multiplayer for that reason.The game functions on a 3 axis control of steer, strafe, and pitch. Most game journalists probably didn't get the memo about pitching or strafing, but those are important control aspects to keep your speed in technical portions of the track. The game is incredibly fast, and knocking out corners and straights at Mach 2+ is an intoxicating experience that I keep coming back to. With the fixing of several horrid bugs and improvements to the engine, this game has never been faster than it is now. This is the best time to jump into Redout 2, and I promise you'll become just as addicted to going insanely fast as I have.This is an official plug for the official Redout 2 discord . It's an incredibly welcome community that is more than happy to offer advice on getting good. Additionally, it keeps the game alive with frequent multiplayer lobbies set up at any time of day. I don't think I would be recommending the game if it had not been for the community's openness to help.This game suffers massively in its multiplayer functionality. In short, it's like there is the bare minimum on what is needed for a multiplayer functionality at times. With lack of dedicated servers or something akin to a rollback of sorts, constant desyncs between you and the host in a direct connection is not a matter of "if" but a matter of "how much". This is further confounded by the inconsistency of collisions in a multiplayer setting through both player-player collisions AND player-object collisions. You can and will simply be put into a state of irrelevancy in a race through no fault of your own because netcode has decided the player in front of you will be teleporting back and forth stealing your regenerating health. It's frankly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ how absurdly  flawed the multiplayer is, especially as a good player and getting robbed. Even if you aren't in it for a competitive reason, you can hardly just sit back and enjoy going fast because of ubiquitous these desyncs are. Trying to play this game competitively, with how bad the netcode is, is a futile effort and is frankly the most abhorrent thing about this game. The game could use a better tutorial system for teaching the player about the control of their ship. I played redout 1 previously and already had an idea of what to expect from Redout 2, but people jumping into AG racing for the first time might find the Pitch and Strafe axes weird. Additionally, the game doesn't convey enough practical information for how to race (i.e., avoid boosting in turns, boost stacking and when to do it, regeneration, speed retention, stability, thrust, etc.), leading to a really confusing learning experience without reaching out to the community for conceptual help.I love this game. With the new patch that has resolved almost all of the active communities's previous gripes, this game is the definitive best racing game I have ever played. No game makes you feel this fast with such control, and no game has ever rewarded me for my time spent like Redout 2 has. The tracks are incredible, the ships feel fantastic, and the community is one of the most enjoyable I've interacted with. The online play still kind of sucks because the netcode is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but can sometimes work fine. The best time to play Redout 2 was in 2022. The next best time is now. I can't wait to see what this game develops into again. It's difficult, but rewards you for sticking through it. If you want a score:

_childDocuments_.review: Alright. I know some of you know that I did music for the game. Being that said, I was hired as a third party by 34BigThings / Saber Interactive to do the music only, so I am not a part of the team, much as I'd love to as they are amazing people. But this is just to clarify that I only saw some references of the game and didn't even get to test any alpha or beta versions. All I knew was Redout 1.So, here's my most possibly unbiased verdict, from a player's perspective.All I can say is, yes. The game is insanely difficult. It also happens to be the absolute best game of its type out there. It has WAY surpassed the games that it tries to pay tributes to. I wouldn't even say it is fair to call Redout 2 a tribute anymore because it is a beast of its own. The graphics, the tracks, and yes... The difficulty. It's part of what makes the game what it is. Anyone complaining about the game being difficult is literally like the people who complained that Super Meat Boy was too hard. It's MEANT to be hard. You're racing at hyperspeed.I personally found this easier than Redout 1 myself, and WAY easier than any of the F1 games, for reference. Everyone is of course entitled to their opinions, but a game being hard says nothing about its quality.I'm honored to be part of this, and I very much recommend you to grab it if you want a real challenge. Cheers to the dev team and the publishers for making this happen, and I look forward to Redout 3!! 🍻

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Redout 1, and have played it quite a lot! In fact I have all the achievements for Redout 1.However, Redout 2 to me is one step forward and two steps back. While there are things Redout 2 improves upon compared to the first game, I do think the first game is the better racing game.First, the difficulty is just all over the place. Others have mentioned the issues regarding the tutorial, so I won't repeat them here. For me the problem lies in that as of writing this I have the game set to "Pilot" difficulty (setting 3 of 6) and I continuously crush the AI, like it's not even close. However, when I set the difficulty one notch higher to "Redout" I will pull pretty far ahead during the first half of a race, but then the AI gets hilariously rubber-bandy and whips past me, putting me all the way to last place with no hope to compete. I have also noticed that the AI seem to have difficulty racing on the tracks, as I've seen them routinely falling off the course after a jump and respawning. And of course with how hard the rubber banding the AI is, on Redout difficulty they crush me no problem anyway. Also the gimmick events like the Speed event are hilariously difficult and don't scale on chosen difficulty.On top of that, if you blow up or crash outside of the course, it's so punishing you HAVE to restart the race because you are NOT going to be able to make your way back up to the front.The game also has a new customization system, where instead of distinct cars and tiers, there's now a point system. This seems great, as the options to bias a car in specific directions sounds great, but the campaign has EVERYTHING locked. The campaign very slowly drip feeds you parts, which you then have to immediately equip because the AI cars objectively outclass you (they have a higher point score than your car), so there is in practice no options at all. On top of that, every single color and pattern type is locked behind campaign events as well, so you're stuck with a purple car for a while, with no options for even basic colors.The racing itself also features a new boosting system, where you have 2 different boosts (a weaker one you can use whenever, and a more powerful one that recharges), and if you overheat your car, it burns away your health. What ends up happening is that you're going to be boosting nearly ALL THE TIME, while in Redout 1 you had a far stronger boost, but had to time it right to get the most out of it.I hope you like the health regen sound. You're going to be hearing it. A lot.The boosting system adds an extra layer of complication that I'm not sure is even worth it to be honest. That and now you have to deal with rotating your ship with the D-pad, so now you're using 2 joysticks, holding down the gas on trigger, and juggling the shoulder buttons for your two boosts. It's a lot of fingerwork for a racing game, and I don't really think it adds anything.The music in Redout 2 is also just overall weaker compared to the first game as well. Redout 1 has really good songs like "Sand Wars," "You Will Burn," and "Arabia Terra" that I listen to on Spotify all the time. Nothing I've heard so far in Redout 2 comes close to those fantastic tracks, and the music is overall a bit more sedate in Redout 2.It's such a shame too because I was looking very much forward to Redout 2, and I want to like it, but between rubber banding AI, a customization system that refuses to give you options to really play with it, and complication seemingly for the sake of complication, I think Redout 1 is the better game.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the first Redout game and completed all the events, including all the DLC, I was really excited to play this game. The trailer looked fantastic and featured some impressive visuals and awesome music. I must admit I was a little frustrated by the delayed launch, but what's a few extra weeks if the developers can produce a better product.My initial thoughts on the game were very good. Visuals were indeed very impressive with beautiful tracks, a pumping sound track and a great feeling of competition. Sadly that initial impression didn't last. After a few hours of play it was clear that a few of the tracks have problems, such as Tartarus Mines: Ixion. Go off the track at the wrong point and you get warped backwards 22km, get it right and you're warped 22km forwards.A few others have glitching through the track issues after a jump, and the overall game design is "Boost until you almost explode". Initially the Speed events were a fun challenge, but as soon as you get in to A class they start to become egregious. For what ever reason the developers lacked any creativity and decided to do the same annoying event in quick succession gating your progress each time.Furthermore, the difficulty setting does not effect Time Trials or Speed events, so if you struggle completing them then you're just simply out of luck.I enjoy a good challenge, and I'm far from the best pilot out there. But after 17 hours on this game I don't feel like I'm getting anywhere and it's already become extremely tedious to play. Sadly I can't recommend this game to others, all I can hope is this review has provided you with enough information and the developers listen to customer feedback.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is an AG Racer for veterans of the genre. If you've never played an AG game and you pick this one up first you are likely to:- Complain about the track design- Complain about the controls- Complain about the repetition and campaign length- Complain about the progression- Complain about the difficultyIf you've spent time in other AG racers before, such as Wipeout, Ballistic.NG, etc. then you'll likely find the track design, difficulty, and control complaints irrelevant. If you haven't played other AG racers before, I strongly recommend trying Ballistic.NG, Wipeout, or Fast RMX first.  Redout 2 is a refreshing and demanding, yet rewarding take on the genre that veterans are sure to appreciate.The control scheme is as unique as it is gratifying, as gratifying as it is responsive; strafing forces a complete re-write of racing fundamentals. Where in a normal game you'd likely brake before a sharp turn, in Redout 2 you oftentimes do not have to break at all, but instead counterstrafe to widen your turn whilst losing minimal speed. This leads to a sense of fluidity that traditional racing games do not provide. And while other AG racers also take on a unique approach to steering in the form of air breaks, those are really just an extension of the traditional steering approach. You really feel the anti-gravity in Redout 2, and a skilled pilot can glide through a track in an immensely satisfying way.There are also two types of boost. Both raise your heat gauge, which, when full, will eat into your hull (which quickly regenerates when not taking damage). Boost timing and hull management, when paired with the unique handling mechanics, result in an insanely high skill ceiling in controls alone.Sense of speed is absolutely bonkers in this game. The ship variety is good, but progression can be a frustrating barrier to unlocking the most satisfying ships. Many of the first ships you unlock focus on tankiness, something that I find antithetical to the aura of the game. However, the base ship is quite good and nine times out of ten picking it until you unlock some of the quicker, nimbler, more fragile ships is a safe bet. Cosmetic progression is equally held back, but performance progression is acceptable.Track design is absolutely incredible, with so many brain-melting turn sequences that really reward track memorization and quick reflexes. Any complaints about track design are in my eyes unsubstantiated because people aren't willing to memorize tracks and expect everything to be easy from the get go, as is the case in many traditional racing games.Track variety is in a similar boat to the design. There is a sufficient quantity of tracks and styles, but many might be deterred by re-used portions shared between tracks. I personally appreciate these re-used portions, as they act as a "safe space" in which I can maximize speed due to their familiarity.The most divisive thing about the game, even among experienced players, are the air controls. They are janky for sure, but once you become familiarized with the courses, you can control the chaos enough to survive any jump.The last thing worth noting is that the game is effectively dead. Portions of the main menu are greyed out, and I don't expect that ever to change. If you want an online race, you'll have to find people on Discord, and they will probably be way better than you. However, there is more than enough content in what is available to justify a purchase at full price.In conclusion: If you're tired of blazing through every traditional arcade racing game without any challenge, pick up Ballistic.NG or Wipeout. If you've already played either of those, and are looking for a modern take on the genre, play Redout 2. It breathes new life into the dying genre of AG Racers, and has unprecedented depth.

_childDocuments_.review: 11/20/2022: Better - much better... KEEP WAITING.Don't be discouraged by the seemingly slow pace of the updates - the problems the game had and still has aren't quick and easy fixes. Things are coming along nicely, and while my verdict is still "WAIT" - there's still plenty of fun to be had with what's here.Still treat the game as if it's an EA release. It's clear that Redout 2 refuses to be a shadow of its predecessor; but development is a many-lap boss track, not a one-lap time trial.I am glad to see that things haven't totally tanked from the initial rough launch. Many major issues have been fixed, but there's still a long way to go.Get the game - just not *quite* yet. Or on sale, if you're getting impatient.==== Original Review Below ====WAIT.As-is, Redout 2 feels like it's in Early Access. It feels rushed, even with the release delay. I'm worried that getting started on the wrong foot is going to tank the game, but I hope it doesn't.Right now, you have a brutally difficult game reminiscent to F-Zero that can and will roll you for a long time. The game as-is expects you to get good - REAL good - and you will be stomped on until you do. The AI is given a bit too much of a leg up in my opinion, but taking first in the tutorial events is possible. Absolutely viciously difficult, but possible. Respawns have issues, multiplayer is super bare-bones, AI difficulty settings don't seem to actually make anything more doable, control rebinding has some issues, and there are only Class 4-equivalent stock craft to play with in arcade mode.Get the game - just not yet.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE Dec '22:I can see that the devs have eased things off; making the speed & time targets more realistic for your average gamer, and rebalanced the difficulty levels in the same spirit.Sadly, while this is a great step, the track designs are still a big sticking point for progression. Tartarus is still part of the novice "B" class career, and STILL contains all sorts of nose cam glitches blocking your view if you play on that mode.It was also SO much fun having to repeat hundreds of stars worth of races, as when I came back all my progress was back to 0. No steam cloud save? Wipe after the difficulty rebalance? Jeez.At this point in time less than 20% of players have reached Class "A" in career.That's a single step up in the career ladder from where you started in B Class after some tutorials. I think that tells you everything about player retention in RO2. They've all moved on to games they find enjoyable.Even with the difficulty tweaks, I don't think this is salvageable unless you have an extraordinary amount of time to no-life the troll-ish tracks. Sadly, most anti-grav racing fans are all grown up with jobs/families and this game is too disrespectful to our limited time. Shame as Japan and Mars are beautiful examples of what this game could be: a low difficulty floor so lower skill players can enjoy while still having plenty of scope for high skill players to shave split seconds off. Everything after those two areas are just designed to catch players out rather than enjoy a race. We wanted more RO1, that's all. Instead we got this. ----------------------OriginalPosted: 18 Jun @ 1:17pmLoved RO1, and I feel in time RO2 will be in a state to really enjoy as well. Especially if the devs can swallow their pride.However, I cannot recommend in it's current state, especially if this is your first time with the franchise.It's obvious this has been pushed out before full QA & playtesting has taken place.Lots of concerns around difficulty balance (eg: AI in races using advanced boost techniques that you havent even been introduced to via a later tutorial yet, as well as needing them to place well in TA or Speed modes). Getting glitches around track booster locations not triggering despite being visibly in the area, odd landing glitches that cause me to come to a complete halt and do a hundred donuts despite being a 'perfect' landing, (rare but happens) track edges for landings also seem not to pair up with the visuals.Early player agency, as well as onboarding are problems. Half the game modes (inc multiplayer) are locked behind a tutorial season, which again relies on you knowing advanced boost techniques you haven't been shown yet to compete.Quality of Life things like a visual aid map on the HUD to assist in track learning would help too.Music is again very good, except for some of the licensed stuff & giga-distorted screech vocals - yikes. If you want a more RO1 like (and better) soundtrack while you play, stick Streamer mode on in the Options.Strangest part is that there are some decisions that show the devs have *tried* to consider new players. For example, there's a thorough list of AI Assists for all the different controls that can even be fully customised. An attempt at a tutorial campaign is also admirable. However, I really think some of the measures have been introduced almost out of spite for people who don't meet up to their vision of a seasoned Redout connoisseur. If you want a more successful product you will need to widen your vision, devs. If you can't do it, then get some industry consultants involved.There are some positive early signs - a day 2 patch to address some AI issues has been released, although the tone of the patch notes still give off a scornful vibe. You can almost hear the ,"How dare these unwashed masses ask us to change *our* perfect game!" under the surface as you read them. Hopefully we'll see more improvements to the early player experience and some more humility in future.At least the Nintendo Switch users will have missed out on the week 1 drama due to delays. Although I imagine Switch players will have even less patience for the dev's snobbery and begrudging concessions than PC players.

_childDocuments_.review: (update patch June 2024 : the game seem more stable than ever)- An unarmed anti-grav (AG) racing game, with boosters and jumps dotted around the tracks.- More demanding driving than a classic racing game, requiring right-stick control (to move sideways and "nose up" / "nose down") and boost / hyperboost management. Boosting increases your heat gauge, which, when filled to capacity, will begin to consume the "life" gauge of your ship (vehicle), which will explode if depleted.- 10 environments (+ 2 in DLC), each with 3 tracks, which can also be reversed (except for the brand new VERTEX environment, and note that certain track sections are sometimes reused within the same environment). This gives a virtual total of 69 (nice) tracks (with DLC, 57 without).The tracks can also be done in "boss" mode where you run the 3 tracks of an environment in a row.- 12 ships to pilot, each with different basic stats but which can be customized with modules (which don't change the ship's appearance) that change these stats, and each of the ships can be customized (colors, ship parts) with a host of cosmetics that have no influence on your ship's performance.- 1 arcade mode allowing you to discover all the tracks and ships directly, with "endgame" modules that can give you an idea of the capabilities of an endgame ship (but the module builds offered by the arcade game are unfortunately generally crappy).- 1 career mode with a very (very) high number of events, with each event giving you rewards (ships, ship modules, cosmetics, stars to advance in the career) depending on your performance, and each event offering a challenge to scratch off an extra reward (challenges such as "arriving 3 seconds ahead of the gold time", "crossing the finish line at over 1250 Km/h", etc.).Many people compare Redout 2 with WipEout, and I think this is a mistake. Redout 2 has its own style, even though it obviously draws inspiration from the best of the genre.In your early days with Redout 2, the game will indeed resemble WipEout a little in its "not so fast" and "soap ship" aspects, but I repeat: you have no weaponry in Redout 2.And the further you progress in Redout 2, the faster your ships will go and the better they'll hold up.As far as I'm concerned, even though I'm no expert in antigravity racing games, I'm seeing more of a F-Zero GX and Star Wars: Racer feel.There's a lot to be said on this subject, as it's what can easily turn players off / demotivate them.The game is demanding from the outset, in the sense that its controls are atypical if you've never played the original Redout. You'll have to spend a lot of time learning how to pilot your ship properly: managing lateral movements, managing boost / hyperboost (you can boost + hyperboost at the same time), managing jumps...Redout 2 also reveals itself as you unlock new ships and, above all, modules to improve your stats. But to do this, you'll need to progress through the career mode and complete a series of events, over and over again.If I had to sum up the game's difficulty, it's on the ups and downs, with a tendency to be more difficult in general towards the beginning (few ships, few modules, learning to pilot) and to simplify later on (more ships, more modules, better piloting on your part after several hours of play...), even if the events are supposed to be increasingly difficult as you progress through the leagues.I recommend that you avoid tryhard challenges too, as some are "wtf, is this possible to do that ?" (and it's someone with all the trophies and 1451/1451 stars who's telling you this), as it's better to progress through the career to unlock as many ships/modules as possible to give you greater flexibility.First of all, you can select the difficulty of opposing AIs (from "Zero" to "Nightmare"), which affects : - the performance of your opponents- but also on the number of "rewinds" allowed in an event: yes, if you fail miserably in a jump, you can click on a button, go back a few seconds before the catastrophe and try your luck again without having to restart your race (note that some events don't allow rewinds, such as time trials).Another point that lets you gauge the game's difficulty at your leisure: the assistsRedout 2 can assist you with literally everything you need to drive.My ego is such that I'm playing with the assistance completely deactivated, but I can only recommend that you try to get assistance if you're having difficulty, particularly with jumps and avoiding walls (then you can gradually reduce these assistances over time).In short, regarding difficulty:- if you're getting crushed by the AIs: reduce their difficulty- if you're frustrated by eating walls all the time and crashing on all jumps: try with assistance on these pointsThe game does its job visually. Each environment has its own style (and music, see below) and is pleasant to navigate.Redout 2's music isn't necessarily all top-notch (although it did allow me to discover a few artists such as Zardonic or Dance with the Dead, even Leonardo Mazzella who is the "main" composer who did some "bangers"), but a great deal of work has been done to ensure that all the music sticks to the environments (giving each one its own style) and these tunes are generally cut into 3 parts:- Before the start (soft)- During the track (generally hard-hitting electro)- Towards the end of the track (faster electro)In short, I'd say that the choice was made to have music that tended more towards the immersive than the artistic (even if there are a few tracks that kick ass), and this fits in perfectly with the gameplay.Sound design plays a major role.Each ship has its own "engine sound" and hyperboost trigger.On the other hand, the boost sound is the same for all ships, which is a pity, but that's a good one ;)And the same goes for the "drift" sound (yes, yes), which you can make by turning in one direction while moving sideways in the opposite direction.Perfect landings are some kind of a delight too.Online only.Multiplayer is almost deserted, and if you want to see other players, I invite you to join the Redout discord, where that's where things obviously happen. Of course, some of these players are among the best of the best.As mentioned above, two environments are available as DLC (each with 3 tracks and their reverse tracks).The first is a Caribbean-style environment and the other takes place on Mercury (in a particular style)If you're hooked on the game, I can only recommend that you buy them, as these additional circuits are not at all redundant with the others.So, Redout 2 is a game :- Demanding at first, requiring a minimum of effort / time investment- A pure pleasure to play, both visually and aurally. This pleasure skyrockets as you master your ship and the different tracks.- Unfortunately little-known and shunned by players who might have been misguided/advised- Make sure your game runs as smoothly as possible: more fps (> 60) and less input lag (turn off Vsync), you'll be just better.- Some challenges are a pain: do not hesitate to switch the game to "Zero" difficulty, so you can rewind as many times as you like! - I think the aim of this game is to have fun / get the thrill of speed. The game will give you the same rewards, whether you're facing "Zero" or "Nightmare" AIs: in short, don't be ashamed to lower the difficulty / use the assists- In career mode, learn to spot events that prohibit rewind and those that immediately fail as soon as your ship explodes- Brakes : use them.

_childDocuments_.review: After hitting 20 hours, I finally had my first actual 'fun' with an event, and figured it was a good time to update the review. I would still not recommend this game unless you already know what you're getting into.Pros:Visual appealCampaign upgrade systemVehicle cosmetic optionsEnvironment varietySplit track pathsCons:The cameraCampaign difficulty and progressionTrack jumps are frustratingRewind system is a bandaid for poor track designBonus goals in campaign range; wildly variable difficulty and no clarity for player ("Did I miss that 1k jump target by 10 meters or by 200? I have no idea")Lunare continues to be the obvious ship choiceThe camera, oh my god the cameraOriginal review followsDespite being a die hard fan of the original Redout, I think that while there are some interesting steps forward in Redout 2, they missed the mark and the experience is painful right now.  The career mode is disorienting, track progression is strange, ship upgrades are placed strangely, tutorials are poorly balanced and mechanics tutorials are gated behind career progression. On the gameplay side, the new system for stacking boosts is conceptually incredibly interesting, but the way it's tuned it becomes the only correct way to play. Stages also have a bunch of "gotchas" with blind turns with no rails which comes across as incredibly cheap with the games forced low camera angle. Also painful are the poorly tuned jumps that require oddly specific handling with little room for error due to weak ability to control your ship once you've taken to the air. I think the devs realize this, and there's now a "rewind" system that allows you to wind time back to a couple seconds before you took the jump but ultimately it's incredibly jarring and clumsy to use and comes across like a band-aid for tracks or systems they knew had issues.

_childDocuments_.review: --EDIT: Original negative review below for posterity, pretty good now, most bugs are fixed, hitboxes of the track and vehicles feel way better and make it less frustrating.--Love/hate relationship with this game. Redout 2 is an anti-grav racer inspired by the likes of the Wipeout Franchise, F-Zero, and similar, this game isn't a cheap knock-off of them though and is very much it's own thing, in-fact I consider the racing in this to be best among all anti-grav racing games. Redout 2 is a twin-stick racer, you must use left analog stick to control steer turning, right analog to control strafe turning, additionally there is pitch control on up/down track bends and roll on jumps, along with a complicated dual boost system with overheat management. If that sounds like a lot to control it is, the skill ceiling in this game is extremely high and I would consider it the hardest racing game I've ever played with the only thing coming close being hardcore sim racers which are hard for different reasons, I imagine it would take the average player at least 50 hours of gameplay just to be able to begin to consistently contend with max difficulty AI on harder tracks, or even start to get to a point where you can do most tracks without crashing into walls or going off edges. It takes a long time to get good at this game and that growth in skill can be extremely rewarding, and the depth to the mechanics of the racing makes it more interesting and fun when you can finally get into that flow state where you're good at the tracks, even on the simplest track you're never going to fall asleep like you might in a simple arcade racer. The racing feels amazing when it all goes right, gameplay is great and there is no real competitors to it or anything else like it with how unique it is. Unfortunately I still have a lot of problems with this game at the moment, the speed at which you race in this game is so fast that some turns, and jumps that also involve rolling and mid-air steering are incredibly difficult, the tracks have signage and indicators to help with upcoming turns and jumps but they are very unreliable and inconsistent, and the pace note images you get similar to a rally car game are overly simplified, sometimes wrong, and sometimes missing turns, because of these problems learning every track in the game is a frustrating process of trial, error, and memorization as you miss a jump landing then rewind time many times in a row, etc. Besides that my biggest problem of all with the game is the Devs and their support for the game as well as communication with the community. The game is full of bugs which affect gameplay, some of them severe, there's environment decoration clipping through tracks which can cause you to abruptly stop and spin-out, there are track sections and railing after jumps with broken hitboxes which you simply pass through as if they weren't even there, UI bugs, texture pop-in bugs, impossible steam achievements and uncompleteable career objectives that don't register, there's even one track that has a branch that leads to a dead-end which is a known bug still not fixed after months. There are so many bugs that the game feels like an early access release and I have legitimately played many early access games with less bugs than this game has. It feels dishonest to me that the game is advertised as a finished product in it's current state. Many of the bugs have been known about by the Devs for a very long time, but the release cycle for bugfixes is painfully slow as the game is cross-platform and any updates are released on all platforms at once, it could take months for even a very small known bug to get fixed. Devs don't have good communication with players either, they don't interact with steam forums at all, bug reports are only through some awkward website system that makes it difficult to follow up on anything as a player, bugs I personally reported weeks ago are still in the game as of the most recent update patch. The point that made me fed-up was the most recent patch released alongside paid DLC, with patch notes mentioning bugfixes, which I can personally verify were literally not fixed. This game doesn't need DLC right now, it needs proper dev support and communication with focus on consistent quality core gameplay, I will change this review to positive if the problems get fixed at some point, but for now it just seems like the Devs don't care about those problems. Worth it on sale maybe, a fun, but potentially frustrating experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I yearn for a neutral review button. This is a game that is much improved in some ways over it's predecesor, but on the other hand seems to be molded exclusively by the half dozen people in the discord server who did time trials ad infinitum. It's a fairly OK game and the design is gorgeous. But by god the cognitive load is higher here than on the previous one, and with no arcade control scheme to simplify the input, it is a nightmare to play on any controller.With that said, it's not a bad game. If you can stomach an overly complex racer with convoluted controls and so many things on screen at once that will make your brain melt, and you don't mind it has been designed around specifically two people in the discord server. Then yeah. You can do the thing.As for me, there are no bunnies on this game, unlike it's predecessor so it's inmediatly disqualified.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Generally an upgrade from the first Redout.+ Better engine sounds.+ Better dynamic music.+ More ships.+ More locations.+ Boss tracks are connected seamlessly.+ Gotta go fast.- Less tracks per location.* The soundtrack is not like the first one. It suits the game from amazing to meh (mostly veryu well) but it's never a detriment. The music tracks are not memorable pieces like the first one, but the licensed tracks do add a bit of flavour.Your ships have 6 stats on how they behave while driving.Each chasis has base stats and then there are 6/7 modules to enhace them further.Different events in the campaign (Time Attack, Race, Arena Race, Speed ...).Quite challenging in the beginning but get easier down the line.Each location has 3 tracks. They all share the same start/finish line.Boss tracks are a lap of each single track in sequence in contrast to the first Redout where the single tracks were connected with teleports.Sense of speed - YES
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is great. The sense of speed is unparalleled, the amount of control you have over the craft both on and off track is great, the boost/overheat mechanic feels both risky but also really rewarding if used right... overall, the games mechanics all feel fantastic, and have a lot of depth to them.BUT.While I do recommend this game, there are a few things about it that need to be addressed. The game expects you to play it a LOT. Currently the campaign is very long (40-50 hrs to complete), which is a bit of a problem as you unlock all of the games content in it. Simply put, you cant play the game properly unless youve completed the campaign, which is a big time investment. On top of that, this isnt really a casual game, it requires a lot of practice to get properly good at and get the most out of.Multiplayer at the moment is basic at best. While it looks like there is a lot more to come with seasonal challenges and ranked mode and the "community" tab, right now you can only really pick a track, pick your ship, and thats it. Cant alter lap count, cant set power limits, cant even reverse the track. Im assuming this will be addressed though.Finally, the game isnt too polished yet, both in regards to bugs and missing features/QOL. Now the developers seem to be hard at work already fixing these things, but at the moment it can be a bit of a mess. Ill update this review once these issues are dealt with, which i believe will happen sooner rather than later. The TLDR is:-Gameplay is loads of fun. like, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it feels good.-requires a lot of time to get into-multiplayer is bare bones-rather unpolished in places.-Also, this game HARD.I definitely still recommend Redout 2 for its excellent gameplay. Just know that, at the moment, its not perfect, and if any of the above mentioned issues are a problem for you, i suggest maybe holding off untill the next patch or maybe a sale. Ill update this should these issues be addressed.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the original Redout most of the skills you learned won't carry over. The driving is much tighter, and the tracks generally more narrow. The music is worse, in my opinion, mostly drum and bass, there's not really anything on top of it all. The layout of the tracks is innovative, The tracks within a set use common pieces, using blockers to change the layout of the track. It's clever, especially in making the tracks reversible but it makes it difficult to learn and memorize the tracks. The AI is much more competent. The goals of each mode and the bonus goals can be trivially easy or frustratingly difficult. It's really inconsistent throughout the leagues. Cosmetics and vehicle upgrades are earned by scoring points in each league event, 1 point for 3rd, 2 for 2nd, 3 for 1st, and an additional point for completing a secondary goal. These upgrades are tied to the events, so if you want everything you need to come in 1st and complete the secondary goal.  Overall it's enjoyable and offers a good challenge, even if some of the challenges are arbitrarily difficult.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's crazy fast, and fixed many of the things that I had issue with in redout 1. Handling is tighter and more responsive, and there's new boost mechanics that basically take the turbo boost powerup from the prior game and make it a core mechanic. This means they pretty much took the most used options, made it the norm, and cut the rest of the useless powerups, and i'm completely fine with that.Wall bouncing was the norm in redout 1, and was entirely necessary to claim a place on the leaderboards. Many were fine with this, but I found the dirty style of racing to be deeply unsatisfying, since a clean lap was rarely the best one. Now, that is completely discouraged. Hull is a valuable resource which is used as an additional boost pool, and it's pretty easy to burn your hull down to nothing with a large boost, so you can't afford to get too comfortable smacking into walls. Clean laps are the way to go, and that feels a lot better to me.Customisation is a welcome feature, with a huge list of paints, liveries, and parts, both cosmetic and performance boosting. This is entirely unlocked through career progression, which gives a good goal to work towards, but some may find it annoying, since there is no currency or quick way to buy exact parts you want.Online is a bit odd. Lobbies are gone, and you can currently only join games through matchmaking. This means that you'd need to befriend a pile of people and invite them to a group to queue, if you want a semblance of a custom lobby. Seems like a step backwards to me, as this will make tournaments impossible to organise.The courses themselves are quite interesting, with a good variety of unique places with different hazards, from massive jumps, to magma that will actively overheat your ship. They all provide interesting challenges, and the more complex courses will definitely take time to learn. You may struggle in some locations to even get around a lap in one piece at first, but once you can finally clock in a good lap on a troublesome course, it is immensely satisfying.Overall, I'd say it has improved in many ways from redout 1, but also taken a step back in others. It certainly feels different in a lot of ways, but I welcome most of these changes. It's been a fun game so far, and I'd recommend it if you want a blazing fast racer with a massive skill ceiling.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: Before buying this game, please note this is not for the casual gamer. If you are looking for a casual racing game, THIS IS NOT IT. Seek elsewhere. Even with adjustable difficulty the game depends on your skill and quick responses. I do not recommend this game if you're not up for the challenge. Anyway, on to the review.TL:DR This game is awesome! The high speed racing gives you the F-Zero fix you need and in my honest opinion, much better than Redout 1. Buy it, sale or not. The only downfall is career is slightly repetitive at times.Need a fun intense racing game? Are you seeking the adrenaline rush that helps you finish your business in the bathroom? Have you been itching for an F-Zero game but Nintendo won't do it? This isn't completely F-Zero but it's damn well close! This game is amazing! So much about it has improved on the first game. I liked Redout 1, but I felt it fell a little short. This one hits everything I like about a high speed, zero to full gravity racing game. Let's talk about the good first.Pros:- Fun action packed racing that keeps your heart pumping. The adrenaline rush you feel from F-Zero is here. It'll keep you on your toes. It'll make you want to throw a controller. (Reminder to add to my list: Buy a new controller). It'll make you question why your car can't go as fast. The game is downright fun racing. It's not for everyone, but the excitement will leave you breathless in some races. - The graphics are really good and cool. The animations of vehicles, the landscapes, and the tracks. You almost get distracted by some of the beautiful environments. Trust me, I've wrecked a few times because OOOOO A BUTTERFLY! Side Note: I play this on Steam Deck. For those wanting to play on Deck, it works flawlessly however the game defaults to Ultra settings. Highly recommend switching to Medium for 60 FPS performance. You will need it. - Controls are good overall, they do take some time to get used to fair warning. But once you get it, you'll realize it makes controlling your machine more fluent than the last game. - Lots of content, with plenty more on the way. The career mode will keep you busy for a while (I'm still going at it). Online works pretty alright overall, and the arcade mode is fun if you want to test vehicles and builds. Apparently we're getting a community update soon? I'm curious what they mean by this. - Not everyone agrees but I love the different racing environments. I love how some have more gravity, some less. Some planets are hot, some are cold. That's just a really cool thing to make you to adapt to different tracks.Cons:- What is pro is also a con. Primarily Career mode. It'll keep you busy and playing, but sometimes the events are a bit repetitive. You'll feel like you played the same level and scenario a few events ago. It's not terrible but for how big career mode is, it's expected. - Some bugs that they are luckily acknowledging and working on. Some have been fixed, some haven't but hopefully soon.Pro Tip: DO NOT SKIP THE TUTORIALS! Especially if you decided not to heed my warning, the tutorials, though text based, actually help you a lot understand the mechanics of the game. Whether you are new to Redout or a Veteran player, I strongly encourage it. Overall, the game is amazing. While we continue to question if Nintendo remembers who Captain Falcon is other than a fighting character, other companies have taken the torch and this is one of those games. If you're unsure, wait for a sale but sale or not, it's definitely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE:I recently acquired a twin-stick setup consisting of a Logitech Extreme 3D Pro and Logitech Attack 3 that I decided to run through an X-box controller emulator (X360CE v4.0) to see if the game was any more enjoyable.TLDR: It was not.I ended up turning off all assists as having the vehicle respond unpredictably to my joystick inputs was incredibly frustrating and made it harder to adjust to the new control format. I realized very quickly that the four biggest issues with this game's jumps are as follows:1. You do not have any truly appreciable control over your vehicle in mid-air other than rolling, so if your nose is pointed anywhere other than the ideal direction, you are immediately screwed.2. Mid-air gravity can be pulling you from virtually any direction and it isn't immediately obvious until you leave the surface of the magnetic track and your ship starts to fall. Sometimes, gravity is dragging you at such weird angles, you have to launch your ship specifically against it to have even a chance of making it to the landing zone. Some even require the use of super boost in order to clear them.3. The landing zones for jumps are standard-width sections of track that are often not in the same orientation as the launch point, requiring you to adjust multiple axis of your ship simultaneously while still having almost no control of where your ship will drift.4. There are annoying weather effects like fog/clouds that will randomly obscure certain tracks and make it impossible to see where you are supposed to land. As if that task wasn't hard enough already. To sum this all up, if I am restarting a single time-trial on a map with multiple jumps over and over again for an hour or two, I should be able to predict what is coming and adjust to it in a manner that allows me to feel confident that I can land those same jumps consistently. Yet, despite having more fine control of the ship thanks to my dual-stick setup with no active assists and restarting this same track repeatedly for an hour, I still only had a 25% success rate for landing any of the more difficult jumps. I knew where they were on the track, I knew where the landing zones were and how they were oriented, and yet I could never be certain if I would land successfully or if my ship would piss off into the sunset because its nose hadn't been aligned exactly right. Because there is not enough control over your ship's movements in mid-air.So why don't I use the provided AI assists then, you might be wondering? Well, it turns out that quite a few tracks have significant shortcuts that are only usable if you have enough control over your ship to leave the standard course. If you have assists on, you will never be able to use these shortcuts.Also, as I mention in my older review, setting the AI assists for mid-air control to 100% still does not guarantee that you will land as tracks with multiple standard paths bugger up the pathfinding and send you off into the scenery for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles. If it's too hard for the AI, you know you have a problem. Ironically, the NPC pilots don't seem to have this same issue, though I have noticed them slamming into the same wall on the same track on the same jump over and over again as if some programmer made a mistake with a decimal point...So... yeah. The game still isn't fun even with a twin-stick setup and it's all thanks to the mid-air ship physics.OLD REVIEW:I decided to update my review for this game after reading other reviews.This game is a mess. Overall the hover vehicles feel more controllable than the original Redout, but only just. However, airborne flight controls are abysmal and the majority of players seem to share the complaint that jumps are miserably designed.Track design apart from jumps is equally terrible. In the original Redout, it was only the harder tracks that required the player to simultaneously control the ship's pitch, strafe, and yaw. In Redout 2 you will encounter these sorts of advanced track layouts as early as B-League. Tracks regularly have missing walls on the outside of tight turns or on the side where the turn is sloped which causes your ship to fly out into oblivion if you aren't careful. There are frequently blind turns that have missing walls or turns with boost pads positioned just before them or in the middle of the turn, which is completely counter-intuitive and feels more like the developers trolling players than trying to design a good level. Jumps regularly require the player to manage the ship's roll, yaw, strafe, pitch, AND thrust in order to (maybe) land the ship. Hitboxes for the landing zones are very small and finicky so it is not unusual to clip through the track if you didn't land the jump exactly right. And unlike Redout, Redout 2's landing zones are incredibly small and usually located at strange angles compared to the jump.And this is where I am going to bring up the most glaring issue. The AI-assist which is supposed to make the game more enjoyable for casual players. It doesn't. I got tired of missing jumps and flying off of blind corners so I adjusted my AI-assists so that all of my Flight assists were at 100% and I upped my Braking assist to 60% so I wouldn't have to worry about the tight corners with missing railings quite so much.Despite having the Flight assists all set to 100%, my ship would still occasionally clip through a landing zone because the AI shorted the jump. On Cloud Ocean in particular, I discovered that the AI cannot find the correct flight path when there are multiple available landing zones, instead opting to send your ship flying off into the scenery.The difficulty settings for the Campaign only influence the competency of the other AI racers in events with opponents. It does nothing to reduce the difficulty level for Speed, Time Trial, or other Solo events where the Time, Speed, or Point requirement to win does not change regardless of which difficulty level you have selected.To make matters even worse, most of these Solo challenges do not allow you to use the Rewind feature. If you mess up, the only way to recover is to restart the race. Combine that with the lack of difficulty scaling for these events and the dreadful airborne/jump mechanics and you have a recipe for an absolutely miserable experience.One last thing: Ship customization. Redout 2 gives you cosmetic and performance mods. Cosmetics do not affect the performance of the ship in any way and are locked behind bonus objectives. Performance mods operate on a point system similar to games like Forza Motorsport. Unfortunately, the variety you might have expected for tailoring your chosen ship's performance just isn't there. As you get access to more powerful mods, the overall number of mods in said tier decreases to the point where you only get 3 choices at the top. Most of the mods don't provide different benefits and are simply "better" versions of a previous mod with a higher point value.My personal experience with the performance mods in this game was that I began skipping any races that didn't award performance parts just so I could collect all of the parts to help refine my ship's performance for some of the more difficult Solo events. I thought this would allow me to give my ship better handling at the expense of some of my speed. However, when I finally had all of the Green level performance parts and a couple Yellow, I discovered that there was no good way to measurably improve the aspects of my ship that I wanted to without completely destroying my top speed stat. The flexibility I expected from the point system just wasn't there because the variety just wasn't there.All that to say, Redout 2 is a poor successor to Redout. It has it's moments but overall the experience is intensely frustrating, and no amount of AI-assist will smooth it out.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played WipEout Omega Collection on the PS4 and platinumed the game. This is what I think of Redout2:Pros:-Beautiful game, good sound design.-Customization is a nice addition.Cons:-Some tracks need to get fixed since if you overjump and try to land you phase through the track and crash.-There is a type of challenge called speed challenge in the game where obtaining even the bronze medal requires the skill level of the 95th percentile of the playerbase or above. I am currently in A-league and cannot progress to the rest of career mode because of 1 speed event. Same goes for time attack events but to a lesser extent. _childDocuments_.review: All the complaints people had have now been sorted. Difficulty has been reduced globally and speed events have been tuned down to the point where you can effortlessly 3 star them, and all the bugs and glitches have been ironed out. If you see anyone complain now they are simply not good at the game. If the known issues were holding you back from buying the game you should definitely go ahead and buy it now. Just remember that it takes time to get used to the steering, and when you do it becomes one of the most satisfying games to play. I've seen a lot of people start with "I'm usually good at racing games but". My brother in Christ this is an anti grav game. You need both thumbs to steer and it's not as simple as steer left to go left, steer right to go right. There's a steep learning curve. Give it a chance. Anyone with three brain cells and a pair of eyes will notice that most of the negative reviews are form Redout 1 players flexing their achievements and/or people with barely 2 hours in the game. It's a different learning curve from the first game. Get over it. It's not something to write off the game over. The Dunning Kruger is strong with people when it comes to this game and they have a hard time admitting they're not good at it. That being said, it has its pros and cons. • Extremely satisfying gameplay. The struggle is real in the beginning but once you learn to steer properly it's so damn satisfying to take corners and bends perfectly. I haven’t enjoyed playing a game this much in a long time.• When you do hard drifts, ships make an eargasmic noise that can only be described as what sounds like a robot climaxing. This noise combined with the perfect drift around a corner? *chef’s kiss*• The music is amazing. Although, I can see why some people might not enjoy the trance style soundtracks. It doesn’t need rock music just because it’s a racing game. I’ve seen people make that specific complaint lol.• Really cool, wide variety of tracks. Good mix of chill and thumb breaking circuits.• Ship customisation is pretty cool. You can change each part, the paintjob and livery design. • The tutorial itself is pretty difficult so you'll struggle to hit the target scores. You only need 3rd place to pass but even that can be a tall mountain to climb. • Occasional clipping issues when you land jumps.• Speed events have targets that are ridiculously difficult to achieve. It does get a little easier with better ships later on but some tracks are stupidly difficult nonetheless.• There is currently a bug in a certain track where if you die at a particular point you respawn several kilometers ahead. The AI seem to be able to exploit this but it’s only happened 2-3 times for me. One small silver lining is it’s not that difficult to catch up to them if that happens.• Not having a currency system to unlock ships and upgrade parts as you want might not be to everyone’s liking. You have to complete events to unlock these in a pre-set order. It’s not a dealbreaker though, because it doesn’t really put you at a severe disadvantage. But it does mean that one ship you really want might be the last one you unlock (sigh).  • Set boost safety to 5-10%. This automatically cuts off your boost when your health reaches the set percentage and prevents your ship from blowing up from overheating.• You’re not going to win events in the beginning because the AI have much better parts, and you’ll probably be struggling to stay away from the walls. But don’t get frustrated, as difficult as that might be. You only need 1 star (3rd place) to unlock upgrade parts. When you have similar parts to the AI go back and 4 star those events (win + trophy) with ease. • The first ship (Esa) handles like garbage. Thankfully, you unlock the second ship (Lunare) pretty fast, and it handles like a dream. Races will become much easier with this.• Once you’ve unlocked Lunare, learn to counter strafe. This is how you ‘drift’ around the track smoothly. Up until this point you’ll probably move both joysticks in the same direction to steer. Once you learn to operate each joystick individually, independent of each other, your skills will skyrocket. Try moving the joysticks in opposite directions when you turn and figure out what that does, and pick up from there. This is how I learned. • If you couldn't complete Speed events before, you'll be able to once you unlock Conqueror. I skipped all the speed events till I got that ship and then went back and completed them after.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a solid racing game, it's fun, but I don't know as it feels like a sequel to the first game. It's like if you took a sim-racer and put the Redout title and partial aesthetic on top of it. Bit weird. The music's *fine*, even decent in a couple places, but there are some tracks (looking at you, Tartarus Mines) where the music is a loop that lasts 10 seconds. That kinda sucks compared to the gigantic, bombastic tunes the first game had. On its own...a 7/10 soundtrack. It's *okay*.The game is respectably challenging, but it has a few places - namely A League - where it gets ball-bustingly difficult to a point where going for the challenges (namely qualifications and a few cheeky 'reach this number of meters travelled while airborne/hit this many perfect landings on a track with that many jumps to do so from') is honestly not very fun. I do like the gameplay loop a lot, but I think the devs should really give the requirements on some of these a once-over and consider whether some things are humanly accomplishable or not. As a big dweebus who platinum'd nearly everything there was to platinum in the first game, this feels like even getting *gold* is on that same level. Overall, a decent game, but if you liked Redout and are expecting more Redout, don't expect much.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Can't help but wonder what happened during the development of the game. Obviously I don't have a lot of playtime right now but I'm not really willing to go through this pain again until some major fixes. I've loved RedOut to death, even with all the early mistakes and issues, but the game did small things, not many things, and all of them equally right.First of all, the game's now basically F-Zero, but instead of always fighting in between health and/or boost you're first filling an overheat bar and then draining your health. I don't see a reason for this change honestly, given also how the game's not handling at all like F-Zero, and same goes for the design of the tracks I've played.The Boosting Tutorial is bugged if you try to play it with custom inputs, which they still suck since the first RedOut: how come we got customization first and not any kind of control input settings and schemes overhaul? And how did a blocker like this get out of QA? No clue.In the first race you get introduced to opponents who have faster and better ships than yours and you simply have to get over it. Goodbye classes and equal cars.Customization's not only on the aesthetics side, but also on performance. That'd be cool if only it didn't feel like an over-complication of an already complex game. And if you want to unlock the components you have to win basically every single race that gives them as a reward. So you're stuck with the path the developers decided for you. At least in the previous RedOut game you had some agency in those choices.Menu's worse than the prequel. The graphic design's downright bad. To whoever did the logos and such... If you ain't The Designer Republic, don't try so hard to sell this stuff to players. Music's ok at least.Regarding art-style, though, it's gone away from the low-poly almost voxel-looking assets you saw in the original RedOut. In RedOut 2 sleek looking vehicles and tracks are crashing with a really bland looking environment which misses the shading and styling of the previous game. This change's also difficult to understand, to be honest.Before you race, sometimes you get an half-a-minute dialogue regarding RedOut 2's backstory. Honestly they could've made them better, like in WipEout Pulse were a distorted voice tells you a one liner regarding the track you're going to race in... And if you don't care, you can skip it. Crazy, yeah. In RedOut 2, instead, you WILL listen to all this lore drop and you WILL have to like it.I find all those flaws personally way too big and "systemic" to be fixed in some kind of patch or update. This shift of direction is not something that's personally adding any value to the product, and if they're going down this road I don't think I'm gonna play this game or any potential sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Well there is a lot to talk about this game.Generally for just racing and multiplayer (I guess there are going to be weekly wallgrinds again), the game is ok. The biggest problem is the current state of the simgleplayer campaign.As for myself, I was quite excited for this game, as I played Redout 1 for 300+ hours and even made speedruns of it, but sadly I was a bit disappointed with the result.First the good parts:+ Racing and Controls. They did improve the controls and added another layer of complexity, to keep it interesting for those familiar with the first game. Racing generally feels really good in this game.+ Visuals have also been quite improved. The game looks a good chunk better.+ Some neat features like the game showing you what kind of corners lie ahead, or rewinds that shouldn't be necessary, but sadly are.Now the problems:- Track design: There are many problems with the track design:  - Every track can be driven forwards and backwards, but haven't really much been designed for that. For example, a sharp corner followed by an uphill-section is not a problem. An uphill section followed by a sharp corner is a blind corner you can't react to. You need to know about it in order to avoid it. There are multiple instances, where problems like these and more occur. - The next issue is with jumps, which are not well comunicated, as in: Where's gravity? Where do I need to land ? How do I need to land ? Redout 1 did a good job telling you where to go. Redout 2 on the other hand not so much. On top of that for many jumps the camera angle is just set up, so your machine, or other obstacles hide the track you are supposed to land on. That just makes jumps more difficult than they should be, especially considering the added complexity with rolling now. Sometimes you aren't even given enough time to react and just die if you don't know exactly what the next jump ahead is going to look like. - last problem with track design is length. Some may like them, but I prefer rather shorter tracks, that are better to memorize, which is especially helpful for newer players, which may not enjoy grinding a single track a dozen times. Longer tracks can be good, but not if the parts of the track aren't memorable, or even unique as some share identical sections. For comparison with its predecessor, the majority of tracks are about 1-2 minutes long, a few of them shorter or even longer than that. In Redout 1 tracks of that length were an exception aside from the last DLCs.- Next we have some visual effects, like motion blur and screen shaking, which are quite extreme here, but can't be turned off separately from other visual effects. I would like to turn them off, so I can actually see what's going on, since that's especially important when going fast- Single player campaign is a mess. There are many issues, I'll list them here: - Lack of variety. What I liked most in Redout 1 was how different the events were. Especially survival, checkpoints and speed were nice additions to your regular races against the AI. Here the first two have been removed and the last one plays very much the same as time trials now, except if you are exploiting the system. Add the massive length of the campaign and repetition on top, that's what you get in this game. - Customization but not: You can customize your machine with certain parts you obtain from events and a point system with limits for each event. That sounds nice first, but as you progress through the campaign, you are usually below the limit with all your best parts equiped, so there really is no choice for parts for your current events, except from the very end of the campaign. - Difficulty ballancing. The difficulty is all over the place, some races are piss easy, others are just unfair and despite having 6 difficulty settings already, they still added a system, that adapts the AI to your skill, making the game already hard enough for a veteran like me on the standard difficulty. Also the part system creates a new problem here. You usually enter events with a rather mediocre upgraded machine, but those were rather designed for fully upgraded machines, so sometimes it's not even possible to get gold with your current gear and need to get further in the campaign, to unlock better parts to be able to fully complete it, or to get a better score. To make it worse, you need to get good parts, placements and records to even progress in the campaign, where especially newer players can get stuck when they enter A-class.- Bugs, translations, other issues. The german translation is not really good, but while that's usually not a problem, there were instances, where the game failed to tell me what to do. Also there are some bugs, like falling through the track, or problems like getting respawned 5 km behind or ahead after crashing. Also the AI can't deal with some tracks and just dies, making it possible to complete events without touching the controller.Summing everything up:The game does have quite a potential, as the core racing is actually really good.However some poor design choices in the tracks and in the single player campaign kinda ruin the experience for me. Originally I planned on completing the game 100%, Now I'm not so sure about that anymore.Overall the game feels a bit rushed and I hope the devs will iron out most of these issues.I'll try to keep this review up to date.
