_childDocuments_.review: The original developers have reacquired the rights to Redout 2. A new review will be written in time.While I love this game and think it could be worth a recommendation in the future, I can't ultimately recommend it right now, it's not in a finished state. Though it's been updated several times, there still remains a litany of bugs and issues that make it impossible to obtain some cosmetics, the "campaign" is still an overly long, repetitive slog of copy-pasted events that lock cosmetics and performance upgrades behind a difficulty curve that's less like a curve and more like an EKG graph.After playing through about half of the campaign by now, here are its biggest failings, in my opinion:♦ I'm pretty good at this game after having 100% completed the first game, but even after 2 separate difficulty patches that make it more accessible, there are still huge difficulty spikes all over the place, no matter what rating your ship is at. On top of some events being unintuitively difficult to beat, some optional-but-not-really-optional objectives in those missions stand between you and some really cool ship parts. Things like "fly 5 Kilometers in a single jump" on a track with only one jump section long enough, but in the middle of nowhere above that section of the track is an invisible wall that will instantly crash your ship if you fly too high. Considering how central the focus on visual customization is, locking cosmetics behind optional objectives that feel infeasible to complete at times is more than just a minor issue.♦ You can still fall through the track or spin out completely at random, or crash out of nowhere due to invisible walls during long jumps, which in about half of the different event types, forces you to restart the entire thing, losing whole minutes of time. This is because:      ♦♦ Difficulty settings still only effect enemy A.I., which isn't where the oppressive difficulty spikes are in the first place, while the rewind function is completely locked during time trial, speed, & qualification events, which are the ones everyone is having trouble with. In the Arena Race & "Last Man Standing" event types, you can rewind, but only if you do so BEFORE CRASHING - If you hit the button a little bit late and actually crash, the event ends instantly, so you have to restart.♦ Multiplayer is completely dead in not only this game, but its predecessor as well. There used to be a small but passionate multiplayer community for the first game, but the devs completely butchered it with an "update" that broke VR compatibility, tanked performance with an unnecessary change in what engine the game runs on, and now requires an epic games account to access multiplayer. So now it's dead, too.♦ There are absolutely no combat mechanics in this sequel which was one of the main draws of the first game. It tries to compensate with "better" driving physics and deeper visual customization, but it's not enough, and those offerings aren't that great in the first place.♦ The visual customization is more of a sidegrade to the old system than an upgrade. Yes, you can change the physical parts of your ships, but every single part is locked behind events, and the color scheme/livery component is much much worse.       ♦♦ Since the overall shape of each ship can change, the liveries DO NOT follow the curvature of any of them, they're just textures slapped onto the models from above and below, as opposed to the first game where each livery was handcrafted for each ship to follow its shape and accent its features. There aren't more color schemes, more than half of them are reused from the first game, and while they removed the requirement of engaging with the Steam market to obtain rarer color schemes for a few cents each, the ones that took their place are just ugly, with no understanding of color theory and no proper allocation of colors to different areas of each livery, which is what made a lot of color schemes visually appealing in the first game.This game is not finished, don't buy it, that would only encourage the horrible design choices made during its development process and tell the devs that they can get away with putting out a product this underbaked.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Wow.... speed. So a bit of a background. Redout 1's largely meta-game was "Turbo-boost" in some shape or form, w/ Magnetic Stabilizer or Augmented Propeller (better traction vs. higher top speed and acceleration; better traction lets you carry speed better around corners). I think the devs for Redout 2 doubled down on the speed aspect.  A lot of reviews on Steam mention that the cars in this game feels heavier--and I feel like it's because they have a bit of Magnetic Stabilizer bolted onto each vehicle at baseline.  The fact that the game revolves around Turbo boost and regular boost stacking w/ an overheat / shield consumption mechanic takes the focus of the game onto turbo/boost management, which is the logical response to what Redout1 turned into. Knowing that, I think this was a logical and also a very well executed refinement of the Redout series from one to the second. A few big things though: 1) The AI is super aggressive even on lower settings. I hope the devs will just ratchet it down a few notches in upcoming updates. 2) I do miss the campaign of the first Redout game. I don't know how they'll fix this, except maybe to give us a few options for each reward instead of the predetermined one. So..... is Redout the sequel the same as Redout 1? No.  I mean, shoot. Mario 1 and 2 are very different. Many of the classic sequels are very different. Not every sequel has to be an episodic retread... Or you can just play more track packs from the first Redout and imagine a 2 sitting behind the title while you're tearing down the tracks on Mars or Rotura or something.Now, cosmetic trappings and mission progression aside, does the actual racing feel good in Redout 2? Oh hell yeah.  30 minutes of straight no-blinking never felt so good.  That sting in my eyeballs is just weakness leaving my body as I learn to go faster.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Overall worse version of the first game. The improvements made in this game are vastly outweighed by poor design choices. Pros: - Boosting system is better  - ships handle better  - ship customization is betterCons:Music: - Music is bland and muted. What happened? It's the same composer as before.Tracks: - Tracks are at least 1 order of magnitude worse. The game would be better off just porting the maps from the first game honestly    - many so far feel entirely uninspired compared to the first game    - instead of adding more levels, the developers opted to change parts of a level and give it a different name. Also added is "reverse" versions. These levels hardly work forwards, let alone when played backwards.     - tracks are generally played with 2 laps and the laps take longer.    - with longer and less numerous laps, and maps with overlapping sections of tracks, learning a map takes longer and is more infuriating - worsened on boss versions of the map which use ALL variations  so expect to take wrong turns into blockades frequently    - many times have boost pads been placed before bends, or worse before a bend with a wall missing so you go flying off    - random sections of many maps just have no walls for no reason    - several jumps you straight-up can not make without boosting, yet with many jumps if you boost too much or far you'll either not collide with the track, or miss it, or hit invisible walls, or hit other props blocking your landing. Am I not supposed to go fast in this game???    - magma biome maps are just awful to play as they exemplify the issues pointed out here    - cloud biome maps have several jumps positioned towards unusable sections of the map intended for different variations of the level   - several times boosting has lead to me flying off the map on turns, upside down sections, or hillsControls: - Game introduced "flight controls" for use whenever you use jumps or otherwise detach from tracks    - this mechanic controls absolutely terribly on a gamepad, requiring to yaw, pitch, and roll simultaneously in order to land jumps       - this is made worse by maps that have the landing spot on an angle and off on a different bearing than the jump surface          - this is made even worse still on reverse versions of the map - No pre-defined control layouts for gamepads for "arcade" or whatever defaults they had in the last game - During the unskippable tutorial campaign required for single-player, various moments that teach you the mechanics which require you to do a specific thing are BROKEN on controller, requiring you to bind and press the keyboard equivalent instead.Campaign:- Only a fifth of the campaign is actually racing against AI- Races against AI very rarely have more than 4 AI opponents- time attack and speed challenges are several times harder than the races in order to get 1st, and are basically the same eventThis game should have been better and can still be better, which is why I find this so disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: The negative reviews for this game from Redout fans truly baffle me--if you're a fan of the previous game, this is quite literally just more of it and with improved mechanics and physics! I adore the original Redout, it's my fave anti-grav racer of all time, and this is a worthy successor. While it's not *quite* as great as the OG, it has some brilliant physics and incredibly fun track designs, with a killer boost system based on F-Zero's classic "your health is your boost" mechanic. The only issues with this game are a bloated campaign mode, a weaker OST as compared to the original, and less "unhinged" track designs overall. If they cut the length of the campaign in half, or at least gave it more variety in the missions, I think it would be better for it. As it is, you'll probably get burnt out on it like i did, and come back later to finish it up. However, since all the tracks/vehicles are unlocked for arcade mode from the start, you can always just play the game for fun single player or multiplayer, so it's not really a big deal. Soundtrack-wise, people are right that it's not quite as good as the OG, but it still absolutely fits the game, and there's still some bangers in there (like the Mars or Tartarus Mines music). There's no tracks that I wanna turn off, there's just less that I wanna jam outside of the game--it's all still well-made and fitting. In terms of tracks, there's some amazing stuff in here (like Black Hole and Lunar City) but the majority of tracks are missing the utter deranged "you will die at 2000 kmh while hurtling into a planet" design of stuff like Europa and Neptune from the previous game. While this does mean tracks are easier to understand, and require less memorization and practice to win on, you lose out on that incredible, overwhelming feeling of "this is literally insane" that the first game gave so much of (except on Black Hole. that one is still absolutely stupid in the best possible way).I see a ton of criticism of the difficulty in this game on here, and I don't get that at all. This game has 6 difficulty options, and the lowest ones require very little effort to win on--heck, you can turn on all the AI assists and have your vehicle basically drive itself. I have no clue how someone could call this game "too hard" when all these assists exist, and don't have a single penalty for using them. They even added rewinds so you can try tricky corners or jumps over and over during a race, which is super useful and really makes the game quite forgiving. Overall this game is a lot easier than the original Redout, which was, quite frankly, bonkers hard--but in a way I enjoyed haha. Huge props to the devs for the difficulty options in this game!Overall, this game is awesome, and if you like the OG, you should def buy this--if you haven't played the OG, go play it first and buy this after if you like that one!
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is in my opinion a perfect illustration of the fact current arcade racers developers have NO IDEA of what they're doing and simply luck out into making good games. It's like a completely different team who barely understands what made the first one so good developed this.I wouldn't say the gameplay is more refined but just... different and it doesn't make it worse so whatever. The track design is damn ghastly however; and the presence of indicators for each and every corner shows they *realized* this and didn't even consider how problematic it is.Most tracks are long for the sake of being long, they all look like the same and mostly have no landmark distinguishing them, you learn them because you're driving and that's about it; there is nothing notable whatsoever about most layouts.To go back to the Redout 1 comparison: where did all the ambience go????? The menu looks like a generic template with a barely noticeable soundtrack; down to the blue hue commonly used in those. Things that were nailed down and contributed to the general feel of the first game like the track speaker or the general UI style are simply gone.The difficulty curve is genuinely horrible, going from races easily winnable at the highest difficulty if you're good to speed and time trials that are barely achievable and don't scale with the difficulty setting.A note on the races: some tracks are bugged (Tartarus) and the AI will randomly glitch through the track right to the finish line; sometimes just one opponent, sometimes the whole grid.I'm not gonna criticize the soundtrack cause subjectivity etc etc but personally I'm massively underwhelmed, especially comparing to the first game.As a conclusion: save your money and pick up the first game instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game having loved the first Redout, but it really falls short in a lot of crucial aspects.First what I think is great:- The ship Customisation and Graphics in general are awe dropping. After playing this I replayed the first Redout and there are Worlds between them. - Ship Handling is improved and feels great the twin stick driving feels so intuitive and fun and the track layout leads to you not only having to steer from left to right but up and down as well.- The Boost being tied to Heat / Ship health is great. It leads to a great flow where you switch between two states for the entire race if you want to go as fast as possible which are: 1. Blasting your boost until you only have a sliver of health left and hear the warning sounds bleeping and 2. Trying to stay alive on that sliver of health while avoiding barriers/other ships and managing the heat bar until the automatic health regeneration starts.Now where I think Redout 2 drops the ball:-  This game has a greater focus on flying and the steering just feels off. The right stick controls your pitch while also allowing you to strafe midair like on the ground.The left stick controls only your yaw while the roll of your ship is tied to the D-pad.Now I don't know about you but I only have one left thumb and if i wanted to, say steer the yaw and roll of my ship at the same time, which you have to do on some Racetracks and rather quickly I have to perform these weird finger gymnastics on my controller where I put my thumb on the dpad while my index finger controlls the yaw and my middle finger on the left bumper which is boost. This could be fixed by remapping the roll to the left and right bumper but then you would have to bind boost to one of the face buttons which wouldn't let you strafe and boost at the same time.The collision is also all over the place. Sometimes you can fly through the racetrack instead of landing and on multiple racetracks you just can fly through the overhead indicators over the racetrack but not all of them, sometimes you'll just explode on impact.Now you could say just turn on the Ai-assist on flying which would be solid but on some maps there are multiple paths you could take while flying and the Ai locks on one of the paths completely random, you'd have to be clairvoyant to foresee which way the Ai would like to go. So if you're not locked in to the right path on liftoff it leads to you missing the landing completely. On some racetracks it actively steers you into obstacles for no reason. If you miss your landing you loose the entire Race most of the times since the respawning just takes too long, if your're lucky your ship immediately explodes because you crashed into something and you loose just a few meters to your opponents but on some maps like the black hole one you can get sucked what feels like eternity into the void until you finally explode and respawn but by this time your opponents gained like 5km in advance because there is no respawn button. This leads me to belive they had to implement the Rewind mechanic to alleviate the problem, but on higher difficulties your rewinds are limited so good luck in that 10 minute race with multiple difficult jumps on multiple laps!- -Speed in which you have to keep your overall speed high for 3 minutes -Time trial which is time trial-Race, a normal race against opponents-Arena race, just like the above but if you explode you're out-Boss race, A normal race but you race trough all track layouts for the location-Elimination race, just like a normal race but you'll get eliminated if you're last after a round until theres only one left Now this all boils down to 2 Modes because there isn't enough to differentiate them from each other.Speed and Time Trial feel the same you're solo in a track and just racing against the clock essentially.Every Race just is the fastest one wins, so there is no real difference in if you loose after 1 round at last place or after 3 rounds at last place. Some Races also want you to complete a qualifying lap which is hilarious because you only gain 100m from first to last place in the starting grid where multiple kilometers of difference are normal, gladly you can skip them tough.- There are 6 unique locations all with a few track layouts and reverse courses, which is fine but the campaign is split into so many events that you'll race trough the same track 5 times in each Event type which gets repetitive really fast. This isn't helped by the fact that all Racetracks feel same-y because of the basic magtrack layout I'll call it. The Courses overall feel a lot more Rollercoaster like compared to the first Redout, which is a good thing I think the twin stick steering really benefits from all the verticality but It doesn't matter now if your rollercoaster is placed next to a black hole or on the surface of the moon. They all feel like the same rollercoaster with a different background, which I get why they did it the game is so fast that you have to have a clear center line that is easy to follow but I wish the locations would get more individuality. The Moon is my favourite Track because there are long stretches of it where you drive "offroad" on the bare surface which gives it a unique feel and I wish more racetracks would benefit from this. Why can't I drive over an asteroid that is getting sucked into the black hole or something? Instead you're bound to the same rollercoaster in the general vicinity to the black hole.-When you play the campaign you'll slowly unlock new ship parts that raise your power level and change the stats of your ship accordingly. Which sounds good at first customisation and building the ship that steers the way you like sounds great right? Well there are a few things wrong with it. The first is a minor inconvenience, you can't see which event unlocks the part you particularly want, which is fine sooner or later you'll unlock every event and see the parts you're missing. The second is more annoying. The parts are all tied to the Class you're racing which means you'll unlock class A parts in the A league and so on. The campaign though is fairly linear meaning you'll race through most races until you go on to the next class and so on. Now when you make the jump from Class B to A for example there might be a part that gets obsolete after 2 Races because you unlock it right before you get to the next class, or the might be a part which you really want which would fit your driving style perfectly but you don't get to see it because its locked to one of the last events of a class, so you'll have to drive the entire class with a different part to the one you actually wanted. And finally the last point which is infuriating in my opinion.You remember how ship parts are tied to power level? Well each class has a range of power like 600-700 where your ship has to comply to. Those who played Forza or something similar should be familiar. Now when you advance into a class your options will be limited to the few new parts you get for the corresponding class. And in my case I had to choose a new part that made my ship steer actively worse to the way I wanted it to but I still had to choose it because it was the only part that raised my power enough to participate in new events.Also the Multiplayer is Dead but that's not the games fault.All in all the Negatives outweighed the Positives for me and I can't recommend this game unless HEAVILY discounted in which case you may get a few hours of enjoyment out of it. I also apologise that this review has turned somewhat into a rant. English is not my native language and I don't know how to put my gripes with this game into a shorter form. I hope this review could be of some help to you even if it is a little rant-y now.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is incredible. It's everything I adore about Redout 1 but they cut away a lot of the chaff, like removing all the worst event types. A few new mechanics add even more depth to an already intense racer. It's fast, it's gorgeous and it's almost a perfect sequel in my eyes.If you like going incredibly fast and finding those perfect lines, this is the ideal racer for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's more Redout, which is not bad, but it's lost the gorgeous minimalist/low-poly aesthetic and focused track design that made the original great. Design choices made strongly in favour of a more arcade-y feel have resulted in garish visuals and track design that lacks variety. Ship handling sees a vague improvement but when every level feels like a rollercoaster rather than a racetrack, there's no longer any real enjoyment in pushing yourself to improve. The original Redout showcased the beautiful simplicity of mastering a track and chasing a new best time, but this simplicity and focus is gone with Redout 2. Also the new soundtrack is trash. Why would you ever get rid of Shahbazians, let alone forgo having an actual composer entirely? His work was a very integral part of the original and it's sorely missed.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Game runs great, looks great, feels great. On a 6700XT I get 110fps @ 1440p avg on max settings with no pop in when going at high speeds. Sound design is incredible, you need to hear it to appreciate it.They got rid of the worthless powerups from Redout 1, except they kept the turbo boost which everyone loved -- now it comes standard on every ship and you can STACK IT with your regular boost. Insanity.In place of powerups you now have a pretty impressive ship customization tool. You can tune the performance and appearance of each ship to your liking and the stats actually matter unlike RO1.Controls are more complex and tracks demand lightning fast reflexes. Many of the negative reviews for this game can best be summarized as "game's too hard". Like yeah, if you struggled with the 1st game you're gonna struggle with this one, it's not any easier. I will say some jumps are total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in that they basically require memorization of where the hell you're going. You will absolutely die on some jumps which is why there is a rewind mechanic in most campaign races on new tracks. Every turn, chicane, and ramp is far more clearly conveyed than in Redout 1, however, with a constant stream of visual feedback indicating upcoming maneuvers. The "sacrifice health as boost" mechanic is awesome. Looks cool visually with the ass end of your ship catching on fire and burning to a crisp, and on Tartarus it leads to some surprisingly complex decision making regarding how much you wanna abuse this mechanic, lest you explode due to ambient heat. It's all about being *just* greedy enough.The game's campaign is extensive, which makes sense because you exclusively unlock new parts/ships/cosmetics thru the races -- there is no more in-game currency to manage.Great game. If you enjoyed Redout 1 you will probably love this. I went into this game expecting to be disappointed due to the lower Steam score, but it turns out the majority of the negative reviews are just people malding that the game is too hard for them.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Seems rushed and unready, elaboration below.-Subjective Problems-* The physics feel all wrong, the vehicles have far too much grip and seem more like cars than the quadcopter feel of Redout vehicles. A big part of antigrav racing's appeal is piloting vehicles with low grip. Compared to HSX and Redout, these vehicles feel wrong, more like GRIP cars than antigrav.* The FOV seems very low. Everything seems zoomed in, as if the viewport is ahead of the point it should be no matter which view I use. I don't know what they did but it feels worse than in Redout.* The purple color of some pads makes them difficult to see. Every important track feature such as these should be very easy to see and contrast well with the track.* Rails are still the same color as the track in some places, they blend together and don't contrast well. This was a problem in Redout as well, except it was red and red in that game instead of the blue and blue of this game.* There are unskippable cutscenes at the start of every race which tell you unimportant bits of lore which don't matter to gameplay. No matter which buttons I mashed, I could not skip this in any of the races I played. These cutscenes show the track overview so it can't even be an excuse for hiding loading screens.* Starting the game throws you right into a forced tutorial, the game doesn't even let you configure options first. * Driver assist is forced on and difficulty settings are locked to easy until you complete the tutorial. The driver assist makes things worse, don't force it on people.-Objective Problems-* Control rebinding does not work correctly. In Redout, I use the 2 triggers on my controller for strafing. When I try to set the controls the same in Redout 2, the left trigger strafes right and the right trigger strafes left. Reversing the assigned triggers in the controls menu doesn't fix this.* There's no option to disable motion blur. My human eyes already have motion blur as a permanent feature, my monitor uses pixels and pixel response time causes a different type of motion blur, so I really don't need a third layer of blur added on. I cannot see ahead of me well enough when moving at high speed because everything is very blurry with no option in the game to disable this.* Setting some options to low seems to do very weird and incorrect things. Setting Effects Quality to low applies a terrible black dithering effect over the entire screens and washes out all colors for example.I didn't experience Redout at launch so I don't know if this is par for the course for 34BigThings or their publisher forced them to release months before it's ready or if they just flubbed it. As it is right now, I must recommend against Redout 2 at least until all of the significant technical flaws are corrected.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: To me it is obvious that Redout 2 is not as good as Redout 1. While both offer an unmatched sense of speed, Redout 2 falls short of Redout 1. I dont recommend getting this game until it is on sale, and even then not over Redout 1. Despite being visually crisper than Redout 1, Redout 2 is more visually boring, it has impossible difficulty, and is more restrictive than Redout 1. In Redout 1, every track took place in separate loading zones. In Redout 2 this is not the case. There are only 9 loading zones, and 3 different tracks per zone. This means that the game lacks the diversity of Redout 1. Every 3 tracks share the exact same skybox, colour, environment, and ending. While looking more visually crisp than Redout 1, Redout 2 is visually repetitive. Difficulty wise, I have 100 hours in Redout 1, and now 28 in Redout 2. There are some events that even on my best runs I cannot get within 5 seconds of the trophy. That is an eternity. I am able to complete every trophy up to that point, but then there is a difficulty spike that feels impossible with equipment gathered up to that point. I like a challenge, but not something that is impossible. Turn down the difficulty on the qualifiers when the AI cannot replicate the same times as what they achieved in the qualifiers. An AI will qualify 1st in 1:24 and then can only complete the track in 1:36. That's just silly. There are more annoyances when comparing to Redout 1. In Redout 1, you could fly past the goal and still get the goal. No more in Redout 2. Do you see a jump that would be cool? Well you had better hope it is intended. Specifically in the Marianas Trench there is a jump that is completely straight that doesn't skip too much of the track, but because of a kill plane it is impossible, it would be possible in Redout 1. This can be seen in every Redout 2 zone. Jumps that look like they would be cool, but there is some silly reason why they are not possible. And before you say it, no, I am not jumping to the wrong track.Overall, no series gives the same sense of momentum as Redout, and if you haven't tried Redout I highly recommend giving it a shot. While Redout 2 does disappoint, I am still having fun with it. I wish it were a little easier, I wish it had more diversity with it's tracks. When this game is on sale, pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, better focused than Redout 1, and the super boost is a nifty mechanic (and a good change over the first game where the speed powerup was the only viable option).But this indie developer did the rookie mistake of selling their soul to a publisher and is now going to be abused until being fired and closed eventually, when costs need to be cut and CEO bonusses need to rise.Never sellout. Crowd fund. Stay indie. Publishers aren't needed in an era without discs and distribution.

_childDocuments_.review: As a someone who spent 500+ hours on the first title I wanted to love this game but I can just hardly bring myself to play more or recommend it. It's just too blatantly hostile towards a casual gameplay.Credits to where it's due: it looks fantastic, environments are well done, controls are tight and it feels  like nothing else  - if you can progress through and master it.My main gripe with this game is its track design. Except for Fuji and Mars to some degree they are more like a rollercoaster rides rather than actual racetracks, and they are . You can't really race until you fully memorized them as they are riddled with sudden twists and blind turns, the turn signs are often plain wrong, there are random visibility drops due to certain in-game effects (this is by design, mind you) and sometimes the track contains some "gotcha!" parts that will kill you on spot if you don't know about it beforehand, like some sudden turn without a railing or a convoluted jump. So yeah, memorization is .Now the memorization is just pain since a) the tracks are long, b) they are rollercoaster-type tangled mess and c) they share segments with other tracks of the same complex. If you played RO1 then imagine each track as the Alaska boss with different track ordering. There are no distinct landmarks to speak of, you memorize the track by grinding it over and over and over.Speaking of the RO1 experience: remember cuts? Those are now actively encouraged as the game has a dedicated method to detach your craft from the track, so on top of all that you need to memorize and properly execute that as well.Track design aside, the difficulty is all over the place with bots being either competitive because they possess a better gear than your own or complete pushovers, the formerly dreaded speed/time attack events are just free points now as you can get gold even after exploding several times and the only echo of those ages are qualifier times that are far better than any AI can achieve on track. The career is a seemingly neverending streak of same-ish events that you must complete in order to unlock the aircraft and upgrade modules that are actually usable when playing against a human player. All the ship cosmetics the game boasts to have are locked behind those as well. The soundtrack is a massive downgrade compared to the first game's as it feels like 10 second loops now. Some bugs here and there that get really annoying when attempting some performance consistency (my favorite has to be the one that doesn't register your input after the rewind if said input was pressed during the rewind, like the acceleration, which you typically notice after a bit, wondering if you're going somewhat slow now when the rest of the roster overtake you). The dev team is completely unresponsive so there's no way to tell what is about to get fixed or when.This is the part where you either love the gameplay enough to do race after a race progressing gradually or you see it as a frustrating grind with hardly any reward in return. I sadly fall into the second category and have very little desire to continue.

_childDocuments_.review: A marked improvement on the first game. Feels incredibly fast and fluid. Tracks are gorgeous. Races can reward the player with new ships, a great range of visual customization and performance upgrades. Progression is a much tighter gameplay loop than in the first installment.Difficulty settings are comprehensive and it was easy to dial in a challenging difficulty where I could still win with a hard enough push on the track.The music is more generic than the first game, but I find it an improvement as there were a few tracks in the first game that I found unpalatable. Most of all, though, the speed feels so good.

_childDocuments_.review: Overview:This is coming from someone who has just beat the campaign. As someone who came fresh from the first Redout, I was expecting this game to be hard, but this was another level of difficult. You have a lot to learn from the start, and after that, you're at this game's mercy right out of the gate. I was frustrated at first, but over time I learned to embrace the challenge of the game, and I eventually became better at this game than I ever thought I could. I guarantee this will be your experience with this game. You'll learn to love it.Pros:- Controls. My biggest gripe with the first game was that you would slide around like crazy no matter what you did to try to prevent it. In Redout 2, that is no longer an issue, as the controls are tighter and the grip mechanic has been improved drastically, and thank goodness for that. It's still damn near impossible to get a clean lap without grinding against a side barrier or falling off the track at least once, but that's no longer a constant issue, and that makes me feel much better about my capabilities as an AG racer.- Skill and progression: You've probably heard this before, but you really can compare this game to Dark Souls. Same deal: High difficulty, higher skill ceiling, and a steep learning curve, but ultimately your patience will be rewarded with a great sense of improvement and progression. Never stop trying and you will succeed.- The AI opponents. Speaking of skill, you're really going to need it to stand a chance against the AI. Unlike the joke that was the AI in the first game, the AI in Redout 2 are good at best, and absolutely brutal at worst (especially during short events), depending on the difficulty you choose for them - perfect for players of any skill level. You'll no longer simply have a time attack with a few moving obstacles at the start. You actually have to fight the AI for the top spot.- The soundtrack. While I will always adore the original soundtrack for the first game, the devs made some great choices for the soundtrack in this game as well. I've never heard of Giorgio Moroder, Zardonic, or Dance With the Dead, but their music is still a great fit for each track.- Environments: The track environments look great for a AA studio release. There are plenty of landmarks to make each environment their own: The colossal japanese castle in the Mt. Fuji track, the futuristic pyramids in Neo Cairo, the chamber of giants in the Tartarus Mines... I could go on. They look great, and I'm sure they'll only improve over time like in the previous game, especially if this game gets the traction it needs.- Customizability: In the campaign, you can really make your ships your own, both in terms of aesthetics and performance, which considerably adds to the sense of progression I mentioned earlier.- Sound design. Just as fittingly dope as the first. The sounds made by crashing into an opponent feel real and weighty, just as would be if it were real. I particularly like the "WUOAAAAOUW" noise that's made by steering and strafing in opposite directions. Nice touch, devs.- AI assist. If that triggers you, don't worry: This isn't what you saw in WipE'out". This is by far the most impressive form of pilot assist I've ever seen in an AG racer. Each and every aspect of the game's mechanics are accounted for: Turning, strafing, pitching, rolling, boosting and probably some more I forgot to mention. It can all be taken into the hands of the AI, which can seriously help you in the early game, especially if your only frame of reference for racing games is something like Mario Kart. And to finally ease into the game and take the training wheels off and really show the game who's boss is such a good feeling.Cons:- The learning curve. Like I said, it's steep. You have to learn and adapt quickly to this game's mechanics and fend for yourself from there. The game does its best to teach you in the tutorials though, and the slo-mo for executing new moves is a nice touch.- Customizability is not an option in Arcade mode. Colours, liveries and performance mods are all exclusive to the campaign. No such thing in Arcade. So much for making your ship your own.- No pipes or teleporters. Seriously, why are they gone? Both of these elements added so much depth and character to the tracks they were on in the first game, and their absence in the sequel feels out of place and very uncharacteristic on the developers' part.- Framerate. There have been complaints of framerate drops and the like from other players, and my case is no different. I'm playing on a measly RTX 1080ti, so my case is doubly severe, but that's just a me thing. I still love this game regardless.Conclusion:Redout 2 is a fantastic homage to the greats. It accomplishes its goal of being immensely fast, challenging, and fun. I'm writing this review just about a month-and-a-half after release, so it's obviously not perfect, but I promise, if you love racing, and you love a challenge, even if AG racers are new to you, you won't regret picking this game up.Good luck out there in the SRRL, and godspeed to you, pilot.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this review by saying this is an awesome game. I played Episode I Racer and F-Zero as a kid and for a long time I've thought about finding another game like that. Redout 2 is obviously that game for PC. I don't believe there is another game like this at their level. Redout 2's gameplay is very well-done. It is 100% worth the money at full price (currently $30), both in terms of quality of content and length of playtime, as long as you have some experience with this type of game or are willing to spend time learning. If you have watched some videos of this game and thought it looked cool, yes it is that cool. A lot of games look cool but fail to deliver and turn out to be not all that fun to play, but this game is not like that. This game is very fun to play.Some people are saying the game used to be buggy, but I wouldn't worry too much about that. Maybe it used to be worse, I don't know. I haven't found anything particularly annoying. Just some trophies in the career mode that are impossible to get and some rare bugs with the game music. Nothing that gets in the way of actually playing the game content.I have some major gripes, though. I hope the developer reads these reviews.First of all, for the love of God, MAKE SOME EASIER TRACKS! Every track except Mt. Fuji is ****ing insane, and even the Fuji tracks are hard. Even the tutorials are filled with lots of twists and turns. I feel like this is just essential to the lifetime success of this game. You have to be able to pull in more than just elite players. There are other reviews talking about how multiplayer is dead. This is a great game, it's just too ****ing hard. (The tracks in the game are great. They're just super insane for a new player.)(Since I mentioned multiplayer though, if you are not familiar with this type of game, you do not really need multiplayer for this to be worth playing. It's a game about going super fast and zipping around tight corners. Just playing time attack with no other racers on the track is fun.)Make some tracks that are not a convoluted mess of twists and turns. Just near-straightaways and more gradual turns. Make anything sharp obvious and visible ahead of time. Make the tracks wider with more open areas and terrain. Do not put them in a DLC! Update the base game and add a C League between Trials and B League with just easy tracks. Beginner tracks are also easier to make because they are smaller and shorter. Just add more laps to make the races longer. People need time to memorize the tracks anyway. I bet you can make 3 beginner tracks in the time it takes you to make 1 expert track.People who are not super dedicated to learning the genre are going to give up when they get dumped into B League tracks with a wall they bang into every 5 seconds.The AI assist is not a good enough solution. It's just like turning the game into a movie and obviously people want to actually play the game instead of cheating.My other major gripe with the game is that the way the career system is organized, you are constantly forced to jump around from track to track and location to location. You don't get to memorize the tracks properly this way. For example, in the first part of B League they throw 3 different Mt. Fuji tracks at you and then throw the boss track at you (which is, as I understand it, a different track for each lap). It would be much better if e.g. every Fuji event in the beginning was the same Fuji track so you got to memorize it and then different Fuji tracks were introduced later with time to memorize them. The tracks are VERY complicated and the way the game presents them to you makes each one feel like a new random track every time.In the career UI let the player pick which track they want to play, and then show them events for that track instead of spreading the events out randomly.It would also help if there was a map of each track visible somewhere. It doesn't necessarily have to be visible during the race (which would be a big design decision), and they don't have to be detailed. Just show it in the menu.If you are a fan of this genre you should show the developer some love and pay full price and buy the DLCs too. It seems like they are doing a good job. The game just came out and they probably don't have a lot of resources to work with. Hopefully they can build out to a point where they can have some real long-term success. They just need to keep working on trying to build their player base, and a lot of that is going to depend on how well they can attract people who aren't already really good at this type of game. New players want to go fast, not bang into walls.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this is a clear recommendation for all those who like anti gravity racing games. But: Since Redout one is (until today) one of my favourite games, this is going to be a comparison. And yes, Redout one clearly winns this race.Why that?- Redout has the more brilliant and clear looking (hence) better graphics. In comparison Redout 2 has much more detailed textures but it also looks somewhat washed out. The simpler graphics in Redout support a better orientation. And that's what we mainly need in a very fast-paced game.- Redout has the more distinct steering. Controlling and timing are simply more precise.- In direct comparison Redout feels a little bit like an anti gravity simulator while Redout 2 feels like a typical/pure acarde game. Nonetheless Redout 2 is a very good video game. Which (not only in comparison) makes Redout simply a superb one!

_childDocuments_.review: Well I think I just found my new favorite anti gravity racing game.😄Insane sense of speed, gorgeous graphics and really good tracks design, it looks amazing and for the most part it's an absolute blast to play.Redout 2 have it all, lot of varied tracks, many different ships to pilot which you can customize and the game also have a pretty good soundtrack.Tbh while everything is in motion Redout 2 is stunning visually and IMHO it's one of the most impressive games we've had in the last few months.Unfortunately there's some balancing issues for the campaign mode.Biggest problems are found in the speed events, the times set by the developers for gold/silver/bronze medals are way too hard.The physics for big jumps that involve pitching and rolling can also be quite random and it doesn't feel right IMHO.It can get really frustrating to fail a challenge or lose a race by crashing into a wall or landing outside of the pre-determined landing zones because of these flying physics.On some tracks it's also very easy to completely lose eyesight of where we are supposed to go.If the developers can fix these problems then what we have here is nothing else but the best anti gravity racing game of the last decade.All in all Redout 2 is a good game but it's also quite technical and may not be for everyone.I have lot of experience with these type of games and yet I really struggle to beat some challenges in Redout 2.There are many different options for assisted controls but I'm afraid that ain't of any help for some races in campaign mode.Personally I play with all assists off except for the boost safety at 15% so I don't blow up my ship at every corners lol.If you love speed and have good reflexes then you will certainly have a great time with this game.The skill ceiling is really high, the learning curve is steep but if your up for a challenge then this is your game.I already know for a fact that this time I can't stand a chance to be in the top leaderboards lol.Join the Redout league and experience the fastest game in the universe !The trailer doesn't lie, I played almost all the worthy anti gravity racing games there are out there and Redout 2 is the most insanely fast game you can think of.

_childDocuments_.review: As this is a sequel, it is bound to be compared to Redout 1. Is it better?In short, Redout 2 is, for the most part, not better or worse - it's just a different game.The flight mechanics are way easier to learn, which is good for new players. I personally liked the old system better. It felt more like you were actually piloting something of a plane that's loosely connected to the track via magnetics. In Redout 2 it feels more like you're piloting a car on a wet street, at least in comparison to Redout 1. I loved having to actually learn to fly those things and it felt really rewarding when you reached the point that you can fly a whole lap of a boss track (meaning all tracks of one region stitched together) without crashing into the border.But I'd guess that this is one of the big reasons that Redout 1 wasn't the astounding success that it deserved to be - it was just too hard for beginners and I personally know multiple people who were initially intrigued by the game but quit after not getting to grips with it in the first hour. And the people at 34 Big Things do want to make money so the sequel has to have a broader appeal. So it's understandable as AG Racing isn't a very big genre to begin with.Boosting got a major revamp in Redout 2. Now your health bar acts as a secondary boost bar which allows some nice tactics, but overall I'd take the more classic approach in Redout 1 even if it results in a specific meta which wasn't overall liked by the community.Another thing is the landing "minigame": When landing, you have to match your pitch and roll to the track you're about to land on. If done right, you'll get a slight boost out of it. That is a really cool mechanic that adds to the stress of the race.What I actually dislike is the change in art direction. Redout 1 with it's low poly style and shimmering track surfaces looked so damn cool, especially after the upgrade to Unreal Engine 4. It had a distinctive feel to it and you could see that it's Redout from a mile away. Redout 2 tries to get a somewhat "realistic" aesthetic which IMHO does still look gorgeous, but it lost something along the way. Something of its identity. Track surfaces just look good now instead of breathtaking, and the variations of it don't look as distinct as they used to. The race itself was easier to read as well which was really helpful at high speeds. But as most things that's just personal opinion.In Redout 1 you earned money in the career and then bought ships in four tiers and upgrades (passive and active, one of each could be active at any given time). In Redout 2 upgrades are drip fed over the course of the campain which slowly makes your car/hovercraft/jet/whatever better.Body customisation wasn't present in the first game. I never felt that it was something that was missing as the design of the cars was really well done.But alongside the campaign everything is unlocked in Arcade mode which is nice if you don't want to grind the campaign.Redout 1's track regions all had a theme to it: Cairo was the beginner's area with long curves and spacious areas to navigate without much exiting stuff. Volcano had sharp turns, P-AR219 was all about speed, Neptune about jumps and so on. Yes, it wasn't THAT black and white, but each region had its feeling to it which was awesome.Redout 2's tracks on the other hand try to go all in from the first second. Already in Cairo (the first region) you're getting loopings, spirals etc. to a much greater degree than in Redout 1. The tracks aren't bad because of this, but they're less distinctive and blend more into each other. I'd go so far as to say that they feel samey, but that's just my opinion.Speaking of opinions: The Soundtrack is a big step down for me. Aram Shahbazians (and collaborators) made a phenomenal soundtrack for the first game which I still listen to at work and in my free time. Redout 2's soundtrack is mostly just some boring beats and some forgettable melodies. But that's just personal preference.I actually like the addition of lore to the game. Having a short clip touting two or three sentences about a manufacturer or region is refreshing and adds to the game.Race tracks have branching paths now. Nice addition.Despite my reservations it's still a solid recommendation. AG Racing is, as stated, a niche and I'd say that Redout 2 is still the best contender for the genre's crown on PC.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm usually not one for writing negative reviews or reviews for any game here on steam. I think after being a veteran of the first game on both console and PC I can speak on this game. Pros:-The customization and load-outs are really fleshed out and it feels like you can build a craft that is uniquely yours.-The environments are pretty and a huge step up from the first game. You can tell this game had some more money put into it.-Different types of craft based on manufacturer (sadly contracts do not make a return)-Lengthy career mode - No micro transactions (yet because I can see where they'll be placed)-Music ranges from outstanding to forgettableCons:-Different play-styles and ship builds are heavily discouraged against( I favor a highly maneuverable craft with a high speed stat) but am forced to play the meta-Difficulty is sore-spot for me in this one as I normally don't shy away from difficult games in other genres but the skill required here borders walk in the park to full on psychotic. (breezed through B league only to be hard stuck in the middle of A league)-Speed events are a joke(especially when the game has a broken thrust stat)-Numerous bugs are still found throughout the multiplayer and single player.-Track Design had a great sense of speed and flow in Redout 1 especially since they were more designed like roller coasters than race tracks now tracks are hampered by random bumps and jarring 90 degree corners.(Though some tracks retain that DNA)-Resource Management is probably the worst addition to this game. It feels like an attempt to add realism to what's already considered as arcade/ag racer to start with. Bring back the fun factor.- The upcoming ranked multiplayer is going to be a joke because track cuts exist and everyone abuses them to some degree (even me)In conclusion if you are looking for an ag racer that focuses on fun factor Redout 2 is not the game for you. It's specifically catered to those with complete mastery of the game and it's boost mechanics and penalizes those of us looking for a fun arcade experience with gimped ships that can't and won't compete with custom ships. The best parts for every ship are locked behind a campaign with a star system meant to penalize struggling players, sliding scale difficulty, and rubber-banding AI from hell itself. I for one will no longer pretend to like or play this game in a regular capacity, only to challenge friends. With a heavy heart I give a thumbs down.*EDIT*After multiple changes to the difficulty changes and DLC content drops, I think this game is finally in good state where both casual and pro players have a game they can both sink their teeth into.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is an interesting experience to say the least. Mind you, I'm not someone who played the original Redout, and I'm still trying to dive deeper into the anti-gravity racers subgenre. So, Redout 2 peaked my interest being its the highest speed, most complex anti-gravity racer on the market, and they have delivered those aspects. Yet, I'm left with a mixed feeling that makes me not want to recommend this game to others.-The control scheme is quite good. I understand why people don't like the much more complex controls. However, being there is no vehicular combat like other anti-gravity racers, the controls offset the missing complexity that weapons usually bring.-The game runs very well and considering how fast you are going, I don't notice a ton of pop in or streaming issues.-Great amount of ships with decent visual customization and upgrades where you can tune your ship for different categories.-The game is quite polished as I've encountered little to no glitches during my time playing.-The game has a good amount of content.-A great sense of speed, even on lower speed classes.-The menu system is not great. For some reason on you nagivate it and how things are laid out, I find it rather confusing at times. Obviously its not a huge issues but I can't say this menu design is winning me over.-The artstyle is god awful. The color schemes for the maps looks like visual diarrhea, and it can be very hard to see where the track is versus the background. It almost feels like I'm playing the game with a color blindness correction put over the whole game. The visual clarity is just not great.-The jumps and in air controls are awful. Who in their right mind thought it was a good idea for us to route our ships using the D-pad? Jumps come up so quick and so short that its hard to react in time, plus setting yourself up for the jump and landing it properly is not intuitive at all. Especially being you encounter angled jumps in B class is CRAZY.-Track design is quite questionable. Putting turns right after blind hills, putting diverging paths on blind corners, putting boosters that lead right into a corner so you are better off not using them, etc. I don't understand why the tracks feel so amateurishly put together.Overall, Redout 2 is definitely a fun game. However, I feel like more refinement was needed to get this in a better spot than what it is currently. If I could leave a mixed review I would, but considering the problems I noted, I'm going have to not recommend this game, which is a damn shame considering how close they got to greatest.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout is basically the goat of modern AG racing games. I would recommend it to anyone who liked Wipeout on Playstation or got bored with the more conventional racing games. I'd even go as far as to say I like its controls better than Wipeout's (might initially feel sluggish, but to me it became really fluid once I got rid of all the AI assists). The controls are rather complex and it's absolutely not easy to truly master the game (the career might initially feel easy, but it's not really representative of the difficulty as the challenges were heavily nerfed compared to early versions). However, once you do, it really feels rewarding.But it's not perfect, although, most of its shortcomings aren't very hard to fix. The biggest issue with it is that devs either abandoned it or took a huge break (possibly the latter, as it was recently confirmed that a patch is coming and steamdb is active again). That leaves it with many features (season challenges, community, ranked matches) in the "coming soon" status despite the game being released back in 2022. A more minor issue is technical - the game has potential to look really well, but it suffers from blur (crappy TAA?) and LOD problems, and could definitely use some better color correction. It's also quite demanding for what it is, and it would be nice to have FSR alongside XeSS for better compatibility with older GPUs (not even necessarily that old - my RX 5700 is in recommended requirements and XeSS cuts FPS in half instead of improving it). Could also use some more environments, as it gets quite repetitive throughout the game (you might think it has a lot of racetracks but actually it's 3 for every environment). Same applies to the soundtrack, though no one is stopping you from blasting some techno and DnB in background.With all that, I still recommend getting it on sale if you're really into the genre (or again, if you want to step it up from the usual racing games), as the development seems to slowly resume. But only if you don't mind it being repetitive and your PC is good enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it better than the original, contrary to the opinions from fans of the first game.For me the ship handling in the first game was just way too slippery which made all ships besides the Koennigsworth and Lunare Scuderia not fun to play. And I always ran the improved grip passive, so every Pure event became a chore when my mods were taken off.By contrast all the ships in this game have better handling and grip stats, and there are no events that mess with your builds. So aside from power brackets which your ship's build must fall into to be playable, you can set up your ship the way you like it and stick with it. That doesn't invalidate the different ships though, as they each have their own unique strengths and weaknesses.The main downside for me is some of the track locations favour a lot of blind corners, or they have really busy visuals behind and around the walls on corners, so you will find there are some spots where you will fly into a wall because the corner is obstructed behind a crest or it will disappear into the visual clutter. But after a few laps you should have those tricky corners memorised.I also like the boost mechanics and lack of active abilities. You get a normal boost which you can use as much as you want until your ship overheats and eats through it's hull gauge, and a hyperboost which is a little bit faster, but has a cooldown between uses and it heats up your ship slower than the normal boost. You can also use both at the same time to accelerate even faster, but it overheats your ship very quickly.Just like in the first game, the ship will self-repair after a few seconds without taking damage, so this means the key to getting better times is to strategically use your boosts, while avoiding collisions so you can boost more.Also the game runs at around 30-40FPS on low settings on the Steam deck, which is definitely playable. But the smaller screen and slightly worse ergonomics than an Xbox controller makes playing on the deck a little more challenging.EDIT: Late into A-Class I found the power level of my ships had plateaued as new orange mods I was unlocking were just side-grades. This becomes most apparent when I completed the event to unlock S-class races and received my first purple mod that didn't raise my ship power enough to enter any S-class races. But there is one purple mod that is given for completing the last trial which allowed me to start playing through S-class.It's a bit weird that they did that, but I just thought that was worth mentioning...

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great anti-gravity racing game, but it's not for the faint-hearted. The game can be quite difficult, and the mechanics and how they fit together isn't obvious from the get-go.The difficulty was quite unbalanced at launch, but the developers really listened to player feedback and toned it down so a more casual play experience is possible. So props to the developers! The developers really keep their games updated. For example, the previous Redout game was released on PC in 2016, and the last update was in December 2022.Visually, this game is oozing style with flashy colors, which is a good thing since you are going to zip across the many racetracks at enormous speeds and you still want to be able to see where you are going.The music is good, some tracks stand out more than others. For example, the track "Takeover" is awesome.There are multiple locations (Mount Fuji, Old Cairo, Mars Memorial, etc.) that each contain three racing tracks. I really like how they were able to interconnect all three tracks from one location. It's like you are racing on different part of one giant racing track. The racing tracks/environment feel distinct, and each environment has its own type of hazard and obstacles to manage.The customization on all the ships is great. There is a huge variety for cosmetic changes as well as performance customization. You can choose a ship you like and completely tailor it to your (play)style.In the options, there is an AI-assist, do not ignore this feature! It can really help you, especially with the more technical tracks and higher speed levels.In short: a lovely racing game with a ton of variety and a unique visual style, but with quite a lot of intricate mechanics that may scare some players off. However,  if you give this game a chance and let all the mechanics sink in, you will have an awesome futuristic racing experience!
