_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER: If you expect something like F-Zero - go away right now. This is nothing like it. Redout 2 is more akin to WipEout and AntiGrav Gran Turismo/Forza.Now to actual review. I want to preface this with a fact that i hated original Redout. I played it because there were really no alternative. I never liked F-Zero but greatly admired WipEout and Redout was the closest we had on PC. Obviously, my beloved "GRIP" was also a "kind of" an alternative, especially after devs added AG vehicles, but it was still quite not it. However there was Redout. And while i liked design, setting and absolutely masterpiece of a soundtrack there were two very heartbreaking "no-no's": Handling and AI difficulty. Handling in original Redout was something i hated with passion - ships felt like trying to steer a Dodge Viper GTS on ice. And trying to master this kind of steering was a great pain for me. But what was even worse than that - is the AI. AI in Redout was inconsistent, stupidly overtuned and blatantly unfair most of the time, making races infuriating. I know a lot of people had no problem with bots in RO1 but for me, they were an absolute nightmare to deal with. Good news is - Redout 2 is nothing like its predecessor and its a good thing in my subjective opinion. Developers got rid of stupid perk system, made Career more straightforward and consistent while delivering what RO1 did very good - insane speed. This game IMO improved on everything that prequel had. -Graphics became more realistic while unique artstyle still in place-AI was significantly reworked. Not only we now have 6 difficulties that finally MAKE A DIFFERENCE, there is a lot of assists to help new players. You can make this game as hard as you want, but it still requires significant mastery of its core mechanics.  -Handling is now precise and crisp. The ship doing what you want it to do. No more feeling like drifting in a Dodge on ice while raining. -Tuning and upgrades now significantly change how the ship feels and behave. You understand that "you made it better" while sometimes trading some stats over other. Not like in Original where upgraded ship is barely different from stock aside from speed. Visual tuning is also very diverse and allow to make ship look unique.Now onto more + and - points:-While ship roster is lowered, i think it is because of the new customization system. I hope we will see more than one ship-per-manufacturer.-Most of the tracks is very interestingly made and very fun to race on BUT at some point you face "Tartarus". This is the most horrible design vomit i saw in my life. Legit cancer of this game. Felt like devs sniffed their RO1 powder again. Insane blind turns, open parts of the maps you falling off from, heat that disallows you to effective boost because your ship will explode, jumps that designed by someone on hard drugs, clipping through map etc etc etc. And all this load of BS is encountered in Class B aka First Chapter. For me and other familiar with AG racing its a big pain but we can overcome by mastering this, personally i can now navigate on this maps with closed eyes, but newcomers ? They will break their controller. Other maps is fine. Except Neo-Tokyo. That second turn can suck my ****.-Jumps. Some of them fine, some of them not. Most of the bad ones - is those where you do not understand where you going or you need to heavily rely on air controls to even land. I would't say its a bad game-design choice, but it can be frustrating.-Boosting mechanic. While i LOVE the idea of combining boosts and trading off your health to more speed i understand that some people can find Hyperboost+Regular Boost+Heat gauge+HP decrease after heat gauge fills mechanic annoying and unfun compared to general "Press A to go faster".-Unlocks is a coin. On one side its exciting to get a new piece of tech or paint or visual part BUT they locked behind star ratings which makes secondary objectives "not so secondary". Personally i prefer money system.-Sometimes AI performance can be a little inconsistent, especially because their ships most of the time have better parts then yours, but if you restart a couple of times, they start to behave as expected. If you see that one AI blasts to the finish without a chance to catch-up just restart the race 2-3 times.-Some secondary goals is too hard, or should i say time consuming. Is it a con ? Up to you.-Performance of the game is hit or miss. Stutters and pop-ups appear often, but its UE4 general issue.-A lot of "Coming Soon" menu items for a released game. No dedicated Hangar to tune ships and no profile statistics page. Also no bots to fill slots in online lobby.-Soundtrack is bland. RO1 had better OST and i listen to it when playing. Subjective though.-Tutorial is lacking. It teaches you very basics but not really tells what to expect. Also most newbs probably never visit it again to play advanced lessons.Summary: Addressing the elephant in the room - most difficulty BS was fixed with patches. Time Trials, Score Attacks now doable and can be completed even by child with least amount of effort. In my eyes this game is superior to RO1 in every possible way and its pros outweight its cons. I strongly do not recommend this game for people who do not expect challenge even on "easier" difficulties, people who think it is similar to F-Zero, people who think their skills from other racing games help them here. However I DO RECOMMEND it for people who loves very fast AG racing and to some extent "realistic" handling, people who want WipEout on PC and as well for those who ready to play it for long time to master it. Redout 2 is a perfect sequel for a flawed original, at least in my perspective.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I almost never write reviews but I feel obligated to here due to how much I love this game and how much criticism it seems to have gotten.I understand that Redout 1 was special to it's community and Redout 2 feels very much like a departure from the approach Redout 1 takes on anti grav racing. I had tried the demo for Redout 1 and it really wasn't what I was looking for.  It had a very "hockey puck on ice" feel to it that I didn't vibe with and to be completely honest it almost kept me from trying Redout 2. Redout 2 feels a little  more in line with something like F-Zero where the ships have a more magnetic relationship with the track. Between the way the ships handle, the sensation of speed, solid courses, incredible sound design, and the BANGER of a soundtrack, this game gets the adrenaline PUMPING. I will say that I'm obsessed with this game's feel.Redout 2 a solid racing game it inspires you to want to draw great lines on the track. It is what I would consider a bit more on the "hardcore" end of the spectrum as far as racers go but if an intense experience is what you want with your anti grav racers then this game will deliver.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm ready to call it, Redout 2 is the best AG racer of the modern era. It perfectly walks the fine line of understanding the simpler pleasures of the niche genre, while not copping out by making an overly anachronistic experience (HI BALLISTICNG!!!!). Oh, and unlike its predecessor, Redout 2 has ample rumble support :p.When you get right down to it, Redout 2 has the traits that every AG racer should have... and then takes it one step further. Handling feels great... but you steer in a twin-stick fashion, which makes it feel more involved, and raises the skill ceiling. The Anti-Grav ships have all the character and characteristics you'd expect, but aesthetic and stat upgrades are separated out into two segments. The soundtrack slaps, but they also configured event-based dynamic music (think Mount Wario and that sick banjo solo :D). And of course, the most important part: the tracks are very satisfying. Redout is not satisfied with having just one track per location, but has a suite of them. You can race several different tracks of Mount Fuji and have very different experiences (and sometimes the game even puts all of the tracks together and has you race through all of them!). The tracks have a great "Roller Coaster" quality to them, with tons of visual spectacle to push the experience to 11. Even better, the boost pads are consistently placed on the ideal racing line, which is a great way to discreetly enforce the in-out-in style of racing.Honestly, calling Redout 2 the best modern AG racer feels a bit insulting, because this is a very simple genre... one that has been botched too many times over the years, or marred by lack of vision. Redout 2 not only meets the standard that the genre should be held to, but exceeds it in some key areas, which I think makes it a noteworthy entry in the oft-forgotten niche genre.Oh, and as of fall 2022, the devs patched out pretty much every major issue. It was a little sloppy for a bit, but it runs like a dream now!*BONUS ANALYSIS!!!!*One item I'd like to address are the jumps and flight in this game, which has caught a lot of flak from the players for being very difficult and very "gotcha". And you know what...? Yeah, they're very difficult and very "gotcha"... at first.... But, if you work your way through this game, you begin to pick up on the visual and audio cues that lead you to a death-defying, perfect landing. You'll hear the music start to drown out, you'll notice that the track suddenly got very straight for good speed boost opportunities. And over time, as you take to the sky (or the void of space, which is awesome), you'll realize that there's a barely perceptible time slowdown effect, you'll finally notice the hud display that tells you exactly how to land (HAS THAT BEEN HERE THE WHOLE TIME!?!?), and look out for the big yellow signs and markers that tells you exactly what your landing options are. You'll begin your landing sequence of rolling your AG racer until you're aligned with the track, then you'll strafe for the same purpose, and IF YOU'RE REALLY GOOD, you'll pull your nose up for a perfect landing.And.it.can.be.the.most.THRILLING.PART.OF.THE.GAME.Don't get me wrong, it's very, VERY difficult, and can be very BS, but once you know what you're doing, it can be immensely satisfying, and I applaud the devs for sticking to their guns on this subject. Memorization is absolutely a factor, but with the multi-variant tracks, it won't be reliable. You'll get caught with an unexpected jump, and it'll be do-or-die. And, really, there's a generous rewind system, and other assist options, so they're not *that* bad.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Is it good? Is it bad? Is it better or worse than its predecessor? I honestly can't answer the latter question. I liked Redout for the sense of speed, the absolute madness it represented. Without the magnetic mod, however, it was impossible for me to even keep myself away from the borders. Braking into corners always felt like a punishment. The mega boost was practically required as well, but could only be used when NOT using your regular boost at all. Enemies were punishing on some tracks, and got overlapped on others... even by me. I didn't feel a huge difference between the different vehicles on each tier.In Redout 2 the handling is better from the start imho, even with the high tier vehicles, which are all unlocked in Arcade, as it should be. The boosts are no longer exclusive, on the contrary, they are supplementing each other. Banking and steering feels overall nicer. I'm never fearful of my durability bar though, because I haven't even come close to receiving enough damage to ever be close to death. More likely is death through overheating while boosting, but it also recovers very quickly. New in Redout 2 is that you not only have to control strafing and pitch, but you also need to roll frequently during jumps, which I'm not the biggest fan of. No matter which buttons I use for rolling, I always feel like I need 3 hands, instead of 2. Something is always out of reach. Having to boost, pitch and roll at the same time, while also trying to steer in some cases, is 2 things too much. Using the d-pad is not an option for me, just too impractical, so I use the shoulder buttons, but now I have to boost with the face buttons (A for me), which means I can't boost and strafe (right stick) at the same time. Frustrating.The tracks in Redout 1 were all hand-crafted and unique. Every location was distinct, every track its own thing, and all of that culminated in the epic "boss" tracks, which combined all 5 tracks of a location into 1 giant challenge. A lap barely took more than 1 minute most of the time, a boss lap like 6 minutes. The tracks were re-arranged and put together with the help of portals. That always felt like a band-aid, like the tracks weren't really connected, a portal just bringing you from point A to point B at full speed, never knowing what's behind the portal, unless you already knew, of course. It was still good fun.In Redout 2 there are only 3 tracks per region ... but they can be reversed. I honestly haven't tried that yet, but I'm wondering how it's supposed to work, when you're usually jumping DOWNWARDS... I'm also not really interested in it, because the tracks feel a bit soulless, to be honest. They definitely "look" nicer (better graphics), but somehow they all feel a bit ... samey, even if they strictly aren't? Hard to explain. In any case, the 3 tracks now share ONE space in a region, meaning they also share quite a bit of their identity with one another. You will recognize the same turns and objects on every track, especially during a boss run, which now just means racing the 3 tracks back to back, no more artificial jumps, you just do a lap, and then the track configuration shifts to the next one seamlessly. That might seem better, but I think it's worse, because it robs the tracks, especially the boss track, of their uniqueness.Career mode is straight up better in my opinion. It's also grindy, though ... but Redout 1's "career" was simply a list of race events, one after another. This one has had a bit more thought put into it, where you unlock higher leagues and more parts for your fully customizable ship.The game also has a rewind feature now, because every racing game needs those. Seeing as to how unfair many of the jumps are and how unforgiving the AI is even on the low setting, I don't really mind, but I wanted to mention it. A way to correct one mistake in a race that takes 10 minutes is always welcome.Performance-wise the game has some inexplicable micro-stuttering at times. It's rare, but when it happens you will probably make use of that rewind feature. All in all I don't think Redout 2 is a bad game, the question is just whether it's worth it if you're used to and having fun with Redout 1. It's definitely pricier, especially the DLC ... and technically, you could argue that it offers less content, but overall this game with both DLCs is comparable to the first game with all DLCs.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write Steam reviews, but there's a limit before I have to write something. I've been playing games for thirty years since I got a NES 8bit and subsequently fell in love with Doom on PC. Redout 1 stands as one of my top five most fun games ever made. There are all kinds of games: story-driven, simulation, action, adventure and so on. Redout 1 topped them all in terms of being raw, immersive fun. Remember when games were supposed to be fun first? Redout 1 was a wonderful challenging flow state that felt like controlling the most beautiful, insane rollercoaster ride in the universe. Then I was like "wait... they made the best game... AGAIN?" And here we find ourselves. Redout 2 is a triumph. Games are never this fun to play. I like all kinds of games and I'm not an 'anti-gravity racer enthusiast' in any sense, but it's undeniable; this is just much MUCH more fun than you have in almost every other single game. Why this isn't ridiculously popular right now baffles me because this is, once again, one of the most fun video games ever made. I'm a video games history enthusiast so I've got a reasonable grasp of what's out there now and in the past. This is so addictive and so beautiful. If you can get it on a 144hz or above monitor then oooweee, it's utterly incredible to witness. I feel like some god of anti-gravity racing because it MAKES you feel like that when you start improving because it's so smooth and fun to master. Like I said, I don't write Steam reviews ever, but like... just buy it. For god's sake it would be insane to not buy this. It's so good. I love that they did this. If it cost a hundred pounds I'd still have bought it (please don't charge that much though). Hey Redout 2 devs, you guys are incredible. Your games stand up alongside the best ever and don't let anyone convince you for a second that they don't. This is my one Steam review. This is one of the best games to play that you'll ever be lucky enough to enjoy. Just get it. It's worth it. This never happens in games development. It's perfect. I love them for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say that I disagree with most of the negative reviews. It feels like they did not even know how to play Redout 1 properly. The game is great and quality is way higher than Redout 1. The game handles very similarly to the 1st game, I did notice that strafing applies more force on your vehicle and you can rotate the vehicle better at higher speeds which allows for higher speed slides. The new overheat mechanic is awesome. It allows you to use your vehicle health as boost, Health regen is decently fast but there is quite a delay before it kicks in after taking damage either from hits or from overheat. This interaction rewards cleaner racing because hitting the wall will delay your health regen which mean less boost. The game starts off pretty difficult due to the enemies starting with upgrades but after a few races you catch up quickly and it evens out. Even then the 1st place AI definitely knows how to play the game and the campaign is way harder than Redout 1 at the start. Have to say though there is quite a lot of frame drops in the cut scenes but other than that the game ran perfectly on my machine. In my opinion the game is way better than Redout 1 and there is no reason for me to ever go back.

_childDocuments_.review: On a surface level, Redout 2 seems like nothing but an improvement over the first game, with improved graphics, overhauled and new mechanics, and the removal of the dumb powerup system, but despite all of these improvements playing Redout 2 felt like an empty experience, and after giving it a long fair shake I think I have earned the right to call it mediocre, especially compared to the first game.For a long while I wasn't really sure what the game was missing, but I think I've figured it out.The most egregious problem is the track design. Despite the additions of varying atmosphere and road conditions changing how you drive, all of the tracks feel the same. In Redout 1, the different environments had what I think I would call different personalities, which led to the tracks varying wildly from location to location. In Redout 2 the biggest difference to me was that tracks were getting twistier and turnier, even locations that were specifically made to be as different to the other tracks as possible like the underwater tracks and the black hole tracks just felt like the previous tracks but harder. The tracks in the first game were also just way more fun to drive, which I was able to confirm for myself because 3 of them were ported to this game as vertex tracks. I believe this is because the first game's tracks give you a greater sense of speed while also being able to mix in (sometimes very sharp) turns while R2 is a maze of short straights and turns with the occasional "boost here" long straight. Its also worth noting that laps could be done very quickly in R1 tracks, sometimes being around 30 seconds while all tracks in R2 seem insistent on making laps last over a minute. I very quickly memorized the tracks in R1 but I don't remember any of the tracks in R2. The most questionable change is that now every location has every track start at the same section of road. I have no idea why this was done but it certainly doesn't help with my issue to remember any track in the game. Why do this? You don't have limited world space like in real life. Not only this but Redout 1 was able to make boss tracks work thanks to very cool instant portals and it was awesome.The way ships control has been dramatically changed, which might seem like a good thing because they are less floaty and feel more magnetically secured to the track, but I think I once again prefer R1. I do think this is more of a personal preference thing but I also think there are some R2 exclusive problems. The amount of speed you lose in R2 for running into walls is pretty dramatic, probably to incentivize braking, but the way the ships controlled in the first game was better for its speed; running into walls would slow you down but not as dramatically, so in sharp turns sometimes slamming hard into the wall and taking damage would allow you to go faster, which could lead to interesting choices and risks being made. The overheat boost and superboost mechanic in R2 seems like a great way to boost the overall speed of the game but it lacks the satisfying simplicity of choosing when I should fire off my very limited, but reasonably quickly recharging boost from R1 and I believe that these mechanics encourage the boring level design. Speaking of boring, because all the ships feature in depth customization, they end up being very similar to control even though their base stats are, and I'd like to emphasize this: SLIGHTLY different. Also, the game starts with assists on, and while I'm completely fine with control assistance in most games I do take issue with having them forced upon me from the start. I went to the options to turn them off but I never got the achievement for doing that, so for all I know there is some hidden handicap option that is on by default that I missed and couldn't find.Lastly and possibly(?) least importantly, the visuals of R2 are a mess. The first game very obviously looks like an indie game, but the low poly hyperfuture stylization gave it clean visuals and the tracks were very easy to see, both where you were and where you were going. In contrast R2 wants to cram as many glowing lights and floaty bits on screen as possible. The kaleidoscope of an artstyle does the complete opposite of dazzle and I feel like half the time the game is unintentionally hiding its own track in an attempt to look cool. Ship design has also suffered. In R1 every ship and manufacturer had a dramatically different ship design and they looked rad. For what I assume to be the sake of vehicle customization, the ship designs have been homogenized a bit, they don't look like they were made my completely different companies anymore, which I guess is kind of poetic because it feeds into how they all control the same now. Vehicle customization is also just not as cool as the dramatic tier differences R1 ships had.Redout 2 isn't bad, but its mediocre to me. It seems like a game that was inspired by Redout, rather than an improvement or natural progression of what Redout was.If you are looking to buy Redout 2 I'd urge you to at least give the first Redout a shot as well, I love that game.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I am speed.Great visuals, incredible sense of speed, beautiful tracks, insane gravity racer controls.This game is kicking my butt and I love it. But it's also due to the difficulty that this game probably isn't for everyone. Redout 2 just like Redout 1 is a game for people who don't mind racing the same track over and over in an attempt to improve.Some nitpicks I hope the developer teams will add/fix later:* Reintroduce VR support. Redout 1 supports VR.* Add the option of having the most important HUD information floating in front of the ship like in Redout 1.* A bit more options when choosing a track in solo time trials, such as the number of laps. (The latest patch fixed this for private multiplayer matches, but not solo time trials).All in all, this is truly a great gravracer and a love letter to the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who both struggled with and enjoyed Redout 1, Redout 2 is an excellent followup to its predecessor. The ship controls and handling feel so much more fluid, the overheat mechanic kicks ass and raises the stakes, and the upgrade modules and customization are a great improvement over buying tiered ships from different teams. I don't think we could have asked for a better sequel.Now that you know my stance, I feel like I should address some criticism (in my opinion, unwarranted) I've been seeing in other reviews:1. Speed Trials - This is something I've seen a lot of people complaining about, saying they're too difficult, and some even saying their progress in the game is blocked by them. They are, in fact, some of the most difficult content in the game, but by far the most important events you'll play. I would recommend to anyone starting out, do the Speed Trials first when you have the option. They make you learn the track: when and where to boost or stack boosts, what the most difficult turns are, how hot your ship can stay while going as fast as possible.Once you've at least gotten bronze on the speed trial for a track, you should ace any races, time trials, and last man standing events. You've mastered the track by this point, and you'll easily win not just the race, but usually the bonus trophies. All the skills you've obtained from the speed trial transfer right over to these events.2. "Losing" in the beginning - A lot of people are miffed about failing to win their initial races. You're a rookie and you have one ship, no upgrades, and you have to come back when you have a better load out. It's that simple. In addition, as long as you make 3rd place or better, you qualify and have stars added to your total, which unlocks more events.3. "The tutorial leaves players in a bad place" - The tutorials tell you everything you need to know to get started. More advanced tutorials on harder cornering, stacking boosts, etc. show up later on in the game, but I fail to see anything that's left out here which would give a player a false impression of how to play the game or leave them unprepared for the initial events. Part of playing the game is learning, and you cannot expect to win every race on the first try. This game is meant to be hard, and requires practice.4. The Soundtrack - I really loved the soundtrack from Redout 1. I have most of it on my exercise playlist because its super high energy and fits well into what I do. Many people are saying this soundtrack is not as good, decrying it as repetitive and "just kind of there". I know music is subjective, but I have to disagree. I've been enjoying the soundtrack immensely and it's implementation in the game.Overall, I'm impressed and have been really enjoying the experience so far. At the time of writing I've just broken into Class A races, but I thought I had experienced enough of the game to write something up. In the end, this game is really really hard, but if you practice, you will succeed, and your victory will be all the sweeter because you earned it.Edit: As of 8/9/22, the devs have lowered the speed trial point requirement for what appears to be all qualifying positions, however silver and gold remain quite high and still provide a good challenge, while bronze is pretty easy to get. They also lowered the star requirements for unlocking events, at least in A and I'm assuming B classes. If you were on the fence about getting it because of the difficulty, it just got more accessible while still providing a solid challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: My feelings about this one is a mixed one...Positive:I bought this game after getting hooked on the firs RedOut game, I really like the new heat mechanic that really challenge you and your patience and timing of boosting. Got the motto of "A un-melted engine is a engine not used" as the maps and races is a challenge to the bone.I'm a fan of souls games and appreciate mechanics that give you a risk/reward game-play.Negative:Repetitive, the maps are well made and gives the options of several tracks in the same map, this is good, but the races and types of challenges fall flat.24h inn now and the game feel like a grind...Cosmetics are locked behind getting every race perfect and I struggle to see how this is "engaging game-play".Swapping back to my favorite ship after half the game just to see there is no cosmetics unlocked is a pain when you realize many of the pieces is just reused parts from the other ships. Unlocking a piece from a different ship as a cosmetic is nice, but unlock it for ALL the ships and don't require the player to grind for the same piece for x ships.On top of the grind, if there is a specific piece you want, good luck figuring what race you need to complete.Otherwise:I miss the contracts from the original game, gave the game some more meaning to the races, you feel like there was interest in the races other than "Oh, you completed another race... here, have this bent metal we found behind the dumpster, good job".There already is names on the different racers, USE IT, give us some challenges against a specific rival. Tie them up to their region, give them personality. Take a look at the old LEGO Racer, your competition had character and gave a reason to beat them.Cosmetically pieces should be accessible, they have no impact on the performance of the ships and allowing the player to customize and personalize the ship is something that made the cars in NFS U2 a gem people still yearn for.The game and the mechanics is a blast, but after a while it falls flat and the replay-ability is debatable...I would recommend this game, but hope the dlc, some polish and balancing can aid this to really shine.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I played entirely through Redout 1 and really enjoyed that but 12 hours into the Redout 2 and I find I'm no longer enjoying a session after half an hour out of various annoyances.The sense of "go-fast" is still absolutely there and it looks pretty. but...I can't quite put my finger on it about the tracks but they aren't as good. It feels like there are way more blind turns and unexpected corners. Some tracks just have terrible, awful flow. Also some of the jumps in the game are very poorly implemented; with default assists there are some jumps that would throw me completely off if I didn't have the exact correct inputs to either go along with, or counteract the assists. Not to mention that some of the landing zones were not obvious until most of the way through the jump.The main thing that is killing it for me is that the difficulty is horribly inconsistent. Most of the solo events like speed or time trial I am blowing away the gold scores, meanwhile I am getting smoked when racing the AI. There are some races where I'm boosting like crazy and still can't reach 1st. I even sat down and tried 10 different ships/configurations for the same race and couldn't find anything that beat the AI on anything but the lower difficulties. And the qualification races... forget it, qualifying first might as well be impossible.If there game were properly refined then I'd totally recommend it, but as it stands, I just can't.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is hard because of the first few levels, while you still don't have the hang of it. Once you 'got it' it gets easier. This is why you will see a lot of negative reviews. If you're a beginner, try to boost (boost+ megaboost) until your health is low, then let your temps get down by being careful with the boost, after a while your ship auto-repairs if you didn't bump or overheat, your megaboost should almost be up again, repeat the cycle. This is pretty easy to do and will help you get through the first barriers. The devs should really look at the difficulty though.This is a very different game from redout 1, while still giving the same sensations. The devs made the ships grippier to fix the first game's wall problem (since the ships were too slippery you had to wallgrind, which was then nerfed, making the game feel too slow sometimes). This will not please everyone, but I really like it. An other change is the boost system, that now allows you to reach stupid speeds at the cost of your health by intentionally overheating. That's amazing. You just keep burning your health to go faster and race clean to get health regen. Genius system that encourages paying attention, knowing the tracks, and rewards you with adrenaline and breakneck speeds.Ship customization is awesome, some ships really feel completely different (try out the Arcade Conqueror, I beg you!).The soundtrack and visuals are amazing, even better than R1, although the low-poly aesthetic of R1 will be missed by some. This includes me but the environments are also better detailed, and the sound mixing is really cool.My only complaint is that I miss the old redout HUD that was around the ship, especially since now you have to micromanage your health and temps, which forces you to look at the new HUD placed on the bottom of the screen while driving at 1200km/h...

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved the first Redout, but I sadly cannot recommend this one.I can tell there is a genuinely great game trying to come out here, but it's buried under a pile of utterly baffling design decisions. The developers shook up the racing mechanics from the first game by removing powerups and the recharging energy meter and replacing them with a heat mechanic - you have a regular boost and a super boost, the more these are used the faster you go (obviously) but you build up heat as you do so and too much will drain your health until you explode. It's a great risk/reward dynamic that mirrors the boost system from F-Zero and there is genuine thrill in trying to get your car as close as humanly possible to the edge without accidentally blowing yourself up. Which I did, frequently.However I found there was a little too much emphasis on 'find the one section of the map where you can stack boosts the hardest', go at ridiculous speeds for a few seconds then leave everyone in the dust. Redout emphasised proper boost timing too, and so does F-Zero, but I find it a little too overbearing here to the point it feels like I have to just remember 'that one spot' on the levels. Redout 1 had more emphasis on its steering mechanics, which I liked. I also wish they played with the heat mechanic more: why not make your cars dissipate heat faster if you're underwater? What about a fork in the road where one lane is faster but has extremely high heat, and another is slower but safer? Maybe it appears in the later levels because I don't think I got that far after six hours.However this is a relatively minor quibble and if this was my only criticism I would still be playing. What got me to stop playing was the frustration I felt with the game's design. First off, the progression system is absolutely awful. You have  car unlocked at the start with no choice of which (unlike Redout 1, which let you pick one free car of your choice), and I didn't unlock a second one for several hours. Redout 2 has a much deeper customisation system than the first game - there are more cars, more ways to adjust its stats and new cosmetic options, but the problem is they are all locked behind specific career events. Want to race a specific type of car? Too bad, you'll have to play for 6 hours and plow through lots and lots of events, unlocking minor cosmetic options you don't give a toss about just so you can finally unlock that one car. I've heard someone describe the progression system as 'glacial' which is ironic for a game all about speed.Then there's the game's difficulty: I tend to enjoy the challenge of a difficult game, but it feels very frustrating here. Rival cars are merciless even on relatively low difficulties (I played on 'Redout' difficulty, for reference, which is 4/6) but I can't see why they are so good, they just seem to be much faster for no good reason. I eventually got good enough to beat them fairly consistently, but then the time attack challenges are even more brutal to the point that I couldn't understand how the gold medal was even achieved. It often feels like you are one mistake from irredeemable disaster and a restart.It doesn't help that the track design is just plain evil at times. One level required me to boost and pitch up to clear a jump (better hope you are not overheating when you see one) and  required me to make a sharp left turn after landing the jump or fly straight off the edge. This happened with almost no warning. Turns out I needed to turn, brake and strafe simultaneously to avoid falling off, which is fine when you know to do it, but it feels like a 'aha, gotcha!' moment by the game and not a genuine challenge of my reactions.Fortunately there is a rewind feature where you can rewind up to three times per race and undo a mistake, but some tracks are so tricky often I ran out of rewinds and then just had to restart. And you can't rewind during a time attack mission (why not?!). Speaking of time attack, they only give you one lap to set a record. Why? Why can't I just keep going around, practising the level until I get better and get a good lap? Redout 1 did this and gave you three laps to set a good time. I can't understand why this was changed."I can't understand why..." is actually a phrase I think of a lot when describing this game. I can't understand why the game ditched the money-based progression system from Redout 1. I can't understand why they put so much lore into a game about driving fast cars, then make you listen to it whenever you find a new area or unlock a new car. I can't understand why the Gold medal requirements in the  are so bloody hard. I can't understand why the speed event has been changed so it plays the same as all the other events. I can't understand why the loading screens show lore instead of driving tips. I can't understand why they added rolling mechanics on jumps so now I have to remember to boost, aim up, then barrel roll left while simultaneously strafing right and turning to keep my car straight.These decisions are so baffling to me that I am semi-convinced that someone on the development team is actually deliberately trying to sabotage Redout 2 from within, as if he's emulating The Hood from Thunderbirds. Because when the game stops being annoying, it has these moments where it comes alive and I have a great time boosting through turns and toeing the line between the fastest car on the track or being the deadest car on the track. And this makes me think the developers do actually know what they're doing most of the time.Unfortunately I eventually had to throw in the towel after experiencing some really infuriating glitches. On one level the AI racers would magically jump about 3-4km ahead on me after one specific turn in Lap 1 with more consistency than my own bowel moments. Somehow I won that event, but then two events later my car kept falling straight through the track after a long jump and I knew I had enough.I hope the developers make some tweaks because I do think this game could be amazing, but cannot recommend in its current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game really doesn't want you to have fun. While gameplay mechanics and visuals are very good, almost everything else is designed with tiny group of elitist AG racing sweatlords in mind.Redout 2 has many difficulty levels, second in terms of difficulty being "Chill", which is very unfortunate naming as this game has zero chill. It is so poorly balanced that even on the easiest difficulties times and scores required for some trials are almost impossible for regular players. Clearly, these requirements don't scale with game's difficulty, which is just a terrible design. What is the point of having such wide difficulty selection then?I play many racing games and enjoy a challenge, but with Redout 2 I don't get what the ♥♥♥♥ it wants me to do to improve. Tutorials suck at explaining basic game's mechanics and lowering difficulty doesn't help as it doesn't scale properly. Enemy AI is all over the place, sometimes staying miles behind, other times becoming ballbustingly hard to catch up to.Track are just as inconsistent as enemy AI. They are visually stunning and some of them have nice flow and fun, challenging technical parts, but most of them are filled with "gotcha" moments where you have not chance to react unless you have the track fully memorized.Racing itself feels great and each ship is very different, but game puts way too much emphasis on constant boosting. You have no chance of winning unless you are boosting, double boosting and overheating all the time. Clean racing line is secondary to boosting, devs seem to be too in love with this mechanic.Flight mechanic and controls for them are absolute garbage. Your ship feels unresponsive mid flight and landing your jumps is at times made super tricky as the tracks are, again, designed to screw you over.Music in Redout 2 is mind numbingly monotonous, it gets annoying really fast and I replaced it with my own playlist.I have reached the final league SRRL, but I'm not going to finish it. Not just because of all aforementioned annoyances, but mostly because this game grossly overstays its welcome. At this point I have seen basically all Redout 2 has to offer and instead of wrapping it up now, they decided to throw extremely long (2-3 laps of Boss events) at you. This is a huge chore and drags down progression even more.Overall I can't recommend Redout 2 to anyone outside of AG racing elitists. Not sure what the devs had in mind, making a game so unapproachable and unfun in its design. I mean, who is this for really? I believe racing games should be scalable so anyone can enjoy them, as not everyone is gifted with some godly reflexes. Looking at this game's reception and non-existing multiplayer scene I'd say gambling on making a game dedicated to hardcore players didn't pay off. Serves them right I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: Now that 34BigThings got their hands back onto their game and are back at providing updates, I can finally recommand this lightheartedly.Redout 2... Is pretty much the one racing game, all kinds confounded, on which I spent the most time (200+ hours to this day).It did start rough for me: its unique strafing mechanic was a hard one for me to get used to. But once I took the time to fully apprehend it, oh boy... This is when I started improving so fast and so noticeably that it became intoxicating!For some reason, Redout 2 is very good at letting you see and feel how far you have come, and how much you have improved. And what is wonderful about it, is that you can still progress more! And after 200+ hours still have that very same feeling of improvement, that very same satisfaction. And as the game does not feature any weapons, it entirely focuses on your skill and boost management, making it all the more satisfying and the less prone to be affected by luck.Aside from that, the game is gorgeous. The sensation of speed, very much there! The twists, turns and loopings, jumps, and reversed tracks that make the fantasy of Anti-gravity racing are not only present, they are everywhere! (when most other games have it but it mostly remains flat until some apex part of the track).The ships all have their own personality, and yet they all have a huge number of customization parts and paints to make it feel more like YOUR version.How to talk about it though without mentioning the game's overwhelmingly kind and helpful community? Whether they dropped on my Twitch kindly feeding me advice, or on their Discord server with people always ready to watch you, provide feedback, and talk, whether it is from other players or the devs themselves... The Redout 2 community made me feel supported and at home, and I owe them a huge lot of thanks.Obviously, the game has a few cons. Like the multiplayer mode unfortunately not allowing people to play all the race modes that exist, the absence of dedicated servers can be a detriment since the host may have some advantage on their opponents... But overall they are very far from undermining the great experience that this game proposes.I could spend the morning praising Redout 2 in this review, but it must end somewhere.All I can say is... If you like to go fast, to drive on technical and impressive tracks, to be challenged by both the curves and speed... Then Redout 2 is made for you.See you on the tarma-... Sorry. On the Magnet-tracks!

_childDocuments_.review: Frustratingly close to being the game of my dreams but falls short in far too many ways, the most significant being that the racing is simply not fun.I'm a UI/UX designer with almost 10 years in game development. I also played f-zero games extensively and used to be competitive in time trial. The difficulty does not bother me so much (I probably have not played enough to encounter the balance issues), but there are numerous other design choices that do.For me, the main problems are UX related. The tutorial is bad of course (which doesn't help), but when it comes to the driving experience I think the main problem is people are experiencing cognitive overload. In other words, there is too much to think about / pay attention to all at once. And at a very fast pace.  For example here is a list of things going on the players need to pay attention to - two stick steering mechanics with up and down tilt, 2 different boost mechanics that need timing, 3 changing bars related to boosting and health, overheating, redout/blackout, jumps, boosters on the track, navigating turns and finding a good drivers line, other AG ships. That's not all, there is also a tun of visual and audio noise to distract the player as well, such as dense visual patterns and details on the track making it confusing to see, distracting overlay detailed backgrounds, blur, boost and overheat effects, UI direction prompts and more. There is too much distraction and the player cant simply focus on driving the track. Sometimes less is more. Trackmania is a good example of a game that's very easy to pick up and play with simple mechanics. It also becomes very hard as it progresses and an ‘art’ to master (it's just an example, redout should not be trackmania). I should also note, that this was not a problem for me in games like f-zero GX which also had boost mechanics.Other issues I encountered were bugs such as my vehicle clipping through the middle of the track on landing a jump. Lack of modes (some seem to be unfinished for an earlier release). Poor menu and UI copy design. Poor graphic design. No fast restart on time-trial. I cant see my personal best on the time-trial menu screen. Unskippable intro cutscenes. Lack of settings and accessibility options. Some issues from Redout one carry over to this game such as the tracks are not as memorable as tracks from other AG games like f-zero, they tend to look the same and I forget what corner should be coming up next. I also think it's ok to have some thinner tracks but over all the game could benefit from slightly wider tracks, especially with so many people complaining about difficulty. I prefer the 3-lap time trial from f-zero (I also prefer their more elegant boost system). I still feel like I want to zoom out the camera more. As other people have mentioned, the soundtrack is also a downgrade.Visually I think the game looks better, especially the ships. However, as I mentioned earlier they can be very distracting as the direction puts form before function.I really want to love Redout but there are just too many issues, I just don't find it fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, but I still prefer the first. While there are more tracks in this one, each location has sections that get reused for each track, which makes the three tracks per location blend together and feel a lot more samey, and it often tricks your muscle memory (at some points you're meant to turn left on one track, but if you're in a different track on the exact same spot you have to turn right). Levels feel a lot denser visually, and since parts of different tracks are on screen at the same time it's sometimes confusing to figure out where you need to go in a split-second - this is especially bad on certain flight sections, the game will often throw you off of ramps and it will take a couple dozen runs per track until you remember where you're supposed to be flying to. The campaign is  longer, which together with the less distinct tracks makes the game overstay its welcome by quite a fair bit. The amazing sense of speed is still there, but I won't be doing all Platinum trophies in this one unlike in Redout 1, and I'd recommend that one over the sequel provided you haven't played either.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is being done dirty by people who have no idea what they are getting into. Redout 2 is not a shovel ware casual racer like you see crop up in your steam feed all the time. This game is made by veterans of the anti-grave sci-fi racing subgenre and the supposed hard difficulty is really just barely harder than the starting point of most games in that genre 10 years ago.My biggest advice is this, if you are new to the genre, or haven't played one in a decade or more, don't go in expecting to place first on your first race, its not even required to progress. That said I haven't played a game like this in at least 15 years and I chose to up the difficulty from it's default setting.Maybe one could argue that the starting diff needs to be lower, but then you run into the issue of the game not being fun. So if you are finding the game hard, clear the first real race, just place 3rd, then go to the diff settings and lower them, we all start somewhere. There is no need to demand the game hand you a first place win on every race, challenge yourself, and you will find a game that rewards your skill growth. Focus on your lap times, not the other racers, just try to take that one corner a little faster and smoother. This is where the joy of racing is.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could write a mixed review because there is a lot that needs to be said on both sides of Redout 2. There is a lot to love with Redout, but I can't lie, the game has some serious problems. The glaring issues, combined with a pretty severe lack of transparency from the development team give me some pretty bad vibes. That all being said, I want to break down piece by piece what's up with Redout 2, whether you are a hardened Redout 1 veteran, or a newcomer to the franchise.Pros:-Environments: Fans of the first game likely loved the colorful and interesting venues of the SRRL and everything you loved there has been cranked up to 11 with improved graphical fidelity in RO2. The locations are genuinely interesting, and also offer some unique environmental conditions. The environment includes temperature, gravity, and other hazards, including dust storms and geothermal vents, each posing a genuine unique consideration for each zone.-Heat and energy: In RO1, you had an energy meter that was responsible for limiting your boost capabilities. RO2 has moved away from that and allows you to boost as much as you want, but with a cost. If you go above a limit on heat, you start melting the hull to boost further. Melt through your hull, and the results should be pretty obvious. This change places a greater amount of skill on managing heat and health, something the first game struggled with. There is more to it now than memorizing when to super-boost. Speaking of which...-Reworked boost and power-ups: In terms of power-ups, we have no power-ups, and that's a good thing. In RO1, if you were ever taking anything other than AP and super-boost you were a lunatic. RO2 has just removed the choice entirely and streamlined the boost system. You can use your regular boost, your super boost, or both at the same time. Each of these choices comes with different considerations for cooldown and heat management and makes a unique challenge.-Improved customization and ship selection: RO1 featured 6 (7 with DLC) teams, some better than others. RO2 extends your selection of teams to 12, and each team has unique strengths and weaknesses that make each one genuinely balanced and suited to different environments. Your Buran might not perform on the breezy hills of Fuji, but it will haul ass in the blazing Tartarus Mines. On top of ship variety, each ship can be further customized both functionally and cosmetically via parts unlocked through the campaign. More on that in a moment.-Flow and feel: RO1 and RO2 both excel in this regard. When you’re in the thick of a race, the game is simply a dream to play. The sense of speed when boosting is incredible, accompanied by extraordinary sound design that just makes your ship feel badass. The satisfaction of perfectly blazing through a turn at high speed is probably worth the whole game to me. The handling and cornering are really cool, and a unique challenge if you are approaching Redout from a background in traditional racing games as opposed to AG racing.-New player accessibility: Although still a tough game to get into, and still maintaining an extremely high skill ceiling, RO2 is more accessible than its predecessor by a mile. It has actual tutorials, poorly designed as they may be, an AI assist feature that helps you maneuver if you haven't mastered Redout's advanced movement yet, and my personal favorite feature is the new turn indicator. The turn indicator in the top middle of the screen makes it much easier to learn levels and memorize where the twists and turns are.Neutrals:-Music: RO1 had a lovely soundtrack by Aram Shahbazians, and really gave the first game a lot of charm. I love hardcore drum and bass as much as the next guy, but there was a certain charm Aram's soundtrack. The new soundtrack feels a bit repetative, with just loud bass and drums overshadowing everything else. They both are excellent in their own ways, but your mileage may vary in this regard.-Progression based unlocks: The good news is you don't have to grind campaign for money to get the things you want anymore. the bad news is the things you actually want may be locked at the end of an extraordinarily long and brutal campaign, with no way to get them sooner. Did you want to fly Mantis? Gee that sucks, sink 100 hours into the campaign and earn it. Parts for stat and cosmetic customization are similarly gated, but this isn't as big a deal in my opinion.Cons:-Speed Challenges: If I'm being honest, speed challenges are probably the biggest dealbreaker in the game for me. There is a game mode called Speed, that has a pretty simple goal. Earn points for going fast within a set time limit. The problem is that the goals for points in these events are absolutely ludicrous. On launch day, I was able to beat the world record lap time for Tantalus by a good 5 seconds and was still unable to even get a bronze medal on its respective speed challenge. Today, I still place in the top 5% for said level, and still can't clear the speed challenge. This problem is made even more maddening since it would be so easy to fix. Just lower the numbers. Or, even better, make the numbers adjusted by difficulty, like every other event type in the game. Speed is the only event type not affected in any way by the difficulty option, and it's the only one I would want to change. The developers have openly stated that it's just a skill issue apparently, despite over 80% of the community voting to change them in a poll on the subreddit. Oh yeah did I mention that they are one of the more common event types in the campaign and that their completion is mandatory for progression?-Campaign: Ignoring the aforementioned problems with speed challenges, the campaign, in general, is just ridiculously long. For some, this level of the content may be a welcome sight, but personally, it's just extremely daunting and draining to slog through the campaign in a futile hope that my favorite ships in the arcade might just be the next one to unlock. I wouldn't have a problem with the unlock system if the campaign wasn't so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ long, but such as it is.-Track design: Although the environments themselves are great, the track design often leaves room to be desired. Most of them are fine, but there certainly are a few problem spots. Especially on levels with longer jumps, the path can be confusing and with little guidance. Better still is when the indicators straight-up lie to you, like that one blind corner with a boost pad sending you off a cliff in Tartarus. Some levels also don't have proper killgrid boundaries like the first game, and you can be forced to fly out of bounds for upwards of 12 seconds on some maps if you fall off, with no self-destruct button. The game also touts its reverse levels, just reversed versions of the standard tracks. Many of these levels just feel like an afterthought made to make the level count higher, and just don't play nice at all. All in all, I would recommend Redout 2 if you fall into one of a few categories. You either have a good group of friends you could compete with in multiplayer, you enjoy trying to get your name on arcade leaderboards, or you are a total depraved masochist who would get a sick kick out of the campaign. If you think you would enjoy any of those things in a racing game, then absolutley give it a whirl.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is a sort of Wipeout with no weapon, and a boost mechanic very similar to Fzero: boosting makes your temperature rise, and boosting while at maximum temperature makes you damage your ship. The game is all about managing your temperature, health and energy on top of regular racing macros, making it a rich experience.There is a good variety of maps with 9 environments (if I'm not missing one) that all have 3 different tracks, and all tracks are playable in reverse. Different tracks from the same environment can have some parts in commun, but since all tracks are quite long, it is more of a relief than a bother to me: they still feel fresh and different, and it makes it easier to learn each parts of the tracks.I think the game has a ton of unexploited potential. I hope the season pass will add a lot of novelties, and not only new tracks, new ships, new parts.However, Redout 2 in it's current state is not for everyone. The difficulty curve is very harsh, especially if you don't want to play with the assist.Talking of the assist, I too was reluctant on using it, but I changed my mind when I hit the 72 stars wall in A League and it certainly made my life easier to get to SRRL League.- The AI on some tracks seems lost and often fall for no reason- On forks, a strong assist will very often make you crash in the middle of the fork- There's a spot in Tartarus in the middle of the road that stucks you in place while making you spin- The assist is unable to do some jumps and even makes you crash by overriding your inputs (one in black hole origin)- The leaderboard in time trial is not updating- Speed trials are very hard, particularly early in the career. The silver and bronze score should be lowered and more spread out for most speed trials;- Changing the difficulty only affects AI. It doesn't make Time Attack trials and Speed trials easier- Some information is missing on trials, like when rewind and assist are disabled on some stages;- The tutorial isn't great. Every tutorial should be unlockable before doing B League (and no more bullet time please). Also every explanation should be available outside of the tutorial trials;- I feel like the game was designed to be mostly played with the assist, without telling you you should use it. I feel this way because on some trials, the assist is disabled and these trials are more permissive.- There's no way to make a custom match with a range of power for all players and AI.- In free play (outside of career), you only have the choice between high-end preset ships or your custom ships. There's no presets for low power and mid-power ships.

Other times, the verticality of the tack road will hide critical sections that require you to make split second decisions making you fail trough no fault of your own.Finally, some later maps, do everything they can to kill you to a rather frustrating point.CAREER PROGRESSThe career progress is simple, though it works, you start with a single ship no other choices until you unlock them (which takes quite some time) so don't expect to pilot a vehicle you like for a while. As for the racing modes, they are all fun, with one being quite problematic. The mode called "Speed" is unbalanced to the point of being game breaking. _childDocuments_.review: Everybody else has already said it. If you like F-Zero then... guess what? This is a modern take on F-Zero; they added TWO boost mechanics: regular boost and hyper boost (and you can do both simultaneously). Boosting raises the heat of your vehicle whereas not boosting will lower the heat gradually over time. If you reach maximum heat then you will begin to overheat and any further boosting will start draining your health (which can kill you if you drain it all). In addition to that, you can start to regain health by not losing any health for about 5 seconds. Regular boosting feels like F-Zero and can give you a quick burst (or you can hold it) but it does raises your heat quickly. The more you use your regular boost, the more your hyper boost gauge is charged. Hyper boosting feels like activating lightspeed in Star Wars and once activated it will automatically hold until the until hyper boost gauge is completely drained. Hyper boosting is faster than regular boosting and slowly increases your heat gauge in comparison. The game is all about rotating your boosts effectively, managing your health regeneration, hitting the free boost pads, keeping up your momentum, using jumps to fly, and doing all this while racing. Is this better than F-Zero GX? I don't know about that but it is in the conversation, I do love this gameplay loop, and this feels like a more realistic simulation of an anti-gravity racing game without sacrificing the speed of F-Zero.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give a mixed rating. But since Steam asked if I could recommend the game... No, I can't. Not in general.Is it a good game? Yes. Is it a game for everyone? Only if you're up for a challenge or like Anti-Gravity Racing.The game takes you back to the time when you first played a racing game - you're crashing into everything and you somehow make it towards the finish line. But you also feel that with practice there is a lot of fun to be had. And when you take that time, you have that rewarding feeling from back then when you finaly started getting better. But it's only then when the game really becomes fun. Unfortunately this will take about 30+ hours... atleast for a casual like me. The game excels at gatekeeping and reminding you to 'git gud'.And that's where the game has its big weakness. You have to be willing to invest time and learn, learn and learn some more. The routes rely on memory, simply driving doesn't work. The route is poorly communicated in many places. What is even further complicated in your career as the routes are constantly changing and it is difficult to get used to individual routes. The jumps are just overly complicated and require you to know where you want to go - because your own vehicle is blocking your view. And no, this is not fun. It's simply bad design and annoying.Only buy this if you wan't to dive in deeper into Anti-Gravity Racing. An be ready to leave your ego at the door.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid recommendation. If you have previously played other anti-gravity racing games you know the deal, adrenaline pumping speed, go fast or explode trying, and this one is no exception.Now onto the interesting parts.Redout 2 has no pickups, that is, no weapons or support items.Instead you have two dedicated buttons, the classic boost (Powerful but needs recharging) and a smaller boost (Weak but infinite).Boosting generates heat, if can no longer be absorbed, it consumes health instead, and health is restored slowly after a period of not receiving damage. . Given that weapons are not part of the equation, you are expected to extract as much speed form boosting as you can, witch in turn, makes you be at low health constantly. So the more durability a vehicle has, the more “fuel” it has for boosting.Air brakes also do not exist and instead of braking you strafe laterally. This is also a huge deal. Strafing does not slow you down, and can be combined with normal steering.On top of all of this you also have to control the vehicle so it is always at an optimal angle towards the ground, and if it is on the air, control it so it lands correctly.All in all the game feels like it has moved outside its arcade origins and more towards a hardcore/simulation racing, and although provides tools to help inexperienced players, in no way will they be enough to be competitive.So somehow a niche game genre has become even more niche, but hey, if this is your jam, it sure feels good to go fast on this one.I could talk more about other stuff, but this review is already long enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Grammar. After around 30 hrs playtime, all points in the review still hold trueFirst: Understand that, while this is an arcade racing game, it is by no means easyI have been a big wipeout fan; been playing for decades, so "high speed anti-grav" racing is my shtick. I can handle speed, so long as the controls are RESPONSIVE. WipeOut has its formula down to a T with it's combination of streering and air-brakes.Redout, on the other hand, replaces air-brakes with strafing. In the first game, I absolutely HATED how slippery the ships were. You want to turn left? Well you're going to be moving right for quite some time before the ship finally changes direction. I couldn't stand it, and left the game untouched when I saw that even the best players were crashing into walls (something that you'd never see in top level wipeout).Thankfully, they have toned down this "slipperiness" to the point that the ships finally feel responsive. You turn left, ship turns left. You turn right AND strafe right? Ship turns right harder. None of that slipping in the opposite direction first before actually turning, UNLESS you want to. If you turn in one direction, but strafe in the other, you will accomplish a similar turning style to what Wipeout offers, albeit a little more exagerrated in the direction that you strafe.Controlability aside, the tracks are interesting but mildly forgettable. They are moreso like roller coaster rides, where you're reacting to sudden twists and turns rather than anticipating them. The devs tried to alleviate this by adding "turn signals" that warn when a turn is about to come up. They come in three colors; green means a light turn, orange means a moderate/hard turn, red means hairpin. Or at least, that's what they should mean, but unfortunately each track has different definitions of how hard a turn is. On one track, a orange turn might be considered easy and might only require steering without the need for strafing, where as on another track, an orange turn requires exact timing of your steering/strafing to avoid getting smashed into the wall. On top of this, the turn signals sometimes appear too late, and you'll suddenly be running into a wall because the track took a blind turn that you weren't warned about until too late.I imagine that if you keep playing the game, you'll begin to subconsiously learn the tracks and won't be as dependent on the turn signals anymore, but having them be more accurate/consistent would be a help, especially since there's 72 tracks (if you include the reversed versions). My last complaint is the air maneuverability. Oh my god I can't describe how much I hate jumps. When you're in the air, the steering of the ship no longer has any effect on your trajectory. If you steer left or right, your ship pivots as if you were turning, but you maintain your original trajectory. In order to move in the air, you have to strafe. Got that? Ok, because now you also have to worry about pitching your ship up and down. Ok, sure, but don't forget about ROTATING YOUR SHIP. In practice, this completely juggles the mind because suddenly your main way of turning (steering) basically get's shut off, forcing you to remember that only strafing works now, and that you have to move your left hand to the d-pad to rotate the ship. This LITERAL SPLIT SECOND of hesitation trying to fumble your brain into flight mode is enough to crash your ship. Devs: Please make steering have an actual effect on your ships trajectory. There's no reason it shouldn't.All of these complaints aside, Redout 2 is very fun. It gives that fast paced action of wipeout with it's own unique style. As mentioned in the beginning, the game is hard, and if you're looking for a racing game where you can win every race in 1 or 2 tries, this will not be it. But if you're looking for a challenge, and a game that offers a great sense of racing at breakneck speeds, this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A good game, in comparison to WipeOut HD. However there are some issues that plaque the gameplay. The Challenges for Time attack and Speed are way too difficult. Those two challenge types require beyond computer level AI perfection to attain. I have had laps where i never touched the wall and was flat out the entire time with boost and still never got close to their times or number values. Mind you, I also have the game set to Zero difficulty, as anything above it, you will place mid field as the AI just blows by you like you are standing still. Best recommendation for the devs is to go back and address these issues, as Wipeout HD wasnt even that difficult on hard mode. What they are asking for is not possible, unless there are cheats I am unaware of. Recommendation is to up the point values you can get while racing for the Speed challenges, and lower the Gold, Silver, and Bronze goals by at least half. 1000 may look cool but if your point ticker doesnt give enough points no matter what you do, it isnt attainable. For Time attack, lower the time goals by at least 10 seconds! When we start out in B series, time attack is possible, but as you go towards the end of the series, even when at max level for the event, there are a few that we arent even 8 seconds close to, and that is on a good performing lap. Times goals are too high and need to be adjusted down.  Lastly, the volcano map and the sky map......I get the need for jump and some of them are fun, but it is super difficult to align on some of these and in some cases you just go right through the track! Not fun. Either add auto align to the game as a non-turn off feature or connect some of these multi jumps into a longer track space so we can land. Further on this but, jumps like 5.0KM/2.14M, seriously?! Lower that value. Granted we may be increasing speed as we levelbut there is not an area on these maps that makes a jump that long. The few places where you think it might be dont even count it. I jump clear from one area to the end of the straight away and that still didnt count! So that tells me the challenge is broken and not registering the jump or there is not a place on the maps requesting that challenge for that type of jump to be possible. Overall good game, but some serious issues on difficulty that make it discouraging to play long term. Not to mention community and seasonal challenges section arent even available and are greyed out! Make it challenging, not impossible. IF these things can be fixed, this would be a solid game in comparison with Wipeout HD and XGRA.

_childDocuments_.review: Bit of a mixed bag this is compared to RE 1, overall I enjoy the game, but I can clearly see why people are dropping it before they get to A rank league which is where the game gets more enjoyable but I still have to rate it negatively until the devs actually fix this mess.Postitives:- Gameplay is a major improvement  over RE1- Tracks are actually challenging- Boost managementNegatives:- Over tuned AI and speed events- Part upgrades tied to events and not in game credits you earn- Career has strange difficulty spikes. Most notably near the end of B rank league and half way through A rank league.- A rank league is far far too long, being double the length of B rank- AI able to use S rank or signature parts in A or B rank events, meaning you have no chance at catching  them due to the sheer stat difference alone...- Tutorial stages teach bugger all and  are full of slow down bs.....- Crap UI and no explination on stability or other stats (Need to look that one up)- So many bugs and track collisions not functioning... _childDocuments_.review: I'm near 50 hours into the game and I find it exciting, cool and flowy, and I want to go on and become part of its commuity.BUT.I find it completely unbalanced;-The difficulty only changes the AI (influencing only races against AI).
