_childDocuments_.review: I put a lot of hours into Redout 1 many of them with friends. Redout 2 was a day one purchase for me. When I started 2, the clunky tutorial threw me off a bit, but was excited with some of the good. I played some multiplayer too and ultimately decided I wasn't having fun.The good:-The controls feel so good-The new liftoff mechanic has potentialThe bad however...-The sign posting in some tracks is so unclear; it's just easy to misread where the track wants you to go when you go off a ramp sometimes-The progression system is a poor choice. You just do not get to experiment with different cars to find one that suits you and you have to unlock specific upgrades for them. You are forced to play career mode the way the devs intended which is wild for a racing game.-The game is actively hostile toward the player. Again. I wasn't the best at Redout 1, but I can play with peeps online and have a good time. This game's career mode is just straight up mean. New players probably will not be able to get past the tutorial and that's just bad design. The AI races just straight up drive better cars than the starter car and you have to hold that.-The arcade and multiplayer mode lets you race with any fully maxed out vehicle, no way to downgrade unless you unlocked the vehicle and the upgrades you want in career mode. That's just throwing people into the fire and going "good luck"-There are balance issues with exploding. If you explode you may as well restart the race in career or just assume your friend will stay 3km in front of you the whole race if you both are racing perfectly. That is way too harsh a punishment for trying to engage with the new boost system to the very edge.-There are some critical bugs that I noticed. Sometimes boostpads just do nothing to do, something you clip through the track when you land on it too close to the edge after going off a ramp (or using the liftoff mechanic to get on an alternate route in some tracks)I can't reccomend this game at all as is. I just felt like I would rather play Redout 1 the whole time and my friends and I probably will do that instead of playing this. It has a lot of potential, I just hope things improve.

_childDocuments_.review: As an AG racing fan I held back for too long on Redout 2; the game delivers and my initial impression is very positive!— No weapons! It's a racing game, a sport; there is no place for weapons...! Thank you!— Flow state...! It's there and it's great! — Controls needs some getting used to, especially if your brain is wired to WipeOut but they make sense and the input feels precise after a while. — You feel the speed! Thanks also to the exceptionally good engine sound design!— Graphics are good with some nice interesting scenarios. — The ship design is awesome!— I'm not a fan of the time rewind feature... it kind of breaks the flow. Maybe I just need to get used to it.— Mid air control seems over-complicated. Was it really necessary to add the cross-pad to the two analog sticks just to correct flight (for now I enabled mid air steering support)?  — The world and tracks are a bit too colorful for my taste. It's also easy to get lost mid-air because everything has the same color saturation. — This bothers me a lot: as mentioned above the ship design is gorgeous and I like to explore the design in the race selection menu. Unfortunately the menu is built in a way that the 360 view is several button presses away... Ship rotation should be available directly through analog sticks. Let's enjoy the art!

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is the most thrilling racing game I've played in a long time; yes it's fast, sometimes very fast...occasionally fast to the point where you physically feel the need to lean back in your chair... But to say "Redout 2 is good because the speed feels amazing" is doing a massive disservice to it; it's a game that demands a lot out of you. it may be "arcade-y" but it is technical; strafing, braking, turning, boosting, and pitching your ship all in a single turn of a track are crucial things to get used to, to gain muscle memory for; and the game will push you to do it with speed challenges and time trials that can at times be a bit cruel... If you exclusively like seeing "1st" appear on your screen then I'm afraid this game will frustrate you to death, you need to accept 2nd and 3rd place sometimes, it's just the nature of it; but it also makes victory feel earned; turning up the difficulty so that you're back and forth with your fellow AI drivers, making those crucial superboosts to escape them at the last minute, knowing that putting your shields that low to do it will make any collision on the overtake potentially lethal.... It is an exceptional feeling!That said to get the most out of this game I want to provide a few tips:1: Assists are nothing to be ashamed of; tune them to your preference as much as you want and only turn them down bit by bit as you gain confidence. The tutorials aren't that great so having the time to learn with a bit of help is great to do, and feel no shame in having them in parts of the game that you feel at your weakest...Also I recommend keeping boost protection on at somewhere around 15%....will stop a lot of self-destructions :)2: Each event tells you what you will earn for how many stars you get; a lot of the harder events will only earn you cosmetics for 4 star completion so don;t worry; often, especially when starting out, 2 or 3 stars is fine, perfection takes a long time and demands a lot out of you; it's okay to get a useful upgrade and move on, a different spoiler or cosmetic will change nothing about how you drive and is not worth the pain if you're super struggling.3: Brake!....Slowing down for a second is not a failure, and you will lose far less speed than you would hitting a wall.4: when you hear the "shields recharging" sound do everything you can not to hit anything or overheat your boost for those moments; shield=extra boost; let them recharge and then you can make up for any lost time with immense speed.and finally 5: LOOK AT THE TURN INDICATORS AT THE TOP OF YOUR SCREEN!  Many tracks you can rely on sight but often times little turns in twists and so on will catch you off guard; just keeping an eye on the colour (green=shallow turn, yellow=moderate turn, red=sharp turn) will massively help your driving and lead to far less restarts on a track. Still keep an eye on the track, but make sure to keep glancing at those indicators and you'll immediately find yourself a better driver for it :)For anyone willing to take the plunge, I wish you the best of luck, and don't be disheartened by a 3rd place on a speed event.... they're really hard, don't beat yourself up about it. Have fun, go fast, do some crazy super boosts and laugh while you do them shouting "speeeeeed!" and I promise you, you'll have a blast :)

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't played much but so far the game is great. If you're expecting just more of Redout 1 then keep playing Redout 1, the game is untouched in it's glory and you're free to keep playing it.Redout 2 ditches the power ups and passives of Redout 1 which is a good thing imo since if you were half decent at the game there was no reason to pick anything but the omega turbo boost and the magnetic or accel passives. Instead you have a boost meter that overheats as you use it and an overcharge boost that recharges after you use it, as this boost overheats you can keep using it to get more speed at the expense of your health which is pretty fun, makes managing engine heat and your health pretty engaging. The music is fine but not as great as the first game and the handling is a lot more forgiving which is fine since it still feels really good to nail a perfect lap going as fast as you can.I read some people complain about the difficulty of the game and honestly I cant see it, I've been playing on the Redout difficulty and it feels just right, I get challenged fairly often by the AI and it's a difficult but fair experience, it's all about managing boost properly and learning tracks, If you're SOMEHOW having issues on the game on the easiest difficulty you should probably reconsider gaming as a hobby.They only REALLY bad thing about the game is that the tutorial is actually forced on you as you are completely unable to disable assists (WHICH YOU SHOULD DON'T BE A LOSER YOU LOSE SPEED USING THESE) and that's pretty bad, but so far that's really my only complaint. The price might be a bit high so if you are unsure just wait for a sale and even then if you just want a fun fast racer you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: You pilot very fast hover-ships & race on roller-coaster-like tracks with twists & loops. Controls are tight & responsive, and the sense of speed is wild when you boost along straightaways.Boosting is "the" mechanic in this game. You have a regular boost that can be activated at any time & will remain active while the input is held down, and a stronger boost that basically shifts your vehicle into high-gear, which can be activated off a cooldown. Both boosts can be stacked together for even higher speeds.Heat management is the next main mechanic. Boosting will increase your vehicle's temperature, and can cause overheating when at maximum. You can continue boosting while overheating at the cost of your health, and will eventually explode once your health is depleted.Interestingly, this seems to be what you want to do - if you aren't overheating, you aren't going fast enough, but be sure to watch your health also.Vehicle control in Redout 1 was more drifty - akin to rally cars, whereas in this game, they're less so & more like Formula 1 cars instead. Turning is a lot tighter and it feels like there is more friction to the track.I don't see this as necessarily a good or bad change, just different.Redout 1 also had a variety of different power-ups you could equip as well, which aren't present in this game.I'm a bit mixed on this. On one hand, I get it - of all the choices of power-ups to equip, the turbo-boost tended to outshine all of them, so they turned that into a main mechanic for this game.On the other hand, I wonder how neat it might've been if they iterated on those often ignored power-ups like they did with the turbo-boost to see if they could've been made more useful in this game.I'm running this on lower-end hardware - NVidia GTX 1050 card.My graphics settings are all set to medium, and the game both visually still looks good & performs at a * 60 FPS (it can go above 60 FPS - I've just capped it here).The lighting & color mixing make for some bright & vibrant environments to look at as well.My only real complaint - and I think this is mainly an Unreal Engine thing - is compiling shaders in real-time.There are short, but large performance hits when the game needs to compile new shaders it hasn't yet rendered for the first time, and it can be jarring & throw off your control when it happens, although it's probably not as bad on up-to-date hardware.When you load into a race, the game will pan the camera across various locations in the track, waiting for you to press start. Letting it pan the camera around for a little while to load the shaders before starting will at least prevent these hits from happening during gameplay.Sound effects are great. Each different vehicle has its own distinct engine sound based around their design/stats. Kicking in the turbo-boost and hearing their engines roar as they shift into high-gear tickles something in my brain. Really helps sell the sheer power & speed these things are running at.Music is okay. It's not bad, but compared to Redout 1, it's really generic & doesn't hit the same.There are different composers for this game, and I personally find that Zardonic's soundtracks are often the best & tend to be more notable compared to the others.The game has this one mechanic where it will dynamically change the current soundtrack based on the gameplay, but aside from the beat dropping when the race starts & when you land after a high jump, I cannot really tell if/when it does otherwise.Tartarus Mines. I saw the complaints people had about the design of these race tracks in particular before I bought the game, and yeah, I think they are justified. Jumps feel like they pop out of nowhere, and the places you're supposed to land don't feel like they're lined up with the jump, especially when you think you can make a jump at your current speed, only to slow down dramatically in mid-air because you were driving against gravity & couldn't tell which way was up because you're on a roller-coaster in a cave.Each carreer event has an optional bonus challenge to complete. Something like, "don't crash once" or "lead every lap". These are fine for the most part - my gripe is specifically with these ones:- "Cross the finish line while going X speed"- "Travel X distance in a single jump"The first is just tedious to try & complete, since you cannot even attempt it until you're seconds away from crossing the finish line. If you fail to complete it, you have to restart the entire race, and then the race is just filler at this point until you can try again.The second is because there isn't any jump distance indicator in the game, so you have no frame of reference for how much distance you've travelled in a jump/how far you are expected to jump. You won't know if you've actually jumped far enough until completing the race. Again, tedious.The "Rewind" mechanic. These are limited-use abilities that allow you to pause & rewind time during a race so that you can retry a turn or jump or whatever that you failed.I don't think the way this mechanic was implemented is bad, I just find it weirdly out-of-place, and it feels like the only reason it even exists in this game is to solve an "X/Y problem" for Tartarus Mines specifically. I.E:- Problem: players are having a hard time making turns/jumps/etc. at specific parts of tracks.- X Solution: give them the ability to undo & try again.- Y Solution: maybe redesign those parts of the tracks if they aren't clearly indicated to the player how to cross them.*Edit: FPS seems to drop in some of the later environments you unlock such as Neo Tokyo and Genesis. Both these environments are set in large cities with a bunch of densely-packed background buildings. My guess is the sheer number of these buildings being rendered is where the performance is being impacted.

_childDocuments_.review: I am honestly mad that I have to not recommend this because it has been a long time since I have played a game like this that feels so smooth, looks so crisp, and sounds better than most video games out currently available.While the game's core gameplay loops, aesthetic, and sound design are some of the best I have ever seen, everything outside of those elements feels under baked.Multiplayer is non existent from my experience. It takes longer than it should to get put into a lobby, and thats IF you are lucky to get into one. Unranked is ok, but having the "RANKED - COMING SOON" option next to it feels really weird.Menu Navigation dates back to early 2000 console era, where you have to use up down left right to navigate the menu. This is one of my smaller gripes, but I do wish I could just use my mouse for selecting things instead of WASD or arrows.The customization is vast but the UI and navigation for it is so constrained and unintuitive that it feels like a chore just to select one new item to apply to your ship. Each ship looks amazing with each of their different customization options, but the game forces you to navigate to it manually instead of allowing you to pick the recent items you were rewardedThe settings are limited and don't seem finished. There seem to be very few options to customize the video, audio and controls considering how graphically and mechanically complex this game can be.I hope this game improves over time. Unfortunately, I can not recommend it with the current state of it as of writing this review

_childDocuments_.review: First AG game to properly scratch the itch for me since Wipeout HD / Omega Collection, and IMO, the very best AG game you can get on PC right now. The first Redout was impressively good but felt a little awkward for me - this one's near-perfect.This game has its own style for sure, but in the best way possible feels like a mix between F-Zero X's drift-y super speed, later Wipeout games detail and technical piloting, and a splash of X-treme G's wild track design. (There's even an in-game brand that's an homage to F-zero X's logo, wearing its influence on its sleeve.)I found the dual-stick turn-and-drift controls a bit more approachable in this game vs the first one - so if you're an ace at that game this one will take re-adjusting to. That said if you're either new to AGs or haven't played one in a while, I think this one has a lower barrier of entry than the last Redout while keeping the skill ceiling pretty high. There are mild assists on by default which can be increased, decreased, or disabled - I love to see this in racing games because it makes them approachable without alienating players who become skilled at the game.Also, holy wow does it look great.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever played Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed Collection? You know how the thrill of a race evaporates the moment your gokart suddenly becomes an airplane for no apparent reason? Well, Redout 2 has the same problem. 95% of a track is like a bowling lane with bumpers on, and then, for no reason, there's random jumps where you have to aim your vehicle like it's a plane. And it really, really ruins Redout 2, which otherwise might have been a pretty good game. No, seriously. If they got rid of those annoying jumps, and stuck to just being a racing game, Redout 2 would be great. But it's utterly mediocre because of the random (and unnecessary) flight mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: A much better game than it's predecessor. Right out of the bat, the game has a much better presentation and feel with better graphics as well. The tracks you drive on have much more compelling visuals, while driving on them feels better as someone who just played the first game.The gameplay has been extended and refined and, with the better track design, thus feels better to play. Now in addition you have tilting, steering and rotating in jumps, which sadly feels really janky, even if it's a welcome addition. Trying to adjust your vehicle to ramps also feels more like it has an impact, compared to the first game.The variety in the singleplayer, however, drops pretty fast. A lot of the tracks start to repeat itself after the first hour and only occasionally get broken up by something new, and while some tracks are reversed, they still feel the same. And if you'd rather say "Well, i like designing and upgrading my vehicle", you have more chances to do so here. However, instead of earning money with which you can unlock things whenever you want, you now unlock aesthetics and upgrade parts by completing events and earning stars. And while the selection of unlockables are way nicer, the way to do so feels really underwhelming.All in all it is a nice game you can play in the meantime of doing something since it's easy to pick up while events don't take a lot of time. Me, sadly, i got bored out of it really fast. But if it's in a sale, definitely pick it up!

_childDocuments_.review: Edit#3After another really long break its time to revise the review again. so, here are my talking points of note:-This game is really hard. There are options to make controlling stuff easier....however it is still a little...odd....that these would be required for some players. None the less, this is considered an accessibility feature.-Rebinding controls works properly now with correct directions displayed for buttons IE left and right instead of increase and decrease (real smooth brain on that one. you'd think that QA would include making sure the UI actually functions the way its intended...I digress, weird stuff can happen in game dev so this can be dismissed if it "works on my machine", and then stopped working for the public launch)-Match making is here to stay. join online and forget about making a room at the time of writing. your only options are unranked match making, and SRL match making with ranks. Instead of making a room, you can add friends from your steam friends list and then invite them to races. It would be nice to make a lobby so anyone can join...but I dont think thats in the game yet. Why not? Redout 1 already had this. Why take the feature away?-There is a replayable tutorial to help get you used to the game. Thanks devs, this is a wonderful feature-UI/UX is overall improved from redout classic. There are some areas where I think it could be further improved, and other areas where I think its COMPLETE and UTTER TRASH. Mission selection in campaigns is made much easier now instead of one giant scroll wheel like in redout 1. everything is in tiles and neatly managed. The HUD ingame is nice and neat though it would be cool if certain areas of the tracks had effects that got displayed on the HUD. for example, enhanced cooling when driving over water. The UI/UX for selecting ship parts and upgrades is ok. One giant scroll wheel near the bottom of the screen that transforms to show all sub options when you select one of the parent options. I wish that when you selected a parent option, it popped up a vertical scroll bar with 5 options so you could see 2 ahead and 2 behind with the middle one being the selection. the scroll bar could be put to either side of the screen to make room for the ship and the statistics display. The devs really messed this part up. Why do I have to push a button to examine the ship? The ship is already there, just let me move it with the second control stick like redout 1 damnit. Serious smooth brain moment. If I am using the UI to customize it, why not let me manipulate the camera angle while I am customizing it with the second stick. The preset angle when you select a asthetic part is often not good enough. Fix this please. The last atrocity is the main menu itself with selecting racing modes. In order to use career ships in arcade you have to push yet another button to switch over. why not just make these 2 separate options. Setting custom arcade races is a nighmare as well. The way to set them with redout classic was nearly perfect, you had all the stats of the race and what you would be racing with on one screan. why did you change this and make it a convoluded sub menu with tabs? Just use a submenu under the main menu's tile theme for each mode and then the settings there in when you select a tile for time trials. This could all be under arcade. Come on guys, this is seriously an EPIC fail for UI/UX design. Take inspiration from mario kart or even your own redout 1 game. Go look at windows 10 live tiles and the folder option for them when grouping them together. Hell, look at android or IOS app folders. you could have easily done something with that with the tile menu for arcade instead of whatever this current garbage is.And then we have simple things like why cant I set lap counts for time trials, why cant I Mirror the track....all of this could be put under a tiled submenu under arcade, but instead its all hidden. Come on guys.-The game is slower than redout 1. now now wait a sec, let me explain. Redout 1 featured open tracks and because you had a significantly larger distance to cover, you went way faster...at least visually without any FoV trickery. Where you were going could change quickly with momentary areas of pure speed. Redout 2 on the other talon uses FoV trickery to make you think you are going faster than you actually are. In addition, the tracks are much tighter in redout 2 with antigrav vehicles that handle much better than redout one. The flat and wide straights that existed in redout 1 dont exist here and as such moving at redout 1 speeds is not required to make this game a fast paced one. This time tracks are significantly more technical than redout 1 and your speedometer will be wrong if you compare redout 2 directly to redout 1. I guarantee it. If you wanted something faster....redout 1 will be the game to play....but if you want something more fast paced, redout 2 will be your poison. That being said, the trophy challenge difficulty is all over the place and in some places are nearly impossible without a spoiler or several hours on a track to figure out where all the death planes are or get the fastest time that would rival nightmare mode gameplay.Now to the music. Ah yes, the music...and audiophile like me loves so much if done well. I LOVE the main menu music. It's as banger as redout classics menu music. Music, a form if audible arts is very subjective, what I like might not be what you like. There should be something for everyone to enjoy here. Here is where we smack into a concern of mine. There are tracks in the game that make up the redout experience while being copyrighted to hell and back preventing you from so much as whispering them on stream. Its not many (only 9 tracks out of 51 tracks) and redout INCLUDES AND OPTION TO TURN THOSE TRACKS OFF FOR STREAMING (thanks devs). "Aww boo hoo im missing 9 of the 51 tracks I want to listen to on stream": SHUT, you have 42 other tracks, deal with it, you wont miss them. Now, my issue is that I cant fully share the experience of the game as a whole with my stream even if it IS only 9 tracks missing, but that's not the main problem here. The bigger problem here is going to be able to actually buy the game. In order to distribute these tracks in the game, 34bigthings has a contract or a licensing agreement with whoever the media labels are that manage the rights to the works....and as 34bigthings should know:Contracts and licensing agreements can:-Have escape clauses for both parties incase one or the other decides the agreement is nolonger viable or beneficial.-ExpireThis could lead to the game nolonger being able to be sold in the future unless the offending content is removed. Want 2 examples? GTA4 and (almost) GTA5. I am making a call right now that Death Stranding will have this issue as well. The good news is that the songs can be stripped if devs care enough to keep their IP on the market.....but why include them in the first place if this is the risk you are taking? I dont fully understand. This is just a concern, it doesnt affect the gameplay (atleast at a technical level) and only affects you if you stream.Overall...this is not redout classic...if you came from redout classic....you're going to have to relearn quite a bit due to the handling of the crafts being very very different. If you played wipeout or ballistics NG or some other form of anti grav racer with tight tracks and bouncy controls, this is gonna be your game, strap in and blast off.Do i recommend the game? Currently....no. Redout 1 is the better game. its got a specific art style, less offensive sounds, a good ui (unless youre in the campaign, then it sucks), and a banger ost that slaps.

_childDocuments_.review: Going from Redout 1 to this one can feel pretty strange at first. I wasn't really prepared for just how much...more there'd be to this game going in. Redout 1 has a sort of simplicity and looseness to it that can sometimes make the game feel empty, or not fully realized. By comparison, this game immediately feels jam packed with new and nuanced mechanics, as well as a more fully realized theme and visual style. It doesn't feel like a sequel as much as a complete generational evolution to Redout 1. With how much more this game tries to be though, it can be easy to feel as if it's trying to go for too much all at once.Redout 1 has a reputation for being complicated and hard. Even after playing the game extensively and becoming familiar with it to the point that that difficulty wore off, I didn't expect for this game to put me right back to where I was then. It can feel like the game is cheating, or is artificially difficult. I don't think this is the case though. Stick with it, get a feel for the new boost mechanics, and memorize the courses, and you'll see improvement. Its still gonna be hard though. Don't expect to take 1st on every event on your first try.I was uncertain about the boost mechanics at first. It kind of just felt that, with this freedom to boost whenever I want, I should boost whenever I can. It led to me edging my ship down to a sliver of health, even as the competitors rocketed ahead of me. After getting used to the boosting and getting a better sense of when and where to boost, it's lead to some really thrilling moments where I have to 'give it all she's got' and just cutting into first in the final stretch as a burning wreck dragging across the finish line. Speed trials are still kicking my ass though.I'm not a fan of the new jumping and aerial controls. There is a lot to keep track of visually in this game, and not much time to do it. The meters for rolling and leveling out are hard to read, especially with how abruptly they appear. The more complicated jumps will usually require you to scramble for the d-pad to roll even with the track before you even know where it is. You're likely to crash unless you are already aware of the jump that is approaching, and have prepared to unintuitively take your thumb off the left stick.

_childDocuments_.review: Since this game launched I've loved every second of playing it.The game is very challenging, but I enjoy challenge and a high skill ceiling, which this game certainly has.Once you get over the initial skill bump, gradually improving, memorizing the tracks and learning fine-tuned precision at very high speeds is beyond satisfying.I did not write a review before this patch because there were still a number of frustrating bugs affecting the game, these bugs have now either been fixed or their impact reduced to a bare minimum.With that I can now recommend the game to those who love AG racing and are looking for a journey of mastery.To get over that initial skill bump, which can be rough admittedly, here are a few rules of thumb: - Use your health for boost! collision damage is pretty weak, so leaving yourself with low hull is not as dangerous as it may seem. To get used to this the Boost Safety assist set to 5% can help you push your limits by preventing you from actually blowing yourself up from overheating. - Stack boosts and acceleration sources! Whenever you can or see an opportunity, use your hyper boost, and stack your normal boost on top of it. If you can find straights with boost pads, long jumps and/or landing zones where you can earn landing boosts you can stack all these sources of acceleration to hit crazy high speed numbers. - Extend your boost time! Once you are at a high speed, it might be tempting to continue to stack the hyper and normal boost until you are out of health, however especially in the early game you don't yet have enough health to get you through most straights. Instead, either cancel your hyper boost early, or stop stacking your normal boost to reduce the rate at which your are overheating. Both forms of boost will do a good job at maintaining a high speed once you have it. - Health Regen is top priority!Having just spend all your health on boost means you have to regen it at some point, but your ships regen is interrupted, or its cooldown reset when you take enough damage in a short amount of time. Being able to spend health as fuel is extremely important if it comes to being fast. Do everything you can to not interrupt your regen. Braking hard for a corner is better then having to wait an additional few seconds for your regen to start. - Improve your top speed!Top speed scales very fast during the early game. As much as your parts allow for it, push it to the second solid white line in the graph at the cost of any other stat. after you've reached that threshold you should focus on the rest to your preference. More top speed after this point has some benefit, but not enough to keep going much further.Bonus tip: Speed events care more about how high your speed number gets then maintaining a high average speed. Don't waste boost between straights trying to keep above the threshold, instead spend all your heat and health at once whenever the track allows, and push that speed number as high as possible.That should be enough to get you through the early game and into the mid game.If you're still struggling join the discord, you can find plenty of people who love to help there.Enjoy going fast pilots.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated review.This game is not bad, but there are way too many questionable design changes and bad decisions that bring it down. It can be good, but the developers have to make some substantial changes. If you are looking for a really good futuristic racing game, get RedOut 1. It's a better game in every aspect.This game does some things good:+ Graphics - really good to look at. 3D graphic designers really put a lot of care and love into their work.+ Career mode (though there are major problems with this mode, I'll explain in the cons section)+ Boosting and managing heat/energy - this is a good "high risk, high reward" system which overall benefits the overall experienceBut now, cons:- Difficulty - I understand that the game is meant to be difficult. Hell, the first one was not a cake walk either, but at least, when I lost in that game, I knew that I will be able to beat any event if I practice enough. Here? I'm often not even close to reach BRONZE in the Speed events. The problem is, that those events are usually placed on really difficult tracks with a lot of sharp turns and jumps (I'll get to those soon). In comparison, similar events in the first game were usually placed on rather straightforward tracks, where after some practice, you could reach platinum (each event had that "click" moment, here, not so much) The requirements also don't scale with the difficulty and it feels like they were created only with the highest difficulty in mind. I wouldn't mind not being able to reach Gold if Bronze was a lot easier (I've managed to only finish the tutorial speed event ffs)- UI/menus - I don't know if enyone tested those, but dear god... I haven't seen such a bad UI in a while. For instance - you unlock a new colour for your ship. The only way to apply it is by selecting an event in a Career mode (yup, no "garage") then going to another screen to customise your ship, then to another to customise the colour and THEN, you would have to search for the new colour as all of them are available on the list (which you can scroll only one by one, mind you) because every color is there, even the locked ones. Seriously, copying UI from any other racing game would be better. This btw. looks the same for every single customisable part of your ship. - Progression - as I like what they did with the progression, how it is executed is something different. You'll unlock certain upgrades/cosmetics/ships from events by gathering stars (by winning and completing certain challenge for every event) This may sound cool, but you'll soon realise that you'll be unlocking parts that you are required to install instantly just to keep up with the AI. Waaaay later on I believe that you'll have some viaraty once you'll unlock different parts that offer different stat adjustements, but after 5 hours I can only tell that it feels totally redundant. This would feel a lot better if you would be given option to customise your ships stats from the beginning, as it would give you an idea what to focus on, based on your playstyle (the only playstyle for now is to do near perfect, or perfect runs)Also, rewards are listed in the event screen,but the game shows you logos that don't mean ♥♥♥♥, so you'll never know if you should do an event or not.- Track design - it's bad. So bad, that they gave you the worst thing in racing game history - time rewind.I'm sure this is an afterthought as this feature is not event mentioned in the initial tutorial. You will get one after you beat some events, right after the game introduces jumps. Those are... bad. Bad and unnecessary. They are often placed in a way that it's impossible to nail them on the first try. Later on, you will be required to do some really unintuitive moves to land on the track. They also had a bright idea to force players to steer your ship while in the air. While this does not sound bad, the controlls are not good while in the air, and often you are forced to do way to many adjustments to your position (the game requires perfect landings for additional speed boost) Those jumps are also being affected by gravity (well... duh!) but in a really bad way. Imagine that you drive a track so fast, that you don't know where is UP and DOWN and you do this jump. You realise, once mid-air, that you are flying to the right. Yup, the track you were on was on a wall, but there was no way to know that as nothing indicated it. At least you have that rewind, but it is still really tricky to land some of those jumps + some times you'll go straight through the track (I guess it's a bug) It took me about 20 tries before I've landed one jump on a lava track (can't be bothered with it's name, but the person who came up with this jump can go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. him/her-self)Another thing is, the tracks are just not fun to drive in many occasions. There are some decent ones, but many have sooo many tight corners and other places where the game just slows down. I haven't seen every track so far, and I doubt that I will at this point.- Music - Feels soulless. I honestly think that RedOut 1 has one of the best racing game soundtracks ever. Each track had it's own music and it added so much character. Here? It feels like it was made for a paycheck. Every single track is just an EDM soulless mess. You will be lucky if you'll hear any melody. It's just kickdrums, psy-trans bass and pointless guitar riffs and solos. I'm a music producer and this really hurts. This game would benefit from letting players upload their own music, or at least, having tracks from the first game.TL/DR - Get RedOut 1

_childDocuments_.review: With 160 hours playing Redout 1, I strongly prefer Redout 2 so far. Yes, when I started, the turning/strafing was so different compared to Redout 1, I completely sucked and I wondered if the game was broken. But when you get used to it, it is deeper and more satisfying. I enjoyed the learning process - it was like playing Redout for the first time (^u^).What I like better about Redout 2: - Controls are so different, this felt like a fresh new game, rather than a big DLC for Redout 1, while also keeping everything I liked about Redout 1. - The new boosting is absolutely genius! Being able to use your health as boost and having over-boost adds so much depth and tension to racing. - AI assist for new players. I loved showing Redout 1 to my friends, but the learning curve was too much for most of them. Now I can share this with more people! - With 0% AI assist, all events were challenging from the start. No beginner levels to breeze through. - Turning is more powerful, so new player don't have to strafe to get around a track. This adjustment is what makes the game feel broken if you are used to Redout 1 at first, but you'll get used to it. It should make Redout 2 easier to pick up - Turning has more inertia, which takes more commitment, so you have to plan more ahead to make your turns flow together. This makes the game deeper and harder to master. - Strafing while turning doesn't kill your speed like in Redout 1, so you can do more extreme drifting if you can handle it. This mechanic is what makes Redout in general the best anti gravity racer ever, and it is even better in #2! - Flying now has way more control. Flying in Redout 1 was too floaty. You can also control roll rotation in this one instead of it being automatic. Harder, like a flight sim, and I love it.  - More level variety, with crazier turns, forking paths and short cuts and reverse directions for each course.  - The individual tracks in each location intersect each other with forks now, so the boss mode is one continuous run through different turns without going through portals. I hated the portals in Redout 1 because I couldn't see enough of the track on the other side, which made me crash unfairly. Huge improvement! - No power ups! In Redout 1, I would either abuse the healing to crash into all the walls and still win without trying or use the super boost to be competitive. I'm glad they are gone, and replaced with a better boost system. - Unlike Redout 1, Redout 2 has enough content at launch to feel like a full game AND we still get DLC!Things worse about Redout 2 - With my mid range computer, Redout 1 actually looked better and ran smooth than Redout 2. I'm using a mix between mid and high graphic settings. - Textures are always popping in and out. It sometimes feels like an early access game. Hopefully stuff like this is a release day bug that will be fixed with an software update. This didn't get in the way of enjoying it, it just lacks polish. - The world building is cringe scifi fan fic and I can't skip the cut scenes. An example of what I think they were going for was the course intros in SSX Tricky, or the countdown announcing voice in Wipeout 3 that says, "3, 2, 1, GO." This kind of thing could be really good, but it needs more personality and the right vibe. I could see it being more elite and sophisticated or fun and tongue in cheek, but it is currently in this middle goofy range. - Some modes need balancing and feel almost impossible. The third tutorial level is way too hard. Again, I hope this is fixed in a software update. - This is true for both Redout 1 and 2, but I don't like their menusAll in all, I HIGHLY recommend this game, and if you have played Redout 1, it will feel broken at first, but if you push through it, in 2-5 hours, you'll love it.

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this a very experienced AG fan, I cannot honestly recommend this to anyone.  (...yet (I really hope A LOT of changes come)) Until it changes I have to give it a 4/10I've played Wipeout 1, Pure, Pulse, HD, Fury, & 2048, F-Zero, XGRA 1 and 2, Repulse, Pacer, and most importantly Redout 1. My biggest turnoff after finishing the beautiful campaign in RO1 was finding out multiplayer is desolate, I was disheartened to see the amount of dirty driving (intentional wall touching) necessary to even be slightly competitive. Disappointing. But even from time to time i'll still open it, play a race or two, and close it. Was expecting a lot of improvement. I only got an oversaturated AG seizure inducer with awful track design.This is absolutely horrendous. The menu is VIBRANT and looks like an apple arcade game. In the campaign, the car they start you off with is bogusly slow. Not in a "here get the bad car and get good at the same track" way, its more like "naw heres the car. get destroyed by Max Spec cars until you Git Gud with a POS".  The AI not only rubberbands at the lowest difficulty it just straight up pummels you and asks you for more. The Non-AI campaign missions are a joke at best, some speeds just straight up cant be reached and theyre asking a breakneck speed thats impossible to reach even at an experienced level.. Mind you, I have to digest 4 chapters of this????? I cannot skip the worldbuilding but I'm also forced to just magically have a great racing line? On Tracks None of which are memorable? With wall-less corners, jumps off screen, and horrendous air bindings??? And then they have the nerve to throw me in a reverse track with essentially Tier 4 type Gold Medal times??????? In this Dog Ass ESA?  yo what?There is literally no rhyme or reason to even WANT to get good at redout 2 besides the very fluid balancing act of 2 boosts and your HP which can be bargained. Cool. I would be down for the ride if tracks could be done in about 20-40 seconds. Not a minute and a half. Only good thing done in a horrible slew of design choices.Bad Tracks, Long Laps, Impossible Speed Challenges, Laughable Difficulty Settings, ANGRY AI, Awful Autosteering assistance, Bad UI, Too much bloom, not enough race. Bad sense of progression, Arbitrary Numbers from minor pointless upgrades like this is an RPG. I cannot even say there is promise. This cant be fixed in a patch. Only a 3rd one that attempts to play like RO1.This is essentially the equivalent of RP MMO servers. Not for vets beginners or die hards. Just straight up for nerds that rejoice over this golden shower of a game meant for those already mouth breathing with the rest of the devs in their discord server. Skip.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Astronomic difficulty barrier of entry, awful tutotial, even worse campaign, initial environments are completely bland, customization is pointless for most of the time you will be playing and game modes are less fun than Redout 1. Fun when(if) you get good. Went in better direction later once devs got their rights of the franchise back but it, sadly, does not redeem the sheer amount of awful the original design direction created that you are forced to play through as you start.In depth: They've committed an ultimate sin: made the game for elite players only. I cannot overstate it, you don't get to "just drive" ever on these tracks even for small stretches. They will force you to eat those walls and you shouldn't expect to be anywhere good enough to not do it for dozens of hours. Comparatively, RO1 was a much smoother entry.Will you have fun once you "get good"? Yes, yes, absolutely. But the sheer amount of grind to get there is ridiculous. Literally every track wants you to know it inside out for anything close smooth driving and the environments *do not* help.There's no remembering landmarks: especially early on they are as generic as they get and it gets more pointless considering tracks of the same location reuse sections so you have to remember which exact version of the track you are on that uses that section. You also can't see ahead basically ever. Almost every turn you *have* to know to actually not crash into the wall. There's like 0 visibility of what you are approaching outside of arrow signs. Admittedly, the scenery gets somewhat better with later tracks, but the onboarding ones are ridiculously cringe. Remember how nice environments looked in RO1? yeah no, prepare to drive your first XX rides in as bland scenery as possible. You can only enjoy so much pink, then it starts grating on your nerves, hard.  They also completely butchered Calima. I loved it in RO1, in RO2 the environment and color scheme are so bland I literally started skipping those before I even decided to jump ship from the campaign completely.Oh right, campaign. I..... do not even know how to start expressing my sheer *hatred* for what they did with it. Instead I will start from what made the game tolerable for me in the end: do yourself a favor and download a completed save. Then play practice maps at your leisure with various parts until you get comfortable with speed/tracks. So what exactly is my problem with the campaign? EVERYTHING. Sin 1: Sloth It starts you with a HORRIBLE craft. I do not use this word lightly. After I got some experience, I returned back just to check if my memory made it seem worse than it is. No, it *is* as bad as I remembered it being. It drives like ass, grinds every wall, feels slow and you will hate your life until several dozen missions in you get to improve it enough to mitigate how much of a cripple the initial ESA is. I have been told it is to "get the player the sense of progression". I call bullsht. All it does is forces you to suffer needlessly. RO1 didn't have that, you got both a sense of speed and actually nice to control craft from the getgo.Sins 2 and 3 Envy and GreedIn RO1 you just had tiers of craft and that gradually progressed you into harder stuff. You could switch beween craft types within a single tier for variety but that was it. In RO2 I can only imagine the publisher was envious of how gacha games made money out of player progression and wanted to eventually introduce paid parts. As a result the game has lots and lots of *completely pointless* parts. Parts that are generic, applicable to every craft, unlock in sequence and only become the tool of variability at the very end. Until then - you will largely be using the currently most recent unlocked  parts as best in slot. This will be the case for dozens of hours and will only be made worse once part point limits force you to play a minigame of "gimp your craft in creative ways using a clunky ui". This system would have been majorly less awkward to use with just dishing out improvement points where you could choose where to improve your craft without doing it jigsaw style.Sin 4: LustThe campaign lusts for your time in the worst way possible. Every "season" introduces just several environments for you to play in and they are repeated *endlessly*. You will see literally infinite variations of sakura, calima, and mars until you get to anything different. It does *not* help that due to the tracks being used for both speed 600 and speed 2000 they take AGES to complete at initial stages. You can fully expect 3 plus minute laps as opposed to a minute and a half of the previous game. Also this infinity of variation is not a good thing because those are just the same 3 tracks per environment driven back and forth with section reuse and largely irrelevant ruleset changes. It doesn't help that those initial environments are also the most boring and you are forced to do them with subpar craft. I've been told the later seasons are even more time hoggy but by then I was done with the game's BS and downloaded the full save to play at my own pace where I wanted to. Sin 5: WrathOh you will rage for sure. See, the campaign as boring as it is commits an even bigger sin: it introduces a lategame difficulty environment intermixed with beginner environments. Worse, it introduces it before the tutorial mission for the types of jumps it requires gets unlocked. You won't really understand how mind bogglinggly stupid it is until you get there yourself but to put it into context: there's a certain jump on this environment that requires you to work against gravity directed somewhere sideways, roll your craft in the air and this jump is at the end of the 2 minutes of twisted driving section. It also comes after a section that a beginner is likely to mess up on, further making approach to this jump complicated. I was trying to make this jump consistently for EIGHT hours. I am not kidding. This is how counterintuitive it is. Your experience may vary.  It could have easily been avoided if these types of jumps were introduced in the tutorial before that mission happens, not several dozen hours after. Sins 6 and 7: Gluttony and PrideThat's literally the players who went through the campaign all the way in without realizing how pointless the experience is and then telling others that you have to play it and you will be better for it (despite these same players openly admitting that the campaign is way, way too long). No no, you won't. If anything you are just as likely to drop the game completely before you get to later seasons. I kinda went sideways with this review because using seven deadly sins seemed fun but I am not finished yet. I've briefly mentioned irrelevant ruleset changes above but it deserves its own mention. Somehow, the game has less variety than RO1 had. All the modes literally feel like they are various barely distinguishable flavors of "just drive". Even boss tracks feel less creative by far. Then there's the tutorial. In a word: awful. It breaks your concentration by having you dismiss prompts because they abruptly stop your driving, it doesn't unlock things when it should be unlocking them (see the awful jump  explanation above) and the environment is actually visually pretty nasty.This is a difference in preferences of course, but I find RO2 Vertex atmosphere actually oppressive. Vertex in ro1 was a colorful joy, in ro2 it feels like you are driving in the bowels of an alien spacehip trying to stop the apocalypse. Tutorial also has a lot of "missions" that would have been better served as text explanations. These types of missions literally have nothing specific for you to do, you just drive as they put some (irrelevant) text for you to read. Why did those have to be driving sections at all is beyond me.I may be mentioning RO1 a lot here, but there's a reason for it: go and buy RO1 instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to its predecessor  takes one step forward from a mechanic standpoing, but many backwards in almost all other aspects.There isn’t one, only a vague sci-fi beef between the many racing garages and something about humanity reaching the stars and colonizing other planets.It’s all hidden in loading screens and item/race/ship description giving it a little more flavour, besides that, it’s just racing.Arcade will see you choosing a car and one of the 54 tracks to race on it on various, yet similar, gamemodes.Campaign will see you start with an underpowered ship and unlock better parts, as well as aesthetic options, as you progress by racing on a developer-picked combination of tracks and modes.AG racing like always is very fast and floaty, being suspended above the ground and all... but the mechanic that brings all others together is strafing.Strafing is a lateral movement that doesn’t have an impact on overall speed, meaning you can use for course correction to take better, faster lines or set yourself up for a turn without impacting the wall first.There is some weird input delay, for example you’re going to get random tenths of a second before the game registers that you made a turn or it keeps strafing for some time after you let go of the button, and I say weird because during the time the game behaved this way other stuff like the boost were fully responsive with no delay.In a game where even a millisecond can change your whole driving trajectory this is a big deal.Random crashes also plague this game.Going too fast before a random jump? Crash.Bumping in a wall in a specific curve? Crash.Pause the game during a certain race type? Crash.[Fixed(?) see note at the bottom]The 54 track number is also a little “lie” as without the reverse version of a track the total drops to 27 and then again track feature pieces of other tracks like swapping Lego blocks because you don’t have enough pieces, dropping it to even less track variety, or identity.The good:Weapons and power ups are removed in favor of pure racing, you either go full kart ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or you go pure racing like Redout 2 did.Health is given use acting like a second boost pool that recharges after a delay.Bumping on walls is now punished by stopping your health recharge for a while, so no more bouncing like pinballs because its faster than braking. [An update changed this, see the note at the end]Braking now rewards with a faster boost recharge while doing so.Campaign has now a component unlock system instead of buying upgrades for a specific ship with money, this means that you can seamlessly switch to different ships or try out different part configurations without having to grind for them every time.Graphics are cleaner and sharper than ever before.The bad:Music is fine for a racing game but the OST isn’t as banger as it was before.Many ships lost their identity, instead of going for a distinctive look like its predecessor, now all seem to conform to the same sleek futuristic jet-car look.Track also lost their identities, beautiful backgrounds but with always the same out of place track pattern/color makes you feel you’re playing always the same thing with only a different sliding background.Track readability is all over the place, the game loves throwing turns at you without giving any visual clues most of the times, and if you think “I’ll just memorize it” consider that F1 pilots are expected to tackle an average of 17 corners in a minute and a half, and you’re expected to do the same but with 50 corners, three times as much.Despite my complaints I still think Redout 2 is still the best AG racing game out there, a recommendation and a must if you like the genre.[Update]: As of 11/06/2024 a big update has been dropped, everything takes five times as long to load and I have random stutters, but the game hasn’t crashed yet, the developers also made it so that you have more leeway about taking damage so a small amount still doesn’t count towards stopping regeneration, but while this helps new players, it also turns the game back into cars pinballing of corners like its predecessor instead of requiring some finesse.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing and enjoying the first game, I was so ready to love this game. The graphics style, the driving mechanics and the content is all great. Wow was I wrong. And that's if you react to it in the forst place because a lot of the time it just throws you immediately into an obstacle.From what looked to be a fun little racing game to play on my steam deck to a sweaty, un-fun experience, I don't know how much more I want to give this game a chance.When it works, it works but the poor map design is unavoidable. _childDocuments_.review: How to "git gud": Visually, it's a lot more "realistic" than the first game. The soundtrack is not for me (I prefer Redout 1's music). The base game has 24(?) race tracks. From Mars, to .There are 5 new ships, and all 12 ships have their own good/bad base stats. You also have components: Some increase top speed, others increase handling or boost power. Saving this into a "loadout", you can build the perfect ship for every situation!Racing has a lot more "grip" than in Redout 1 but this also depends on the race track. Unlike the first game, you must rotate and pitch your ship in jumps (Though in both games, you can't play properly with JUST steering alone!). It can be very overwhelming at first, because of how much controls you get. This game takes away powerups, but gives you a turbo and a rechargable super boost. You can overheat from boosting, which then burns down health. The career mode lasted a bit too long for me. The gradual progression of stats DOES help you get used to the tracks and the increasingly high speeds as you play. However, there are so many items to unlock through >100 career missions that it can feel sluggish for some players.When this game came out, there was a  issue with the difficulty being too high and the Thrust stat being broken Luckily, the game's overall difficulty and some jumps are now easier. Thrust is working, too! The goal in RO2 speed events is to get as much score as possible in 3 minutes. You need to boost a lot. Score increases exponentially (Example: 2 points a second on 800km/h becomes 6 a second on 1000km/h or 12 at 1200), so you'll want to go fast and stack both boosts.Newcomers might find this game challenging. It has a high skill ceiling, with several layers to its controls. Because there are no powerups, making a mistake is very punishing. It's almost unavoidable that some players will be far ahead of you. Still, if you want a super fast modern antigrav racing experience where skill means victory, this is for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'll literally just copy & paste my Redout 1 review here, since everything I said there is relevant here (notable changes listed at the end):By far the best track racing game I've ever played.What makes Redout's gameplay and control feel different from your normal racing game is that you also need to rotate your ship up and down to follow the road - so it's not just a road that happens to sometimes have vertical turns or loops, but you need to manually react to those turns too. The ship will still follow the road through vertical turns automatically (you can't fly off the road), but turning it manually has a big impact on your speed so you'll want to do it.It's a really simple but effective change to the gameplay and control feeling, which helps make it feel more like a special levitating/flying ship rather than just a car on a magnetic road.The first ships might feel kind of slow compared to what you see in the trailer, but you'll quickly unlock faster and faster ships.PS. The OST is great, and it fits well in the game.---Then for the changes from Redout 1:- As you progress in the game, you'll unlock parts for your ship, and you build it up from 6 different categories. Each piece affects one or more of the following stats: Durability, Thrust, Top Speed, Stability, Steer, Strafe. So instead of picking from preset ships, you'll basically build your own from multiple parts.- Boosting has some changes: you have a basic boost meter that you use to boost. But if you keep boosting even after the boost meter is used, you'll "overheat" and start losing Health - so you can take risks and boost for longer, but it will require not hitting anything for a while so your health can regenerate back.- There's also a Hyperboost, which locks you into a fast boosting mode for a couple of seconds - using almost all of the boost meter. You can pair this with normal boost and go *really* fast, but it's really risky as you'll quickly end up losing almost all of your health. Really need to know the tracks.- Abilities (magnet etc) have been removed, probably to focus more on this boost/hp resource balancing minigame - personally I like this change.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I played the first game a lot and as far as first impressions this looks great. The new boost system of eating through your health was intimidating at first but was a nice and intuitive change. As well as getting rid of different power ups and combat gimmicks the first game had. And now there isn't classes, now you progress getting better parts. And you can even customize each individual ship. And it is pretty indepth you can change most parts as well as the livery and color palette. Honestly this is such a step up from the original game. I was surprised at how they made everything look soo much better but still feel similar. Honestly still love the first game but this is already has surpassed it and feels great to play. I have lots of content to look forward to, and many completionist things to do. edit: After playing longer and getting through the first league in career mode I understand why most people said it was repetitive. And that is because it is. There could have been so many events condensed down, considering some don't even give an reward for getting the 4 stars. Not really a big problem for me considering I played to almost the end of the first game/s career mode. But still a fundamental issue that carried over into this game that they had years to correct. I don't agree with it but still enjoy playing it if that makes sense. I enjoy just playing the game. And mainly the gameplay is the real selling point for me. Getting more and more chances to play and get shiny new things is fun. But it is a bit extreme the amount that actually is there in front of you and how many times different tracks are reused. I didn't get to experience over half of the tracks the game has to offer in the first league.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun but difficult, a lot of people compare it to wipEout but i feel its more similar to speed racer. No air brakes but a dual joystick steering system adds depth and makes it very satisfying to chain turns together. This is not a game like Forza where you can pick up and just play, you really have to spend time to learn the courses if you want to get good times.Maps and ships look fantastic and the visuals are bright and flashy but not overwhelming.The customization is quite good. I do think the paint scheme unlock is a little jank, maybe something where you unlock the colors/paint material over time would be cooler.Multiplayer is good but a server browser + some more map selection/game mode options would be nice. _childDocuments_.review: Probably the best AG racer i've played ever. Love the sence of speed and quick decision making. The different locations all feel very unique and have their own quirks. This game is not trying to recreate the Anti Gravity Racing genre (f.e. Wipeout), its doing its own thing. No vehicle combat or item pickups other than boost pads. Just pure speed with a regular and a superboost that are combineable. If you dislike its features like the flight system, you can enable automated control assists for it and many other controls.Only downside are somewhat frequent framerate stutters when playing certain tracks for the first time of a session.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I gave it a positive review, BUT this game is inferior to the first Redout in every way except graphical, still a good pick if you know what you’re getting. The racetrack progression is weird at best, so is the AI. In terms of difficulty progression this game has none really, it is difficult from the first race on, but not in a fun way. You have no time / space to learn the fundamental mechanics of the game, but are expected to instantly know tracks etc. The AI is a beast, with perfect boost control, great lines and insane rubber banding it is just not fun to race against if you are new and still learning and ok if you know what you’re doing. So how can you resolve that issue? Easily! Just lower the difficulty from Redout to a lower setting that makes you feel like a complete fool, who can’t even play the game on the “normal” difficulty setting. All in all, if you are looking for the best, most fun anti-gravity racer nowadays just pick up Redout 1 enhanced edition. Sure, it may look less impressive, but it has its own stylized look I am quite fond of, also the races and progression are just way more fun in the first iteration. Thanks for reading my review, I hope it helped!

_childDocuments_.review: Not a game for the uninitiated. It also doesn't help that many of the tutorials appear long after the player is required to learn Redout 2's unique controls on their own in order to pass specific tracks that could've benefit greatly from said tutorials.Unfortunately, Redout 2 is a niche game in an already niche, dying sub genre (AG racer) of a somewhat niche genre (racing). This leaves the multiplayer dead right out of the gate with the exception of a small community of toxic elitists. Redout 2  the savior of the genre that many hoped it would be.Here are a few pros and cons.

_childDocuments_.review: More redout, what's not to love?Flight controls have added rolling with the D-pad vs autorolling in Redout 1, boosting is now tied to an overheat mechanic. _childDocuments_.review: I really like Redout 2. But it is a challenging game. Don't be afraid to use the drive assists when starting out. They really help to make the game more enjoyable when you don't know how to strafe efficiently. (Also it's OK to skip the early speed challenges until you get a better ship.) I bumped up the steer, strafe, and break assists up to like 20% or 30%. But I started to tone them back after I got the hang of piloting my ship.There's a lot of content in the career mode. I'm trying to go through the events in order, but after nearly 24 hours, I haven't finished the first league. (Although, I've had the rank up event available for a while now.) It can feel like a grind, especially since the early career only uses the first 3 or so locations. But man, it's so much fun to just fly the ships that I keep powering through.The ships are very fast, but are still feel very responsive. I especially like the little animations on the wings and fins. Strafing is an awesome mechanic that adds a lot of depth to every corner. It can kinda feel like drifting in other racers, but with more control. The two stage boost bars is also a clever way to make a traditionally simple mechanic way more interesting.The tracks are long, and each one feels unique. My main complaint is that every track at a location shares a starting line, so it's hard to immediately distinguish which track is which during the countdown. The long length also makes each a bit more difficult to memorize, but career does a fair of getting you familiar to previous tracks before introducing a new one. TLDR: Redout 2 is a challenging racing game. The ships are fast, the controls are tight, and over all it's a blast.Oh. Also the OST, and the situational audio effects are a delight.Edit: Since this review, the -dx11 workaround is no longer needed and it's a great experience on desktop Linux. (Still stutters and eventually crashes randomly on Deck tho.) Still not done with the career mode tho. I'm like 80 hours in and I'm a little stuck at the end of class S.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of Anti-grav racers. I've played everything from F-Zero, Wipeout, and the original Redout. I've had a blast with them and would consider myself someone who enjoys this genre of games. When I say that Redout 2 is fast, I mean that it's . I don't think I've reached speeds like this since playing GX on my Gamecube. The controls are easy to learn but difficult to master. The tracks are well designed and are technical enough to require real effort to navigate but still feel satisfying to complete. The air roll mechanics, while a bit clunky at first, are extremely satisfying to pull off. This game looks and feels far better than its predecessor. _childDocuments_.review: IT is brutal. Its not an easy game, reminds me of the stories of how hard F-Zero GX is and I would call it in par with Xenon Racer in terms of mastery and difficulty, but both are fun for a lot of people and I love Xezon racer and even Quantum Rush Champions which is another anti gravity racer with is brutal!Redout is all about being a twin stick racer with breakneck speeds with a high risk high reward with boosting that one mistake can cost you. You need to know how to play chicken with your health, when to break off a boost before you destroy yourself.The controls are simple to learn and hard to master. The one thing you need to know is when to break and let off the gas, took me a bit. To put it simple, ever drive a racing game where your car is clipping into the ground dragging on the track slowing you down? You try in vain to tilt your control stick to tilt the car, but it won’t?  Its why the dual stick is important as you can tilt your ship to match the curves of your ship.It's also to avoid gets red outs or black outs like a real fighter jet pilot has to do. Hence why they named the game Redout. Now the only hard thing about it is the tilting controls. To barrel roll your ship left to right when in mid air you need to use the D-Pad. If you got an elite control or one like it map the back paddles to left D-Pad or right D-Pad. This is easier to race with and its just harder to move down to the D-pad so fast or not.Luckily if you want the Mario kart controls of auto tilting it comes with assists. Think like in Forza Horizon. Each assist is for breaking, tilting and everything to help you learn and get better at it. I barely use any but Boost Safety. For me I wish they handled Boost risk like in Quantum Rush Champions with how by default ships will not explode due to you using boost for too long and eating up all your health. They did have a ship line that did ignore that and select modes that had it disabled but for Redout 2 it has no safety system unless you use the assist.Lastly the music is good! Now its is not like the Redout 1 music that each track felt like a different environment or remain in your mind when you are not playing. But they due all fit in and work great for the tracks you are racing on. Just not always memorable in the I want to listen to them out of the game. Granted if I sit down that might change.All in all, if you like hard racers and ones that are fast and breakneck speeds you should get it. IT is hard at the start, but you are not suppose to get 1st on each race, just not last. It’s how the tutorials don’t teach you everything but over time goes over more and more advance tricks on its mechanics. It’s about going back and mastering the tracks and challenges. It’s the classic;  So when you get it, just keep at it. It’s a rewarding game and a high skill ceiling.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is different to the first one in some ways, but the formula is still there. The tracks are tough the first few times until you memorize the layouts. It's then that you can take full advantage of the straights. The sense of speed is incredible when you get that double boost going at the right time.I see many people complain about boosters right before a corner. Keep in mind that all tracks have a reversed version in which those boosters will become useful. Also, you get 3 rewinds in case you fall off the track. Another thing that may put off some fans of the first game is that many of the tracks can't be completed with full throttle throughout the whole track. However, it does make the brake button more useful now. Lastly, the only issue I've come across is some hardcore lag on tracks from 2 different worlds. I am certain it isn't my connection, just a bug from these worlds that will get fixed in time.Other then that my experience thus far with this game has been fun. 4/5 StarsUpdate:Now that I'm at the final boss races of the career I can say that the game is super fun and challenging. About what I said previously, the lag in two of the worlds has been fixed. And the part where I said you can't full throttle every track was just lack of experience on my side. If you steer into a turn and strafe away from the turn at the same time you can basically drift sharp turns. All ships are viable with the right build. Tons of variety in terms of tracks. Knowing that the chance of DLC is high, I am very excited to see the future of this game.Keep it up devs! You're doing an amazing job with game! New rating: 4.5/5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: A racing game that ins't "boring"! Now hear me out. I like racing games. It is just they get a little predictable and repetitive. Skill only helps so much. Get the fastest car and power-slide around corners. One direction is to add chaos with items and such (Mario Kart). _childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is a major improvement over the first game. Graphics have improved, but are still simple enough to run at higher settings and achieve high fps.The controls remain largely the same, and I vastly prefer the new loadout system over the module system in the first game. The addition of assists also help a lot if you are new to the game or need to get back into the groove; a very much welcome feature. I also really like the rewind feature, which is very similar to Forza's but actually better. Gameplay has actually been improved a solid amount and the tutorial levels are very helpful. If you don't have Redout but are interested in getting into the series, I would honestly just start with Redout 2; unless of course you are an anti-grav racer nerd, the first game still has lots to love. I really don't have anything bad to say about the game. Any gripes I have could easily be rebutted with "git gud." At it's core, this is a very hard game. Even on the easier difficulties it manages to have a high difficulty curve thanks to the complex controls and wicked speed; and when you crank up the AI difficulty, it becomes even harder. Even on the easiest AI setting where you can breeze through races with little effort, some other game modes require a lot of skill and mastery of the game mechanics. Time trial levels are very difficult to take gold medals in, and I have yet to even get bronze in any of the Speed trials. Personally, I am not a huge fan of the soundtrack this time around. Don't get me wrong, the soundtrack is great and very fitting for the pace and style; but something about it feels off compared to Redout 1's soundtrack. I also find it somewhat comical and disappointing that they use Dance with the Dead in the marketing, but only have one of their songs on the soundtrack...I'd probably like the soundtrack more if there was more Dance with the Dead, lol. Overall I highly recommend the Redout series to fans of Wipeout, Ballistic NG, F-Zero, and other anti-grav racers. It is absolutely worth the price, and if the first game is anything to go by, the DLC will keep coming for a while and always be top notch.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long-time fan of AGR games and have several hundred hours across the F-Zero franchise and Redout. I have waited patiently for this game to be released while 34 Big Things continued to put out garbage like Space Assault and for the money I spent, I am a very happy customer.I am very much in love with the meat of the game. It FEELS fast, smooth, and real. It looks beautiful on my medium graphics setup and doesn't lag much if at all. The soundtrack, though less listenable as standalone songs compared to this game, works better with the active mixing system and is very immersive. Several changes from the first game, including the reworked boost system, removal of power-ups, and vehicles that are more similar stat-wise have removed uselsss mechanics and put emphasis on the inherent high-risk/high-reward concept of AGR. The skill floor has been increases albeit a bit too much at the beginning of the game. The skill ceiling seems so high that no one can reach it (this is a good thing unless you are a casual gamer). This may be the greatest AGR game of all time after some fine-tuning.That said, currently I believe that the goals of nearly half of the events in the campaign I have played so far are unrealistic and generally not possible without making over a dozen attempts at each individual event. The gold-level goals for speed trials, time attacks, and qualifying rounds are just too much to ask for. Some events want you to qualify in at least first place so that you can unlock a cosmetic item, but give you a time that not even the AI can come close to when they actually race you on the same track. I'm just wondering where they came up with the numbers. In races, the AI you play against seems to inconsistently play much better than you or allow you to win. They clearly rubber-band if you start to accumulate a nice lead in most instances. There is even one track where they crash at a specific spot seemingly on purpose then respawn several KM ahead of you. They are also not subject to the same rules you are. If they crash on an arena race, they respawn. You don't. The campaign feels grindy so unless you are in love with the game like I am, it may feel like a slog.In short, the game succeeds at what it needs to, and has its work cut out for it in order for it to be optimized and more accessible not just to new players but veterans such as myself. I am getting my ass kicked in good ways and bad ways. I would have payed way more than 30 bucks for this game. I will buy the OSTs and any DLCs as soon as they become available. 34 Big Things can go far picking up where Nintendo left off if they stay on track (please make another attempt at Space Assault and don't make it a mobile game, that is not what your fans want).Go fast.
