_childDocuments_.review: Compared to Redout 1 this game is lacking in every single department except graphics (it looks gorgeous).Music is forgettable. No idea who made the call to replace Aram with Zardonic but music lost its soul. Difficulty is all over the place and dev's solution to lackluster AI is extreme rubberbanding. I really hope R2 will get the enhanced edition treatment like the first game did coz right now it's just not fun to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: First 2 hours gameplay impressions in brief:The game is incredible. Coming from a huge AGR fan and one who placed Redout 1 at the top of the AGR list (yes even on top of WipeOut Fury and F-Zero GX etc), I think Redout 2 is worthy of stealing the no.1 place from Redout 1, but I'm going to give it time to see how progression goes in the game. Otherwise everything feels much better than R1.It starts off a lot faster, tracks are a lot better, sounds are better, a few more ship classes which are nice, some classes like Conqueror/Koeniggsworth feel very flexible to use now, Lunare is not longer the go-to noob ship, new boosting system is based on heat, and then when heat it maxed it takes away from your hull health, but you don't have to wait to keep boosting, you just have to keep your ship cool, there's a LOT of career events, you can play with all the ships without customisation in Arcade mode, but you start with only ESA-AGR on the Career and have to build it up slowly as you go.Responding to the negative reviews about difficulty: if you learn to control the ship properly and manage your boosts, you wouldn't have 'rubber-banding' issues. There is not rubber banding, it's that the ships behind you will boost to get in front of you, and you can do the exact same... just outplay them, otherwise there's no shame in putting the difficulty down, unless you're going to publicly complain about rubber-banding which doesn't exist in the game. Higher difficulty = better AI management of boosts.In proper criticism of the game, Tartarus Tantulus and Ixion need reworks. These levels prevent the players from performing at their peaks due to some misplaced boost pads which throw the race instead of helping it, and ridiculous jumps on Ixion which are severely affected by sidewards gravity, but the player must somehow fly straight. I've died trying that jump about 90% of the tries. Otherwise, the tracks are amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a confusing, frustrating mess that punishes you for mistakes, and also has technical issues.The first problem I ran into is that at the default settings the game constantly stutters and hitches. This was resolved by setting the quality to low, and I suspect it has to do with asset streaming but stuttering should never happen in a high-speed racer.The second major issue is with track design, which is that the jumps are terrible. As the tracks get harder, there are more frequent and harder to land jumps. Often it is difficult to even figure out which piece of track you are supposed to land on, and air control of the vehicle is somewhat tricky. Often the hardest jumps happen near the end of the track, so it is hard to practice them, and they just kill you.The third major issue is that the controls are too complicated. You have to use both joysticks and the d-pad to steer the ship. For some reason there are two boost buttons (small and big boost). For the most part to turn a direction you push both joysticks in that direction. Does this add anything beyond pushing one joystick?

_childDocuments_.review: Visually exciting, audibly visceral, mentally taxing, and a great challenge. Unlike the first Redout, which demanded a focus on planning your cornering and pitching to keep your careering craft from smashing into a wall or flying off the track, this game focuses on playing chicken with your ship's health by constantly pushing your boost to its max, mainly due to what feels like a kind of wind drag effect that requires you to constantly boost to keep from slowing to terminal velocity in a way that reminds me of the one thing that bugged me in Wipeout Omega Collection when you were maxing out your speed down the vertical drop on Empire Climb. This makes the game feel completely different to the first one, leaving me exhausted after a session as though I've been riding a motorcycle with an open-face helmet all day, unlike the first game, which left me exhausted in a more adrenaline-dump kind of way, like after getting off a rollercoaster, or how I imagine one would feel after careering down an ice tube in a bobsled. Steering feels more forgiving in this one, while jumps are more difficult, with some requiring you to use boost just to make it. Blind corners are as frequent as before, so memorization is key. The learning curve can be steep for non AG racers, or non-Redout players, but once you master the controls, and realize that some events will need revisiting later with upgraded ships to be fully completed, it's a super-satisfying challenge. The campaign is looooooooooooong, and upgrades, liveries, and ships get drip-fed to you one event at a time.  Sound is bigger in this one, there's so much going on, and the effects are really satisfying, with engine and boost sounds whining and whooshing convincingly. Music serves its purpose well, with some great thumpers and aggressive tunes that keep you on edge, which fits in with the general theme of the game. However, it's taken more of a back seat this time, and doesn't reach the epic and memorable heights of the first, which, let's face it, would be really hard to pull of a second time in a row. In summary, the game's an absolute blast. If you go in expecting the same experience as Redout, you could be initially disappointed, but keep at it and it'll keep growing on you.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel many of the complaints about this game are a bit overstated because there is definitely more good than bad.  Easily the best antigrav racer on the market with it's fair share of bugs and annoyances.pros: - controls, streamlined mechanics, and increased variety in ship performance and upgrades make this game wonderful if you want your ship your way.  However they take some time to unlock.  Campaign is tough-tracks have ditched the portal system and instead opted for branching circuits similar to Extreme G 2.  each track has 3 circuits + a boss mode which combines all three circuits into one gigantic lap.  this allows for more focused and crazy sections of racing, which is aided by direct callouts for incoming elements.  - the campaign mode is hard, but incredibly lengthy, allowing for varied events with unlocks aplenty.  cons:-few bugs, some really bad, but sure to be addressed in a future patch (few bad colliders)-some track elements are almost too crazy, meaning you'll need some memorization, practice, and plenty of rewinds to get though them safely.- music is pretty forgettable minus a handful of licensed tracks.  Wish there were more inspiration for music based on the fun of the first game.- ♥♥♥♥ SPEED EVENTS.  in their current state they are nigh impossible to place.  they need an entire rework.- unlock progression a bit too slow, with many ships hidden behind multiple racing speed classes.  10 hours in and only four ships have been unlocked for me so far.overall mostly recommended.  thing to remember is with this type of antigrav racer, it's niche because it's less approachable than many other games.  It's hard and gnarly by design so prepare for a fight.  That said, if antigrav racing is your thing, it's hard to find anything else that comes close.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: While the criticisms of my original text below still apply, honestly, I'm changing this to a positive review after seeing the post about wresting the rights away from the publisher. Good for 34bigthings. Explains a lot about the game.Man, the more I play this game the more it makes me want to just play the original Redout. There's a lot done right here: controls are generally better, game runs better, game balance isn't Lunare City. However the new music is awful, the career mode's a slog even more than Redout, and most of the tracks are just boring. The latter is a clear consequence of having to make every track reversible for padding purposes...sigh. Also, what the hell is wrong with the flight controls? I don't want to necessarily put that in the negative bin because I might be missing something, but boy howdy does it not feel intuitive or responsive...like, it's based on setting up the jump in advance instead of having air control like the previous game.I don't entirely dislike the game--it does feel good in the moment here and there--but I'm struggling to recommend something that I can't say much good about. Moving away from Aram Jean Shahbazians and Nils Iver Holtar was a mistake. This trance music is about as appealing as eating paste.[EDIT: fixed a typo]

_childDocuments_.review: I'd say this AG-Racer is absolutely ballerI love how challenging the track itself is within Redout 2. A lot of people with negative reviews bring up how the game has a lot of blind turns and turns with no borders which makes you spin off the track. But I'll let you in on a little secret... you're not supposed to be hitting track borders in the first place as it makes you loose speed. You'll usually hit a blind turn once or twice and then you'll instantly know how to turn. That and the game actively notifies you on which bends or turns are coming up next, so I wouldn't quite say they're completely blind turns. This comes with almost everything in Redout 2, like the jumps people complain about. And if people are so hell-bent on completing it first-try, then there's a VERY generous rewind system.The game has an emphasis on boosting, as with Redout 1 (but to more of a degree than the first). A lot of people take displeasure in it since it's the meta. But for me, this only contributes to the sheer amount of speed I feel on straightaways and other spaces on the track where I can fit my turbo in. Next is the difficulty. A lot of people say the game has no chill when it comes to the difficulty. And all I gotta say is... what? I do not get people's issues with the difficulties with the game as I'm often finishing at 1st with either over a kilometer (it seems much bigger than it actually is) or finishing with a good few seconds. All I gotta say with this one is skill issue, especially since it's a twin stick racer (steer and strafe) that can be complex to control sometimes.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely phenomenal game and damn near almost flawless. If you've been waiting for another game like F-Zero this is it. Every course is brilliantly crafted and every car looks exceptional. I don't have enough adjectives to throw at this game, it really is that good.  The only aspect of this game that I don't like are the speed challenges. You're supposed to drive as cleanly and as fast as possible to rack up as many points as you can. The issue is that the threshold for success is far too high and the ramp up in difficulty is jarring especially when you absolutely demolish the competition in a previous race of the same skill level. It's quite disheartening too as some of these speed challenges house either valuable rewards or act as a barrier to progress. If you have the patience, you just have to "git gud", but I do hope that the devs reevaluate these speed challenges. The curve in difficulty, especially in early in the game, is far too steep. Other than that this game is the best racing experience I ever had. The sense of speed and the rush you get hitting those well timed boosts and jumps is unparalleled. The fact that a small team can achieve something like this speaks volumes for 34BigThings. All of my praise goes towards this studio.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, Redout 2 unapologetically demands that you git gud.  There is a lot of nuance in moment to moment gameplay.  Track knowledge and understanding how best to leverage your chosen vehicle are critical to success.You will almost certainly be running the same event a couple times as you learn the racing lines and best places to boost.  If that doesn't appeal to you, probably stay away.If that does appeal to you, I can't think of another racing game that will give you the same sense of speed or satisfaction when you're in the groove and performing well.  Blasting through a section at full speed that was previously giving you trouble is extremely satisfying.  It is a game where a primary source of fun is seeing yourself improve and pushing your limits to perform a little bit better the next time.There's a few bugs (some of which are major) and some features yet to be implemented so it wouldn't hurt to hold off for some additional updates.  Even its current state though, the game warrants your attention if it sounds like a style of game you would enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll get this out of the way, this game is both the most accessible and the least accessible game in the Redout series. How so? There's tutorials for each aspect of the game... but most of it is stuff you'll be exposed to before the tutorial is unlocked. You'll encounter things like how the temperature of each location affects the heat buildup and heat dissipation of your boost meter. Furthermore, you'll run into how different terrain types and gravity affects your vehicle's handling. You'll get familiar with these before the game ever explains them to you and, for the record, I've yet to unlock these tutorials myself at the time of writing this. I thankfully already knew about that stuff, and more, going into the game because of the videos that I watched.So, yeah, that's why I say the game is both fairly accessible but also not very accessible to new players. How many games have you honestly played that explained important to know mechanics far after they came into use? Typically, at the latest, they'll do so when you first encounter them... if they do so at all. Figuring things out on your own is a great feeling I'll admit but when a game has a tutorial system and fails to utilize it well then that's a big problem.Other than that, this is a legitimately challenging racing game even if some parts I'd say the developers went too far in that regard but that's a 'me' problem right there. If you want to grab the game anyways then go right ahead. Just be mindful that not everything you need to know, outside of the basics, are explained when they need to be.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: They've already patched the difficulty in the tutorial that many users mentioned. I don't like racing games because I suck at them. I love this game though and I think the reason why is based on how the vehicles control. See, I play flight simulators, space simulators, arcade flight games, etc. And with a few changes to the control scheme they control like a fighter jet in Ace Combat. Cars are hard to control with a controller I have found but not jets, while I don't use a HOTAS (I don't think you can or would want to) it still follows the same logic that I have mastered throughout these games. Pitch, Yaw, Roll, left and right rudders (game calls it strafing) etc. Thought the game holds you to the track except in some instances where you fly (think mario kart where the glider initiates). Once I realized that they control this way I fell in love.Oh, also the graphics are great, the music is amazing and the tracks are beautiful. The track introductions are so relaxing and this really is a "sit back and enjoy the ride" kind of experience. Fun races and fun trial modes. I am hooked.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the original Redout, Redout 2 is an excellent antigrav racer. It's different from the wipeout series in that you don't aggressively turn with air-breaks, rather you can turn and strafe.Comparing to the first game it has a way more fleshed out career mode, it might seem slow at first, but it definitely gives you a lot of building variety as you keep playing. The difficulty can be mitigated a lot by skipping events and coming back later with a more specialized build.The jumps and tracks have gotten a bit harder but the difficulty, assist mode settings and tutorials are excellent.Visuals are different to the average antigrav racer, less grounded in reality but instead everything dialed up to 11.Colours are vibrant and the soundtrack absolute bangers throughout, just like the first game.Lastly, you can gamble your health to boost more, absolutely amazing mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall very good racing game. I didn't have a issue with the beginning trials as other people said they had, I just played the trials and completed them on the first go. My only dislike with the game is the time attack and speed game modes in career; THE TIME TO BEAT IS INSANE FOR TIME ATTACK to me at least 1:35:997. And you never know what the time to beat before hand, it only shows after you finish the race. That 1:35:997 is all i ever saw for time attack and of course its always on the most annoying type of map to race on, odd turns, boost near sharp turns that you'll wall bang on etc. Speed is nearly the same thing, as far as the map selected goes. Now the racing is where this game feels most rewarding, aside from a few maps that have jumps ( too short of a jump you'll crash, too long of a jump hmmm you'll crash, you think you landed the jump...nope just missed it...good thing for that rewind feature) or no railings which lead off the map for you to crash and burn. Not every race level is like that from my time playing, but they are there. Ah yes the racing, it is pure fun. Everything just flows right, the level design, the speed, it all blends very nicely. I wish i could praise the other modes in the career mode like this but they are annoying to say the least. This isn't my go to type of racing game ( I mainly play console for racing) but this is really good, if they can update the time attack and maybe the speed modes in career to favor better maps more suited for the cause i believe it will be even more enjoyable experience ( or remove those crazy 1:35:997 run times, I have always came in at 1:40 and some ) The bots for the most part aren't a problem, but they seem to be rocking upgrades before you even earn 1. And some of the early goodies to upgrade or customize your ship are locked behind ( you guessed it) the time attack or speed modes in career Yayyyy. If you like this type of racing, it's a really good choice to select and add to your collection. I don't know what PC specs you're rocking but if you don't meet the requirements maybe pass on this game until you can upgrade for a more enjoyable experience. <MSI GS76 Stealth, 2070, I9>

_childDocuments_.review: ANOTHER EDIT: THIS GAME HAS BEEN UPDATED SINCE I POSTED THIS REVIEW, AND IT IS A LOT BETTER NOW. Still not recommended for those who are easily frustrated, but a lot of the issues i mentioned in this review has been solved.I can't give a complete recommendation, it's fun to play once you get used to the controls and how fast the game actually is, however, i can't give a full recommendation until something is done about the difficulty of the Time Attack challenges and the Speed challenges. They're way too high and too difficult to achieve, even at the very start of the game. Sometimes landing on the wrong track or too far on the right one as intended will have you fall right through the track. It's good when preventing cuts, but it's very frustrating when trying to land normally.Edit: Okay, i played through the game a bit more. Again, it's not that bad, but it can be better.First off, the campaign is LONG. About 1,449 stars are there to collect over 5 chapters. For reference, each race can earn you 4 stars. 3 stars for finishing first, and one additional star for completing a certain objective like reaching a certain speed. As i write this now, i have finally unlocked the 5th and final chapter, AKA the SRRL Invitational. If you want to receive every part in the game, every ship part and livery, good luck. All of that is locked behind super long campaign, and you will have to 4 star everything to unlock everything. Currently, i don't think anyone has done that, and i wouldn't be surprised if i was right, because there is a HUGE difficulty spike right at the beginning of the game with the Speed challenges and the Time Attack challenges, which do not scale with difficulty and is extremely hard when you encounter them for the first time.I guess a part of me is still waiting for a patch to fix those challenges, but until then, i still can't give a complete recommendation.Some of the positive things about this game are: the handling, which is hell of a lot easier to control over the first Redout, and the music, which is actually really good. Redout 2 is a mixture between F-Zero and Motorstorm with an extreme sense of speed and a huge difficulty spike and is a hella well made game for an indie game. If you like anti-gravity racing at a really high speed, this game would be for you. But it's not for those who are easily frustrated.EDIT: THIS GAME HAS BEEN UPDATED SINCE I POSTED THIS REVIEW, AND IT IS A LOT BETTER NOW.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun to play once you get to S class upgrades. There are some issues holding it back.1. Some of the building-heavy maps like Mars have awful optimization after the updates, it wasn't like this on launch. Even on lower settings you'll still end up with crippling stuttering, which WILL prevent you from completing challenges. The worst offenders are all of the Mars tracks.2. The soundtrack is incredibly mediocre compared to the first game. Boring electronic slop you'd expect to see from a corporate project. I'm not exaggerating, it's like the Imagine Dragons of Synthwave.3. Inconsistent subtitles and audio recordings when unlocking a ship or map for the first time.4. Does not play as well as the first game until you get to the Class A and S unlocks which allow you dump stability. The first game controlled excellently even with class 1 ships. This one is rough: much, much less drifting potential, much slower ships, boosting feels incredibly lethargic and unresponsive.

_childDocuments_.review: ... *Sigh* ... I don't hate how this game turned out. The problem is that I also don't LIKE how it turned out. It's kind of depressing really. Lemme explain why:Let's start with the introduction itself: You're given a Forza Horizon-style introduction to the game in the new Mantis brand ship and a feel for the game as a result. That alone isn't so bad. It lets you have a taste... The problems immediately follow with the most HORRENDOUS Tutorial I have ever experienced. It held my hand so much that I felt like there were hands constantly patting my face and plugging up my nose whilst smothering my mouth, I HATED it. "Don't run too far, Jimmy!"Piss... Next up is the tracks. The tracks feel... Kind of small, a bit too flamboyant, the boost areas are not the most easily noticeable thing in the world, which is a problem, the red and yellow wall lines of the first game are completely missing in this one, making it hard to get or keep your bearings...And then the cars... Ohh... God, the cars. You only get to use ESA's ship first. That's uhh... That's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ PROBLEM! What the hell!? What the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ happened to being able to pick our brand to start off!? This isn't FUN! I HATE THIS! It's actually enraging! I thought the customization system was going to be neat, instead it felt kind of exhausting and like it got in the way of the game! Not a single fraction of this felt fun, and I have a personal dillema with that!Over all, I can't tell which is the more disappointing launch for me between this and Shadow Warrior 3. I'll give Redout II credit where it's due, 34BigThings didn't try to do anything that the game wasn't meant for... But what they attempted took away from the identity of the first game. I'm just not a fan. The music for the tutorial and first tracks you race in the campaign also aren't very fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a negative review, but I wanna start by saying that I really enjoy this game. This is a style of game I love and it checks almost every box exceptionally well. The music, the stages, the visuals the mechanics (not counting flying) it's all great. Even the weird lore they squeeze in is goofy and silly and makes me laugh often despite how nonsensical it is. I mean c'mon, why is capitalism still alive in a future with such boundless resources? It's so cartoon-ish that I can't help but laugh. But on to the negatives. The multiplayer is unfinished. 1v1 random matchmaking is un-fun. It leads to players leaving the race as soon as they think they'll lose. Ranked is not yet implemented over a year later. The career mode is extremely tedious and required to unlock parts--parts which only can be used in career mode and have no other purpose. It makes the career mode seem like a waste of time in the grand scheme of things. That's all. The game is great but without solid, completed multiplayer this game is doomed. I hope if they have a ranked mode or multiplayer update coming that they implement it sooner rather than later. Until then I'd suggest you wishlist and follow this and wait for a sale or maybe a big update--fingers crossed.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is fun.I loved the original, and jumping into the sequel feels new and exciting while still being familiar.Only first impression gripes I have are the annoying tutorials, and having the game's assists locked to 'on' before completing the trials and having the reigns handed to you.Plus, many will complain about the boost tutorial..Your health bar is basically an extended boost bar; boosting past full overheat drains your health, but it's encouraged; balancing risk and reward. You can also boost  a hyper boost; which is what the tutorial wants to teach you to do.If you want the old feel of the original Redout, you'll need to turn off the assists (which come automatically enabled) and do some control remapping. The ships will feel grippy and sluggish with the assists pushing and pulling you toward the racing line; but without them, it's the same chaotic energy as the first game.The starting (un-upgraded) ships don't feel slow, but they  handle like crap. You won't be winning many races starting out, since you have no upgrades and your opponents will be better.Too many people have been goaded into this false sense of 'every event must be winnable right off the bat.'Wrong.Racing drivers don't win every single one of their races, it just doesn't work like that.In Redout 2, you have to  advance, upgrade, and return to older races to beat them. This makes winning more satisfying, since it isn't just handed to you on a silver platter.Even on difficult settings in Redout 1, beating the AI always felt stupidly simple (at least to a half-decent player).If anyone is unhappy with the difficulty curve of this new game, just turn the difficulty down to 'chill' and enable all of the assists. I don't understand why adding difficulty to a game is a bad thing, when there are lower options available right off the bat...Personally, and so far, I love the game. It gives you speed, new toys to play with, an interesting boost mechanic that rewards taking risks, and beautiful track designs and environments.Any fans of the original can use the settings to tweak this game to their liking; otherwise, if it's 'too hard' go find something easier to play...

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: If you are new to Redout 2, do not listen to the negative reviews.  Most of the negative reviews are from people who put many hours in to the first Redout.  While that isn't a huge problem, it doesn't give Redout 2 a proper unbias assessment.That being said, I am new to AG and Redout 2 and this game is PHENOMENAL!  As oppose to just Gas, Brake, Steering, and turbo, the game adds more "depth" to racing.  That leads to more engagement when you are racing, which I truly appreciate.  You have to focus when playing Redout 2.Speed This game is very fast and you honestly need to pay attention more so than any other racing game.Career Mode: A lot of people complain about the career mode and I can't understand why.  The career mode is LONG, but that is a good thing.  There is so much to this game, that you shouldn't just jump in to arcade or online mode immediately.  You need to LEARN how to play this game effectively and efficiently.  It guides you through the different race types and gradually increases stats so that you can see and feel how different components affect your ships performanceMusic: I don't listen to the in game music.  I listen to Sonic Riders OST and it works PERFECTLY!Difficulty: The game is HARD.  From understanding the race types to understand the track layout, it is very challenging.  It is also very rewarding.  You will get an adrenaline rush from this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The soundtrack is a straight downgrade from the first game and no amount of balance patches can fix that. Legend of Anxanum was one of the weakest tracks in the prequel and i can tell you that the majority of the soundtrack in Redout 2 actually undercuts it by a long shot. It's mostly just inoffensive, lukewarm, limp wristed drivel that only ever gets you hyped when you pause the game because THEN the game decides to turn up the bass boost to 11, which makes you momentarily believe theres some actual banger going on until you accidentally unpause and its just the same uninspired elevator music as before.Also, so far career mode has been a letdown in terms of player agency (on top of dragging on way too long with same-y events). You get upgrades to your vehicles when you have headroom in terms of class limitations and if you play all events in a row you'll never be in a situation where you wouldn't just slap that new upgrade on your vehicle the literal moment you acquired it.Track design is ... different from the prequel, to say the least. Jump sections don't rotate your AGR towards the landing spot (of which there can be multiple now, anyways) so the whole flying part is not just strafing and pitching anymore but also rotating your vehicle to align yourself properly to the track to get a speed boost. In general, the track design now involves the player way more with the more complex jumps as well as more tight corners that force you to use the brake more, and thats good.Whats not good about track design is that overall, tracks feel less inspired. While playing them is generally way more involved I can't help but notice that there are several sections in every biome that just feel like they needed to add more "stuff" so they just slapped a bunch of random winding curves down and called it a day. This design choice isnt helped by the fact that each biome has 3 courses that all reuse several parts of the whole circuit, because the starting location is always in the same spot.The tracks have also been designed to be driveable in reverse. Reverse tracks are honestly one of the better ideas the devs had here, since they actually feel less same-y than having 3 tracks that share a lot of their design with each other.There are driving aids to help the player with the on screen route notes similar to what you'd expect in a rally game, for instance. But in my opinion those are relatively useless in more situations than not, since they dont take the player's speed into account. On a course that i don't know yet like the back of my hand (which is hampered by the repetitive nature of each biomes 3 courses), boosting makes it so that by the time i actually processed what is showing up at the top of my screen i have probably already rammed myself straight into a wall. So a QoL change that I would welcome is to be given more than just one or two notes based on how fast i am going.I'm not even going to touch on the difficulty of each event because let's be honest, people need to get good and from what ive seen on Redout difficulty (the one before the AI starts to get genuinely stupid, probably with the help of cheating), everything is doable and people just need to focus more.That all being said, there is a lot of things to unpack about this game, but i'll also try to summarize it: The sequel is definitely a continuation of the prequel, that much is for sure. But it is no successor because the word "successor" implies "success", and this game does not succeed redout 1.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute garbage.What is the point of making a racing game if you are not even allowed to race?The level design constantly makes you take blind turns. The levels are narrow, have fun not bumping into anything.Taking corners the "correct" way, as in breaking or strafing loses you more time than just ramming into the rails and sliding on them.This drifting with pulling the right stick in the opposite direction of the turn is counter-intuitive and complicated. In general you shouldn't need to watch tutorials to understand how a game controls. Why they did try to reinvent the wheel with this game's controls is beyond me.The pitch mechanic isn't interesting. It's just extra busywork for your fingers and is barely utilized. They could cut it and the game would be better for it.No rebindable controls and all the schemes are questionable, asking of you to press multiple buttons at once for some maneuvers. It's tedious.The jumps are ridiculous. This is the first racing game I've ever seen where boosting before a jump is a BAD idea. Overshooting, crashing into "safety nets" and into other objects is common. Not needing a boost applies to most jumps but not all, so it's a trial and error nightmare. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥ air control doesn't help.Most of the items you can equip are garbage.The AI feels super artificial and cheaty. No matter how fast you feel like you're going, unless you're significantly ahead it can zip past you at any time. And a single mistake, even if you're way ahead can cost you the whole race.Convoluted and imprecise controls and handling.Good luck mastering that and have fun bouncing from fall to wall.All gameplay is based on trial, error and memorization, which means that you are not playing, you are working.Garbage developer.

_childDocuments_.review: Now, you may notice the developer actually says in the warning they present to let you know they're going to be harvesting data about you, and that if you're under 13 that means they'll be breaking the law when they gather all this information about you (so, if you're under 13 they want you to not play the game to help them avoid doing their law-breaking pastime of spying on children), that there's an opt-out mechanism.   There's no way to opt out of the game and you can't start playing unless you agree to surrender your legal protections over your privacy to Saber Interactive... I'm not even sure about the legality of that, but it's not okay. Redout 2 is a console ported "anti-grav" racer which just means it's an arcade racing game that has loops and other generally non-gravity obeying jumps and stunt sections in it.  Despite being a shallow arcade racer they tried to add some needless convoluted mechanisms like heat management to the game, which comes across as a little schizophrenic as the game doesn't know if it wants to be a dumbed down shallow racer or if it wants to compete with the latest F1 game on the highest difficulty... and neither of these two conflicting states of mind results in a game that's going to appeal to a lot of gamers.  Console peasants won't enjoy anything that involves pressing more than 2 buttons on their console peasant childrens toy controllers, and PC gamers will be annoyed by more console crap polluting the place. Having said that the visuals are pretty good (if needlessly noisy, I guess the console gamers need bright flashing lights to maintain their attention) and the game is optimised okay for a console port, so you could, if you really wanted to, play this while the developer harvests all kinds of interesting, personally identifiable information about you for sale to third parties.  Of course they'll say they don't intend to sell your private data for profit, or profile you, but can you trust them?  If they were trustworthy, They also ask if you would like to link your game to Epic Games (backed by Tencent/CCP) to increase the amount of spying and profiling they can do to you.  They might as well have asked me if I'd like to have bowel cancer.  You don't have to do this, but it makes you wonder what kind of agreement they have with Epic and how much of your data flows to them anyway. As always with console ports, because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.I know a significant portion of my review has been about warning gamers about the privacy risks and concerns associated with this game than the game itself, but those are important considerations.  Developers must not treat gamers like cattle or property as Saber Interactive are doing here. The final reason to avoid this console game is the almost comically insulting pricing.  Redout 2 is the kind of game that would go almost direct to the bargain bins outside the games store in the brick and mortar days, but they've given this pretty much full AAA pricing for what is, at best, a B- game.   Redout 2 has the ridiculous price of $30 USD, plus another $46 in DLC.  That's right, an eye watering $76 if you want to own this complete set of spyware with a simplistic console game wrapped around it.  Jesus wept.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated and incredibly fun racing game.They absolutely nailed the sensation of crazy speed that you want out of an antigrav racer. The tracks are complex and visually impressive. The gameplay is incredibly engaging.However, the skill floor is quite high - you will probably struggle to navigate the tracks at the beginning. Luckily, the game comes with a bunch of ways to make picking it up easier: Playing through the campaign introduces you to the tracks and gradually raises the speed of your ship, letting you work your way up to top speed. There are rally-style turn indicators. There are also highly customizable assists, which are in the game for a good reason. You should not be too proud to use them at the start unless you're prepared to mess up a lot, and some of them always remain useful. You can turn them down as you get used to the game, but if you simply disable all assists and jump straight into arcade mode, you will have a bad time and probably crash every corner/jump. The same goes for your use of the rewind feature, which will save you restarts and frustration from crashing out horribly on the final stretch of a race. The developers clearly put a lot of thought into ways to make the game more approachable and easier to pick up without compromising the skill ceiling.And once you get into it even a little bit, it's incredibly fun. Blasting down a straight, burning up your entire hull in the process and navigating the following turns with your ship integrity at a sliver is an absolute blast. With 10 environments each containing 3 tracks for a total of 30 (without the DLC), plus the combined boss tracks and a reverse version of everything just listed, there is plenty of variety as well.I personally also greatly enjoy the absolutely absurd tidbits of background lore casually delivered to the player through the context of racing, but maybe that's just me.If you like the idea of going very very fast in a videogame, then I highly recommend Redout 2.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 is an amazing experience, more polished than the first Redout, but not necessarily better, rather a different flavor.After playing for a few hours:Music: RedoutTracks: RedoutAtmosphere: RedoutDifficulty: RedoutHandling: Redout 2Races: Redout 2Customization: Redout 2SFX: Redout 2I feel the skill ceiling has been lowered quite a bit, ships have much more grip and durability, tracks are bigger, turns longer, it has been dumbed down, this makes the game generally easier, less frustrating and more accessible (with the exception of jumps, which suck now), which is fine given the first one was hardcore.There are some performance issues, games freezes for a tiny bit quite often and given the Mach 2 fighter jet speeds there would be a lot to gain from higher fps. It doesn't look that much better to justify the big performance cost.Maybe it's just bias but the first one felt more authentic and cohesive, this one feels more commercial, more candy crush.It seems like I'm trashing the game, I love it, I hope they keep working on it. I wish they will go back to a more serious tone for the next one. Keep the gameplay and make the rest grittier, more ships (there are more ship makers now, but less ships), more customization, more tracks, less cringeworthy stuff like the narration.Maan the experience of piloting these things is incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fun, feels very much like Redout 1 which was great. Music and sound design are great, game looks nice, feels really fast. Love what they did with the boost system, instead of a boost meter that fills over time that you can spend on little taps or dump the entire bar for a huge boost, they now have a Heat system, where both the standard boost and the mega-boost generate heat. Go over the heat cap and you'll take damage. This is awesome, because now it gives you an incentive to avoid pinging off every wall like in Redout 1, since you can trade health for raw speed. It's now more important to avoid the little chip damage that resets your ship regeneration since it'll cut into your effective boost capacity if you can't heal up. Minor nitpicks though:- The AI feels like it will straight-up stat-check you at several turns. Their ships are rarely maxed out for the rating that you're racing at, but they'll often be sporting upgrades to engine or boost that you don't have access to yet, so they'll just be flat-out faster than you at all times.- Bonus trophy challenges are wildly inconsistent in difficulty. Every 'Time Attack' that requires you to win with a 1-second lead is basically a freebie, as is any 'Race' that requires the fastest lap time; if you win 1st in either of these, you're practically guaranteed the bonus trophy. Any 'Race' that requires a win by 500-1000 meters is a toss-up depending on how badly the rubber-band AI wants to cheat, and which track you're racing on. The 'Finish at x speed' challenges are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ though. If I have to do ONE MORE 'Finish at 1250 kph' on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Rainbow Forest where they put an S-curve 100 meters before the finish line, I am going to lose my mind. This barely matters for progression but if you're a completionist this is going to piss you off.Overall, very good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: This so far is probably one the most challenging AG games I've ever played.That's not to say it isn't merciful either. It's more merciful than Redout 1 IMO with the combination of it's difficulty slider and tools to help control the ship if you don't want to control the roll, strafing, pitch and whatnot. Very considerate!But I'm playing on Redout difficulty and controlling with no help. I want the full experience! That said. The game's got a high learning curve. Moreso than the first one from what I can tell.Not only that, the game wants a lot of your time.... and that's what I've come to love the first game for.The second? To me, is a large improvement.No items. No annoying EMP to disrupt the action. Just tuning up the vehicle with modules you earn, far more style customization, and a beautiful three-tier boost system. Outside of the tuning up, the only way forward is basically just get better at the game, and I love it. It's boost system is a very intense risk versus reward mechanism as well that can simply eat through your health fast if you're not careful.I think my only complaint about this game so far, I'm about 60 hours in, halfway through A-class. Feels like I'm only racing Sulha, Ahkal-tech and Conqueror here. All the others just seem left behind, but I'm hoping that changes over time! It doesn't go against my bias though, I'm a Sulha fan. I like rockets on my rockets, simple as that. (Edit: Good news, almost 100 hours in now, seeing other companies again. That was fast!)And to end on a higher note- The OST. Not everyone seems to agree, and that's fine. I regularly listen to both Redout 1 and 2's soundtrack back to back, but I am a little more biased to 2. To me, it's got more variety. While still maintaining a mostly trance focus like the first game, but when it does diverge from that... it's all Zardonic EMD from there. Literally. And this game is the reason I'm a Zardonic fan now.I'm hoping the DLC's ost will be released on steam sometime though. Gods I love those songs just as much as the main game.It's definitely different from the first game, that's for certain. It's easy to see why some decisions are even a bit divisive. But fortunately, I exist on the end of the player base that considers this an improvement instead of the opposite.I hope this isn't the end of support for this game! I'd love to be taking for a ride through DLC like I was through Redout 1! Because as it stands, Redout 1 would be my favorite AG racing game and racing game in GENERAL, if they didn't make this one!Don't leave us, 34bigthings! You've created a beautiful piece of work here! I only hope it's sales numbers go up like it deserves!

_childDocuments_.review: I want to keep it short and sweet seeing as there's plenty of reviews that say the same or similar things:Pros:Similar to Redout 1 but with enhanced visuals, music, graphics and more choices with maps, customization and vehicles. _childDocuments_.review: I went into this expecting a bitterly challenging, blinding fast racing game and Redout 2 did not disappoint. It's one of those games that pushes you to the limit trying to master it. I really like the time rewind ability, since it lets me see exactly what I did wrong and experiment with different approaches to the more challenging sections.With that said, not all the things that make the game challenging are necessarily positive. The aerial controls are difficult to handle even after 80 hours of practice, and not just because they're slippery. By default, the game wants you to use the D-pad to control your orientation in the air, which requires temporarily leaving the left analogue stick while you rotate your ship. Thankfully, I have macros on the underside of my controller and was able to use those instead, but without them, I'm not sure I'd consider playing the game at all. As it stands, I still struggle with this aspect of the game in a "there's only so much I can do with my hands at once" sort of way.The game also seems to have very high expectations of you, especially on the later time attacks. I know that kind of sounds like "the game's too hard" but that's not...exactly it? I've played a few of these tracks dozens of times, often consecutively. I've got a good loadout for the track, I'm racing well, but I'm consistently getting ~2:09 and the game wants 1:58 somehow. I am genuinely unsure how to shave off those extra eleven seconds. I'm not saying that out of frustration either, I signed up for having to try things over and over again until I get it. I mean I legitimately do not know how to improve.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall really like this game as someone who played a lot of anti-grav and high-speed racers, but it's not without its problems.The biggest one I find is the flying, because the first couple of times on any track it can be exceptionally difficult to determine where the game wants you to go and you will inevitably blow your ship up either hitting the terrain or trying to land on the wrong portion of the track. There have also been situations I've seen where it appears I'm going to land correctly and instead fall through and blow up. The rewind feature is nice in those situations, but the game also likes to add limitations on when you can use it. It doesn't feel so much that the game expects you to already know the tracks, but it damn well expects you to learn them QUICK.Other than that the game is gorgeous. The strafing and pitching system is so cool, it makes you feel like you're actually piloting these things rather than just driving it. It necessitates the use of a controller which may be a negative in some eyes.Price point is a little steep for what you get, but some hardcore racers may not mind that. Definitely worth picking up during a sale I think.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best racing games on the market, AG or no. If you haven't played, you're missing out.First of all, it's fast. I'm not a huge racer, but when I do race, I want to go fast. Redout 2 scratches that itch like nothing else I've ever touched. The original, while very technical and fun, always felt like I was getting funny readings from my speedometer. Redout 2? On a fast track, with a fast ship, when you hyperboost down one of the straights you're actually going fast.Regarding difficulty: Yes, it is a hard game. It is a bit strange that some events like Speed or the qualification times don't scale. Some of the 4* events are insane (more on that later). However, I've found that every time I put my head down, tweak my ship build, and race again - it's winnable. Progression is rarely gated to perfecting single races - plenty of them genuinely need parts found later to 4*. You can just grind through and get to the next rank then come back later - it makes no difference even if you're achievement hunting. Just takes some patience.The trophies are in some cases annoying. That said, I've ticked them off one by one and there's plenty of proof out there of them being achievable legitimately. Whether or not you want to try and nail a 2km jump off the edge of the track out of a hairpin... I get it if that sounds annoying. It is. But it's so satisfying to nail them.Honestly, my only gripe besides the stutters (seemingly not hardware dependent - I've tried on several rigs) is the music. I can't remember a single track from this game offhand and I still regularly hum the original game's soundtrack to myself. It's good, and it matches the pace well, keeps up the energy, it just doesn't crawl in your brain and stay there like the first games'. Maybe that's a plus if music gets stuck in your head easily, but I do miss the music. Everything else is leagues ahead of the first game and I would consider this a better jumping in point for new players.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: A true love letter to anti gravity racing, old school full game with DLCs that only add more fun and beautiful tracks. This and Redout (the first game) are a must have for any racing lover. Colors, biomes, sound tracks, ship designs...everything in this game is at the highest level you could imagine.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game, though the controls do require some getting used to. While steering is a lot easier compared to Redout 1, strafing is now also a thing. Besides that, at several areas on many tracks you'll have to fly over gaps, which now also involve rolling, pitching and yawing to the correct area.Don't be afraid to enable some assists to a certain point, the game is definitely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews, but this, this game deserves one.Redout 2 has found it's place in my heart as one of the few recent gaming experiences that actually makes me Genuinely happy to play.For some reason, it supercharges my long lost childhood sense of wonder to race around at 800+ mph through radical locations and blasting that kick-ass soundtrack till my ears bleed.It gives off a "chuck-e cheese arcade racer" vibe, in the best way possible, the kind of game you'd spend ALL of your tokens on cause it was THAT. FUN.The locations in the game are gorgeous, ranging from the Mariana Trench on Earth itself, Tartarus Mines on IO, or even within a field of wreckage just outside of a Black Hole.It's the small things in these levels that really get me, Racing through mars and part of the track goes through water, "WHOA! THERE'S WATER ON MARS?!" Speeding around in the Mariana Trench seeing Beautiful colors and wrecked ships on the seafloor, and being terrified of the ocean the whole time.Blazing around a black hole and having the colors shift is absolutely psychedelic, and the strong gravitational pull of the Black hole pulling your Racer around while you're in the air is freaky.Surfing through the Cloud Ocean and looking down is sick, and the track itself has some really awesome design, since it's all just floating in the sky.Zipping around in the Tartarus Mines is an unforgettable experience, the music gives off such a perfect "Industrial Danger" vibe, and all the machinery and lava everywhere are cool as all hell to look at.The music in this game is something special too, the custom tracks in the game are 1:1 perfect fits to their respective areas. almost as if the music was made first, and then zones and tracks to go with it.Redout 2, I love you, and thank you, for rekindling my childhood sense of wonder, and for a game that makes me happy.and if anti-gravity racing ever becomes real while i'm alive, i'm quitting my job, and camping out to be first in line <3
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Ships look way nicer than in R1 (although they still change color based on the track's reflection, just...why)No weaponsUnlocking mods by winning feels more rewarding than just buying them with the money gained from races like in R1Trading your ship's integrity for more boost makes you feel always on the edgeThe possibility to customize an assistant for every single driving aspect is a nice touchThe rewind option (contrary to my purist beliefs) is actually useful, but I feel it was implemented due to the absurd difficulty that is gap clearing (more below)ConsBland music compared to R1, muted after a couple of hoursThe jump perception is awful, most of the times you think you have cleared the gap just to discover you are falling through the pavement. In addition adjusting direction and orientation while mid-jump is frustrating and counterintuitive, and who the hell thought that implementing non-straight jumps when you are going this fast was a good idea??Unlocking new ships is a loooong process: 12 hours in, I've gotten only four.Career mode makes you race the same tracks over and over, that's a way to bloat the gametimeThe tutorial is fragmented to the point that they'll give you useful information when you have already figured it outTracks are very confusing most of the times, due to narrow turns and lighting.Finally, : race tracks feel all the same.No matter the environment, you'll always have the perception of doing the same kind of loops and turns, with an overall feeling of racing inside a mix of a giant pinball machine and the Mario Kart Rainbow Road. No matter the background, it will never actually blend with the actual track you are racing on. I reinstalled R1 because I remembered it not having this problem and man, couldn't have been more right, the comparison is embarassing, it's so much better.I might play it more because ultimately I like fast arcade racing games, but this issue makes my enjoyment of R2 way too low to reccomend it. Get the first one with all the DLCs instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good racing game that is nothing like Fzero. Sure everything happens in the blink of an eye, you feel the breakneck speed, and you have to stare with such intensity you can't even look at your hud.Sure its exhilarating and takes advantage of modern hardware and high FPS that Fzero fans have desperately wanted forever.BUT WHERE ARE THE SICK F***ING HEAVY METAL LICKS?How am I supposed to get my Fzero fix if there isn't a cranked up guitar righteously shredding that s***? There's not nearly enough. What am I supposed to do? 0/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels severely undercooked, even still.the visual ugprade is welcome, the sound design is still good and the keybinds being configurable is great. I'm in support of the removal of pointless "combat"-perks as well... but... too much changed in the wrong direction.Air control feels . The vehicles change direction like bricks. Even Redout:EH's League 1 ships feel more alive, more agile and more fun to maneuver than these bricks - probably atleast partially due to the way the game handles keyboard inputs now.The titular feature seems  important than in RedOut one.Pitch control basically only matter where the game gives rally style pace notes to 100% signpost it. Even then, ground contact seems almost nonexistant. Impact feels minimal.Ships take ages to unlock, since they're hardlocked behind campaign progress instead of a flexible credit/money system. You're forced into a single ship for like 10 races, before unlocking the second one.There is also no speed league system - just a nonspecific upgrade pool, where any ship can stack upgrades into any 'skill'-category.The ship type or 'brand' just changes the minutiae of the pre-upgrade starting values, as opposed to the core characteristics, but presumably, you can blow out the upgrade budget to make any vehicle to perform like any other...It's a progression system where a flat, fixed car selection pool or open credit store for vehicles would've genuinly been better (see BallisticNG or RO1).Equally, old racing tracks make a comeback, but their race design has changed critically - with almost none of the previous prime setpieces having the same impact.Track design in general is pretty mixed. Some tracks are ace, but some are just downright crap. If I'm shouting "oh fuck off" at every blind jump, every sidewall-less corner, then something in the player teaching & signposting is not right. The fact that this game needed rally style pace notes to begin with is kind of a clue...The track QC is dodgy as well. I barely played 5 hours and have already - clipped through the floor of a track , broken through a sidewall instead of wall bouncing once, and also clipped through the landing of a jump. I'm also not certain if the AI doesn't cheat like hell sometimes. They can be seen barreling past you at mach 2 even while you're coming of a boostpad under active turbo - only to  slow down 50m ahead of you.Give this some more time - assuming developement is still happening - or just play RedOut: Enhanced Edition instead.I certainly need more time get warm with this - but the 5-hour-impression is poor.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time, I write a review, I just want to boost the reviews for this game, because I think it is criminally underrated and I want more anty grav racing games. You know the Anime Redline? I kinda feel like, I'm part of it, if I'm playing this game, especially if I hyperbosst and my ship is faster than 2000kmph and I'm close to exploding. That feeling is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. (sometimes I got goosebumps from it) I absolutely adore this game. It is not for everyone, yes it is hard, but it gets easier, if you get faster in later leagues. LET ME TELL YOU. IT'S BEEN SO LONG SINCE A GAME HAS MADE ME SCREAM IN EXCITEMENT FROM WINNING. _childDocuments_.review: Game starts very easy (but still very fun), apart from impossible things in the tutorial (that don't  matter for scoring they're here for the tutorial's sake), then suddenly you get bonus challenges so hard you have to almost cheese them, then you get races that are impossible to get first, and you end up feeling good barely making it third.Another huge problem is that the Turn Warning system in the game can be VERY inaccurate, or even straight up missing, making it extra difficult to anticipate turns when you have poor visibility, and you end up generally wingin it as best as you can more than you rely on them.Opponent's racing ships have unlimited boosting and I have caught them boosting WAY beyond what is possible, which could be added to the fact that, just with like most racing games, stats do not matter for the AI.Some issues with frame drop when at high speed with more than 1 racing ship on the screen.I end up regretting this purchase

_childDocuments_.review: jesus ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ christ FINALLYwho in their right mind thought 50+ hour campaign in a racing game is alright???So obviously - the game is far too long. People usually already don't finish racing game campaigns and I feel that if you make it 50% longer than what other racing games offer, it isn't going to make that statistic go up.The game is alright. It's a very competetive sci-fi racer and it does deliver. All maps are beautiful and most of them are fun to drive on (except Neo Tokio which is just a constant of unexpected turns that will handicap the speed of your vehicle). I feel that this is probably the best sci-fi racer PC gaming has to offer for now. All pointless powerups from Redout 1 were removed and now everyone just has the boost by default (good change). I really like the nitro mechanic which increases the game's competetiveness.The game surely delivers a lot but a huge turn off is still the optimisation which did get better with time but it's still not the best. I think optimisation in a game like this is very important but even considering all flaws I mentioned, I'm not going to downvote the game because it has been downvoted enough already and it really has the potential to become something amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. Name of the game is high speed, high reward. Just dont be too reckless, lest you burn out on the wrong turnEdit: Its quite unfortunate that we haven't received an update in a year or so. I know that things are being worked on, but a little more of an update on what exactly is going on would be nice. As i've been playing i've noticed a few quirks on some tracks where I've just been shoved to the side for no reason, or it seems like gravity is just ten fold in that spot (not in the black hole ones, ik that's because there's a literal black hole next to me). Also the ship hitboxes could use a tweak. Lunare especially, she really scrapes hard on some tracks that the others don't.One thing I really miss after going back to the first game for a bit is the portals. It was exhilarating to go through one of those and suddenly be on a whole other planet, or in a new area. It also made the boss tracks unique in that instead of looping to each one, it like shuffled each section of the tracks. If there's a way to include those, that would be amazing. It just added a bit of fun to the tracks and just looked cool.Lastly I do have to agree with a lot of people, the soundtrack is a banger, but it just doesn't quite have the same punch as the first and can get a little stale. _childDocuments_.review: I know I'm not alone in wanting a neutral button for reviews of games, but this game is both amazing and awful. The campaign is so incredibly padded out that if you make it to S league, you should be given an award for your patience.Tracks are repeated so frequently that trudging through the leagues is undoubtedly a dubious chore. Tracks are beautiful but have some of the jankiest collision. Think you'll land that jump? Sorry, no, you clipped through the geometry and have to start over. But what's the reward for even winning? Oh, it's a flaps that don't change the performance of my ship. Cool. And most races are like that. Not to mention the difficulty of either the A.I. or the challenges of some courses. They're sometimes way over-tuned and a colossal headache for average players.Anyways, the customization is nice but shallow, the rewards for winning races are trivial, and tracks often don't feel fair in a lot of places.I recommend this game if you are interested in AG-Racers but if not, I'd point you towards Ballistic.NG for a much more solid anti-gravity experience.

I keep thinking about the "tilt" in mind or the recurrent "you need to boost but not maneuver in a jump" kind of new things. I just hate tilting in jump makes me want to die to lower my thumb to do this.The star  unlock progression mechanic is also pure garbage. I finished the first one, beat the last event (few of us did, less than 2%) but I skipped aaaaaaalot of events, here wont be possible.... wich is dumb.Others features are pretty welcome, like the "new"(because it really isn't) super boost.Some technical issues came but didn't ruined my experience, especially cutscenes... and some "stops"... _childDocuments_.review: I was a really big fan of Redout 1, and while Redout 2 inherits most of what made it good, it only made small improvements and sidegrades. I would recommend getting 1 instead if you haven't already and this game interests you.I used to think Redout 2 looked worse than 1; on further inspection that was not a fair assessment, as the graphical quality remains about the same (which is worth criticizing in and of itself for a sequel), but the performance has significantly decreased - I have experienced stuttering and frame drops. What I will criticize is that the tracks in Redout 2 have almost no landmark locations (any ones they do have are just dumb, like the giant robot in neo Tokyo) or anything that is particularly eye-catching or beautiful. I cannot tell the tracks apart in any way, they are all just random pieces of tracks with generic background and no set pieces to set them apart.The high speed AG racing from Redout 1 is still here, and it's still very good (I definitely did have fun in Redout 2), the tracks still have insane twists and turns. They also got into the habit of removing random pieces of guard rail from the track, leading me to fall off a lot.The upgrade system is expanded upon, there are more ships and upgrades to collect, and I like the new boost mechanic where you can sacrifice health to keep boosting, adding a great deal of risk and reward. However I didn't like that you now have to manually aim your ship in a jump, the game is too fast and the control too confusing for me to able to do that. Thankfully there are assist options for jumps, but sometimes they don't work and will just let you crash.I also have to mention the music, Redout 1 had great music, but here except the main menu theme all of them are very boring, a lot are basically a 5 second riff repeating over and over.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Totally recommend.Redout II is like a fine wine – it keeps getting better as it ages. It was a bit rough out of the gate, which was a bit disheartening given the amount of love you could feel was put into making a fitting successor to the original. But now with a few patches added to it, you can tell this one is only going to keep getting better.The good (things I like): Customization: Gone are the tiered bodies and customizations of the original. Redout II really takes customization up a notch and makes it feel like its your ship. Swap out body parts and performance parts as you unlock them to make your ship look and run how you want it. Awesome! Visuals: There was something nice about the angular style of the original, but this just looks pretty. One lap around one of the Fuji tracks is a great showcase of the visual polish, but each locale is stunning in different ways. And its not just the tracks, the ships look amazing too – especially now with all the customization options. Gameplay: The original Redout felt like you were piloting a rocket – steering had the grip-free drifty feeling. Here, it seems the rockets now also have some magnets to keep them somewhat stuck to the tracks, which feels a tiny bit more fun given some of the other things added in. Weather and temperature play a much bigger role – reduced visibility adds some extra challenge, and racing in hot environments makes moderating boost usage more interesting. Additionally, the flight controls allow for some awesome rolls in midair. Line up your landing perfectly, and you get an additional speed boost. Just be careful to adjust vector else you’ll end up flying off away from the track entirely!The not so good (meh):Track design: I get that they wanted to expand on the flight mechanic that was very basic in the original, but blind jumps and weather obscured turns are terrible ways of shoehorning difficulty into otherwise moderately technical tracks. Granted, some people may enjoy that experience, but optional HUD navigation hints would go a long way to improving the overall experience. However, overall, the tracks aren’t bad. Aside from a near 90-degree turn on a certain Neo Tokyo track… Can I get an emergency brake for my rocket? Soundtrack: This is a tough one. The soundtrack isn’t bad, and there are some real bangers, but compared with how awesome most of the soundtrack was for the original, a lot of the music here feels like an afterthought. Race modes: Speed events are neat. Time attack is classic. Races are fun. Boss events are a blast! Last Man Standing and Arena are… alright? The last two are just different rules for regular races, but outside of the obvious rule changes (Last Man = slowest racer DQed each lap, Arena = exploding = instant DQ) they don’t do much else to stand apart from standard races. The extra speed and damage modifiers should be looked at to make them more interesting with each lap.The bad (things I don’t like):Difficulty: Yes, its supposed to be difficult, I get it! But there are still instances where it seems like I’ve done as best as I can with the limitations for certain events, but the AI just seems to be miles ahead. Speed events seem to ramp up in difficulty a bit more nicely now (perhaps even a bit too over-easy), but races seem to go between laughably easy and frustratingly difficult.Performance: Really, this is a minor gripe, but for a racing game, its more than a bit annoying when the game stutters the first time you run a track. This should really be loaded up front. Outside of that, performance in general is great.

Amazing graphics that you wont be able to notice because you're going past them at 2,000km/h.Like Wipe-out and the other zero g racers, there is a learning curve, but there are ample tutorials and options in place to assist those looking for a more relaxed experience.The games pace does a good job of easing you into the speed, but there are noticeable spikes in difficulty as some of the lower speed concepts become higher speed ones on tracks you thought you had learned, but its a nice problem to have.Amazing depth for a racing game, well worth the asking price. At 14 hours I'm halfway through the second 'license' and think I could do another 14 before even thinking about multiplayer.Come for the sense of speed, stay for the sense of accomplishment of wrangling a 2,500 km/h corner.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really love this game. The sense of speed has been enhanced since the first game, the controls (generally, barring aerial controls)  feel a lot more fluid, the soundtrack still absolutely slaps. It's a passion project that brings Wipeout, Star Wars Podracer and F-Zero in to the 2020's in a way that no other company has been able to do. It's thrilling, fast paced, challenging as sin, and really really fills a niche that has been missing from games for a long time.Loves:- FAAAAAAASSSSTTTT- The game looks great- The game is long!!! There's plenty to play through- Game mechanics are presented in a virtual training area that lets you put them in to practice before you take them to a "real" race- The ships feel very different from each other- Ships can be visually customised which is a great touch- Soundtrack really does slap (though I do miss what Aram Shahbazians and Nils Holtar brought to Redout 1's soundtrack) and with new environmental incorporation (bass hits on contact with border barriers, hi/lo pass filters on boost and bandpass in the air) the soundtracks feels alive and reactive as much dance music does when DJ'd live.- THE REWIND FEATURE- I play on xbox controller and tapping B lets you rewind if you flung yourself off the course on a harsh corner with no border. It makes the game so much more forgiving- No more weapons- the game is a racer, and has really leaned in to it in this iteration of the game. You might think that makes the game less exciting, but with the new boost system you'll always find yourself with other things to monitor and juggle that make you grateful that you're not being EMP'd every lap. Speaking of boost...- The new boost system that lets you drain your health to boost longer. So dangerous. So satisfying. So clutch. It's the perfect measure of risk/reward- especially when you stack your hyper boost with regular boost. It can drastically change the  outcome of a race in less than a second. Awesome.There are a couple of things I don't like so much:- Currency is no longer a thing. In Redout 1, you played in events and built up currency with which to purchase new ships and upgrade owned ships in career- it made it a rewarding experience to attain your own goals and progress in a way that you found personally fulfilling. In Redout 2 its far more linear. You get given upgrades for completing courses. You will always have access to Lunare before Asera if you follow the upgrade progression etc.- Contracts have been swapped for trophies. Contracts added a lot to the replayability of levels. It also made you feel more in touch with the game world to be approached by the organisations you were in a contract with. (Please note, with 12 hours in the game I should say I have seen contracts YET)- Detailed lore about the companies and universe has been removed from the ship info and put in to sound bytes and simple descriptions throughout career. I loved reading about the organisations that make the in-universe sport possible in Redout 1. It was a beautiful touch that really showcased the love 34BigThings had for the original Redout. - The aerial controls aren't intuitive. They have the capacity to be so, but when you spend so little time in the air it's hard to get used to them inherently. On a controller when you're already controlling your strafe and nose turn via the analog sticks, leaping down to the d pad to suddenly control your rotation for half a second is really jarring in such a fast paced game. By the time your fingers have moved and your brain has caught up with being in the air you're already back on the ground and doing 4 loop-de-loops. In the end I kinda just accepted poor landings and relying on the rewind function.- The world itself is a lot more zany, or at least is presented as such which is more of a personal taste thing than anything else.- The very linear progression applies to cosmetics inclusive of colours. I feel like there should be a far more extensive base selection of colour combos in the game from the start, with less being locked behind career progression. Everyone knows red ones go faster.I got the game in the Christmas sale 2022 on Steam with all the DLC currently available. I'd highly recommend giving this space age racer a shot- especially if you played Redout 1 and are looking to shake off the rust and get back in to the cockpit. The devs seem pretty active, and I'm stoked to see what's next!

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from Redout 1, after an hour or so of Redout 2 I can safely say: it is very, very good. The ships handle like a dream, there's a handful of control assist options which you can tweak and max out, so your friends can enjoy Europa-esque epileptic tubes and loops.New: Aerial ControlsGeting used to aerial controls takes you a while; back in Redout 1, your ship would just snap into the track; now you have to *roll* and land properly to avoid damaging your ship, and control the pitch so you won't crash face-first into a 90-degree track.New: XeSS and graphicsGraphics are improved across the board, the tracks are brimming with detail and the ship designs are a definite step up from R1. To handle the antialiasing and the performance impact 34BigThings had implemented Intel XeSS, and it gets the job done.New: Boosting and HeatThe old range of weapons, equipment and the energy meter from R1 are replaced with Boost, Hyperboost and Heat. Boosting builds up Heat. Overheating drains your ship Integrity. Hyperboosting can be used after a cooldown in addition to Boost; use both and go nuts.New: Environmental HazardsEvery track contains at least a couple environmental hazards that affect your ship in many ways; you lose traction over dirt, move slower and cool down in the water, and struggle with the gravity near a Black Hole. Yes.New Tracks:Run through the Event Horizon straight into the heart of a Black Hole, Interstellar style. Get suspended in mid-air because you didn't have enough speed to reattach yourself to the track. Become increasingly worried as it's pulling you away.Black Hole smiles at you with eternal malice.New Ships:- WALLACE-RGA new variation of the jack-of-all-trades. ESA-AGR with an emphasis on maneuverability. Turns on a dime.- AKHAL-TECHAwesome speed and acceleration, bit more balanced than SULHA, can take a hit, too. Pleasing Thunder Force aesthetic.- BURAN (dishonorable mention)In Redout 1, the *ussian cinderblock is as unpleasant to look at as it is to drive. Got to give it to 34BigThings, now it's at least manageable and you can change the looks.- BEHEMOTHTartarus mines; a guy piloting LUNARE is sweating profusely, integrity alarm blaring as he watches his last pixel of health.You charge straight through a lake of lava, unphased, sipping a Mai Tai.A SULHA struggles to push you off course. You do not veer off a single degree. Sulha is squished against the next wall, screaming.KOENIG is a turtle. This one is a heatsink that is slowly inching its way toward the finish line.Feel the weight of a ponderous BEHEMOTH.Feel every molecule of air struggle against the sheer volume of your heat-dissipating slowpokium.
