_childDocuments_.review: I have to start by saying that I haven't really played a supersonic, anti-grav racer since the likes of PS2 era Wipeout or F-Zero on Gamecube. With that admission in place, Redout II is not for the faint of heart! It is NOT Wipeout with a shiny new paint job and it ain't no F-Zero! I don't mean that negatively at all. Instead of a complete arcade racer, Redout leans more toward the "sim" side (if you can indeed simulate anti-grav racing at 900 MPH). Holding the throttle wife open and bouncing off the walls ain't gonna cut it here. Learning the tracks and the individual machines is key to not being, literally, miles behind.My first suggestion would be to remap the controls so the ground controls more closely resemble aircraft controls. For me personally, they feel more intuitive this way and they're not all switched around when you actually have to fly this damn thing every now and then. And I rarely have to turn on assists and drop the difficulty all the way down but to learn the game, I had to resort to using "Zero" difficulty. I do like how you can turn individual assists (one for each individual control) up or down as needed. As you figure out how to drive, you can ease them back to tweak the challenge as you see fit.I do have to agree with the consensus that the jumps are oddly (and wildly) random. Either it seems like you barely make it with boost or you're flying past the intended landing zone by miles. Speaking of boost, my personal biggest gripe would be that, for whatever reason, it's hard to tell how fas you're going unless you're stack boosting and redlining the heat right on the verge of blowing up. But that eye for speed comes with practice.All in all, Redout II is tough, especially for what you probably think is an arcade racer. But once you get the hang of it, it's exponentially more satisfying. If you want a hypersonic anti-grav racer that you actually have to drive/fly, I've not seen better recently. Recommended!

There is 6 types of acceleration: usual, boost, hyperboost, boosters on track, inertia return landing zones and gravitational. Up to extreme 3600 km/h, and with all of these you can still not hitting any walls.- Tons of customisation, both visual and performance.- Huge variety of different stylistically and technically tracks.- Good optimisation, even for an UE4 game (especially if you tweak engine parameters, this will run on everything).- Amazing dynamic soundtrack.- Huge career mode if you like progression, fully customizable arcade mode for single runs, multiplayer if you want to make sure that your skills are drastically below 'average' player.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: more than the sum of its parts, parts are good to begin with, the titanfall 2 of racing gamesReally loved the first Redout & have kept picking it up again & again for years, & this one improves on virtually every part of it & fleshes it out into a much more immersive & engaging game overall. the devs find the sweet-spot between arcade & hard sim everywhere it matters -- controls are deep but forgiving; garage is complex & key to performance enough to have to pay attention to your decisions, but simple enough to avoid choice paralysis; career lets you find a balance between pushing your parts to the limit on the way up to the fastest event classes & combing back through for upgrades; the focus on high effects & shaders paired w/ low-poly models looks beautiful & runs great even on older hardware. The controls & the heat/boost system are the best in the AG racing genre; the precise control over understeer/oversteer makes it feel more like DiRT than wipeout, & the resource management involved in boosting (regular boost - always available & raises heat, hyper boost - requires battery to charge & raises heat, braking vents heat, boost types can be stacked) feels like a more active & dynamic version of the fuel & ERS management systems in the F1 games.Re: a lot of the comments on difficulty -- the game does a great job with rewarding the player for learning the system & not ignoring mechanics that seem too complex, not ignoring cars or stats that seem uninteresting to the player's own comfort zone, etc.; for example, you might skip a track because you don't want to deal with a bunch of jumps or hairpins that you can't quite nail & just want to go fast, but you'll eventually need to come back for the points or upgrades, and can tune the car for the track in a way that will let you drift through the hairpins at full throttle without touching the wall, boost to a certain speed you need to hit for a challenge criterion, etc.Unique visuals + immersive controls + high skill + casual-friendliness + fun customization = titanfall 2 of racing games

The only major change is that now instead of having maximum throttle you have thermal throttling that deals damage once you overheat, but banging into things and enemies deals close to nothing. _childDocuments_.review: Short: The game has really satisfying racing mechanics, but individual tracks lack identity and Career mode needs tweaks.The intense speed of the game is incredibly satisfying, and once I changed a few controls, it felt really good to have so much freedom of movement. The game also has a great strategic choice between drifting turns and strafing turns, and both playstyles are fun. There is a massive amount of longevity to this game because it has extremely satisfying basic mechanics. There's good variety to the levels and some of the ones that are unlocked later (Origin Black Hole) feel incredible. The campaign is very long, which is nice but problems crop up from time to time. Each mission has a "Trophy" that is unlocked by completing an optional objective and worth an extra progression point. Some of these trophies are fine, like getting 5 perfect landings or finishing at a high speed, but others are more problematic. "Qualify in 1st position" and "Get 3 seconds past Gold" (time trial) are artificially locked behind a very high difficulty and most players will not be able to get them even after several attempts (difficulty has since been rebalanced and this is less of an issue). Others I personally dislike because they dampen the fun of the game. Playing a race is most fun when you're able to set the difficulty so that the AI challenges you, but when the Trophy requires you to lead every lap or win with a kilometer lead, you're incentivized to lower the difficulty to a point where the AI is no longer a challenge. Throughout the game I found myself in an awkward position where I wanted to play on a higher difficulty so that I wasn't just leaving the AI behind all the time, but couldn't because I wouldn't be getting the trophies anymore. One final issue I had was with the abundance of reverse tracks when you first start playing. They make it take a lot longer to learn the tracks, so they probably shouldn't show up until you've raced a track 4-5 times. This wouldn't be as big of an issue if the tracks weren't so much harder to learn than in RO1. There's an "upcoming turn warning" feature now which is nice but it's hard to learn the tracks when all the ones in the same region share some segments and have very few visual differences. The game's progression also feels inconsistent. At the very beginning you get so many upgrades that you can't equip them all without going over. In contrast, Class A has a string of several dozen events that don't give out any ship upgrades, but the difficulty keeps going up to a point where you're barely able to meet the minimum.  Each track region has a 'ship' that is built to suit it nicely, but in many cases you don't unlock the ship until much later, even though the Time Trial Gold time will usually be from it. Because of this, some events are very difficult early on but become easy later with the right ship. There were a few instances where I encountered bugs or the physics felt wonky (particularly when landing after jumps), and hope those will be fixed before long.

_childDocuments_.review: Final Score 4.25/5Verdict: Worthy successor to Wipeout series that brings mature and rewarding racing mechanics, challenging career mode to battle for upgrades, and beautiful graphics,  ------------------------Pro:- Fast, challenging, cool loooking- Responsive controls- Pretty visuals- Awesome soundscape- Thumping dynamic soundtrack- Lasting career mode------------------------Love/Hate: Difficulty - Player reviews around the internet sometime complain about difficulty. I think this is is because of misunderstanding the career mode - you are starting in basic rugged down ship and by playing career mode you unlock "racing modifications", to increase power. Each configuration of ship has speed rating. You will not be immediately winning races with ship rated 208 against ships rated 298.  I like it, as it makes sense to me - I will try to finish 2nd in this race to unlock better rudder unit, so I can be faster on next attempt. Now none of this is explained well in-game, you have to find it out by trial/error. So I understand the confusion, however the game difficulty and career progression is well done by me. Controls - are also new, if you have not played the predecessor. Left stick to turn, rights stick to strafe and control ship yaw - in Wipeout this is was on triggers and left stick respectively. This poses some challenge to master. Make sure to play with assisst if you struggle.Music - If you are into psytrance, dnb and in thumping music, you will like this one. It has interesting dynamic soundtrack model where you can gauge speed by how close to peak techno you are. If not you can always disable music.Announcer lady telling track stories - Not fan of autotune chosen, content is fine but script would deserve a rewrite (english version)------------------------Really bad:- HDR is broken. It does not work. Just do not even try to enable it unless there is a patch with specific fixes.- Control scheme probably could be reworked, maybe the Wipeout scheme is better?- Written description of developers logic behind career mode would honestly be enough (Play races to finish 2nd-3rd, earn upgrades, rerace and win.)
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is not like the first game, and I strongly recommend playing through the first game first - both for the quality of content and the difficulty curve you will be guaranteed to hit going straight into Redout 2 blind.Redout was an Arcade racer with a progressive campaign that eased you into faster and faster tracks. By the end of mastering the campaign you might not have been the best racer, but you felt accomplished getting each gold medal and a platinum medal or two. You customized abilities and picked a team that suited your play-style, with the more tanky teams being good for less experienced players, as the health pool in the first game was about 1/10th what you are given in Redout 2. It had amazing and unique tracks and event modes, each felt unique and immersive.Redout 2 is an immersive and competitive beast. Coming from the first game, you've had the boost upgrades completely unlocked to the point where you can keep using them until your ship explodes - no more power-ups, meaning the tanky ships are designed to boost for longer with their additional health. From the very first track, you feel like you've been dunked into a difficulty harder than the first game could provide, and that's not necessarily a bad thing, since...You can now put training wheels on your ships in the settings, helping you corner faster and keep your ship from exploding. The tracks themselves now have multiple paths, each environment affects your ships differently, and above it all the music is just as great as the first game.Vertex maps have been redesigned from the first game into actual tutorial levels, showing players ~some~ of the intricacy of the controls, but I feel neglects to show some of the most important tips, like how to drift. (strafe opposite of steer)Another change from the first game is the intricacy of jumps and landing, needing to pitch as you fly. The biggest bug that needs to be fixed is the collision box with the track as you land as you will fall through unless your landing was perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly awesome game, but with a steep learning curve.When I started playing it, I found it too hard.  I got quickly frustrated.  I wasn't even winning the trials.   After a while of almost never winning any speed challenges, I figured I was doing something wrong.  Turns out I was!    I was strafing the wrong way.  When you have some sharp turns to do, you cannot strafe in the same direction you are turning, you need to strafe the opposite way and before you start the turn and then adjust the strafing during the turn.  This changed everything.   I was able to complete the B league and I'm working on the A league now.  This game is very challenging, but it is great.   The first one was only truly challenging in the dlcs and in some specific events.    This one feels more like Wipeout-level challeng.   What a rush you get when you complete a hard event after several tries.   I'm not even in the hardest part yet.   Can't wait to see the insane speed of the last events.  It's a long game too.  I'm close to 90 hours and I'm not even halfway through.    I often need to redo events several times before winning and there are "trophies" in each race that sometimes are really hard to accomplish.  15 perfect landings, dammit!The music is great, but not as good as the first one, I think.   This game looks incredible too, the level designs and the car designs are amazing.   Some tracks need to be fixed (or explained?), sometimes when you jump too far, you go through the racetrack even if you should just land on it.    Some of the time challenges are wrong too (1 in B league and 1 in A league so far).   I finished them with something like a minute and a half faster than gold.  It made no sense (I'm nowhere near that good).   I also sometimes start spinning in circles when I hit the sides in a specific way.  These are small issues that will be possibly be fixed in upcoming patches.I highly recommend the game for any fans of Wipeout and F-Zero out there.

_childDocuments_.review: So far 3 hours in and its a 4/5 from me.After the first 90 min and completing all the tutorial levels things started to click and things like boost stacking made for some interesting gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: DON'T LET THE NEGATIVE REVIEW SCARE YOU!Most of those were written at or shortly after launch when the difficulty curve was insanely unfair and the game was a bit buggy. The devs have worked hard to rectify these issues and the game is now much more approachable.That's not to say that it's easy. The controls themselves are their own challenge to newcomers. For the uninformed, simply steering your ship around the track will not do. You have to use both control sticks to control steering, pitch, and strafe. Coupling this with lightning fast speeds, edgeless tracks, blind corners, and learning how and when to boost most effectively makes getting around the track in one piece quite the challenge at first.But rest assured this is one of the most satisfying control schemes to master. As you progress through the (appropriately difficult) campaign you'll progressively upgrade your ship with new parts to help you fly around the track faster. There's not a lot of variety in locations at first, but once you get to where you're racing on the more complex and beautifully designed tracks things really start to heat up.I also have to shout out the AI driving assists. You can adjust how much assistance you want with any aspect of driving. While I recommend using as few of these as possible, I still use the Boost Safety and Air Roll assists after 30 hours.I also cannot recommend the season pass enough. These track designs are some of the best in the business and it's totally worth the money.So yeah, from a veteran arcade racing fan, this is one of my all time favorites. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is wonderful, I didn't stick with Redout 1 not because I disliked the game, but because I felt late to the party and hardly felt like I understood what I was doing, Redout 2 feels more complex yet I can actually understand what i'm doing and how to go fast, I'm not someone who plays racing games at all, but I dip my toes into a few interesting ones and so far this is by far my favouriteIt has a wonderful sense of speed and tight controls, breezing through a match feels and looks masterful, this game feels like it's less about taking tight corners and more about maintaining and gaining speed, same as Redout 1, the visuals and music are fantastic and I want to specifically mention whatever dynamic music system they have in place is perfect for this game,It isn't perfect however, UI could use some work in some areas, the singleplayer has a daunting amount of content that while has variety, it's not enough for how much they want you to play. Some tutorials being locked behind singleplayer progression which while having good intentions of not flooding the player with information, is a weird choice for players looking to learn, something a difficult game like this will have a lot of, and multiplayer is all matchmaking with no server browser which while isn't bad, is a downgrade in my opinion.Difficulty is something people have talked about, I'm finding it to be easy outside of the speed trials, but I didn't play before the patch that made it all easier, my other complaint is weirdly enough, the lack of rubber-banding, It feels like I get ahead in every race and never interact with the other racers again, rarely any give or take with the lead.I am loving this game, aside from the singleplayer balance it feels more polished than redout 1, On current patch it's still very enjoyable and i don't feel like i'm missing out on the few odd singleplayer missions that seem unreasonable, it's a fantastic pick up and play game that I hope has a good life ahead of it.

_childDocuments_.review: I love futuristic racing games like F-Zero and Wipeout, games like these are the pinnacle of the racing genre (in my humble opinion :^)Thing is though that these games are pretty rare, there were a few during the 90s and early 2000s but nowadays it is really difficult to find any new entries into the "Futuristic Racing" Genre. Luckily we got some top tier entries "recently" with the first Redout and BallisticNG and now we can add Redout 2 to the list.If you ever played any of the games I mentioned and you like them then you have to get this game! _childDocuments_.review: I’ve already written about it extensively in both my Beast Sides and Best B-sides of 2020 features but I still haven’t run out of ways to praise this track. _childDocuments_.review: Yeah if you wanna get max stars then the game is pretty rough.. but that's the whole point of these arcade X00mph futuristic racers. It might not be easily accessible for people new to the genre but as someone that grew up playing Rollcage, Wipeout, Burnout, XGR etc. I can wholeheartedly say that this is it chief.The artstyle isn't anything to write home about but it lends further to the performance and when you're whipping around a corner fast enough to nearly black out then the last thing you should be looking at is the slightly low res sphinx in the far distance.The difficulty... let me start off by saying that I played redout 1 and thoroughly enjoyed it. Only complaint about redout 1 is that the difficulty was inconsistent, at times I would blaze through a course and get gold and others I would be stuck for 30 mins retrying to get the perfect line. Redout 2 on the other hand is far more consistent.. consistent at crushing your balls because ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is unforgiving, that is exactly why this game is so much more enjoyable (imo) than the endless slew of modern racers, I've never restarted a race so many times and still been eager to give it another go just out of sheer determination. Let me tell you about boost management.. because if you're anything like me then you'll get a stiffy from watching the boost meter fall as you rip through the course and then start to eat into your ships own health pool for the first time. Oh you want to mega boost everytime it's off cooldown? yeah no sweat.. just make sure you never touch a wall because you're gonna be riding at 1% health the whole game. You might think this sounds awful but it's actually such a great mechanic imo, think of the possibilities.. having the large health pool is a great fallback for newer players just getting the hang of things but where it really shines is for the more experienced racers, it's a game of chicken to see how far you can push it at all times constantly riding the knifes edge.Conclusion.. if you like a bit of c*** and ball torture and also happen to enjoy racing games in equal measure then this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has played the first game, I feel that the controls have been changed for the better. Taking out dedicated buttons for air strafing means your right thumb can stay on the right analog stick and allows you to boost whilst navigating turns. The AI assist that can be fine tuned for just about every aspect of using your hovercraft also serves as a great way to ease yourself into the controls and gradually take the training wheels off.Taking out the usable gadget slot, while it decreases variety in gameplay, also serves to better focus this game on racing, especially when almost everyone was using the ultra boost gadget in the first game.Lastly, it feels like Redout 2 rewards players better for masterful driving and boost management. Instead of being limited by how much fuel you have in the tank to boost (hence the low variety of attachments and gadgets used in the first game), you're limited by your craft's structural integrity. This greatly separates those who are constantly crashing into barriers and those who don't, creating a steeper but more satisfying skill curve to master.Couple everything with it's already sick artstyle, framerates and techno OSTs, and this feels like a newer, improved version of an already amazing first game.

_childDocuments_.review: Takes a step in a different direction from the prequel, feeling like it combines Redouts traits with F-Zero GX with its energy boosts tied to your health. Then it turned me over to see if I was still breathing--then it dropkicked more of the same set of tracks some more.I couldn't take it anymore and spoiled myself seeing the rest of the zones past that in the free modes. Customization is nice but feels sorta minute with the payoff save for the livery and colors. The tutorial could be introduced a bit better with everything all at once and not really in the bits and pieces format. I found myself questioning some of the newer features that weren't answered until a few successful races later when it was finally addressed - by that point I dismissed the question and moved on hours later.Speed Mode? _childDocuments_.review: It's good, but it could have used another round of balancing.Legibility is much improved from Redout 1, with a bright neon line running through the center of the track as well as rally style callouts for turns. Jumps are much more drawn out affairs, giving you time to adjust after takeoff and being more tolerant of speed variations. However as the game progresses and the tracks look more and more like rollercoasters, this shows its limits. The callouts have less than perfect accuracy. There are still a few hills that conceal immediate turns, and many more that hide the straight lines you want  to be boosting on. Your high speed jump will miss its mark because you couldn't tell you'd be falling sideways after this many loops.Despite the experience of the first game, the developers have still not sworn off blinding the player, with clouds occasionally traversing the course and veils of waters blurring your craft's canopy. The loading screen might tell you that low visibility "really brings Redout to the next level", but there's no way you're getting a good idea of the unannounced right-hand turn right after entering the first habitat in Ahti, unless you pull it back a notch and go through it at 30km/h. At least Neptune's pipes are gone.The game is difficult, as many of the other reviews note. Thankfully the game provides 6 different difficulty levels, as well as rewinds that let you undo your mistakes including crashes. It's a shame then that these options only work for races, leaving the other half of the events, ie Time and Speed Trials, unchanged. There's about a 20% difference between what's needed for Bronze and what's needed for Gold, and Gold typically requires a performance that would beat a Master level AI for that single lap. And you'll need golds to progress through the game's second league.Races with a time trial for qualification are even more amusingly off the mark, with the times demanded for first place being higher than what Platinum requires. Narrowing the bracket of target times and scores, letting players use rewinds in these solo trials, and scaling all of that based on difficulty would have completed the laudable inclusion of difficulty levels, but as it stands things were rushed.

_childDocuments_.review: Give this some time, and you'll see it's an outstanding sequel to the first game, whilst leaving a few areas for improvement.The handling is tighter, which suits its more technical track design, and more so the faster you go. And faster, you will have to go, much faster than in the first game. The campaign is brutally HARD, and there needs to be a bit more balance, especially with the 'Speed' challenges. You have to very strategically pick your upgrades and then fly more or less perfectly to be in with a chance of earning some stars on some of these. That's actually a point of contention for me. I was going in expecting to pick my preferred team, and build it up throughout the campaign, but for certain challenges, you really do have to switch it up, swapping out parts to be within the homologation limits. it can get finecky changing your setup so frequently to suit the event.All that said, my biggest gripe with the first Redout was a lack of challenge from the AI. That has been comprehensively remedied here. You will much more often be neck and neck with opponents, boosting past one another and jostling for position, which really adds to the drama.The music is actually for me of a more consistent quality than before, though it's not packed with as many killer highlights as the first. The score is solid and does a great job of getting you pumped up.There is some bugginess at times when landing on tracks, in that it's possible to fly straight through them when you could have sworn you contacted it.  It can be hard to tell at such high speeds and, as others have pointed out, the track can be particularly hard to read when transferring between tracks over long distances, often with a choice of track, along with obstacles to avoid. Moreover, knowing how much extra pitch and boost you'll need to make the gap is largely a matter of trial and error, with certain jumps having some quite counterintuitive physics to them. Once you've learnt the track though, it's much less of an issue. The aesthetic customization is pretty awesome, though it takes a while to unlock things. I'm standing at 15 hours and the vast majority of parts and liveries are still locked. The campaign itself is pretty straightforward, much like the first with a mixture of its different event types across a nice, large range of biomes. I wouldn't bet on the multiplayer being too lively, based on the first game, but you never know.I'm actually going to say this is the superior game to the first, for the overrall experience.Again, be aware this game is hard as nails, but if you give it a chance and focus on strafing and counter-strafing to make it round corners, there's a hell of a thrill to be had here, once again.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I played Redout 1 and I played a lot of the WipEout games, so I'd consider myself an AG Racing fan.And this one is a mix of emotions.In comparison to Redout 1, I'd say this game is an absolute improvement on almost every level. Unfortunately that doesn't mean it's perfect and it carries over and creates enough issues for me to frequently get frustrated with aspects I feel like aren't my fault as a player.But let's start with the .The amount of blind corners, jumps and open edges is just depressing, and no arrows or pacenotes or rewinds will get you out of that.I love myself some challenging maps, but I want to have a chance at succeeding.Honestly the rest are just nitpicks. I really,  want to love this game but the frequent bad maps make it very hard. I'm still absolutely gonna recommend this game, but it's just such a mixed bag.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from the perspective of someone who played Redout 1, I would say I much prefer Redout 2  to it. Redout 2 is a lot more technical than Redout 1. It has steep learning curve, even for returning players. If you come from Redout 1 expecting to slip into Redout 2 like a familiar pair of gloves, you'll be in for a rude awakening. However, if you get yourself accustomed to the game, its much more engaging than the original.Redout 2 has taken out most of the powerups from 1, and it's better for it. Most of the powerups were either very situational or very unpleasant to deal with. The only powerup that saw consistent use in the first game; the Turbo Boost, they've taken and incorporated into the main mechanics of 2 as hyperboost. Sparing the details boost management is now much more involved than just doing it whenever you can. It's a tricky system and results in the player having to strategize and adapt depending on the course they're playing on.Now if all this sounds really daunting, don't worry. There have been some very helpful features added to compensate for the higher difficulty level. For one, a very robust assist system has been implemented that automatically tunes itself to your needs from assessing your tutorial performance. The assist system can then be manually customized if you feel unsatisfied with it. If you really have trouble, I'd suggest cranking those up and then turning it off after you get a better sense of how to handle yourself. There is also a rewind feature that allows you to wind back time at will to try again if you make a mistake.Overall, a very enjoyable game. Unlike most modern games, it has a steep learning curve but it tries its best to hold your hand.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute blast! _childDocuments_.review: It's more Redout, with a steep curve to get into (a few hours, so keep that in mind) and a more convoluted Career upgrade track. Since I primarily play solo, Career mode is the only thing I'll discuss.At time of review I'm clearing the last bits of the starter B-league.The upgrades to ships now are modular and tied to a point-value used by the career missions. Since the upgrades are rewards for clearing specific missions, you might not have the proper stats to beat an earlier mission.The other part of Career missions are the star-rating, 3-stars on 3rd-2nd-1st and 4th for clearing an objective regardless of placement. These are usually 'go fast', 'beat the top time', 'finish fast' etc., but there are a few ones that are counterintuitive to the way the game is meant to be played (go fast) and some that are a nuisance to get, specifically the Promotion race to A-class, where one jump on the Tartarus track unassisted flew me into the wild unknown many times until I turned on the assist.. and even then it was tricky. It could be fine in a ~2min lap, but this was a 2-lap boss run, so effectively 14 minutes of 'perfect' play in the relative early-game.The customisation has the color schemes and patterns again, but with the upgraded classes swapped for modular upgrades, the cosmetic aspect of ship design has also become modular. You have the base chassis per ship archetype, and unlock modular parts (and schemes and patterns) through the missions as well.The soundtrack is good, but is missing a bit of the original's vibe. It could be part of the new track-blending tech they use for the music, but they lost the stand-outs from the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: At the moment, Mixed.For now i can absolutely not recommend this to Casual players, its baseline difficulty is far too high.While it does have Difficulty settings and Driver Assits, the Difficulty settings only affect how well the AI drive.In Qualifiers, Time Attack, and Speed Gamemodes the Difficulty setting have 0 effect and are very overtuned making even veterans break into a sweat.That'd be not so bad unless almost all of the unlockables be it Liveries, Paint, Upgrades and even Vehicles are locked behind these gamemodes, unlockables you really want if you want to play Multiplayer and i guarantee this will frustrate most of you.Unlockables also locked behind bizarre bonus objectives like landing perfectly 15 times... on a track with no jumps... in a 1lap race.For Veterans however, be prepared for a real challenge.The Tracks are tighter, punishing, more frustrating followed by then adrenaline inducing after practice.The time requirements are tight and even for some of you seemingly unreachable.Eventually after 30 hours i can almost see the light at the end of the tunnel and i am starting to feel more confident playing this game.Be prepared, this is not an easy beast to tame.Other DetailsThe tracks are one outlier, The Boss tracks this time are directly linked, kudos to that, the bad news is that the reversed tracks feel very disorganised in comparison.To the point that in one track, known as Cloud City: Mistral have the AI dying constantly at the reverse.And Tartarus: Ixion where the AI will teleport 4km infront of you if they are forced to respawn at the reverse.Other bugs is where you either fall through a track or worst one, hit an invisible object in the middle of the track and bump back, or more commonly just start spinning like a pulsar, stuck.TL;DR, the game is still in a early state with early release issues, is not reccomended for Casual players, and also Veterans need to be warned that the difficulty curve is way higher.

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is way, WAY harder than the first but I love it so far.Redout 2, like the first, will remind you of the days you spent in some sticky gross arcade playing F-Zero AX with the whole two friends that showed up to your birthday. It's a fast paced, chaotic, extremely high skill ceiling game, even more so than the first. It ditched the items from the first game to raise the bar on the boosting and vehicle handling, and honestly I dig it.I've seen some negative reviews regarding the difficulty, and while I don't wholly disagree, I kinda like the challenge? I haven't got too terribly far yet, but it hasn't been too bad, barring a couple exceptions (COUGH speed challenges COUGH).I'm going to defend it though, honestly many games don't bust my ass these days, and I appreciate a game that does.I think the main issue is how woefully unequipped you'll be for those first couple races; AI will have items and you will not, and you start out with an extremely minimal, all rounder ship that really does need those items to compete. The tutorial, especially the very first ones, are simultaneously very barebones and very handholdy, and you may find yourself having to figure stuff out on your own (combining strafing and turning for new players for example) for a while. I think the main issue with the tutorial is that you don't really need to  what it asks you to. During a cornering tutorial I was smashing into walls left and right but it completed all the same. There's a tiered result system (gold, silver, etc) and yet the completion is all the same 1 star.In spite of that, I think as you get over that initial hump the game comes into its own, and it only gets better. I ain't gonna say get gud, but I will say  stick with it a bit more if you struggle. You can clear that hump. Once you do the difficulty feels especially more fair and the reward is so very worth it.The environments are even prettier than the first game, and I thought the first was already stunning. They included more in-depth vehicle customization which I absolutely ADORE, being able to pick apart aesthetics with a goodly amount of pieces and being able to mix and match certain gear gives all ships a bit more wiggle room in terms of versatility than the first game.Still love how the game plays, handling and boosting is very difficult yes, but so very rewarding, and I wish more games were like that.Few bugs I ran into, though they bear mentioning:Some jumps I launch WAY over what's seemingly intended, especially on one Cairo map, and clip straight on through where I should land.I know the AI is cheating on Tartarus. I KNOW THEY ARE. THEY DON'T WHEN I FOLLOW THEM BUT IF I GET AHEAD OF THEM JUST AFTER A LAP  4KM AHEAD. I'M NOT CRAZY.You know what this is. Like F-Zero (especially AX/GX), or WipeOut, this is your cup of tea. Don't mind a bit of ball-busting? You'll be all right. Especially to GX players. That game whooped my ass as a kid. I love a nostalgic ass-kicking. If you're on the fence, give it a couple months to iron out some stuff, particularly in the early game.

_childDocuments_.review: Torn right now. I really wish there was a thumbs in the middle option..I really do enjoy the fast pace style of this game. There's a severe learning and skill curve that makes it hard to get going but rewarding to get better.. The ai is trash and will rubber band and or be forced to catch up to you unrealistically even when you've raced perfectly for 90% of the track. One little bump and all of a sudden, the 2 mile lead you had on ai is instantly lost and they're ahead of you and it just doesn't add up. I hope to see the ai become more realistic and the game can become a bit more rewarding to players that are actually doing well. The multiplayer as of right now is absolutely awful. Not only does matchmaking suck super hard but it often fails, and doesn't properly track the performance of each player. I just finished racing someone online in an un-ranked race and they must have been new because I destroyed them with an over 5 mile lead.. They didn't finished and at the end, it said that I lost.. WTF, okay... stupid.. The graphics, physics, and car customization / unlocking system is pretty cool. I really have enjoyed the actual racing part itself and I've gotten through most of the 3rd league but and can win most of the races but I've gotten to a point now where its just too difficult to progress to be fun.. It needs to be loosened up a bit so that I can actually unlock the parts needed to progress. I'm now stagnating because I cannot unlock more upgraded parts which I need in order to unlock more start on the next races. I'm not complaining about not getting first place or not doing perfectly on a race, I'm complaining because as others have said, its just too poorly optimized and isn't well balanced in terms of unlocks, vehicle power available vs the ai driver difficulty going against you, etc. The other thing that annoys me a lot is the way it looks when you hit a ramp and you need to rotate the car quickly in order to land on the other side of the ramp.. It can be so fast and so hard to even see ahead of the track to know what direction you need to rotate.. I shouldn't have to memorize tracks in order to keep up with that. Its annoying AF.. I wish it would at least indicate which direction you need to rotate. Im not asking for it to be easier, I just want to be able to mentally keep up with the next move needed like it does when it indicates turns, winds, hills, etc as you race.All in all, its the fastest pace racing game I have ever played and its pretty rewarding to get good at. I think in time as they balance out the ai handicaps, unlock parts requirements, make future upgrades a bit more in reach, fix the stupid jump rotations to be more visible before hitting them, and finally, spend some time investing into the multiplayer interface, matchmaking, invite system, and scoring post race, it could be an awesome game. I am hesitant to recommend it right now for the reasons above. I am glad to own it and still play but it can be very annoying at the same time.Cmon devs, pay attention to the common complaints you're getting for Redout 2.. Don't ignore them and then wonder why your game dies in a few months.. Be better than that!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm absolutely sucked into this it's just perfect for me. I love the new risk reward system with how the heat and health bars react to each other on maps you know well you can pretty much be always boosting your shields and heat should never be full otherwise you're just wasting potential speed and once you under stand this the game becomes so much fun and just stupid fast. there is a lot of shortcut potential with the ability to get of the track and boost onto another part of the track I accidentally skipped an entire loop doing that cant wait to see some of you speed runners in time trials. _childDocuments_.review: I would like to preface that I have never played the original Redout game or any anti-gravity racer before, so I cannot give a comparison. However, as someone new entering the genre and franchise I have been blown away by the visuals, the amazing high octane gameplay, and just how fun the game is. The game is challenging but very rewarding especially when you are finally able to make a turn perfectly or beat that time trial that was troubling you before. The game puts you in the deep end, giving you a pretty crappy first car that isnt the best at cornering or strafing. It kind of acts as you training wheels so you can get a feel of the game. I have unlocked 4 cars atm. The game becomes a lot easier when you get the 2nd and 4th car. Makes you feel like a badass going around a massive bend at over 1000km/hr. The are a few issues with the game however. I would say that this game is definitely not for everyone, and the poor design of the tutorials don't help either. For example, there is a mechanic called "Boost stacking" and the way the progression works is that you unlock the tutorial missions as you progress through the game. However, you kind of need to using this mechanic the beat a lot of the missions before you can even unlock the tutorial. The deliver of the tutorials themselves are pretty poor also, It slows down time awkwardly to teach you and it just doesn't work that great. Another issue/bug that I have encountered was on one of the tartarus mines races where some of the AI would teleport 4km ahead of me at the start of the race. luckily I was able to catch up and beat them. Bit of an all over the place review but the bottom line is that the game is very very fun. There is a tone of races to do in the campaign and the game for me is a great mix of challenging and fun. I play on redout difficulty and I havnt had any issues with winning races. I wouldn't recommend this game to someone who is bad at racing games however, there is a bit of a skill filter.

_childDocuments_.review: The previous game, Redout 1 is a fantastic futuristic racing game. Roller coaster tracks requiring you to pitch your craft up and down, beautiful vistas, a complex steering and strafing system, different(or no) gravity on some tracks leading to wild track design with huge jumps or free flying sections, fantastic sense of speed, great electronic soundtrack.Redout 2 has all of that and tries to build on it in three key areas:1. HandlingThe handling is much tighter than in the previous game. It is much easier to avoid the walls and thus tactical grinding or bouncing off the walls is just not the way to go anymore. A good change over all, sacrificing a slight bit of the flavor of the original for an overall tighter experience.2. Skill FloorThe game has a wide range of AI difficulty options. Sadly this doesn't do anything for events without AI as far as I know(time trials and speed events).The game has a tutorial that the predecessor lacked, although it is not great, a bit annoying and weirdly structured (some of it only unlocks once you've already done other campaign races)The game has asssists you can enable in the menu without penalty. If you don't know how to steer, strafe, roll or not blow up from boosting, you can hand it off to AI.The game has a rewind system. A few times per race, depending on the difficulty you can pause the game and go maybe 20 seconds into the past to correct your most recent mistake.3. Skill CeilingYou have two different boosts on three seperate cooldowns(heat, health and hyperboost ability). Boosting with full heat depletes health. You can combine both boosts at the same time for massive speed for massive health costs. Managing these bars cooling down each at their own pace is key.You can control your roll in the air now. You can choose during some jumps where to land and you can adjust your craft accordingly. Also there's a system in place rewarding a perfect landing in pitch and roll with a free speed boost.You can take off of the tracks if you pitch up and boost over a bump in the track, allowing more creativity, but this also influenced track design where some alternate paths can be reached by actually jumping off the track instead of sticking to it. As it stands, it is a pretty great sequel. It's still a bit rough around the edges right now, especially for newcomers I'd imagine. But sticking with this game and improving at it will be very rewarding.I'm personally very happy with this game and having a lot of fun with its challenges. Looking forward to more updates and patches.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall an incredible game, the pinnacle of anti-grav racers and a worthy successor to Redout 1.Pros:* Looks fantastic, nice colourful, shiny graphics and beautiful art design* Runs great on my GTX1070, solid 57-60 FPS on max settings* Blazing fast sense of SPEEEEEEEEEEEEED, playing this game is like an injection of DMT straight to the brain* Overall a hard game. However there is lots of lower difficulty settings and AI assist controls (where the AI will control some things) to help people who want a more chill experience, or people who might be missing fingers etc* The courses are truly crazy, like the world's most epic rollercoaster* A great soundtrack (although I think Redout 1s soundtrack is slightly better)* A huge career mode with 250 events and loads of upgrades for your ship* Tons of cosmetic upgrades as well, colours, liveries etc which you unlock in the career* There is global leaderboards for time attack in arcade mode* Actually has some lore, which is niceNeutral:* A more involved control scheme than most other racers. There is steering, accelerate, brake, boost, hyper boost, boost pads on the track, pitching, strafing and rolling in midair.Cons:* The speed events are currently disproportionately hard, much harder than races. This really needs a balance pass from the devs.* The unlocks in career could stand to be a bit faster paced at the start. Later on you have tons of options to customise your ship, but early on it's too limited.* The difficulty and AI assist options don't unlock until after the first few tutorials* Multiplayer is currently pretty bare bones. You can form a group with friends, and queue for races. But the ranked mode isn't working yet (it's planned), there is no lobbies yet, and no player cards yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Still delivering the fantasy.Like the original Redout, this is hands down the best version of that WipEout / F-Zero experience available today, and terms of concept I think it's an improvement on its' predecessor, stripping out the 'weapons' in favour of a more F-Zero style boost / hull strength balancing act, with the customisation going back into the performance parts you pick.It is however, not for the faint of heart: where the original Redout rewarded you for excellence, Redout II punishes you mercilessly for anything but perfection.  Thankfully, races vs the AI are a little more manageable after a day 1 update, but some of the time-attacks and speed events feel downright impossible without the perfect ship and part selection.All in all?  Still a gripping AG racer, but very much the Dark Souls of its' genre.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this game is an improvement over the original in (nearly) every regard.I had plenty of issues with the original. While it could be fun in some regards, I couldn’t recommend it both because it grew stale rather quickly and because of a lot of issues I had with it, many of which are addressed and fixed in this sequel.- The biggest is that ships are no longer extra floaty now. In the first game, even ships with high grip handled like flying bricks and were super-slippery. Now ships are more solidly connected to the tracks and move the direction they’re supposed to and strafing is much more responsive. I admittedly struggled with it at first as I was not expecting it to be as responsive as it was, but I got used to it. Beforehand, it was hard to take even soft turns without bumping the walls, but on that note...- Wall-bouncing is no longer a thing. In the first game, the fastest lap route was not a clean lap, and often bouncing off the walls would be faster than taking the lap clean, odd as that may sound. Now hitting the walls is very punishing and getting a clean lap will be faster, as it should be.- Gone are the useless upgrades and power-ups in favor of a more focused boost mechanic. In the first game, there were plenty of power-ups one could apply to their ship. But, most of them were only useful if you were just starting out, and it would become clear that AP (extra acceleration and speed) and turbo boost were the strongest pairing while all others became obsolete. Now they’ve focused it all down to a simple boosting mechanic instead, with the ability to customize the stats of your craft.- The boosting is quite sophisticated, too. Boosting builds up heat, and boosting while overheating will drain your health. You can use a simple boost, or a super-boost that needs charging. Or combine the two for extra speed. But along with this, the “thrust” stat means boosts are more powerful and heat less, while durability not only means taking more punishment but also that the ship can take more overheating before exploding. This allows even ships with durability as its main selling point to stay competitive in the game, something which wasn’t so much a factor in the first. You’re even rewarded for braking to take turns, too, as braking cools your ship off faster!- Tracks are overall much more intuitively laid out, and there’s even a rally-style warning system to alert you of turns and hazards coming up so you have adequate time to prepare for them. This has helped me out a lot and I wish more AG racers had that! It’s not perfect, though, as some warnings show up too late and some are bugged (there’s one track on Mars that warns of a U-turn that doesn’t exist). Overall, a welcome addition!- AI is much more competitive now. In the original, the AI quickly became obsolete and, once you kinda knew what you were doing, they stopped being much of a challenge unless you really screwed up. Here there’s a constant pressure on you from them, and you really need to get used to abusing the boost system to get ahead.Although that brings in the biggest criticism I have of the game. It. Is. HARD. I’m normally pretty okay with this, and it works really well for the game and the devs’ vision behind it, but right out of the tutorial you get thrown into a race which is extremely punishing and brutal. After that, the game remains challenging, but reasonably so...mostly. Speed events (where you score points by remaining above a set speed) are extremely unforgiving and I struggle to even reach bronze on many of them.Overall, my criticisms pale compared to praises, and overall I feel the game is a massive improvement over the original!

_childDocuments_.review: Good game.Very steep learning curve though. This game's 1st race picks up where the Redout 1's campaign left off (at least without DLC) in terms of difficulty, it feels.There are 5 or 6 different difficulty settings which ought to counteract this, though it baffles me that this only applies to the AI opponents, not the hardcoded scores fore some modes. 2 game modes (time trials, and "Speed" challenges - where you gather points essentially only when hyperboosting) are completely unaffected by the difficulty options. (Devs! Please fix this, scale the scores by the difficulty!)For people returning from Redout 1, please note that the gameplay is focused around a new mechanic, which might not be to your liking necessarily. (More on that later)Gone are the equipment choices from Redout 1. Every car has the magnetic grip module, every car has the hyper boost module. Instead there is a tuning system, similar to many other racing games. Playing the campaign unlocks new tuning parts, transforming your subsonic soap box into a hyper sonic lightning bolt over time.The way you unlock those parts is strictly linear (The same applies to cars & cosmetics). While I like the constant drip-feed of new items, I recognize the blandness and grindy nature of this approach.Gone are also the vehicle classes. Every manufacturer has only 1 car to offer. Based on the installed tuning parts it gets a score - determining on which events it may be used.The main new gimmick of this game is boost stacking. You got 2 different boosts: One which you can use at any time and dose to your liking, and a hyperboost, which charges up until it can be activated. The trick is, that you can use both boosts simultaneously, catapulting you forwarding with absolutely ridiculous speed. What is counter intuitive: Boost stacking is more effective than using both boosts after each other. It gets explained briefly in a tutorial, but in my opinion this has to be taught as one of the 1st things in this game.Gone is the energy bar of the 1st game, instead there is a heat bar. Any kind of boosting heats up your car. At max heat it damages your car, but you can keep boosting as long as you want (and have health to spare)The cars repair quickly when not taking an damage for a few seconds. So where in Redout 1 the focus was on mastering the track, and the boost being a simple button tap when appropriate, in Redout 2 the focus is on mastering the new double boost mechanic. In addition to mastering the track.I was unsure whether I like this. But it grew on me after I got the hang of it after a few hours. However that makes Redout 2 certainly more difficult than the 1st game.Gone is also the awesomeness of the soundtrack, sadly. The music is what I would call "an okay background noise" - its not annoying, just very forgettable :(If you don't mind a considerable challenge, this game is pretty fun. As a casual arcade racer it somewhat fails, stemming from the missing difficulty scaling on ~ 1/3 of all races in the campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been keeping an eye on other opinions of this game, and I'll agree with the consensus that this game is tough - and probably daunting for newcomers to Redout and AG racing games. But I have to say that I love the challenge. This game isn't without its flaws, and I have complaints of my own, but the priority from the developers seems to be replay value - and this game definitely has it if you want it.I have played mostly campaign so far, but even experimenting a bit with the maxed out ships in the Arcade mode has led me to the conclusion that the racing itself is nearly flawless. I think the mid-air/flight controls are a bit frustrating and un-intuitive (rotating your ship with the d-pad??), but the handling and raw speed of this game are just so sublime. To me, it's like F-Zero GX and Wipeout 3 had a nearly perfect baby. No weapons, but if you want a challenging racing game where speed kills, this is it.There is a ton of content in this game, with 36 huge tracks (27 + 9 boss tracks that combine the 3 individual layouts from each location). Each ship has its own suite of visual customizations ranging from minor and hard/impossible to see mid race, to silhouette altering eye candy that you can enjoy if you race with the chase camera. The campaign has a huge amount of events, and incentive to retry them so you can unlock more things. Some unlocks are not great, and I wish there were an easier way of accessing different ships, but I certainly can't accuse the developers of giving me a barebones singleplayer experience.Lastly, I just want to reiterate that this game is not easy to pick up and play. You need to give yourself some time with the controls and you'll be hitting "Restart" often. Try not to get discouraged and push yourself to play better. It's such an intense and fun feeling to hold off another racer as you barrel down to the finish line at 1300 km/h, while the music is blasting along with the beat of your ship's warning alarm and you desperately try to feather the boost so you don't burn up at the last moment.Great game, 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: At first I was hesitating to buy RO2, since I already owned RO1 twice, on the Switch and on Steam, and I was not sure, if the game offered anything new justifying its medium price tag. But some reviews comparing it to my favourite anti-gravity racer, I got curious and could not longer resist. I bought the game... and it is wonderful.This games feels like the modern interpretation of F-Zero GX which is largely due to its modified boost-mechanic. Everytime you boost, heat builds up, and when your heat-bar is full, you ship starts to loose energy. But this does not mean, you should stop, in contrary, just like F-Zero, the game requires that you boost so long until your energy is almost depleted (your ship explodes, if you continue to boost) in order to have a chance on the higher difficulty settings (I am playing on Red-Out). If you stop to boost, the heat sinks and if you manage to avoid any damage for a short periode, the your ship starts to repair itself. Note that these are two independent processes, which means, as long as your heat-bar is not full, you can still boost without delaying your repairs, but of course, the faster you are the more difficult it is not to hit a wall. This adds an additional layer of complexity over F-Zero, but thats not all. You have two kinds of boost, a small one, which you can use at every moment, and a big-turbo boost that needs to recharge. You can also use both simultaneously for hyper-speed and extreme heat build up. This risk and reward system is together with the thight controls addicting.Many negative reviews are complaining over the difficulty. Maybe there was a patch, but I had no bigger difficulties in beating the AI-pilots on the level "Red-Out" and I am not an expert player. I could not witness any extraordinary Rubber-Banding, I often finish the race with one kilometer distance, but I also make extensive use of my boosters, always depleting almost all of my energy. Other challenges are more difficult, but I am fine with getting a gold medal only after a few tries, since you can also continue with much easier bronze medal and also because my expectation of an anti-gravity game is to be a hard game. Some people mentioning that the soundtrack is less memorable, and they are right. The different tracks are inferior to the one of its predecessor, if you want to listen to them like to an ordinary music track. But they are superior in supporting the game play, together with the remaining sound design, the warn signals when you overheat or take too much damage, they produce a rush of speed and adrenalin.If you are a fan of F-zero, I recommand this game to you. But you are more in line with WipeOut and you liked RO1 because it was similar to WipeOut, you may not like the new play style. But this is something you will immediately notice in the first two seconds of the game. So maybe you should try it and refund it, if you dont like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Bigger tacks, better tracks, harder tracks, FASTER TRACKS.Redout 2 is most certainly harder than the original if only due to the sheer complexity of the tracks.but that complexity is EXCITING. branches, shortcuts, switches all make for a dynamic racing experience instead of the same track loop over and over. the handing model is much more finely tuned and enjoyable. the graphics are beautiful, especially the lighting and reflections, though you may need to turn graphics down since the game is genuinely difficult to play at too low a frame rate due tot he sheer speed.I have my minor gripes about the upgrade and progression system, as well as the way you unlock liverys and colours schemes. Id prefer a credit system for sure, but that doesn't overall kill the gameplay for me.overall, gets a good 9/10 from me. there's some things that need polishing that may yet come with updates, most of my gripes are minor.

The AI rubber band themselves from over 1.2KM deficits through really bendy spots that B class shouldn't be able to, and I'm just barely scratching the wins. Another issue connected to this is trying to get the 4th star on most races, with the AI being able to just snap to you at about the 75% point in a race (watched mutiple 800M leads get closed immediately starting at that point) it's really frustrating to try and get 'Win by 500M' or ' Win by 1.0 Sec" when the AI (even with lower or equal vehicles) just gets to keep these stars out of reach until I can come back fully upgraded. Customizable in that you can select premade parts, liveries, paint palettes, but I wish you could at least mix&match some of those pieces more.Picked it up because I heard it had a really reasonable solo campaign and so far that is not disappointing (outside of the aforementioned star issue) Would recommend picking up if you're willing to grind and really feel success when you get those corner strafes right. _childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 straddles this strange line between arcade insanity and technical precision.  This is *not* f-zero or any of the other old sci-,fi racers. Redout has so much crammed into vehicle control that is hard to get a handle on.  To understand this game, we need to talk controls.As with most racers there's accelerate, break, turn left and right.  Instead of the slide or drift mechanics common to arcade racers we have the ability to strafe left or right. I'll get back to this.  We can also pitch the nose of the car up or down to maintain traction and avoid bottoming out on the track.  Finally there's not one but two different boost mechanics. They both generate heat and damage your vehicle, but one is time gated, and they can be stacked for extreme speed.  The game doesn't really explain this and it's required to finish the tutorial.   Finally, we have boost pads on the track like many other arcade games.These mechanics combine to to create a few unique things you have to pay attention to during a race. First is the pitch mechanic that adds just one more thing to think about as the track whips in every direction.  Second is the strafe mechanic. Racing lines have a different meaning when you can strafe to tighten turns or fix heading coming out of one, and when you're having to hit the boost pads. In some instances you can avoid steering entirely. Finally is the dual boost mechanics. Health in redout is a resource. The best drivers will abuse boosting to be within a sliver of life left, and in most cases after stacking a boost you end up entering the following corner with entirely too much speed.In addition to all the control complexity, (and I didn't even touch flight controls) the game also has differ gravity, heat, atmospheric density, and hazards on different tracks, I have confirmed how the atmospheric density works yet, but most of the others do what you expect, including a black hole that changes gravity in different areas of the track.Redout 2 is a fantastic sequel and improves in the gameplay of the original and takes it from being a standard arcade racer to its own unique experience. I can't wait to see how the leaderboards develop over time.

_childDocuments_.review: Different than redout 1, but in a good way i think. The controls are slightly more complex (with the addition of mid-air roll and pitch) and they've let go of the active abilities and ship energy in favor of a more in depth boosting system. Both generating speed and finding ways to maintain it got etched into the core of the game moreso than its predecessor making it far more punishing if you have difficulty with that.However, with the new addition of the "AI assistance" function you can still race without needing to instantly learn how to perfect strafing and mid-air control. Additionally this function can be tinkered to your personal liking letting you play the game however you like, Rookie or Redout Professional alike.Should you not want to grind through the campaign to unlock all of the ship parts, and instead just get right into the multiplayer, the game provides a decent preset garage that can be used from the get-go so you don't have to worry about all the tinkering.Overall:Good game if you like racing games,Great game if you want total control of your vehicle,   The best game if you're like me and love all of these things and all the tinkering the game lets you do.

_childDocuments_.review: After nearly 60 hours of playtime in a 2 week period, I can say this game is very good. Some of the most fun I've had in a racing game, ever. Huge skill ceiling, a meaty campaign with tons of unlockables, and a very solid collection of tracks for 30 dollars. To be more in depth with the track design, its a step up from Redout 1 in nearly every way. They twist, wind, and invert in many fun and unique ways that reward mastery with the new boost system and just how much more grippy the ships are this time around.       Special mention to Neo Calima which is a remix of Calima from Redout 1, Sisyphus being a windy and challenging early game track that features tricky turns and heat management, Mistral for its incredibly unique jump at the end of the track, Ahti for having very fun rotation jumps, Neo Roppongi for its tight and precise turns through the city, all 3 Genesis tracks for having amazing track flow, and Sputnik for being an incredible track set right next to a black hole. Every single zone is unique and varied to have its own style of driving and track design with different environmental modifications to fit each location, like the atmosphere being set to 'Dense' in the Mariana Trench since you race underwater there, causing more drag to be generated losing you speed faster than normal.       Every track can be played backwards too, some of those being even better than the normal version like Mistral, Ixion and Neo Shinagawa. Overall the track design is brilliant and that's more than enough reason to spend hours grinding for top leaderboard spots on your favorite maps.      The soundtrack is also excellent and features some great music that can stand up with Redout 1's superb soundtrack. Big shoutouts to Raging Revolution (Time Attack Mix) which plays in Genesis, Lights Out which plays in Origin Black Hole, and Gaijin's Prooving which plays in Neo Tokyo.        However, the career mode has a crazy high difficulty spike extremely early on in the game that will cause frustration to people that are less experienced. It's not very beginner friendly. What does help though is that if you can push through B League and early A League, the game becomes monumentally easier the further you get. I'm struggling less with the highest league tier on Nightmare compared to B League, the difficulty balancing is awful for the start of career mode. If you are interested in getting the game, I'd recommend joining the Redout discord for tips and advice if you want to get better, especially during the early game.       But overall, once you've really mastered the games mechanics, nearly every track in the game becomes a ton of fun to drive on and it's just pure racing fun. It's just a steep climb at the start of the game that can drive people away from getting to experience that fun.       For me, this game is giving some other games I've played this year a serious run for its money as my GOTY, even in its current unbalanced and rough state. And it's only going to get better as the game gets updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 in my opinion is a great AG Racer. Compared to the first game the controls are a lot tighter and the AI is significantly better and more challenging. Career progression can take awhile due to its difficulty and since its the only way to unlock new ships and parts, you won't be getting all the ships for a long time. At times it can feel like the AI is rubber banding and gaining massive speed out of nowhere. For the soundtrack while it is pretty good, imo Redout 1's OST was WAY better and its a shame the first games composer didn't come back for the sequel.I am overall having a good time with the game and would highly recommend it to any AG racer fans! _childDocuments_.review: For most of the review, I’ll be comparing the game to the original Redout. Just like its predecessor, this game is not easy, although I would say that it is definitely easier to pick up. It’s not for everyone, so bear that in mind as you read on.Gone are the days where you have to choose between enhanced grip or speed boost in order to get the bets lap time. Everyone has the exact same abilities: a small boost and a big boost. You are in charge of using them at the right time to maximize your speed.The small boost and big boost increase your heat, which when maximized, causes your ship to overheat and eat into your health. You can use the small boost for as long as you want, until you run out of health. The big boost is on a cooldown, but canceling the big boost reduces its cooldown, allowing you to use it more frequently. If you want to go REALLY fast, you can combo them together, but this further increases the rate at which your ship heats up, and it’s easy to destroy your ship if you’re not careful.The steering mechanics are in theory the same as the original Redout, but in practice feel very different. If I were to compare the two, Redout 2 steering feels more precise, and a bit more responsive than Redout. Redout 2 feels less like you’re piloting a ship and more like a car, as many others have said. Make no mistake, however, because you can still strafe just like before. As with the previous game, strafing is absolutely essential to getting better at the game and earning faster lap times. Pitching your ship into a loop is roughly the same as before; you need to lift your nose up or down in order to avoid scraping and/or maximize speed.Flying seems to be massively improved. Because you have more control overall (even in the air) it makes the portions where you have to fly more enjoyable. Plus, there is an added mechanic where if you land your ship correctly, you get a speed boost. Lastly, there is an assist system that works pretty well. It won’t help you against high difficulty AI, but it can help you on some tricky turns and even show you how you’re supposed to do some of the jumps. You can turn all assist settings up to the max and pretty much just watch the game play itself, albeit with a few wall grinds here an there.The biggest improvement is the inclusion of paste notes! Now, even if you’re new to a map, you’ll at least have a general idea of which direction and how hard to turn.They’ve moved the health and boost away from your ship to the bottom of the screen, making it appear more arcade-like, at the cost having to glance down to check your stats. However, the bars are much brighter and visible, so that’s a plus.You can also see how far ahead/behind you are, with arrows that change color based on how close your opponents are to you.Gorgeous. Stunning. Will the graphics age as well as the low poly scenery in the original Redout? Definitely not. But they managed to achieve a Wipeout-level of polish on most of the surroundings, resulting in more memorable landmarks as you zoom past.The track layouts start out even more tame than in Redout, but quickly evolve into the chaotic twisting and turning mayhem that you know from before. Most of the features you’ve already seen before, like huge loops, spiraling sections of track, and massive jumps. One new addition is divided entryways, where you can choose from 2 different routes. Oh, and the tracks are WAY longer too! Many of them take 1-2 minutes or more to complete a lap!I will say that there are jumps where there is an uncomfortable amount of air time, and portions where even with the paste notes, not knowing exactly how to pitch and steer your ship before going off of a jump presents a huge problem. There are also parts where it it is unclear where or when to land your ship, and in a last ditch attempt, you may be forced to land sideways or upside down.There are six in total, and they’re all great, except Speed. I don’t know why they they didn’t just keep Speed the same as the previous game, but here you can earn more points the faster you go, and there is a time limit instead of a lap limit. It sounds good in practice, but it makes is more frustrating because there’s not a clear target anymore, which makes it harder to gauge how fast you REALLY should be going. Plus, the difficulty scaling on Speed is actually ridiculous -  I have yet to get a gold time for most of the events.There’s not much to say about Race, Arena Race, Last Man Standing, Boss, and Time Attack. They’re all good, with plenty of available difficulty scaling for the AI. The Time Attack levels can be pretty tough, but not as ridiculous as the Speed events.There are double the difficulties from before! One of the biggest complaints in the orignal Redout was that the hardest difficulty wasn’t hard enough. That is definitely no longer the case! I’ve played numerous races using the 3rd highest difficulty (“Redout”) and it’s a decent challenge. Only the most skilled players would be able to win a race against the highest difficulty of “Nightmare” – which is precisely how it should be. Everyone should be able to enjoy the game at whatever level they feel comfortable.The AI also seems to be better at using boost in this game. There are many instances where the AI will actually prepare to use boost directly coming out of a corner instead of waiting another second to use it on a straightaway. One of the main points of using boost is to accelerate back up to a reasonable speed quickly, and seeing the AI use it in this way makes it feel like you’re playing against real people.You can play with friends, or just join a match. When enough people ready up, you start. This makes things simple enough, and is better from the perspective that matchmaking will get you in a game sooner. Apparently there’s going to be competitive in the future, but I can’t help but wonder how they’re going to deal with cheaters – they were definitely rampant in the previous game. Sadly no splitscreen.There are currently a few issues I’ve noticed:-Glaring respawn issues.-Some maps don’t have a barrier going completely around the track, causing you to fly off in that direction forever.- In multiplayer, you sometimes get put into a race after it has already started. Whether or not this is intentional, it’s frustrating to play if you’re already behind.-As already stated, the difficulty of some events (mostly the Speed events) needs to be turned down a notch. I’ll update this review as I play more as well, particularly if the issues get fixed. Like I said earlier, definitely recommend this to anyone who likes challenging AG's! It feels different from Redout, and so I recommend giving it a try even if you haven't played the first one.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely pick up if you're a fan of any hovercraft racer. They're few and far between, and honestly the genre deserves some AAA quality, which Redout 2 comes close to. It's not indie by any means, bringing a lot of professionalism and polish to the table compared to Redout 1, like great visuals, UI, music & audio, etc. But, it could definitely be bigger in scope like a big budget game (more online play / features, which are coming soon with seasons & ranked play). That being said, if you're just interested in singleplayer/offline, it's NOT short by any means, with tons of events and challenges at different tiers to train you up. It might get a bit grating seeing the first seeing the same few tracks with the fancier ones being held for later in Career mode, but that might be because I'm trying to 100% everything / get every star. If you just play through normally, you'll probably be seeing new tracks all the time.It's also a big step up from the original in gameplay. Redout 1 didn't have items or weapons like a lot of other action racers, but it did have 'Abilities', 'Passives', 'Classes' and flat upgrades you could get with winnings. They've all been removed in favour of swapping out internals of your ship, of which there is now only one for each manufacturer/team (but there's a lot more teams). This only really applies during singleplayer career. In multiplayer, everyone gets to use maxed out ships from the get-go, bringing it down to the skill of the player and the choice of the ship for the map being played (some will definitely be more useful on one map than another). But no matter how you play, keep in mind that Redout 2 is a challenging game, it takes some practice to learn how to swerve around a corner with both turning AND strafing, and avoid walls.Boosting also works differently. Instead of being a limited meter that recharges, you can ALWAYS boost, which fills an 'overheat' gauge instead. Once full, it starts draining your ship health to continue boosting, which provides some fun risk/reward to reach higher speeds, and more caution to avoid bumping walls to start health regen sooner for more boost, rather than worrying about health as some separate isolated thing. E.g. if you're confident with a track, you can keep running your ship within an inch of its life for the best speed, but one mistake could have you respawning!All in all, it might be annoying at first to be bumping into everything, but once you get the hang of it and make a flawless lap with the music pumping and the sound/visual design on the speed, Redout 2 is a blast.And yes, the trailer music is in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games where you can feel yourself improving after each race. But try not to explode, obviously.Also, feather the brakes on turns, and feel free to let go of the gas as well. I am still improving myself. Again, there's a lot to learn, but so far I'm enjoying my time. The soundtrack is also full of bangers.
