_childDocuments_.review: Fresh off the heels of the first race with Ai: (For context, I have played the first game. loved it till the new update cause I lost all my progress. I'll try to get that progress again on another time. Ill talk about how the game feels later.) I was doing good against the Ai till seconds before the first lap ended... one of the Ai just flew past me. thought it was cause they had boost, so I thought nothing of it. Later, near the mid, the Ai passed me again, and I went to 2nd place. The other racer passed me and stayed that way till the end netting me a bronze medal. I know that this is the start of the game to give you a feel of a real race, but C'mon, at least give the new people a chance to win or not have to REALLY know how to use the tools to their fullest. I'm more upset that the Ai was well-equiped unlike myself. I imagine new players would have a HARD time trying to get into the game: and even when it came to the earlier missions to get used to the controls, I disliked how they slowed time to force you to make the basic moves such as: moving left, moving right, and don't forget, strafing!  I'm going to go back to finish the races to get to the meat and potatoes of the game but some other things I did not like: the ability to choose a frame was taken away for a uniform start. That would make sense if it was like say, Pokemon or Warframe with their different starters to give the player (new and old) a way to choose their play style. maybe even give them a decently leveled up kart via Handling/Hull, Speed/Accel, and Energy/(Stability?). Then take it away in the real races so the player already has a taste of power and are willing to climb the ranks for it once more. Okay, as someone who put a 'few' hours into the original game, it feels weird. not bad weird or good weird. I need to race a bit more to truly understand how the karts work, but I don't hate it. It feels a lot more grippy versus the original game and I can't yet say if I Dislike it or not. Same thing with the new boost mechanic. I'm going to need a lot of time to get used to burning my health to go faster while not smashing myself into the walls. ALSO, I did not mention in the first paragraph, but the boost (it felt more natural to add it here) feels off with regards to regular boosting and hyperboosting. I read around that people had issues with the boosting level since they had to learn to mix hyperboosting and regular boosting to beat it, I simply mixed the two and beat it with silver since I was scraping the walls a lot. During the race, it seemed that there is a delay between hyper boosting and turning off the boost, so I had to restart the race since I came in 4th (which should still give the new players a star or something at this current stage of difficulty. And as much as it is a sequel, I rather liked how the first game had their events and progression: after a few training levels, here: play in all these events to see what you like.) and I even still had issues in the rematch with it not turning off the hyperboost when I want it to. Thankfully, I beat it, but mayhaps I have yet to get a grasp of the mechanics. My first kart from Redout 1 was the Koniog (or however you spelled it) and I used all that extra health to safely get to terms with the game as I had not put lots of time into racing games, let alone anti-grav racers. I like to try new games that seem interesting, and I was glad I got the first game, but after the recent update to the first game, and now how this game feels, its a weird change, but I'll stick with it to see how it goes.Other issues have to be the introductions to tracks have audio issues with the narrator, and some weird visual stuff, but I don't really mind it too much, I overlook lots of stuff, since I'm sure making a game is no walk in the park.I was hooked by the music from the first game, and same here so far as some musical artists worked here too is awesome. however, I'll simply say as a warning, the game feels weird as a veteran, and I imagine perhaps unfair to the new racers. Ill still recommend it, but beware, it has a few "interesting" design choices.(Edit 1) Just got to the second race with Ai (after typing this long-ass thesis) and I will have to reiterate the fact that the Ai a "tad" bit too powerful versus you. I may just be a bad player, but it really feels like the Ai is just better than you and not because they have rubber-banding (you don't) or that the Ai know the maps better than you do, but they seem to have better equipments. *I can't really tell since I don't know all the parts very well*(Edit 2) New patch rolled out, but I guess it helped(?) but I have a slightly better understanding of the boost mechanic now. I am still not familiar with it, but I am welcoming it so far. I moved from the second race and am trying the other modes -- I got upset and turned off the game but came back to try the other races -- and now have a slightly better feel for the game, though it is not much, I'm happy to say that I was able to get new parts for the ship. I guess while I am used to the old game, I just had to let go and keep pushing myself to understand the new things the game had to offer. If I could offer one "reasonable" change, it would be to maybe be able to have an easier way to visualize the health and boosts, only because my blind-ass can't see manage health and speed, but in all seriousness, maybe being able to move those hud elements closer to the ship or something. Otherwise, I just have to get good. I'll probably get used to being to know when to boost and to conserve health.

_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game of its kind where I feel that no matter how insane your speed is, you always have full control of your ship and your gameplay: the main feature of the game is a peculiar control system which lets you accelerate, break and steer as normal, in addition to lateral strafing as well as tilting your ship up and down, while you'll boost throughout the entire races, pushing your vehicle to its absolute limits to get as much speed as you can - literally, since your health is essentially a second boost bar that regenerates over time.You have this sense of high risk high reward that permeates the entire experience, and even in time trials you'll be on your toes, fully focused on everything that's going on without ever feeling overwhelmed by it. It's an absolute blast that I would recommend any fan of the genre, or any fan of racing and speed in general.Just, no matter what experience you have with previous games, when you start your singleplayer career, don't expect to win. The game is NOT designed to be won when you first start, which seems to throw off many, many people who believe the difficulty to be badly balanced.At the start you have a weak, standard ship. Your enemies have upgraded ones, and they'll know the game mechanics better than you, since the tutorial unlocks bit by bit as you progress the first races and won't fill you in on everything you need to know right away. No matter how much experience you have from other games, you'll likely lose.BUT, you'll progress anyway, because unlocking your ship's upgrades, as well as new ships, only requires you to get 1 star out of 4 in events, which, in a normal race, means getting third place out of 4 contenders (max stars only gives you cosmetics). It's something challenging but reasonable, a simple goal you'll have to chase as you learn the game, unlock new tutorials to further understand the game mechanics, and gradually get your vehicle up to speed with the others. In due time, you'll start fighting for second place, and before you know it you'll suddenly be winning, consistently - and it's an incredible feeling of growth and progression, no other game has ever given me.And then, the game will throw you a roadblock, telling you "you need more stars to unlock the next event". And you'll go back to the first races you couldn't win, and this time you'll be competing on even grounds, and finally push your way to victory.It's a beautiful experience all through and through, and it's so sad to see so many people being thrown off because they couldn't get first place right away. Just go with the flow the game guides you through, and you'll have no issue growing to the point where you'll dominate the races you once dreaded.For the rest, this game fixes every single problem I had with the first Redout - the tracks are now much easier to see even at incredible speeds, designed to let you know what kind of turns and twists are coming next, also with the help of little indicators at the top of the screen. "Weapon"-like special abilities are removed, and everything is a pure blooded race now, and thanks to the increased grip of your ship dying from impacting the walls is now a very rare occurrence, which is a big plus considering you'll spend a lot of time on the verge of destruction to push your speed to the max. Every track is truly beautiful, the dynamic music fits the action's pace perfectly, and there's not a single dull moment in the entire experience. And the content, just the singleplayer alone has hundreds of races and unlocks with great replayability due to its progression system encouraging you to return to past events to get more stars. It's incredible, and more game modes and contents are going to come in the future, too.This game is probably the best racing game I've ever played, and it breaks my heart to see so many people bashing it just because it's different from Redout 1 instead of keeping the exact same gameplay. Give it a try and don't be discouraged by its difficulty, as you learn and grow you will not be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't like the original Redout, but it did try to sell me on being like Wipeout.This game seems to have taken some considerable inspiration from F-Zero, and with that, old neurons fired up and immediately found it enticing. For people coming from an F-Zero background, this game plays fairly similar with some modifications to make it more Redout-like.- There's considerably more control over your ship, and the controls work differently- The difficulty of the game will auto-adjust after you start playing to give you the best experience, I personally didn't find it as hard as other people are saying, maybe the original Redout was simply too easy or they got put into a higher difficulty?- You get that same sense of intense zoomies when you're health is yelling at you while you blast at insane speeds down a straightawayI think if you like F-Zero you'll probably like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright first impressions: A worthy sequel to Redout 1.Some others have said that there are performance issues and some bugs, I've luckily not experienced any and the game runs buttery smooth on highest settings, there will of course be some kinks to iron out after release like with any game but this launch has been flawless for me.I'm so excited to race in a fresh Redout experience again!
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I shouldn't leave a review only after playing it for 1h, but I saw some negative reviews there and feel the need to post my first impressions right now as the game is released. Obviously I'll come back to update this after playing more. The new system works wonders, truly. You gotta drive and think about how you're gonna use your boost ; just hyperboost, or coupled with normal boost, but then your health will go down faster ? So am I gonna get to 5hp and make sure not to hit a single wall, or play it safer because the upcoming turns are tough ? And then what remaining hp is acceptable ?Do I trigger the hyperboost right as I have it in order to be efficient, or is it really not gonna be worth it because of my health / the curves ahead ?All that while going at 1000km/h :) Some people may not like it, but to me that's actually a very clever way to have two things to think about, that other racing games would do through the usual item system.The weapon system from Redout 1 just did not work (it felt useless) : having the focus on managing your speed and health and getting the curves pitch-perfect is exactly the direction the game needed to take. As for the tutorial difficulty : I literally exploded my car from overheating (one particular rotating straight line is... very exciting to boost in) and still managed to get 1st on my first try. I'm not even that good, as I remember getting owned in Redout 1 multiplayer. And since dificulty (+ assists, although I think it's better without any of those) can be tweaked after that, I wouldn't consider difficulty an issue. As for performance : I run a 2060Super, and am getting 80 fps (so far, I don't know if some future tracks are more demanding) on 1440p with high on settings (except shadow on medium) and epic on antialiasing. So, pretty good I'd say.Cheers!
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: 3 Hours in I think I've a good handle of the mechanics and upgrade system, and even then the AI on easier difficulties is cracked to high hell. In old arcade high speed games (extreme g, jet moto) and as far as I remember, I don't recall racing games being this frustratingly hard. The vehicles feel slidey and non-responsive for these speeds and amount of curves.I would be hard pressed to go through another... what 10-20 hours of crushing defeat thanks to the AI and handling.Visuals and music are really good which makes that much more frustrating as even starting out the AI is annihilating you from making just a couple mistakes.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Hold off until there's some balance patches, especially if you're new.Difficulty for some of the early tracks seems extremely overtuned (especially the Speed tracks, which don't seem to get easier when you reduce the game difficulty); just getting a Copper medal on some of the speed tracks requires almost flawless play for two straight laps, including knowledge of ideal boost patterns. I'm fine with gold being unreachable without spending a while practicing, but especially this early in the game it should be fairly easy to land a copper and decently achievable to get a silver. I'm also getting the occasional graphical bug in cockpit view where the camera seems to slip inside of the ship every now and then, usually after a hard landing or similar. Not sure exactly what causes it but it blocks all visibility when it happens, which isn't great in a high speed racer.I like the risk/reward system of using your health pool as additional boost. I am concerned that as the tracks get more technical, the novelty will wear off, since the target numbers for good laps seem to assume that you are burning your health as a resource regularly, and not just for an extra burst of speed at the very end, but for now it's fun.Overall the racing feels great; the problems are mainly the overtuned difficulty (especially the target numbers in time trial and speed events; racer AI became a lot more satisfying when I turned the difficulty down) and the odd bug. Hopefully this gets fixed soon; as is I imagine a lot of new players will bounce off the early wall, and even returning veterans will probably get frustrated that they're having such a tough time so early in the game when they're still just trying to unlock things.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's definitely a different game from Redout 1. And that's not a bad thing either. It's got the soul and essence of the original, but much of it feels cleaner and nicer. It's also far, far more accessible than it's predecessor as well, with a ton of tuning for ai assistance with controls if you should need it. The game is gorgeous, the audioscape is great, and the soundtrack is a banger too. Few games give you the feeling of real speed like the Redout series so expertly manages to do.If you're into hover racers, you really cant go wrong with Redout 2. It's very well fleshed out with tons of customization options and upgrades to tweak and tune your craft that you unlock through the career. While I personally would have preferred a credit/point buy system ala RO1 style, it works well and forces you to get better.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute masterclass of a game. The most fun "arcade" racer i haver ever played.The more i play this game the more i prefer the actual gameplay over the first part. Boost and risk management is a lot of fun and there are quite a few visual and sound aids to help you keep track of your health and your overheat status. Would recommend starting the game on pilot and then progressing to redout after grasping the basics. The tracks themselves feel a lot more diverse and challenging. Some of them offer stunning visuals.Also i like the fact that the AI can blow up too if they go too fast or smash into walls all the time.The new turn-indicators are much appreciated.I don't mind not being able to costumize my vehicle in multiplayer when it comes to tuning because usually what ends up happening is that everyone just ends up using the same parts anyway.Disbanding every lobby after every race in casual multiplayer seems kind of uneccessary...maybe atleast let the people play a cup together or something.The soundtrack is absolutely incredible!Overall i would say its a big upgrade over the first redout despite a few crashes i had when opening the costumization menu. The game still needs some polishing in terms of AI and circuit bugs. For example the game respawning you 20km forwards for some reason.But i am not a huge fan of a day 1 season pass. I sure hope that there won't be multiple seasons...i am done with being expected to spend 100 plus euros for every game.Finally for the love of god please do not split the multiplayer into dlc/non-dlc lobbys. Either you make the new maps available for everyone or restrict them to the singleplayer. Whats also possible is that only 1 player in the lobby needs to have the dlc.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: The tracks are great. The control of the ships feels spot on. The ship upgrade/customization is deeper than the first game. Boosting has a different mechanic than the first game, adding a heat meter and overheat/health damage. Health is readily replentished and hitting the walls is far less punishing to health. You are far more likely to fall off the track than to die by hitting walls. The active modules are no more and there are still NO WEAPONS! :( Overall this game is super fast and smooth and the tracks are all exciting and fun to play. A very welcomed new version of Redout and aside from no combat racing, is hands down the best hover racer out ther for the second time running!
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Redout 2 hits all the right notes for an antigrav racer for me. Great visuals, great sound design, great OST, absolutely insane sense of speed... honestly, it makes the first Redout look like a tech demo. Everything just meshes better in the aesthetic and gameplay, and i'm loving it. I especially love how they reworked boost, so instead of your boost being a resource that you run out of, it's heat that you build. Use too much of it and you'll damage your ship, but you'll get the highest speed when you push it over the limit. As a result, you're constantly balancing speed while essentially using your health as a resource, and it makes the moment to moment gameplay so satisfying. However, it's not without issues. There is a pretty nasty difficulty curve at the beginning, but it's worth noting that you don't have to get 1st in the tutorial races. The game selects a difficulty rating and assists depending on how you do at them. You can also unlock upgrades without getting first in every race, which makes things a lot better the further in you go. That said, if you aren't experienced with these kinds of games it might be worth waiting for a patch to make it a tad bit more accessible at the start.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent, absurdly fast successor to Redout. I still believe it's the only worthy spiritual successor to F-Zero. The soundtrack is even better than the first, which is saying a lot, the ship customization is excellent (before it was just color schemes and a single upgrade per category that you'd never swap out, now you can tune a ship for handling, boost, speed, etc.). Be wary, there are a few obviously day one bugs that will hopefully get patched quick, nearly all involving the ruthless AI. The AI is extremely overpowered right out of the tutorial until you can get several upgrades to your ship, and this is coming from someone that got all the platinum medals in Redout and multiple top-20 leaderboard times. Even if you lower the difficulty, the rubberband is so bad they'll regularly beat you at any difficulty and set world record times, so don't feel bad until you upgrade your ship into the upper 200s. The AI is also bugged on a few of the volcano (mines) tracks, where they will teleport 5-10 km ahead of you lap over lap, making a couple of the races impossible to beat currently.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of early complainers that this game is a bit different than Redout 1. Well, its true. It is also true that F Zero X raced differently than F Zero GX, and Wipeout games all had their nuances. Xtreme G2 was not Xtreme G3.Time moves on, and great racing games are hard to come by. This is one of them. I was 8 when I first played F-Zero X, now pushing 30. Many folks didn't even try Redout 1 because "it isn't like Wipeout". Nostalgia is a powerful thing, and would be a shame to miss out on the Redout series because of dedication to one single other game. In Formula 1, the best championship-title level drivers can adapt to any car setup. Are you seeking a challenge, or the same old?They set out to not just update Redout 1, but refine it. Powerups that were questionable have been refined into upgrades, and the boost system is now about how much you can handle. Get it and enjoy the fact that for $30 someone is still dedicated to making great sci-fi racing games, and that there is a community to race online with every weekend.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: i think most of the negative reviews on this game so far are the result of conveyance issues, so i want to just use this review to try to clear up the two biggest things people aren't understanding:-you can use regular and super boost at the same time. in fact, you absolutely need to be doing this. the boost tutorial doesn't mention it at all and a lot of people are finding themselves much slower than the game expects them to be because they don't know they can do it. hopefully the tutorial gets updated to mention this-you're not supposed to win races in career mode on the first try. i don't know why they structured it like this without really explaining it, but you're supposed to run through and get 3rd places in events so you can unlock enough upgrades to actually try to win them on the second run through, i guess so you get more mileage out of each event? honestly i don't even mind that system but it's kind of baffling to just expect the player to know they're not meant to win. anyway, once you understand those two things, the game's pretty comparable to redout 1 so far, which is my favorite racing game of all time. there are things i think are steps in the wrong direction, like increased emphasis on correct boosting, but the increased ship customizability and the new areas are pretty cool and i'm liking the new tracks so far. don't let the mixed review score scare you, i'm not going to say the negative reviewers are "mad because bad" but i think a lot of them aren't understanding some of redout 2's... kind of alien, unexplained decisions, is all.

_childDocuments_.review: Changed my review to a negative. I can't recommend this game.I do not have any issues with the difficulty of the game itself, while a lot of players do. I even took the time to make guides to help other people get Gold / Platinum on speed missions.The sheer amount of things that do not work properly such as..1: Terrain issues.. It is common to lose a track because your ship will clip into the floor itself and start spinning.2: The thrust stat being coded in the reverse (The more thrust you have, the less you can boost) This is double frustrating because at some points in the campaign you're forced to add more mods because of the minimum power your ship can have.. So you have to purposely make your ship worse.3: The tedium. You will have to complete several hundred missions to be able to unlock most upgrades. Until then, you're gatekept out of good scores in multiplayer or arcade.4: The arcade ships themselves suck. This kinda ties in with point 3.5: If something happens to the install of your game, you have to start the whole tedium again.I'm too exhausted by this to even think about more negative points.. Just make sure you know what you're getting into, because blackdesert and maplestory felt less tedious to me than this.And i'm not even sure if anything will change because of the massive amount of positive circlejerking that I see that all the above points are positives.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm an avid fan of F-Zero GX (my best game ever, completed 100% multiple times and won a few tournaments by Nintendo in 2003-2004). I also played quite a lot of Redout.At first, I wasn't sure about the new gameplay.But after a few tracks, it just clicked. The game is incredibly awesome. Everything I didn't like about the first is not there anymore (especially items). Also, the gameplay is much tighter and feels a little bit more like F-Zero GX. You can also customize controls 100%, which is great (I use the same layout of F-Zero GX and it works like a charm).Just remember that the strafe is mandatory, but doesn't work necessarily like F-Zero. Sometimes, you have to strafe the opposite way of the turn so you can drift a bit and then strafe on the other side so you can take the turn properly (feels like pressing both L+R in F-Zero and then strafe on only one side so you peak the turn at 90 degrees). Learning this, you don't have to brake or release the acceleration at all after,Also, hyperboost + regular boost + on track boosts makes your machine go so much faster and it's satisfying. If you find the game too difficult, you can lower the difficulty.In summary, an extremely good evolution of the Redout series. I'm sad to see it has mixed reviews, but oh well.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Previously, I stated that I would not recommend this game, especially due to the difficulty. However, after returning to this game, I have found it to be more bearable. First of all, set your game difficulty to pilot at the most, as the default ai will be very difficult, especially to newcomers.I will say though, the progression is a bit tedious. From what I can tell, the intended progression is to pass the events with some stars, then return to the event with the better gear from higher classes to beat them. It has worked for the most part for me, but I find it to be a bit annoying, especially due to how many events there are in the career. While this is not much of a problem for races if you lower the difficulty, it is apparent with the speed and time trial events, which as far as I can tell has the same records to beat across all difficulties. This is made even worse when getting gold in a time trial is mandatory to get the upgrade.Probably my second biggest gripe is the unlock method for customization. What's that? You want that really cool tip for your ship? Good luck finding the event that unlocks it and pray that it isn't behind getting 4 stars in a time trial where you have to beat gold by 3 seconds for the fourth star.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: I had a bad time with this game on release, but kept it in my library because I'm a fan of future racers. I went back to it now that it's had a few updates and I'm having a much better time. Good:+ I really like the feel of the race crafts. They feel a lot more solid than the original Redout, and there's less "messy racing" since you no longer want to bounce off the walls for optimal times. Ships do lose speed faster though, so less momentum based strategy (+ or - depending on your taste).+ Looks nice, good sense of speed when it gets going. I will say I have performance issues when I use anything but the highest level of AA... not sure what that's about. Nice ship models with aesthetic customisation. + Game is better balanced now. On release it took forever just to make it through the tutorial. + Game is complicated (turning, pitch, strafe, roll, two kinds of boost), which can be rewarding depending on what you're looking for.+ Dynamic music has its moments.+ Is a future racer.Some things that still irk me a little:- Boost strategy really is a big part of it. Not my thing but not a deal breaker. At least you can set the ship to automatically stop boosting at 5% health, not sure if I overlooked that when it came out or if it's new. It should be on by default IMO, I'm not looking at meters while I race.- Jumps can be annoying for a few reason: Unclear landing position, landing obscured by ship, needing to control turning (left stick), pitch and strafe (right stick) and roll (dpad). I only have two thumbs! I guess this encourages you to line up your jumps so that you at least don't have to worry about one of those dimensions, but many of the jumps are blind for the reasons above, so they're annoying when you start learning them.Old Review:I'm a fan of future racers. I love games like Wipeout, F-Zero and Redout 1. I want to like this game, but it is too in love with boost mechanics and bars filling up. I do not want to watch bars while I'm racing.You have a heat bar that is basically your boost bar. If you boost it fills up, if you stop boosting it cools off. If you boost too much you take damage. If you don't take damage for awhile you repair yourself, so in that sense your health is also like a boost meter that just refills differently. There is also a super boost which relies on a battery filling up. Using the super boost also fills your heat meter the same as a regular boost, and you can regular boost and super boost at the same time. So you have two meters strictly related to boosting, and one meter that is both health and auxiliary boosting, and they are all changing all the time. I don't want to micro manage meters while watching high speed racing. There's just too much strategy around boosting. Do I want to trigger all of my boosts at once for ludicrous speed, or portion out my boosts so that I'm constantly boosting? It's really hard to tell which is more effective.There are also boost pads which are fine because at least they don't have an associated meter I have to watch.I am very sad because this isn't exactly a popular genre (RIP Studio Liverpool) and the original Redout was one of my favorites.
_childDocuments_.name: Redout 2

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly Redout 2 is great. As my friend put it, it's basically like going between F-Zero games; it's the same as the original Redout, but at the same time it isn't. Balancing health as a resource with the new boost mechanics feels really good, and there are some slamdunk bangers that we've heard in the soundtrack even at just a couple hours in. I feel like this is an easy recommendation for folks who enjoyed Redout or are new to the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Before the patch, my review was summed up like this:-Too high scores for the Speed 180s and Time Attack challenges-Multitude of bugs-Poor progression system for unlocking everything, AND a lot of it is blocking people from playing multiplayer. Thus a lot of people don't play because they literally can't-AI DOES rubberband. and most often then not, they have better upgrades to their ships. No, it's not just "game good, you're bad". No they legit have higher level upgrades, the scoreboards actually show this-Good controls, handling and speed feels good. Double boost system is fun and rewarding and worth it's riskMy review after the patch is summed up like this:-Decent scores to achieve on Speed 180s and Time Attack Challenges. Although some need to be adjusted-Multitude of bugs, random crashes for entering water in some tracks, disgustingly low FPS drops for no reason at all when I wasn't getting that before this patch-Poor progression system for unlocking everything, AND a lot of it is blocking people from playing multiplayer. Thus a lot of people don't play because they literally can't-Haven't done any races other than the challenges post patch, so I can't say anything about the AI. However 34 did say it was tweaked to be easier in the patch notes-Good controls, handling feels good. But they somehow broke the thrust and boost system with the patch and will wait for the DLC patch to fix it.34...REALLY?! Who is going to buy the DLC when the base game isn't even fleshed out or optimized. The progression system makes me want to NOT play, it's so unrewarding and locking mostly every upgrade behind a backwards speed class system is just stupid. The player feels drained, I can get through maybe 2 challenges before I turn off the game because of how bored I am. The game isn't fun with this progression system. Unlocks are fun if you let the player build up to it, this is just based on pure skill, which might work in some other games. However, this literally blocks progress from playing multiplayer. It's either use, pre-built and uncustomizable ship, or don't play multiplayer till you unlock everything.I'm done with this game, and I can't even get a refund because I really tried to love it.Waste of $30. Don't buy it.

Do the campaign and don’t worry to much about winning or going fast right off the bat try to understand the ship controls and the tracks on where and where not to use boost or ultimate.Very fun game, fast and overall very enjoyable

_childDocuments_.review: Having gotten over the honeymoon period I can no longer recommend this game.TL;DR the campaign is a slog, non race events are way too hard and frequent, the manner of unlocking everything is very grindy. Tracks lack wow factor a lot of the time, music is a downgrade.It feels both half baked and as if it is trying very hard to be as dissimilar to redout 1 as possible. Tracks in 2 are much longer, but also slower. Technical sections are frequent but there are also few real setpeices. Stuff like tubes and pipe sections are totally absent and while the offerings have plenty of inversions and jumps (most taken at awkward angles that need midair manoeuvring to land) for the most part the game underutilised the possibilities offered from being anti-gravity and having multiple routes. Instead of clear tiers of ship that grow visually more complex redout 2 features a core roster that you upgrade the performance and look of during your career, I like this.However the rate of unlocks is glacially slow, everything being strictly tied to career progression. If you want x part you must win y event to obtain it. This even extends to the ships themselves whereas in 1 you could unlock and upgrade any ship in any order you wanted via an ingame economy. It is incredibly arbitrary and arcade-like now and due to the slow progression often leaves you well behind the curve performance wise. It's only when going back to earlier races with later unlocks do you have some manner of choice over how you build your ship. When going through the game normally you simply bolt on everything you get as you get it since you are so under powered.This even extends to arcade mode, if you choose to use your own garage of prebuilts the AI will not scale down. Then there is the career itself. It is simply bloated. There are fewer event types this time around and some, like arena race, are so neutered as to be barely different from the basic race. You'll be doing the same races, speed trials and time trials in the same few areas again, and again and again. The original redout somewhat had this problem too of classes only using a small selection of tracks until class 4. The difference is the early classes in 1 went by very quickly. Here it feels like a slow, unrewarding slog of the same events over and over with gradually increasing difficulty. Worse still due to the unlock system of 2 you no longer have the luxury of simply skipping certain events you loathe. Doing so can deprive you of cosmetics, parts and even entire ships as opposed to 1. Then there is the difficulty, Redout 1 was not a particularly difficult game. At least in single player. The real challenge was in multiplayer and leaderboards where people compete for fractions of a second. Still the game did recognise when you were truly fast, having hidden platinum trophies for a number of events. But even if you were legitimately terrible at the game you could see and do everything even if it meant farming the few events you could win over and over to afford all the ships. In 2 the skill floor has been massively increased now even qualifying in speed and timetrial events can be incredibly difficult. Part of this is, again, due to the horrendous unlock system leaving you always weak. But the fact the difficulty options only scale AI means these events have a hard limit on how good you must be to progress. This alone would not be a massive issue however non-race events in the campaign practically outnumber the race events. It's a slog when you are gated off from races and upgrades because you don't enjoy the over tuned gimmick events.Finally mechanics, I'm neutral on most of these. Ships in 2 are gripper in general but the tracks are also much narrower and more technical to compensate along with hitting the walls now being more punishing. Powerups are now removed too, not a huge loss as most of them in 1 were useless.In addition to this there is a new boost system. Instead of energy which refuels boosting is now always available but heats your ship up once it is overheated further boosting erodes your health. This will regenerate on it's own after a few seconds of not taking damage. Finally to achieve real speed you need to stack forms of boost. All ships have a hyper boost on a long cooldown, this boost is actually very ineffective on it's own and is designed purely to be stacked with regular boost. I don't mind the boosting system, pushing your car to the edge of exploding for speed is exciting, but your ship also barely maintains it's speed when you do get going. Stacking boosts is also a mandatory technique to remain competitive even against the AI rather than some manner of hidden tech. The sound effects for being low on health and repairing are also obnoxious for how often you will hear them. The bones of a great game are here but the execution is sloppy.

name: Lucky's Tale
detailed_description: Lucky Swiftail is a brave fox on a quest to save his best friend Piggy from the monstrously tentacled Glorp. Together, you'll run, jump, and climb your way through a bright, colorful world full of charming characters, boss battles, hundreds of secrets to discover, and exciting 3D platforming action. Lucky’s Tale broke ground as one of the first 3rd person perspective games in virtual reality, showing the world VR can be much more than 1st person experiences. Its pioneering approach to camera, character motion, environment, and gameplay provide a thrilling experience that allows players to freely roam immersive environments that are at once both toy-like and vast in scale. You'll feel as though you've gone inside the world of a nostalgic platformer! Become a hero and save the day in the groundbreaking game that launched a beloved franchise, now remastered for modern VR headsets. NEW in this version : remastered lighting, audio, rendering; optimizations for modern HMDs NEW in this version : refined player movement and an updated character model for Lucky (as seen in New Super Lucky's Tale ) Diverse levels featuring lush swamps, underwater ruins, an active volcano, secret foxholes, boss fights, and more 3rd person perspective camera built for virtual reality and designed for thrilling yet comfortable platforming action Headset tracking for aiming, throwing, finding hidden items; touch controls for interacting with Lucky and menus Additional timed-based and collectathon challenges that reward replays Cute, cuddly, and made for all ages and skill levels

_childDocuments_.review: Lucky's Tale was definitely made for kids primarily. 8-12 year old me would have loved this game, but 32 year old me really likes it too. It's a platformer, we all love them right? It's also not overly easy, I find myself dying occasionally. Maybe not as much as Crash games but probably as much as a Mario game. The level design is pretty amazing, there are no pre rendered backgrounds to add illusion of depth. Everything you see is your level environment. The graphics are highly polished in VR and even a potato can run it. My absolute favorite parts are when you dive into a hole and do a side platforming bit, they are just that extra touch that makes me keep playing. The story is basically non existent, but it's a platformer. There is lots of replayability here too, though I don't think it is that long. I would say wait for a sale but $20 is reasonable, and this genre just works so well in VR. I find myself always searching for the next 3rd person platformer that is actually worth playing. I can't think of that many cons to this game but one major one for me is there really isn't any puzzle solving that is of any depth. I would have liked to have seen mini puzzles that would shake up the monotonous enemy bashing and coin collecting. The voice of lucky is also kind of annoying and childish, but not too bad.Overall I am enjoying it, but I don't think I would have touched this game on flatscreen. VR just makes it really worth playing. I hope they bring Lucky's Tale 2 to VR as well! Would definitely buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Good VR platformer game. At the time of writing, I haven't played Moss or Trover yet, so I can't compare it to another vr platformer yet, but it was pretty good. _childDocuments_.review: Lucky's Tale VR is the third installement of the super-cute true 3D jump'n'run platformer which unites a lot of ideas from other known genre representatives.Difficulty ★★★★☆☆☆☆☆☆ (add 4 stars for gold medal timed trails)First of, this game comes in 3 versions if you buy it in the bundle (release order):* Super Lucky's Tale (SLT)* New Super Lucky's Tale (NSLT)* Lucky's Tale VR (LTVR)While NSLT is a remake of the SLT, TLVR is a complete game of its own and is not directly connected to the story of the first game(s). I think the devs just wanted to test out how Lucky's Tale would perform in VR.The overall game experience is quite good and super-cute, and in some cases can compete with NSLT. The big issue is yet again the difficulty. The devs don't have any sense of making a fair and square challenge, neither in the games before, nor in this one. The overall difficulty of LTVR is easy, unless you try the speed trials. To get the gold medal you have to stay super close to the perfect line and keep running always, and take any hazardous shortcut to compete. But this is when the VR limitations kick in. The game has too much control issues for the task they demand from the players, so getting the gold medals is just very frustrating. * well made VR* super cute game* simple but pretty graphics* good and clear rendering (no blur effects)* good gameplay* lots of levels and challenges* good final boss fight* for my taste the camera is too close (but you can fix this with recentering the camera while leaning forward)* camera panning is aweful for backtravelling sometimes* camera does follow Lucky too slow (especially in vertical maps and timed trials)* the return of the insta-death (I really didn't miss it)* fights could have been more challenging (but this is an issue of all Lucky's games)* Lucky does run on two feeds, but this time at least it looks more natural (in New Super Lucky's Tale it is aweful)* timed trials (gold) are too difficult compared to the rest* the game does get repetitive after some while, there is no progress or and skins to unlock like in the former games* aerial control not very good (unfortunetally the same with the other Lucky's games)* if you die in red coin quest you will be teleported to level beginning (annoying in big levels)* level design not as creative than in (N)SLT* no NPC you can talk like in the former games, it is a pure platformer* enemy can spawn right inside/underneath you and insta-damage you* game uses invisible walls for off-bounds that sometimes you notice to late and die because of it* some objects don't have a hitbox although they look like they should have* no music/sound when you start the game (the volume is set to zero in the options everytime you enter the game)* sometimes the fox shadow is drawn on the ceiling as well* puffer fish does damage you although the needles are already retracted* sometimes you will get no double jump although Lucky connected to the ground properly before (happens often with logs or crates)* hitboxes of enemies are weird* it can happen that the game glitches out and you will get a gold medal for timed trial with a 00:00 timer, yet the game breaks permanently your in-game rewards and Steam achievements along with it. You have to fix this by manually editing your savefile. Common, this totally shouldn't happenI would have really wanted to like this (VR) experience, but two things killed it for me, so thank those devs for the overall negative review:1. insta-deaths: why the hell did the devs went back to the insta deaths? I mean, they knew what stupidity they did otherwise they wouldn't have given you unlimited lifes in the timed trials or removed it in NSLT completely2. timed trials: I really hate to say it, because this kind of a challenge I always waited to get for (N)SLT, now the devs deliver it for the most difficult to control game in their series, but I absolutely have to say it... which lunatic thought that demanding players to chase for a world-record time to get the gold medal with bad aerial control, weird hitboxes and bugged double-jump mechanics would ever be a good idea? I guess we have to wait that they do a 'New' Lucky's Tale VR before we can really enjoy it. On the other hand, just adding VR headset support to NSLT would have been the better option probably than doing a whole own VR title like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Good story and good gameplay. Bosses are good for the most part, I felt like some fights leading up to some of the bosses were kinda stupid. For example, being shot by a cannon across the bridge, yes you have cover but its hard to fight the swarm of enemies in front of me while im being shot at by multiple gunmen and cannons. If you want an easier way around it, i'd say just change it to easy mode temporarily. The story was by far the best i've experienced since Yakuza 0, the pacing was good and not too much extra rambling/side quest involvement to the story. Glad I dont have to hear some npc's life story for like 20 minutes just to get back to the main story. The story cutscenes are like either bound to 30 fps and some are 60, it seemed like the promotional ones got about 120 fps compared to the rest. Its not the worst thing in the world but it could be better. The combat remained similar to most yakuza games if not better, the style is like a mix of kiwami 2/6 and yakuza 5 which to me is a perfect combo. One last thing I will say is DO NOT buy the dlc (unless they fix it but they most likely wont) because right now its only one per save. If you delete a save forever you will have to rebuy the dlc, not really optimal at all. RGG please fix this because believe me this is not the smartest move for dlc on your part.Overall, 9/10 close to 10. (If they fix the dlc thing I would gladly give it a 10)I do recommend for anyone looking to pick up a new game, regardless if you've played the yakuza/like a dragon franchise or not.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:- Story is top notch. Lots of liberties taken with the real history, of course, but overall feels like it's up there with the best of the franchise- Fitting use of previous characters as model cameos. A few odd ones out, but most are adapted very well, despite technically being new and unrelated characters- "New" combat styles are a lot of fun, very satisfying. Sword-focused bosses feel very different from anything else in the series- Runs VERY well on Steam Deck. Completed the game entirely on the Deck.The bad:- More of a remaster than a remake. Feels very much like the Y5/Y0 era, and not at all like the Y6/Kiwami era.- Porting to Unreal instead of using the Dragon engine is questionable, and came with a lot of drawbacks. Occasional performance hitches and frame drops (thought this was a Deck issue, but seems to be common). - Side stories and filler content are especially lacking compared to the rest of the series- Combat can be very frustrating at times, especially on higher difficulties. Ending sequence in particular has one specific room that's legitimately worse than any boss in the game.- Crafting system is absurdly expensive and grindy - I finished the entire game without engaging with it even once.Overall, very much on-par with the rest of the franchise, and while I would highly recommend it, I definitely would suggest playing on Normal and just playing the main story out. Just be aware that this is VERY much a PS3-era game, and more of a remaster than a remake.

Think of it as a play with the cast playing the different roles they have.Music STILL a certified banger, and they even remixed some themes like   theme from yakuza 5.Content is still top RGG standard, full of variation to entertain yourself in the city of Kyo.Due to its engine change to UE, it suffered with few problems like stuttering on cutscenes and gameplay, which makes it jarring. Graphics wise, it looks great but i prefer the old engine honestly.Another problem is, well you know it, the Bath House which is sucks considering i am really looking forward for it.  Okay that aside, i don't like the trooper system to be implemented in the main game. I just don't like them and the boss using the special skill is just feels really off. I mean sure you can play the game without the troopers but boss still uses them regardless.and minor nitpick from me, is the font choice. I don't really like the font for the game, feels too basic and doesn't fit the setting of the game. Thankfully there are mods for this so i guess that is easily solved.Overall its a great game but not perfect, not my favorite RGG game. But i brought it because i like RGG studios and i want to support them. I am sure they can improve, hopefully. And for RGG studios, don't let the success go over your head.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna be honest. This is a horrible remake of a good game. Ishin has some design choices that make people have vast opinions on it, stuff like  friendship quests with boring objectives, the way the combat is stiffer like the older games  or the story being based off japanese history which some people don't care about.I'm one of the few people who liked those parts of ishin anyway....Though when i say "like" i mean the original ishin, not whatever this ""remake"" is. If you are someone who hasn't played the original ishin or just a newcomer to the series, you might end up liking ishin kiwami.However as someone who's played the original i can easily point out some heavy flaws that make the remake considerably worse in most aspects: Nearly every single boss in the game got some sort of change that decreased or outright prevented the chance of them getting knocked down, ruining certain combos from the original. Unreal engine seems to have nerfed  the grabs, certain bosses slide off while  the others are outright ungrabable in kiwami for no reason.Back blows don't stun bosses as much anymore, they can randomly gain super armor and just ignore your attacks.  Ask any no damage youtuber  and they will say that og ishin has kiwami beat in every aspect combat wise.Combat wise it seems they rebalanced the styles, and by rebalance i mean they nerfed the worst style (brawler) from original ishin and made it even worse, while gunner and wild dancer remain kings.Brawler tanimura parry buff (maxed, gives you combo speed and makes attacks bounce off you.) lasted 9 seconds in ishin and only 3.54 in ishin kiwami for some reason??Even worse is they nerfed brawlers damage to the point where it only exists for certain heat actions, like imagine maxed brawler  tiger drop dealing less damage than 2 sword swings?Certain bosses outright don't do their full combo due to the unreal engine breaking the ai, a certain tutorial boss  for example is a joke (beginning boss is meant to have long combos suprisingly ) but him and his grunts just do like 2 swings and cancel it for no reason.THEY REPLACED A UNIQUE BOSS THEME WITH TOWN BULLY FROM YAKUZA 6 (this happened since they mixed up the ultimate battle and story folder, so  it plays in ultimate battles instead of the story part it's meant to play in like wtf.)on the topic of ultimate battles, og ishin made bosses use their qtes during em, ishin kiwami just makes them go into heat mode and use their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ superpowers. (Which i hate very much since they ruin the mood and are very boring to play against, like imagine having a serious sword fight only for the guy to kamehameha you.) Small gripe, but ultimate battles don't have a  pause at the start so enemies can hit you while the ultimate battle is still fading in.Og ishin has a boss who can throw projectiles (won't spoil) he doesn't spam it too much and uses his melee after hitting you (which stuns you)  or missing (his moves are dependant on that),Kiwami broke that and he just spams projectiles half the time lol!(his ♥♥♥♥♥♥ magic is also a projectile lol, the follow up attack he does after stunning you with a projectile is broken and only works half the time, since unreal can make it randomly miss.)(In og ishin the follow up attack had a green flash because his aura was a unique green, kiwami changed it to orange but the flash is still green because the interns making ishin kiwami ported it and didn't realize that).The giant enemies are spammed everywhere in kiwami, they are unstunnable and can't be heat actioned, truly so "fun" to fight against unless you cheese them.AMON got nerfed. he went from one of the hardest ones in the series to kinda being slightly wimpy since his sword got nerfed and his moveset isn't as fancy. OH and you can stun lock him with certain swords if you want (cough lightning).Graphically: The game was made on Unreal Engine (which makes it a stuttering mess) to make it look more beautiful than original ishin, which is ironic since the game looks like a blurry unfocused mess (where characters look like they are wet and covered in oil) compared to the original ishin, the only positive is that the night lightning looks beautiful but that's about it. Certain fights have their atmosphere kinda bugged or ruined: a certain fight happens in a steamy sauna and the steam is horribly rendered compared to the original. A certain  boss arena has this beautiful atmospheric moonrising overlooking it, kiwami ruins it and dependant on your luck, the moon either doesn't appear or is not correctly shown in the phase transition cutscene due to them incorrectly placing the camera.Another small gripe but a certain boss in og had a badass intro where the music started playing after his name title pops up, kiwami screwed up and the music starts playing before the title even fades in.Certain facial animations for characters are just horrible due to model swaps (yakuza 6, 0 and 7 characters stick out sometimes due to the obvious port). a certain VERY IMPORTANT boss (AGAIN NO SPOILERS) has way worse line delivery in kiwami, they also use his incorrect costume for some reason? Good old recasts. Very minor gripe: They removed a cool post credit scene where ryomas statue is shown (based off the real one.) (Though i understand this since the voice actor in that scene has passed away).The Ishin completion list is notorious for being very grindy, and thankfully... Ishin Kiwami made the grind even worse :D.Grind was increased: chicken racing exploit patched, blacksmith is worse ( Requires Rng), the game is designed to be played with the cards  and your damage is low if you don't use them, even with a heavily maxed sword (unless you use a certain overpowered seal that requires virtue). They totally didn't increase the grind so they could sell you the  paid dlc (exp and crafting packs????). Sega would never do that......Ishin Kiwami obviously has new voice acting, for the most part it's great, but i do love the instances where you literally hear nothing because the voice actor talked quietly, or you hear the mic peaking into your ear, utterly ruining the serious scene.I have more complaints but i genuinely have to write them down somewhere so i don't forget.All in all. I hope emulating stops being buggy and the ishin translation project discord completes it's job so more people can emulate the superior ishin.They really should have just localized it and then just ported it without any of this padding.I feel really bad for the interns or b team that had to port this game  on unreal.if they remake kenzan and ruin it i will cry.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin!~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~After being in exile for many years, you, Sakamoto Ryoma an expert in sword fighting, shall we say a Samurai, has returned to his native city of Tosa. There, Yoshida Toyo, whom you consider your father, and your brother in arms Takechi Hanpeita have a plan to restructure Japan. You are invited to their latest meeting in the Tosa Fortress, where a Ninja assassin ended up slaying Toyo and many of his soldiers. As more reinforcements arrive at the meeting place, they see Toyo in your arms and assume that you are his assassin.  After managing to evade the soldier’s reinforcement, you reach the wall of the fortress, where you come face to face with the real assassin as your brother lay down on the floor injured. The masked assassin’s uniquely skilled swordsmanship is unbeatable.  After he flees the scene, you swear to find him, whatever it takes.Like a Dragon: Ishin! is an action-adventure beat ’em-up game developed by Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio and published by SEGA on the 22nd of February 2023 on the Steam platform. I must say that I have never played any game from Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio before this game. The first reason for this is that I am not a real fan of console gaming. The second is that I was never really attracted to the games these developers have produced so far, and the third is that I can’t stand crazy high-pitched voices as I suffer from tinnitus. What tickled my fantasy about Like a Dragon: Ishin! is that it is based on historical events. So, I decided to give it a serious go.  After 40 hours of gameplay, I must say that I have enjoyed playing the 14 chapters that make up Like a Dragon: Ishin of! I can see now why people enjoy games from this developer. All the components of the game are extremely well done. The Story is compelling and well-structured from start to finish. What I also appreciate is the fact that they have chosen the right music to associated with emotions such as sadness, betrayal, euphoria, etc. The only thing I thought was slightly overboard for me is the recap of the chapter just finished. The other thing that you may find a bit much is the shear amount of reading, as the entire voice acting is done in Japanese. You can definitely fast-forward the conversation by clicking on the button “A” on your gamepad if you wish to, but you’ll probably miss many interesting twists within the story if you do.The story is linear, and you’ll have to complete several tasks within each chapter to move on to the next one. However, you can take your time and explore the city of Kyo (Kyoto) where you’ll find plenty of restaurants to dine in.  As the story evolves, you’ll be able to enter new establishments, such as the Chicken Races Betting House.  Maybe you’d fancy a Japanese checkers game or to participate in the Japanese The Voice contest. There are fun little mini-games. One of these mini-games is the cooking game. This game can be played in your second residence which you can access at the docks. One man will be waiting for you when you are ready, and you’ll be travelling by boat to your house. There, you’ll have your own vegetable patch where you can grow stuff. It will be small at first as you have to unlock plenty of upgrades for your house as well as for other things within the game. It is a fun little thing to do, and even more important is that food will regenerate your health. Yes, you can sit down in restaurants, pubs and tea houses and order food and drinks which you have to pay for. Being a good cook will save you a few coins and most of the recipes you successfully cook will generate more health than you would achieve by purchasing meals in these food establishments. Sometimes you’ll have to eat out anyway as you will be far from the docks.This brings me to the combat aspect of the game, and let me tell you, you’ll encounter many battles all the way through the game. In fact, Kyo is full of warriors, ruffians and bandits that walk through its streets. In fact, every couple of corners, you’ll cross paths with some of these groups. You can run away if you don’t feel like fighting or just have fun and try to earn orbs for your four fighting techniques, which are Brawler, Swordman, Gunman and Wild Dancer. The first three are pretty easy to figure out.  Each of these styles has an ability board that looks like an original Japanese solitaire game. As you progress through the levels of each of these styles, you’ll earn orbs of specific colours. For the swordsman abilities, you’ll receive blue orbs which you can use on the board to unlock specific moves or upgrade a capacity such as your health. You also have grey orbs or training orbs which you accumulate throughout the game by fighting. You can use these orbs on all four techniques to boost your capacity and moves. There are also locks on each of the techniques boards and you need to visit specific places like Dojos or the arms dealer to learn these new techniques so you can remove the locks. The fights are fun and I thoroughly enjoyed the fact that you can swap between techniques during combat. As you level up, so do the Ruffians, Warriors and Bandits and expect tougher encounters as you progress. I strongly recommend taking on as many fights as you can to level up your characters as you will need plenty of experience when you face other battles with key characters throughout the chapters and at the end. For me, the combination of the Swordman and Gunman techniques was the most suitable. Great arcade fighting, and I was only playing the normal difficulty level! And yes, I died more than once in all the important fights! The graphics, cutscenes and soundtrack are very good. It’s a very good linear story and you can do your own things as well around Kyo if you want to. As I mentioned, I played for 40 hours and achieved 50% of the substories and other things as well as finishing the game. There is plenty of replayability here, which is just great. I didn’t experience any issues whatsoever from start to finish, with all my settings turned up to Ultra. Positives:~~~~~~~ + Great graphics, cutscenes and soundtrack+ Compelling story with plenty of twists+ Four different combat techniques+ Fun, addictive and challenging on the normal level of difficulty+ Several mini-games to find and play+ Many hours of entertainment+ Achievements and trading cardsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ - A fair bit of reading as the voice acting is all in JapaneseLike a Dragon: Ishin! brings you fabulous storytelling and a combat system that will keep you entertained for many hours. A top game!9/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Rating this down not because the game itself is bad (it's actually very fun and im enjoying it so far) but because there are lots of dumb issues and I don't think this game should have been Kiwami'd First off the game is technically a Kiwami (even named that in the jp release) but its more just a UE4 port of the original with some cast changes and some extra substories for 0 and 7(Y:LAD) fanservice. The gameplay itself is entirely the same which makes it incredibly weird to have this good looking game with Yakuza 5 type combat, i'm not saying its bad (I quite like it as I enjoyed 4 and 5 alot) but both Kiwamis have actually done stuff to the combat. Looking at footage of the original it does not even look hugely dated, it was only 1 year before 0 and thats the most popular game in the series that anyone interested in Ishin would have played.There was absolutely no reason this couldn't have been just translated and made a Remaster like 3,4 and 5.Other issues to note:Poor performance, lots of stutters when heat actions happen (apparently a UE4 issue where stuff isnt cached properly) but in general it's not a good PC port. Runs better than Kiwami 2 tho.The lack of legit ultrawide support, the game is unsure if it supports it giving constant bars at the side of the screen but still rendering some text and the karaoke under those bars, hoping for a community fix or a patch on this as this is apparently a UE4 default settings issue (thanks Tim Fornite Sweeney)The game also has one time use microtransactions to get gun and sword parts?? These aren't even good and I don't know why they were added.TL;DRThe game Ishin! itself is fun, game should have been a remaster instead as this isn't a good Kiwami.

_childDocuments_.review: If you ever played a Yakuza/Like A Dragon game, the beat 'em ups not the turn-based RPGs, then there isn't much new here.That can be good or bad depending on your enjoyment of the other RGG games. Like a Dragon: Ishin! feels lower middle of the road compared to the games in the series I've played. I like the historical period piece the game is going for, and I enjoy seeing Yakuza characters playing different parts like they are actors at the RGG studio.The melee is good, if the same stiff button mashing the series has always been. And like every other game in the series, starts to wear thin with its lack of depth and hundreds if not thousands of opponents fought.  The mini games are a little lackluster. I can't point to any I particularly enjoy. Many of the gambling and gaming staples made the cross over from modern setting of Yakuza to this game. As did fishing, karaoke, dance dance revolution and not entirely unfamiliar courtisan mini games. Perhaps the most interesting mini game here is the cooking ones. Which I found none entirely satisfying to play for very long. And for the life of me I don't know why the develops do a singing rhythm game line by line with the cursor moving at differing speeds. That is beginner trap central.What I did enjoy is much of the charm that found in the series. Little side stories and missions, an convoluted main mission story and like able characters. And I think the game would be an much easier sell if the grinding and padding was cut way back. There's a number of decisions that seem there just to waste the player's time. Several button inputs to pick up a prize ticket or open a jar, forcing the player to return to the same NPC multiple times to do the same action until filling the meter to resolve the substory. None these things hurt the game in isolation, but they had up cause the game to be less satisfying than it otherwise could.Which is why I think the Yakuza/Like A Dragon series has always been niche. I enjoy the quirky fun enough to overlook the fundamental flaws and old fashioned/wasn't fun back then either game design and mechanics of much of it.  So, I do recommend Like a Dragon: Ishin!, but with many caveats. If you don't already like Yakuza games, this game isn't likely to change your mind.

_childDocuments_.review: Totally recommend this game. It feels and plays much better than for example Kiwami or Yakuza 0. No offence to those games, but this game feels a bit more streamlined. _childDocuments_.review: This game has an amazing story and yes I know everyone was disappointed in regards to the graphics and that they expected more for the hype however the game has an amazing story with lots of content for you to enjoy. There is a bit of a grind but that is ok you can change it up with all the extra content. Money is a bit of an issue in the first play through but by the second play through you have a lot to work with so no worries. The game really brings you into old time Kyoto however not sure how accurate it is to actual history as it relates to the historical time period in Japan known as the Meji Restoration or the Restoration of the Emperor. I am surprised Nijo Castle was not used as it hold great significance during the Tokugawa Shogunate. I do like the use of one of Kyoto's most famous temples in Eastern Kyoto however Kyoto is dotted with tons of Temples with rich history. However I love this game and Ryu Ga Gotoku Studios and I hope for more content like this to be produced by the studios. Without giving any more potential spoilers I will end my review here. If you love the pre-industrial Japan, the time of Samurai, and western influence at the start of the 1800's then look no further than this epic story from Ryu Ga Gotoku Studios. Hands down loved the story.***Also don't believe the hours recorded as I did a lot offline.***

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying I intend to put as much effort into this review as much as they did in the remake.Specifically the part that justifies full price for a game that was originally a PS3 game.First, they did the bare minimum.Second, Third, they decided to sell it for full price.Alright, I'll elaborate anyways.What they didn't bother with:- English VO- Work in Ultrawide- Work to get rid of shader stuttering- Story happens in 1860's, just like the combat mechanics - QoL improvements to make it more than PS3 gameWhat they did:- Copy pasted it all into UE4, e.g., 30fps cutscenes- Improved the graphics from PS3 to PS4~ish- Subtitles, glossary- Acknowledged messed up UW layout (layout only)- Decided to sell more of one-time use per account DLC's- Made a DLC pack of Twitch StreamersConclusion: 25-30€ for this I would have understood. _childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing this, I've put in 37 hours which surprised me.  It absolutely does not feel like I've played for more than a couple hours.  You can't go more than 5 mins without finding something new to grab your interest.  Between the side quests, engaging combat, and mini games there is always something to keep you running around Kyo.  This is the first entry in the Like a Dragon series that I have been able to play at launch without having the thought in the back of my mind that I have more entries to go through.  Maybe that fact is why I am able to let myself get lost in the game and engage with the content available without trying to advance to the next title.The Yakuza series has always had varying combat styles to chose from but they all largely revolved around unarmed combat.  It's refreshing to have combat styles that focus on permanent equipment.  The gunman style is straight broken but it is so cathartic to unload on an enemy that has been giving you issues.  I can't help but laugh after re-enacting the Indiana Jones scene in a hard combat scenario.  I started my first playthrough on Ishin difficulty and oh boy does it go hard.  Most trash mob enemies can kill you in two hits.  Bosses almost always one-shot you.  Don't say I didn't warn you.The story is essentially a who-dun-it revenge story. A colorful cast of characters who have been staples throughout the Yakuza series return but with different names and in feudal japan.  It's easy to find a character that quickly becomes your favorite.  If you've never played a Yakuza (Like a Dragon) game prior to this entry,  you can easily start with this title.  You don't need to know a single thing about the series to follow the plot of this title.  Honestly, you'd be doing yourself a disservice by passing on this game.The twitch content creator troop cards is dumb.  Nyanners and these other random e-celebs stick out so hard in a feudal japan setting.  However, you can completely ignore the content creator trooper cards if you don't download the DLC.Still dumb though.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a captivating spin-off in the Yakuza series, transporting players to 1860s Japan with a gripping story centered on samurai Sakamoto Ryoma. The game blends historical drama and the series’ signature over-the-top action, offering a mix of versatile combat styles and engaging side activities. The beautifully crafted Kyoto setting, rich in detail and atmosphere, immerses players in the Bakumatsu era, while the dynamic soundtrack enhances both intense and quieter moments. For fans and newcomers alike, Ishin! delivers a refreshing take on the Yakuza formula, combining heart, humor, and history seamlessly.

_childDocuments_.review: I found this boring and repetitive compared to other RGG games I played. RGG games don't shy away from repetitive or stretching things out but there's a lot of immersion in the setting that this does, with side stories and characters giving different angles of this world RGG has built (or recreated in this case).I know it's a remake of a classic but that unfortunately carries a higher bar, not a lower one. The dialogue and storytelling is wildly inconsistent, with what is really a very short tale that is dragged out (when so much more could be told within or alongside it) being held together by some very enjoyable set pieces and twists. I wanted to care about deaths and setbacks but really couldn't find myself doing that.Can't believe I have to say this but you really can't have this many people in a game who exists solely for you to give vegetables to. Lazy.No issues playing this on my setup, is also something positive.

_childDocuments_.review: A treatise on historical storytelling through video games. "Like A Dragon: Ishin" does what few other games have managed to pull off. It tells an engaging and interesting historical narrative, conveys a powerful message, and provides a fun and rewarding experience. If you enjoy "Fall of the Samurai", "Rurouni Kenshin", "Gintama", or "The Last Samurai" then you will likely enjoy this game and time period. I am not normally a fan of JRPGs but I found myself deeply invested in the characters and locations. The combat can become repetitive but it is well worth it to get to the next story or scene. The story itself is a creative retelling of the Boshin War and Meiji Restoration and takes some creative license while still managing to stay true to the historical end result. Take the time to read up on the true events and appreciate the effect that a few individuals can have on a nation's history. With 30 hrs in my first play-through I have only completed 25% of the game. I am satisfied enough to walk away now but could easily be convinced to walk around and attempt to get further toward that 100% mark. This is a must buy for lovers of history, the Samurai, and the JRPG genre.
