_childDocuments_.review: - - - Story - - - Excellent main story as usual - it's a traditional tale of revenge told in typical Yakuza/Ryu Ga Gotoku fashion which never get boring. The less known the better. The side quests lack any charm whatsoever; I've actually been skipping almost all of the dialogue which I have never done in the seven Yakuza games I've played. I'm not sure why, but I haven't found any of them interesting at all. I can't put my finger on it, but I just don't really care. We don't get many distinctive characters like Miracle Johnson or Mr. Labido.- - - Performance/visuals - - -Although a patch has been put up to address it, stuttering is still a big problem and has actually got me killed in a fight, which is a big problem when you're playing on Ishin difficulty like I am, where you die after being hit two or three times. The visuals are great, but I do think some of the post-processing effects are quite unpleasant. The texture quality and world geometry all appear to be the same as the PS3 original, with he exception of a few textures that appear to be upscaled in some way or another. Now I understand that the setting does limit the artistic freedom the artists would have had, but the world lacks a sense of depth and clutter - this is not a remaster on the level of Yakuza Kiwami 2, which is what I was hoping for. With all that said, the world is authentically Japan as of the Edo period. It definitely looks the part, but they really haven't pushed any boundaries with this re-release. It's a fun world to explore, and there are some flickers of genuine beauty in some isolated areas of Kyo. This game was updated to run in UE5 and it has some of the best hallmarks of the engine; the modern lighting looks more natural compared to the original. Ambient occlusion looks great, the depth of field effects look great in the cutscenes. One very nice addition is that most of the original Shinsengumi and other characters have been replaced with characters from Yakuza games released after Yakuza Ishin on PS3. As an example it was wonderful to see Hitoshi Ozawa (Awano), Riki Takeuchi (Kuze), and Hideo Nakano (Shibusawa) from Yakuza 0 reprise their roles once again, albeit in a Japan under feudalism - those guys are great actors. Not to disrespect the original PS3 actors as they all performed just as well, but I have more of a connection with the characters that replaced them. The character models in the cutscenes are of a very high quality and look great, however in-game they look about the same as their PS3 counterparts, which is slightly disappointing.To disable the awful motion blur, depth of field and chromatic aberration, paste this code at the end of the engine.ini file. However, I do like the DOF effects in this game, I'm just aware others might not:[SystemSettings]r.MotionBlurQuality=0r.SceneColorFringeQuality=0r.DepthOfFieldQuality=0 - - - Side activities and mini-games - - -All the traditional mini-games you expect from the Yakuza series are here, from casino games to a combat arena, all about the same but in a different era. Utamaruya is the old-school karaoke which is one of my favourites with the excellent soundtrack that uses traditional wind and string instruments. What are unique mini-games are as follows:Nichibuza, a form of traditional dance where a fan is used. There's some lovely choreography and becomes increasingly more difficult, a little bit too difficult for me :)Chicken racing: need I say more?Courtesan visits: you can visit a courtesan and play some fun, innuendo-filled mini-games. The voice actress has a lovely voice.Farming/cooking: at some point in the game you gain access to your own villa out of the way of the hustle and bustle of the city which mirrors Kiryu's Morning Glory Orphanage to some extent - it even comes with Haruka! What you do here is farm and cook what you grow into a surprisingly diverse range of dishes. I don't really find it that stimulating compared to running a cabaret club in Yakuza 0. Plus Haruka is the only best girl. Shinsengumi captain: once you become a captain you can partake in policing activities in the form of missions and management of soldiers. I never enjoyed this mini-game too much because of how limited it was. I don't really have much else to say - it's a repetitive, pseudo-management game that has you retreading the same few maps over and over.I've probably forgotten a load more things to do as there's loads to distract in this game, in typical Yakuza fashion.- - - Combat - - -Bare in mind I am only playing Ishin difficulty which is punishingly hard, so it might differ on easier modes. With that in mind - - It's pretty good, mate. It's typical Yakuza beat 'em up brawling with the interesting addition of... A GUN. Yes, you can shoot people in the face and stab them at the same time! The combat is surprisingly balanced considering you have a katana and a gun, you never feel truly invincible even when you've risen in level and understand the nuances of the combos. Everything is beautifully animated and the Heat actions are as bodacious and over-the-top as you'd like, and fun to look at. It doesn't feel anywhere near as repetitive as other games, and isn't as punishing as Yakuza 4.Like most Yakuza before it, you gain additional abilities for each of the four fighting styles from trainers. You even get an ancient Komaki! There's not much else to say, it's basically the same as the previous games.- - - Crafting - - -Unlike other Yakuza games crafting is essential in Ishin; most games in the series you can completely ignore the crafting side, however you need resources to craft and upgrade your guns and swords at the forge in Ishin. Luckily crafting materials are abundant in the world and you get at least one every time you defeat some delinquents or ronin which are this game's version of yakuza and gang members. You'll find materials on the floor, in wells, in random pots. Certain materials are very rare and you'll have to buy them or earn them playing mini-games. It's quite fun.- - - Soundtrack - - -It would be remiss of me not to mention the soundtrack. The Yakuza music has it's style rooted back in F-Zero GX (developed by Sega) that still carries on with it's composer Hidenori Shoji who, 20 years after GX came out, is still making music in that distinctive style in the Yakuza series. Electronic and rock fused into a soulful and visceral style that really sticks with you, that also complements the often high-octane action and emotions of Yakuza. Ishin is no different in that it has these elements; the addition of traditional instruments like the koto and shakuhachi mixed in with the more high-energy tracks for combat really help that distinctive style to fit into the world.Outside of the heavier, rock/electronic music, the ambient and slower-paced music is beautiful. The wind and string arrangements are soulful and distinct. Though, I would have liked more tracks comprised entirely of instruments like the gottan and shakuhachi, I still appreciate what is included. - - - Conclusion - - -Leaves something to be desired on the visual side of things, and the sub-stories are genuinely dull. However, what you get here is an excellent Yakuza/Like a Dragon story, decent combat and an awful lot to do and explore. Long-time fans will be delighted if they're in it primarily for the main story.I hope my review was helpful.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever considered how a “shot-for-shot” videogame remake would look and play like? Well, now we have the answer – Like a Dragon: Ishin! is, for all intents and purposes, a remake of the 2014 Japanese-only title Ryū ga Gotoku Ishin! (and to avoid confusion the Japanese title of this remake just added Kiwami, just like with previous remakes). But unlike the Yakuza 1 and 2 remakes, this one feels, looks and plays almost exactly the same as the original game did. Is it good? Is it bad? Probably neither, but the result is a pretty cool entry in the Like a Dragon franchise that, however, does feel like it’s from the past in more ways than the setting.Just as with the majority of Like a Dragon titles, this is an open world action adventure title with beat ’em up combat and a cinematic story, where the open world part is not that big but rather dense with events and stories. However, being set in the Bakumatsu era of history of Japan, presumably in 1867 if we align it with real world history it… let’s say “takes inspiration from”, it also prominently features usage of weapons and not just fists or feet. In fact, for the most part this is more of a hack and slash than a beat ’em up title, even though those familiar with combat of the series will quickly adapt to the tweaks and changes.As the original title was made in the period between Yakuza 5 and Yakuza 0, a lot of the design decisions were and still are very close to that period of the franchise. So going from Lost Judgment into Ishin! might not be the smoothest transition. Thankfully, the auto-save and ability to save anytime are here and even though most of the mechanics and concepts are more or less the same as they were in the original version, they were updated to be smoother, more responsive and just easier to enjoy. Although, again, it’s a far cry from just how comfortable and user friendly the latest entries were, with very limited fast travel points, limited inventory and the need to drop items off in the storage, no auto-pickup for items that drop from enemies, slower in and out transition for combat, no way of seeing substories (side content) on the map without a special item… Lots of great quality of life features that the later game added are just not here and you will feel the absence. And also, in my personal opinion, the mini-games for some activities in this entry are pretty bad. Then again, even in newer titles there can be stinkers.I wasn’t joking about “shot-for-shot” remake nature of the game otherwise, however, as despite being completely remade from ground up on Unreal Engine 4, despite changing some of the character looks and voices, despite tweaking the music here and there the presentation and storytelling of the game is exactly the same as in the original. To the point where I have to wonder if the RGG Studio somehow managed to reuse all of their capture work and camera movement from the original game in UE. The only notable change I know about is the absence of one post-credits segment which looked at the events of the game from the modern time perspective, but everything apart from that looks exactly the same, just prettier.Luckily, the lack of story changes doesn’t feel bad as the tale was interesting enough as is. In general, it is a reimagining of the historical events that directly led up to what is now known as the Meiji Restoration and it features fictionalized takes on real historic figures and moments, but all told with the usual Like a Dragon melodramatic flair. If you’re not used to it, some moments can be very frustrating as the characters often make decisions that in real life would feel really dumb, like this game’s Kiryu – Sakamoto Ryōma, who survives through the story just because he’s so honest and idealistic that people can’t help but admire him, even when they should probably kill him instead.And also there are moments, especially the whole ending bit, that are very patriotic in their message to the future people of Japan to keep fighting for the better future, from the perspective of the characters of the era when Japan was on the verge of being colonized by western powers. It’s a bit awkward for me, but at the same time – this is a tale about an extremely important moment in Japanese history so I get where it’s coming from. Especially as a Ukrainian who at times caught myself thinking of direct historic parallels with our history and how we could probably make the game with at least a few similar messages that would feel important today.Nonetheless, the story is good, the characters are fun, most of the gameplay is very good and is both fresh for the series and also pleasantly familiar. The way the leveling up works is really nice and feels surprisingly natural and not grindy. In fact, apart from a lot of the side content, most of the game is far less grindy than what Like a Dragon games from that period of the franchise were and the game is overall less tiring than Lost Judgment even. Plus, since it doesn’t have any connections to the other titles in the franchise, it’s easy to just go in with no extra knowledge and enjoy the game as is.I liked Like a Dragon: Ishin! quite a bit, even if I did feel at times that maybe more things could’ve been remade to fit better with the quality of life features of more recent titles in the series. If you’re going in just for the main story, you’re going to have fun (unless, of course, you somehow hate Japanese history entirely). If you like to 100% these titles, it’s going to get a bit frustrating, but it’s not among the worst entries in that regard either. Honestly, though, I wish to see more Like a Dragon titles from older times, but no need to tie them so directly to real world events, they can happen in the background.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally after almost 10 years we have Ishin in the west! RGG has delivered yet another BANGER with the kiwami version of Ishin. The game is overall phenomenal and it has potential to be up there with the greats like Yakuza 0 and Lost Judgment. However it does suffer from a couple of small flaws that I think hold it back by just a little bit. 1. CombatThe combat is great and it feels super satisfying. Ishin has 4 fighting styles: Brawler, Swordsman, Gunman and Wild Dancer. With many different fighting styles in the game one is bound to be less popular than the others and that would be swordsman, however in swordsmans case here the style just isn't good at all compared to the other styles and feels really lacking. Brawler and Wild Dancer are good for crowds or for one-on-one fights while gunman is great for crowd control but some use can be found in boss fights as well. Swordsman is only good for boss fights and even then you're just better off using brawler or wild dancer in bosses as they are much faster with better mobility and defense abilities. Swordsman has a slightly bigger damage but it's still really slow even when upgraded and I just never really used it. It was the only style I hadn't maxed out when I reached the final chapter. It looks cool to use? I guess?2. Trooper cardsThe player being able to use trooper cards is not a problem for me as you can just... not use them and call it a day. My slight nitpick about this is how the story bosses are able to use them. If they would use it like once a fight it wouldn't matter at all but sometimes they just decide to spam the special abilities. This happened to me with  boss fight and it felt like a really cheap way to amp up the difficulty. I played the game on legend so usually these abilities just instantly kill you as well especially in the early-mid game when I hadn't crafted good enough gear yet. A "classic mode" would have been nice to experience the game as it was originally intended.3. Bathhouse fight QTE was censored4. The GrindThe game has a pretty agonizing grind when trying to get the right material drops from dungeons as RNG is always involved. I would point out the need for money grinding as well but since the chicken race exploit exists you can completely remove the grind for money with that.5. Unreal Engine stutteringAs the game is on unreal engine the game has some stuttering issues. Doing a new heat action for the first time for example will always result in stuttering. Not really a big issue at the end of the day but worth pointing out I think.All this aside, everything else in the game is absolutely fantastic! Everyone can have their opinions about the cast changes for example but as for me most of them are pretty solid. There's a couple in the OG that I would have liked to return but I think there's nothing wrong with the new cast members. They also created some new music for this remake  and all of the new tracks and remixed tracks sound gorgeous as well.Overall this game is an easy 9/10. If you're a fan of RGG and have not yet played Ishin (Not this one or the original) I highly recommend you play it.Here's hoping one day we get Kenzan and Kurohyō 1 & 2 in the west either in the remastered form or in the kiwami remake form as well as Dead Souls finally making it past the ps3 and getting either a remaster or the kiwami treatment as well

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game and its Yakuza style twist on real historical events, but the gameplay itself does have some pros and cons. _childDocuments_.review: After years and years of waiting, we finally got a western localization of Ryu Ga Gotoku: Ishin! in the form of...Ishin Kiwami.Well, to cut a long story short - the main story and everything around it is easily top-tier RGG material if there ever was, but in my opinion the side content is below average.The few actual side stories that are here feel on par with the older PS3 Yakuza games, while the rest are just "Hey, you started a friendship with a person/store!" type of deal.The friendships are a bit of an excessive grind, and are certainly not a fun thing, nor were they ever.In hindsight, they were a bit much even in Judgment, though in that game it was still better handled.As for the mini-games, you have the usual suspects - Karaoke, a dancing minigame (which is actually not nearly as piss easy as what we had in Yakuza 5 and is actually harder on average than 0 - probably closer to the difficulty you can find in the dancing club in Lost Judgment), two of Yakuza 5's minigames (chicken racing betting and an udon ship minigame) with the regular assortment of Japanese board/gambling minigames.As always, your mileage may vary, but I'm sure you'll find something to enjoy there.As for the battle dungeons - well, you either love to grind them or hate to go through them as they go on and on and... ON...Actually, I'd like to shout out the absolute state that is the way the game's balanced and how it hinges on crafting. I don't like it. The sword style just isn't satisfying - almost any enemy that isn't a small fry can block your rush combos with ease while also getting hits on you even though you could've sworn your dodge was well timed or your block should've triggered those sweet, sweet i-frames.What isn't helping is how the crafting system has SO MANY materials that you need to collect, and boy is the game not generous with the ones that count.I'd be lying if I said I recommend playing the game without using mods and/or resource cheats.(Seriously though, I would absolutely DESPISE playing RGG games on a console, where I can't use save editing, install mods or apply specific, pinpoint cheats where they can really count. It's a real shame that some of the best you'll find in gaming has to be bogged down with mindnumbing grinds and questionable design decisions.)Despite all of my complaints, I still recommend the game overall, seeing as all the criticisms above notwithstanding, if you don't find the quality of the side content to be that important or conversely you LIKE grinding the same gameplay loop for crafting materials, then you'll find one of the best main stories in the Like a Dragon franchise here, with combat that can be uneven but still pretty good (bless the Wild Dancer style for letting you run wild on enemies). You'll get much more out of it if you give yourself a crash course on the state of Japan's society and politics circa 1850-1870 beforehand, though.Just, uh, hold fast to your suspension of disbelief, ok?

_childDocuments_.review: It's amazing to finally be able to play this game! Overall it was incredible starting with:Story: Not a really big surprise as a RGG studio fan they've always delivered amazingly written stories. This one is no exception. _childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! is up there as one of my favorite games of all time. To finally get a remake of one of the most beloved entries in the series and get it localized for the first time is a real treat. One of the best parts of this game is the combat. Combat is one of the most important aspects in these games, because I know I will spend a good portion of the game engaged in combat. So I was really happy to see the combat done well in Ishin. There are multiple battle styles to switch from with each form having their own unique properties. The Wild Dancer style is possibly one of my favorite combat styles in the whole game, just because how well it flows and how good it is when you master it. All of the other styles are amazing as well. Trooper cards are also an addition to the game. They are fun to use and make things a little easier, but if you want to play through the game traditionally, just don't use the cards. My only complaint with the combat is that it takes a lot of time to level up your battle styles. Even after 40 hours of playing at the time I am reviewing this (this is after completing the main story and doing a bunch of the side content), I am still far from mastering all of the styles and utilizing all of the abilities in the game. Of course, you can easily get experience points from the Shrine, but they take up a lot of Virtue points that would've gone to other useful features as well. Besides that, the combat is one of the best RGG combat systems that I have played in a while. The music is something I love about this game. Most of these songs were from the original Ishin game, but there are some new ones for bosses such as "Soar" and for karaoke songs such as "Baka Mitai". Hearing all of these tracks in game was such a treat with some being remixes of songs in other games. But there are a few nitpicks (spoilers ahead): . Regardless, the music also goes hard in this game. The story was also very good, and I like how the narrative is based on the events that propelled Japan into the Meiji Restoration (the shift away from the Shogun's rule and the restoration of the Emperor). I really love to study Japanese history in my free time, so combining the history behind the Meiji Restoration with the Like a Dragon series made me so excited. If you search up all of the names of the characters in this game, you will actually find people with the same name who actually lived and played a part in this story, including Sakamoto Ryoma. Side content is also very good in this game. The substories are fun as always and some will have you create bonds with the people of Kyoto. The home life side game was also fun and was a great way to make money and take a break from that unravels in Kyoto. It's like Animal Crossing, but just the part where you pay off the debt. I haven't had the chance to try everything in the game, but from what I have experienced so far, it's really good.Finally, I'm really impressed how well Ishin turned out in Unreal 4. I thought we would get dragon engine games from now on, but I'm happy Ishin was not on the dragon engine. I really needed a break from the dragon engine games and all of the things that make it so frustrating to play on. Basically, everything in this game is really good with the exception of some minor nitpicks. I hear people have complained about the frame rate and the PC port in general, but I haven't had any trouble on my end besides a few frame rate drops occasionally (for reference, I played through this game on a Steam Deck). Hopefully more updates will make the PC port better for other players. The only thing that isn't great is the DLC, which many people have complained about since it is only a one-time use and is only tied to one save file. In addition, there is a difficulty setting locked behind the paywall as well. I'm not sure what went through RGG's mind to come up with something like this, but it is my biggest gripe with the game. I would personally not recommend buying the DLC and just get the base game. You're really not missing out on much by not purchasing the DLC unless if extra cosmetics and an extra hard difficulty setting is something you need. Besides all of my criticisms about the game, Like a Dragon: Ishin! will definitely go on the list of favorite games of all time and is my favorite game of 2023 so far. I'm really looking forward to future entries from RGG Studio including the upcoming Like a Dragon Gaiden game later this year and Like a Dragon 8 in 2024. If you are a fan of the series or just wanting to check out a Like a Dragon game from this year, this is definitely a great game to pick up and play.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, it's important to clarify that this is a remaster, not a remake. The original game used a different engine, and this version has been rebuilt using Unreal Engine 4, with additional visual adjustments. This is significant because it requires much less effort than a full development cycle, resulting in a faster and more cost-effective product.The base game is currently priced at 59.99 EUR, with the Digital Deluxe edition priced at 69.99 EUR. Comparatively, Hogwarts Legacy, which was released in the same month, is priced at 59.99 EUR for the base game, and took approximately five years to develop with an estimated budget of 150 million USD. Despite using the same Unreal Engine 4, Hogwarts Legacy features the latest technology, such as ray tracing, and boasts impressive visuals and performance, including shader pre-compilation on PC.Although the remaster might have been worth the price if it were flawless, it unfortunately falls short in some areas. For example, cutscenes run at only 30 FPS, which is a jarring contrast to the game's 120 FPS, which can be immersion-breaking. It appears that the cutscenes are rendered in real-time, not as video files, so there is no reason for them to run at a different frame rate.Additionally, the intro and other cutscenes are not skippable (*), and there is no shader pre-compilation. Despite being a brand new remaster, the visuals are completely dated and do not compare favorably to other games in the same price range. For instance, Judgment, a game from the same developer that is older than this remaster, can run most of the game at 120 FPS, including cutscenes (with only a few pre-rendered scenes), has skippable cutscenes, zero stutter, and looks even better than this game.In conclusion, while the base game is great, the current state of the remaster does not justify the price tag, especially when there are other games available at the same price point with better visuals and performance.* I've started the game with mouse+keyboard and tried pressing several buttons to skip the intro, including the ESC key - none worked. Apparently, you can skip intros by first pressing "M", then some other button on the keyboard. With a controller it's more natural: pressing the start button (which is usually mapped to ESC on keyboard, but not in this game), then pressing "A" / "X".

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a spin-off of the Yakuza series that takes place in the Bakumatsu era of Japan. The game has an engaging story, a fun combat system, and a rich open world to explore. However, it also suffers from some major flaws that prevent me from recommending it.First of all, the PC port is poorly optimized and lacks basic features such as shader pre-caching and ultrawide support. The game often stutters and crashes, making it frustrating to play.Secondly, the DLC policy is very unfair and restrictive. The DLC items are tied to one save file instead of one account, meaning that you can’t use them again if you start a new game. Moreover, one of the difficulty levels is locked behind a paywall, which is unacceptable for a full-priced game.Thirdly, the game requires an internet connection at all times to play. This means that you can’t play it offline or on devices like the Steam Deck. It also means that if your internet connection drops while playing, you will lose your progress and have to restart the game.These issues overshadow the positive aspects of the game and make it hard to enjoy. I hope that the developers will fix them in future updates or patches. Until then, I can’t give this game a thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily one of the best Yakuza/RGG games made to date. It is a love letter to the entire series, with characters from every game returning, although with a new name. The combat is probably the most different out of the whole series, with sword and gun combat taking a major focus, but it is done very well. The story is also one of the best in the series, making you care about every character you meet. The substories are a bit of a weak point, as they are much more boring and forgettable than the other games in the series, especially games like yakuza 0 and yakuza like a dragon. The mini-games are very strong, however, with the return of the almighty karaoke bar (now a singing bar) and many other fun mini-games like dancing. Overall, an amazing remake and one of RGG studio's finest works.

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who loves the Like A Dragon series to death, Like A Dragon Ishin was one of the games that I most desired to be released internationally and on all platforms. So when it was announced it automatically became my most anticipated release for early 2023. Like A Dragon is the remake of Ryū ga Gotoku Ishin! which was originally released on February 22, 2014, exclusively in Japan, serving as a launch title for the PlayStation 4. Set in the chaotic Bakumatsu (1853–1867) phase of the Late Edo period of Japan, players take on the role of Sakamoto Ryōma, who is distressed resulting from conflicting pressures and uncertainty about one's self and role in society. Being embroiled in the middle of a Tosa coup d'état and bent on finding the murderer who assassinated his father figure, Ryōma burrows himself with a hidden identity in the streets of Kyo and joins the grim Shinsengumi. This remake of Ishin! retains most of the gameplay system from the original game, with the exception of the Trooper Cards, which can now be used optionally in regular combat. In addition, several characters of the game were also recast with new actors, who have previously portrayed other characters in the mainline titles, notably from Yakuza 0, Yakuza 6: The Song of Life, and Yakuza: Like A Dragon. The singing bar (karaoke) minigame features two songs not featured in the original: a new arrangement of the series' fan favourite karaoke track, "Baka Mitai" (ばかみたい, I've Been a Fool), and an entirely new track, "Ichizu Samurai" (い・ち・ず・侍, Truehearted Samurai), alongside the five unique songs featured in the original game. The game's depiction of 19th-century Kyoto A.K.A Kyo is brilliant and the environments are gorgeously rendered in this remake. The combat is super fun and so unique compared to the usual Like A Dragon combat. The Soundtrack is absolutely fire and the remixed songs are absolute bangers. A Solid 10 Out of 10 From Me.

_childDocuments_.review: Rode its way to one of my favorite games in the series. Instead of Kazuma Kiryu and modern yakuza this game follows the story of Sakamoto Ryoma and the shinsengumi during the bakumatsu era. You can still expect everything from this game you would find in a mainline title, from the many weird but funny moments to an actually good story which puts its own twist onto the story of Sakamoto Ryoma. Although the characters share the appearance and some character traits from the characters we know and love they are still different people with their own goals and motivations, which I all found to be interesting and entertaining. I also recommend reading about Sakamoto Ryoma, the actual person, a little after finishing the game. It makes the story and some major moments hit much more and really adds to the experience. The game uses the “four style” system again already known from 0 and kiwami. They all feel unique to one another, swordsman giving a well-rounded and heavy hitting kit, gunman offering spammy distance fighting and wild dancer a very fast mix of both with a wild set of moves. The only style feeling very lackluster is brawler. I basically only used that style for the tiger drop, but other styles offer similar moves with better damage because the damage in brawler is not affected by the gear system which makes the other styles much stronger. The gear system allows crafting of swords, guns, armor and other special weapons. Some of these weapons bring special abilities like elemental damage or life steal with them, which made experimenting with different weapons and armors fun. I really wish there were gloves or something like that to make the brawler style stronger and usable. The only negative of this system and for me in the entire game is the grinding. I basically save scummed to farm money because the higher tier gear would have taken hours of farming to get otherwise. And that still requires farming the necessary materials from the battle dungeons which aren’t guaranteed, meaning you must play the same missions over and over again just to get these materials.       The game also offers a ton of side content again ranging from small things like the karaoke (search for “ishin truehearted samurai”, thank me later) or fishing to bigger things like the farm management and the battle dungeons. The card system was fun to use too, offering a lot of abilities to mess around with but also some really strong ones like the time slow.All in all, I hope they remaster kenzan too if it gets the same quality treatment as this.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin is definitely one of the more controversial titles within the Yakuza series with the weird transition into the unreal engine which is a first in the series (and probably last), along with adding the Trooper Cards system into the rest of the game which a lot of fans were skeptical with that decision to say the least. However, what do I think? I think that this game is a new personal favorite in the franchise for me.Gameplay - Now if the idea of a samurai wild west gunslinger strikes as exciting for you, it pretty much is. The whole concept of it is exciting but it plays so damn well. You get introduced to the 4 combat styles of the game being fists (for parrying/defense), swordsman (burst dps), gunslinger (ranged dps/heat generator), and wild dancer which is the best style in the game and even upon its nerf its still so damn good. Now using these styles in unison was confusing at first, especially when a style is just both the 2 styles mixed together (sword and gun = wild dancer), but each style has its own situational use, and when you finally get the flow and muscle memory of the styles down you glide and navigate through combat like a trained killer. All the styles felt fleshed out and useful, even if the unarmed fist style did feel super weak on damage even fully maxed. You are also able to equip additional weapons from the skill tree of the styles like spears, odachis, and a cannon. They aren't as fleshed out as the main styles but they were still fun to mess around with in random street fights.Trooper System - After a few chapters of getting used to your stock styles, you will get access to the trooper system. Basically you will be able to activate different cards in fights that give you abilities. This system before was only usable in the dungeons side content of the game, but has been expanded upon and made available throughout the entire story, in fact even bosses can use these insane powers. Now, understandably a lot of players don't like the inclusion of this system in the rest of the game, but for players who have played the original this is definitely some much needed spice to the gameplay. For many this is their first experience of Ishin, and I think the game would of benefited from having the trooper card inclusion be accessible in new game + or the Ishin difficulty or just an option to toggle on or off. It didn't ruin my enjoyment, mainly because I have the original game so that could definitely give me a bias here so take that with a grain of salt.Setting - It's great taking a break from Kamurocho and the modern setting of the Yakuza games, and the new location for this game being Kyo is definitely hitting for me. I have to place Kyo as one of my my personal favorite locations in the series next to Okinawa from Yakuza 3 and of course the iconic Tokyo streets of Kamurocho. Kyo for me is a totally fresh take on what we have seen in the series thus far. Its a completely different Japan set at the end of the Edo period in the 1860s. The environment changes in different sections of the map, whether you are in the bustling streets of Rakunai, the markets and riverbay of Fushimi, or my personal favorite location, the bandit city of Mukurogai. Everything just looks so damn nice, especially in the Unreal Engine. The shadows and lighting is the best in this game compared to the other releases and honestly I wouldn't mind another game in the unreal engine. Don't get me wrong, the dragon engine is probably my most favorite engine in gaming period, however to see the devs go back from time to time into their old game design to recapture the original game is a nice and much needed breath of fresh air. Minigames - My favorite part of these games are the side content to lose yourself in, and where to start? Karaoke is rebranded as the "singing bar" since karaoke didnt exist yet time wise and Ishin's line up of songs are another reason to just give this game an install. I love me my dancing mini games since they never seem to miss and Ishin even has that with Buyo dancing (fan dancing). Sounds lame but trust me you will need to be on your toes on the higher difficulties. You have chicken racing which was my favorite way to make money in this game, and really is going to be your bread and butter for the grinding sections of the game and oh boy I have section on that, that's how bad it is. Then the hostess mini game is replaced with the courtesan games. You basically play 3 different mini games with a courtesan, one being sake showdown (a drinking game), rock paper scissors, and then finally sensual healing which is a sex bullet heal mini game and my god is it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard. I would definitely have to say the asura mode on the sex mini game gave me the most trouble in my completion like what the hell I was not expecting that much trouble and bottlenecking from the sex mini game of all side content.Another Life - The big mini game of Ishin is titled "Another Life". Its Yakuza's take on a slice of life where you farm, take car of your house/pets, cook, and even sell the before mentioned items off like the stuff you cook or your produce. The money you can make accumulates over time with the more and more orders you put out, but honestly I just had myself coming here to take off stress from the grinding and just relaxing because they definitely nailed that aesthetic. Really for the money you are just better off with the Chicken Racing mini game but i'm still happy for this whole mode's inclusion, was super fun.The Grind - Now this had to be a whole section of its own. Yakuza games can be a little grindy here and there. Especially if you focus on crafting or completion, but its usually not THIS GRINDY. In this game you grind for everything. Need troopers? Gotta spin the gacha mechanic case opening that can drop 1 of 400 troopers. Need materials for grinding? Perfect, which material because there are 4 other sub categories of which supply you are looking for (seafood, produce, etc.).  Need materials for another life? Go grind the 4 different fishing spots for the unique fish, aswell as wait on the farming timer for your crops.  Need a specific high grade material? Its either random world drop, or farm the specific dungeon for a chance at it dropping, and of course the worst part had to be crafting weapons and gear. Which I say with a heavy heart because that was what peaked my interest in the combat of the game to begin with. All these cool different pieces of gear, fully modeled, performing different things, whole seals giving you a chance to socket a bunch of neat stats to optimize the gear. Like, that all sounded so sick. Until you actually start trying to gear up and you realize the big problem which is the resource sink. Even fully upgrading your blacksmith (which gets you a reduced rate of money/materials spent on gear), you are still sinking tons and tons of money and materials into these weapons. There is a whole section, and mechanic for the gun style that has you swapping out different ammunition types that play super fun like flash bullets that daze the enemy, lightning bullets that stun, poison that adds a DoT to the target, etc. But, these cost so much just to fire 30 OF THEM (which is as much as you can craft in a max stack), like that goes away quick on a maxed out gun. So I couldn't really get experimental without having to shave away hours grinding for more mats and money just for all of that to be spent on merely an hour of shooting off the thing. It just was not worth it. Its true that you can completely ignore the crafting section of the game since story missions give you upgrades on items nonetheless, but this is still a big part of the game, and a big part that could help you not struggle as much in fights.Other from those gripes, the story, the gameplay, the world of Ishin is phenomenal and even know this remake hiccups here and there I do still think this is worth a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been thinking for a while about how to review this game because I think it's not that easy. It's a good game and a good Yakuza game, but there's some things that bothered me during my playthrough. If I had to answer "should you buy this game", I'd say yes, but wait for a sale, and if not, only if you like the era it's set in or if you're a Yakuza fan as is. I'll let just give a list of things that I think it did well and it didn't do well.The good:- The atmosphere is great as is always the case with Yakuza and Judgment games, the map is pretty good and exploring is rewarded with finding substories or content in general- The game runs well, I know I've read that others have had issues with the port but it ran flawlessly on my computer- A lot of the characters are from previous Yakuza games, I think it's a cool nod to fans of the series but new players also won't feel like they're out of place- The cinematics look great as usual, they felt like a reward sometimes for how well they're madeThe meh:- The combat didn't feel nearly as good as in most other Yakuza or Judgment titles. For reference, I played on hard. The styles didn't feel cohesive at all in my opinion. There's four styles which are Wild Dancer, Swordsman, Gunman (I think it was called?), and Brawler. Wild Dancer is your "AoE" style, but honestly once I made it past the early game it felt a bit underwhelming, I just found myself using the same simple move set in it. Gunman felt, outside of it being used for special ammunition, like it was just a cheese style to shoot enemies from far away, but I also didn't put many points in it so I don't know if it gets better late on. Swordsman felt like the most fleshed out of the four and was a fun style to play in, but it also got meh towards the end because again, it just felt like I was using the same move set and the same two heat actions. Brawler felt underwhelming the entire game long and was overall just weak and not fun. I put more points into it towards the end of the game and I still didn't feel like it was fun. Everything I could do in brawler, other styles could go better. Generally I also think switching between styles wasn't fluid and they didn't feel cohesive. It felt like there's little heat action variety. Besides that, I also felt like I spent a lot of time in combat on the floor because everything knocks you down in this game.- The soundtrack wasn't very memorable apart from some iconic ones, the absolute bangers that I am used to from Yakuza games were far and between. I didn't even notice each style had a separate soundtrack because it felt so same-ish to me.- The story felt like it dragged on, towards the end of the game I kind of just wanted it to be over already and be done with the game.- The side content ranges from great to awful. There's some fun side content like the second home feature, but most of it and the heart "side content" (to me at least), the substories, were mostly boring. Most of the side content I tried wasn't very engaging or fun, usually I tried it and left it at that, or if I did it more often, it wasn't very long. I think it's because the combat hindered a lot of enjoyment, for example there's a scarecrow maze thing where you have to destroy scarecrows in a specific style (usually) within a certain amount of time, and I didn't complete too much of it because it felt very clunky.- On the topic of substories, felt like every other substory was turned into a bond (which there's so many of). If I think back to Y0 for example, there's so many memorable substories, but in this game most of them boil down to "give me this item", and then they turn into a bond, which means to finish it, you have to give them an item (sometimes a specific item) five times or something like that. That's just flat out boring and feels like filler content. I mean why are there at least three bonds related to you giving vegetables to someone?- Trooper cards. I'm not sure how I feel about them, I think at first they were pretty fun but they became a thing I didn't even think about much outside of "just using them" fast. They are OK.The bad:- This might just be me being lazy, but this game needed more taxi spots, I had to walk a lot and maybe I'm spoiled from the other games having much easier means of travel- Everything in this game is so clunky and slow. Opening menus, picking things up and so on. It feels so non-responsive and it just wasn't fun to "navigate" the game sometimes, I don't recall it being like this in past gamesI don't think I've ever written such an elaborate review for any Yakuza game, usually I just feel like "yeah, it's more Yakuza but improved from the last game" and I am happy with that, but I didn't feel like that with Ishin, but I do recognise that this game is a port and remake/remaster (?) from a game that's been out for a while. All in all I enjoyed the game, but it's not their best work.

_childDocuments_.review: Just because Kiryu hit someone with a sword using enough strength to cut them in half and then shoot 30 times with a Glock it doesn't mean he kills people... they are alright.Oh man this game is great! Of course it has its flaws (any game has) and I can point to the fact some of the optional content to get trophies/achievements requires a crazy amount of grinding for no good reason and the DLCs are despicable (don't buy it!). However if you don't care about those things then it's smooth sailing all the way to the end even playing on the very hard (Legend) difficulty, just don't bother about trophies/achievements.The game is kinda like Yakuza 5 but with some enhancements (more like a hybrid half-remaster half-remake) so you might feel that it's slightly behind what we saw in Kiwami 1 and 2, but both of those games are more like "extra games" while Ishin is surprisingly a fully new game with a new city filled with hundreds of details and so much content everywhere. It's nothing like the spinoff "Yakuza: Dead Souls" (or "RGG Of the End") because this here is really like a main title. This was without a doubt my biggest surprise.I always dreamed of playing Ishin on the PS3 and now (10 years later) seeing it being released in English for the first time was such a joyful moment to finally put my hands on it and spent almost 100 hours enjoying all the cutscenes, mini-games (I even learned how to play Mahjong this time!), sidequests... all in full HD while running on an SSD which made the experience even more enjoyable than playing it on the PS3.

_childDocuments_.review: Being a Yakuza fanatic, I obviously had to get Ishin on pre release and play it as soon as it came out.I took my time, not wanting my time with Kiryu *cough* Ryoma to end and played many of the substories and minigames.First of all let me say that Kiryu with a bun is a viiiibe and I absolutely loved the character. I played a lot of the "Another Life" substory, getting to know Haruka more and above all learning all the cooking recipes and expanding my farm. Eventually I also got all the pets which was nice. I like that the cooking actually achieves something in this game. The self-made recipes restored A LOT more health than any medicine you can purchase; plus there were some substories linked to cooking your own meals which was cool.I liked that you can only get certain fish in certain places at certain times. _childDocuments_.review: I believe this is an incredibly rushed, buggy and (in my opinion) boring game from RGG Studio. If you’ve never played a Yakuza game before, go look at Yakuza 0, Yakuza: Like a Dragon or Judgment, all three of these will scratch a similar gameplay/storytelling itch minus the Edo Japan setting, and are not only great starting points but are also just amazing games. They all have their unique pros and between the three there’s something for everyone. For RGG veterans who absolutely must experience this long anticipated game, I'd recommend you either watch it on YouTube or wait for it to get patched so at least the bugs listed are fixed, then buy the game on sale without the comically useless and scummy DLC in the Digital Deluxe Edition. Otherwise I think you're wasting your money.Review:I'm going to be as objective as possible here, and I really hope you spare a few minutes to this read review before you consider buying the game in its current state. This review is not only , but also a little long.Firstly, this game is incredibly buggy, not unplayable by any means, but I was fed up with it by the end. Multiple times character models would disappear during cutscenes, the cutscene camera would start flashing intensely or go into walls, obscuring what’s on screen. I once had the water textures bug out and obscure the game in all directions and had a boss’s theme play twice simultaneously with delay. This is just the tip of the iceberg for strange occurrences, and I've even had friends whose games crashed on them, which I’ve never heard of happening with any other game by RGG Studio.The game also suffers from many frame drops when displaying blood, when some bosses use their "superpowers" for the first time and in action sequences, which made timing QTEs especially difficult since not a single one of these sequences in the game didn’t have a frame drop or freeze. Another thing I took issue with is the new cast changes leading to very off-putting face movements from characters. The main example I point to is Yamazaki Susumu, whose counterpart is Joon-gi Han. They cast his face over a character who had very unique facial movements. However despite the model change his animations were not adjusted, making his facial animations unnatural and uncanny. This applies to all the new characters who were cast over old faces to a lesser extent as well.Denuvo usage and the scummy DLC practices are very disappointing to see. Many DLC packs are one time purchase, meaning if you lose your save, you must buy the DLC again to use it only one more time. It’s not worth it, and despite buying the Digital Deluxe edition for the Early Access I never once had to use it. Denuvo means you need to play an offline game online, which is questionable at best.Finally, while this is a more objective point than the rest, I found the game to be incredibly tedious. The enemies in this game feel like they have way too much HP, especially if you opt not to play with the Trooper Cards. RGG Studio went on record saying you didn't need to play with the card "superpowers," to enjoy the game since many community members didn't think they fit into the game, but that could not be further from the truth.It also felt difficult to maintain any momentum in this game. A lot of the fun of RGG's combat is about trying to experiment and come up with your own style of gameplay. In Lost Judgment, you had style switching juggle combos, in Yakuza K1 you had to try maximise heat gain while also maintaining max speed with well timed moves and style switches. In comparison, Ishin's styles are all very unbalanced. Brawler does way too little damage, Swordsman is slow even with speed upgrades, Gunman is barely interactive at all and while Wild Dancer hits a decent balance it's limiting to only use this style. Heat actions also lose their impact as they do minimal damage and the more you them the less damage they’ll do. It's a mechanic in most of the other games but it’s especially harsh here. All of these factors lead to an overall underwhelming combat system which makes the game difficult to get through.A lot of these issues are things patches could fix, and I think this game has many positives too. The story is incredible, one of the best by this studio, and that says a lot. Your usual offering of side activities and distractions is here. It’s the blueprint for a solid Yakuza game but held down by horrid performance, weak combat, disgusting DLC practices and a frankly sloppy job from RGG Studio. Their move to Unreal Engine 4 is mostly to blame for poor optimisation and bugs; and the kinks of the original Ishin are still here unimproved because this game is a port from it's original engine to Unreal 4, rather than a ground-up remake like Kiwami 1 and 2.For now, I recommend taking the advice in the TL;DR. I adore RGG Studio, and this review is harsh because I don’t want this to be the future of their games. I still really want to see the other Japanese-only Yakuza games like Kenzan or Black Panther (Kurohyou) get localised through remakes, ports or otherwise. I believe this studio should absolutely be supported; this just isn’t the quality standard I think warrants your support.

_childDocuments_.review: Intro starts off with Majima and several others recast characters you know you'll be in a crazy ride from beginning up until the end and there's no exceptions here. If you wish to experience Yakuza series but in a medieval setting with lots of crazy encounters, fighting & non sense situations then hop on in. I'm sure many fans wanted the 4 style system from pre-modern Dragon Engine to be back and they certainly kept its diversity offering us a Yakuza 0 type assortment. There's a clear sight of high effort put into animations and combat as everything is visually pleasing when you cut, shoot or simply rampage through everything that stands in your way. Beautiful environments enveloping medieval looking Kyoto with realistic lighting & shading especially during sunny mornings. Katanas, guns and all the weaponry available are superbly designed with attention to detail to the tiniest component part. Facial animations & textures of characters are massively improved coming back from the original with life-like graphics vastly enhancing the immersion during cutscenes. The choreography is designed like a true masterpiece; every start of a boss fight is pure raw hype that blends near perfect into the in-game combat itself. OST is as always a banger with some comebacks meant for the respective character in their original appearance. Lore itself is displayed purposely to fit 1860s Kyoto and Japan in general, narrative choice is one of true honor or simply dirty deeds and backstabbing just to obtain more power and a higher title in these harsh feudal transitioning times. Don't expect the more contemporary worldliness you have previously encountered in the series, it's vastly meant to be authentic notably for those unfamiliar outside of Japan. The minigames are back and in full force offering everyone something to their preference, be it wildly hilarious or more serious toned. Additionally the trooper card system is welcoming addition for those wishing to bring third party elements stylishly to the table.- character cast quality- extremely diverse combat- feudal japan immersion- voice acting - OST & ambience- ee ja nai ka- bond system overused

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has played all the Yakuza games including the original Ishin, it's more than safe to say this is a dreadful remaster. Just like Y7, this game has a bunch of scammy DLCs which just include half-assed retextures, weapon materials, and finally the god-awful, poorly edited guest cards without even mentioning the cringe fanservice. This is essentially a 9-year-old game repacked on UE (which was its final nail in the coffin) with added microtransactions and it somehow manages to be worse than the original in every single way. Like a Dragon: Ishin! took an absolute nose dive when it comes to quality. Frankly, I refuse to believe some aspects of this game were even quality checked. The only good things about the game I can think of are probably Fly and Affected fight remixes and the fact that the dog follows you now, while when it comes to bad aspects:-Awful AI-The engine itself-Price-DLCs-Laughable lighting (or the lack of it honestly...)-Localization (As someone who knows Japanese I can safely say the Judgments localization teams did a pretty bad job but this is on another level)-Cards-Bosses and their special abilities (Most are just reused card effects)-Brawler absolutely sucks-Spear enemies-Blacksmithing system-Addition of those huge enemies for whatever reason-Fanservice -Hanpeita's recastI'd unironically rather pay the same price for the original Ishin localized on PC than for this. _childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommendation, if you have put up with the problems of past RGG games or Yakuza titles and don't mind experiencing the same jank again and again then you'll be right at home. The problem I have with this game is more of a long standing issue with RGG and not really the game itself, I'll go more into detail.  Normally I'd give a pass to developers who aren't used to the way western audiences perceive quality, (look to Kagura games library of copy/past JRPGs) but if I can hold lazy western Developers like Rockstar and Bethesda accountable then I can do the same to RGG. Speaking of which, Atlas includes all the DLC as a one package deal for Persona 5, so that you won't have to purchase it seperate or have a "digital deluxe" edition. Food for thought as to where your money should really be going. So why can a Japanese developer who puts out regular bangers get their collective ♥♥♥♥ together for a re-release of their content on a new platform, but RGG doesn't and or can't? (Lets not talk about Persona 3's port lmao)The game itself is pretty good, the performance on older systems is untested and bad, constant stutters when blood is shown or spurted over the ground or surrounding area, makes the game a living hell with combat. The voice acting, while good, starts and ends at cinematics and in game cutscenes, no side-substory voice lines like in Y7. For those who liked Yakuza 7's ENG VO, (not me), say sayonara to that because it's only the JP VO.  The newest update allows for you to reaquire "lost" DLC weapons, no idea if this covers all the DLC weapons and if lost how many times you can reaquire.It's nice to see subtle improvements to the AI but its lost when the AI barrel roll straight through your attacks like you didn't just slash them 1 second ago. I can get stun locked for 5 seconds but for them they shrug it off, very infuriating. Major disappointment in the settings that the cutscenes cannot be set to 60fps, every single Yakuza game that's on Steam at this moment has the option to set cutscenes to be 60fps, why is it different for Ishin? Nobody will ever know but RGG. The 60fps issue extends to the Minimap as well, it stutters when rotating because that's locked to 30fps or lower, extremely weird design choice. Texture loading on a M.2 SSD takes longer than it should, idk if its the way the developers stacked priority within the application itself but Yakuza 7 and Judgements do not have this issue, and those games are using the more newer version of the Dragon Engine. (This actually makes sense because Ishin is running on UE4/UE5 and Unreal Engine games like Fortnite run like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ unless you force DirectX11 on the launch settings, which by the way fixes the majority of the stutters, not all unfortunately).Honestly if you're on the fence, just wait until you hear that the game has been updated with fixes. If not, jump on it with a sale because while its fun in the short term, there's a lot of problems with it.

_childDocuments_.review: ~FINISHED THE GAME UPDATE, 02/24/2023~I may very well be in the minority, but my disappointment in this game carried the entire 30 hours and the game is less than the sum of its parts. I honestly didn't enjoy myself as much as I thought I would and this will end up as my least favorite RGG game I've played--yes, even the laughed-at Yakuza 3, which I think had a lot of heart and great points. I didn't hate all of it, and the highs are extremely high, but the lows were far, far too low for me personally. I walked away more annoyed than anything, and that hasn't happened before in this series.I don't have much else to say, so I'll sum it up very quickly: the combat didn't work for me; the gearing system took up too much time, and the reliance on gear didn't gel with me; the story was slow at first, got really interesting, and then completely lost me at the last 1/4. Those are basically the main sticking points (not including my complaint below about this being a so-so remaster).I still recommend this game cuz it did a lot of great things, but maybe wait for a sale. Don't let the cool samurai aesthetic fool you, the crime drama modern era games are far superior in my eyes. ~ORIGINAL 02/21/2023 REVIEW~This is the exact game fans have been clamoring for since 2014 and we finally got... basically the same game from 2 generation ago with a nice coat of paint. I'm enjoying this game just as I expected as Yakuza/Like A Dragon fan and fully expect to beat this game and see a decent chunk of the side stuff. The world is fully realized and fun to explore, side quests can be entertaining, the combat is cathartic and bloody, and the story--while it takes a couple hours to get going--is captivating and well written. This series is one of the few where cutscenes feels like the reward itself, I'm always excited when the frame rate goes to 30 and the mo-cap is in full swing. The graphics are impressive, as usual, especially with the Unreal Engine 4 powering everyone's pores to the max; lighting and texture work are a major highlight, especially the detailed haoris and weapons. But I can't help but feel a pang of disappointment around the whole thing. For starters, as I mentioned earlier, this is same game that was released in 2014, almost literally. Kiwami 2 this is not--this is more in line with Kiwami 1, complete with all the stiffness the series had before the Dragon Engine, for better or worse. I'm in the camp that loves the Dragon Engine despite some combat downgrades, so having an Unreal Engine 4 skin over a PS3 game feels dated off rip. The lack of voice acting for 80% of the game (read: anything not main story) is particularly heart breaking since you know they have the budget and a top class cast. I find myself skipping side quests now thanks to games like The Witcher 3 spoiling me, and I find myself only stopping occasionally when something seems extremely goofy or especially thoughtful or emotional seems to occur. You really start to feel how awkward and cheap it is to not here music nor sound effects during most of this, just the typewriter sound of the text appearing on screen and the occasional grunt. I also find myself missing the seamless exploration of the Dragon Engine games that had no loading screens when entering buildings, getting into fights, etc. Kiryu may've controlled like a bus, but the immersion, for me, more than made up for it. I never fast traveled in those games, but I look for the nearest palanquin in this one. I miss Bus Kiryu. The pacing, too, is disorienting. Realizing what this game is and not what I wanted it to be, I decided to just focus on the story and do the side stuff in a later Yakuza game, like Yakuza 7 that I have yet to finish. But in the first 10 hours or so, be prepared to stop at every alley while Ryouma does his best Kiryu impression and tends to the needs of every man, woman, child, and whimpering animal that stands immobile until approached. As a whole, it's a familiar and mostly exciting formula, but again, it's 2023 and they've already done better. To regress (or rather, choose not to enhance) in so many ways technologically and mechanically effects me a lot more than I thought it would. I typically love older games and their jank, but Yakuza series is huge, storied, and has a LOT of titles. There's a lot I love about this game--the combat, the world, the story, the performances, the exploration, the fact that it feels like a movie cuz all the faces are the same--but the stuff that bothers me really sticks with me, like a splinter under my fingernail.I recommend this game, I really enjoy this game, but I am disappointed. I'm just glad we finally got Ishin in the west, and it was worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe I'm leaving a negative review on a Like a Dragon game, but what it all comes down to is, after years of goodwill, years of excitement for this story in particular to be localized, too, I went through 40 hours of this game repeatedly saying to myself "okay. Alright. Just hold on, it's gonna pay off eventually". And now I have finished it. And it absolutely didn't! People definitely worked hard on this but a few terrible design decisions likely forced in at a board meeting now very clearly rip open and destroy the gameplay balance in every feasible way.Let's start with the good, the REAL good. Combat animations and impacts are really, really satisfying; the upgrades you get for them make them feel better and better as you learn them, and there just isn't anything like swinging your sword and sweeping around to reach for your gun mid-slash, fire off a shot, slice through your opponents, and sheath your blade just to get right up close and personal and deck that last guy.The music, while strangely missing some of the original tunes in some spots, is superb fanservice with lovely new mixes of classic series tunes, as well as just some lovely atmospheric music overall. I listened to a lot of it before playing this version and I'll sure as heck be listening to it after.Translating a story like this was no easy feat, and they do a wonderful job of immersing you in the setting while also keeping terms that truly don't have any direct translation. It trusts you to understand without just sort of leaving you on your own on that front; many of the cast are returning from other games, and they do a great job. This has an enormous cast to keep track of and yet, though I'll admit I lost track of some names, it's one of the more follow-able bizarre conspiracy plots of this series, and they really do try to wedge in an irreverent take on actual history whenever they can. It's educational in the sense it gets you to go read a book on the things that happened because it very intentionally isn't getting much right, and I think that's fine when you're having fun with it.So why would I come away from this disappointed if it's a tight story, interesting setting, great music, and fantastic combat flow?Because every single facet of that's been kind of broken to bits in the remake. Which it isn't labeled as such, but this IS a remake.The Trooper Card system. Play the Combat Demo and if you aren't sold on it, you won't be. This was formerly for a small portion of Ishin before, but now it's the whole game. I would be lying if I said I wasn't excited to equip Kenny Omega the whole game and hit bosses with the One-Winged Angel, that's very funny, I try to take it in the spirit it's meant, but the problem is twofold.A. These cards were designed for some bonus dungeons. These are still in the game, bearing most of the game's loot drops (more on that later) and they are fantastically boring, bland empty locales bereft of much but enemies and crates.B. The rest of the game is rebalanced for their addition, and by rebalanced I mean all foes are now overpowered until you spam these or start grinding for really OP weapons (which requires the above aimless tunnel wandering). This in particular ruins the tone and flow of the boss battles, where they all now have instant stunlock elemental attacks with... man I don't even care about no explanation, sure, you get magical powers, they might as well, too, but it's just not fun when a fantastic final boss meant to be an exam of every single fighting style you've learned just KO's you again and again not from superior fighting technique, but from becoming Emperor Palpatine and blasting you with unblockable inexplicable Force Lightning dozens of times. It isn't fun. It makes the great big payoffs of each chapter a miserable slog until you press the "let somebody else do it" button and demolish their health bar, undermining *all* the fantastic combat mechanics in the game.Weapons require smithing. Smithing requires resources you find in the empty sad dungeons, and also grinding to increase the level of the Smith. Or just buy something OP on Steam, sure, whatever.The recastings are... notable. Heads sometimes seem clearly stuck on to a different body, particularly during the emergency meetings. A trend in the recastings kind of instantly blows the majority of the plot points and allegiances which is not great.Substories typically involve all manner of wacky bizarro things that make you believe this world you're living in is, well, lived in, by all manner of lovely strange characters. Nine out of ten of them in this game are requests for vegetables that you have to grow in your farming sim which by the way you also get a farm here. Most people in the town will ask you for vegetables. There is a boy next to one of the key locations you'll be returning to whose mom won't let him eat veggies. You can click on him, and then offer him a vegetable. However, due to each line being animated, you cannot actually skip ahead once you do this, so if you'd like to complete the game thoroughly, be prepared for"Oh boy!""Veggie time!"*eating noises**gauge slowly increases*and multiply that by many times for the lady that lost her wallet and the woman that's definitely not using them for the intended purposes and the sumo wrestler that needs to eat to win and the guy looking out over the water thinking a picnic sounds great right now and it's just... tedious.Everything about this fantastic bombastic samurai drama is ground down into .And that's painful.The ending was... such an ending I just uninstalled from there. Should've done it 15 hours in when I wanted to quit then. But now I can say I've played it, and I don't think you have to. (I'm not saying this lightly, either. I liked Dead Souls.)

_childDocuments_.review: This review was made in mind after a Legend difficulty () play-through of this iteration of the game and in retrospective of the original, mind you, not having played the original but rather having compared the "Kiwami!" version to   videos and comments made by those who  played the original.First of all, the pros are all largely ones that are present in both versions of the game, that being the setting of the game is a historical adaptation of the end of the Bakumatsu period with familiar Yakuza/Like A Dragon/Ryu ga Gotoku characters playing historical figures that uses the adaptation to tell a compelling story with the usual gamut of mini-games and sidequests sprinkled throughout the game to give the player a bit of levity throughout the game.  Ishin in comparison to the mainline series rewards experiencing everything the game has to offer through its prototype version of 0/Kiwami 1's Completion Points system with the Virtue system, a secondary wallet that is filled by doing all manner of the game's secondary content that can be redeemed for miscellaneous skills and potent healing items that would otherwise be harder to stock up on with cold, hard cash through game-play alone.Unfortunately this is where the pros of the remaster end, as numerous,  changes were made to the gameplay loop itself that completely detaches the game from the satisfyingly tight, beat-em up feel of the other RGG Studios games, and even the original itself.  Ryoma does completely pitiful damage at his baseline, forcing you to rely on the memetically broken Gunslinger style to slog through the early game, which itself has been nerfed from the original, not to mention the other 3 styles, most notably the Brawler style, all received nerfs to their damage and capabilities.  Not only can you deal no damage, you also have nothing resembling durability for a large portion of the game, owing thanks to sparse and meager base health and defense upgrades, and the game starving you of valuable healing items early on too.  In addition, numerous encounters and setpieces have been "rebalanced," by way of adding several magnitudes more of enemies while also buffing their health and damage compared to the original, not even mentioning two  mini-boss encounters against literal 3 meter tall giants () who on their own would be trivial to fight, but are flanked by several allies who will mercilessly gank you while the giant stunlocks you to the continue screen.Now you may ask:  "How would I go about increasing Ryoma's stats in order to combat these ridiculous sounding balance adjustments?"  The answer is, not easily, and its not very fun.  The first way of increasing Ryoma's damage and resilience is simply to upgrade his equipment, which sounds easy enough, the mainline games that featured equipment crafting often had simple requirements, typically only requiring one or two crafting materials you were bound to find at some point and taking them to the right NPC, and even then equipment crafting is largely optional in those games as the protagonist's arms and legs are more than enough to trounce their local conspiracy.  But once you're introduced to the game's blacksmith and his not only completely extortionist prices and the obnoxious requirement of having to level up the blacksmith to access stronger equipment crafting, all sense goes out the window.  The original game featured comparably  reasonable crafting costs, only costing around 3-5 Ryo/30k-50k Mon for some of the strongest equipment in the game.  Rather un-sensibly, these crafting costs have been MASSIVELY inflated to upwards of 100s of Ryo, in a game where you'll be struggling to scrape together even a tenth of that, not including the crafting costs of previous tiers in the crafting trees, in addition to the necessity of grinding out upgrading the blacksmith in order to even access the higher tier gear, which will also cost you several hundred Ryo buying swords, upgrading them, then donating them to the blacksmith.Now having been turned off from interacting with the blacksmith at all to upgrade your stats, your other option is the contentious Trooper Card system, which was present in the original, but was only utilized inside the basically optional Battle Dungeons and had no effect otherwise on the rest of the game.  In the remaster however, the Trooper Cards have been integrated into normal game-play, and can grant you various buffs to your health, attack and defense, in addition to giving you powerful, zany magic- wait, magic?  Infamously, the Trooper Cards can give you activated abilities that give Ryoma the power to shoot Kamehamehas, throw fireballs,  stop time, smite enemies with lightning, and much less notably give you flat stat buffs or invincibility.  Alongside the integration of the Trooper Cards to normal game-play, this coincided with the aforementioned "rebalancing" the game experienced, meaning the Trooper Card system is no longer optional if you want to finish the game without the cement shoes of your inability to deal or take damage.  And to top it all off, many of the major boss fights have received new special attacks that are all based on the various special attacks the Trooper Cards can grant you, and all deal such high damage that if you don't dodge them, they will one shot you.To cap off, the remaster offers a localized version of the original Ishin! for non-Japanese speakers, while completely butchering the game-play of the original to the point that I literally researched the differences between the remaster and the original to formulate my points on this review.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a spin-off of the Yakuza series that takes place in the Bakumatsu era of Japan, and while it's not the most polished yakuza game, it still manages to be a fun experience. Here's my review of the game: After playing Lost Judgment, this game’s combat doesn’t feel as smooth. Parrying doesn't work half the time for some reason. Dodging doesn't always work because some enemies have the wide slash move and they will always hit you no matter how well you time your dodge. Despite the issues described above, the combat styles in the game still manage to be fun in their own way, with "Wild Dancer" being my favorite because of its style and agility. The graphics in this game are beautiful and the attention to detail in the environments is amazing. The world feels alive, and since this is still a „yakuza game", there are plenty of charming substories in which you can partake. The game features a lot of minigames to enjoy, and the voice acting is really good.The soundtrack is amazing, with my favorite song being from where you train at the Ginryu Dojo. Heat actions are dope as always, and the weapons have cool effects that impact combat. However, some people might be turned off by the amount of grinding required for said weapons and equipment. Another thing is the introduction of trooper cards. Some people might hate them because of their unrealistic nature in gameplay, but I think they are a cool way to incorporate cameos from other Yakuza games. If you don't like them you don't need to use them to enjoy the game.
