_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a spin-off of the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series set in 1860s Japan. The game's story is based on that of the historic figure Sakamoto Ryoma's, but with many additions and changes that make it much more entertaining and bring it more in line with the rest of the series.Ishin! has a huge cast of characters, the majority of which are loosely based on historical figures, all primarily being portrait by various characters from games within the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series. The bulk of the characters in Ishin! are portrayed by characters who have similar personalities to those that they are portraying, however, the characters in Ishin! still manage to stand apart and feel distinct from the ones they are portrayed by.The world of Ishin! is one that feels familiar to other worlds within the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series, the crowded streets and substories encounters scattered all throughout the world are exactly as you would expect from any game in the series. But the overall setting of 1800s Japan makes the world feel very distinct and unique from the rest of the series, leaving Ishin! feeling somewhat refreshing despite it's overall similarities with the rest of the series.The combat in Ishin! plays the same as other games Yakuza/Like a Dragon series, the main difference to the combat here is the unique combat styles present in the game, Swordsman, Gunman and Wild Dancer. These three combat styles are each very distinct from one another and each have their own uses. Swordsman sees you utilising a katana for close one-on-one combat, Gunman lets you use a firearm for a variety of ranged attacks, and Wild Dancer combines both sword and gun into a more all-round combat style. The game also features brawler combat style which plays similar to the hand-to-hand combat typically seen in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon games. Overall the combat feels well balanced, although the Gunman style can easily trivialise much of the game's combat by staying at range.Ishin! also introduces the trooper card system. While originally constrained to a side mode, the remake of Ishin! now allows you to utilise trooper cards throughout the whole game. This system allows you to assign various cards that grant various abilities when used, these can range from small temporary buffs to damage to unique powerful attacks. The cards have a cooldown between uses to prevent you from spamming their abilities. The rarer cards can be massively overpowered, allowing you to trivialise any encounter. The cards don't seem too bad in the context of the side mode, but utilising them during the main story will destroy any sense of challenge the game could have provided.Ishin! also has a wide assortment of side content available. Much of the typical side content found in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon games is present, such as gambling minigames, karaoke, and the arena. However Ishin! also comes with an assortment of new side content, buyo dancing, chicken racing, cooking and tending to your farm. The side content in Ishin! is all good and offers a lot of variety, providing you with a huge assortment of interesting things to do outside of the main story.Overall, Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a unique spin on the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series that feels familiar yet provides an experience that is both unique and engaging. The world, story and gameplay are all excellent and all come together to make Ishin! a game worth playing.

I love that RGG and SEGA decided to bring this to the international market and I hope to see Dead Souls come around to finish it out. Things I wish were there was instead of the render scale only reducing the resolution, I would have loved to see the options increase it to 2x. Love that XeSS was included -- giving love to us rare Intel Arc owners.I highly recommend this game whether you have played any of the previous installments or not from an action or story point of view as this is taking a loose interpretation of a historical time in Japan. All playing the previous installments will do is pretty much say "Oh yeah, that's Kiryu! Oh! That's definitely Majima!"

_childDocuments_.review: As it stands I can't recommend this game for this price - UNLESS YOU'RE A MASSIVE RGG/YAKUZA FAN! I am, that's why I paid £70 just so I could start the game on the toughest difficulty (Ishin). That's right, you have to pay to start on Ishin difficulty. For a single player game. This is greed that is unworthy of a studio of RGG's class. Or so I thought.The graphics are basically polished PS3 graphics - they're little better than Y0 but little uglier than Y7, which is one of the RGG games with worst graphics. I just came from playing LJ and the downgrade of the graphics quality was a shock to me. _childDocuments_.review: : The gameplay is fantastic, the world is beautiful and feels alive, the minigames are fun, the characters are memorable, the visuals are impressive, the cutscenes are breathtaking and the soundtrack is great as always. That being said, the story is not the best in series; imo it's a bit boring and suffers from major plot holes, most of the substories are short or just downright boring, and the deluxe content is ridiculous (for $10 you'll unlock the hardest difficulty from the start, as well as overpowered items that make the game so much easier). The game was unplayable a while ago (keeps stuttering every 10 seconds, as well as glitchy cutscenes), but the last patch fixed it. If you are only interested in the story then I recommend getting it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure about Like a Dragon: Ishin going in as it was set in a completely different time period to other games in the Like a Dragon/Yakuza series, and it runs on Unreal Engine instead of the Dragon Engine used by every game from RGG Studio since Yakuza 6. However, my doubts were short lived, and I think Ishin is one of the best games in the series, both story and gameplay wise. The story is filled with mystery, and while there are a lot of familiar faces, you're not sure who to trust and who is a threat, as characters can take on completely different roles compared to their modern counterparts. The combat feels exactly like the combat from Yakuza 5/0/Kiwami and all of the new fighting styles are interesting and have their own strengths and weaknesses. Overall though, this is a solid game, however I recommend if you're planning on playing it to wait until after beating 0-7 first, as you'll recognise all the faces in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: As a recent newcomer to the franchise, I've played most of the mainline games in the franchise and totally loved the unique blend of drama and seriousness, over the top action, and ridiculous humor and side quests present in all the Yakuza games I've played so far, which are basically all the mainline titles except Yakuza 0 and Yakuza 6. It's a very unique experience that I can only describe as "Imagine if Grand Theft Auto was steeped in Japanese pop culture and you didn't actually drive all that much, if at all, but also every game in the franchise was a direct sequel telling the extended story of the same people across literally a decade" and the only other game series I can vaguely compare it to as far as long-form storytelling is concerned is probably the Trails franchise, and even those games change the main cast of characters every few games, while in this series you spend the vast majority of your playtime across most of the different games playing as the icon himself Kiryu Kazuma.So this one, being a spinoff that is set in the late 1860's piqued my interest because, well, "Yakuza but in Samurai times" sounds like an obviously amazing concept. And I'm not disappointed because, other than realizing you don't actually have alternate versions of the main cast but as people living in the 1860's as much as you have the character models represent other entirely different characters that resemble them and their relationships as if the Yakuza cast was acting in a samurai historical drama, the game is pretty much giving me everything I expected and wanted from it.The change in scenery and gameplay focused on swords and guns instead of just martial arts is also helping me avoid burnout after playing the gigantic and seemingly never-ending Yakuza 5, so that I will be able to jump into Yakuza 6 and finally Yakuza 0, before moving on to the more recent Like A Dragon titles, without needing to take a really extended break to detox from so much Yakuza in a row. Sure, this one may be "more of the same" in comparison to the main Yakuza games given that it's not all that different except in mostly superficial ways and I get how some people might feel that it doesn't really bring much to the table as a result of that, but the differences in setting and gameplay, while not exactly radical, did help to make it feel like a fresh experience for me, and you might find it does for you as well if you're into this kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: While I REALLY want to recommend "Ishin Kiwami" and I am very happy that it finally came to the west, the advertisement for this game has been quite deceptive. This is not a "Remake" or "Kiwami" as suggested by the Japanese title as well as all the advertisement materials. This is at best a "Remaster" of the original "Ryū ga Gotoku Ishin!" similar to the 2019's Remastered Collection which included enhanced versions of the Yakuza 3, 4, and 5. Although there have been noticeable changes such as recasting many of the characters and adding a few minigames and mechanics, "Ishin Kiwami" looks and plays almost identical to the original game. So, definitely keep that in mind before paying full price for what is essentially a late PS3-era title.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Yak- I mean Like a Dragon  If you like these games, get it  If you've never played these, though, perhaps start elsewhere  This has its own self contained story as a past era spinoff, but the historical characters are essentially played by Yakuza/Like a Dragon characters, and knowing their normal incarnations is part of the entertainment of this game   But keep in mind that Sega has introduced microtransactions into the "trooper card" system  Please do not pay for these   Editing after putting in quite a few more hours and also finishing the main story:   I stand by the early review I did, as I enjoyed the game quite a bit  The game is pretty much exactly what I expected from a Bakumatsu Yakuza spinoff, and the game had me glued to my seat for many hours   But I am also a little disappointed by the overall situation of this release   Cutscenes and minigames capped to 30 FPS  Additional difficulty locked behind paywall (This personally doesn't matter to me as I play Normal, but shady business practice is shady)  Consumable items sold as "DLC" that work only for one savefile, and you have to rebuy them if you want them again in a different playthrough  Game sold at a $60 pricepoint as a "remake" but outside improved graphics and character replacements, nothing is really remade, and the gameplay has seen no improvements since the Ishin/Zero/Kiwami1 era  (Ironically, it's not faithful to the original either due to the character replacements. But at least this shouldn't be an issue for most English speaking players who haven't played the original Ishin)  Switching to UE4 is being marketed as some big deal, but in the end the only thing it gave us is DX12 shader compilation stutters (use the command line switch -dx11 to reduce this problem). I do hope this is the first and last time they use this   Feels a bit like Sega executives are letting the recent success of RGG games get to their heads

Ishin is a game I can recommend wholeheartedly.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin!Wow what a game. It's actually much easier to hate on it and find everything that is wrong with it rather than to focus on the good. Ishin is almost indefensible and I could easily see how people new to the Ryu Ga Gotoku games would totally hate and ♥♥♥♥ all over it. Game is very dated, what was acceptable and cool 5-10 years ago now is not, it's time to move on yet the game is stuck with it's archaic formula. Pretty much all side content is busy work - dungeon - busy work with good rewards only in 3rd dungeon, 2nd life - total trash waste of time with no rewards, as side note it's nice to see Haruka and all but you can't engage with her. Although game says that you can talk to her and bring her gifts or that someone will come to collect 100 RYO for the farm but for me it never triggered, can't talk to Haruka, can't give her gifts nothing,  just cook for her which is so slow and mindbogglingly dumb way to interact, it just sucks. Fishing is there and 1 substory requires you to get a king tuna for the cat, doable but not fun. Graphics also feel very dated, especially when it's not main characters or the expensive brothel, think most generic substory npc's are taken straight from last decade. There are 4 fighting styles - bare fisted but with ability to use special weapons - trash with moderately fast attack speed and like 10 damage, swordmaster with sluggish but strong attacks, gunner, once you get VORTEX gun this is the way to fight, poor mouse though and finally blade dancer style is the way to go fast, strong endless combos and easy to dodge. Game difficulty - easy, not only can you have food that restores gazillion hp but you can also apply medicine in the middle of a fight. There is crafting but it's so basic no point even mention. Some weapons better than others, read fire or lighting swords better than anything else.I've completed game on hard difficulty with 47% completion, which is a lot for Like a Dragon series and while I seen most of the content not a lot of it is a good content mostly busywork.Map design is okay. Annoying that Ryomas name is not Kiryu Kazuma, almost feels like you're playing a different guy however he, himself is still the headstrong bigger than the world character, very charming with awful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ clothes. Those trousers are ♥♥♥♥.Reflecting upon it no way I would ever be able to recommend this game to anyone who is not already a fan of Yakuza series games, judgement excluding because judgement series is a trash. So this is a hard sell for new players and passable experience for series veterans. Now when game is done, I don't think I'll ever pick it up but I might pickup Yakuza kiwami series as those were brilliant. Also btw the story is trash for anyone who is not Japanese, looks like they needed some patriotic inspiration but as a non Japanese player I can't relate to this crap, not a fan. The villain reveal in the last act is mega cringe, a parody and they even added the over the top evil laugh...yeah ok.So finally it's a pretty bad game, looks like all the good writers have left studio and now interns took their place. Definitely not the way to get fans on board to spawn an epic game series like they did with Yakuza, need way more effort.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice remake of a little forgotten game. This game was never released outside of Japan so it was a nice to play it after all those years of waiting. Its typical Yakuza-style game, with awesome story with alot of fancy plot twists, and likeable characters. As usual the amount of the content in the game is overwhelming, after 110h of gameplay i was not even close to 100% it. I did all the substories (they are still silly/funny/creepy/interesting to do) and battle arenas tho, i took me plenty of time. arenas were espiecially grindy. Farming simulator was crazy time taker too. Its always something to do right? :DThe things i didnt liked at this game are: - combat is not as fluid as in Yakuza games, feels slow at first but its get better later on when you get a little more decent equipement and cards (special abilities with cooldown) from your army- Enchanting/upgrading weapons is way too pricy and too complicated, its very hard to get any seals (which can be inserted into weapons/eq), and even harder to upgrade them to gold status. Did i mention the prices for every action at blacksmith costs like a whole mountain od gold? And the only way to get cash in this game is either farming, abusing minigames or playing arenas over and over again untill u die of boredom.. Still at least those activities are far better than Cabaret clubs minigames from Yakuza series ;)- graphic is bad.... really bad.. Not counting the cutscenes - its just looks terrible and theres plenty of problems with the textures dsnt loading correctly - Theres way too many boring repetative battle arenas, and you will do them over and over to get materials for items. It took me 3 full days to beat them all, because enemies there are like a HP sponges. Prepare to mash attack button for a long time- The game needs an balance - the fire sword is way too overpowered compared to rest of the gears. Did someone tested it? Even last secret boss was not able to protect himself from the fire effect, its.. lame.. And ofc i abused this mechanic to the limit-getting up both skills and levels tooks way too longOverall its a good game, but its not as polished as Yakuzas. Also a slighty lower price would be better looking that its a remaster of a very old game. Still i love what Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio and SEGA is doing, and i will support them no matter what :D

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend “Like A Dragon: Ishin!” to existing fans and newcomers, but with some caveats. I’ll start with the good and then mention the bad!Positives:-An engaging melodrama based on an exciting time in the history of Japan-A helpful “Glossary” function to help clarify things that those of us not familiar with Japanese history (myself included) can benefit from-Exciting combat with four unique styles-Lots of minigames, including Karaoke!-Great (Japanese) voice acting-No performance issues on an older rigNegatives:-It’s a remaster of a ten-year-old game, and the game mechanics are a bit outdated-Still has some of that Yakuza-cringe with how women are represented in minigames-Similar to other Yakuza games, it’s not especially polished in the graphics departmentAll in all, it’s a fun Yakuza game and easy to recommend. If you’ve not played a Yakuza-style game before, this is a great point to jump into the series! In my view, the Yakuza games have always had a B-movie charm, with serious melodrama juxtaposed with silly side activities, and this game doesn’t disappoint. Even though I’m only a chapter and a half in, it’s already making me laugh.

The mini-games are fun and I sometimes get lost in time while playing Ishin.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played all of the Yakuza games released in the West on PC, and out of all of them this is the one I've put the most hours into. It doesn't have the best main story (that belongs to Yakuza 0 imo) but what it does have is an absolute truck load of very engaging side content. Another Life alone will take you hours upon hours to complete, and then you have all the combat masters to do, the Battle Arena, the Dungeon and all the little side stories.There's also an in depth weapon, armour and accessories  crafting system. I'm 130 hours in so far and I'm still not done.Highly recommended for fans of the series and also worth your time as a first game in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Like A Dragon Ishin is a great game. It is very unique from other Yakuza games because of how different the setting is. The story is fantastic, and combat is really fun and I really enjoyed it from beginning to end. The only downsides I would say is the cutscenes stutter whenever blood splatters everywhere, and I think RGG should stick with Dragon Engine over Unreal. Dragon Engine is so much better. The story so far is great you never know who is on your side. Seeing faces we know and love but not attached to the same characters keeps me on my toes. I really love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Another excellent RGG game, I loved the characters, the story, the twists throughout and the environment, everything about the main game. I didn't however overly enjoy 90% of the side quests, a great many of them in fact revolved around providing an item, (mostly food) to the person over and over again, slowly filling the bar until it was full. Adding to the irritation was 2 facts: Firstly the dialog in the fat middle of each quest is identical, so only the first bit and the last tended to be different, secondly whilst the character is moving, you cannot progress and skip, so for example giving a young boy vegetables meant waiting for him to complete his bow for 2 seconds before I could hit X and move on, that got very annoying...especially when you have to visit him like 8-10 times before reaching the last stage.I also disliked the blacksmithing, they make a big deal out of it, but I didn't even use it once because I got excellent weapons from the story missions, so it seemed sadly wasted.Lastly I somewhat enjoyed 'Another Life' but unlike recent RGG games, (I know this is a remake of a 2014 game) it didn't have the same addiction for me to complete it, like my building empire in Yakuza: Like A Dragon, which gives you a solid reason to keep going. In Another Life there didn't feel like there was any real reward for bothering with it, that's a shame.This might seem negative given the meaty middle of the review, but rest assured, I loved the game, although it might not seem it, but for me side quests are a nice optional aside, not the be all and end all, the main story is fantastic, I loved the combat too, characters as I said are AMAZING throughout, it was such a riot and I will not forget it anytime soon, just wish the side quests and mini games were up the standard of Y:LAD and Judgement 1+2, but like I said, they're from the 2014 era, so I give them a big old pass on that, at least their new games are getting better and better in that regard and that's what counts.Hope this review helped you but generally if you enjoyed the Yakuza, Judgement games, you'll enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: Wild Dancer style is definetely the way to go in this game:- boss too fast? Wild Dancer him to death.- a lot of mobile enemies? Wild Dancer them to death.- enemies use guns and stay far away like some cats? Use your own gun that comes with this style to knock them out and then Wild Dancer them to death.- you miss blocking? Go to a dojo that's dedicated for this style and unlock parrying so you can protect yourself and Wild Dancer your enemies while at it. Or just spam dodging while Wild Dancing all your enemies, that works too.If you lack green orbs and have a lot of the white ones, just put them all into the Wild Dancer style because this one's the most fun to use honestly.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! has the same magic of Yakuza 0. This has got to be the most fun RGG game I've ever played. The minigames are outright addictive, the substories are so funny and the world is incredibly immersive. I also really love the combat! Fighting with a sword is incredibly satisfying >:D The main story is also really engaging, although my Japanese friends who played the original said the localization left a lot of details out, so I'm a bit disappointed we aren't getting the authentic experience.All that being said I think the "recommended" PC requirements is the baseline in order not to get a laggy stuttering mess. I have a beefy PC and haven't experienced many problems aside from the annoying 30fps cap on cutscenes, but a lot of people have been having issues that seriously affect playability. This was the fist time the studio tried using Unreal Engine and since it's a straight port from the base game it leaves a lot to be desired in terms of graphic optimization. I hope if the RGG team fully makes the switch to unreal in they work hard to optimize their future titles.

_childDocuments_.review: On the same tier as Yakuza 0 and LaD (aka Yakuza 7) for me. Tons of fun. Amazing music. Has a neat little sidegame like those games did where you grow crops and cook, and it has excellent writing and story like the other games. It's still both hilarious, and dramatic/hard hitting all at once, just like the others.I don't think it's quite as large or as long as those maineline games, but it doesn't feel small, either. I'm playing it at a relaxed pace, messing around, using no guides, and I'm way past 60 hours. Although I've beaten it now, my total completion is at 50%. Easily enough here to sink your teeth into for many hours and have a lot of fun. _childDocuments_.review: "The core of the game is being eroded by this." - Masayoshi Yokoyama, Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio Head on the Like a Dragon: Ishin (Behind the Scenes of Like a Dragon! – Ep 2: The Road Ahead 8:09)Before I start I want to mention I've refunded the game a fair while ago, so let me know if anything has changed. I'd consider myself a massive RGG Studios fan, I've played every Yakuza/Judgment game available on PC, so it disheartens me to say that this game is the worst the series has been, and I don't mean that with any exaggeration I dislike this game. I will admit I wasn't super excited for this game as I didn't have much of an interest in the original Ryu Ga Gotoku: Ishin! But after playing this remaster (I'll discuss that more later on) I have even less of an interest in doing so. "So what are the flaws?" you may ask, and to put it simply this is a cheap and poorly put together remaster. You might ask why do I keep referring to it as a "remaster" rather than a remake which is what this game is being sold as. Well to put simply half, if not a majority of the original games code, animation, models, and overall gameplay is still in the games files, it was ultimately a port of the original to Unreal Engine 4. With that out of the way I want to point out another glaring issue, the port to Unreal Engine 4. I can make a comparison but I want you to keep in mind it's not as bad, is Grand Theft Auto: Trilogy Remastered. The game overall uses a variety of models, some characters got changed as apart of the cast change, and this can vary on the quality of them as these models come from as early as 2014 with the original Ishin (Ryoma's model is still his original model), or head models that are either from 2020's Yakuza: Like a Dragon (Kondo has Adachi's head), or completely new ones such as Ito (while it uses Hitoshi Ozawa/Kuze's facial scan data from 2015, it seems like they made a new head based off it) and it just becomes a mess in terms of quality as some are higher quality than others. The map and models looks off, as it was completely made in a different engine, and then ported to Unreal Engine 4, except for in cutscenes where they seem to actually be able to take advantage of Unreal Engine, and they do look nice when they work that is. This game would've benefited from a ground up remaster made in the studios own Dragon Engine. The next issue I'll point out is bugs, they are littered throughout this game and they range from minor annoyances to major issues, here are some I would like to note, bosses would sometimes unintentionally teleport throughout the boss fights, cutscenes would start flashing to black and back to normal horribly, sometimes the cutscene camera is inside of a wall preventing the player from seeing what's going on, music would overlap over itself with the second repeat being delayed, the water would sometimes glitch out and cover the screen, and that's just to name a few bugs I've encountered and seen from my friends. I will point out some personal points, I don't consider these as strong and they are up to personal preference. I don't like the trooper card and boss super attack system. The trooper card system from my knowledge was exclusive to the dungeon system, and I think that's fine, but in this game, they are technically unequippable, but they give stat bonuses, that and the cards on the U.I take up too much space, while they make the game less tedious than without them, they should give you choice. I can say the same about the bosses super moves (example: a boss has fire balls come out of his hands), from the same documentary I got my quote from the beginning of my review from, it is mentioned they added these in an attempt to appeal to a wider audience, and I personally agree with Yokoyama on it eroding the core of the game. Despite being a RGG game, they tend to have limits on how silly they'll go, especially in the main game (story). The extracts in Judgment/Lost Judgment which are similar to the trooper cards, are completely optional and you have to go out of your way to use them, so I am completely fine with that. The easiest thing I can compare the boss super attacks to, is the mortal attacks in Judgment/Lost Judgment, but the thing with those is they aren't super silly, they are still relatively grounded. I'd also make another quick point about a thing that bugs me is that they have the original cast of this games model, and as proven by Ryu Ga Gotoku: Online (a Japanese gatcha game), they still are able to use the likeness and voice of the original cast so I don't see why that isn't a toggle especially with the controversy towards the new cast, while I don't personally mind the new cast this is a 80 dollar game. I'll wrap this up with my last point, the price point, and DLC. This game is 92.99 Canadian Dollars for the Digital Deluxe edition, which is absolutely insane. For comparison Resident Evil 4 (2023)'s Deluxe Edition is only 89.99, and that's a ground up remake, and not a port with unnecessary DLC that wasn't in the original. The DLC for this game isn't an issue because it's a "support the devs" option, but because most of it is a predatory EA, Ubisoft type of microtransaction, why do I say that? The DLC can be divided into two things, a DLC for cosmetics (Shinsengumi Captain's Set) which is fine, but it also includes a difficulty mode, which I really don't like but okay. But then you have materials for weapons crafting, and high quality cards, that is an issue, especially the weapons crafting as this game is notorious for grinding. But also another main issue is that these are all ONE TIME USE, so if you get them on the wrong save, or your save gets corrupted, it is gone. This is the most worrying aspect of the game as I can see how it can easily be implemented into Like a Dragon: 8. I want to conclude with, I am genuinely really unhappy with this game, I am hoping that this is a one time thing for RGG, as I feel like every game prior to this has something I really like about it, this doesn't, and it's a shame because everyone has been hyping this game up, and I never was onboard, in a way I'm lucky as I would hate to be a fan of the original Ishin just to be disappointed by this. Personally I hope moving forward, RGG focuses on it's Japanese audience primarily for the decisions they make in their games (in the same documentary I mentioned at the beginning they've mentioned that Sega of America gave them suggestions and they took it.) as it's why we love the games, they move forward using Dragon Engine because they truly made something special with it, it's an inhouse engine that they've improved greatly as shown in Lost Judgment, and I want to continue to see what they can do with it, and also I just hope they drop the predatory DLC, just stick with cosmetics, and story expansions (price them better as well). I still love RGG Studio but I can't recommend this game.TL;DR: Like a Dragon: Ishin! is an overpriced poorly made remaster that calls itself a remake, that has a lot of annoying bugs, a lack of options, and predatory DLC practices.

_childDocuments_.review: What is there not to like.Its our favorite characters from the Yakuza series put into a feudal japan setting while u slash and beat people to pulp again as Kiryu (Ryoma). Im sure people missed the brawler beat-em up / slasher em up style from the good old Yakuza 1 - 6 games. (i love the rpg style too from LAD dont get me wrong)Seeing Kiryu being a bada** again and still being kind as f*k always make me smile. The game as always starts with the main story build up where u have to follow it to a certain point, but its pretty good and the VA's are top-notch (not dubbed but i feel like playing in English would take away from the experience tbh) .Once u get free reign, u will most likely skip story stuff because in every cram and nooky there is a side-quest. Some are kinda meh, others are surprisingly fun and other times they just make u cry. (yea the game can definitely play with ur heartstrings) The story so far is pretty good, already seen a lot of the familiar faces from the yakuza games and theyre still doing an amazing job. I don't know if its a story everyone will like, i certainly do, but i love the feudal Japan type of thing and there's a glossary for explaining some of the stuff that u might not know what it is/was. The mini-games so far are pretty fun. (Singing, dancing, Udon Chef, chicken races, shogi, chopping wood just to name a few with still a lot more! ) There are 4 different fighting styles each with their own grid, but u will get orbs that u can use on any of the paths. I'm sure eventually if u grind enough u are able to max out all of the grids but obviously its not necessary. I personally enjoy the wild dancer stance (the one with a gun and sword) but u could just play brawler style and never touch a weapon.All in all, i will recommend this game if u are a LAD fan or if u want to play a Feudal Japan setting game with amazing cast and great story.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm happy to see that Like a Dragon: Ishin! has finally been translated and released internationally. I've never played the 2014 Japan-exclusive PS4 game (duh), so I'm even happier that after the first hours I can already tell that it has all components that make for a great Yakuza/Like a Dragon game: suspenseful main story, dozens of fleshed out characters with their own agenda, silly side stories, great soundtrack and satisfying combat.It doesn't improve on the "Yakuza formula", but it doesn't have to - it's a game series that reliably delivers.It's a great spin-off that anybody will enjoy who enjoyed other Yakuza games. For newcomers, this could be a great starting point, provided the setting in 1860s Japan sounds interesting. If it doesn't, it would be better to start somewhere else, e.g. with Yakuza 0 or Yakuza: Like a Dragon. At the same time, there are a few glaring issues that can't be overlooked. The movement outside of combat is clunky and feels very 2014, even on a controller. The story has some pacing issues, after the intro it pretty much slows down to a crawl. On top of that, there are technical issues, that will hopefully be addressed with future patches. Some of those are really unforgivable in 2023: UE4 shader stutter; missing ultra wide screen support (come on, Sega); 30 fps cut scenes (really?).

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr this game is very good and you should play it unless you have a fatal allergy to non-dragon engine games. combat is excellent at its core but some of the things built around that core aren't great, side content is more or less what you expect in terms of RGG quality, story is good but crams too many characters in.PREFACE:I didn't play the original version of RGG Ishin, because I cannot read or understand Japanese. There are pretty substantial graphical and gameplay differences between the two. That being said, I don't think you can buy the original anymore on Steam.GRAPHICS/SOUND:Ishin's graphics look more or less like Dragon Engine graphics, though the animations are more like the pre-2016 games. Sakamoto's modeled after Kiryu, but not the Dragon Engine Kiryu, but that's the only real divergence aside from the complete model replacements. Some of the characters that were modeled after real people (and then some others) in the original had their models replaced with remastered versions of the post-2014 RGG characters e.g. Joon-gi Han, Jun Oda, the Dojima lieutenants (those are modeled after real people, but I assume their likenesses either didn't expire or were renewed because more people like Yakuza 0 than are familiar with the original likenesses). I don't have much of an opinion one way or the other, but I think it is sad that some of the obscure characters don't get to shine. Did they need to get rid of Hamazaki? Hamazaki was cool. He wasn't even that obscure, which sort of undermines that part of my point, but I think it still stands more broadly. The soundtrack is good, as is usual. Get to the last part of the "Wanted Men" side content to hear a blood-pumping guitar song.GAMEPLAY (COMBAT):This is not a Dragon Engine game, so no physics and no running from combat. The gameplay is most comparable to Yakuza Kiwami, but they're hardly similar. Weapons play a much larger role in this game, for one. You have four styles, and only one is hand-to-hand, with that style being focused on Heat gathering and Heat Actions. The other styles cover a broad spread: a slow but heavy-hitting swordfighting style, a fast gun-and-sword style that requires you to dodge instead of block, and a gun-only style that is pretty intuitive: you shoot people. All 4 styles are a whole lot of fun and cater to pretty much every type of person. Despite the centering around weapons, the number of actually good weapons in the game is very limited. The number of weapons in general is massive, but most of them are middling at best. The most expensive and difficult to obtain gun in the game, the Dragon Hawk, is almost certainly not worth the effort, completionism notwithstanding. The same is true for swords. There is no real "golden gun" equivalent (there is a literal golden gun and it is quite good but nowhere near the best). Weapons can be upgraded via seals. Getting seals is a massive pain because they are obtained at random from crafting weapons and rarely from enemies. Applying seals has a chance of failure that can't be reset via loading which makes it even worse.From what I can gather the old Ishin had the system from Yakuza 5 where eating food could give you buffs and a second health bar, and this was gotten rid of. I liked that system and the "trooper cards" that replaced it (at least regarding the health bar) are a bit of a needless overcomplication. Most of them (there are literally hundreds of unique troopers) do the same thing and I barely used them except for grinding.Nearly every boss battle has a thing where the boss is capable of literal magic. I'm not talking about the heat aura thing, I'm talking about the bosses summoning fireballs and tornadoes like a wizard. It's so weird because there's not reason given for it and pretty much every RGG game has reserved this sort of stuff for side content, except for Yakuza 7, which has that whole "overactive imagination" thing going on for the main character. Also, you sometimes fight giants who are at least as tall as a bus. That's also weird.Lastly, there are optional "battle dungeons" to grind materials and XP from. The menu makes it look like there should be more than 3, but there are only 3. They're nothing outstanding, just going through rooms clearing dudes, pretty standard. GAMEPLAY (OTHER):There is a thing called "Another Life" which is basically the game's way of introducing Harvest Moon-type stuff. You grow crops, fish, and sell the fruits of your labor so you can decorate your house. It's a good break from the other, fast paced parts of the game, and the crops don't grow agonizingly slowly like in Nier Replicant, so there's not much wrong with it.Most of the minigames are unique to Ishin, such as buyo, but karaoke comes back, as does chicken racing.PLOT:It's a good old tale of honor, betrayal, and the dark side of patriotism. The only thing not to love is the game's overstuffing with characters, which doesn't seem to serve much purpose other than invoking nostalgia. There's a character who plays barely any role in the plot and doesn't even appear until the end, and when he does appear it still left me confused as to why he was even afforded an appearance. There's a guy who's revealed to be a spy for the enemy and gets executed. Does that matter? Not really. He's just a vehicle to cast doubts on the main character, meanwhile Mr. Spy's spying is never brought up in any real capacity again. I think one of the good things the swapping of models did was give the opportunity to subvert expectations with the "casting" of characters. Even though Majima is Majima and Kiryu is Kiryu in this game, you get to see some interesting ideas like a calm "Kuze" and Machiavellian "Adachi".

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr only buy if it's either on sale or you really like the other yakuza games.Ishin Kiwami is a mixed bag of good and bad. It is obvious how much effort RGG put into this remake, however if anything, it feels more like an enhanced port, just on a new engine. Coming off the heels of Lost Judgment, Ishin Kiwami feels like a downgrade in almost every department.While the visuals aren't terrible, at times they look rather disappointing, especially considering that this is the same studio that have made some beautiful looking games. There are times where the game can look rather sloppy, even on the highest graphics settings. At points i'd say it looks worse than Yakuza 0 or even Yakuza 5 During cutscenes the visuals are stellar, which only reinforces how disappointing the rest of the game can look.The cutscenes look great, though they only run at 30fps, despite the fact they are not pre rendered. And even still, the beautiful cutscenes are not prone to problems. Sometimes there is stutter, frame drops or camera jittering, which really takes away from how polished they feel. Considering how the rest of the game runs at at a constant 120fps on the highest settings 1920x1080, I don't think the issues present during the cutscenes are an issue with my hardware. The 30fps cap is not limited to the cutscenes as it is also present in activities such as Karaoke, Buyo Dance and Cho-Han.While visuals are a minor gripe, a much more prolific issue is the technical issues at play. There have been accounts of instability as there is a lack of shader compiling though I haven't experienced this all too much. (whether that be to hardware or having the game on an SSD) An issue I have experienced is very rarely, there are battles that have no music, which just feels really weird and uncomfortable.Combat is refreshing, although a bit underwhelming at times. Gunman is a broken style that turns the game into Devil May Cry 2, even on legendary. Wild dancer is a fun style to use, though not as versatile as Swordsman which is clearly the main style that should be focused on. Brawler is really disappointing and underpowered (even with the loincloth that gives a 90% increase to brawler attacks). To coincide with brawler being a letdown, heat actions feel incredibly weak, weaker than they were in Yakuza 3. Not even from an aspect of damage, but visually, they look very underwhelming and do not pack any sort of punch, which even Yakuza 5 and 0 did, not to mention Kiwami 2 or Judgment. This was probably done to provide more emphasis on the new Trooper Card system.The new Troopers that can be used in combat are a cool addition, if not a bit strange as even on Legendary, it makes boss fights seem pretty trivial (how this fairs on Ishin, I do not know.) It is cool to see some characters such as Ichiban, Nishitani and Makoto as well as the appearance of some guest characters and even animals from the series such as Nugget, Mame and Yama-Oroshi, though these cards can be disabled if one wishes to do so. It is unclear if RGG will keep this new feature in upcoming games or if it was just a one off thing specially made for Ishin Kiwami.The substories are some of the weakest, or even, the worst, the series has seen, as a significant number of them end up being speaking to a person, giving them an item or doing something for them and then unlocking a "friendship" with them, akin to that seen in Judgment, however, unlike Judgment or Kiwami 2, these provide no benefits and only act as underwhelming filler, though not all substories are bad as in some of them we get to see some characters from other games such as Bacchus, Miss Tatsu and Shinji, but that still doesn't detract from how uninspired a portion of them tend to be.Even with all these downsides, Ishin Kiwami is splendid and rather enjoyable, given you've played the other games in the series. The recasting done for Ishin Kiwami is great as well as the return of characters from the original Ishin as we get to see fan favourites such as Mine, Nishiki, Kuze and Ryuji (sans the best part of the shower scene) come back. The story is solid and a well done historical fiction from 1860s Japan with Yakuza characters portraying historical figures.Finally seeing Ishin localised is great with a clear amount of high effort, however significant downsides that do detract from this being one of the better games in the franchise, and if this is a precedent of how Gaiden or Like a Dragon 8 will turn out to be, then I'd be rather worried. RGG's transition to the Unreal Engine has clearly not been smooth, and an important thing to note is that this is the first game without Toshihiro Nagoshi at the helm of the project. Hopefully this is only a small setback for the RGG team and future games will hopefully be stronger and more impressive than the preceding titles. Depending on the success of this game, RGG may hopefully decide to remake or port previous entires that are either region or console locked such as Kurohyou, Fist of the North Star: Lost Paradise or even the infamous Dead Souls (I wouldn't get hopes up for Kenzan considering the nature of the content within.)One day I plan to play the original Ishin to see how Kiwami stands up to it, even if it does have a language barrier to cross.

_childDocuments_.review: Ishin, more than any other game in the Yakuza franchise, is a game for the sickos, and potentially only the sickos. It's the kind of game that provides a rewarding experience first and foremost to those players who have already played every game in the series already, and are deeply invested in the characters and character interactions. By using the faces and voices of major and minor characters across all eight (at the time) main series games, the game does provide a touchstone for players who aren't familiar with the historical narrative being told (and for those who are, given that it takes plenty of liberties with the historical record in its narrative), but the fact remains that, in story and gameplay, Ishin is probably the least accessible game in the franchise, the kind of game where you really need to want to play it specifically.This is a remake of a PS3-era game, ported from its original engine to Unreal Engine 4, and it really does show its age in its animations and combat. The brawler-style Yakuza games very rarely miss in their combat, but Ishin provides a stilted, uncomfortable experience in basically every fight. You have four styles to work with, but one of them is uniformly useless, and two others tend to be situational at best. Most likely, you'll be spending most of your time in the swordsman style, and it makes the combat feel repetitive and not very engaging. Traversal can also be tedious, as the taxi equivalents are few and far between across the surprisingly large map, with a slow standard run speed and a harshly limited sprint. All in all, it makes movement feel unpleasant, which is a shame for a Yakuza game.The games in the series that falter in gameplay tend to make up for it in story, and I do think that Ishin does a decent job of this - even though the story is a historical retelling of the Bakumatsu period, and thus a far cry from being relatable for Western audiences especially, the game deploys its actors in fun, sometimes unexpected ways. Of course, most of the casting is straightforward - Kiryu as protagonist Sakamoto Ryoma, Kazama as a mentor figure, Nishiki as a rival, etc. - but there are a number of characters whose faces and roles in the main Yakuza series make their roles here quite intriguing. Keep an eye out for Mine and Shibusawa in particular, with Zhao and Joongi also creating intrigue in how they're used. Like I said before, it's a great way to help players connect with the characters of a story that would otherwise feel a little too far away from relatability, like watching a stage play.Side content is about as plentiful as you'd expect from one of the PS3-era Yakuza games, with fun spins on staples like karaoke and gambling dens. I personally found myself not really wanting to engage with much of it, given that I was kind of slogging through the game, but I definitely had a lot of fun with karaoke and the Haruka-related minigames, and there's plenty to do to space out the main story. This includes the weird dungeon-crawling side game related to the trooper cards, which I admittedly didn't bother with for a single second because it all seemed exhausting. The trooper cards and equipment upgrades are a huge grind, one that could end up being necessary for making the combat go a lot faster by giving you stronger weapons to work with. It's easily the most griped-about part of this game, which made me glad that I didn't end up really needing to bother with it.On the whole, despite the tone of my review, Ishin is not a bad game - I don't think there's a bad Yakuza game. I do think that you need to understand what you're diving into when you play it, and it's a game whose appeal is much narrower than the mainline games, but if you fall into the demographic who will get a lot out of it, I'd suggest picking it up. Just wait for a sale, and probably make sure you've played all of the main games before this one for the best experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is filled with a lot to do, some extremely rewarding tasks, some menial enjoyable tasks, some downright intrusive & not so much fun at all tasks (which is to be expected if you've been playing the entire RGG collection). All in all; this is a great game and a serious 8/10. The reason why I won't give it a 9 or 10/10 is because in my humble opinion, the combat, while incredibly satisfying and visually appealing for the player, leaves much to be desired when coming from the flawlessly capable and snappy combinations and styles from (0). The fighting feels slower (by the frames) and as much as I'd like to attribute that to realism on the developers part, it seems more like they over looked this minute detail in the grand scheme of this game. That high energy slow fighting kind of worked in 4,5 & 6 when you adjust to it and slow down so that the engine could actually render the right moves. Same goes for the story, while I might add the story is incredibly immersive, it also gets incredibly boring and as much as I love the dramatization most of the time in the RGG series, however, with the older characters I found myself almost rushing through the story trying to get somewhere the chapters are kind of strung together like this review, and even the most dramatic parts don't really sit how I feel the developers wanted them to, knowing that in canon the characters were "acting" metaphysically. Besides that and some initial graphical issues upon release, if you're into RGG storytelling and an almost entirely brand new IP using old IP characters consisting of edo period Japanese culture, subculture and socioeconomic turmoil please give this a try it has much to offer as far as actual open world game play & roleplay elements, cutscenes, incredible acting and minigames the majority of my gripes where intentionally critical considering these guys are making some of the greatest games on the market. Still can't wait for the rest of the games to drop, I'll be checking it out for sure. I really can't think of any thing else besides the chicken race glitch that got patched.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty much your Yakuza 3, 4, 5 or 0 set in a 'historic' setting but can be very much enjoyed even if you don't know or dislike history since it's all anime bullshieet anyway where freshly cut or shot down foes get back up their feet like nothing ever happened after suffering fatal wounds. Don't get me wrong though there's quite a few people dieing within it's story as usual but just the overall combat is typical japanese like that. You'll spend a lot of time eating your pain away when hurt which I can't say is unrealistic but it's like those old River City Ransom beat em up games: fight, eat, repeat. A formula all the yakuza games had anyway, so that didn't bother me or anything but do know what you'll find here if you're not familiar with these games or was expecting something else like say a Ghost of Tsushima.The main deal is it's humor and all the substories and minigames that can be done but you could decide to skip a few or even all of these and still have a grand time with a more fluent main story that way (just a harder time completing it on say a hard difficulty without some 'grind' or preparations in unlocked combat skills).That being said I always thought of the Yakuza series as something familiar other then just 'River City Ransom but 3D' but I couldn't quite put my finger on it until now: it's essentially Gintama.You're an oddjob self-exiled ronin instead of a robinhood yakuza this time around that's the main difference and you'll be helping or disrupting all kinds of exploits in and around town all the while having a main goal to figure out who's behind your father's murder. It is however to the player how fast or slow-phased this can be done.The presence of Haruka gave me quite a jumpscare as she is literally what ruined the series for me but the good thing is that she is way more optional this time around and she and her manor can be largely if not completely ignored (A big difference from the dreaded Orphanage of Yakuza 3).Another fellow I didn't quite miss was this Komaki the 'karate kid trainer' guy, he too is there but here's hoping he gets pancaked by a palanquin someday but other then that all the characters are amazing in their own right.It's overall another great edition and perhaps one of my favourite yakuza games so far even but it's not without it's common quirks and shortcomings in both wacky combat or graphics department though considering it's a remake of an older game that finally saw a release and translation one could look past that stuff after giving it a good few hours.There seems to be alot of folks complaining about it's graphics or combat mainly if not the mandatory xbox controller overlay when played with any controller, which I admit has been confusing for me as well especially with all the quick-timed-events in some of the cutscenes and minigames.The only real downside for me personally was that some of the pre-order extras got bugged and cannot be retrieved to this day... because I've got this pre-order edition from a friend I went the extra mile and mailed Sega about it but they point towards Steam and Steam back to Sega in a long story short: I couldn't retrieve these because of playing the US or Canadian version on a EU based Steam account apparently. Now I realise even before this problem occurs that I should not be within the EU but well.. I do hope they might fix it one day but it's not something that prevents me from playing the main game either so it's no gamebreaker. In fact all the free downloadable content doesn't seem to be affected interestingly enough only the pre-order or paid ones are.So there's a lesson in that :P

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's played all the games in the Yakuza series, I'd recommend skipping this one, unless you get it for half price or less. Here's why I don't think this game measures up to the other ones: is probably the biggest miss. Out of the 4 combat styles, only two of them (sword and sword+gun) are usable overall. The third style, unarmed, deals about 20% of the damage as the other styles, and on harder difficulties, this means you're just pounding away on each random thug for 90+ seconds before they finally go down. The final style, gunman, has so many oddities and bugs that ruin the combat. The biggest one is that when you shoot an enemy in gunman style, there's a 50% chance that they'll start an infinite loop of taunting you, so they just stand there while you spend the next 15 seconds shooting them to death. There are some flashy moves in each style, but you'll find yourself going back to the same two styles over and over again, just so you don't lose every fight.  , which are those comedic side-quests which characterise the Yakuza series, have lost almost all entertainment value due to the implementation of the "friends system". In this game, you meet characters on the street who will ask you for things from your inventory, and then give you some short dialogue to thank you. To maximise the "friend gauge" of that character, you need to give them the same kind of item, and listen to the exact same dialogue about 10-20 more times before that character is complete, and they give you the comedic end of their painfully dragged-out story. It's like being told the setup of a joke, and then being forced to complete 15 identical fetch quests before they tell you the punchline. The huge time delay between the start and end of each substory makes them a lot less funny than in the other Yakuza games.  is alright, but slightly worse than what a fan of the series would typically expect. The main appeal is that they've included a huge cast of returning characters from all the previous Yakuza games, so for example, a longtime fan might get really excited to see how a conversation would play out between Kuze from Yakuza 0 and Mine from Yakuza 3. The game definitely delivers on the ensemble of characters, but the game fails to give enough screen time to anyone. There are times where major characters die off screen.  There are also times where important characters literally disappear from the game, and are never even mentioned again. This alone isn't enough of a reason not to buy the game, but it certainly doesn't help justify the game's $80 CAD price tag.Here are some other issues I had with the game, but couldn't sort into the above three categories:If you're a hardcore Yakuza series fan who would get excited about this game's ensemble cast, I would recommend waiting until the game is at least 50% off before purchasing, since the main story one of the only reasons to get this game. However, with RGG Studio releasing 1-2 Yakuza games every year, it might be best to wait until the next game comes out this November.

_childDocuments_.review: As of posting there is a shader compilation stutter issue. Every time an effect happens for the first time you'll get a stutter, sometimes a big one. Thankfully this isn't the kind of game where new effects are happening all the time, but when it does happen it's extremely annoying.The move to Unreal Engine is devoid of benefits, there's no HDR support, no raytracing (at least give us shadows), no modern features such a move should create. And it looks as good as previous games but not really better, maybe lighting in some areas (at least it doesn't have the generic unreal engine look).Not only is there no HDR support the game forces the setting off if you try to modify the config. I hate that, I wish studios would stop doing that.The worst issue is 30fps cinematics, thats absurd, I can understand a 60fps limit for technical reasons but 30 is an unreasonable compromise to me. I hope that can be fixed cause when you can easily play a game at 120FPS, 30fps REALLY stands out.There's some nitpicks about camera movement where it just feels off for some reason, not very smooth.Another nit pick is the pause screen does not confirm if you want to skip a cut scene. IMO it's otherwise same old Yakuza, I played 13 hours straight today by accident. I love these games and the samurai ♥♥♥♥ is fresh as ♥♥♥♥, I love seeing old characters in a new context and see how things play out. I can fully recommend this despite my issues above. I'm posting my complaints in the hopes they fix these issues but truthfully they don't detract from the game entirely.I hope by launch the shader comp issues and 30fps cut scenes are fixed, and I hope they add HDR support before I finish the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Like A Dragon: Ishin! is a very interesting spin-off from the Yakuza franchise, I really like its setting of Bakumatsu Era Japan, the map of Kyo is very expansive and beautiful with a lot cultural decorations in the tea parlors and shops. I often find myself walking around taking in the sights, especially during sunrise and sundown. However the NPCs around me don't seem to know their way around all that well, I often see them running into walls or floating on objects and it really breaks my immersion.I find this map so much easier to navigate than Kamurocho was in Yakuza 0, that might just be the much improved mini-map which has zoomed out a bit to give you a better view of whats ahead, but I find the decorations and theming of important buildings really help build landmarks to help me find my way around.Something that I wish they'd change is how often these random encounters occur, I run into bandits far too often and it really makes it hard to get around town.Combat in this game is incredibly fun, its smooth, fast paced, and very experimental, I love the Wild Dancer fighting style but its great to have a full arsenal of different fighting styles for different situations. Especially having the long-range gun fighter style. One thing I feel makes the combat clunky is how the guns aim especially in Wild Dancer style where my gun will seemingly aim at either nothing or some other NPC that I am not currently facing, it makes it a bit annoying to lose my combos because the gun isn't behaving how I think its supposed to.The Yakuza games have always been very story rich, and this game is no different. While I like the story its telling and I enjoy how theatrical the cutscenes are, some of them go on for extremely long amounts of time and then are followed by very long conversations. I found myself losing interest in some of these sections just for how long they can be. One thing I find weird about this game is that all the characters are clearly the Yakuza characters wearing period appropriate attire, and it makes it trippy to see them with different personalities then they have in those gameThis game also is very grindy, mainly in the blacksmithing system. You'll have to win a lot of battles, search around the city for hours and do odd jobs around town just to get what you need to upgrade your weapon for the harder fights. I haven't seen too much of the grind yet, but many other reviews point it out so I imagine its quite a core part of the game.I give Like A Dragon Ishin! a 8/10, its a very fun spin-off to the Yakuza franchise, and the new setting and story really help keep these games feeling fresh. Combat is fun and fast, with lots of experimentation to be had. With the main drawback being its grindy gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: After 64 hours into the game on Hard difficulty I can safely say:- Fix the DLCs being one-time use only. That is unfair and predatory.- Fix the Minigames and Cutscenes being locked at 30FPS. Most PCs out there are capable of handling such, and it's sad to see in 2023.- Rebalance the difficulties. They are not exactly what I'd call "fair". Enemies are plus on basically every attack, some can't even be staggered, and some go as far as being so unrelenting they will hit you as soon as a fight scene starts without giving you a chance to react.- Rebalance styles. Swordsman plays horribly, and I avoid the style like the plague because of how minus it is. You get animation locked on so many moves, because apparently the move speeds up, but the actual mechanic of it isn't, so you're stuck sitting there taking all the hits. Plus, either I'm doing it wrong, or Wild Dancer's quickstep avoids probably like only half the attacks.- Rebalance smithing. Sure, it's meant to be grindy, but when I'm actively avoiding a whole mechanic of the game because it's just that bad to get a hold of? Then something's probably wrong. I would rather run a dungeon 30 times and hope I drop a better weapon, than use the blacksmith. (I avoided doing such by simply going through the story, no spoilers.)I would die for this company but, with how this game is shaping up to be I can't, in good conscience, recommend it to my friends and tell them "Sure, you'll have fun, trust me."I understand wanting to use a different engine and be experimental with it, and I appreciate how you guys have translated basically almost the entire Dragon Engine 1:1, but I'm sad to say it doesn't work. I hope you guys aren't working on having Gaiden and 8 use Unreal Engine too, and if you are, fix these issues while you're ahead. Please, act while you're ahead and do better.If I have any more issues, I will edit this in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This was such an awesome game! For context, I started playing the Yakuza series just a couple years ago (started with Yakuza 0, then played through the PC remakes of 1-6, then Like a Dragon, and now this), and I have thoroughly enjoyed the series so far. Note that I never played the original version of this (I didn't even realize there  an original release), so this was my first experience with this game.It was really cool seeing the characters I recognize from the original Yakuza series play through this plot in feudal Japan. A small thing I actually  appreciated was that the dialogue boxes included a "show definition" type button when historical Japanese terms were stated: it was a cool learning experience (I don't know a lot about feudal Japan), and it helped me remind myself of key terms the characters kept saying so I wouldn't get lost in the plot. It was a subtle but really nice touch, and I hope they (and other game devs) continue to do so in the future!As far as the game itself, the graphics were solid in my opinion: they were what you would expect from the modern Yakuza games (great scenery, fairly realistic textures, etc.). The non-cutscene character interactions look robotic like the other games, but I think that's fine. The music was also really great. The gameplay was like the other Yakuza games in terms of beat-em-up combat style, but this time, you have 3 combat styles: one where you just use a sword, one where you just use a gun, and one where you use both a sword and a gun simultaneously. I thought this was a nice touch, as there were some enemy types that I preferred fighting ranged, and others that I wanted to get in and fight in close combat.The story was also pretty good; pretty much what you would expect from the Yakuza series (except instead of it being a Yakuza-centric plot, it was a plot about the political system in feudal Japan; similar feeling, though). It was really interesting seeing the interactions between feudal Japan and the British Empire; a really cool historical adventure!Overall, I definitely recommend this game: it's another excellent entry in the Yakuza series :-)

_childDocuments_.review: It hurts me to leave a thumbs down on an RGG LAD game. I absolutely adore this studio I've finished every mainline PC game, and with this I've now finished every spin-off too that's come on PC. (the Judgements are really good, look into them)The biggest gripe I have is that the story constantly loses me. There's this dissonance of the "Guns only kill in cutscenes" narrative that feels especially egregious here. So much so that it repeatedly takes me out of it. Ryoma doesn't like to kill in that recognizable old Kiryu fashion, but... he's using a pistol, and a sword, both being very excellent tools of KILLING. Yet every non-story fight I've gone through feels like I just smashed them with a Boken.And you may think "Yeah, every Yakuza/LAD game is like that.", sure, but there's a difference with a story fight in a Yakuza cutscene brushing off any in-game weapons as Kiryu *actually* using his fists. In Ishin though? Every fight's a sword fight, and they've definitely been shown to be fatal. A tryout almost gets gutted and is told to find a doctor before he bleeds out. Swords are repeatedly established as killing tools in cutscenes, but when a boss-fight ends it repeatedly seems like they've gotten away with just scrapes.Y'know what? That's one point we can look past. It's RGG, playing loose with what's fatal and what isn't is just how they roll and after seven Yakuza mainlines games and the new direction with LAD, I'm usually pretty used to it. And of course there's the fact that LAD Ishin is a remake of the original Ishin, so they couldn't really change the story. Seeing old faces replaced with recognizable faces and voices is pretty neat. I liked all the Y0 callbacks, as that one still remains as my favorite. Feels just a little fanservicey, though.I just wish the combat didn't feel this samey.Brawler is useless as a style compared to the rest, it almost feels present out of obligation to the series. And I get that, but it could've been more useful. What if Brawler came with a disarm out of the box? Which is something the other styles have to unlock. Could be a good cheap source of Bundle Swords for crafting before you get your hands on a lot of cash through Chicken Races.Swordsman is for fighting bosses mainly, though it's useful in any situation. This is the style you'll probably lean on the most out of comfort. It hits hard, has a lot of interesting techniques and in general just feels the tankiest.Gunman is there to mop up mainly as anything remotely threatening can rush you down far too fist. You're either spamming bullets or throwing special ammo repeatedly, which can be a drain on resources. If special ammo stood out a bit better, it'd at least have a fighting chance compared to Swordsman. As it stands though, it's only good to invest in its tree in order to unlock the cannon, which is just too goofy of a weapon to not at least give a try.Wild Dancer combines both weapons, which leads to a fighting style that's fast, low-damage for either weapon, and primarily defends itself through dodges and very narrow parries. It's main use is for dealing with a lot of enemies at one time, since enemy AI loves to attack you in the back while you're using Swordsman.None of it particularly wows me. One of the greatest features of the Yakuza/LAD/Judgement series was that you had plenty of ways to spice up combat. Mainly heat actions and building out a skilltree that organically complements that past few unlocks. In LAD Ishin though, it's a mixture of stat boosts, attack speeds, Heat action unlocks and maybe a couple of actual interesting systems thrown in like a disarm or a combo rush move extension. It's nowhere near as interesting as Yakuza 0, which I will admit to be an unfair comparison.The cards system isn't bad, but it's rather forgettable. Damage skills really don't do as much damage as they ought to (even the overpowered lvl99 ones you get from that free Youtuber DLC), and the damage buffs don't seem to do a whole lot either. The best use I got out of them were the free heals, which took the pressure entirely off of any healing items in my inventory. The system's not a detriment, but for how flashy it looks and predominant a place it takes in the UI, it sure doesn't feel very significant.Ultimately I would say that you can do much, much better than this if you're looking for an RGG game on PC. Both Judgement games are stellar, the mainline Yakuza series maybe gets a little rough at its numerical middle, but feels like a heartwarming epoch when you finally finish Y6. Yakuza LAD is absolutely GOATed, too.LAD Ishin doesn't tarnish my faith in RGG. I'm more than confident that the two new games coming out are going to be beyond stellar, and I honestly can't wait.

_childDocuments_.review: Remember a few years ago when Deus Ex tried to sell single use skill point microtransactions in a single player game and it went so poorly for them they never made another game in the franchise? Well here we have the same thing happening again but they're trying to keep it quiet to avoid the inevitable backlash. Just to be clear, it isn't single use per save. It's one use ever. That alone isn't the reason for a negative review though it certainly puts the game in a bad standing. The fact they also increased the games price after release also doesn't help the game much when talking about the game's value. If you haven't played all the other games in the franchise I would recommend literally any of them over this for the price to content/quality ratio. Also since this is a kinda fan service throwback game a lot of the references to characters will be lost if you haven't played at least the main Yakuza franchise without the spin offs. Then you also have the stuttering and 30fps lock in cutscenes, boring repetitive substories, then incredibly grindy crafting mechanics. Every new action requires the game to render the shader for the animation. (Not too dissimilar to the issues The Callisto Protocol had/has on release) This means the game will stutter every time a new animation is played for the first time. So every heat move, every unique boss battle, every time you use a new weapon with a new glow on it. The game can be running a solid framerate without ever dropping in gameplay but then stutters like crazy for anything new. It basically ruins any interesting boss battle. "Oh they're doing something cool... oh I missed it because the game was stuttering... I can only hope they do it a second time or I'll never know what happened." This also happens in the 30fps cutscenes... so playing it a second time for NG+ you won't have these issues but you also won't have any of the dlc you paid for (including what you got from the deluxe version.) Then the lacklustre substories. At this point I've played pretty much every game in the franchise plus the spin off games and I honestly can't think of any game that had so many boring repetitive substories. So many are just you come across a person, they want an item, you give them an item, wait a minute later and give them the same item again, repeat 10 times and that's a substory complete. There's not even a unique interaction every time you give them something outside of the first interaction and the final item. This is the vast majority of substories. This isn't the maxing out a shop owner either, which feels like it takes a lot more transactions than it does in previous games as well. There are a few unique substories but they feel so rare. This makes the substory from zero about getting toys from the claw machine for the little girl look like a breath of fresh air since you actually have to do something before you return and do the same task again and again. Then the crafting. Honestly playing on hard, just ignore it. The whole mechanic is so grindy for so little reward it isn't worth the effort. It feels like something that's there just for NG+ and the new difficulties that come with it where everything has it's numbers bloated. You can buy weapons very early on that are better than 3/4th's of the swords you can craft. Then you're given weapons through main story battles so you never need to craft anything yourself. It requires so much money to level up the crafting to be able to make something better than what you can already buy elsewhere then the costs to build stuff is crazy. You do get 200 ryo for completing the game which will offset a lot of the costs, hence it feels like a NG+ thing. Also I dread to think how much grinding you would have to do in the battle dungeons to unlock all the materials you would need to craft anything worthwhile. All in all outside of the main quest and the minigames there isn't much in this game to recommend. In previous games the substories were some of the best parts. They were always so crazy and unique almost every time whereas in this they're all so mundane and they feel so copy and pasted in what you have to do. The game has performance issues which we're still waiting on getting fixed. Then the monetisation of the game is questionable at best. If you really want to play the game I would wait until a deep sale, maybe by that point the game will have it's performance patched so its enjoyable to play on the first run not just the second. Also if you do play I'd highly recommend getting a trainer, something like WeMod or something, in order to get what you would get from the paid consumable dlc for free. It would also remove the grinding if you really wanted to craft something for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin is another great release from RGG Studio. In the past, changes in platform/engine have had combat that just doesn't feel right (Yakuza 3 & 6), whereas their first entry using Unreal Engine 5 feels amazing to play and is spectacularly beautiful. I thoroughly enjoyed the more in depth sword combat and the revolver with infinite bullets. The story is fantastic and gives a (dramatised) insight into the issues and politics of Bakumatsu Japan. The substories are as hilarious as always and there are a plethora of minigames to enjoy.I did have a few gripes however. I loved the addition of the new characters, but was disappointed when some didn't have Ishin versions of their music but instead played the original track. In addition, the implementation of the relationship system is really boring, as all you need to do is  hand an item to someone and reload the area, just to get the same dialogue 10 times before ending with the "relationship" with a different scene. Furthermore, after 40 hours without crashing, my game closed right as the end credits finished, but before I got a clear save to start Premium Adventure, which was quite disappointing.All in all, I really enjoyed Ishin, and despite comfortably playing other RGG games on hard, it was quite challenging this time around, which was quite fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game expecting a Yakuzah opus situated in feudal Japan. And while there is a lot less humor, it's still quite similar: Lots of side missions, mini-games and stories that give life to the ingame world (the udon minigame is stressful but fun). The cinematics and the story are just as good.But after 10 hours of playing, I have to admit it:The combat system is simply and purely catastrophic.In a serie known for its over-the-top fights, what we have there is below mediocre; The fighting styles rank from useless to barely passable : -Brawler style, useless except for picking up the few tools you can use (then you quickly realize they do less damage than your weapons.)-Swordmaster style, kinda usable against mobs, not really against bosses. Stiff and unresponsive.-Gun style, button-mashing cheese. Game is too hard ? Walk backwards and go pew pew pew.-Wild dancer style, the most useful one (not saying much), At least, allows you to quickly dodge.Another problem shared by all styles : they're all boring to use, even with unlocked skills. Same with the Heat actions : you either go *slash* or *bang*, nothing extraordinary or original. Even Way of the samurai 4 on the PS3 has a more interesting and complete fighting system.Add to that weird pauses when doing actions like picking up items or clicking in the menu and you get a game that's only interesting during cinematics. So you might as well watch a movie.
