_childDocuments_.review: Overall Score : 9/10Verdict: An amazing story, great visuals and great LaD gameplay.Review:Oh man.I feel like I have to say that, aside from 2 hours in Kiwami 2 this is my first Yakuza game and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ man I wasnt prepared.WritingI've played a load of games with sub-par/almost non-existant storylines recently so this game was a massive, massive breath of fresh air. The level of writing in this game is on par with some of the best movies I've seen. You can definently feel the level of care put into this series as i've heard the story of the other games is equally as, if not even better than this. _childDocuments_.review: I still have this very special connection to Ishin serving as a sort of departures from modernity into a world that stands at a crossroads of what has been and what is. The feudal Japanese setting made it feel special and calming even. This remake of the original Ryu Ga Gotoku: Ishin! enables Westerners to immerse themselves into a beautiful Japanese world that appears familiar to players of the LAD franchise, and due to its 19th century setting, while at the same time feeling distant due to the traditional Japanese customs and difference from those games of the series that are set in modern Japan. The accordance of distance and nearness creates an amazing setting.The combat was fun albeit it had poor hitboxes. Often, Ryoma doesn't even visually touch the enemy for it to count as a hit, or the weapon swing isn't even executed yet, but the hit already connected. Other than that, the combat can feel very fluid and fancy or heavy and methodic.The story was very interesting and full of exciting political intrigue. It felt special to see Kiryu's face actually do some important political ♥♥♥♥ and kill people. Without spoiling too much, you are not looking at a historically 100% accurate depiction of Sakamoto Ryoma's life during the Meiji Restoration, but instead at a fanfiction of a cooler version of Sakamoto Ryoma by a very talented author. The grind, as usual, is terrible, not respectful of the player's time and agonisingly slow.I have played the game for about 75 hours, and have not 100%ed a single of the four fighting styles. If you strive for 100% completion on Steam, don't. The game, like most LAD games, is littered with nonsensical quests, heaps of minigames out of which not all are fun or based on luck, and to complete the Blacksmith you are forced to loot so many more enemies or do so many more missions of the same to collect enough loot to craft everything. _childDocuments_.review: As always with the Yakuza series, you promise that it will be the last because this is always the same gameplay loop with weird and somewhat broken (but fun) gameplay, the same characters and plot strings with annoying encounters in the street and blurry graphics...but after one or two hours you are just trapped in the game and you cannot leave it until the end !I mean, the overall direction and story (even if the somewhat always the same) are enthralling and the characters (which are also the same archetypes) are so charismatic that you forget everything else. The side quests, not that great in this episode but still good, even if very limited in terms of gameplay builds a great atmosphere and all contribute to the immersion in this period. To sum up the plot and characters, they are really similar to Yakuza 1 which was one of my favorite (plus Majima, here Soji, was a normal character and not a complete clown in this episode).Anyway, the greatest strenght of the game is the same as all games in the series : the pacing which is very wall balanced to make you play a substantial adventure without make you become tired. I would say that Ishin is a bit better than many episodes because it started from zero, without having to carry the weird dramas like Y5,6 etc.The atcivities are various, with many typical ones (karaoke, fishing, shogi...) with some new ones (like chicken racing, farming), not the best in the series and generally average but they help to balance.The fights are not as messy as late PS3-engine games (Y3, Y0, YK) but the styles are really really unbalanced. WIth some ennemies at the end, you can use all of them, but for the most part swordsman is the most effective stance. At the end Sword gameplay is not as intense as brawlers styles of classical episodes but this is less messy. Add it to average boss fights and you get an OK game. The powers added by you infantry (because you are a captain) are a nice addition to help making the fights less bland.FInally, graphics are great for the main characters but blurry for the buildings, etc. The best way to greatly improve it to make them sharp enough is to play with DLDSR (x2.28 makes the game clean, not impressive at all, but sharp enough).To sum up, Ishin is a typical Yakuza games with many flaws in the gameplay and with "unbelievable" plot strings (I mean litterally) but with the same magic that makes you play from the begining to the end, guided by the desire to see what will happen in the next chapter. The only thing that was a bit frustrating in this game, aside from the annoying goons in the street (like in every game, but here it is hard to skip them) was the inability to get enough money and the inability to spend in in meaningful things. You start to earn money at the end with fights while farming gives you almost nothing. Aside from that, if you like Yakuza (even if you promise that it will be the last...I personnaly started with Y1 on PS2 and played all of them since), you will like it for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin!A flawed gem.This game does a lot right and for the most part, is pretty damn fun. Unfortunately it gets a lot wrong and there are some big misses as well. To wit;---Graphics - 7.5/10 || The remaster of the 2014 original release looks pretty good on modern hardware cranked up, but it's obviously just that, a remaster. I wouldn't consider this a full-blown remake in any sense of the word in terms of graphical fidelity. It's still very dated overall in appearance and art direction - regardless of this game being a period piece of feudal Japan, or not. It's not amazing, nor is it abhorrent in it's appearance either. Just solid.Performance - 7/10 || The biggest universal complaint you're going to hear from just about anyone who has played this game on PC is the God-awful shader caching issues that accompanied the release client (v1.02). RGG/SEGA is supposedly working on a patch to address this in due time, but who really knows when that will be as historically they're beyond terrible at supporting their products on PC in a timely fashion, if at all, as numerous games in the Yakuza universe on PC are still fundamentally broken for many people - just go take a look at the massive bug-reporting threads on any entry for proof of concept.With the shader-cache issues out of the way, once those are actually built, the game indeed runs quite well for the most part. I had the settings cranked to the absolute max with FSR on Ultra-Quality and unless I was in the middle of town with tons of NPCs roaming around, I barely ever dipped from the enforced 120FPS cap. Just have to build that pesky shader-cache first. This even occurs during the locked 30FPS cutscenes, so theres really no getting away from it. I'd advise anyone on the fence about experiencing this game to simply wait until this has been addressed as it can really break your immersion in whats going on.I also surprisingly enough didn't have a single game breaking bug or crash in any capacity in the 60 or so hours it took me to finish the game. Which is extremely impressive considering RGG's track record at this point for these games on PC.i76800K 4.0 OC'd32G DDR41080 STRIXGameplay - 7.5/10 || The gameplay is pretty fun in Ishin for the most part. Combat feels fantastic once you get your styles leveled up and is the closest thing you're going to get to Yakuza 0 since, well, Yakuza 0. Some styles obviously fair better then others but with some research and grinding you can make anything viable. I ended up making the gun-style extremely busted by the end of my first playthrough, making enemies essentially trivial. Brawler funny enough also ended up being extremely powerful once I had the right gear - it can make any combat encounter in the game an absolute joke with the heat actions it has access to.On heat actions in this game specifically - these are some of the best in the franchise to date, mainline entry or not. They're animated well, and many of them suit combat situations perfectly. I was very impressed with these this time around.Theres also plenty to do when you're not cutting down people too, being a Yakuza game after all, this time with a feudal Japanese touch. Singing, dancing, tests of skill, having a woman of ill repute play rock-paper-scissors with you, just to name a few. They're all pretty entertaining, funny, and a nice breath of fresh air from what we've been doing in modern-day Tokyo all these years.The biggest negative/black mark on this game in general besides the shader-cache woes when it comes down to it is how exceedingly grind-heavy certain aspects of the game are, and the absolutely ATROCIOUS balancing in combat. Leveling late-game takes painfully long, the blacksmith aspect of the game is almost prohibitively expensive to level it up in order to get access to gear that makes an impactful difference on your character, and the difficultly level in combat relative to how much damage you do, and how much punishment enemies can take, is simply put, for lack of a better word, stupid.Enemies have dump-truck loads of HP, hit like trucks, and attack/dodge aggressively, even on normal. This was esp. apparent when I got into the Sanada Stronghold dungeons later in the game, when it was so brutal I actually ended up scumming it and switching to easy to be able to complete and farm it for materials I needed, to switch back to normal afterwards and finish the remainder of the game up on the mode I started on in the first place. I'm not sure I'm compelled to try Ishin mode if I ever force myself to get maximum stats as I've read even on the most basic of encounters you can essentially get 2-shot.Whoever designed the balancing of the combat system in this game needs to be relocated to a different task within RGG, or simply terminated. It's some of the worst I've seen in a video game in a very, very long time. It's awful. Being a game ultimately from 2014 is no excuse.Story - 9/10 || The story in this game is easily the best part. It's consistently compelling and will keep you enthralled from start to finish. Some really great characters with faces you know and love and some great twists. Thats all I'm going to touch on here for risk of spoiling something. For a game that was based on real individuals and events during a period of Feudal Japan, I can honestly say it had it's hooks in me more then any mainline Yakuza game, or Judgement, for that matter. It was absolutely fantastic.Sound - 7.5/10 || Nothing really to write home about here, that being said, RGG keeps the bangers coming on boss themes.Replay Value - Very High || The RGG standard fare, premium adventure, ultimate challenge, it's all there. If you really want to you can keep playing this game to your hearts content, esp. if you're trying to get Ryoma to maximum power with the leveling system.---A note on the DLC discourse:As I've called out in each and every single DLC release for this game in their own review sections;It's a black mark on RGG as a studio to make the DLC for this game -single-use- rather then account bound. It's abject garbage and an insult to the consumer. RGG needs to take a step back and see the serious disdain for this practice, and never do something like this again with any game they release, ever. I for one will -never- purchase another piece of DLC for any RGG product in the future if something so hilariously out of touch gets executed again. Unacceptable.---In closing, Like a Dragon: Ishin! is a very fun, if allbeit dated journey with some technical/design issues. If you're a Yakuza universe fan, you're probably going to love it all the same. I'd wait until the shader-cache issues get fixed as to not interfere with your immersion and the experience before making the commitment.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: As far as RGG games go, this one has a decent story, not their best, but not their worst. I think the first 80% of the story is really engaging but then the ending I started losing interest.It has good gameplay and a good upgrade system, but there are blemishes like Brawler style being under-powered and very difficult to scale up its damage (Tiger Drop is still very good, and its easy to crowd control with Brawler since every finisher make just about any enemy fall down). Another gameplay issue is how you're either under-powered from not making enough weapon/armor upgrades, or you are overpowered and the game is easy for 99% of encounters except bosses, because you quickly just grind'd and made all the best stuff fairly early on. It never feels tightly balanced.The setting is awesome and unique. The main hub is really good, filled with great side content as usual. The new setting specific minigames like the farm, cooking, and deliveries are great. The dungeon mini-game is pretty good too, good for grinding xp/materials plus it has some good boss fights. The world looks really good and authentic and is a great change of pace from modern Japan. Adding the Troop cards to the whole game was probably a mistake. Adding influencers cards to it was very weird, felt like Sega of America meddling in RGG's original design. Saw a mini-doc on Ishin Kiwami's development and it seems like RGG had to set SoA straight a few times because they went off the rails, the cards is an example of that and I think RGG should have stopped them from adding them. I don't really like or hate the cards gameplay-wise, but I'd just prefer if they weren't there at all.The port was not perfect, some heat actions lag the first time you use them and then get better after use #2 and beyond. Some cutscenes are locked to 30 fps for some mind boggling reason. Some minigames are locked to 30 or 60, which seems understandable given how high fps broke other RGG PS3 games in the 3/4/5 remasters.On the RGG scale of 1 to 10, I'd give it an 8. I wish the ending was better and I wish the combat was more balanced, because it was just too easy if you finish the side dungeon content during your playthrough, since doing that gives you all the materials you need for all the insanely OP weapons/armor.

From what I can tell, on higher difficulties, the game doesn't make the enemies super tanky, it makes you very easy to kill which I think causes a lot of great adrenaline inducing moments as you hang on to a tiny amount of health waiting for one of your healing cards to recharge as the enemies try and hit you. The story is excellent and the members of the Shinsengumi are mostly very interesting. Not my favourite RGG game (that one still goes to Judgment) but still up there as one of my favourites and the idea to make Legend difficulty available from the start is a brilliant change.

Ishin is a love letter to the fans and the series as a whole in almost every single regard, and you owe it to yourself to play it for that reason alone. _childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of heart and sincerity, much like what people have come to expect from these games, but it also does a lot to set itself apart from your traditional Yakuza experience. About a day before I picked up Ishin I finished Yakuza 0 for the first time, and oh man am I in love. I enjoyed Yakuza 0 but I had a lot of problems with it that this game fixes entirely for me.If Yakuza 0 is more of a beat-em-up River City-esque game in a 3D space I would say Ishin! is an Action-RPG with brawler roots. Potentially this might turn off some fans of the series but I'd like to run down a list of things that really set this game apart for me: -New abilities are no longer paid for with money. Using your different styles levels them up and allows you to spend orbs on them to learn new abilities. This means that using your favorite styles rewards you by making them stronger, rather than grinding out a separate resource for them.-You can block or Parry out of almost any rush attack immediately which means that combat feels extremely responsive. Even if you are in the middle of an attack if you time your guards right you will cancel out of it and parry the enemy. Overall this makes the combat feel far more aggressive if you're able to pull it off consistently. -The heat gauge is no longer tied to unique moves on the different styles. This means that if you go for a tiger drop, or one of the other parry options you don't have to worry about where your heat gauge is relative to what you're able to do. I remember in Y0 there were some moves that were only usable at heat level 1/2/3 and this would lead to unnecessary clunkiness. The heat gauge is now almost strictly used for Heat Actions and each style's 'Ultimate' attack. It no longer drains in combat either, but it goes up a little slower, which makes heat items a little more valuable. -The enemy variety is good, and the styles have more niche uses. There are by far more enemy types in this game that demand you to pay attention to their movesets a little more than normal. The minibosses also all feel by far more unique than anything I encountered in Y0. Even between enemies using katanas you'll notice there are 4+ different stances they'll take that change up their movesets.-There is a monster hunter-esque weapon tree for the 5 different weapon types and armors in the game that require you to farm materials from different places along with a weapon quality and enhancement system using different gem sockets to further customize your play style. There are some +5% skills here and there, but there is also a mix of unique modifers that change how some things in combat function, like a special glove passive that allows you to block with brawler and gunslinger syles for example.-The trooper cards aren't too obtrusive and you're not required to use them, but I think they're fun an add another layer of customization to the game. I don't mind pouring over their active and passive effects, and so far there seems to be a decent amount of configurations therein. I can see why they would turn someone off, but they just add another layer of depth to the game for me. As for actual combat challenges there are now dungeons to explore that drop loot, different weapons, and allow you to further level up your styles and character. If you enjoy the combat you can now more freely just engage with these combat encounters alongside the arena with special boss fights as well. If you ever felt there wasn't enough ways to just jump into Yakuza's combat and try out your new moves on mooks and bosses alike this game really rectifies that in multiple ways.There is a lot going on with this game that makes it hard to cover everything. The locales are all bright and colorful. They feel lively and well put together. The CP system is gone in favor of a more easily accessible Virtue system that gives you points for pretty much everything you do, meaning you no longer have to seek out to do specific tasks in order to access the meta-progression systems. The mini-games are all rather fun. Some returning, and some new. I particularly like the farming and cooking mini-games that function as this game's primary money-making activity. The substories are still a mix of silly and touching. Some are better than others, but none of them feel outright bad. The story and setting are a huge draw for anyone who misses old games like Way of the Samurai, and similar life sim-esque games. The cast is extremely strong, obviously there are a lot of character 'cameos' in a sense that historical figures are replaced by Yakuza character models and voice actors. Also you can finally quit the game from the pause menu rather than having to go back to the title screen or hitting alt+F4. You can save anywhere, so you're no longer stuck having to run to phone booths or being stuck in longer stretches of gameplay without a way to save. If some of these QoL features are in later titles I wouldn't know, but they stuck out to me in particular jumping right in from Y0.There is a problem with this game's shader optimization. You WILL get a lot of microstutters in the beginning of the game until it finishes building a shader cache, but once it's done it runs extremely well. This game might be a strong contender for my personal game of the year, but we'll see what the rest of the year holds. Well worth the asking price for me. Even if you're not a fan of Yakuza, or you bounced off of the other ones, give it a shot on sale maybe.

_childDocuments_.review: I found  to be a bit of a mixed bag, but would recommend . is a remake of 2014's Playstation and Japan exclusive , which is a samurai-themed spin-off of the main / series.The action moves from modern day Kamurocho to Kyoto during the  period of the 1860s. This was a pivotal point in Japanese history, as it led to the overthrow of the Bakufu military government, the Meiji Restoration and ultimately, the modernisation of the country. We play as Sakamoto Ryoma, a ronin searching for his foster father's murderer. Ryoma travels to Kyoto and discovers that the killer is among the leaders of a notorious Bakufu-organised police force, known as the Shinsengumi. Ryoma is forced to infiltrate the organisation in order to find the culprit.Ryoma has the likeness and voice actor of Kiryu and several other series mainstays appear in alter-ego form, such as Majima, Akiyama, Saejima, etc. Many of the characters are loosely based on real-life historical figures and the game has some fun with this set-up.As in any  game, you can engage in a variety of mini-games, such as Karaoke, Gambling, Fishing, Mahjong, etc.  also has a few unique side activities in the form of "Another Life", where you manage a farm and "Battle Dungeons" where you fight through a series of labyrinths to gain rewards in the form of XP, money and crafting items.Fighting styles return and Ryoma has 4 options to choose from: Brawler, Swordsman, Gunman and Wild Dancer (a combination of Sword/Gun styles).-I found the historical setting to be very engaging to the point that I was inspired to read-up more on the real-life events.-It feels like a tribute to the  series as a whole. There's fan service aplenty and long-time fans will get a kick out of seeing some of the returning faces from past games, like Nishiki, Ryuji Goda, Mine, Kuze and Awano, along with some more obscure ones.-As in all games in the series, the music and voice acting are top notch. Some iconic series themes make a reappearance in remixed form.-"Another Life" is a fairly chilled out diversion from the main game, where you can grow and sell vegetables on your farm and cook meals with Haruka, as part of a side story where you need to raise money to pay off her debts.-Karaoke as always is thoroughly enjoyable - there's a few other interesting mini-games like the buyo dancing, running the noodle shop and cannonball training.-Some of the substories are up with the usual  fare of zany and surreal - the "Ee ja nai ka" series comes to mind. There's some neat references to real-life figures like Natsume Soseki as well, helping to reinforce the historical setting.-"Majima" aka Okita Souji, plays a prominent role in the game.-The story definitely loses its way in the 2nd half - without spoiling too much, there's one particular plot twist mechanic that gets overused.-The Battle Dungeons are a real drag to play through. They tend to be filled with lots of spongy enemies and can be quite difficult to navigate. They're also required if you want to fully engage with the game's crafting systems. I think there's 40 of them in total to play through, but honestly I lost interest after the first batch.-Speaking of which, crafting the best weapons and gear is going to take a hell of a lot of grinding. The top end items will cost obscene amounts of money, not to mention all the materials you'll need.-Combat in general feels quite stiff (especially coming off of ) and I found I only used 2 of the fighting styles regularly. Gunman is very situational and Brawler simply doesn't do enough damage.-One of the most controversial changes implemented in this remake is the implementation of the Trooper cards system outside of the Battle Dungeons.  Damage and health values have been adjusted for both Ryoma and enemies to account for this and use of the cards feels essential to avoid every fight turning into a long, drawn-out slog. Many bosses will now have "super moves" that can quickly drain your health as well.-Many of the substories are really lacklustre - so many of them revolve around bringing a character X number of items (usually vegetables) to complete a friendship and they're so tedious to play through.-There's not a huge variety of mini-games, unless you happen to enjoy gambling!While I'm glad I played  and generally enjoyed my time with it, I found it to be one of the weaker entries in the series and it's definitely not worth it at a full price of €60 (or your regional equivalent).Any fans of the series should enjoy the callbacks and nods to previous games and it's worth a run through the main story. I'd advise anyone interested to temper their expectations though -  does suffer from some frustrating mechanics and unless you're a masochist, a Completionist playthrough should be avoided.

_childDocuments_.review: The 2023 remake of Like a Dragon: Ishin! brings a fan favorite entry in the series I will continue to call Yakuza to international players for the first time, albeit with a Kiwami-style treatment. Ishin eschews the normal crime drama of contemporary urban Japan in favor of an Edo period samurai drama with the roles played by major characters from the rest of the series. This change in setting makes for a nice change of pace, even if Kyo is awkwardly structured. This game also lets you switch between different combat styles on the fly a la Yakuza 0, and these new styles are for the most part quite fun to play. The new Another Life side activity also adds a nice, slower-paced farming sim-esque component to the game. Otherwise, this is Yakuza, with all that that entails.Ultimately, I find myself preferring the series' more typical tropes, but this is a very worthwhile detour if it at all intrigues you.

_childDocuments_.review: i love the LAD games, but definitely skip this one. major problems abound, including:1. so, much. grind. the game's reliance on skill tree upgrades to increase combat damage is good, but all but one of the styles rely on weapon damage to bring damage up to snuff as well. how do you get good weapons? grind hundreds of thousands of units of currency, collect materials on stacked rng systems, and you'll still feel like you hit like a wet noodle. why? well, that brings up complaint 2 and 3.2. brawler. just as a fighting style. has some of the most useful counters and heat actions in the game but does utter garbage for damage. even the tiger drop is generally useless in this game, but fully leveling the style is necessary for major sections of side content (as well as essential upgrades like faster heat build, quickly changing styles, and health upgrades)3. the engine and combat. like a dragon: ishin! was remade by a studio that is not RGGStudios, and consequently, they didn't use any of RGG's in-house engines like the dragon engine or yakuza 5's engine (the engine that the original ishin!, yakuza 0, kiwami, and of course yakuza 5's gameplay are based on). for gameplay this means two things: firstly, juggles are gone. completely gone. enemies do not bounce off of walls or the floor, enemies can't be cornered for long combos, etc. secondly, the rules of engagement are completely screwed up; frequently bosses and enemies will turn around during a backturned rush combo, resulting in frustratingly inconsistent damage opportunities. all of this compounds with the following...4. you feel weak. damage always feels too low, and enemy damage always feels punishingly high. the only way to remedy this seems to be dropping the difficulty down, but as someone who has played many many past LAD games on hard or even legend difficulties, it is a stark and frustrating difference. only a few mistakes can result in complete failure, but your damage is so low and your combos so slow, damage windows so inconsistent, that playing the game itself feels like spinning a slot machine. in conclusion: this game sucks, play literally any other LAD/RGG/Yakuza game to have an infinitely better time. if you're a newcomer, play yakuza 0. peace

_childDocuments_.review: So, I've unreviewed and re-reviewed this game a bunch of times.I love this game, but I have minor nitpicks with this remake itself.History time, this game is actually a remake of a Japanese-only PS4 game of the same name, with some changes. The original game was released around the same time as Yakuza 0, so if you're wondering why some things look similar, that's why, a lot of the face actors are the same people. Pretty much every familiar face is all based off a specific person, like Bacchus for example is based off a real person.Trooper Cards used to only apply in battle dungeons, now they apply everywhere, but the game isn't balanced around it so they break the game outside of battle dungeons. In the original game there were food bonuses instead, that provided passive stat buffs, but they weren't as high.Randomized affixes were turned into seals, at original launch of the remake people complained about them being less varied, turns out the drop rates were ♥♥♥♥♥♥, this got fixed. Almost all of the affixes now exist as seals, which can be collected and used as you please, rather than being even more at the mercy of RNG.The crafting system in general was reworked, with weapon paths being more cleanly displayed, and the single timed button press "minigame" being removed. That being said, it's still cryptic as ♥♥♥♥ where to find the dude who lets you make magical weapons. He's in Mukurogai, if you didn't check.The battle styles were reworked slightly, as in Gunner was changed, but not nerfed. In the original, gunner's attack speed was relatively constant, allowing for run and gun, and it was actually pretty powerful, because knockdowns are a mechanic. In the remake, shot speed is tied to movement, if you stand still, you fire faster. The actual DPS is about the same, but now you play as a turret. Wild Dancer still works if you like run and gun.Brawler always did the damage of a wet noodle because you were expected to use affixes or seals to improve Brawler, use the Fundoshi you get after the Ryuji fight, it multiplies your brawler damage pretty high. However, if you don't like this, I recommend using a mod that changes brawler damage, they exist already. The Yakuza/LaD/Judgment modding community is very active, and Ishin got a lot of good mods close to release. The modding discord is a friendly place filled with a lot of people who put effort into their projects.The story is very loosely based off Japanese history, so if you want to complain about the story, it's basically the TV Soap Opera version of the very real legacy of Sakamoto Ryoma. All of the characters are based off people in that era, but played by face actors who played people in the main Like A Dragon series.The top review complains about how sidequests work, Only an admittedly sizable fraction of the quests use it, and the friendship system isn't new, it's actually used in a ton of the later numbered Yakuza games, as well as Yakuza 0, but is also used in Judgment, and in my opinion, Judgment handles that system the best.I actually like the battle dungeons, they have problems but I just like actually having long encounters in these games that aren't apart of the story, where you move through a big area. The Kiwami 2 bouncer missions are similar, and I like those too.All this being said, I do think the price is too high for a remake that isn't terribly expanded over the original. This game has about the same amount of non-dungeon content as Judgment, which is reasonably priced on PC, and is also based off the PS5 remaster, similar to how this game is based off the PS5 remake.The game had some shader stutter on release, but it's not as bad now. There's a hidden DX11 mode that might help you avoid shader stutter if you get it.8/10, not the best Like A Dragon game overall, but I like it and it's worthy of being put up next to the others.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the series who has played every game available, even down to emulation, LAD: Ishin is something I'd say you need to buy only when its on sale.First, the positives. The setting is very unique for these games, and the combat can be just as satisfying and punchy as the mainline entries. The story is enjoyable, with its fair share of twists and turns, and the side content is as stacked as usual.This game, however, has obvious negatives that originate from both its status as a SEGA branded rerelease, and as an experimental series entry. The combat having 4 styles is nice, but only two are properly balanced, Swordsman and Wild Dancer. Swordsman suffers from godawful combo speed in the early game, and Wild Dance not having a proper guard sucks. The other two options, Gunman and Brawler, are on different ends of the usefulness scale. Gunman is far too easy to abuse, even in the early game, and tears through most non-hyper armor encounters. Brawler, by contrast, despite having all of the previous Komaki tech, does no damage unless you equip items that heavily buff the style. Boss fights also suck, as they utilize way more hyper armor than the original game, which makes them wars of attrition, and even ruins the drama of certain boss fights (looking at you final boss).The graphics make it really obvious that this is the RGG team's first delving into the Unreal engine. While I do agree it was necessary in order to better portray the more naturalistic tone of this entry, it comes with all the traditional issues of shader compilation stuttering and fps slowdown, along with low res textures. Side Content is probably where the experimental aspects of Ishin shine through, for better and for worse. On the one hand, currency for side content completion and Friendships are cool. On the other hand, most Friendships are either lengthier repeat fetch quests, or merely reskinned completion parameters, such as money spent on stores. The content centering around the home is cool, but either incredibly repetitive (farming and cooking) or fetch quests. AGAIN. The crafting system is probably the worst part though. The original game had sane costs for upgrading weapons, but the material grind did suck. Here, money required has increased one hundred fold (I am NOT kidding), and still keeps the old materials grind. The method by which you get these materials? Battle Dungeon. Which has higher enemy health pools than the original, necessitating use of the cards system, which clashes heavily with the more grounded themes of this game, and also alters the base game's content (reducing skill wheel health upgrades to incentivize card use, which inadvertently makes content that locks off cards way harder) The battle dungeon was a big grind in the original, but here it might as well be a part time job for the player in the worst sense of the phrase. And the only way to grind out the cash requirements for this game is through the chicken race, which is a lengthy and hellish process. Just use mods if you're trying to 100%, unlike in other games, its just not worth it. All in all, Ishin is a clearly experimental franchise point both at the time of its initial PS4 debut, and now in its rerelease. The gameplay hasn't either aged well, or has been marred by the quality of this rerelease. Some concepts that come with this are cool in theory, but they just cannibalize the original game to be properly integrated. This isn't a bad game by any means, but it sure is one of the worst Yakuza games I've played, which should tell you all you need to know.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Ishin is an exceptional game that offers an incredible story and setting that will transport players to a different era. The game's narrative is beautifully crafted, and it tells the story of the samurai era in a way that will captivate players and keep them engaged throughout the entire experience.One of the most remarkable things about Like a Dragon Ishin is its setting. The game takes place during the Edo period in Japan, and the attention to detail is absolutely stunning. The streets and buildings are meticulously recreated to give players a true sense of what life was like during that time. From the architecture to the clothing, everything feels authentic and adds to the immersion of the game.The story itself is also exceptional. It follows the character of Sakamoto Ryoma, a real-life historical figure who played a significant role in shaping Japan's future. The game presents an alternate history that allows players to see what might have happened if certain events had unfolded differently. The writing is top-notch, and the characters are all well-developed, making the story feel like a compelling drama that players won't want to put down.Overall, Like a Dragon Ishin is an excellent game that delivers an exceptional story and setting that will transport players to a different time and place. The attention to detail and writing make this game an unforgettable experience that anyone should check out. It's truly a masterpiece of gaming and storytelling, and it deserves all the praise it gets.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you beat the last boss in Sekiro and go “I wish I was that guy”? Have you ever wanted to be in a Kurosawa film? Look no further.In Ishin, you too can be a Glock Saint in a samurai tale full to the brim of: love, revenge, secret techniques, secret identities, political plots, manly men yelling at each other, manly men crying at each other, manly men beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of each other, and epic one-on-one duels. And in between? Karaoke with the boys.Ishin is a Yakuza game through and through. And that is the best recommendation any game could ever receive.Unfortunately, there are some technical issues that hinder the experience. Partly due to the fact that the game is the first one made by them with the Unreal Engine. It’s a very good first effort but issues to show. Micro stuttering is definitely an issue throughout the game. Much more during the beginning but some will happen sporadically in cutscenes later in the game. The lighting in the game also has a couple miss steps. There are occasions where a character seems way too bright for an interior scene.Gameplay wise, the actual fighting can seem a little rough. Especially when you're using the gun where it seems like the game needs two to three shots to miss before it actually targets an enemy in a group. Smithing in this game is basically non-existent due to how grindy it is just to make stronger gear. However, on Normal difficulty, that's not an issue. The game will drop stronger gear sporadically after specific boss fights.The game is friendly to new players of the series since it's basically a side story. However, because they use faces from characters throughout the whole series as well as their theme songs, the game is much more appreciable for people who have played the other games.Still, if you can ignore the negatives (which is a pretty easy thing to do, in my opinion), you’ll have an awesome time with the game. Best OST of the series. One of the best stories in the series. Probably the best final fight in the series. Because of the issues, the highest I can give it objectively is an 8/10. If they can fix their stuttering and lighting (or if you can ignore it), 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Like A Dragon: Ishin is either the first Like a Dragon game in the West or the latest in a long line of a major franchises, depending on your view of the naming convention.  This was created by RGG Studio and they are well known for their “Yakuza” series, though that series is now named “Like a Dragon” which is a direct translation of the original series title, Ryu Ga Gotoku.However, Like A Dragon: Ishin, or Ishin as I’ll call it for brevity’s sake, is a stand-alone title, for the most part.  However, the connection to the entire Like A Dragon Franchise is important.  While this is a fresh new story in a new time period with new characters, every major character in Like A Dragon: Ishin uses a similar face to the rest of the Like A Dragon Series.  This might be the most important part of the game because for some it’s a little too on the nose, and for others, this is pure fan service, which is what fans of the series might enjoy.  Many characters who no longer are part of the larger franchise, appear once more in Ishin, and in many ways, this works. Seeing some of the great heroes' and villains' faces tell a new story is entertaining, however, there’s a bit of an uncanny valley for many of the characters.  It was often that I could tell that certain characters were people I knew, but sadly with a change in hairstyle and clothes it was hard to place them, again this is something some players may love, and some players may hate, and this time around it bothered me just enough that I feel like I should mention it. The one big negative though with this is that every character plays to type, meaning if the character is a villain in Like a Dragon as a whole, they’ll typically be a villain here, the same with the heroes.  While every character is different, it’s a shame that there wasn’t more of a mix between the heroes and villains of this story.That being said, the story told here is rather solid.  The game focuses on “Kiryu Kazuma”’s character Sakamoto Ryoma who is based on a rather famous historical character.  After a tumultuous first chapter (This is a Like a Dragon game after all), Sakamoto Ryoma adopts the name Saito Hajime.  Rurouni Kenshin fans will instantly perk up because that’s also a name of a major villain there, and sure enough both Ishin and Kenshin have characters based on the same historical character.The basis of most of Ishin’s story is rooted in historical facts.  Saito Hajime eventually joins the Shinsengumi, which is run by Kondo Isami, he’s befriended by Okita Soji (played by the same face as Majima Goro), and they are defending the Bakufu (shogunate).   This and much more of this story is based on historical fact.However Saito Hajime and Sakamoto Ryoma are not the same people, and a majority of the story is fictionalized, this is historical fiction, but similar to Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Like A Dragon: Ishin will make players more interested in the time period and the real characters behind this story.  Though Romance of the Three Kingdoms is a little more historically accurate, both of these are entertaining for the fictionalized accounts.The story in Ishin is mostly well-paced.  There is at least one chapter that just seems to have a minor reason for existing and the final chapter seems to load multiple unnecessary diversions for time, but overall, if players enjoy the typical Like a Dragon style, born from Yakuza movies, Ishin will feel right at home even if it’s based on the Samurai and the Bakumatsu time period (essentially the time period after the Black ships have arrived in Japan to “open up the country”).Sadly what is supposed to be the biggest twist in the story is given away almost immediately especially if players are familiar with Like A Dragon’s flow, but overall the story is well told and still will hold many surprises for fans of the series.  Though the story is only one of the major features of this franchise.  The combat will be where players are spending most of the time and in that Ishin is a little unstable.  The main draw of Ishin is to return to the Samurai time period, and that may make people think of a lot of sword fighting, but within the Bakumatsu time period, guns have entered into the mix.  The good news is Sakamoto Ryoma can use both, as well as combine them and use a bare-handed style as well.  That means there are four different fighting styles in the game, and each one feels different enough to be worth including.  Even the combination of sword and gun feels unique to both.  Bare-handed brawling against sword-wielding goons sounds dangerous, but there is an enhanced amount of defensive parry ability that helps offer a higher risk-reward structure in theory.In practice, however, Ishin boils down to two styles.  The sword is so powerful almost no other style is necessary, and there are only a few moments when the range is required.  The guns on the other hand can stun-lock large groups of enemies to the point where if players want to they can just rain fire down on enemies.  Ishin tries to balance this with enemies who have armor, which does weaken the gun’s power but just requires players to switch to the basic sword mode.  Bare-handed and the combined sword and gun style have neither the power nor the utility to be necessary and even though I tried my hardest to use the Barehanded mode, it’s a foolish move that will only make the game harder. Add in the fact that equipment exists in this universe and players will be able to get better guns and swords, and the focused styles also will provide more of the bonuses of either, there are only two of the four styles worth spending time with. This isn’t a negative per se, as long as you’re a player who is willing to accept that there are styles of fighting that have no purpose, but it’s a shame that the developer couldn’t balance the four styles to be more useful.As for the rest of Ishin, it has all the typical drapings of a Like a Dragon title.  Outlandish side stories, interesting characters, unique moments, a wonderful self-contained map, and a memorable location.  Mini-games return and with new additions added players will have everything from the classic Karaoke, mahjong, shogi, and casino games, to chicken racing and a Geisha set of mini-games that feels just explicit enough to make someone blush. But this is ultimately what a LIke a Dragon title is, which is also how Like a Dragon: Ishin has been sold.  Ishin was intended to tell a different story, and provide an odd form of fan service in that many characters already in the universe could return for one more game.  At times it feels almost like a play, with characters playing similar characters to their originals but telling a different story, but that’s also what makes this charming, it’s a chance to see new pairings, but also one more chance to fight Ryuji Goda, a chance to see an alternate history for Majima Goro, a chance for Kiryu Kazuma to hang out with friends once more and fight against a secret cabal once more. And in that, Like a Dragon Ishin succeeds.  It also succeeds in one other way.  As amazing as the Like a Dragon franchise is, many characters feel so well developed it’s hard for them to surprise characters once again, and Ishin allows a way to tell a new fresh story using characters fans are already quite familiar with.  Ishin is a breath of fresh air in that it can show there’s still a lot of life left in the Like a Dragon formula, even if it isn’t in a typical Like a Dragon game.   That’s perhaps Like a Dragon: Ishin’s strongest point, it’s the perfect game for someone who has played the entire franchise and wants to play a similar game, but not another of the main series entries.  And you know, I’m really happy to have played through this entire game and go another wonderful story out of it. 8/10 If you enjoyed this review, consider checking out my Youtube channel where I review games .

_childDocuments_.review: unfortunately, like a dragon: ishin might just be my least favorite RGG game. as a big fan of the yakuza games and having played through all of them including the judgment spin-offs, i can't help but feel disappointed by ishin and here's why:the plot:simultaneously rushed and very slow, which is quite a feat but nothing new in a yakuza game. even though i did enjoy most of it, the ending left a sour taste in my mouth - particularly the instance when the "puppet master" shows himself. not only was this moment rushed, it was incredibly jarring. he jumps in the middle of an emotional moment between two characters as the story is about to wrap up and acts like an absolute cartoon villain. i was actually flabbergasted by how terrible it was. you've got the whole nine yards: shows up out of thin air? check. machiavelic laugh? check. starts spewing his entire plan with a smug expression? check. pisses and ♥♥♥♥♥ himself when his plan takes a turn for the worst (surprise) in the matter of a few seconds? check. the yakuza games are notorious for having moments like these, but MAN this one was horribly executed especially because it's his first appearance in the story as well. combat:you've got four styles this time around: the swordsman, the wild dancer, gunsman and brawler. out of all of these, only the swordsman and wild dancer are actually useful in a fight. - the swordsman is the most frustrating style in probably the whole series. it's slow, clunky and you will fail to connect most of your attacks, but it deals the most damage. recommended for 1v1's against stronger enemies. - the wild dancer is very fun and also the only style you should really use throughout most of the game. even though it's very fast and flashy, it lacks any substance. after you've unlocked a specific rush combo ability, you will be able to mash the dodge and the basic attack button through literally ANY enemy in the game which becomes boring very fast. - gunman: you shoot guns. that's it. you don't even have to reload! just run away and shoot them at a distance (if they don't deflect the bullets).  - brawler: even though it can get very fun, it hardly does any damage. i could kill my enemies faster with words of affirmation than with my fists in this game. shucks.overall a very frustrating experience. enemies will hit you anyway after failing to connect their attacks, your swords will go through them and not do damage at all, the list goes on. crafting:the blacksmith is a very interesting mechanic that sadly falls short. you've got these massive trees to craft different kinds of swords but all of that becomes trivial when you realize the game hands you over much stronger swords by simply completing the main quests. what's the point of grinding in the dungeons, collecting materials and saving money only to get a better sword anyway by just progressing through the story? i spent around 5-6 hours gathering everything i needed to craft a good sword only to get a much stronger one for free an hour later. the music:both the new songs and the remixed ones from past games sound great and they're one of the strongest points in this game. unfortunately, RGG had the bright idea of reusing awano and kuze's theme for their respective boss fights here. why not just remix them and turn them into their own thing? what's the point of reusing them? i'm not sure if it was laziness or fan-service but either way i didn't like much of that.conclusion:if you're a die-hard fan of these games, try this one out. the cinematics are still very entertaining and every character has the charm and presence you'd expect, so everything will still feel very familiar - but do be prepared for the worst features of every yakuza game to be present here and dialed to 11.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! Is a perfect standalone experience to get yourself into the Like a Dragon franchise. You do not need to know any of the other extensive personalities that surround the franchise and can perfectly stand on its own without its older brothers. There is little to complain about when it comes to this game outside of a few gripes when it comes to balancing and one hundred percent completion. There are four unique fighting styles you can experience, however to be frank you'll most likely use two out of the four extensively and towards the end of the game just one due to how broken it is. The mini-games in this collection are great and can keep you busy for hours if the dramatic story becomes too much for you to handle and you need a break. You can do anything between fishing, working at a noodle shop, hunting down bounties, the infamous mahjong that Like a Dragon is known for within the community and plenty more. The story is a fantastic setting set within 1860s Japan during the Bakumatsu era at the end of the Edo period. You play as Sakamoto Ryoma a real-life historical figure who gets tangled in his own revenge scheme, finds himself embroiled in the tumultuous socio-political climate of the era. I have left out countless activities and didn't even mention the RPG like leveling up system, down to the blacksmith where you can upgrade your weapons and armor.If you like feudal japan settings, drama, RPG like qualities, goofiness within minigames, and can look beyond a few questionable balance choices! You will undoubtedly find a fantastic time within Like A Dragon: Ishin! PS: Okita Soji is husband.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin! Follows the same structure as the rest of the Yakuza games, there’s a lot of story and narrative, most of which you can skip if that’s your thing, and there’s an open world to explore as well, in this open world there’s a ton of different activities to complete, from interesting side quests that range from generic to some being pretty interesting in their stories, to other activities involving a set of challenges to complete, like dungeons filled with enemies to defeat, or target practices.There are restaurants, karaoke games, and a sort of different neighbourhoods all with their own unique styles and people; there’s the marginalized areas that are mostly riddled with crime, whilst there are others that are filled with dojos and temples in which to train and interact with a multitude of characters from the main narrative.Overall, it’s a pretty darn good game, but there are issues when it comes to the pacing of the game, and some of the combat, which in a lot of aspects is a step back from other Yakuza games, but I wouldn’t personally say I found it to be bad; the combat here is much more focused, it asks you to choose from four different styles, some that prioritize melee unarmed combat, others that combine your swordsmanship and gunplay, and even one unique one that makes you a master gunman. Generally, these are all fun to use, but you’ll have to make a choice as to what interests you the most to level up and focus on. There are also a ton of different dojos and trainers that are specific to your abilities, so you’ll want to progress their stories in order to get better and better combat skills. In the end you get a new game plus mode which is a staple of the franchise -thankfully-, and there’s even the option to respect your points to prestige them and get better buffs to your core abilities. Definitely recommend this game, but know that it can be quite slow at times, specially at the beginning and with its narrative presentation, but the world, activities, and combat make for it more than enough.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a mediocre version of a great game. They ported the original engine into Unreal Engine which introduced a lot of jankiness and bugs and general graphics inconsistencies which really bug me after playing the original version previously. I really wish they just ported the original version instead.For the story, it definitely will help to have some knowledge of the Meiji Restoration period otherwise there are a lot of Japanese factions and general terms to keep track of that might get confusing at times.The combat has been changed from the original in ways that make it feel very clunky and slow at times, especially the sword style, and it does amplify some of the annoyances of Yakuza's combat like getting knocked over constantly after getting hit with weapons. The original version did have some issues but this new version introduces annoying mechanics like complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boss super powers (where they have complete melee damage immunity while doing them) and they removed most ways of knocking boss fights down, only a few particular moves can knock them down or you just have to use heat moves (which there is a very limited amount of). You also do barely any damage in a lot of fights against higher tier enemies (mainly in side content like the dungeons) which isn't very satisfying. You're expected to keep upgrading your weapons at the blacksmith but it is very tedious as it requires levelling the blacksmith up (new to this version - makes it EVEN MORE grindy) which is very slow and also requires a lot of money which is pretty slow to earn unless you do chicken racing which is extremely tedious but very profitable.Now for more annoyances with this version in particular:- Don't you love having a cool sword fight with a Shinsengumi captain for him to them put his sword away and start shooting fireballs at you. Sounds really cool doesn't it? Worst change by far- Inconsistent graphics due to porting the original engine to Unreal without modifying models. They seem to have redone textures and character's eyes but this has led to problems such as Hijikata's left eye having an oval-shaped pupil. It feels like there was a lack of care. Hair especially looks terrible. And you can see distant geometry lacks any detail. When paired with realistic lighting it really can look flat a lot of the time.- UI is extremely slow compared to the original game. For example, backing out of the abilities menu takes multiple seconds and if you spam the button you can hear the sound of backing out play multiple times- Shader pre-compilation not enabled which leads to stutters the first time you see effects. This is inexcusable- Some of the character replacements are strange. The character who was Baba from Yakuza 5 is now Zhao from Yakuza: Like a Dragon. This would be fine but this character in particular had Baba's character traits like being kinda shady which fit having Baba's likeness and voice, but now it's just a completely different character. Doesn't really fit with the original intention to me. Also when fighting some of the newly replaced characters, their boss fight themes are just their unchanged theme from their original game. It doesn't really fit having a dubstep sounding song in a game set in the 1800s- Missing multiple health bars. Every boss just has a single red health bar. Pretty sure this was a big complaint with Yakuza 6 which was changed afterwards in Kiwami 2 onwards. This adds to the enemies feeling tanky situation as every hit takes down a tiny slither of their health bar compared to taking down a big chunk of one of many health bars- General lack of polish. Enemy fight intros can sometimes have them facing the wrong way. The transition between multiple phases of some heat moves have a little gap where it shows the regular combat again.- Single use DLC which was not advertised as single use. Many people have used the DLC and then loaded their save and have lost access to it.- Made the main menu a boring image instead of Ryoma on a ship. Why?- They made the dharma tumbler animation faster but you stand still for a second afterwards completely negating the change- Missing little details, such as separate running animations when on stairs- They went way too far with catering to new fans from Yakuza 7. They added wacky stuff to the main story like random giant enemies and added the trooper cards from the dungeons into the rest of the game. While you can ignore the trooper cards, it feels like they rebalanced the game around using them so you feel like you're at a big disadvantage at times, especially when bosses start using the powers from the cards.Don't get me wrong it's a very good game but I hope they put a lot more effort in if they're gonna be using Unreal Engine going forward

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, and outside of some stuttering on DX12 (just use -dx11 launch option), runs very well.Loving the story and characters so far. I've played Y0, Kiwami 1 and 2, Y3, and LAD (aka 7). I don't recognize everyone; there's certainly faces from 4, 5, and 6, but that doesn't matter since this story is entirely separate. I guess it is similar to playing 7 without 4-6, in that regard.So far I'd say the combat is closest to 0, which is a good thing, imo. I enjoyed 0's combat much more than 1 and 2; and ergo I enjoy this a lot too. Very fluid, fun, and a bit mindless. Feels very solid compared to Kiwami 2's engine.Only downside is there aren't a ton of heat actions (for my tastes). I feel like 0 had a bunch, but mostly because you could pick up so much stuff and use them with heat actions. Here, brawler can pick stuff up, but it isn't common, and the heat actions don't have a ton of variety. Not a big deal though, just means some animations are a little repetitive.Also I'm not sure if I'm a fan of the "relationship" sidequests which are very samey. e.g. "give this dog a bone 5 times" or "give this kid a vegetable 30 times". Especially since there's a cool down and you can't just get it out of the way.Also also the Taihei Boulevard Coin Lockers were basically replaced with a "lottery"; you find tickets for it all over town. Unlike Taihei these are unlimited and randomly spawn. But playing the lottery has a little animation. I now have 100 tickets and legit think it would take about an hour to use them all. So tickets are either too common, or there needs to be a way to play 100 tickets in one go. Again, super minor.

_childDocuments_.review: LIKE A SAMURAIThis game takes place during the end of the Tokugawa period or the Edo period, a piece of history that is not really abundant in current modern entertainment and media, or atleast not from my experiences. From what I know, a samurai is a katana-wielding warrior usually highly regard by the people for their bravery, skill, and more. This game delves in deeper about being a samurai that is actually very interesting especially the time period being kinda the end of the samurai. Unlike in most other entertainment, samurai here is depicted as wielding guns too since the British made contact with Japan exchanging weapons such as firearms and such. I don't know realistic it is when compare to the real life period but this tiny bit of piece adds to how unique LAD: Ishin! is when compare to other samurai-focused entertainments.Like A Dragon: Ishin! is a brand new Yakuza game by the chads in RGG Studio and also a remake of the Japan-only 2014 game Ryu Ga Gotoku: Ishin. This game is rebuilt from the ground-up with Unreal Engine 4 and new additions compare to the original. I haven't played the original RGG Ishin unlike other Yakuza games since its not available in my country and also I need PS3 hardware or an emulator to play this game. Therefore I will not be making any comparisons to the original but from what I've seen, the games is pretty much faithful with the addition with a new mechanic which is the Trooper System.In this game, you play as a samurai, Sakomoto Ryoma, on his journey to find out the truth of a certain event that happened earlier in the story. Eventually, you playing as Sakamoto Ryoma, in typical Yakuza fashion, will find out about the pieces at play being controlled by the powers of Japan, samurai organisations, other warriors, and more that is very enjoyable to experience. More importantly, the events you'll experience as Sakamoto Ryoma also happen in real life during that period of time so some context about history adds more to the experience. Not 100% accurate though but the additions for me are very creative and well-thought by the writers team.In typical Yakuza way, the action here is phenominal. I'm referring to both the combat and action scenes. For combat, the game have the style-switch system that is present on other Yakuza games like Yakuza 0, Yakuza Kiwami, Judgment, and DMC 5 where you have the Brawler style which is the classic Yakuza style, Swordman that is good in 1v1 situations, Gunman which is a more range and fast style, and Wild Dancer which is a full-offensive style combining both sword and gun. Combat is awesome with combos you can string together in-between styles. Addition to the combat system is the Trooper system where you can assign 3 or 4 cards in one style to execute special moves that rivals Yakuza 7's specials. Most of the cards are just stat buffs but the special ones can make Sakamoto Ryoma shoot a beam of light between his palms or open a black hole to the shadow realm. Personally, I didn't use much of the Trooper system except in the Battle Dungeon minigame. Battle Dungeon is a mission-based minigame where you can do to get materials for equipment and crafting. Equipment here felt much better to use here than other Yakuza games since it is realistic to wield swords and polearms in this game. The crafting system is also similar to Monster Hunter which is an A plus in my book.Returning back to the story, the story is good. I'll admit I didn't fully understand since there were many factions and terms at present like the Choshu Domain, the Bakufu, and more that kinda made me confused on how the world works in Tokugawa Japan. To alleviate this, the game has a glossary that highlights certain terms that are important to know like Sonno Jouie, Shishi, Joshi, Goshi, and more during dialogue scenes. Being Japan af, the names of every character are also arranged accurately to how it is called in Japan with the family name being the first. Sakamoto Ryoma with the old arrangement is Ryoma Sakamoto with Ryoma being his first name. Like Naruto Uzumaki changed to Uzumaki Naruto, or Kazuma Kiryu to Kiryu Kazuma. Since the game is Japan af, might as well go all in. This is also applied to the actors name and the devs in the credits. Although I was dazed and confused during the credits, a quick Google search about the history of the characters and the time period really brings out all the references the game made along the way. I do understand why it wasn't released in Internationally since it has too much content and references about Japan. I commend the translation team for the effort in bringing this internationally and making it more accessible.The soundtrack is straight up fire. Other than that, the main story is only a percentage of the full game. The side-content is usually one of the important things to do and have fun ingame. You can do Karaoke, or Singing Bar, a typical Yakuza staple, Buyo Dancing, a traditional Japanese dance, selling Udon, farming, selling crops, cooking, and more. Yakuza games can be defined as a hybrid of action and slice of life game where you not only do what the character does, but also become one. Other than the activities you can do, there are also substories which are little events that are very entertaining. These substories other than giving you rewards, also give you features in other minigames, tidbit lore of the world, and more and never are there a chore or bore to experience.Alas, not every game is perfect. This game have a friendship system where you have to interact multiple times in order to maximise them. Not all of the NPCs you interact gave any meaningful reward, atleast from how much I have played. There are tons of NPCs, like TONS of them in every nook and cranny, shops, that you have to kinda interact with either giving items they want multiple times. Some are funny but most are just kinda tedious to do and felt like giving out items that I could have used better in other situations like in the Battle Dungeon. I have not done all of them so my opinion may change, but for now, the relationships are tedious to fulfill and have no reward in fulfilling them.Other flaw is that there many spelling errors, like too much for a Yakuza game. Kinda sloppy. The translations confused me especially the differences being Joshi and Goshi, which I can understand it being mistakenably written. More quality assurance for better spelling please. And also some button prompts can bug out, menus being slow, but these tech issues I can give forgive since I have a high tolerance for it. Its just the spelling errors that are quite many that its noticable.Overall, a classic Yakuza, or Samurai game.5/5

_childDocuments_.review: I'm about 33% through and this is a top tier game in a series full of fantastic games.Fully recommend to newcomers as well as Yakuza fans.Pros:- The combat styles are a ton of fun and once you get the hang of switching between them mid-fight you'll steamroll enemies.- Substories are hilarious and always a highlight of these games. Fantastic comedic writing.- The plot is pretty simple and engaging! I usually lose track of the plot but this one is great.- The minigames (Dancing, serving food) are challenging but fair. - There's a side story (Another Life) where you work on a farm and upgrade the farm. This can be overwhelming at first but once you get into it, its a ton of fun fulfilling orders.- The environment is a lot more entertaining to move through than Yakuza 7's , which I found boring. It's easy to memorize: not too big, not too small.Cons:- The combat system and level ups seem to want you to use the "Heat" mechanic, but it's really hard to generate a lot of Heat, even against the most basic enemies. Previous Yakuza games didn't seem to have this issue.- The weapon crafting/upgrade system is too tedious. It costs a ton of in-game currency and materials for seemingly very little rewards.- Some of the minigames are so much fun that I wish there were MORE of them!- I simply do not understand Mahjong. I've tried to learn it in every Yakuza game and it doesn't click with me.- You can press "Pet the dog" but it doesn't SHOW you petting the dog

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Ishin is one of the more interesting entries in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series, and though I had some issues with some of the systems it has, I enjoyed the game overall. The story is based on real historical events in Japan, so I took the time to read the history a bit because the game made me curious about the period.  It was also fun to see characters I loved from the other games play totally different characters.  Compared to the other Yakuza/Like a Dragon games I've played, Ishin has one of the better stories and I liked it more than the story in Yakuza 6 even though they share some plot points.  The minigames are generally good.  There's a fan dancing game that reminds me a lot of the disco one in Y0, though it's a bit easier.  Obviously, there are no arcade games, but the courtesan minigame gives you a shooter to play if you are hankering for one.  I haven't finished all of the Battle Dungeons yet, but I like it more than the other collectible-type games such as Majima Construction in Y2 and Clan Creator in Y6.  The card system is a bit overwhelming at first but it's not too hard to grasp and you can get a lot of nice cards without needing to purchase DLC.The "Harvest Moon" side business is quite addictive, though I wish they would have added more challenges to the Cooking Mamaesque cooking portion.  It's a good early game way to make some money.  The substories are overall not as wacky as the ones you encounter in Y0 and Kiwami 2, but I liked several of them.  I especially enjoyed the Wanted series of substories since they involve ninjas and goofy thieves in Tengu masks.  As for the combat, I loved the sword-based styles the most.  I found Wild Dancer to be even more fun than Breaker since you can chain attacks forever if you get good enough at it.  The Swordsman style starts out kind of slow but over time it becomes extremely powerful and varied.  If you pair Swordsman with a great crafted weapon it can easily carry you through the whole game.  Gunman isn't bad, but it felt a bit simple and situationally useful.  Once I crafted a rapid fire gun, for example, I could just mash the x button and get good results without having to worry about special ammo or trick shots.  Brawler, unfortunately, felt extremely weak and I had to rely on the invincibility frames you get from parrying to score more hits.  Overall, the combat system is heavily affected by the weapons you craft.  The main issue I have about this game is the crafting system. It's a bit complicated but the game does little to explain the system and I had to use guides.  Crafting also requires lot of grinding to get the materials you need, the cash to craft the items (and upgrade the blacksmith), and the seals you need to enhance your weapons and armor.  Unfortunately, the seal system has a lot of RNG, so if you want them all you will have to do a lot of farming and crafting.  Fortunately, the main story didn't seem too hard to beat and one of the best swords in the game isn't as expensive to make as some of the others, so the heavy grind is reserved for players who want 100% completion.  If you're a more casual Yakuza player like me who doesn't need to 100% complete everything, then you should have fun with Ishin.  It's an interesting spinoff and nice change of pace from the main series.

_childDocuments_.review: Best Yakuza that is not technically Yakuza.Has all the jokes, emotional stories and cool moments just like in 0.Story actually makes sense as opposed to Yakuza games..Ryoma is amazing and is very quirky, even more so than Kiryu.I love Kiryu but he's way more sad and tragic, which can sometime be unfitting of the jovial vibes the mini games have.Imagine just seeing random people doing a dance on the street and joining them. That's Ryoma for you.Or better yet play house with some local children. Ryoma gets to live the life Kiryu's always dreamed of, and I'm here for it.Every interaction matters and is either a substory or leads to a short storyExample: You feed a cat 5 times wondering "why am I even doing it, it's tedious"You then get to see the cat's story and you adopt said cat.Or you buy from a certain merchant a few times, he gradually tells you his supplier is late, you then get to sell him produce from your garden that you grew yourself.This makes this game very unique and cool.It makes you feel like you're always in an arcade.The graphics are amazing. Every location is gorgeous.UE4 really made this game shine.Usually Yakuza games have heavy problems with aliasing (the edges always dance and shimmer)The newer Dragon Engine is particularly bad in that regard. (also the physics are wonky)The facial (and idle) animations of dragon engine are stiff and lifeless.Such problems are absent here. Really wish they'd use UE4 for all Yakuza games.Best LAD game in my opinion. I mean look at my hours (and I'm not even done yet)I usually binge game but not to the extent this game makes me.It's just too fun to stop.Every few steps you make there's an interaction.You never feel lonely in the world of Ishin.You plan to go somewhere, and then get derailed a 100 times (of your own volition) and end up doing something completely different.I mean, can you really walk by the cat without giving it a fish?nahhhhhDon't listen to people saying it's grind-y.You can choose whether to grind or finish the game in 15 hours insteadThe grinding isn't mandatory and doesn't really affect progression (i.e. you're not forced to grind to better your gear, because gear good enough to finish the game randomly drops and very often so)But in case you want to grind, you will be rewarded with story bits and world building.You only grind because you want to see that extra scene/interaction or complete an achievement.Anyway amazing game easily on par with Yakuza 0.This game is what westerners so desperately seek in order to refresh the open world formula.This is how you make an open world feel alive as opposed to the barren lands of western games.

_childDocuments_.review: First thing that I gotta mention is that this game is RICH IN CONTENT! And not just bloat or just existing and going unnoticed like those side activities in Yakuza 5. This game locks you into playing all the minigames and side activities/stories and they are fun mostly. I have never played the fishing minigame this long in any Yakuza game but this one and the farming/cooking minigame just keeps me coming back. 40 hours into the game and I'm still finding new people to "bond" with when I thought I've seen everything at that point. The world of Ishin feels more alive than what I've seen in most Yakuza games. It definitely represents the busy feudal era with its people minding their own businesses buying or selling stuff in the noisy market. Another thing that this game does that other Yakuza games don't is that for some reason, the combat isn't the best part of the game. I played on Legend in my first playthrough (casually without looking up anything about it) and the first 10-12 hours was just a horrible grindfest. Even when I'm finally strong enough in the end game, the combat just feels strange. The bosses can one hit kill you like FromSoft bosses while they tank all your attacks, it's just not fun. I will say though that it does get better once you start upgrading your abilities and gear. The story is what you would expect from a Yakuza game. Rubber bullets, plot twists, betrayal, angry old men arguing, the usual. It's definitely engaging and I always like how in japanese games you start with save a cat then the last mission is kill god. This one is like that too but the last mission is you save Japan. And I wouldn't call this a "remake" more like a "remaster". It's not a Dragon Engine game either. The combat is pretty much the same as the original. The graphics received an upgrade but there are some moments that it looks like Yakuza 0 with graphics mods. One thing that I hate with games these days is that, TAA is forced enabled and when you disable it with a mod or by tweaking the ini file, it looks sharp but bad, it's like you get to see what the game actually looks like. TAA produces these fuzziness in the graphics as it is constantly erasing jaggy edges and it always doesn't look good. I will say that Judgment and Kiwami 2 looks better than this game. I think maybe they should've used the Dragon Engine and revamped the combat and then that would be a "remake". Content is worth the money but if you're unsure, get it on a discount (like I did).
