_childDocuments_.review: I am here for the same reason you likely are; I saw metroidvania, I saw souls-like, I immediately thought of Hollow Knight. As a TL;DR for this massive review: if you're thinking of buying this game to scratch your silksong itch, do it. It's not as good as Hollow Knight, but it's pretty high up there. Though if you do buy it, give it until the fourth Sol before you decide if you want to keep playing. I know you won't be able to refund it, but this game has a very poor start in my opinion that needs time to grow on you.Having just now beaten the game, I can safely say that this game is absolutely worth the $30 price. I was very on the fence seeing an indie game priced that high, but after things kept popping up on the game for me, I finally gave in and paid the full price. I was expecting a much shorter game, or a game that is poorly inflated with excess content, but instead I was blown away by the sheer quality and size of this game. It was rarely too much; the only overwhelming thing for me was the parts of the game where I spend 40 minutes getting through the massive queue of character interactions i had built up. However, this game is NOT for everyone. If you are bad at or dislike parry mechanics, this game is not for you. If you dislike excessively difficult games, this game is not for you. If you don't like taking on the same boss 20 or 30 times before you finally beat it, this game is not for you. If you are someone who absolutely despises games filled with character interactions at every turn, this game might not be for you. It fills a very particular niche, and for people who enjoy all this stuff, it is a genuinely amazing experience that I couldn't recommend more, especially once you master the mechanics. However, if you buy this game, you should absolutely give it a lot more than a few areas before you decide whether or not you want to keep going. The game gets much better as you keep playing, and i only fell in love with it halfway through. With that out of the way, let's get into:Starting off strong, this game's combat is one of the most satisfying and fun combat systems I've ever played. Its much higher complexity makes it so that performing well and proving your mastery of the system becomes far more satisfying than a simple combat system like Hollow Knight. The enemies also complement this system near perfectly, mostly being designed with the system in mind. That may sound like an obvious thing, but it's surprising how many games make enemies that are made without thinking about how they would function with the combat system. Even some enemies in this game feel more like they were simply made and forced into the combat system, but those are few and far between. The way you fly around in late game combat from consecutive parries is incredibly fun and being able to take advantage of a perfect opening to deal massive damage just feels amazing. The shining jewel of this game is easily the boss fights. For clarification, when I say boss, I am referring to any fight with a health bar on the bottom of the screen that is either a sol or has some sort of comic intro or defeat scene. There are very few that I consider bad, and my absolute favorite boss in this game is an experience I will never forget. The fights can be done with such perfect, fluid motions that often when I lose, I am just in awe at how fun the fight really is, I am excited to take it on again just because it was so damn fun and exhilarating to play. I've also often found that people's favorite bosses are incredibly varying, which is a testament to how fun nearly every boss in this game is.The story of this game is honestly pretty good overall, I enjoy getting to learn the answers to a lot of the questions I have about the game, but it is definitely a weaker part of the game. I do love the interactions I get to have with my allies as well, they are often funny and cute, or are a nice progression of that character's story. Lastly, the level design is very good, the theming of the areas feel perfect and I love nearly every gimmick that the areas present me with. I'm not great at analyzing the greatness of level design, so I don't have much to really say beyond this, but trust me when I say it's very well done.To start this section off, I would like to say: Red Candle Games, if you ever make another game like this, please do not ever make a group fight boss again. The two that are in the game currently, being Goumang and Kanghui, are easily the worst fights in the entire game. Goumang is an Ornstein and Smough style duo fight, facing off against an agile and rapidly attacking smaller enemy and a slow but powerful large enemy. However, unlike Ornstein and Smough, the Goumang fight does not pair well with each other. The large enemy often uses wide unblockable attacks that take your priority while the smaller one peppers you during this, aiming to catch you when there is literally nothing you can do, or throwing a projectile at you that feels like it was made to just piss you off in the worst way. It's a shame, because Goumang herself has such an amazing character design for a one-phase fight where she sits and watches you fight the most BS pair of enemies in the game. Kanghui on the other hand just feels fundamentally awful. He sits, stuck in place, summoning a horde of enemies for you to take on where it feels like every enemy is simultaneously the priority, making for a fight where you will deal with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ constantly changing situations where you can do nothing.With that out of the way, I also will say that this game has one of the weakest starts I've ever seen in an actually good game. It sets up a story, only to end that story within the first 30 minutes or so, then makes you wait around for the first few areas while it sets up its actual story. The combat system at its most basic form also doesn't quite make for the kind of moments that i love this game for, you are just learning the basics. The first boss isn't all that interesting, one of the early minibosses I came across felt like it had insane expectations from a new player like me, the second boss is Goumang, and at that point I was struggling to keep playing. I managed to push through, despite the fourth sol, Jiequan, being a package of everything I hate, and eventually I fell in love with the game while I was fighting him.The story is highly predictable, which took away from a lot of my enjoyment of the story by the end as i could see the twists a mile away. But the gameplay had already snagged me by then, so i was in it to finish the game just for the fun of it. The minibosses are the exact opposite of the main bosses in the game. Some of them can be fun, but by the end of the game they are way harder and way more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ than the actual bosses, and even some of the early ones put awful expectations on new players. The final one I fought was easily the worst, it felt designed to actively ignore the combat system, throwing attacks at you during attacks, giving you very little time to react, etc.Lastly, the design of the enemies gets a lot worse near the end of the game. Once you beat the 5th sol, it starts to feel like some of the newer enemies are, instead of testing your prowess with the combat system, trying to find ways to ignore the system entirely. Making attacks impossible to react to, demanding focus when you're fighting a enemy that needs that focus, or even throwing in contact damage out of nowhere on an enemy they put in groups. It dampens down the ending sections of the games, but the bosses are just so fun that it keeps me going, plus not all the enemies at this point are that awful.Though despite these bad parts, I think the game is such a fun and even unforgettable experience at certain points that it is well worth experiencing it if you think you'll enjoy its niche.

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is a spectacular platformer game that admittedly took a little bit of time for me to get the hang of, but once you get the hang of timing parries and everything clicks, the combat becomes spectacularly satisfying when dealing with both bosses  and high numbers of low-level enemies. From a narrative standpoint, the protagonist is one of the more compelling ones of gaming, whose journey of vengeance slowly transforms to one of redemption as he forms bonds with the characters around him. From an appearances perspective, the art style is unmatched, reminding me somewhat of Thunder Lotus Studio's Spiritfarer with an Eastern slant, with everything from the characters to the stages exuding both traditional Chinese aesthetics and sleek cyberpunk features. Altogether, I was totally satisfied with this game, and I highly recommend for anyone who's a fan of platformers, unique visual styles and Chinese culture (even with fun Easter eggs of character names that reflect Chinese mythological counterparts). 10/10, no notes. Just don't give up on the first or second bosses and you'll be fineEDIT: Plus boss rush mode added!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Did you like Hollow Knight? Did you ever wish it was brighter, harder and Taopunk? Do you prefer to play as a cat instead of a bug? Did you ever wish that Souls games have two modes, one "Standard" and one "Story"? If your answers were mostly yes, then this game's for you. Nine Sols puts the "Sekiro" in the 2D souls-borne/metroidvania franchise. Your primary defense mechanic is a parry, which also gives you charges to blast foes. Glancing blows are a thing, and will count as mitigated DoT effects. Dodging is your secondary defense mechanic without being rendered useless. Both of these have their own advanced uses when you combine them with other basic mechanics like jumping or other ways of upgrading your character. It's simple as an idea, but it branches out brilliantly. Which brings us to boss fights, which are designed to man-handle you in a manner similar to Sekiro. I won't spoil but they're tough. The first Sol boss is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ skillcheck in the same way FromSoft skillchecks you with their first boss of each game. After that, the game keeps giving you clear upgrade paths that feel appropriate for each stage of the game you're in. I cannot underscore how smooth progression feels.Hollow Knight has a more interconnected world, while Nine Sols feels more linear; however, I'm feeling that this is intentional. The game drops you to the bottom of the map and then you're climbing upwards, as if you're exploring a tree. Which incidentally is also where your game points as your final destination. At the same time, it builds, with both mandatory and extra areas, on the platforming legacy HK and its spawns have built - but does so with creative twists that make Nine Sols stand tall next to its predescesors.It boasts an obscure but precisely implemented theme which governs story, atmosphere and overall aesthetic: Taopunk. If you haven't played the game, you can't imagine it, but once you get in you'll know exactly what I mean. I wish this theme was explored more often in stories.The story is so far is cohesive, with well-fleshed out characters that feel real, whether they are cats or not. It revolves around the main character's relationship with a little kid... and you know how these stories go. Also, no spoils. The cutscenes are comic-strips which make you think the story could be told in that medium as well if the company really wanted so.Overall, it's staying in my favorites folder. You can nitpick it and find minor flaws, but the overall experience is a 10/10. I wish they give us the option to replay bosses, or even a pantheon feature where we fight extra difficult versions of bosses. If a DLC comes out for this game, it'll need to include this feature. What a fantastic game you put together Red Candle, congratulations. I'm definitely keeping an eye on that company.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I have been this addicted to a game in a long time. For the description of this game people would call it "Hollow Knight + Sekiro" which I think is fitting, but this game is more than just that. I would even say I enjoyed this game as much as Hollow Knight, maybe even more.The world and characters are just really charming and the art style and combat are what I really love about this game and those are the big highlights of this game. The Sekiro type combat mixed with 2D Metroidvania gameplay is so fitting. The bosses are super well designed and every boss and area feels unique and the game experiments with a lot of different things for each area, which makes the game really fresh to play. This game left me with my jaw open so many times. Awesome game, with awesome art, music, bosses, combat and all around awesome. One thing to note for some people is that the game is quite dialogue heavy which I liked, but some might not. I would definitely recommend this game to everyone who find it even a little bit interesting, and for people who have played Hollow Knight.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a parry-combat fan and enjoy the difficulty of hard, but fair boss fights, then this will be a 10/10 game for you.Combat is crisp and reactive. Every parry or attack connect is backed by strong sound effects. Most of the enemy attacks are well telegraphed both by audio and visual cues. Bosses can be quite challenging (the last one took me about ~2hr to defeat, others ~30m or less) and I got my ass beat many times. Fortunately, on almost all occasions, the game communicated with me clearly what I had ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and it was easy to find a solution/react faster on my future attempts.Worth nothing that exploration and platforming are well-made, but not the focus of this game. To my surprise, the story was not half-bad and featured some great animated sequences. Both the characters and main theme were well-crafted and managed to deliver a emotional and satisfying conclusion to the plot.As a huge fan of Sekiro, I enjoyed this immensely. Playtime: ~20 hrs for 100%TL;DR - If parrying activates your neurons, buy this ASAP.

_childDocuments_.review: Very early into the game as of writing this, but I can't imagine it gets much better. The game looks cool and flashy, but after a while you realize that's all it has going for it. Combat is extremely simple, with it just being quick time events into holding down the talisman button. You don't really get much options for movement either, so the loop is, use your free invincibility to wait for an easily parry-able move, parry, attach a talisman, repeat. Now, that could be a fine enough loop for combat, but with the game trying a lot on its visual style some moves are simply just harder to parry, and thats even if the hitboxes line up with the moves at all. There are very minimal i-frames if any when hit, so there's been a good few times where because of the layout of the arena or environment, you just get combo'd and die instantly. I want to talk about the exploration and map, but there isn't really much to talk about. Mostly uninteresting layouts and easily noticeable secrets. Maybe i'm just not used to noticing everything yet, but the artstyle and design of the different areas just feels really same-y and bland. semisolid platforms look really similar to regular fully-solid platforms, so you'll just jump is place trying to go through platforms a lot and not be able to flow through areas that well. Overall, the game just feels kinda rough, which is understandable considering my knowledge of the developers, but I can't find myself to recommend this game at the time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent metroidvania. It's Hollow Knight x Sekiro. The combat is fast, expressive, and very satisfying. The traversal and platforming don't really reinvent much, but they're competently made. The narrative really surprised me with how well written and emotional it was.Honestly, the only real con to this game is the awful map. It's barely functional enough to figure your way around. Most metroidvanias live and die by the map. Red Candle, for some reason, split the full detailed world map into non-detailed chunks. When you view each "area" up close, you get to see the parts of the current area that you've explored, but the transition points between these areas are just arrows with no labels or easy way to see where you're going. There's no way to put your own markers on the map to remember where you need to come back or where you've been. Some parts of the map are these doors that go into back rooms, which don't have any maps, and they also aren't marked in any way when they're "done".The rest of the game is EXCELLENT, and I still recommend it. The entire package, minus the map system, is honestly a masterpiece. I hope Red Candle puts some more work into the map so that people with less patience than me can still enjoy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR game is great at its price if a bit shortI'm really not a fan of parry focused combat systems in general but the rest of the game still managed to keep me around for the full playtime. The story and world building kept me interested from beginning to end. I got more attached to the characters than I expected within such a short time. The environments were beautiful and varied. Animation was stellar. Art was more gruesome than expected from the cover, and better for it. Only real issue I had with the game was the difficulty spike on the final boss. I actually quite liked the fight itself, but why is one boss taking up 4 hours of my playtime on a 29 hour long game. Other bosses took me around 5-30 min with their difficulty seemingly more tied to their lore than their placement in game progression.I also feel if you came to this game straight off the back of Hollow Knight you may find yourself somewhat dissatisfied with the depth of the exploration. There were only a few real puzzles and nothing heavily hidden away to discover. You get basically everything with just your first walk through each zone and some short backtracks when you get a new tool to explore with. I don't personally count this against the game and enjoyed it for what it was, just a comparison I thought of near the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a perfect game, but one with lots of heart put into it. If harder games tend to make you rage, I wouldn't recommend, however if you're up for a learning experience, pick this one up! The highlights include obviously the gameplay, and less obviously the story. The gameplay is punishing at first but gradually more satisfying as you go on and fall into the beat of battles. Excluding a singular boss that keeps on spawning mobs over and over, low point of the game for me, every boss fight is incredible! As for the story, I would've never thought I'd grow as attached as I did to this cast, especially Yi and Shuanshuan's relationship, very touching moments! I admitedly haven't played that many metroidvania so it's hard to say how good it is for the genre, especially when it's a much lighter experience on exploration compared to genre staples, but I'll confidently say I had as much fun playing Nine Sols as I did Hollow Knight!

_childDocuments_.review: High highs and low lows. Went in with very high expectations seeing 95%+ score.:Story, characters and world-building are surprisingly interesting. Combat and traversal can feel really satisfying. Finding secrets and optional mini-bosses is fun. Some bosses are very creative and surprising.:Exploration: Pretty quickly levels start feeling samey and not that fun to explore. Loading screens for every single room you enter, for some reason. Backtracking can feel a bit tedious, even later-obtained fast travel forces you to go to the home base first, then to your destination (+2 loading screens). Map is clunky to use.Combat: You take a lot of damage from bosses. It can be frustrating to learn their moves or attack patterns if you die within seconds. Why do you die withing seconds? You can get stun-locked into multiple hits, then into spikes/fire/aoe hazards, and just die if you get hit once (there is a skill that you can unlock later to help with this, but it's pretty mandatory and should be there by default). There are 0 iframes after getting hit, so bosses or enemies in general can one-shot you with multiple damage sources at the same time (bomb clusters for example). Fighting multiple enemies at the same time is definitely not something this combat system was designed for, so it's just frustrating more often than not. Healing is too slow for how fast some bosses move or teleport around the arena imo. Overall just a bunch of small flaws with combat that add up to an unnecessarily frustrating experience.Edit after finishing the game: Many hitboxes are atrocious. Unskippable cutscenes. Bosses get very confused when you stand close to them/behind them. They start jumping and attacking backwards, or just doing a 180 in the middle of attack animations. Unbounded counter is a clunky mechanic. This game demands a lot of precision from you, but doesn't provide much of it in return.:There is plenty to love in this game, but two core things for me, exploration and combat, just had one too many frustrating quirks.

_childDocuments_.review: This game took me by surprise: I didn't expect it, moreover, I didn't know about its existence. How happy I was when I found it! From the first second, I knew that I would love it. After just 10 seconds of the trailer, I pressed pause and immediately bought it. Now, after finishing it, I can finally say that this, gentlemen, is one of the best Metroidvania games I have ever played. To be fair, in my opinion, this game shares first place in the league together with Hollow Knight. I loved it so much—the combat, the mechanics, and especially the story. However, I do think it was a bad decision not to let the player choose between skipping the dialogue and not skipping it.I played the game at 60 FPS on medium settings on my Steam Deck, and believe me, this game was made for this device. It looks wonderful, the controls feel very responsive, and I wouldn't be lying if I said that I craved the very this kind of experience as a kid.My favorite boss is Lady Ethereal. By this point, I had mastered a decent level of the parry mechanic, and it felt like the fight was choreographed—it looked so beautiful. All the bosses are extremely well done, needless to say, but there is a special place in my heart specifically for this Lady. Her theme is marvelous, and the story behind it is masterfully intertwined with the theme, which makes it a thousand times more compelling, even heartbreaking.Finally, I just wish more people could play this and enjoy it. I don't think the game is very difficult, but for people seeking a good challenge, I think they will be very pleased with what this game has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely the best metroidvania I have played this year. It's made me start enjoying Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown after I fell off earlier in the year.  Combat (parrying) is definitely a major element but I have found it to be difficult but fair. I also appreciated the story and world with its East Asian influences. It follows some standard metroidvania conventions as for as these stories go but the developers take you on a somewhat morbid journey that left me with thinking.  There are some puzzles and platforming but I never found those elements to be overly difficult. You could also say its a little linear but I think that helped to make the story stronger. Overall, Nine Sols is just a well executed game across game play, sound, music, and art.  This is the first game I have played from Red Candle Games. It looks like they have done good work across several  genres. Hopefully, they will revisit the metroidvania space again.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game. It's easily a 9/10 for me.Praises:1. The art and soundtrack are AMAZING. Truly nuts how good the atmosphere of this game is. The big tree, the transmutation zone, the dream scapes – these are memorable environments. The boss music is next level. The manga panels during key moments are such a creative touch to the story. I'm really glad that there is a story mode, because I know so many people who I want to recommend this game to based on the aesthetics of it, who aren't into hard games. 2. The combat system is so neat. The game bills itself as Sekiro-like combat, and I understand why they do that, but I think the devs are selling the game short in some of the innovations they have in the parry system. The unbounded counter is a really great evolution of the parry system, and the talisman system is a great and natural way to make parries beneficial without ripping off Sekiro's posture system. Yes, it's clearly inspired in many ways, but it's a very unique system and not just a Sekiro-like.3. The lore of the game is so good. I know people criticize it for lore dumping, and there certainly is a lot of lore dumping through NPC dialog. But the amount of lore that characters drop in endless conversations is only a small fraction of the total lore. There's so much about New Kunlun and Penglai society that is assumed and hiding in plain sight, things that are known to the characters but not to the player, that nobody says and that you have to piece together yourself. The story itself is good, but the standout is of course the worldbuilding. "Taopunk" is not actually how I would describe it. I feel like the Taoist themes are a bit over-marketed relative to what the game actually has. But it absolutely is a unique kind of sci-fi, and a very compelling one.Criticisms:1. The lack of invincibility even 0.01 seconds after taking a hit can lead to some pretty frustrating deaths in mob fights. 2. The jades are mostly not that great. Not nearly as cool as the Hollow Knight charms from which they take inspiration. 3. The lack of a universal fast travel system until the midgame can lead to some dull running around the map, until the midgame when they give you the ability to fast travel between every save point. (Tbf, Hollow Knight never gives you this.)

_childDocuments_.review: I've been keeping an eye on this since it dropped the little demo almost two years previous.  I'll start this by saying This game is  gorgeous.  Its hand drawn environments and fully animated cut-scenes ooze style and originality in their Taoist come cyberpunk setting.  There are even some sections that are done like little comic strip cutouts along with a wealth of  distinctive flairs that set this apart from other hand drawn games that have been copied to death recently; *cough* Hollow Knight clones.  The combat is  inspired by Sekiro to the point where this feels like I am actually playing a 2d version of Sekiro; right down to bopping people on the heads when they charge a red unblockable; the only thing missing is a kanji symbol.  The controls are hyper tight, the parry is well timed and very responsive and the enemies are vicious and formidable after the tutorial.  Gameplay and exploration is along the same line as Blasphemous or aforementioned Hollow Knight, but there is a genuinely intriguing and grim/beautiful narrative unfolding that's a little less vague than a lot of soulslikes and metroids in the way that it is delivered. Be prepared to stop and take a little beat every now and again instead of all out action continually, especially at the start where there is a decent bit of exposition; don't worry though this doesn't disrupt gameplay flow after the first hour/tutorial zone. >You start with a very minimal toolkit but you WILL unlock all the things you might imagine would make both the combat and traversal more fun, just give it a while to let the game unfold. >Enemies and bosses start super manageable but quickly amp up in difficulty. They never feel unfair, but rest assured to those looking for a challenge, don't be put off by the gradual ease into difficulty.>This game is dark as ♥♥♥♥, with a lot of violence, brutal narrative decisions and world lore. It's also really beautiful and heartwarming in equal measure, but don't be fooled by the cute character design and art style, this setting has a lot of grit to it. I have loved pretty much everything about the game so far and I urge everyone with a spare 25 euro to check out this absolute gem of a release if anything I've said in this review sounds interesting or appealing. It's beautiful in content and presentation, its combat mechanics are amazing and there is a metric tonne of heart and soul pouring from every pore and pixel.
_childDocuments_.name: Nine Sols

_childDocuments_.review: This is my few 10/10 games (one of the other being Hollow Knight) - and guess what, I hate platformer.When I first know about Nine Sols, I thought "oh, HK, but with cat instead of bug". However, this game was not "just more HK" as I first thought: it reminds me of the first time I played HK. I feel like I never actually wanted "more HK" (that is what Silksong is for), I just want to experience the joy of playing a wonderful game like I did with HK.While the game takes a fair amount of inspiration from HK, the vibe and feel are different. First of all, this is a story focused game, and it has a very good story imo. While I love HK, that game story is pretty much Dark Soul 1 (and I do like both games, I cannot really say their stories are engaging). If you are interested and familiar with east asian culture and mythology, you will have a great time spotting the influence and messages. I also like that its story is rather straight forward, but complex due to the theme and characters, rather than just twists and drams like modern writings. I guess I should not be surprised given that the developer's previous 2 games are highly rated story games.The second thing worth mentioning is the difficulty. I do think the game is on the challenging side, but somehow I always feel the game is "easy". Perhaps it feels so because the gameplay is "fair" most of the time: you can dodge and parry pretty much anything with very forgiving windows. However, the game is very punishing when it comes to misplay - you have fairly low health and can be two-three shot by the bosses if you button smash. The playstyle is also surprisingly flexible, having multiple styles to choose from and mostly balanced.I want to note that I consider myself an awful platfomer player, hate it even, and I also play only on keyboard and mouse. Yet this game feels much easier and better than Hollow Knight (I believe keyboard and mouse is just awful to play for platforming games like HK, since you need very precise movement). Some people complain about the hitbox, which I guess is kinda fair, but then again most enemies and bosses have easy to recognise attack pattern. Again, unlike games like HK, this game is less about precise movement (so it's not like you try to dodge enemy hitbox), but about timing. The game has more Sekiro DNA than HK as it does suggest in the game description. I actually like Nine Sols combat slightly more than Sekiro because Sekiro combat later on relies too much on counter.Do note, if you do have trouble with parry-style combat, the game has a very flexible difficulty adjustment in the Story Mode! I consider the story a huge part of the game, so it's total ok to enjoy the game with less punishing combat.There are quite a lot of other praise or nitpick I can say, such as the music and sound, characters and tropes, etc. but that would be too long for a Steam review. I had one small bug while playing but it is fixed pretty much the next day; performance is much better than HK at launch as well. The ending makes me quite moody for a while, both sad and happy. Really though, it was quite an emotional experience and I hope people will also enjoy the game.

My only minor suggestions to the devs would be to visually outline some of the projectiles a little in some of the Boss Fights near the end, and maybe explain (maybe they did and I missed it, but I don't think they did) that grounded parry must face the opponent's attack, I didn't find this out until late, late game, and I could see others not figuring this out on their own.  Really great game, I will buy whatever this dev makes next.  Lot of passion in this one.Two things of note1.  This is more combat focused with a metroidvania style sprawling map, but there is not a lot of backtracking for exploration and super hidden secrets, though the exploration is not mind numbing either, it is still there, just minimized and takes a back seat to the very fun combat and excellent story. _childDocuments_.review: It's hard, but if you like Sekiro, which focuses on reacting to enemy attacks, once you're familiar with the parry timing, this will be the most satisfying Metroidvania combat for you. The core of Nine Sols lies in its parry combat system. The mechanics are intuitive yet challenging, requiring precise timing and strategic thinking, making each enemy encounter a test of skill rather than mere button-mashing. Boss battles are intense, multi-phase encounters that require a deep understanding of the boss's mechanics (I tried the final boss for 3-4 hours until I beat it... other bosses may take 20-30 minutes to get familiar with their mechanisms). Additionally, character customization allows players to tailor their abilities and playstyles; I did change my setup a few times to make some boss fights easier.Art style plays a very important part in a Metroidvania game, in my opinion. Since we run around the map a lot, the background must be interesting enough to keep players enjoying the journey. And one of Nine Sols' most striking features is its art style. I think it might be the most unique style in the Metroidvania genre right now. The game world is beautifully crafted with detailed, hand-drawn environments with Taoist mythology aesthetics.Must also mention that Red Candle is known for making horror games, and the nightmare part of this game is very unnerving, even if the boss there is a furry lynx mommy.Both are incredibly good. The perfect parrying sound effect is really satisfying, and every time you attack, you can hear the long sleeves swinging. The soundtrack of Nine Sols is another highlight, perfectly capturing the mood of the game. Every main boss has their own unique theme; some of them even change with their phases, really hyping up the fights. I love the Chinese religious vibe of the music mixed with the electro genre; the soundtrack is well-composed and complements the game's tone effectively.The narrative provides enough context to keep players engaged. Plot might be the weakest part of this game, but I still enjoyed the interactions with NPCs and bosses.A must-play for fans who appreciate reaction combat systems and the Metroidvania genre. Its Tai Chi-style parry combat is a breath of fresh air, offering a level of engagement and challenge that is both satisfying and addictive. The overall experience of playing Nine Sols is one that will definitely stay with you long after the credits roll.    A very polished game, as seen from the boss and map designs.    Fluid and engaging parry combat    Unique art style    Well-composed music and satisfying sound effects    Some respawn points are a bit too far    Early stages may feel annoying hard if the player hasn't found abilities like air dodge or double jump.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best indie soulslike games of the year—and potentially of all time if you're into this kind of game. Given how popular Hollow Knight is, I'm surprised this game hasn't gained the same level of recognition. As many have noted, it plays like Hollow Knight with a unique twist on Sekiro's parry system. The combat is simple yet incredibly fluid, offering a challenge without being overly punishing (you can change to lower difficulty if you prefer). Once you become familiar with the wide range of available skills, you'll find yourself pulling off impressive and satisfying moves.The art style is stunning, and the story is engaging. However, if you can read Chinese, you'll find the experience significantly richer. Many of the characters and locations are rooted in ancient Chinese mythology, which adds a fascinating layer of depth. While this cultural exploration is a major plus for me, I can see how the names and references might feel obscure if you don't speak the language.Although the overall world-building is decent, the weakest aspects of the game are probably the dialogue and character development. The dialogue can feel a bit flat, and most characters come across as one-dimensional.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing combat with a low skill floor and a high skill ceiling, and I cannot express how UNREAL some of the boss fights are, namely a feminine character around the mid-game and the final boss, both of which take a TON of practice to beat on your first time. I didn't use it, but the "Story Mode" option to make the game easier at any point at the cost of losing one achievement was a kind thing for the devs to add.The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard, , , and of course  are breathtaking pieces.The artwork needs praise, from start til end Nine Sols is a masterpiece of visual design, the mixing of cyperpunk themes with eastern Tao designs is seamless and a treat to look at.And the story. I sobbed by the end of my master file. The  last 3-4 hours of content were some of the most gut-wrenching moments I've witnessed in any media, elevated during the final sequence.My only gripes are how little time you spend in the world, and how short the game is. Things move very fast near the start with a bit of exposition-dumping, and the game can be beaten 100%-with or without a guide-in about 30-35 hours. _childDocuments_.review: I'll get the negatives out of the way first. The thing that bothered me the most about this game is the fact that there's a ton of cutscenes and dialogue, and you have no option to skip them aside from fast forwarding the text. Why this is still a thing games do in 2024 I will never understand. It especially sticks out as a flaw in a soulslike / metroidvania like this because a lot of players will naturally want to replay and speedrun it, and they'll end up spending a lot of time just sitting there waiting for the cinematics to end. Even playing casually I found it just slowed down the pacing too often for my liking. There's also a little bit of jank with the hitboxes. They're consistent once you get used to them, but some attacks just aren't very intuitive visually and lead to that feeling of "wait, how the hell did that hit me?"All that put aside, I still think this is a fantastic game overall, and definitely the best game in its genre I've played in a long time. While it's easy to tell it takes inspiration from Hollow Knight, I think it sets itself apart through the style and setting more than enough. There's a really cool blend here of eastern mythology and cyberpunk aesthetics that makes exploring and getting lost in this game's world a joy, and each area feels completely distinct through both atmosphere and gameplay. I'm also just a big fan of the artstyle overall, I always love 2D hand drawn art in games and this is a beautiful example.The combat system also strays pretty far from what you'd expect in a typical metroidvania, being highly focused on blocking / parrying attacks and waiting for openings rather than playing aggressively. There's definitely a learning curve, but improving at it and taking down some of the tougher bosses feels extremely satisfying. I honestly think it feels pitch perfect, and the fact you're still getting new attacks and modifiers to add to your kit late into the game make it stay fresh to the end.Lastly, the map design. In the grand scheme of this genre, this game isn't all that open ended compared to something like Super Metroid or Hollow Knight. With a few exceptions you'll be going through each area in the order the game wants you to. It's something I'm personally fine with, since it allows for a better difficulty curve, but I could see others being a little disappointed with the linearity. Each individual area does atleast feel pretty open and expansive, with tons of secrets to find. I also appreciated how you never feel like you do too much backtracking in this game, especially since you unlock fast travel not too far into the game.Overall, this game will definitely be a highlight of 2024 for me, and I'm really glad I decided to give it a shot. I'm usually pretty intimidated by soulslikes just because I've definitely dropped off of a few of them pretty early on, but this game felt a little more reasonable with its difficulty than most. (Plus, not having obnoxious runbacks every time you fail a boss is a nice bonus.) I had so many moments where I felt overwhelmed when first attempting a new boss or learning certain attacks, but eventually being able to overcome those parts was just so rewarding in a way games haven't made me felt in a while, and I think that feeling is what I took from this game the most.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid game. I love the paper-esque art style, like the whole game was written on a scroll. _childDocuments_.review: I was recommended this game by a friend. When I first started playing I was slightly skeptical, as parry-based combat is not something I was familiar with and the game felt really difficult. But the story and art intrigued me to keep playing, and I am glad I did. After finishing Nine Sols, I can confidently say that I am in love with this game. The sound design is clean, the art and animation is amazing, and the story had me on the edge of my seat throughout. But, above all of that, the combat system has become one of my favorites. After I got accustomed to parrying, I was amazed by how smooth the combat felt. When I was doing good, I felt untouchable. Even when I was struggling, I was still having fun. Each boss was a new puzzle to solve. I loved mixing, matching, and strategizing with the different tools and abilities the game has to offer, until I found a combination that helped me overcome the challenge I was facing. Having finished my first play through, I am now working towards 100% completion. If you are considering playing Nine Sols, do it. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Well made metroidvania game. It is very parry based, which can be intimidating at first, but it is not that bad. Really enjoyed this aspect, which makes this game stand out. _childDocuments_.review: An absolutely amazing metroidvania game, the music, combat, and story all really come together to make a memorable unique experience. The combat is fair with the balance for parrying being really solid even if its not perfectly timed the game encourages you to keep trying with the internal damage mechanic which definitely sets apart from other games parry systems where if you miss it or time it improperly you are punished severely. Basically non perfect parry will still counter the attack but you take regainable damage. The Taoist tech aesthetic is fantastic in showing the thematic argument between science and spirituality in the game's story. The music is great the whole way through with tracks specific to certain regions in the map making them stand out more. Definitely worth full price and I hope the devs continue to make games like this. Big warning for newcomers the final boss is a big difficulty spike, recommend collecting every improvement before facing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially recommend Nine Sols by a friend who pitched it as 2D Sekiro. I've never been that big on metroidvanias (bought Hollow Knight but never made it past the first few hours), but I absolutely adore Sekiro so I decided to give Nine Sols the good ol' college try. RedCandleGames has really created quite the gem here. While Nine Sols is by no means perfect, it absolutely nails the rhythm-game-esque feeling of Sekiro's parry system, and there is a decent amount of customizability through the jade system. The boss fights are a joy, and the two 3-phase bosses for sure rank up there with the likes of Sword Saint Isshin, Lady Maria, and Malenia (not to mention the OSTs!)What honestly surprised me the most was the storytelling. While nothing absolutely groundbreaking/mindblowing, the story is well-written and well-executed, and definitely has moments where it hits you in feels. For a game that I expected to just rush through smacking things, I found myself actually slowing down to read bits of lore and dialogue. TLDR: Play Nine Sols now

_childDocuments_.review: It's so disappointing that this game hasn't received all the attentions it deserved.The combat system inspired by Sekiro is very well-made, while the atmosphere created by the handmade drawings and the story itself are truly something that I did not expect and left me speechless.Even the characters are very-well written, some of them better than others.The only slight problems that I've found are two:- The map, for being a metroidvania, is very "easy" to explore : I've rarely done backtracking, since the items are very easy to find, but I can understand it since it's mostly a story-driven game.- There's little variety of enemies : Most of the enemies you fight later in the game are "enhanced" versions of the previous ones, with the only difference of one or two attacks.Despite these two points, I would still reccomend playing this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is a phenomenal Metroidvania which I would on par with Hollow Knight for one of my favorite games. _childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a neutral option for reviews here on Steam.The mechanics? Gorgeous. Parrying is fantastic to do, and in general very worth it.There is very little endlag to moves, everything is snappy.I've played Hollow Knight,  I'll try my best to refrain from comparing Nine Sols to it, that seems unfair.Healing is something I would like to compare though. You have limited charges in your healing pipe, and you can't get them back without properly going to a "bench". That, on paper, is perfectly fine. Several games have done similar for healing, such as Tunic's Healing Potions. You have an innate autoheal, but I dunno about you, I don't wanna wait in the case of me getting on low hp.But the issue isn't in the healing. It's in the damage you need to heal.I'll admit- it's probably a skill issue and I might be salty. But it feels like enemies do just too much damage. It feels like enemies kill you in ~4 & 1/2 hits. Weird metric, but hopefully that gets the point across. At least where I'm at at the time of this review, an annoyingly consistent number of enemies typically use multi-hit (2 hits 90% of the time) attacks. So that ~4 & 1/2 hits goes down to ~2 combos.It doesn't help that this game has a mechanic equal to HK's Shades or Tunic's Spirits, you lose your stuff until you get back to where you died.Here's the kicker for me though- if an enemy kills you, it inherits your stuff. You need to  it to get your stuff back.But if you died to a tough enemy, and now that still tough enemy has your stuff, how do you beat it?My overall opinion of this game is just meh. The best way I can put it into words is that a gem of a game tries its best to make you dislike it. I am constantly switching between great joy and insane frustration.Not for the faint of heart!Edit: Final boss has some total bs in there, took me >1hr, a lot compared to the other bosses

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, truly. Probably my personal GOTY, at least as of the time of this writing.Both the story and the combat start out a little slow (especially in the first hour or so of gameplay), but after playing through the game twice now I actually kinda like this - the primary combat tools that you start out with (parry, dodge, slash, talisman) are going to be your bread and butter for the majority of the game and so spending a while getting acquainted with them makes a lot of sense, and from a narrative perspective I appreciated getting a feel for the characters a bit before they started dropping a ton of Proper Noun Exposition into the mix. Once the game gets going though, it really gets going - both the plot and the combat evolve in fun and interesting ways, and while the combat remains focused on parries throughout I was pleasantly surprised at the variety of different "builds" you could do, though once I found my favored setup I mostly only switched it up a few times for very specific enemy types towards the end of the game.Story wise, this game pretty easily has one of the best stories and narratives of any metroidvania I've played in the past few years. At first it felt like they were going with a "we're not really going to give you a clear plot" idea that so many metroidvanias have utilized recently, but that was just a setup to get you familiar with the setting and the characters - the story and world are fleshed out both in some story scenes and flashbacks, but also just in the world around you through lore pickups. By the end I was very invested in the characters and the story, which is impressive to me in a game where probably a full half of my first file's playthrough was spent bashing my head against bosses.All that to say - if metroidvanias appeal to you, you should probably give this game a try. I thought for sure that the combat would be too hard for me, but once you get the hang of how the game works it is actually fairly forgiving - and the story is well worth the time it takes to get used to the combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. The artistic style is fantastic, the characters are amazing, and the environments stand out, each new zone having an unique theme and score to it. However, I am still unable to recommend this game as the combat, which is its primary feature and mechanic, is the most frustrating thing about it. This is exemplified extremely well with the boss Yanlao: the game has a stun feature where Yi can get knocked to the ground by certain attacks; however, like games in the Soulsborne series, Yi is NOT given some i-frames to recover here but is entirely susceptible to damage. This becomes a clear problem when fighting Yanlao since missing a SINGLE parry in the second phase can knock you down, get you hit, thrown into a laser and hit again and you will die in one single combo that you cannot do anything about. Outside of this particular boss, this mechanic has killed me so many times where it is straight up unfair and can only be boiled down to poor game design. In addition to this, the game's respawn system is the most atrocious thing I have ever seen. Once more, if you get hit by spikes or something of the likes, you respawn, ONCE AGAIN without a single i-frame meaning that the enemies around you immediately attack you without you being able to do anything about it, often leading to undeserved and stupid deaths. This is honestly game-breaking and I am stunned that it made it through testing.

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols really surprised me. The level of detail and thoughtful craft put into this game is seriously impressive. It’s one of the most satisfying experiences I’ve had with a game in years. If you’re a fan of Metroidvanias and Souls games, this game is worth your time.You’ll no doubt read about how the game is hard. It is, sure, but it’s equally rewarding, and you  have to be a Sekiro player to enjoy it. I wasn’t. I’d never played game that placed such a strong emphasis on parry mechanics. From my perspective, the game does a great job onboarding players with that style of play in the early game by being thoughtful about enemy density and attack patterns. As the game progresses, there’s appreciable variation in enemy behavior and quantity, such that there’s a benefit to approaching encounters in different ways fairly often. Some enemies benefit from being engaged aggressively, some defensively. Developing a sense for that and learning how to execute the games mechanics skillfully was  satisfying. The implementation of the internal damage system, in particular, was something that stood out as novel design which yielded satisfying gameplay. The game also provides the player with a fair amount of progression and customization options in its static skill tree and separate configurable skill slot systems. Nine Sols rewards thoughtful selection of Jades, talisman style and arrow type, and in the cases of its most difficult challenges, demands it.The bosses, in particular, are what elevate this game from an experience that I liked to an experience I loved. Yes, I died . However, for me, learning the attack patterns of bosses—when to parry, when to punish—was the ideal mix of frustrating and rewarding. The game has that exquisite alchemy of making some encounters feel nearly impossible at first, but each attack, each movement of the boss communicates how to approach it, so that when you’ve learned to read a boss and defeat it, it is immensely gratifying. I’ve played Hollow Knight, Dark Souls, Elden Ring, etc. For me, Nine Sols has among the strongest, most consistent quality of boss design I have ever seen in a game. The final boss, in particular, was an incredible challenge, and the experience of overcoming it cemented Nine Sols as an all-time game for me.As a frequent Metroidvania player, I found a lot to love in the level design. The game does a great job of tucking away secrets and rewards, difficult to access areas, and hidden bosses. The game really rewards exploration and I had a great time scratching the corners of each map trying to find everything. The game doles out movement abilities over time, such that playing the game a dozen hours in feels significantly different than playing the game just a few hours in. The game is also good about ensuring that these new movement abilities have utility in combat as well, giving you different ways to approach or deal with enemies apart from using the standard parry. The game gives you some prompts about where you might go, but it absolutely does not hold your hand. In my playthrough, I wound up in a few frightening areas on a couple occasions just from exploring thoroughly, which I always enjoy, because it serves as foreshadowing and makes the world of the game feel expansive and non-linear.The narrative of the game took a while to get its hooks into me, but when it did, I found myself invested in the world, characters, and mysteries of New Kunlun. The lore, delivered both in dialogue and found objects, really drew me in over time, and I was engaged by how the long history of the Solarians informed the aesthetic of the game and its narrative direction. I do wish there was  more to directly reference in the game’s database (“what was the difference between  and  again?”), but I suspect the lack of an explicit glossary was intentional. The net affect is that it takes some time for the full picture of the world, and context in which Yi is operating, to unfold. The different elements gel really well by the end of the game. The full scope of the events which preceded the game and the core thrust of the narrative arc unfolding in the present reveal themselves around the same time, in way I really enjoyed.I was not  drawn in by the characters at first, but the game does a fantastic job of giving them depth and complexity over time. Shaunshaun is an excellent example of a character who I did not like at first and who seemed to be operating in a fairly flat way, but over time really grew on me. I think the game still may be guilty of saving its most interesting characters for the end of the game and not giving as much screen time to some of the Solarians who engaged me the most, but on the whole I think the game punches above its weight in its character development and dialogue. That’s not necessarily what I come to this kind of game looking for, so the game far exceeded my expectations on this level.Similarly, I was not  captivated by the taopunk aesthetic. However, after combing through the different areas, admiring the architecture and level design, taking in every frame of the lovingly detailed animation, and listening to its gorgeous score, I walked away enamored with it. Nine Sol’s aesthetic feels distinct and unified in a way that is rare and notable. The game has a visual identity that, over time, is layered and coheres, leaving a strong impression. One particular element I loved was the way that scenes were occasionally conveyed in manga-like panels. This is not just an interesting stylistic choice, it gives more opportunity for shifts in scene perspective and character expression. The game packs a lot of drama, tone, and characterization into these scenes. I’d guess that the effectiveness of this visual style plays a large part in why I grew more engrossed in the narrative and characters over time.On the whole, Nine Sols is among the best experiences I’ve had in years. There’s so much to love here. If you’ve taken the time time to read this, I hope you will consider giving this game a chance. With Nine Sols, Red Candle Games has crafted something stellar and singular.

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is a recently released Indie Metroidvania set in a hand-drawn Taopunk world, with challenging combat that puts a main focus on parrying mechanics. TLDR at the end for those who don't want to readPros:I don't think I've had as much fun with challenging combat since my first playthrough of hollow knight; The main character is snappy and responsive to control, with a satisfying parry mechanic which can be pretty hard to get perfectly right. The combat itself is intuitive and pretty easy to grasp, but takes a while to get good at, and the enemies are varied and relatively interesting (I'll get onto that later).The story is also of a very good quality, with a seemingly well detailed setting & some good old mystery to keep you engaged. The story also seems to be (so far) trying to tell a more morally grey tale than the average game, the protagonist especially has very pronounced flaws and the beginnings of a really compelling character arc.Another thing to mention, though rather obvious, is the art. The art looks really good and the aesthetic is interesting. Not much more that I can add there really.Cons:The game is not without drawbacks though. The currency system is quite punishing; you die once and your money is dropped or absorbed by the enemy that defeated you, if you die again without picking it up, the money is lost. Considering how easy it is to die in this game, it is quite easy to lose all of your hard-earned currency due to a few small mistakes or bad RNG, which can be very frustrating. Another issue is the dialogue, which is just text (and there can be a lot of it), which some players may find difficult to read, and the font does look a bit goofy at times.To elaborate on the enemies in the game, the AI is... not good. Enemies have a habit of standing still for a while in front of you without attacking, which I assume is to make it more manageable to parry when fighting large groups, but when fighting single enemies, waiting 2-3 seconds for them to make an attack while standing directly in front of them can be a little immersion breaking.To concludeI think that 9 sols is something special, from what I've played of it, it has been imaginative and engaging with gameplay mechanics and (to a lesser extent) story. I would definitely recommend it to anybody who enjoys metroidvanias or even anybody who is just interested by the combat shown in the trailers.TLDRpros:-Really fun combat-Interesting story-Pretty artCons:-Punishing currency system-Lots of text to read-Lobotomised AIAddendum: I am probably biased in this game's favour, as I am a MASSIVE fan of Metroidvanias, and will generally enjoy a game if it's a Metroidvania. This is also the first time I am writing such a long review for a game, so my apologies if the format or language is hard to read / interpret. There are also a few things that I found a bit too subjective to insert into the review, a lot of which is covered in  (which I also ripped a few points from), so read that if interested.

_childDocuments_.review: "Enjoy a sublime eternity amongst the evergreen foothills! New Kunlun: the second home of your dreams."I find it funny how incredibly sinister, obvious, and stereotypical that message is. Where we are is doomed, alright, we must trust the Council and migrate to this other plant in which life will return to normal. The game even plays on this by allowing the player to find an item, its description is about a guy who has been super unlucky his entire life, all the annoying things happen to him all the time but when he gets accepted as an immigrant to new Kunlun he thinks he finally caught a break: "Could all those unlucky things that happened to me were the price to pay to get this ticket?" little did he know that this ticket will be the completion of his bad luck, and the one that will end his life in one of many heinous ways.Furthermore, even those who didn't get accepted to migrate were also doomed... The scale of the tragedy engulfs all and everything, in the face of such a predicament, difficult choices must be made. Or so did the Council believe.Why? How did it come to this? Yi said once: "Greed is in our very nature". Maybe none of this would have happened if we, or them, the Council members, were content with what we have. We always want more and they wanted more, they wanted immortality. Maybe none of this would have happened if people didn't lie if they admitted that their technology cannot do what it's being asked to do. There's always a price to pay for the lies that we say. The debt is accumulated and eventually demands to be paid. The bigger the lie, the bigger the debt.How Nine Sols merges religion and science is nothing short of amazing. We are in space, we are in a virtually created world yet we see the temples of those before us who worshipped and prayed tirelessly. We come from religious tribes and people yet Yi refuses to embrace it or even accept it, "Superstition this, superstition that". Yi's life was once saved by the same superstitions that he refused to accept: "No! It was my mentor who saved me."Yi the kind of person who thinks everything can be understood by science.Throughout your journey, you see how one person's views can change thanks to their newfound experiences and... friends.The NPCs in this game are verified souls-like NPCs. Their humor, functionality, and importance are just perfect, itched in my memory, and will never forget them. It's always great how those darkest games have the brightest humorous moments as if it is to say: "No matter how bad it is outside, between friends, all is well."We, humans, like to boast about our human rights, the right to live and exist, the right to freedom, happiness for all, dignity, liberty, equality, brotherhood, and so on. But let's assume hypothetically that on a distant planet lived a different species, to whom our existence is tied. We must kill them to live and survive. Would our human rights theories stand in our way of surviving and doing what we must? No, it won't. But why? Because this species isn't humans? is our human rights theory a lie? Is it because survival is more important than anything else? Is it because they are not as smart as us and they would go extinct on their own anyway?Well, and so did the Council of 10 went on to justify, each according to their character, the invasion and enslavement of a different species. And so did the the lies begin and so did the debt started to accumulate for centuries. I don't think any of the 10 envisioned or imagined how grave their mistakes were or the cost of it all. Not to excuse them, that is.The thing that I probably found most interesting about this game and at the same time, most annoying is how blurry the lines are. It's never black and white: "What is justice? black and white? Good and evil? It all depends on the eye of the beholder." said Ji, leaving me very conflicted about how to feel. Even in my moments of victory, the game would never let me have it. Would never let me believe I did a 'good' thing and instead the opposite, making me feel like I'm the bad guy... and maybe I was.Ultimately, no matter your circumstances, your actions have consequences. We could sit here and try to justify them till tomorrow, but it won't change the fact that Pengali is a deserted deathbed and the Pale Blue Planet is nothing but an apocalyptic farm where delaying the inevitable ever sinks us deeper into a delusional coma.The combat is fantastic. It's very Sekiro-like, your parry is your everything. Exploring the world was fun, side quests were meaningful throughout which you saw the world and your friend change as you went on your self-righteous journey. The music. Now this is what I like. It knows when to be quiet and when to take the stage, again, an incredible mix of religious serenity and scientific disruption.I loved this game, it's a very special Metroidvania with its story, world, NPCs, and gameplay mechanics. There's a lot more that could be said but I leave it to you to find out for yourself. I close by saying: "Oh, to go back, and be as innocent as ShuanShuan."

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is an excellent game and absolutely worth it for the current asking price. Nine Sols is a solid take on the metroidvania genre - If you've enjoyed games like Hollow Knight, Metroid Prime, or Ori and the Blind Forest, then Nine Sols is a must try. The game also combines elements of Soul's likes well, particularly Sekiro. It's a very parry heavy game. The combat is tight and engaging. Puzzle platforming is fun and of expected difficulty, although it doesn't quite reach the White Palace challenge of Hollow Knight. A unique element of Nine Sols is your AI Whisp companion that allows for limited platforming to unlock mechanisms further away from your character, it's fun, but under utilized.The story of the game is good, not new, but good. It's not often we get to see Cyberpunk Taoism and the atmosphere and lore kept me consistently engaged. The game doesn't really have any twists or turns, but the characters are well-written and interesting throughout. It's very trope heavy, but the tropes are done interestingly and compellingly. The scope of the story starts small and rapidly pulls back creating a compelling narrative, even if we've seen stories like it before.All-in-all great game, worth the asking price, and it did what any good game should - I was sad when it ended because I wanted to engage with the world more.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure this game has already drawn a lot of comparisons to Hollow Knight, and even though it's an apt comparison, I think it's worth examining more closely. It's not similar in worldbuilding, gameplay, or art style; the level of difficulty is arguably harder (it involves a lot of precise timing of attacks with little wiggle room, precision being one of the worst things for me personally), and you start out with most of the tools needed to navigate the map, making exploration a lot more accessible. These are all traits that make Nine Sols stand out among competitors, and worth playing.But the ways Nine Sols is similar to Hollow Knight also makes it unique, in a way. I keep bringing it up because I (along with many people) think Hollow Knight is the industry standard of the Metrovania/Souls-like genre, the one to imitate or surpass. And although Nine Sols will probably never reach the same level of popularity or notoriety, I think it gets the closest to capturing the essence of what makes the game truly great. Whereas a lot of games would've tried to match the art style, mechanics, or tone of Hollow Knight, Nine Sols rebuilds it from the ground up, creating something both like and very different from other Metroidvanias.The way the story unfolds is far more akin to an RPG than anything else, populated with a lot of colorful characters to interact with, a set goal known from the beginning, and a heavier emphasis on exploration outside of the typical "point A to point B" formula. I've only played about 12 hours at this point, and I suck at boss battles (especially in games this difficult), but I've still traversed all over the map. Instead of new equipment or skills needed to proceed, more often than not, the main roadblocks for progression are extremely powerful enemies that will wipe the floor with you if you aren't strong enough; so, technically possible to beat, but far smarter to go a different way first. This is emphasized by the fact that you have a home base that you can fast travel to, but you can't fast travel from one location to another, making the map more of a web than a dungeon: if things get too hard, go back to the beginning and go a different way instead.The art is beautiful as well; filled with saturated colors blended in a way that evokes Chinese watercolors. A lot of Metroidvanias focus on darker, dreary tones or expressed through the kind of lens filter a DC movie would use. A downside to the graphics, however, is that it really slows the computer down. As long as I have my laptop plugged in, I can run most 2D games without any trouble, but I had to greatly lower the quality to run certain parts of Nines Sols smoothly. A little lag isn't always a big deal, but when a game focuses so much on timing and precision, lag can be fatal.The other positive for players like me, who are terrible at Souls-like games due to difficulty but find less challenging games too easy, is that Nine Sols has a custom scale option at the beginning, instead of the typical "easy, normal, or hard" modes. Here, we have "normal" or "story mode," which allows customization. I chose to play it at normal difficulty, of which I'm honestly regretting, but if I decide to go back and start a new save file using story mode, I know the game will be fun enough to retread old ground.TL;DR I cannot recommend Nine Sols highly enough. $30 seems like a steep price, but I don't think it's asking too much.
_childDocuments_.name: Nine Sols

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols is quite comfortably my GoTY for 2024 as of mid-June, and I fully believe that it is the new champion of the Metroidvania/Soulslike genre, and by a comfortable margin as well. While it might not be top of its class in every single field, I think that there's a real argument to be made for it being a runner up across them all, which is extremely impressive. I don't think I've ever played a game with such a strong fantasy style. Taopunk is such a fresh take on a very traditionally medieval genre, and the bar Nine Sols sets is not one that will be topped any time soon. The game's philosophical and touching story are a real breath of fresh air when contrasted with its muddy and more speculative Souls siblings. The world is rich and a lot of quality effort has clearly been put into expanding on the cultures and histories of the various Solarian factions. While I don't think that the game's music is best in its class, I feel that simply calling it serviceable is disrespectful. I didn't have any big Greenpath Theme or Slave Knight Gael moments with it, but it was reliably pleasing nonetheless. The world and movement are all quite good; exploration is smooth and the enemy populations are well balanced. Nine Sols understand that its combat system is oriented towards one-on-one fights and for the most part it allows you to isolate each enemy, while also leaving room for enemies to bunch up if you get careless.All of that said, where Nine Sols really shines is its combat. I'm of the opinion that Sekiro has the best melee combat system of any game I've ever played, and the inspiration shines through extremely brightly through Nine Sols, a game that, if I may be so bold, rises to Sekiro's challenge, and perhaps even surpasses it in areas. While Sekiro places a greater emphasis on rhythm, which does make it a more consistently satisfying system to learn and pull off, Nine Sols incorporates Sekiro's parry system with a more weaving-oriented approach. Given that there is no posture system, your goal is instead to sneak the heaviest attack you can in between each of the enemy's, parry, and repeat. It works fabulously. The internal damage system is a bit superfluous when it comes to enemies; most of the time only serving to encourage aggression. However, talisman blasts have the delightfully satisfying side effect of converting all internal damage to direct damage. Often you will build up a large amount of internal damage on a boss and then consume it all to decimate its healthbar. It's a deeply enjoyable experience, and in my opinion rivals the satisfaction of breaking a boss's stance in Sekiro. A place where I believe Nine Sols has a leg up on Sekiro is visual readability; the 2D medium makes boss attacks much easier to perceive and react to quickly, which is essential for the fast-paced combat. The readability alongside near-impeccable difficulty balance and hitboxes make for one of the fairest combat systems I've ever encountered in a game. Despite the game's pretty challenging boss fights, there was only one where I ever got frustrated. When the game slips in this regard (which it does on said boss, in my opinion) it is very noticeable, though that does come with the side effect of it being all the sweeter once you get back to the status quo of the game absolutely nailing it. Nine Sols's combat is its most impressive achievement among a series of genre-defining accomplishments. It means a lot when the only complaints I can think of for a game feel more like nitpicks than real, significant problems with it, especially when they are so few. I cannot praise this game more highly. It is rare that a developer's vision for a game is so clear and so purely, perfectly realized. The already high bars for the Metriodvania and Soulslike genres have been substantially raised. I strongly recommend Nine Sols to anyone who is willing to overcome the ample challenge it offers, you will be rewarded with one of the best gaming experiences I've ever had.
