_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't leave reviews for most games I've played, but Nine Sols is probably one of the best games I have ever played.     It is a cross between Sekiro styled deflection (parry) centered combat, and a beautifully stylized 2-D Metroidvania similar to Hollow Knight. Though the size and scope of the world is not quite as big as Hollow Knight, there is still plenty of secrets and other hidden items to find. It also has a very unique style of what could be described as a mix of Taoism and Asian culture, and a Cyberpunk sci-fi setting, or "Taopunk" as the steam trailer describes it.   Nine Sols is also much more story and character focused than Hollow Knight or similar Souls-like games, and has some of the most interesting and compelling writing I've seen in a game in a very long time. The protagonist Yi also becoming a new favorite main character of mine. I know that not everyone has the patience for games with a larger narrative focus as they just want to get to the game-play or "meat" of the game, but if you are looking for a game like Hollow Knight or Sekiro, or just a fantastic Metroidvania with a somewhat larger focus on the characters and story without any sacrifice to the quality of the game-play then Nine Sols is definitely worth playing. Also, for those who don't care about the story or characters, it is not too difficult to just skip or speed through much of the dialogue and cut scenes if you want to, though I strongly recommend to give them a chance.   The boss fights and battles against common foes can be described as a dance of sorts, just like with Sekiro, with a satisfyingly strong blend of offense and defense. The bosses in particular (the Nine Sols) are definitely a highlight of the game, and are some of best, most memorable, and fun Bosses I've fought in a long time. I would rank some of these fights as being worthy of some of the best bosses from Sekiro and Hollow Knight, as well as Furi for anyone who has played that. They also recently added in a battle memory mode into game that lets you re-fight any of the Sols if you have achieved an ending in the game. It is not a true boss rush, but it is a welcome addition regardless to be able to enjoy these fights again, and to be able to practice them without having to replay the entire game to do so.   Also for anyone who may be hesitant to give the game a try due to the inherently higher difficulty of souls-like games, fear not for there is a story mode that can be enabled that allows control for damage taken and given, though I would encourage to give the standard difficulty a chance as this kind of combat is not as satisfying if you adjust it to just let you tank through everything and kill enemies in a few hits. The difficulty I would argue also helps to enhance the atmosphere and the at times bleak and brutal feeling of this world.   It is also worth touching on that not only does Nine Sols has a beautiful art style, but much of the sound design and music in the game also matches the visual quality. I would describe some of the sound track as being hauntingly beautiful and somber.   I also did not experience any notable performance issues with the game, as it ran quite smoothly for me with a stable FPS and no notable glitches. But I also have a good quality PC, so your mileage may vary depending on your setup.   Overall I have very few issues with this game as I feel it is as close to perfect as game like this can get, but while I may not have any major complaints about the game I do have some minor nitpicks. There are a couple of attack animations that do feel that they could have been tweaked to telegraph the attacks a bit better on a handful of enemies as they feel a little weird, but these are very few and far between so its a rather minor issue that many people probably will not notice. The hit boxes for a couple of attacks also seem to be a bit larger than they appear to be which can make it look like you got hit by an attack that shouldn't have been that close to you, this is also a rather small issue but it is worth noting.   I should also mention that while it did not bother me, this game can get rather gory and violent and does have some moments of cruelty, so if you are easily bothered by such things you may not enjoy this game. I will also note that while I did not have a issue with this, some people have complained about the final boss of the game having a rather sudden difficulty spike, especially if going for a specific ending. While I personally think the final boss is perfect as is, I can understand that it may be a bit much for some people. So if you struggle with this fight I would recommend to try changing up your strategy with equipment and abilities to see what works and what doesn't as I also had to do this. Some optional abilities you may have glossed over during the rest of the game may be very helpful here, I would recommend the water flow talismans when learning the fight and attack patterns, and the full control talismans for more damage to get through the fight more quickly once you get comfortable with it. As a tangent the full control talismans became my favorite style to use after beating the final boss and will definitely be used more on future playthroughs.   I could go further into describing the different aspects of the game and the combat and story, but this review is already rather lengthy and I don't want to spoil the game too much with regards to mechanics or said story. Though I will say that I would consider Nine Sols to be my personal Game of the Year for 2024.   TLDR: Nine Sols is an amazing parry focused Metroidvania with strong characters and story that I would strongly recommend to anyone that enjoys games like Sekiro or Hollow Knight. And even if these kinds of games are not something you would normally enjoy, I would at the very least try playing through with story mode to experience the story and characters if you more interested in the narrative of the game than the game play. Also you play as a lonely, depressed, and sometimes very vengeful cat boi so I'm sure that's a plus for some people.  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

_childDocuments_.review: really hard, really good. some of the most creative and visually inspired boss fights and world, and now i'm kicking myself because i was one quest away from reaching true ending before fighting the final boss. like a lot of other reviews say the final boss is definitely the most difficult but it felt so satisfying to finally beat them. highly recommend.i read some other reviews about the combat system being unpolished, specifically the need to face the same direction to parry and getting comboed by enemies; but i would say after getting used to the gameplay facing the same direction is second nature and getting comboed is not a real complaint to me, because you should be appropriately punished for messing up. there are a lot of options to avoid getting trapped in a string and parrying is pretty lenient, all things considered. so if you don't want to struggle too much then just play the story mode, but you're really missing out on some of the best adrenaline rushes out there if you do.The story is also pretty good, there's a lot of environmental storytelling and bits of lore to find, and you get a lot of the story shown to you through flashbacks so piecing everything together isn't too crazy. _childDocuments_.review: Updated Review:I've spent 24.6 hours with Nine Sols, most of it repeating a loop. _childDocuments_.review: Never have I ever written a review for a videogame, but I think this one deserves it. Nine Sols is a game that excels in every department: art/presentation, gameplay, storytelling (I loved the manga-styled cutscenes and almost cried at the end), and especially the soundtrack (jesus christ the OST... you get this banger during one of the first bosses:) I could spent hours admiring this game, but instead of stirring up expectations, I prefer to warn you that...- Though the 2D models are gorgeous and have their charm, it's pretty grim, dark, bloody and even have some small body-horror elements. .- . Sometimes you feel you are getting the hang of it, then suddenly you are retrying a boss fight more than 10 times. I didn't test the "Story Mode" difficulty, but I can tell you that "Standard Mode" will test your perseverance over and over again. If you are not into repeating (pretty amazing) boss fights until you can master them, then the "Standard Mode" isn't for you, especially with the final boss. I don't meant to flex, but Sekiro's final boss felt like a pushover compared to this one. This is surely subjective, but in my decades of playing challenging games, I never thought I would have to repeat that kind of (lovely) experience again where I had to spent at least 1 hour trying and trying until I beat it, but I can see why that may frustrate some players.- . You can tell the developers had pretty competent writers and it's truly a labor of love. But if you are not into reading lots of dialogues, interacting with every single character and logbook, you will be missing on a 50% of what makes this game so great.- . Sure, it borrows one or two mechanics from that game, but just like the game description says, it's heavily inspired by Sekiro, which means you need to have a sense of rhythm and reflexes in order to parry instead of attacking. I have to make this warning because I suspect people will buy this game thinking "oh, I loved Hollow Knight, I'm surely going to love this one". Nah, they are completely different experiences. I'll quote what another user said "Hollow Knight is the 2D version of Dark Souls, while Nine Sols is the 2D version of Sekiro". The only thing I can gladly admire that it shares with Hollow Knight is that every area plays a role in the storytelling, instead of what most Metroidvanias do where they insert random traps and monsters here and there "because it's cool".- Also, , though it has the basic elements of exploration and platforming, which are very satisfying, and you always have the liberty to go wherever you want as long as you have the necessary powerup, this game is mostly linear and there aren't that many optional areas to explore.- If I had to list the things that I personally think they could improve:Nonetheless, it's a pretty complete 20-hour package, with an amazing story told with philosophical elements, a good pacing that keeps you wondering about the main character's true intentions, and thankfully it doesn't rely on overly-expositional dialogue: it's not until the very end that you get the whole picture of what's happening.Since the very beginning you can tell that every piece of this game is high quality and made with ton of effort. I highly recommend supporting the developers even if you buy it with a small discount.

_childDocuments_.review: A platformer that looks and sounds absolutely gorgeous.Unfortunately, it's more about combat than anything else. While classified as a metroidvania, it's pretty linear with little reward for exploration, and no real sense of getting lost in the world. Not only that, exploration is actively punished by its money dropping mechanic. Also, if you die on the way to your money-holding gravestone, you'll lose everything you had. No joke.Gameplay here is ALL about fighting, and to be more specific, about parrying. This isn't a metroidvania!It's a parrying simulator with all the rote memorization that comes with the territory. It's more like a punishing rhythm game, where you absolutely need to know every enemy/boss telegraph by heart, and even that's often not enough. Some prompts are virtually indistinguishable from each other, and if you fail to react correctly a couple of times, it's game over. (Then again, I assume that's what they mean by the "Sekiro-inspired" marketing phrase.)This is a huge issue, as bosses kill you in a few hits, while you have to get in dozens. On its "normal" difficulty, even mini-bosses are ridiculous sponges.As for the inevitable "git gud" choir of unemployed gaming gods: practicing fights in Nine Sols sucks, for the aforementioned reasons. You die fast, and to get another try, you need to make your way through the mostly boring environment to where you died - and most likely be forced to wait for elevators and whatnot while you're at it.Not good, unless you have unlimited time. You either check the correct strategy on Youtube or play the trial-and-error game for extended amounts of time.Note: The game does have a story mode which can be adjusted make everything more tolerable. Personally, I wasn't that interested in the story, so I opted for just uninstalling.I bought in to the "stop waiting for Silksong and buy this" hype and it really didn't pay out.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE AFTER COMPLETING: It remained very strong all the way through! There was a bit of a difficulty spike with the last few bosses but it was sick. Like... 8.7/10. Fantastic execution of the hollow knight formula.They updated the map system to make it friendlier. I was fine with it being more obscured previously but I can see how that would have alleviated some of my personal pressure points earlier in the game.THE REST I WROTE ABOUT HALFWAY THROUGH THE GAME BUT STILL AGREE WITH: An excellent entry in the metroidvania + soulslike fusion genre. It takes many mechanics from similar games and executes most of them very well, all while featuring a great art style and soundscape.Map exploration has been great so far. I like how large each room is and how it shows up as a defined area on the map, and then you can find a data chip that unlocks a detailed view of the area later on. There's a few bugs with using a controller on the map screen so I've ended up having to use my mouse a few times to be able to navigate to areas.Root nodes (the game's benches/bonfires) provide the ability to teleport back to your hideout, and then later on you can teleport to any root node that you've found. This is pretty standard amidst these games, though I personally prefer Hollow Knight's travel systems with the stagways, trams and dreamgates over simply being able to teleport anywhere.In usual fashion, dying gives you the opportunity to lose accumulated money/exp. There's plenty to buy with money and I mostly run with the charms that give me more money, so I haven't felt like I've lost much progress even when I did make some silly mistakes and die. It definitely felt a lot more punishing in the first few hours of the game though. At the point of the game where I'm at, I have a few shopkeeps in my hideout so I'm never more than one node away from spending money.Exp and the skill tree feel like extraneous systems to me. In terms of losing exp, you can only lose accumulated exp to your next skill point which really isn't that punishing imo. In general I'm a little tired of skill trees but it doesn't necessarily detract from the game.Combat and movement feel very smooth. Directional parry took a bit to get used to but feels great. Enemies from above can occasionally cross you up but it's not a big deal. Some enemies also turn on a dime so dodging through them during a flurry of blows is dangerous if you're not careful. A horde of enemies surrounding you is genuinely dangerous. I'm still feeling out the 'unbounded' counter move which lets you absorb/reflect completely unblockable moves though at the moment it feels very strange.There is a good bit of unskippable cutscene/dialogue that (if it remains unskippable on repeat playthroughs) would hurt the replayability of the game. I enjoy the characters quite a bit otherwise, though a few cutscenes are a touch too long in my opinion.All in all, a great package so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Deep, emotionally rich, and meaningful game that, like a lot of Red Candle games, speaks eloquently to the Taiwanese identity, in a way that very very few pieces of literature can do. Really fun and reactive gameplay that makes you feel like a tai chi master reacting to the environment, but can often feel frustrating in its difficulty as all the negative reviewers are saying. I get the same "me vs. game" vibes going through this as I got with Elden Ring, which is not necessarily a bad thing if you're into that. That being said, the developers do have an "easier" story mode that you can switch to if it gets too frustrating at any point. So if you feel yourself frustrated at any point, or just want to experience this rich and deep world and story with minimal frustration, there's no shame in switching to easy mode (honestly I might switch soon myself because I'm just so engrossed in this story)Also this targets a more mature audience. This isn't a game for kids. Be warned.

_childDocuments_.review: Its Hollow Knight but with Sekiro/parry style combat instead of dashes and dodges. I will say some of the minibosses are sometimes recycled with just an additional move thrown on to them, still fun to fight but it could have been something unique instead.Movement and platforming is fine. I've got no complaints about it and I did not run into anything I felt was unreasonable even when playing on mouse and keyboard.I'm not much of a story guy but I enjoyed the comic style cutscenes before every major boss and the true ending did make me feel a bit emotional after so many hours playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: What a genuinely amazing game! From the very beginning I was having an absolute blast. The combat feels really good - it's difficult, but it's fair and as long as you're learning the different movesets, you can progress in a fight. Each boss fight also felt really unique and interesting.Also, the art style is so beautiful! There are short snippets of the story that are told through a comic format and I thought that was really cool. And the story itself was top-notch. The true ending had me tearing up and feeling emotions that few games have successfully been able to do.I just...it was really, really good and more people need to have this game on their radar. People keep comparing it to Hollow Knight and I would consider Nine Sols pretty on par with that game. I hope that people take away from the comparison that they're both fantastic combat-based metroidvanias, and even if you didn't love Hollow Knight to give this one a try. Besides some base mechanics that are similar they are very different and unique games.Anyways, have fun! Please play it. It deserves everything.EDIT: If this game doesn't win some kind of award this year, it will have been a severe disservice. I haven't played such a beautiful, fun, and wonderfully written game in a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished with almost 100% completion, all endings.The amount of effort put into this game is a must experienceI would give this game a solid 7.5/10.The story with its creativity and originality deserves a separate rating, solid 9.5/10. Red candles absolutely cooked.I would love to give it a higher rating, but I will discuss both the pros and cons for my rating placement below. The game quantity is high but quality is average. Generally the problems with the game shows as this is Red Candle's first metroidvania game, but given that this IS their first attempt it's outstanding. The cons are mostly what I find interesting about this game.What Nine Sols is:Nine Sols is a combination of very heavy storytelling, exploration, and boss combat. The game lore delves into a discussion of reasoning (science) and spirituality (taoism), and questions where both has a place among each other- described as 'tao-punk' by the devs. There are other minor themes of philosophy and morality also brought into the story. The main star of the game is the storytelling, and obviously the parry mechanic that it sells for. Other than that, it follows a typical metroidvania formula that you would expect with exploration into boss fights, as its main combat highlight.Pros:Storytelling is greatDrawing panels for every boss, many cutscenes, and even character drawings created just for unique one-off appearances or which get barely used laterMap visuals are greatMap themes are creativeCombat system is complex and interesting (as the game progresses)Parrying is amazing, they nailed it on the headUpgrades generally feel fair and well deservedBoss designs are greatMusic is 'average' for me (purely personal taste)Final boss () is an absolute 10/10 bangerEnding is amazingCons:The game, despite being ~45hrs worth of high quality gameplay content to finish, has many things that 'feel' strangely unpolished.The game has a very strange lack of 'direction' pointing for the player. The game initially reveals your next main objective through dialogue, however it is not emphasized at all prior that the dialogue is the only thing that will point you to your next objective. There is no dialogue replay option. And if you can't remember the initial strange names of the locations mentioned, you are generally left to assume on your own. This IS bad because this basically was my experience- skipped all dialogue (was planning to read midway through the game) until I realized they were actually important but couldn't reread any of them, became lost, did a WASD exploration of the map. And ended up doing almost pure exploration for my first 15hrs of gameplay, only to be subjected to almost a 4 boss rush sequence at the end.The game is an absolute slow-burner. The story and combat is initially very slow and only picks up around the midgame point, and then actually takes off at the endgame. If you weren't invested in the game from the beginning I feel there is actually very little to catch your attention and continue playing. It actually almost feels as if you can tell the devs development from when they begin to where they get really good and comfortable with designing the game system.Exploration early is greatly punishing and frustrating, which matters because they give you the ability to explore ~65% of the map from the start with no obvious "you need this mechanic" signals. ALL mobs have high health and damage, you barely deal damage, you can only heal twice, and when you die reclaiming your gold and exp is hard and frustrating because most of the time you died due to the length of your journey, not "I couldn't deal with something". So there are times you reach there and die again, just losing everything. Midgame exploration difficulty feels where it should be right. But waiting until the midgame for a metriodvania game isn't what a player would normally do.While I'm not sure if bosses are fixed in a fighting order, (subjectively from my experience) boss difficulty tends to fluctuate quite significantly, either spiking in difficulty or being a complete pushover. I can think of two mini-bosses () who felt significantly harder than actual main bosses you fight. And some main bosses () felt like complete pushovers compared to others ().I'm unsure if boss balancing is based around assumptions of your expected power level (from explorations/upgrades) by the time you reach them, but either way it makes some boss experiences quite unenjoyable. If the core combat mechanic is parrying, then the combat experience should revolve around parrying complexity, not "I literally can't kill this boss because he almost oneshots me, and my dps is so piss low this would take 15mins").)There are two specific bosses in mind where they are absolutely miserable to fight unless you figure out the specific counters to some attacks or attacking windows, which to me were either strangely specific in the same that none of the previous bosses had any emphasis or build up to that mechanic. )The Jade system is nice but I don't like that some of them have pros/cons attached while others are strictly power boosts. It's inconsistent. I would rather all of them have pros/cons than to just have powercreep augments.If you are heading for the true ending, the criterias for it are just literally not ever specified. It turns out it borderline requires . So it is almost impossible to achieve unless you look it up and spoil yourself, which subjectively, ruins the game experience for me.Some weird glitches/details not ironed out:There is no way to return to before your endgame "" . Yes they gave a light warning, but the fact that you are stuck with your decision until the  and have no way to undo it is strange. This is bringing back the whole "bosses are balanced around your expected power level" pointer.Enemies can attack you during cutscenesOpenable Doors and locked doors look verryy similar except for the engravings on the openable doors. It actually matters when you've been playing for more than 3hrs consecutively exploring and are struggling to tell the difference anymore. Dark backgrounds or getting chased while trying to tell the difference isn't helping.Some items are just hidden very unintuitively. Some very subtle hints at pots that actually contain very important items, and . There is one puzzle () that is also wtf unintuitive.There is no way to undo power system progress. Not for the reason of reallocating skill points, but because I want to nerf myself and undo power progress to challenge myself for bosses. Yes, there are mods, but with the game this long and this big in content I find it strange.

_childDocuments_.review: There are some really nice bosses, the movement and combat feels really great and snappy, the environment looks clean and the artstyle is great... but above all.. the story!I'm not one to read blocks of texts from descrptions and notes normally, but i got a little invested in it, and ended up shedding a tear or two at the end of the true ending.I also kinda feel like having to compare it to Hollow Knight.. Not only because i think Hollow Knight is still one of the best Metroidvanias currently out there, but also because i think Nine Sols has so many good aspects, that it's worth comparing it to one of the best titles.They both have great combat and enemie/boss design, a beautiful artstyle, smooth platforming, well designed zones, and they share a similar system with the Charms/Jades, so how could i not..So here's a few of the, in my opinion, more notable things when looking at these two games, for those interested:- Nine Sols is pretty linear in how you progress through the zones and veery few optional zones. (There is optinal secrets, rooms, bosses/minibosses and stuff tho)- new dialogue is much clearer displayed with an " ! ", and (most) special items clearly tell you who you can/should give them to, making it harder to miss out on story and NPC interactions.- I wanna say "less enemie variety", but i think that just comes with Nine Sols being a shorter game, which is probably also why it didn't bother me at all- Oh yeah.. and there's some gore and creepy/horror aspects that might not be for everyone, for me it was just the right amount to convey the state and the stakes of everything, without overdoing it, but people might be put off by itOne more comparison i wanna make is in the combat, so everything from here on is just me nerding about the combat..Where in Hollow Knight combat is focused around dodging and weaving in hits and choosing between using your spell vs saving the charge for healing, in Nine Sols you also have the option to block/perfect parry/counter different kinds of attacks, which simply gives you more options in how you wanna approach a fight, and your healing has a set amount of charges that you can increase and upgrade, Dark Souls style.One might think that blocking/parrying is tedious, and i'm normally that type of person aswell, but i like the execution of that system in Nine Sols.Blocking and perfect block are the same button, its just your timing that makes a difference. So you will take reduced damage if your timing is off. (and because of how quickly the game responds to your input, you can oftentimes get a very quick block in, even after attacking, where in other games you'd be trading hits if the enemy attacked right after you finished your attack)But even if your timing is off and you take some damage.. some of the damage you took is recoverable by either not getting hit for a few seconds, with a Jade for example, with which you can even make that health recoverable by attacking!.. Bloodborne style!And you get rewarded even more for blocking properly, because doing that gives your enemies "internal damage".Internal damage is basically a portion of their healthbar changing color, and when hitting that enemy with your Talisman, they take the entirety of that colored portion (+ Talisman damage) as damage.So essentially, even if you feel like you can't find easy openings to get attacks in, you can still work on enemies and bosses health bars by blocking their attacks and removing chunks of their health with your Talisman.This gives you the choice of what attacks you want to dodge, to then weave in attacks, and which atttacks you feel comfortable blocking, then weave in attacks, and then benefit even more from them with the internal damage system.Normally just sitting there, blocking and waiting for an opening would feel slow and not as rewarding, because the boss's hp doesn't change from blocking, but this way you still get rewarded for it.And that all, when used in conjunction on some of the tougher bosses  can create a beautiful dynamic in combat, where you can still dodge and weave in quick attacks to chip away health, but also block/parry attacks, still get hits in during your attack window, and use your talisman to remove an EVEN bigger chunk of their health bar, if you get comfortable with blocking.I really really hope RedCandleGames makes more games like this, i'd be very excited and interested Nine Sols has been a great journey!So thank you if you read this far and find this useful.And thank you RedCandleGames for this gem of a game! :)

_childDocuments_.review: To summarize this game in three words: Chinese Metroidvania Sekiro.I do recommend it and so do most people here on steam, so I'mma criticize it as much as possible. If you want a positive-only review, scroll away.Chinese: tropes, names, music, and stuff like that. Mr. Main Character's name is "Yi."Metroidvania: This game might've been a lot more fun if it was like Furi, where you only have back to back boss fights. All the in-between stuff are metroidvania elements which bore me. Sure, you go around a big area, jump around, unlock abilities and stuff -> and then access newer-ish areas in places you've been to before, uncover secrets and chests for money and loot... then eventually get to the next area. It's not a particularly deep metroidvania experience but it is solid. The reason it bores me is because it kinda collides with:Sekiro: It's designed to be difficult where you're expected to learn attack patterns and how to parry and/or dodge them. Every enemy in the game DEMANDS you respect this formula and will absolutely punish you for trying to skip it. Imperfect parries result in "internal damage" which slowly heals back over time. Like how Sekiro can't get stance broken if you keep parrying, you can't die in this game from internal damage. If you do get hit, you will lose all internal damage and take normal damage on top of that, so, carefully walk on the razor line.Furthermore, every boss fight is effectively: enter for the first time, see stuff happen, die, then go back and do better; repeat until you win. Walk-backs to bosses aren't long, which is a plus. While it is possible to win some fights on your first try, don't expect to. This is actually a huge flaw because the best fights, the ones I enjoyed the most -> were ones where I was able to actually fight and learn the fight as I played; instead of just dying and trying again. Importantly: you'll most likely NOT die after you run out of healing because of how this game is set up -> with bosses taking you from full HP to dead in a combo; a combo you're going to learn to heal with on your next try, or the try after that, or the try after that... or- etc.The final boss in particular is thoroughly designed to kill you until you just learn the fight. I did not find it fun because I was not engaging with a fight but I was literally playing rock-paper-parry-this-you-filthy-casu-"okay, parried it" - 3rd attempt or something. You stand ZERO chance to learn this fight as you play it because, despite having max possible HP, the boss hits like a truck. Not only does the final boss deal an absurd amount of damage to you per hit, the boss combos and combos and combos -> resulting in the fact you won't really get to heal easily. The boss is design to take you from full HP to dead in an instant.It says a lot about a boss fight that I wasn't excited that I beat it because I was half-watching a youtube video on the other screen and just playing on auto-pilot. I'd like to note: the Final Boss is not the worst boss. That honor goes to a rampaging axe wielding dude who... doesn't even swing you at half the time -> instead it knocks things from the ceiling which are unparryable and deal stupid damage. I didn't even feel like it was hard, just a stupid fight that killed me because I was trying to play the game.Other:There's a plot that's obtuse and sad (literally sad). It only earns two specific sad moments so it mostly lost me. With that said, the characters are well written and importantly: your "Firelink Shrine" area changes as you interact with characters and as the game progresses - to the point that it is changes quite a bit. On the topic of not_Firelink Shrine, being forced to teleport to it is a pain; Bloodborne style.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece.The best parts of Hollow Knight and Sekiro in one game.Beautiful art and sound design.Charming world with a Count of Monte Cristo esque story loosely based on the mythological archer Hou Yi.Satisfying Metroidvania platforming mechanics, and unparalleled combat in all aspects.Excellent pacing and the perfect level of complexity (more than a Foddian, less than a Fromsoft so you don't need to google anything).Sekiro-level difficulty (if it's too hard for you, you can can still enjoy it through story mode with difficulty sliders making it accessible to all kinda like Skyrim).Play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine if Hollow Knight and Sekiro had a child. That is the best way I can describe this game, and it's amazing. My play through lasted 30 hours, in which got almost every achievement except for two I missed that I will have to re-do. Though I find most bosses to not be too difficult, if you are going for the true ending then you must absolutely prepare yourself for some of the optional bosses that are no joke. The story is told in a very open ended way, where questions considering the lore and the world are mostly left up to interpretation, but the main story is very well conveyed to the player, with many many character interactions to enjoy. Speaking of which, if you at all enjoy visual novels, then you will feel quite at home with how the story presents it self, as most of the main story is told entirely through different characters, either by gifting them or just triggering character events when they become available. The artstyle is drop-dead gorgeous, being so imaginative at times with the ancient-punk(?) aesthetic, which lends it self so well to the theming of the story. The combat is where the Sekiro DNA comes in, as it is parry based, which is implemented on such a high level that only Sekiro rivals it in terms of parry systems in my opinion (yes there is a mikiri counter equivalent). 10/10 game that deserves all the praise, especially considering this is RedCandle's first action game, let alone metroidvania.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't want to make a review until i finished this game, but the whole way through I was resisting the urge to give this a thumbs up because of how incredible this game is. I have just finished the game with the true ending and have almost 100% the game, and it is easily one of the best I have ever playedThe highlights for me were easily the beautiful and fluid hand-drawn animation that made the game so easy for the eye and definitely is one of the most well-animated games out there, this games art helps build such a great world with so much variety and makes it feel so alive , the music is so atmospheric and really emphasises all emotions this game throws at you. Speaking of emotions this game has a beautiful story and endings that left me in awe after beating them. One of the best aspects is seemingly controversial and that is the combat, its a sekiro-like parry based combat that is INSANELY BRUTAL, it's super punishing but each fight is fair (except Kanghui ♥♥♥♥ him) and so well balanced, all the sols have such great settings to fight in and the best movesets possible. Although at some times it can get a little tedious (like if you fall into spikes you dont get invincibility frames and can get hit, and those blob things that dont have moves but just damage you whenever they touch you they pissed me off) but its clear the game WANTS YOU to get better, you may need to die tens and hundreds of times but its so rewarding and the feeling you get once you beat a boss you have been stuck on is unparalleled. Speaking of all the bosses are so well designed story wise and visually.The game also has a HEEP of mechanics that are super cool and are so fun the play with (although I didn't like the unbound counter as it automatically releases after 2 seconds) but other than that they are all well implemented into the gameplay to make the combat the whole way though feel so unbelievably fluid. Ranting about the story again: the story of this game whilst a bit confusing at the start all wraps up in the perfect way, being so motivating the whole way throughout to uncover the secrets of New Kunlun and seek revenge for Yi, for me the True Ending was easily the best and the most rewarding even though it broke me, and the whole way through I am so immersed in the Taopunk theme and story. This games characters build such an emotional connection with Yi and all have such great chemistry that there wasn't a single one I disliked.The exploration in this game is also genuinely fun, there isn't LOADS to explore but I don't find it at all a hassle and was actually enjoying myself looking for every treasure possible, and the short few side quests really made me feel so connected to the world and super immersed.I cannot stress how amazing this game is and its really amazing seeing a game studio that has been through so much with their past games create such an artistic masterpiece. If you like any game ever you will love this game, just dont give up because it gets HARD.

_childDocuments_.review: ****Just beat the game, so I'm editing this review to post my final thoughts****    As a fan of Red Candle for their previous horror games, I was surprised to see the change in direction with Nine Sols. While nowhere near the level of their previous games, it still maintains a decent amount of body horror and dark subject matter. The "Taopunk" setting is very interesting, having a blend of spiritual imagery and sci-fi technology, and the artstyle is very detailed and shows off some cool set pieces for bosses and their zones. In terms of story, Nine Sols is just as good if not better than their last two titles, having a very driven main character, interesting story with lots of twists and turns, and a fun cast full of charming, detestable, pitiable, and cool characters galore.    Gameplay-wise, Nine Sols is a huge jump forward from their previous works. It's a very fast-paced and combat heavy Metroidvania-style game, with a big focus on parrying and/or dodging different styles of attacks in order to charge special attacks or exploit openings. Animation and sound design is pretty good at telegraphing which method to use against which move as well, though this can get muddled if you're fighting a crowd all bunched up in one spot (you probably should be avoiding that regardless though since you'll get your ass kicked, lmao). In terms of exploration, there is a lot of freedom in allowing you to tackle batches of levels in the order you please, being able to just grab whatever upgrade from the earlier portion of a level and then just dipping out to fight another boss entirely instead, lmao. Locations are very varied, both in terms of mechanics and art direction, with some later levels really messing around with the platforming in interesting ways. In the circumstances where I needed to backtrack, the teleport system was very convenient and you're never too far out of reach from the main zones. Shortcuts and traversal upgrades make running through old zones even easier in case you're combing through for secret treasures or trying to go a different route.    In terms of difficulty, the standard mode will NOT hold your hand, with some bosses and elite enemies being able to just two shot you at your starting health. You can heal mid-combat via a limited amount of heals per rest, but doing so will require that you be grounded and stationary for a duration of time, making it tricky to find the timing for it and usually costing you damage opportunities on the enemies (basically Estus Flasks from Dark Souls). Similar to Hollow Knight, you can get Jades to equip that will customize your functions and features, such as healing as you deal damage to enemies, easier parries, burning health to empower attacks, etc., with most of these being hidden across the levels or available via merchants. You also can learn new moves via a level up system that grants you skill points, with most being significant additions to your moveset. Overall, while the difficulty isn't a pushover, you have a lot of avenues to power up and customize the gameplay to your liking. If things are too hard for you, there's also an easy mode that presents itself as a very "just see the story" mode, but I have no familiarity. Having beaten it on Standard, I can confidently say that this is not the type of game you'll be able to bulldoze through without meaningfully engaging in the full depths of the combat system, with later content demanding nigh mastery of all the available moves at your disposal.    If I have any complaints, it'd be the relatively pointless death system that follows the Dark Soulsification of single player games for no good reason. I hated it in Hollow Knight as well, and I'll probably hate it anywhere else it shows up, and it's definitely no better here. If you die, you can retrieve your exp and money at your death spot, but dying again before doing so will erase the lost resources. If not for so many upgrades and items being locked behind significant amounts of money, I wouldn't consider this too punishing overall, but you really gotta save up for some of the more important upgrades.    My time with Nine Sols was one of the better experiences of my year so far. The plot, gameplay, and cast were so engaging that I constantly found myself playing far longer than I expected to after sitting down, finishing one portion and then getting spurred on to the next out of curiosity at the next room, feverishly rematching a boss and honing my skills, or just wanting to punch some insufferable villain's face in and rushing on ahead. I found myself naturally scouring every nook and cranny in the game, and by the end of it all I felt extremely engaged with the gameplay system and fluidly navigating combat. I had a really great time with this game, and I'm only sad that it's over. While I have been a fan of Red Candle's work for a while now, this game truly stands out not just among their own, but as both one of the better games I've played and better games in the entire genre. I eagerly wish to see Red Candle's future achievements after having my expectations shattered with this game. If you're a fan of their previous works, or just a fan of Metroidvanias in general, Nine Sols is a must play.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes you play a game that clicks with you so well it feels like it was made for you specifically. That's Nine Sols for me. It takes the best parts of Hollow Knight and Sekiro and puts them together in a unique package that is absolutely dripping with style. The combat is incredibly tight, its central pillar is a loop of parrying to build up charges that you detonate with a special move. It demands you fight for your openings, since explicit damage windows are rare, forcing you to remain on your toes at all times. This can get very difficult to pull off, especially in large groups but that just makes managing it all the more satisfying. The early game bosses are quite good, the later game bosses are god tier, the sort of quality I'd expect from Fromsoftware. Your limited toolkit (Though there is still room to make your own build) allow for bosses that require unique approaches and test your skills in different ways. Mid-game boss  is one of my favourite bosses ever, being both great to look at and super fun to fight.Exploration is pretty good. Unlike some other metroidvanias, it is fairly linear in its progression. You won't get the dash move and gain access to 3 new areas immediately. Instead, you typically unlock one zone at a time and can explore 90-100% of it with the tools you have available. This could be a turn-off for some, but I appreciated the effect this has on the narrative, allowing it to unfold at a consistent pace. Each zone is full of secrets to uncover, and you will be well rewarded for doing so, either with some story beat or character upgrade. Zones typically have some unique gimmick not seen elsewhere that makes them feel unique, and there was never a risk of it feeling stale as you get to grips with the movement. In a shocking break from souls-like tradition, the story is very up-front and comprehensible. It's bleak, heartwarming and hopeful in equal measure. The main narrative is communicated clearly through short cutscenes and dialogues, thoughtfully placed to not interrupt the flow too much. I especially appreciated that upon beating each major boss you get a short summary of their life and what led them to be one of the Sols. It's a nice additional reward that wraps up that act, before you move on to the next Sol. The background lore is communicated through your classic item descriptions with the occasional flashback establishing Yi's personal story and how much of a giant nerd he is. I adored my time with this game

cats are in the game. 10/10the art - i didn't know a game could look this good until i played nine sols. the animations are fluid and it's simply satisfying to do any move in the game as they're all beautifully crafted. i could gush over the art for hours but i'd prefer to keep this briefthe soundtrack - _childDocuments_.review: TLDR if you have a single video game-appreciating fiber of your being, you owe it to yourself to play this all-caps MASTERPIECE.I didn't quite know what to expect going in--this is my first time playing something made by RedCandleGames--but for anyone who likes to surprised by a game, I wouldn't dream of robbing you of the joy of discovering this richly illustrated (and often disturbing) world. All I'll say is that beyond all the "plays great, sounds great, looks great" superlatives, this is a game that zigs when I expected it to zag, especially when it comes to the story. Just when I think I've got the story and characters figured out, it goes in a direction I never would have expected and whoever wrote Shuanshuan deserves a medal (maybe several). The exceptional story is anchored by combat that's reminiscent of Sekiro with its emphasis on timing based parries but with a fascinating twist that made parrying my favorite verb in the game. Special equipment and level-ups allow your parries to damage enemies, restore health and charge up energy for a supremely satisfying special attack where you literally dash through crowds of enemies as they explode behind you. I probably could have finished the game in less time, but I kept coming back just to savor the fluid exploration and impeccably tuned combat. The fact that the music is never less than excellent made every victory feel like a third act climax and every loss feel devastating. If I could delete my memory of this game to play it for the first time again, I'd do it in a heartbeat; if you like Metroidvanias, Soulslike games or just good video games, this one is worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: What if Shadow the Hedgehog was your dad and also had SEVERAL substance addictions?For real tho, this game is great. Very story heavy, which may not be to your tastes for a metroidvania, and there isn't (yet) a way to easily skip cutscenes for future runs so keep that in mind. The devs have been sneaking in QoL changes since release, so I don't think this will be an issue for long.The combat and platforming are tight and satisfying to an insane degree. Your tools are deceptively simple and seem restrictive at first, but the better you get and the more abilities you find, the more ways you can chain different mechanics together into some truly stylish moments. Upgrades have good variety and can significantly change the way you use core systems, making experimenting with solutions to difficult fights quite fun. (Did you know that you can cancel the Swift Descent jade ability into an aerial deflect that actually make you fall faster while covering your descent from both sides? It's sick. this game is sick.)In terms of exploration and metroidvania level design, the story focus does hamstring it a bit. You can still do things out of order to a certain degree, as important abilities aren't usually given as major boss rewards, but there are a lot of hard "lock and key" obstacles that will require you to at least visit certain zones before others. Zones can also be quite linear, with more focus on interesting combat/platforming scenarios than secrets or exploration. It's no Hollow Knight, that's for sure, but that's not a comparison I like to make.Overall, it's not a flawless game and it certainly isn't for everyone, but if you want tight risk/reward based combat, meaty bosses to sink your teeth into, endearing characters, amazing art, and some BANGER tunes, I can't recommend this enough.

_childDocuments_.review: The directors of Nine Sols had a precise vision in mind and they have made what feels like no compromises in its execution. In a genre full of games with largely hands-off stories, vast and open maps, and simple combat, they chose to create an almost masterpiece of a game that has a direct and impactful narrative, a tight but focused map, and an intensely polished action combat system. And they did so with stunning precision: there are few dull moments in its lengthy story and its combat and world have fewer flaws still. Experiencing the evolution of the combat as you traverse the skill tree, peering into the various tragedies and joys of the cast, and traversing into the depths of a world that combines Chinese myth and sci-fi is a genuine treat.  Nine Sols likely isn't for everyone, it will have too many story beats or characters for some and entirely too much combat focus and not enough exploration for others. But if you want to experience a genuinely touching narrative, sharp sekiro-lite combat, or an amazing tao-punk world, than it's ABSOLUTELY for you. It is beyond impressive that a studio with experience making only horror games created a game that manages to stand among the very best entries in the ever-popular metroidvania genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I had heard of this game's combat and art-style being excellent (and I fully, completely agree), but what surprised me the most is how amazingly the story was executed. Initially it felt heavy on exposition, mostly because the player character is not some nameless entity but an already existing person with a strong personality in a world with its own rich history. This introduction to his life therefore was a bit hard to get through, but getting through that opens up an incredibly well-told tale that stands strongly on its own, yet flows nicely along the gameplay. Returning to the 'central hub' in most games to progress some NPC questlines usually doesn't interest me a lot, and yet I could really enjoy the relationship between our protagonist and Shuanshuan basically through their little interactions alone. And this is similarly handled for other relationships, the overall execution is quite touching and makes this game worth it to play for the story alone.Of course we are also treated to an excellent combat system with a smooth difficulty curve starting from the first boss and peaking right at the end. The first boss and the last boss both seriously kicked my ♥♥♥♥ in but the former helped me understand the combat better and the latter led me to that coveted perfect dance of 1v1 combat where it really feels like you have the answer to their every move. And besides that there are honestly no real lows in terms of bosses or areas either! It might be difficult at times, but the journey is definitely worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols deserves way more love than it’s getting. Yes, it’s tough, with parry mechanics that aren’t for everyone, but once you push through the early challenges, it transforms into an incredibly rewarding experience. If you’re struggling, invest in the skill tree or switch to story mode—there’s no shame in making the game work for you.The combat is all about rhythm and learning from your mistakes. Every boss that seems impossible at first becomes manageable as you upgrade and adapt. The visuals are stunning, blending a unique Taopunk aesthetic with haunting sound design. The lore is deep, and the world-building is rich—perfect for those who love to dig into backstories.Sure, there are some minor issues, like item tracking and arrow switching, but they don’t overshadow the game’s strengths. Nine Sols is one of the best metroidvanias in recent memory. If you’re waiting for Hollow Knight Silksong, play this instead. It’s that good.

_childDocuments_.review: My thoughts on the game after getting the true endingPros -combat is excellent and is essentially a very successful translation of sekiro-style combat to the second dimension. for those unaware of the differences and try to play the game like hollow knight you will die FAST, hollow knights combat is about positioning yourself, and being as aggressive as possible, in Nine sols heavy emphasis is placed on timing, and knowing when to counter attack, parrying is king-the bosses, especially the main bosses are great, With special attention being drawn to the 4th through 9th sols-This game has one of the best final boss in a video game that I have played in a long time- The characters, I was worried that this game would do the classic bad anime thing by having characters with one defining trait but then overcome them at the end to have an artificial character arc, but this game thankfully doesn't do that. Its characters appear one note at the beginning but acquire depth and personality as you play. The story does a good job of making you form an emotional connection with shuanshuan especially-art, the game is beautiful* with the occasional fully animated cut scene-the world building, the describes itself as taopunk which is cyberpunk mixed with Taoist mythology, I would love to see this setting explored more-this is a rare souls-like with an actual difficulty option, I beat the game on regular difficulty but I appreciate that the option was there for the people who wanted one.MINOR COMPLAINTS-*I couldn't help but feel that some areas didn't meaningfully differentiate from each other, (you will spend a lot of time in this game in dark-blue metal corridors) some areas looked close to identical to each other or were a simple color swap, however there are enough unique areas that this isnt that bad.-hit-boxes, I'm not someone who generally notices these things so Imagine how bad some of these have to be for me to take note of it, for example I can be blatantly out of a grab attack and be teleported 10 feet right into into the attack, some attacks I can be very clearly outside of and still get hit. however 99% of the time the hit-boxes are actually really good, its only a few examples on some of the larger enemies that I actually noticed-fast travel currently requires you to go to the pavilion first before going to another node which feels really unnecessary especially because you already have multiple reasons to go back there even without the mandatory visit, if you were allowed to teleport to any node it would save a loading screen.-the game is relatively linear for a metroidvainia with only a bit of open ended exploration towards the end of the game-the reusing of mini-bosses, I'm not against the idea but most were re-used twice or even three times-no boss rush, but I hear they will add that in eventually.Conclusion, this is an excellent game, I would recommend it to people who enjoyed Sekiro style combat, hollow knight fans and people who enjoy hard games generally. Red Candle games knocked it out of the park in there first attempt at a metroidvainia and I for one am looking forward to what they do next. And if you play this game, PLEASE, leave a positive review to support these devs, they really deserve it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols managed to take the essence of Sekiro and Hollow Knight and innovate in such a way that maintained their greatness while still presenting a fresh take on the Soulslike and Metroidvania genres.- The story is deep and full of foreshadowing and subtle details.- The exploration is satisfying and rewards you with not just upgrades, but also heartwarming emotional moments.- The combat manifests as a dance between parrying and counterattacking, with a rhythm reminiscent of Sekiro’s best moments.Nine Sols follows the Soulslike storytelling style, where the player is thrust into the remnants of a ruined world following the events of an apocalyptic event. It is through dialogue, data logs, and flavour text that the player is able to slowly piece together what actually happened.Where Nine Sols differs from most Soulslikes is that the protagonist, Yi, actually knows (most of) the truth. This brings me to where the game truly shines:On your first playthrough, the game throws a bunch of fancy jargon at you, while characters engage in conversations for which the player lacks context.Although some of these questions and mysteries are cleared up near the end, a second playthrough allows one to see just how expertly the developers weaved details into the narrative right from the opening moments.Speaking of details, part of what makes Nine Sols’s storytelling so good is the sheer amount of subtle details present everywhere: from character models to even the beautifully (and grotesquely) crafted backgrounds.I spent so much time just staring at the backgrounds, taking in the narrative implications each pixel represented for the story.English localisations for East Asian games can often be a little, uh, awful. Fortunately, Nine Sols’s localisation is largely acceptable—easily top 20% of localised East Asian games. It’s certainly nowhere near as terrible as the Engrished to hell Chinese gachas or the JRPGs localised by pandering morons who don’t understand Japanese grammar.Nevertheless, there are several details that suffered from the decision to transliterate instead of translate/localise. For example, 山海 was transliterated as “Shanhai” instead of translated to “Mountains & Seas”, and 天禍 became “Tianhuo” instead of “Divine Calamity”.As for dialogue, there are instances where grammatical errors, overly casual language, and the spamming of outdated idioms make the characters sound tacky and weird. (Idiom spam can work in Chinese; it doesn’t in English.) Some Skills’ and Jades’ (i.e. equivalent of Hollow Knight’s Charms) descriptions also don’t match their effects.Nine Sols is filled with a bunch of fun platforming and combat puzzles that make exploring each new zone an absolute joy.The game also respects your time by including a system that tells you how many bosses/items/places of interest you have left to find in a single area.This is vague enough to preserve the joy of exploration but also specific enough to not drive you insane searching for that one thing you missed.One of my favourite moments in Sekiro was how you could find and gift different types of Sake to various characters for lore and greater insight into their pasts. Nine Sols takes this concept and builds upon it, with rewards for defeating a boss or completing a platforming section often being gifts for other characters.Said gifts trigger cutscenes that provide the player with lore, emotional moments, and character development. The hub also undergoes some very interesting and heartwarming evolutions to reflect this.Without spoiling anything, this type of reward system achieves spectacular ludonarrative alignment with the philosophical messages being conveyed.More specifically, Nine Sols’s message is One thing many Sekiro-inspired Soulslikes fail to realise about Sekiro is that it’s not simply a parrying Soulslike. It’s more accurate to call it a  Soulslike, which is something Nine Sols understands.Some of the best parts of Sekiro were those where you heard the Perilous Attack sound cue, saw the red 危, and had to decide which counter to implement in the split-second afforded you. Succeed, and you’d inflict a lot of posture damage, with the opportunity to follow up with some health damage. Fail, and you’d just dashed into a sweep or gotten stabbed out of the air.In Nine Sols, we have Crimson Attacks—attacks during which the enemy glows crimson and unleashes a powerful, unparryable attack. Fortunately, you’re able to unlock a pair of countering techniques that mirror the high-risk-high-reward paradigm of Sekiro’s counters.Further complexity comes in the form of deciding whether to dash through these attacks or attempt a counter. Successfully executing these counters often stuns the enemy for a brief moment, granting you a window to follow up with powerful attacks of your own.An example of said powerful attacks is a system unique to Nine Sols: the Talisman system. Parrying and countering attacks grant you Qi Charges, which you can expend for Talisman attacks where you dash behind an enemy, mark it, and let loose an explosive burst of damage on said enemy.Put all this together—the parrying, the counters, the Talismans—and you have a system where fights look as spectacular as choreographed anime fights. It is very rare for combat in Soulslikes to feel like this—the constant dashing back and forth I had in certain boss fights made me feel like I was playing DMC.If I had one critique, it would be that the protagonist got so powerful in the late game that you could easily one-shot normal mobs in a variety of ways, leaving the boss fights as the only source of challenge. I would really appreciate a boss rush mode where the bosses were scaled to the player’s stats.This was Red Candle Games’s first foray into the oversaturated and highly-competitive Soulslike and Metroidvania genres—and they’ve created a damn masterpiece.Nine Sols has joined the ranks of Hollow Knight and Sekiro on my personal list of best Soulslikes of all time. There is a lot of potential here for both a sequel and a prequel, and I really hope that the developers are open to the idea of expanding the Nine Sols universe.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Some genuine criticisms:- VERY linear progression. You explore whatever area the game gives you, and you rarely get to go in other directions or explore on your own without being blocked because you needed to acquire something in a different area (quite crippling for a metroidvania).- Simple combat. Although this works in the games favour by having the player focus on its few core aspects as the upgrades the game give you expand only expand on existing abilities, it leaves very practically zero variety in how you play, and gives the game no replay value after you've beaten it once.- Quite short. I explored the entire map, beat every mini-boss, and beat the regular ending in 25 hours, which is a good time for what the game offered. I can't expect much larger from the average indie studio, but more side content or some replayability could've gone a long way and encouraged me to actually find more of the jades instead of just using what was already working for me (I hardly changed my set up at all until the last fight).(this one is quite small but still)- Dialogue shenanigans. I absolutely despise whenever games give this false sense of choice or 'optional dialogue' which is only ever 2 options. Whenever the options are actually different, it just leads to the same conversation anyways. This isn't our story, and we don't choose 99% of the dialogue, so why are you giving me pointless options? _childDocuments_.review: Nine Sols, when it first appeared on my radar, was a fairly interesting game. It had a cool aesthetic, and promised challenging gameplay with a parry focused gameplay loop that enticed me, though the game admittedly quickly fell back off my radar. I picked it up when it was running on a decent sale and finally got a round to playing it a little while after it had first came out. Now, I had fairly recently finally gotten around to finishing Hollow Knight, a game I heard endlessly praised and came out with just a solid experience. I had decently high hopes for Nine Sols, but hadn't really heard much about it. That's why it came as a very pleasant surprise that the game was so damn amazing. A vaguely metroidvania, Nine Sols pretty much has it all. It has a super interesting world that unfolds before you as you progress; a host of likeable and hateable characters to get invested in; a gripping story of morality, power, authority, life and death; and of course, an extraordinarily responsive combat system with satisfying parries, flashy attacks and the right level of difficulty that challenges you without being too unfair (mostly). If you looked at Nine Sols, if you took a glance at the gameplay, or heard a few buzzwords like "metroidvania" or "Sekiro inspired", pick it up. This game is a fantastic experience, and if you give it a shot, you'll either drop it in time to refund it, or watch as 30 hours fly by.

_childDocuments_.review: As a short warning, my writing style is ♥♥♥♥ and might be hard to understand I apologize, that is all.I played the game on standart difficulty and will not switch to story as standart is the way the devs intended the game to be played, and so it should be critiqued through the lens of standart difficulty. I love the aesthetic of the game and even a lot of the gameplay. I don't want to put too much thought into the structure of this post, so I will just write my grievances as a list: - The absence of i-frames after getting hit is an odd choice to make. I believe this is because Sekiro does not have them, thus a game inspired by Sekiro won't have them either, and in most cases that would be fine even here if not for the huge knockback that attacks in this game have where you will get hit once ragdoll and get hit by another attack that likely came from the same guy shooting multiple shots in a volley. There is also an issue with enemies like bugs in farmlands that shoot 3 blobs at the same time that are supposed to seperate from one another and go in different arcs. The issue appears when you try to kill one with your melee attack, and since there is no stagger for enemies (as of that point in my game anyway, some jade or skill might give it later on), the bug will just hit you with all 3 of them at once because there are no i-frames.-The ragdoll mechanic, I can't think of reason for this to be here except for "Sekiro has it and so do souls games" the issue with that logic is that both Sekiro and souls use 3D space meaning that when you fall prone you are harder to hit and can by default roll out of prone, here when you are prone you are easier to hit and cannot roll out unless you invest 2 skill-points just to unlock the privelage of attempting to salvage your situation.-Skills: some of the skills that I have seen and unlocked should not have been in the skill tree at all, like the above-mentioned roll from the prone position and the sprint ability. I have no clue why you would lock the ability to move mildly faster behind a level-up.-The loss of XP and money on death again "Sekiro has it, and so do Souls games." Even in those, I can easily argue that this mechanic has no point to exist, and I love Souls games, but if I'm being honest, there is really no point to it. Ok,  you died a second time, and your progress gets a soft reset. What does this accomplish? You get to spend more time clearing a room of trash mobs that with the money making jade give you ~33 money when worth while upgrades go for 600 for half of a health upgrade to 2000 for another jade slot or pipe charge, cool.-The gimped fast travel ability—this is dumb—just give the stupid horn the ability to travel from checkpoint to checkpoint right away. The only thing that having it be a "homeward bone" accomplished is that I didn't want to explore knowing that if I go into a sideroom and find a different path with its own checkpoints, then I will have to later backtrack either from the pavilion or from the room that will be at the end of that path because I can't make progress in it since I don't have some ability or item to progress there yet. -The stop gap before a mini-boss. This is a complaint about level design. I have found 3 different mini-bosses, and all 3 of them had some dumb speed bump right outside of their room so that every time you died you had to do parkour or wait for those moving blocks to move out of the way. The fact that I died lost (even if temporarily) my XP and money have to run back from my checkpoint. You then have me just wait and waist my time while this block meanders it's way over to me while I'm just stewing in my frustration just so I can go and try again.-Similar to the previous point are the cutscenes that play when you enter the main-line boss arena. I'm fine with you having them; they are cool, but they happen every time you enter, and you can't skip them. Also,  there is a separate one for the second phase of the fight.-Double attacks, I mean any attack that has a follow-up right after the first one, almost immediately after the first one. The ninja's double slash is a good example. I do not doubt that you can parry both attacks in this combo; personally, I could not. I can parry one, but no matter how quick my button press is, I can't seem to ever parry. The second one holding down block seemed to not help either. This is largely a minor complaint as you can just dodge this attack.-The talisman should function like a dodge. The talisman attack is a dash that lets you go through enemies and looks a lot like the dodge, but if you try to use it like the dodge, you will get hit. Personally,  I feel that the dash portion of the amulet attack should let you go through attacks as if you used dodge, as this would make bosses less of a rhythm game by giving you more agency by letting you choose when to deal damage to them.Instead of waiting for them to finish whatever combo they are currently doing, to clarify, I don't mean make the entire amulet attack invincible, just the dash part.-Combo attacks, if you played Souls game you should get this concept easily, a boss hit's you once and you are effectively dead because here you will get rag-doll'd and get hit by the rest of their combo that's it, I don't like these in any game because having attacks like these makes having a health bar in boss fights mean nothing, the combo might as well not exist just make the first attack in the chain an insta-kill and the result is the same.-The parry direction, the ground parry, and the jump parry have one very large difference, and that is the jump parry is omni-directional while a ground parry only works in the direction you are facing. This is a huge misstep. the amount of fights where you are being hit from both sides even early in the game is quite high, I personally feel that making ground parry omni-directional would have been for the best, I might be in the minority in this case though but I feel that I'm having issues with because I stop paying attention where my character is facing during the fight since I have to reposition so much in prolonged fights that having to move back and make sure to face the enemy every time eventually slips my mind because of how much is happening, this is not a lesser problem in games like Sekiro because of not only lock but being able to move backwards while still facing the enemy here you can only go forward ant thus you have to turn around every time.-Hit boxes feel very bad. I really hate to say this, but a lot of attacks feel awful because of how often I would dodge past the attack and be behind the enemy (or in the case of the centaur boss inside his human torso area) and still be hit by what is shown to be a forward-facing attack. The same thing happens to sweep attacks that go along the ground that look like you can just jump over them, but no, they still hit you somehow.I have more problems, but during the process of writing this, my head has cooled, and most of the anger has left me along with the complaints that I had while playing the game. They will of course come back once I return to this game, and I might add to this list as a sort of calming ritual. If I could, I would rate the game a maybe in recommendations, but since I can't, it will be a no.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Beat it, I'll say the same stuff I liked and disliked generally stayed the same, although, like with most games, you get used to the negatives the longer you play it. The bosses and setting are fantastic and it's probably the hardest metroidvania I've played, but also one of the most enjoyable in the long run. I love the narrative and the setting to bits, and the combat is just so juicy and good, especially near the end of the game. Definitely a must buy if you're someone who enjoys the genre.My favorite parts:Combat; The combat is based around parrying with some attacks needing to be dodged. At first it may be hard to flow with, but much like Sekiro, when the game starts to get into motion the combat shines heavily. Fighting a large enemy one on one swiping at them while parrying every hit makes you feel amazing, and, much like sekiro, this IS the way you are expected to handle encounters so it's tailored well, each fight feels good with this system.Boss Fights; They're great. Every one, except maybe duos/add fights, feel great to take on, and learning them, while sometimes a process, feels good once you've gotten into the flow of it and are parrying/blowing them up. They also feel pretty memorable, the bosses generally egging you on through the level before you finally encounter and take them out in a dramatic multi phase fashion.Art Design; This game has a unique setting and visuals. I think it calls itself tao-punk which makes sense given the aesthetic. Every setting from your home base to each new area feels unique and I'm never tired of exploring the environment. The way the game uses comic panels and animated cutscenes to convey dramatic story moments also lends itself to being fairly impactful and I imagine I'll remember this one for some time.What I didn't like:Encounter structures; This game suffers from its encounters to some degree. Maybe others will like this, but there were several times where a fight I might of enjoyed turned into tedium due to 2 or 3 other enemies being tacked on just to increase the difficultly. It doesn't need this. These fights can just work on their own, but they like to add on adds all the time and for no particularly good reason. There was one fight later in the game too where I believe, if I hadn't done a certain objective, I would of had to dealt with adds, which is a great disappointment given how good the fight was.Input loading; This game requires you to act quick, and a big issue I have is having to press a button multiple times because I'm not finished with some other animation. There are times where I've gotten hit or in trouble purely because It takes me multiple taps to heal or do an action before my character acts, which is annoying since the speed of the action could of changed the outcome of the battle. I just wish inputs didn't get dropped as much.A great game with some frustration design decisions. It's a Sekiro inspired metroidvania with a unique setting/art direction that lends itself to quite a memorable experience. When the game truly gets going with its combat, especially when fighting certain enemies or bosses one on one, it feels amazing and looks amazing too. My gripes mainly lie in the decision to add too many mobs to certain encounters, which, in a game where you can get multi-hit and monsters don't necessarily act in a fashion that is always tenable, can be quite the opposite of fun. Still, the narrative, the setting, and the combat, all draw me back to finishing it.If you like metroidvanias this is a definite buy. You will probably get frustrated at points, but stick with it, it's a good experience overall.
