_childDocuments_.review: If you're reading this because you've already bought and been playing the game, this is yet another GLOWING review (shocker). But for the uninitiated, HIFI RUSH is an high octane rhythm action plat former with more personality than you can imagine, and while I could write a 10 page essay on why that's the case, let's stick to the basics, because honestly, you need to be spending less time reading reviews and more time buying and playing this game.Soundtrack is at the core of this game, and it is no slouch. The game feels so satisfying with it's indie rock aesthetic tracks. And they are catchy while also being musically fitting to continuously play through the game. If licensed music is a huge turn off because you like to record or Stream, HIFI RUSH has you covered with fully in house free-use banger tracks that replace the licensed tracks that would otherwise get your content in trouble. It's such an immense undertaking for a small attention to detail, and you will find this a common theme in this game.The Story and Characters are simple, but it's fun, humor filled, and you may find yourself cheering on the cast as you progress through the games story. There's plot twists you won't expect, and other cliches and tropes that may make you roll your eyes while still smiling because damn it, it's still executed so well despite how cheesy it might seem. The whole cast is lovable, and the villains you not only love to hate, but provide comedic and serious moments that make not a second of this game feel boring as you traverse their respective levels and fights.The game play takes the premise of any good rhythm game and multiplies the satisfaction by tenfold. It's simple, but can very quickly get complex and if you don't take your time to find the groove you will struggle. Combos feel exciting and impacting, with just the right amount of variety in moves that the more you learn the more situations you can handle and keep your flow going. However, it never feels overwhelming because the game cleverly introduces you to all its mechanics as you progress through the whole story, giving you time to learn the mechanics and prepare yourself for new ones to challenge you.The level design is SCARY GOOD. The game manages to feel accessible to everyone while still proving to be a challenge to overcome as each stage gives you new obstacles, enemies, and interactions you've yet to come across in your journey. This makes HIFI RUSH never feel repetitive or stale as it's constantly giving you new challenges and obstacles, or even building upon older game mechanics for fresh new interactions. HIFI RUSH's level design never makes you go "Oh great, time to do X for the tenth time in a row." Achieving this was absolutely one of the most applaud-able aspects of the game.Finally, for now, lets touch on the animation and art style. HIFI RUSH takes heavy inspiration from the current Renaissance happening in western animation studios, whereby 3D rendering pipelines are changed to include elements of 2D animation, onomatopoeia, movement lines, and using frame rate to emphasize movement. By combining traditional animation with 3D rendering, HIFI RUSH creates an aesthetic of a Cell-Shaded, indie rock music video printed on comic pages. The cut scenes are gorgeous and blend so smoothly between game play and animation that it keeps you constantly immersed in the world that's been created.I've seen some real gem games come out before, many games I'd still give glowing recommendations for the level of heart and soul put into them. HIFI RUSH is a once in a decade gaming experience, topping off even some of the greatest most charming games out there. The level of polish and detail in HIFI RUSH would lead me to believe even the studio janitor gave it their all cleaning the places that contributed in making this game. It's practically criminal that an game this well developed from start to end is only 30 dollars. I'd happily pay 90 dollars for this easily. I could go on and on and on about how stellar this game is, and everything in this review barely scratches the surface on how much FUN it is to play this game. But it's time to close the set out on this review.If you're one of the few that found this review and used it to decide whether you should pull the trigger on this game. Here's your decision. Get this game. You won't regret a single second of it. Great Job Tango Gameworks, your passion paid off immensely.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS GAME ROCKS!!It's been a long time since a game came out that just oozed style, and Hi-Fi Rush is style incarnate. The levels are alive with the beat of the music, the environment is splashed with vibrant color, and the soundtrack is up there with the best of the best.It's a spectacle action game (think Devil May Cry or Bayonetta), but combat is heavily tied to the music. Every attack (friendly and enemy) lands on the beat which makes combat flow beautifully. Switching between attacks, dashes, and parries is a ton of fun when you're jamming to the awesome soundtrack. As you gather allies, they add a new wrinkle to your combat options with ways to defeat certain types of enemies, keep an aerial rave going, stagger opponents, etc. There's a shop where you can buy new moves, so your fighting arsenal is always growing with new combos to master.The narrative is a pretty tight experience. You need to defeat the evil corpo bosses and stop their dastardly plans. Every character (friend and foe alike) has a ton of personality. The humor is pretty much on point. There were a number of times, I burst out in laughter at a visual gag, or dialogue exchange between characters. While there was plenty of humor, the serious moments didn't suffer and were allowed to rest before moving on. One of the best parts about the story is that it has an ending. There is no cliffhanger, no sequel bait, and no open ending. It's very refreshing to have a game where I'm not left wanting more. It's not a long game, but it's well worth the ride. I give this an easy 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: [Steam Deck]WHAT. A. GAME!!Hi-Fi Rush is pure joy. I don't think I've grinned like a baboon so hard from start to finish in a game before. The writing, the humor, the characters, the MUSIC, the art direction...everything is firing on all cylinders here. Play it, I implore you.Now, more objectively, Hi-Fi Rush is such an interesting take on the cyberpunk genre, to the point I'm sure many people would argue it doesn't even fall into that category. It uses all the same cyberpunk tropes and critiques - high-tech, low-life - but with a confident, positive energy that felt so refreshing. The whole game feels like an American Saturday morning cartoon with the energy of a Japanese anime - a perfect fusion of western and eastern styles. I couldn't get enough of it.Gameplay and music are intertwined here, obviously. You fight to the beat of the music, with options to relax the timing if rhythm games aren't really your thing. While I didn't care for the quick time events and thought some of the unique boss encounters were a bit confusing at first, the hack-and-slash rhythm gameplay is so utterly addicting and empowering that it makes me feel like forgiving the very few shortcomings of this game. And holy hell, what a FINALE!!Tango Gameworks has created nothing short of a masterpiece here, and I eagerly await their next project. A+ work.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi Rush is one of the few genuine masterpieces to come out of the AAA space in the last decade. It's impossible to put into words how fantastic this game is, even on a level that eclipses the game itself. To get the obvious out of the way, the music, visuals, and combat are all spectacular. I'm honestly shocked how well Tango nailed the spectacle fighter genre on their first go, while also infusing it with something entirely new to that genre. Sure games like BPM, COTND, and Metal Hellsinger exist, but Hi-Fi Rush's beat is  beautifully interwoven with the game in every aspect of design, something that the aforementioned games couldn't nail. The world *breathes* to the beat, and the rhythm can come almost as naturally as breathing for those who are willing to let the combat click. Not only that, but I am also extremely surprised Tango pulled off such a beautifully designed and stylized world, especially considering their past works. The game is wonderfully animated, the worlds are richly detailed, and  the characters really do shine with how lovingly the cutscenes were animated. But I think what really shines from this game is how, for the first time in ages, can I feel the soul of the development team in this game. Take it from someone who is currently working in a AAA studio, most of the AAA games, regardless of quality, are almost polished to a fault. They feel almost inhuman, with so many people coming and going to a project, they come out feeling like something made in a machine. But even ignoring the heartwrenching (in a "ive been there" way) credits song, I can really just feel this games dev cycle. A pitched passion project thats been workshopped for ages, constantly fearing cancellation, with budget cuts and arguments with the finance team in droves. Injokes and dumb ideas becoming implemented parts of the game, while cut content was turned into a joke rather than flogged back as DLC. But at the end of the day, despite all of the troubles, this feels like a passion project fully realized, that everyone is proud to stand behind. I know all this "soul of the game" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ makes it sound like I'm high out of my mind, but I really do mean it. Hi Fi Rush is a masterpiece, not only because its a great game, but its a great game with a soul.

_childDocuments_.review: So as probably many others mentioned, this game is great:It has style.It has the lighthearted, cheesy comedy.It has fun gameplay.It has a fun combat system, and a soundtrack to match (original AND copyrighted)It has a real nice upgrade/progression system with using special modifiers which use limited slots, making you think what you need most.There's also a nice completionist-friendly system with challenges giving you rewards visible in your hub area as well as other rewards, like resources for upgrades or the in-game currency, and sometimes even cosmetics!I've only three nitpicks: 1) You cannot see how many collectibles you've found per map, meaning that if you REALLY want to find everything, you might end up licking every single wall to find a clue for that one thing you need to finish your progression.2) While I dare say this game is what would be described as rhythm-based, cartoony Devil May Cry, there is no reward for doing a no-hit encounter in a form of a score multiplier or anything, meaning that even if you do no-hit runs of levels, if you don't get the highest score, too, it won't show up in the level selection. If there was a way for the game to prioritize showcasing that, then that would be great.3) At times it feels as if some parries didn't register, but this is a very minor thing, because sometimes I can clearly tell that it was me messing up. _childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi Rush is a rhythm spectacle fighter game with some platforming elements. The game is Devil May Cry hack and slash action while trying to keep a beat. This game has a fantastic soundtrack, a wonderful combat system with a fun gameplay loop, likable characters, a lovely art style with a comic book feel to it, and some funny comedic moments. The game is a breath of fresh air with its combination of action and rhythm gameplay elements. Hi-Fi Rush is a highly polished experience that knows exactly what kind of game it ones to be and succeeds at that goal. The story is pretty simple with a very punk/rock star vibe to it, but the narrative really excels with how it tells the story in its stylistic manner. The blending of the cartoon-style graphics with animated cutscenes flows really well, and gives the feeling of watching a good anime or watching a Saturday morning cartoon. But the cut scenes are pretty brief, not taking you out of the action very long before you get back into gameplay.Hi-Fi Rush has 12 levels that each take about 60-90 minutes each to complete (with about 2 short levels that can be beat in about 15-25 minutes).The game took a little under 13 hours to beat on Hard difficulty.The game has some unlockable post-game modes, but most of the post-game is focused on replaying the main game to achieve a higher score, play at higher difficulty levels, and to complete challenge rooms hidden throughout the main game.I got this on sale for around $20 and it was well worth that price for the level of quality and fun I got out of it.The game has plenty of original music that are great to groove to, but does have a fair amount of licensed music to help spice up the playlist - though these songs are often relegated for boss fights. I quite often found myself bouncing in rhythm to the music while playing the game in order to keep the beat when in combat. The game is well thought out in many elements and has many different visual/auditory indicators to let the player know if they are keeping a beat. The player character's idle animation, the enemies, the game's UI, and even the environment all move, attack, and snap to the beat. If that's not enough, you can even enable an additional UI element to have an ongoing metronome present to track the beat - toggling this on/off with a simple button press without even having to enter the settings menu.Even outside of platforming, you get positive feedback for jumping or dashing in beat (in fact, you can only triple dash if you sync all three dashes with the beat). This connects the out of combat exploring/platforming sections with the combat sections to always keep the player in tune with the beat. It's a small, but highly effective with making the game a cohesive experience.In combat, you do additional damage if you time all your hits to be on beat. Enemies only attack you in sync with the beat and will telegraph their attack one beat before their attack lands - allowing the play to parry or dodge in beat. This is fantastic and feels great to pull off. I've played rhythm action games where the player is incentivized to attack/dodge on beat, but the enemies would be able to attack with no regard to the beat of the song. This would pull you completely out of the groove of the song as you would dodge on-beat, only for an enemy to attack off-beat. This is not an issue in Hi-Fi Rush and it allows you to always stay on beat.This game is for people that:*Enjoy spectacle fight style combat (a la Devil May Cry).*Enjoy rhythm games and do well with keeping rhythm/being able to maintain precise timing.*Enjoy grooving along with the soundtrack and gamplay.*Enjoy light-hearted characters/stories that have a very comic book feel that doesn't take itself too seriously.*Enjoy meta-humor (or at least has a good tolerance for it).*Enjoy linear games that are focused on doing one thing really well instead of an open-world game that tries to be everything.*Like cute cats.*Like to pet cute cuts.*Also, there is a Twin Peaks reference in the game that got me to crack up.While I absolutely adore this game, there were some grating issues that affected my enjoyment:*Unskippable cutscenes.*Unskippable tutorial sections.*If you lose a fight and have to retry, you have to rewatch the unskippable cutscene before the fight.*If a fight had a tutorial section to teach you a new ability before the fight and you die in the fight, you have to replay the tutorial section again.*Many QTE/parry sections require you complete them flawlessly in order to progress (even getting 1/10 wrong requires you to repeat the entire section over until you get it 100% right).While none of these things are gamebreaking, they can disrupt the flow and therefore diminish some of the fun.The game has 4 difficulties available at the start: Easy, Normal, Hard, and Very Hard - with a 5th difficulty unlocking after beating the game on any difficulty. Easy difficulty allows for looser timings on rhythm elements as well as makes the combat easier. Both normal and hard are the same in terms of most aspects with rhythm and enemy health, but in hard you receive more damage and health items are less plentiful. In very hard, you need "tight" rhythm timing, and all enemies are harder to kill and hit harder. On the unlockable difficulty, all this is even harder, as well as having an additional failure condition of needing to keep your rhythm meter (e.g. score) above a certain grade, or you get an instant game over.I have experience with action games and have decent enough with timing, but I wanted to focus on grooving - so I played through the game on the Hard difficulty for the additional challenge in combat. Even though I enjoy challenging combat, losing a combat and having to retry a fight (especially if you have to rewatch a cutscene before a fight) can really disrupt being in a flow state. I honestly think I would have enjoyed myself more if I played the game on normal instead of hard so I would not have those interruptions. For this reason, unless you enjoy the challenge and are proficient with spectacle fighting/action games, I would recommend most players to play on normal. If you are a player with slow reactions or struggle to keep a beat, I would advise playing on easy. The game has a handful of accessibility options to make the rhythm and action sections easier for players that do not have the reaction time for the precise timing of sections that require you to parry or require flawless execution of certain rhythm sections in order to progress. Some of these options include:*Only having to press one button for timed rhythm sections (e.g. you only have to time hitting the "X" button instead of all 4 of the face buttons).*On Easy or Normal difficulties, you can enable an auto-battler option, allowing you to just press any button and the game will essentially play for you (choosing what attacks/combos to use automatically regardless of player imput). This is clearly for people that struggle with memorizing all the different combos to vary attacks with and just want to focus on attacking on beat.*Enable auto-parrying/dodging attacks.*During parrying/dodging sequences, the playing only needs to time the first parry or dodge, and then just hold that button to avoid all subsequent attacks.*During certain rhythm quick-time events (QTEs) you have more generous timing with inputs and you can pass the section even if you do not complete the section flawlessly.I did not play with any of these enabled in order to get the intended experience/difficulty. However, I honestly wished I played with the QTE one enabled because missing just one input means you have to repeat that entire section over again until you get it all perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: It is so difficult to review this game. It's a weird mix, that may not work for everyone, but will work very well for others.GOOD STUFF: Extremely good.BAD STUFF: Extremely bad.Among all the serious world saving games that make a seasoned veteran gamer approaching 30 mostly indifferent towards the newest boring oh-so-epic universe that needs saving, HI-FI RUSH is a colorful, out of the blue game that is like no other. It's charm comes from it's genuenely good, albeit childish humour, it's surprising ability to constantly pleasantly surprise you with gameplay and(!) story twists, and it's highly varied storytelling method that constantly jumps between in-engine 3D animation that goes on during gameplay, 3D inengine animation cutscenes, 2D cartoon style animation cutscenes, 2D animated comic book page style cutscenes, is just such a joy to experience and it's so fluidly and creatively mixed there is really nothing else like it. Imagine this:You take Spiderman: Into the Spiderverse (and the following movies in both animation style, theme, and vibes) into Shrek, then put them both into Ghost in the Shell, then mix in a little of actual physical comic book you hold in your hands. It is incredibly lighthearted while dealing with very serious topics that are thought provoking and serve as rich discussion material such as the role of marketing trying to take control of your life, the role you play in supporting this machine, the somewhat stereotypical cyberpunk evil corporation theme, even some family tragedy (which could've been handled a little better at the end though), and somehow HI-FI RUSH is the most life celebrating, funny, all positive vibes and fun game I possibly ever played. Excellent writing, good humour, creativity in boss design, great music, fluid gameplay, it's all there. And not only you can pet the cat, later you can even dress it up.It's... *chef's kiss".Imagine you take Devil May Cry or Metal Gear Solid as action games, and make a slightly watered down version of them that makes it more accessible for everyone, but the depth you lost (which is not much, the the game is absolutely worthy to stand among those titans) is made up with RPG elements you may be familiar with from NieR Automata. The good kind of RPG elements: no loot, no gear grinding (pun intended, you'll see), no leveling, none of the crap that doesn't belong to a good action game but plagues the genre anyway. It's *cheff's kiss*. While it may appear so, this is no casual game on higher difficulties: invincibility frames matter, and the game is openly talking about these kind of tech-stuff on character chipset customization (passives) and combo descriptions, however, on easy difficulty it is also very accessible to anybody! Your first playthrough you won't be able to afford unlocking every move which also sort of adds a little "build" building feel to the game, and it's a positive element that you can also sell combos and special moves that you may not like so you won't acciendly spend your hard earned special move meter on those. I mean, the 3 games I compared it to: those are masterpieces competing for the throne of action games, also they are my most beloved games I think very highly of, so HI-FI RUSH earning a positive comparison with those for gameplay and content richness (see below) is the highest praise I can possibly describe this game with.However, this is also a musical, rythm based game and much of your success will depend on getting in sync with the music and the animations of various enemies in form of QTE's, which... can be hard to deal with.This game has a lot rythm elements to it like many musical games do: shoot on rythm otherwise you do no damage in Hellsinger, or your stage is being created from your music in Audiosurf. It has a lot in common with those, except the action gameplay is only rewarding you with additional score and AoE effects on your attacks if you stay in rythm. However, it adds QTEs. If you've played every game in existence that has QTEs and you combine them all together, this game is towering above that abomination with how many QTEs it has, and it's so extremely annoying if you are bad at it that it's frustrating beyond to the point wher kills the joy and positive vibes and experience but turns it outright POISONOUS. That's a word I don't use lightly. You get this hard earned victory in a bossfight, but no! Enter: weirdly timed QTE where the game throws at you 5-20 or even more QTE button press prompts, that not only you have to press before they disappear, you have to wait a little and press the button with perfect timing(!), timing can vary(!), and the pop ups are randomly thrown all around the screen(!) and may god have mercy on your soul if you play this on a big TV like I do. You miss out on entire cutscenes, in fact a very large number of otherwise so well coreographed cutscenes that are important for the flow such as the final showdown with a boss, even the final boss. This is spammed everywhere: elite enemies execution, phase switching in boss battles, simple "break the wall" buttons... imagine retrying the same very hard QTE 40 times over in the middle of a bossfight and you lose a little health every time, locked into replaying this animation 40 times! 40!! It's poison that I felt slowly turn my fun and joy into physically hurting sorrow. Honestly, it's a game killer if you can't get your head around this, and it's possible, but not easy at all and requires dedication from you.13,5 hours. Levels vary between 20-60(!) minutes+ 4 difficulty levels (normal highly advised for veterans of the genre even, it gets really hard later on if you start on hard!)+ Additional 2 unlockable difficulty levels (one where low combo score - if you let it drop - kills you, and one where missing even a single beat kills you)+ Unlockable secret levels (after first playthrough)+ Arena mode (after first playthrough), which sadly has a very strict timer that is incredibly disheartening to play this, it should be far more forgiving, and actually requires a patch that stops the timer when your big special move "cutscene" animations play out, because otherwise you are just not supposed to use them and that feels very bad when you face this situation.+ Challanges that reward ingame currency, and also enrich your home base (there is one!) graffiti wall!+ A character customizer opens up that let's you mix and match indepth customize Chai, the main character, and also all friendly NPCs with full costumes.+ There are little side objectives in some missions. For example, a birdpoop cleaning robot is very annoyed with the nearby pigeons, so you have find them all hidden nearby and get rid of them, and who knows, maybe you get something of value in exchange!+ All of this is supported by Achievements!+ None+ Ingame currency not purchasable.+ There is a huge difference between games designed to be grindy to unlock stuff, and a game well designed to be highly replayable but also keep offering unlockable stuff for quite some time during that. This is the latter, so when I say there is no grind, remember this when you feel like you can't buy all combos during first playthrough.+ FREE 30€! At full price is half price of an AAA game, and this is very much one that puts those to shame.+ Flawless KB+M support+ Flawless X360, X1 controller supports (friend gets Xbox button prompts using Dualshock though)+ No crashes, rock solid 60 fps on an old config.+ Photo Mode!- 3D inengine cutscenes can desync image and audio. Set "cutscene quality" to speed over quality (not much difference).

_childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi Rush is surprisingly mid. As many have stated, the work the dev team did on this is very apparent. Animations are extremely crisp, character design is unique and entertaining, and the voice acting is good. But that's the problem, right? This would be fine if I was watching an anime. However, these are all things that generally are a secondary feature in a game, with the primary being the gameplay itself. And the gameplay...? It's just kind of meh.This is less of a rhythm game, and more of a fighting game (akin to DMC, Bayonetta, No More Heroes etc.) with the mask of a rhythm game. Yes, everything happens on-beat. Yes, you can time your blocks and attacks in rhythm with the music but... that's kind of it. I prefer Rhythm games that make you feel like the music depends on you--like you're playing a song. This just felt like I was playing Kingdom Hearts, but Sora would only attack and defend on every eighth-note. When it comes to enemies, some enemy attacks in Hi-Fi don't feel terribly telegraphed, forcing you to just memorize what an opponent does. Others are better-telegraphed, but occur on a screen with so much visual noise that you'll probably miss it anyway. Instead of each enemy feeling like a musical puzzle, they just come across as another thing you need to button mash your way to get through.The platforming is serviceable, but only just. It's the most basic of basic--jump on platforms, some move, others need timed switches. Dash when you need to close a gap, magnet-link when you need to close an even bigger gap. Use Blue Ally for blue switches, Green Ally for green switches, and Red Ally for red switches. The same ally logic applies to enemies when you fight.The music itself was also fairly forgettable, apart from a level or two. It all blends together to sound exactly the same from one level to the next, which is sad since you could really build up a lot of good energy had the songs pushed for more.The "vibe" Chai as a character introduces does a lot of heavy lifting to make things feel fun. Some of the scenes were amusing and a boss fight or two were mildly entertaining. When I step back and look at the big picture though, I'm left unsatisfied, wondering why I'd rather go and play BPM or Muse Dash instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi Fi rush is a very good game. Its such a creative idea to combine just frames with actual music rhythm. The flow of combat being dictated by the beat combined with dmc-esque combos makes a great game play loop. Boss sequences use the rhythm excellently.The level design is great with surprisingly good platforming, which is also tied to the beat. In my eyes this surpasses similar titles like dmc5 in this regard, if only for the elegance of keeping with the theme of rhythm. I enjoy the writing for the most part. Its rare in these sorts of games to actually get competent character development over the course of the game. The satirical corporate humor is good too. My only complaint is that there is a lot 4th wall break and lamp-shading that is kinda funny at first but gets tiresome at times. My first play through I saw minimal bugs. No crashes. I occasionally got a bug where an attack wouldn't come out but it was too the beat so it still comboed. I think it happened like twice. I have accidentally caused a certain bosses grab to occur but not actually grab me (got stuck to them while they were moving, I eventually broke free). Also during cutscenes, occasionally animations would trigger when they shouldn't. But these are the only bugs I've encountered and for the most part they didn't take away from the experience (that boss grab wasn't great)I love action games where combat mastery is a key part and this game definitely scratches that itch.

_childDocuments_.review: Something that I have a hard time describing other than a "Perfect Game"Of course you have to take into account my biases towards of action games and favor for very well designed mechanics, however Hi Fi Rush feels like a game where everything just absolutely works polished to an immaculate sheen.The designed interplay of combat mechanics that flow into one another, the way how players are rewarded in game for better performance and resource management, the visceral and satisfying audio design of every hit, the amount of absolute coolness instilled into the animations that breathe life into the game! I could go on forever about how well these mechanics are designed to give an ultimately satisfying experience but to even add to that, the art direction is just top notch and just OOZES style, overflowing with a punk rock rebellion and a childlike nostalgia that thought was lost as the game industry shifted into a direction to the point its reached a point of saturation. This game is absolutely a breath of fresh air and one of my favorite games that has left an INCREDIBLY strong impression due to the amount of incredible polish in terms of technical programming and enemy encounters! I do have some very few gripes about the game such as not being able to skip certain cut scenes or dialogue options especially on failure attempts, and making it quite hard to backtrack for collectables due to not having a proper hidden collectibles tracker, those are small issues compared to what an astounding achievement this game is in the current year of 2023.I think if i too delve into the story and soundtrack which are course are incredible on their own merit, this would be way too long to read, but if I could summarize it in a metaphor, HI Fi Rush is the rainbow showing in a sky of cloudy gray, something that truely breathes life in excitement after years of skepticism of high production videogames, and better yet gives people an exciting glimpse into the future of the possibility of developers taking more risks into making more creative visions that don't adhere to the industry norm. _childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi RUSH is a polished, fun, unique action game that conforms to (and in some ways, improves on) the typical conventions of the genre while also carving out its place among the best with its rhythm game-infused mechanics, colourful environments, great soundtrack, and overall fun, lighthearted vibe.The combat is addictive, the visuals are awesome, the voice work and script are excellent, and the music (licensed and original) is stellar. There's even a solid amount of post-game content beyond simply replaying on higher difficulties, which is above and beyond for a game like this.I legitimately struggle to find things to complain about. In a year stacked with incredible releases, this one stands out as one of my favourites. Worth every penny for fans of action games, and those new to the genre will almost definitely find something to love as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty damn good. Great music, voice acting, gameplay, animation and level design. Great balance of difficulty. I played on hard and never felt like something was out of my control, and every mechanic is introduced at a great pace and explained well. I also enjoyed the story more than I thought I would.Skips the execution barrier of more complex combo games by having combos relying on the beat of the music, meaning that doing long powerful combos is much easier since the timing just goes by the beat instead of being more specific. As soon as you get a feel for the tempo in a level, you can do pretty much every combo without having to stress about it. It makes the game a lot more fun and you feel a lot more powerful.Overall, very solid.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the freshest experiences I've had loading up a new game in years. The first boss fight had me about the same as the scene in ratatouille where the guy is blasted back to his childhood after taking 1 bite of the food. Everything was very expressive and had a whimsical tone with a comic book artstyle i enjoyed a lot.Absolutely loved playing this game, and i'll see if I can try and get around to 100% it. I could talk about all that I liked but this review would be insanely long. Just to name a few, Korsica would definitely be mentioned multiple times in that essay. Every time she was on screen I was having a blast. 808 the robot cat is named after the Roland TR-808 drum machine and all the sounds she makes are from the sound effects of that machine. Phenomenal tidbits like this were in a lot of places.A few things fell a bit short for me but I want to stress these did NOT impact my overall view of the game by the end. Just worth noting.- Movement was janky sometimes, if you jumped off a ledge toward a magnet hook and got closer than it wanted you'll lose the prompt to snap to it and fall which I thought was strange. Momentum didn't carry with some heavy attack moves which means i'd stop dead in my tracks trying to slide a big hit into something and miss.- The game railroads you with QTEs and for me on a PS4 controller looking at mandatory Xbox button prompts it was rough at some points (this was recently patched as an adjustable setting but before I had this option it was a pretty big dent on my enjoyment.)- Combat could stand to be more flexible. I felt like a lot of sections grinded to a halt to make you do things a certain way before you were allowed to keep going, rather than just pace it better. With that, a handful of enemies REALLY want you to kill them "the right way" and it felt a little stiff at times. Also some enemies kept walking out of my super move(s) so that was pretty cool.- There are very brief sections you can play as characters other than the MC and they both happen at the end. I really wish they didn't do it that way! I wish we had more of these opportunities. It was a great idea that was cut short once I learned it was on the table at all.Overall though, keep the first things I said about this game in mind above all else. This game was really enjoyable!

_childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi Rush is one of the best video game experiences I've had so far. _childDocuments_.review: If Devil May Cry married a rhythm game and they had a baby, it would be this game.In a time where so many "AAA" games come out with monetization up the oiseau and try to justify with "high-end" graphics, this game came in with little to no ad campaign and reminded everyone how games can just be FUN.Gameplay: Beat em up combat, reminiscent of DMC and Bayonetta. In my opinion, it's probably the more accessible of the genre, due to the emphasis on on-the-beat gimmick. All actions, even enemy attacks, occur to the beat of the background music. Having trouble? just listen to the song and time your actions!Even then, there are visual cues to assist players. It's easy to get into the flow by fighting on the beat.Graphic: sort of cel-shaded, cartoony art style. Characters and enemies have distinct, eye-catching design. The story content isn't deep or anything, and the art style perfectly complements it.Soundtrack: catchy tunes and pretty sick rock tracks that will get you pumped for combat.A selection of songs from other famous artists make boss fights pretty hype.A very appreciated feature is the option to replace these tracks with similar-sounding songs to help with avoiding copyright issue, yet these are pretty solid in their own right.
_childDocuments_.name: Hi-Fi RUSH

_childDocuments_.review: Originally, I left a joke review, but this game is genuinely amazing and I recommend it at full price.It's a character-action rhythm game. It takes aspects of Devil May Cry (and many of Platinum Game's titles) and combines it with a rhythm-based combat system, something that you would see in Guitar Hero. The story was simple, but very enjoyable. The characters were fantastic thanks to the hilarious and charming dialogue. It isn't Shakespeare, but it gets the job done. I seriously played through this whole thing with a wide smile on my face.The boss fights were incredible. And the music gets you pumped. Nine Inch Nails does that. There is also some fantastic original music.Overall, it reminded me of a past where I could go into a GameStop or Blockbuster and buy a game for my PlayStation 2, expecting it to be just fun. _childDocuments_.review: In 2023, a game like Hi-Fi Rush is a miracle. No marketing, no microtransactions, and nothing to judge the game on but the quality of the game itself. It was games like this in the early 2000s that made me fall in love with video games, and my feelings towards this one are no different. I dove in skeptical of the hype, and came out a true believer.It's worth noting that I played entirely on the Steam Deck, mostly docked, and experienced no technical issues whatsoever. Hi-Fi Rush's story is pretty straight forward and you get into the action from the second you pick up the controller. There's never really a lull—the story doesn't stop for the entire 15-18 hours you're playing the game. If nothing else, the writing is efficient. It takes you where you need to go and shows you what it needs to show you in order to tell the story that wants to be told.Personally, I enjoyed it a lot! It's cheesy and hammy and a little cliché but it's fun, and that's what matters. The voice acting isn't over-the-top and I found myself invested in all of the characters by the end. There's a lot of sequel potential with this one too.This game is definitely Devil May Cry meets your favorite rhythm game and it's a match made in heaven. Even if you don't have rhythm, the game has accessibility options and various difficulties to make sure that everyone can enjoy it equally. I consider myself to have rhythm, but I don't have very good mechanical control to make combo-heavy action games easy for me. I played on the Hard difficulty and still had a blast. I used a lot of continues so my stage ratings were usually poor, but that's okay. I found that the increased challenge let me appreciate the combat more and ultimately made me better—even if I had to redo some encounters and bosses so much that my thumb cramped up.The only thing that I hesitantly wish for is a more precise—or at least visually apparent—targeting system. There's no real way to manually control which enemy you're locked onto, which makes some encounters difficult to safely navigate and can ultimately lead to fatal errors. There's not much to say about the music. It was perfect. The mixup of classic songs with songs recorded by the game was a great choice (although scary for licensing in the future). The game takes a similar approach to Nier: Automata where the songs change based on your environment and gameplay, an obvious choice for a game so heavily focused on music from both a gameplay and thematic point-of-view. The UI in this game is cute and completely serviceable. It's not without its shortcomings though. The game tries to educate you on how to equip certain items fairly early in the game, but you don't actually have enough money to really experiment at that point, so I found myself unable to figure it out later on when I actually had more money to experiment. It's easy, so it didn't take long to find, but I distinctly remember being confused for about 5 minutes. (Hint: You can only equip items in the shop, and you want the Left Trigger button on shop screens where you can buy equippable items).It's incredible that Tango Gameworks decided to shadowdrop Hi-Fi Rush without any sort of marketing, but that confidence was well-placed: this is an incredible game. It takes modern game design and marries it with the best of the more experimental gaming eras. At $30, this game is a steal and everyone with access should play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Verdict: My favorite game this year so far. I'm happy this genre blend (Rhythm-Action) is going on a roll lately, although it is a pretty niche genre,but for me Hi-Fi Rush solved the biggest issue on the rhythm side: Example of active punishment is breaking or off-putting sound when you miss, like the standard rhythm game.Sure, you will still have some sort of a punishment in form of final score rank at the end or progress block for certain sections, but there is an accessibility option for that progress blocker (Easy/Normal only) and I appreciated that.Some way this game could improve if there will be a sequel (fingers crossed):1. SoundtrackWhile I do think the overall soundtrack, both OST and licensed are  (I even bought the OST), it lacks the iconic OST for the game (e.g Devil Trigger/Bury The Light from DMC5). Working with a higher caliber composer hopefully will be a huge improvement. More banger soundtracks are always welcomed!2. PlatformingJumping as Chai takes time to get used to, because it's more on the bouncy side. I basically just double jump and/or Jump-Dash to pass between platform.More magnet-grapple platforming is also pretty good for me.3. Option to lock-on targetsIn this game, magnet grapple to the robot is basically your "target lock-on". In the sequel I hope there will be an option to manually lock on the target.4. Misc: Achievements or "speedrun side"Not all of the dialogue/setpiece are skipable. This will be quite tiring if you are planning to 100% this game, because you basically have to finish this game at least 5x to 100% it.Extra credit if the achievements clears faster if you do the harder difficulty first (e.g if you achieved something on Hard, it also applies to Normal and Easy)PS: I think the game will ultimately benefit on the replayability factor if this is improved, because action game emphasize more on replayability to make better score.From the The Game Awards side, I would love to see this game nominated for Best Action and Art Direction!

_childDocuments_.review: When people say games have gotten worse over the past decade or so, it's because we stopped getting games like this.Everything from the visual style, the choice of music (both copyrighted and music made for the game!), the combat, the short sections of different gameplay entirely, seriously everything about this game, save a few very minor gripes (mainly the platforming at times) is pure good game design.The story is super simple and fairly predictable, but that's okay! I realize that most games we're accustomed to have super complex or dark stories to tell, and there is nothing wrong with that! But wow, is it refreshing to play a game where you can just go with the flow of both the story and the gameplay. I also think it's worth noting that I haven't played a singleplayer game that made me genuinely laugh this much in years.The gameplay is DMC meets BPM, or Metal Hellsinger. If you're like me, that probably already sold you on it, but if you're not very musically inclined that's fine too! While the rhythm is an integral part of the game, playing to the beat only really gives you benefits, you don't really get punished for, say, attacking or jumping off beat. In fact, the game will do everything in its power to MAKE everything you do sync up, even if you know you hit a button off beat. The majority of the combat encounters are fun, although they can tend to feel a bit repetitive when you have 2 or more encounters nearly immediately in a row, but that doesn't happen often enough to really detract from the game as a whole. The bosses, on the other hand, are the absolute peak of this game, in my opinion. Each one has unique music chosen specifically for that fight that succeed on so many levels: They are just good tracks, they match each boss perfectly, especially the songs made for the "streamer mode," some of the songs even give insight into the personality of the boss you're fighting, it's just awesome. If I could add one feature to this game, it would be an option to skip straight to the bosses upon replaying a level, I just love every boss fight so much!At $30 USD this game is a steal, great value for your money in my opinion. This game was somehow able to recapture the feeling of coming home after a long day and being super excited to keep playing that new game you got, a feeling which I haven't truly had in years. If this is the best thing to come out of 2023, then I think I'd be alright with that. The only thing that could be better for the time being, is having more Hi-Fi Rush content from Tango.

_childDocuments_.review: I had recently gotten back into this game a few days before the news broke out, having finished and enjoyed the hell out of the game when it first released. Hi-Fi Rush is, to put it simply, one of the best games to have come out in recent years, and should be the gold standard for games going forward. The game is primarily an action game, along the lines of Metal Gear Rising, Devil May Cry, or Bayonetta, but with the twist that everything moves to the beat. And I do mean everything; stage elements, your attack, enemy attacks, even cutscenes are synchronized to the beat of the background music. You aren't required to stick to the beat, but your attacks will still land on-beat, and you're rewarded with extra damage for landing on-beat.This leads to the game having a very interesting feel, as it leads to beats in the music feeling almost like frames in a fighting game. All your light attacks take one beat to execute, and your heavy attacks take two beats, and most enemies have a tell a few beats before they actually execute their attack, allowing you to perform a combo that ends right before their attack, and then bust out a parry on the next beat, before continuing your combo. The story is also extremely good, and all the characters have unique and memorable personalities that feel just over-the-top enough to not be obnoxious. Chai may feel like a protagonist you'd get tired of after a bit of time, but his personality and development lead to him being the perfect character for a game like this.Along with these, the game has incredible replay value. There's a short postgame storyline involving 16 "Challenge Rooms" that demand you to fight a wave or two of enemies with a special condition, such as not manually moving, only dealing damage with parry counters, not taking damage, or getting above a certain percentage of perfectly on-beat attacks, ending in a humorous final encounter with the game's antagonist. Afterwards, you're offered the ability to replay the game at higher difficulties, to go for higher performance ranks, or the three side modes, Rhythm Tower, BPM Rush, and Power-Up! Tower-Up!Rhythm Tower serves as a 60-floor gauntlet of the game's areas, challenging you with a short timer that you can increase by performing well in the fights, and every 10 floors, you're challenged with one of the game's corporate bosses, before facing the final boss at Floor 60 and getting your final ranking and payout based on how much time you had left.BPM Rush and Power-Up! Tower-Up! were added as part of the "Arcade Update", and are both accessed from an arcade machine in your squad's hideout. While they aren't integrated with the game's 'Achievement Mural', a large mural on the wall that fills with characters and details as you complete challenges and accept your rewards, there's a separate Arcade Reward Tracker for them, holding a bunch of exclusive rewards, such as outfits for characters, new super moves, and photo mode poses.BPM Rush has you fight an endless wave of enemies, with a bar at the bottom that fills based on your performance. Once this bar is filled, you get a "BPM Rush", where you must defeat a buffed mini-boss enemy, after which the BPM of the background music will go up and you have to repeat the process, up until you're hammering buttons at 200 BPM.Power-Up! Tower-Up! is essentially a Roguelike mode. At the start of a run, Chai is zapped, and his stats brought down to abysmal levels, but between waves of enemies, you are given the option to accept buffs that'll bring him back up to and even above form, with more powerful upgrades including a temporary "bug" that will affect the next wave of enemies, such as causing enemies to explode when they die, damaging you, or "Setting the video feed to 480p", which serves as a humorous visual impairment.Overall, Hi-Fi Rush is an AMAZING game if you're looking for something with a ton of personality and replay value. I would say I hope for a sequel, but unfortunately recent news has not only revealed that Tango was in the process of pitching one, but that they were also shut down by their parent company, essentially shuttering any hope of a good followup.EDIT: Recently news came out that Tango Gameworks, the developers of Hi-Fi Rush, was saved from closure by Krafton, with specific mention that they'll be persuing more games in the Hi-Fi series, meaning that we effectively have confirmation that we're getting Hi-Fi Rush 2, so you can ignore most of that final paragraph lmao

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty charming and fun experience!The Story is pretty simple as its meant to be a casual type of game, however it does a good job at moving the game forward. Sound and Audio are fantastic (with it being a rhythm game of course) with the Soundtrack feeling bouncy and a perfect guide for the combat beats and i also like the choices of licensed music that they went for. In terms of gameplay, its really fleshed out. The whole premise of doing everything on beat is done to a perfection with movement and combat reflecting this really well. _childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, Devil may Dance!As a woman beater myself I can really relate to Chai as he beats women twice. Very cool character.Wait, what?!This is one of those rare games that deserves a 10/10. It is faultless. Everything works as intended as is fun. It is so well polished. Best rhythm game ever.Took me about 10 hours to beat it. Initially I thought it was a neat concept but kinda simple. However, the more I played it the more I enjoyed it. The second half of the game had me smiling non-stop. The game feels oddly nostalgic, like it feels like an old PS2 game in the best way. It took me back to the days of me playing PS2 games when I was younger. I found the characters charming, the combat was pretty good, I loved the music, and the bosses were great. There wasn't really a point in my run where I felt like I was having a bad time. I'm surprised such a high profile dev literally released a PS2 game in 2023 and I mean that as a good thing. Just the entire design of the game is old-school PS2 era. That whole "insert Sonic meme saying I want shorter games with worse graphics and I'm not kidding." It's hyper focused on delivering fun gameplay without bogging things down with an open world. And the cel shading and smooth animation makes the whole game pop. A lot of attention to detail as well.Some of the boss fights and set-pieces are incredibly creative and exciting. I was struggling to stay on rhythm initially but as I started to vibe with the music I naturally started to stay on beat. The rhythm based combat was super cool, it reminded me a bit of the old days playing Rock Band and Guitar Hero but as combat instead. It took me a little while to feel comfortable with, but once I came to terms with how enemies will only hit you on the beat, juggling parries in with my regular combat started to feel a lot more natural. The soundtrack was great, with 2 Nine Inch Nails songs and the level that used Whirring by The Joy Formidable was amazing the way it used the build up to the end of that song as the ending to beat the boss, oh man, so great! The voice acting is an absolute treat. Robbie Daymond does a great job making Chai a Peter Parker-type everyman and Erica Lindbeck does her usual thing but it works well for Peppermint.Also, as someone who works with disabled people, it was so amazing seeing how this game has such great representation of disability. Hi-Fi Rush's cast is predominantly filled with disabled characters. Like Chai for example, he uses a prosthetic arm because (as confirmed by the creators) he didn't have full function of his arm. Peppermint also uses a prosthetic leg, Korsica and Roquefort are basically on life support, etc.  It's not all in your face about it and made to fit naturally into the plot. It just feels natural, which is rare in media. I think part of the reason it feels so natural is that in the game world it feels… normal. And That it's normal and okay to be disabled. Which is something I really loved, it's not focused on extensively, it focuses on the characters themselves, rarely ever the disability. They're fully fleshed characters who happen to have disabilities! I'm super thankful for this game.I'm almost in disbelief at how great it was to just play, like "Wait a minute, we could have games be this fun on a moment to moment basis?" I've always appreciated Insomniac for putting gameplay first and just making something a joy to play. Then this comes along and does that with presentation and a theme that clicks for me even more.I cannot recommend this enough to everyone, it's been awhile since I've seen something be surrounded by so much positivity in gaming discussions and it's great to see. Also realistic graphics or not, this might be the best looking game I've ever played.  Gotta say, this could easily be a $60 release with all the content and its quality. It's an absolute steal for $30. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I typically don't write reviews, but...Tango Gameworks's Hi-Fi Rush is a game with a fantastic concept and excellent execution, especially considering its complexity. Essentially, through Hi-Fi Rush, Tango Gameworks effectively explores the scenario of "What if Devil May Cry was a rhythm game?" Like Devil May Cry (of which I am also a huge fan), Hi-Fi Rush is a hack-and-slash game, but its approach to gameplay is unique due to its rhythm-based mechanics, which are integral to the overall experience. The combat centers around executing light and heavy attacks and various combos in time with the music, making listening to the music an active component of the gameplay and enhancing the overall immersion. The soundtrack consists of both licensed and license-free tracks of excellent quality, akin to an alternative/indie rock album. This genre of music complements the happy-go-lucky vibe and bright anime cell-shaded graphical style presented in the game, proving that graphical fidelity in video games isn’t what truly matters. This is something that the triple-A gaming industry, for the most part, doesn’t seem to understand.While the combat in Hi-Fi Rush may take some getting used to, its skill curve and complex mechanics are far easier to master than those of Devil May Cry. Though I could compile a long list comparing the two games at a mechanical level, there are two main aspects that highlight how Hi-Fi Rush is much more accessible compared to Devil May Cry. First, Hi-Fi Rush uses an auto-targeting system, unlike Devil May Cry's manual lock-on targeting system. Second, Hi-Fi Rush’s version of the Devil May Cry style meter, referred to as the Rhythm meter, primarily builds up based on landing combos with good timing, rather than simply executing as many varied combos as quickly as possible, as seen in the Devil May Cry series. What makes Hi-Fi Rush’s Rhythm meter even more accessible is the game's consistent beat, which strikes a perfect balance. The beat is fast enough to maintain the fast-paced flow integral to real-time action combat systems but not so fast that your hands begin to hurt and fatigue after a while—an issue I encounter with the Devil May Cry combat system (a game that generally plays as fast as you and rewards your self-inputted fast gameplay). Overall, Hi-Fi Rush’s combat and gameplay are fluid and polished. More importantly, all of its inner workings and complexities, centered around its blend with music and rhythm game mechanics (which must have taken forever to get right), contribute to a fun gameplay experience.Narratively speaking, Hi-Fi Rush isn’t anything remarkable. It tells a relatively basic, straightforward story that complements the level design. This isn’t a bad thing, as narratives across all mediums don’t need to be complex or thought-provoking to be good. The characters serve their purpose; they aren’t terribly complex, nor do they need to be, given that the narrative itself is written to accommodate this. Protagonist Chai, in particular, is a great character. While he’s written to be annoying, you can’t help but like him, which is exacerbated by Robbie Daymond’s excellent voice performance. Daymond is known for roles such as Goro Akechi in Persona 5 Royal (Atlus), Megumi Fushiguro in Jujutsu Kaisen (MAPPA), Prompto Argentum in Final Fantasy XV (Square Enix), and Lloyd Bannings in The Legend of Heroes series (Nihon Falcom). On a personal level, Chai resonated with me because he represents my close attachment to music, specifically my evolving love for rock music. Chai is a character that represents individuals like me, who at one point didn’t know how to play an instrument but still had a profoundly deep understanding of music. In particular, there is a cutscene towards the end of the game that effectively emphasizes this.As a writer, what I appreciate most about Hi-Fi Rush narratively is its dialogue. The game has a comedic structure similar to movies like Deadpool (Marvel Entertainment) and video games like Sunset Overdrive (Insomniac Games), both of which are effective in their endeavors. This aspect of Hi-Fi Rush is particularly impressive since it’s typically very difficult to write a script with this type of comedic structure that doesn’t feel cringe-worthy. In contrast, Square Enix’s game Forspoken is an example of how to mess this up, resulting in a script that is wholly cringe-worthy.As I finish writing this, a sense of sadness washes over me as I confront the realization that Xbox has shut down Tango Gameworks without any known sensible reason. The creative minds at Tango Gameworks produced one of the best games Xbox had published in many years. Consequently, Hi-Fi Rush, with all its amazing innovations, will never see a sequel, as without Tango Gameworks, there is no possibility of one. Hi-Fi Rush was clearly created by developers who were deeply passionate about crafting the best and most enjoyable gaming experience, rather than focusing solely on monetization. This dedication is sadly rare in the triple-A gaming industry, where companies with vast financial resources often refuse to take creative risks due to an extreme and at times unreasonable fear of financial loss. Hi-Fi Rush serves as a symbol in the triple-A industry of what it means to create something with passion, with the end goal of producing the best product rather than merely the most profitable one. While Hi-Fi Rush isn’t the best game I've ever played, I deeply appreciate it for what it is and what it stands for. And in an industry where the triple-A space often refuses to innovate, Hi-Fi Rush is more than enough for me.- PC OPTIMIZATION -☑️ Amazingly Optimized🔲 Meets the PC port performance standard🔲 The Port has some issues🔲 PC port is in an Unacceptable State🔲 Unplayable- WORTH BUYING @ FULL PRICE -☑️ Yes🔲 Its Free🔲 Wait for sale🔲 NoENGINE: Unreal Engine 4GRADE: B+/A-

_childDocuments_.review: Through densely inspired skatecore aesthetics, HFR is a combo-oriented hack n slash with enough campy writing to stay in your memory past its completion.Where HFR suffers most is that it attempts to coast so hard on its visual and thematic style, that it ends up with often flat and near-insufferable character dynamics. Chai is exactly who you expect him to be- a jabbering protagonist who bickers with the female lead despite being stronger together. These tropes are not explored, subverted or even seemingly acknowledged. The characters are simply action figures with a little button to say something that their personality would say in response to any moment. The Rhythm combat is also underexplored- All music stays within one genre, and it fails to even give that longevity. All rhythm is stuck to basic 4/4 timing, save for the occasional doubletime or QTE. You are never inputting combos like a lead guitarist, only like a rhythm guitarist. For the first 10 hours of the game, you barely have the resources for more than a few combos which means the combat is crazy repetitive up until late game.With all that said, it hits its stride after the middle point of the game and without elaborating much it's the exact type of game the world needs more of. Short, contained stories with a unique central mechanic and a clearly invested creative team who takes the time to add charm to every level- props that bob and weave with the rhythm, seamless transitions between cutscenes and gameplay, and a willingness to not drag out levels longer than needed.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi-Fi rush is one of the best rhythm action games ever created. I would encourage anyone to give this beautiful game a try, even if you have no sense of rhythm. Every aspect of this game is beautifully crafted. The artwork is cell shaded and gives a comic book feel. The characters all have charm that isn't forced on you and all the characters, even the lowest minion all have a memorable feel to each of them.Let's talk about the story for a second. Chai, the main character, is looking to receive a cybernetic implant to help him become a rock star, only to find out that he's supposed to be a garbage picker. Once the system breaks, he looks for a way out and along his way, discovers a very believable plot about how this evil corporation is trying to do nefarious things.Do yourself a favor. Pick up this game whenever you can. However, I would recommend that you wait for a sale because Microsoft shut down Tango Gameworks and they should get very little of your dollars. However, you should sing the praises of this work of art and treasure it. This type of game is a rare commodity in the world of squeezing the dollar out of the players through endless DLCs and micro transactions.

Definitely worth to try.

_childDocuments_.review: A fairly standard character action game or whatever they're called with light/heavy attacks, combos, and a letter-based grading scale, but with rhythm mechanics. You do more damage and get other benefits if you're on beat with inputs, and moves for you and your enemies are always on beat. Not a ton of depth, but elevated by the music integration, support characters and varied enemies. The combat is challenging without being frustrating, and fighting on beat feels very rewarding. Overall has a nice 'in the zone' feeling that I really like.Writing isn't brilliant but it feels like a genuine attempt at making a fun script; the characters are likable and fun despite being rather two dimensional. Some good humor, especially the physical humor, but some pretty corny jokes. They (arguably) venture pretty closely into summer animated film quality at some points, but the game has so few jokes it's moving through both verbally and visually that it doesn't bother me. Plus, it feels sincere rather than snarky, like the director is just a cornball, so it's fine.I think the visuals and music are good too, but that's subjective. Has some licensed music that scenes were built around, but also "streamer mode" tracks made by an in-house band or something that sound like slightly different versions of the licensed stuff. TL;DR: A solid feel-good game with a neat gimmick. Korsica is best girl.

_childDocuments_.review: This was an impulsive buy where I saw some of it's gameplay and thought "Hey - this would be perfect for the Steam Deck" (And by the way - it is perfect for the Steam Deck). The cell-shaded graphics are brightly coloured and cartoon-like, it fits the game style well. The gameplay is focused around the rythm as the main character of the game has the aspiration of being a rockstar. you around the levels by platforming your way through in a classic 3d-platformer fashion. Overall it's a mix of Guitar Hero, AudioSurf and Mirrors Edge. It also reminds me of "No More Heroes" but I ever played it, so I can't really comment on that. Each level of the game is different from the other and I don't think that there are any two levels that are the same, they're well designed and I didn't feel like they were dragging on or became boring at any time. And as the game progresses you keep learning/acquiring new skills/abilities (and companions) so the gameplay doesn't get repetitive thanks to this. The two improvements that felt like could have been made - 1)Co-Op - for a classic platformer 2 to 4-player co-op seems like would have been perfect; 2)More open-world - having linear levels is probably what leads to the level design working out so well and keeping the interest as you make your way through them, but man that title screen seems so inviting ... makes you wish you could platform your way through that city!

_childDocuments_.review: - Top notch presentation with a wonderful story awaiting you.- Endearing, likeable characters with fleshed out personalities. Characters have a high level of cuteness and quirkiness.- A rhythm game that'll scratch that punk rock itch! - Great soundtrack with very creative audio effects. - Multiple difficulty levels to choose from.- Plenty of achievements and collectibles.- Hidden gems for perfectionists and explorers.- Gorgeous varied environments made in its specific style. Somewhat reminiscent of Borderlands.- Charming references to movies, tv shows, books and games.- Lots of meta humour in a game that doesn't take itself too seriously but is seriously well developed. - Characters and objects move to the sound of the beat! Seemingly simple but perfectly executed.- Accessibility options baked in from the get-go.- Very well optimized for the Steam Deck. I had a blast! - No bugs/glitches/crashes to report and near instant wake from sleep so you can resume exactly from where you left off. So cool!- All in all, the game is unique. There's nothing quite like it. Hoping it acts as inspiration for others and paves the path for a potential sequel. - The platforming aspect isn't for everyone at first, but you can get used to it. Much like the Spyro remastered trilogy.- Timing for certain moves can be tricky and lead to some frustration but with plenty of patience you can proceed. Understandable as to why they did it, story-wise, but still. - What Microsoft did to Tango Gameworks is beyond words. Despite that, the studio is still kicking and hopefully in more capable hands.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanna start off by saying the sheer amount of content in the levels and visual style are all excellent high points of the game. This is clearly a game with a lot of work put into it which is why it's kinda a shame I didn't really like it. The writing overall fluctuates from having some genuinely funny jokes to some really just corny and bad dialogue. The overall plot was pretty basic nothing too bad or too good. I kinda expected that going in so it's not a huge deal. Where the game kinda fell apart for me was in the combat itself.                                                     I played through this game on hard mode and that might have been a mistake for my enjoyment of the combat. I think the combos are really cool but enemies love to attack you in the middle of them. Now the game does give you two options to deal with this, 1 being a parry and the other a dodge that gets you out of the situation entirely. The problem is there is so much visual and audio noise in some the fights its basically luck if you know an attack is coming. Because of this I found easily the best strategy is just to run around avoiding attacking anything and spamming partner abilities which while effective for getting past all the encounters wasn't fun.                                                                                                  You could very well have a better experience playing on normal mode but for the experience I had I can't recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Bethesda and Tango Gameworks' surprise 30 Dollar release is worth buying but I don't think its GOTY if I'm being honest. I understand why people feel this way given it feels like a statement against Modern Game Development practices (And critically executing Forspoken which is admittedly hilarious). But as a game detached from all of that, I don't feel its quite to THAT level, even if it comes close a couple times.Reason being, Pacing, The first third and The Vandelay museum can be sloggy with its overemphasis on platforming and tutorialization. I also feel like it could have used its music better or perhaps another look at the music direction. Poor Nine Inch Nails feels like gets drowned out with the rest of the game's soundtrack but The Prodigy and the Joy Formidable are both used incredibly effectively at their respective moments in the game. Invaders must Die in particular was Perfect. That said to swing it back to the positives, They nailed combat. Especially when those two aforementioned bands kick in. Hi Fi rush is at it's best when you are headbanging to the beat with your combos and action platforming as you enter a flow state to blow through hordes of Vandelay Robots, which when it does happen thats where it feels like its hitting that GOTY Territory. Most of the time it doesnt quite hit that but its still very solid. Art direction is great, with the game world synched to the beat and characters being very expressive without going full anime-overdesign.The story is...okay, its basically a better version of Streets of Rage 4's plot which was pretty bad, the characters are all charming enough to keep you engaged and everyone has their moments of glory and shame. Comedy is generally solid and helps alleviate some of the story's rougher edges I did have a few moments where I spat out Coffee (Decaf) laughing and I don't recall cringing at any attempted jokes.Otherwise its polished, with very minor bugs if any, and is a pretty full single-player playthrough with its own post-game.So 10/10 GOTY? No but I do think its well worth the 30$ asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a prime example of the kind of games the industry needs. Not so much the stealth release, but the interesting setting, music, art style, the presentation etc. Just something that isn't an open world realistic, "deep", over the shoulder 3rd person shooter/psuedo RPG with repetitive map markers spread all around. Something that qualifies the A and B tier state of gaming instead of needing to be supported constantly or make a bunch of money off anything other then the sales of the game. Literally the only slights I can give hi fi rush is the main character being a massive cringe lord but that's probably by design. The parry needs to be introduced earlier as that mechanic becomes the entire meta of the game and makes it more enjoyable. I've also seen people  say the rhythm fighting gameplay is also a turn off judging from some comments as well, but I at least liked it and it felt it just needed to be a little less overwhelming with options at the start. I feel like this is the kind of game No straight roads was trying to be, but with a much higher budget. My only fear is no sequel. (My greatest fear has come true)Also scottish women are hot

_childDocuments_.review: First,, the game doesn't stutter during gameplay, but you can very clearly see the framerate drop during cutscene to the point where it's very jarring.This game is part spectacle fighter, part rhythm game, and part platformer. The platforming part is pretty boring and the levels are really dragged out with it to the point where they overstay their welcome. Where the game really shines is the combat. If specticle fighters are your thing (DMC & Bayonetta) you will no doubt have a great time! The rhythm, like many people are saying, can be ignored for the most part... BUT... there were a few mechanics of this game that I truly despised because I just...could not. And it FEELS really bad when you mess things up because of doing poorly on timings, like, it strikes your ego and you get bummed and maybe a bit pissed. I had that feeling far too much throughout the whole game because I just kept missing the timings of button presses. Up to the very last levels... :((Also beware some unskipable cutscenes, and not being able to pick up collectables while someone is talking)I won't be replaying this game, since the combat is definitely not my cup of tea, and the platforming is a slog, but I'm still recommending it because, again, if the gameplay is your jam you'll no doubt love this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I've still got a ton left to do in this game but with only about 20 hours played, I can seriously sit here and say this is a 10/10 game that deserves every bit of love it's getting and it's a damn shame Microsoft screwed the studio over when they made a masterpiece of a game in an era full of AAA slop.The performance alone is enough to make this game stand out. So many games in recent years are full of optimisation issues that take forever to get fixed but right out of the gate, Hi-Fi Rush offers a completely smooth experience with absolutely zero frame drops even in the most intense situations. This is the standard that all games should be aiming for.With a colourful cast of characters that all flow perfectly in the combat and a combat system that is very unique, Hi-Fi Rush gives a once in a lifetime experience that everybody should try-even those new to games like this one, it's so easy to drop in and get the hang of things real quick. With plenty of tools to help you, the combat feels so rewarding and hits all the right spots to just make you feel good after winning fights.The story itself is nothing over the top or extreme but that's to it's advantage. It tells a really enjoyable, goofy story that has a great cast of characters that are all lovable and special in their own ways and you just can't hate any of them-even the villains.No review is complete without mentioning the music though. Whether you use the licensed music or streamer mode to get the in-house music, it all fits the game so perfectly and every single one of the songs feels perfectly suited to the environments and characters you come across throughout the game.Whether you get the game on sale or at full price, this is one game that everyone should play. This was one hell of a bang to go out on by Tango Gameworks and this will go down as a game that could've lead to so much more if not for Microsoft's greed. The devs should be proud of this passion project.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything about this game hits right. Hi-Fi Rush is similar to Devil May Cry with the combat and score for each encounter. The game has an in-depth combat system which has a rhythm that you can take advantage of to get extra damage. The combat is expressive and there is tons of moves you can add to Chai. You can add chips which change how your partners function, like faster cooldowns or double damage. It's got a unique charm to it and while I didn't play for the story I was surprised how well it was put together. The bosses have their gimmicks and they are all enjoyable.There is a surprising amount of post-game content including in-game currency to unlock music for your hideout and unlocking costumes for the characters you meet throughout the story. While I didn't play it, there is an entirely new mode which functions like a rouge-like where you advance a tower with buffs/powerups which you obtain on that run. I fully recommend this game, even if you only plan to play through it once.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game so hard. The art is awesome, the music is amazing, the combat is varied, the platforming is excellent, and the story (so far) is interesting. But so far, only about halfway into the tutorial zone, I hate this game.The key game mechanic is that everyone and everything syncs up to the music, meaning that one's ability to do the combat and platforming are directly tied to their ability to keep the beat. We have seen similar game mechanics in the past, from the popular "Crypt of the Necrodancer" to the adored Nintendo series "Rhythm Heaven." I am a drummer and have been trained to keep the beat, so I should be able to pull off amazing combos. Unfortunately, I have scored a D for timing on every combat segment I have faced thus far because I face too much input lag. I have tried playing with the timing visualizer on, with my audio playing through headphones, and using numerous other strategies to attempt to minimize input lag, but the input lag is unbearable. It makes the game completely unenjoyable.I have given this a positive rating because in theory I love this game, and I will continue to try to find a way to reduce input lag enough to make the game playable. But I warn you: do not buy this game until you are sure your gaming setup is fast enough to handle it. Check your specs before wasting money on a game you will not enjoy.Also, if anyone has recommendations on how to reduce input lag, please let me know. I want to have fun with this game.
